[p0013-l0001] [25.22pt] Preface
[p0013-l0002] [18.92pt] The Machine Learning Tsunami
[p0013-l0003] [10.5pt] In 2006, Geoffrey Hinton et al. published a paper1 showing how to train a deep neural
[p0013-l0004] [10.5pt] network capable of recognizing handwritten digits with state-of-the-art precision
[p0013-l0005] [10.5pt] (>98%). They branded this technique “Deep Learning.” Training a deep neural net
[p0013-l0006] [10.5pt] was widely considered impossible at the time,2 and most researchers had abandoned
[p0013-l0007] [10.5pt] the idea since the 1990s. This paper revived the interest of the scientific community
[p0013-l0008] [10.5pt] and before long many new papers demonstrated that Deep Learning was not only
[p0013-l0009] [10.5pt] possible, but capable of mind-blowing achievements that no other Machine Learning
[p0013-l0010] [10.5pt] (ML) technique could hope to match (with the help of tremendous computing power
[p0013-l0011] [10.5pt] and great amounts of data). This enthusiasm soon extended to many other areas of
[p0013-l0012] [10.5pt] Machine Learning.
[p0013-l0013] [10.5pt] Fast-forward 10 years and Machine Learning has conquered the industry: it is now at
[p0013-l0014] [10.5pt] the heart of much of the magic in today’s high-tech products, ranking your web
[p0013-l0015] [10.5pt] search results, powering your smartphone’s speech recognition, recommending vid‐
[p0013-l0016] [10.5pt] eos, and beating the world champion at the game of Go. Before you know it, it will be
[p0013-l0017] [10.5pt] driving your car.
[p0013-l0018] [18.92pt] Machine Learning in Your Projects
[p0013-l0019] [10.5pt] So naturally you are excited about Machine Learning and you would love to join the
[p0013-l0020] [10.5pt] party!
[p0013-l0021] [10.5pt] Perhaps you would like to give your homemade robot a brain of its own? Make it rec‐
[p0013-l0022] [10.5pt] ognize faces? Or learn to walk around?
[p0013-l0023] [8.0pt] 1 Available on Hinton’s home page at http://www.cs.toronto.edu/~hinton/.
[p0013-l0024] [8.0pt] 2 Despite the fact that Yann Lecun’s deep convolutional neural networks had worked well for image recognition
[p0013-l0025] [8.0pt] since the 1990s, although they were not as general purpose.
[p0013-l0026] [9.0pt] xi

=== PDF page 14 / printed label 12 ===
[p0014-l0001] [10.5pt] Or maybe your company has tons of data (user logs, financial data, production data,
[p0014-l0002] [10.5pt] machine sensor data, hotline stats, HR reports, etc.), and more than likely you could
[p0014-l0003] [10.5pt] unearth some hidden gems if you just knew where to look; for example:
[p0014-l0004] [10.5pt] • Segment customers and find the best marketing strategy for each group
[p0014-l0005] [10.5pt] • Recommend products for each client based on what similar clients bought
[p0014-l0006] [10.5pt] • Detect which transactions are likely to be fraudulent
[p0014-l0007] [10.5pt] • Forecast next year’s revenue
[p0014-l0008] [10.5pt] • And more
[p0014-l0009] [10.5pt] Whatever the reason, you have decided to learn Machine Learning and implement it
[p0014-l0010] [10.5pt] in your projects. Great idea!
[p0014-l0011] [18.92pt] Objective and Approach
[p0014-l0012] [10.5pt] This book assumes that you know close to nothing about Machine Learning. Its goal
[p0014-l0013] [10.5pt] is to give you the concepts, the intuitions, and the tools you need to actually imple‐
[p0014-l0014] [10.5pt] ment programs capable of learning from data.
[p0014-l0015] [10.5pt] We will cover a large number of techniques, from the simplest and most commonly
[p0014-l0016] [10.5pt] used (such as linear regression) to some of the Deep Learning techniques that regu‐
[p0014-l0017] [10.5pt] larly win competitions.
[p0014-l0018] [10.5pt] Rather than implementing our own toy versions of each algorithm, we will be using
[p0014-l0019] [10.5pt] actual production-ready Python frameworks:
[p0014-l0020] [10.5pt] • Scikit-Learn is very easy to use, yet it implements many Machine Learning algo‐
[p0014-l0021] [10.5pt] rithms efficiently, so it makes for a great entry point to learn Machine Learning.
[p0014-l0022] [10.5pt] • TensorFlow is a more complex library for distributed numerical computation. It
[p0014-l0023] [10.5pt] makes it possible to train and run very large neural networks efficiently by dis‐
[p0014-l0024] [10.5pt] tributing the computations across potentially hundreds of multi-GPU servers.
[p0014-l0025] [10.5pt] TensorFlow was created at Google and supports many of their large-scale
[p0014-l0026] [10.5pt] Machine Learning applications. It was open sourced in November 2015.
[p0014-l0027] [10.5pt] • Keras is a high level Deep Learning API that makes it very simple to train and
[p0014-l0028] [10.5pt] run neural networks. It can run on top of either TensorFlow, Theano or Micro‐
[p0014-l0029] [10.5pt] soft Cognitive Toolkit (formerly known as CNTK). TensorFlow comes with its
[p0014-l0030] [10.5pt] own implementation of this API, called tf.keras, which provides support for some
[p0014-l0031] [10.5pt] advanced TensorFlow features (e.g., to efficiently load data).
[p0014-l0032] [10.5pt] The book favors a hands-on approach, growing an intuitive understanding of
[p0014-l0033] [10.5pt] Machine Learning through concrete working examples and just a little bit of theory.
[p0014-l0034] [10.5pt] While you can read this book without picking up your laptop, we highly recommend
[p0014-l0035] [9.0pt] xii

[p0015-l0003] [18.92pt] Prerequisites
[p0015-l0004] [10.5pt] This book assumes that you have some Python programming experience and that you
[p0015-l0005] [10.5pt] are familiar with Python’s main scientific libraries, in particular NumPy, Pandas, and
[p0015-l0006] [10.5pt] Matplotlib.
[p0015-l0007] [10.5pt] Also, if you care about what’s under the hood you should have a reasonable under‐
[p0015-l0008] [10.5pt] standing of college-level math as well (calculus, linear algebra, probabilities, and sta‐
[p0015-l0009] [10.5pt] tistics).
[p0015-l0010] [10.5pt] If you don’t know Python yet, http://learnpython.org/ is a great place to start. The offi‐
[p0015-l0011] [10.5pt] cial tutorial on python.org is also quite good.
[p0015-l0012] [10.5pt] If you have never used Jupyter, Chapter 2 will guide you through installation and the
[p0015-l0013] [10.5pt] basics: it is a great tool to have in your toolbox.
[p0015-l0014] [10.5pt] If you are not familiar with Python’s scientific libraries, the provided Jupyter note‐
[p0015-l0015] [10.5pt] books include a few tutorials. There is also a quick math tutorial for linear algebra.
[p0015-l0016] [18.92pt] Roadmap
[p0015-l0017] [10.5pt] This book is organized in two parts. Part I, The Fundamentals of Machine Learning,
[p0015-l0018] [10.5pt] covers the following topics:
[p0015-l0019] [10.5pt] • What is Machine Learning? What problems does it try to solve? What are the
[p0015-l0020] [10.5pt] main categories and fundamental concepts of Machine Learning systems?
[p0015-l0021] [10.5pt] • The main steps in a typical Machine Learning project.
[p0015-l0022] [10.5pt] • Learning by fitting a model to data.
[p0015-l0023] [10.5pt] • Optimizing a cost function.
[p0015-l0024] [10.5pt] • Handling, cleaning, and preparing data.
[p0015-l0025] [10.5pt] • Selecting and engineering features.
[p0015-l0026] [10.5pt] • Selecting a model and tuning hyperparameters using cross-validation.
[p0015-l0027] [10.5pt] • The main challenges of Machine Learning, in particular underfitting and overfit‐
[p0015-l0028] [10.5pt] ting (the bias/variance tradeoff).
[p0015-l0029] [10.5pt] • Reducing the dimensionality of the training data to fight the curse of dimension‐
[p0015-l0030] [10.5pt] ality.
[p0015-l0031] [10.5pt] • Other unsupervised learning techniques, including clustering, density estimation
[p0015-l0032] [10.5pt] and anomaly detection.

[p0017-l0001] [10.5pt] Part II, Neural Networks and Deep Learning, covers the following topics:
[p0017-l0002] [10.5pt] • What are neural nets? What are they good for?
[p0017-l0003] [10.5pt] • Building and training neural nets using TensorFlow and Keras.
[p0017-l0004] [10.5pt] • The most important neural net architectures: feedforward neural nets, convolu‐
[p0017-l0005] [10.5pt] tional nets, recurrent nets, long short-term memory (LSTM) nets, autoencoders
[p0017-l0006] [10.5pt] and generative adversarial networks (GANs).
[p0017-l0007] [10.5pt] • Techniques for training deep neural nets.
[p0017-l0008] [10.5pt] • Scaling neural networks for large datasets.
[p0017-l0009] [10.5pt] • Learning strategies with Reinforcement Learning.
[p0017-l0010] [10.5pt] • Handling uncertainty with Bayesian Deep Learning.
[p0017-l0011] [10.5pt] The first part is based mostly on Scikit-Learn while the second part uses TensorFlow
[p0017-l0012] [10.5pt] and Keras.
[p0017-l0013] [9.6pt] Don’t jump into deep waters too hastily: while Deep Learning is no
[p0017-l0014] [9.6pt] doubt one of the most exciting areas in Machine Learning, you
[p0017-l0015] [9.6pt] should master the fundamentals first. Moreover, most problems
[p0017-l0016] [9.6pt] can be solved quite well using simpler techniques such as Random
[p0017-l0017] [9.6pt] Forests and Ensemble methods (discussed in Part I). Deep Learn‐
[p0017-l0018] [9.6pt] ing is best suited for complex problems such as image recognition,
[p0017-l0019] [9.6pt] speech recognition, or natural language processing, provided you
[p0017-l0020] [9.6pt] have enough data, computing power, and patience.
[p0017-l0021] [18.92pt] Other Resources
[p0017-l0022] [10.5pt] Many resources are available to learn about Machine Learning. Andrew Ng’s ML
[p0017-l0023] [10.5pt] course on Coursera and Geoffrey Hinton’s course on neural networks and Deep
[p0017-l0024] [10.5pt] Learning are amazing, although they both require a significant time investment
[p0017-l0025] [10.5pt] (think months).
[p0017-l0026] [10.5pt] There are also many interesting websites about Machine Learning, including of
[p0017-l0027] [10.5pt] course Scikit-Learn’s exceptional User Guide. You may also enjoy Dataquest, which
[p0017-l0028] [10.5pt] provides very nice interactive tutorials, and ML blogs such as those listed on Quora.
[p0017-l0029] [10.5pt] Finally, the Deep Learning website has a good list of resources to learn more.
[p0017-l0030] [10.5pt] Of course there are also many other introductory books about Machine Learning, in
[p0017-l0031] [10.5pt] particular:
[p0017-l0032] [10.5pt] • Joel Grus, Data Science from Scratch (O’Reilly). This book presents the funda‐
[p0017-l0033] [10.5pt] mentals of Machine Learning, and implements some of the main algorithms in
[p0017-l0034] [10.5pt] pure Python (from scratch, as the name suggests).

[p0019-l0004] [18.92pt] Code Examples
[p0019-l0005] [10.5pt] Supplemental material (code examples, exercises, etc.) is available for download at
[p0019-l0006] [10.5pt] https://github.com/ageron/handson-ml2. It is mostly composed of Jupyter notebooks.
[p0019-l0007] [10.5pt] Some of the code examples in the book leave out some repetitive sections, or details
[p0019-l0008] [10.5pt] that are obvious or unrelated to Machine Learning. This keeps the focus on the
[p0019-l0009] [10.5pt] important parts of the code, and it saves space to cover more topics. However, if you
[p0019-l0010] [10.5pt] want the full code examples, they are all available in the Jupyter notebooks.
[p0019-l0011] [10.5pt] Note that when the code examples display some outputs, then these code examples
[p0019-l0012] [10.5pt] are shown with Python prompts (>>> and ...), as in a Python shell, to clearly distin‐
[p0019-l0013] [10.5pt] guish the code from the outputs. For example, this code defines the square() func‐
[p0019-l0014] [10.5pt] tion then it computes and displays the square of 3:
[p0019-l0015] [8.5pt] >>> def square(x):
[p0019-l0016] [8.5pt] ...     return x ** 2
[p0019-l0017] [8.5pt] ...
[p0019-l0018] [8.5pt] >>> result = square(3)
[p0019-l0019] [8.5pt] >>> result
[p0019-l0020] [8.5pt] 9
[p0019-l0021] [10.5pt] When code does not display anything, prompts are not used. However, the result may
[p0019-l0022] [10.5pt] sometimes be shown as a comment like this:
[p0019-l0023] [8.5pt] def square(x):
[p0019-l0024] [8.5pt]     return x ** 2
[p0019-l0025] [8.5pt] result = square(3)  # result is 9

[p0021-l0013] [18.92pt] Changes in the Second Edition
[p0021-l0014] [10.5pt] This second edition has five main objectives:
[p0021-l0015] [10.5pt] 1. Cover additional topics: additional unsupervised learning techniques (including
[p0021-l0016] [10.5pt] clustering, anomaly detection, density estimation and mixture models), addi‐
[p0021-l0017] [10.5pt] tional techniques for training deep nets (including self-normalized networks),
[p0021-l0018] [10.5pt] additional computer vision techniques (including the Xception, SENet, object
[p0021-l0019] [10.5pt] detection with YOLO, and semantic segmentation using R-CNN), handling
[p0021-l0020] [10.5pt] sequences using CNNs (including WaveNet), natural language processing using
[p0021-l0021] [10.5pt] RNNs, CNNs and Transformers, generative adversarial networks, deploying Ten‐
[p0021-l0022] [10.5pt] sorFlow models, and more.
[p0021-l0023] [10.5pt] 2. Update the book to mention some of the latest results from Deep Learning
[p0021-l0024] [10.5pt] research.
[p0021-l0025] [10.5pt] 3. Migrate all TensorFlow chapters to TensorFlow 2, and use TensorFlow’s imple‐
[p0021-l0026] [10.5pt] mentation of the Keras API (called tf.keras) whenever possible, to simplify the
[p0021-l0027] [10.5pt] code examples.
[p0021-l0028] [10.5pt] 4. Update the code examples to use the latest version of Scikit-Learn, NumPy, Pan‐
[p0021-l0029] [10.5pt] das, Matplotlib and other libraries.
[p0021-l0030] [10.5pt] 5. Clarify some sections and fix some errors, thanks to plenty of great feedback
[p0021-l0031] [10.5pt] from readers.

[p0029-l0001] [16.82pt] CHAPTER 1
[p0029-l0002] [25.22pt] The Machine Learning Landscape
[p0029-l0003] [9.6pt] With Early Release ebooks, you get books in their earliest form—
[p0029-l0004] [9.6pt] the author’s raw and unedited content as he or she writes—so you
[p0029-l0005] [9.6pt] can take advantage of these technologies long before the official
[p0029-l0006] [9.6pt] release of these titles. The following will be Chapter 1 in the final
[p0029-l0007] [9.6pt] release of the book.
[p0029-l0008] [10.5pt] When most people hear “Machine Learning,” they picture a robot: a dependable but‐
[p0029-l0009] [10.5pt] ler or a deadly Terminator depending on who you ask. But Machine Learning is not
[p0029-l0010] [10.5pt] just a futuristic fantasy, it’s already here. In fact, it has been around for decades in
[p0029-l0011] [10.5pt] some specialized applications, such as Optical Character Recognition (OCR). But the
[p0029-l0012] [10.5pt] first ML application that really became mainstream, improving the lives of hundreds
[p0029-l0013] [10.5pt] of millions of people, took over the world back in the 1990s: it was the spam filter.
[p0029-l0014] [10.5pt] Not exactly a self-aware Skynet, but it does technically qualify as Machine Learning
[p0029-l0015] [10.5pt] (it has actually learned so well that you seldom need to flag an email as spam any‐
[p0029-l0016] [10.5pt] more). It was followed by hundreds of ML applications that now quietly power hun‐
[p0029-l0017] [10.5pt] dreds of products and features that you use regularly, from better recommendations
[p0029-l0018] [10.5pt] to voice search.
[p0029-l0019] [10.5pt] Where does Machine Learning start and where does it end? What exactly does it
[p0029-l0020] [10.5pt] mean for a machine to learn something? If I download a copy of Wikipedia, has my
[p0029-l0021] [10.5pt] computer really “learned” something? Is it suddenly smarter? In this chapter we will
[p0029-l0022] [10.5pt] start by clarifying what Machine Learning is and why you may want to use it.
[p0029-l0023] [10.5pt] Then, before we set out to explore the Machine Learning continent, we will take a
[p0029-l0024] [10.5pt] look at the map and learn about the main regions and the most notable landmarks:
[p0029-l0025] [10.5pt] supervised versus unsupervised learning, online versus batch learning, instance-
[p0029-l0026] [10.5pt] based versus model-based learning. Then we will look at the workflow of a typical ML
[p0029-l0027] [10.5pt] project, discuss the main challenges you may face, and cover how to evaluate and
[p0029-l0028] [10.5pt] fine-tune a Machine Learning system.
[p0029-l0029] [9.0pt] 3

=== PDF page 30 / printed label 4 ===
[p0030-l0001] [10.5pt] This chapter introduces a lot of fundamental concepts (and jargon) that every data
[p0030-l0002] [10.5pt] scientist should know by heart. It will be a high-level overview (the only chapter
[p0030-l0003] [10.5pt] without much code), all rather simple, but you should make sure everything is
[p0030-l0004] [10.5pt] crystal-clear to you before continuing to the rest of the book. So grab a coffee and let’s
[p0030-l0005] [10.5pt] get started!
[p0030-l0006] [9.6pt] If you already know all the Machine Learning basics, you may want
[p0030-l0007] [9.6pt] to skip directly to Chapter 2. If you are not sure, try to answer all
[p0030-l0008] [9.6pt] the questions listed at the end of the chapter before moving on.
[p0030-l0009] [18.92pt] What Is Machine Learning?
[p0030-l0010] [10.5pt] Machine Learning is the science (and art) of programming computers so they can
[p0030-l0011] [10.5pt] learn from data.
[p0030-l0012] [10.5pt] Here is a slightly more general definition:
[p0030-l0013] [9.3pt] [Machine Learning is the] field of study that gives computers the ability to learn
[p0030-l0014] [9.3pt] without being explicitly programmed.
[p0030-l0015] [9.3pt] —Arthur Samuel, 1959
[p0030-l0016] [10.5pt] And a more engineering-oriented one:
[p0030-l0017] [9.3pt] A computer program is said to learn from experience E with respect to some task T
[p0030-l0018] [9.3pt] and some performance measure P, if its performance on T, as measured by P, improves
[p0030-l0019] [9.3pt] with experience E.
[p0030-l0020] [9.3pt] —Tom Mitchell, 1997
[p0030-l0021] [10.5pt] For example, your spam filter is a Machine Learning program that can learn to flag
[p0030-l0022] [10.5pt] spam given examples of spam emails (e.g., flagged by users) and examples of regular
[p0030-l0023] [10.5pt] (nonspam, also called “ham”) emails. The examples that the system uses to learn are
[p0030-l0024] [10.5pt] called the training set. Each training example is called a training instance (or sample).
[p0030-l0025] [10.5pt] In this case, the task T is to flag spam for new emails, the experience E is the training
[p0030-l0026] [10.5pt] data, and the performance measure P needs to be defined; for example, you can use
[p0030-l0027] [10.5pt] the ratio of correctly classified emails. This particular performance measure is called
[p0030-l0028] [10.5pt] accuracy and it is often used in classification tasks.
[p0030-l0029] [10.5pt] If you just download a copy of Wikipedia, your computer has a lot more data, but it is
[p0030-l0030] [10.5pt] not suddenly better at any task. Thus, it is not Machine Learning.
[p0030-l0031] [18.92pt] Why Use Machine Learning?
[p0030-l0032] [10.5pt] Consider how you would write a spam filter using traditional programming techni‐
[p0030-l0033] [10.5pt] ques (Figure 1-1):
[p0030-l0034] [9.0pt] 4
[p0030-l0035] [9.0pt] |
[p0030-l0036] [9.0pt] Chapter 1: The Machine Learning Landscape

=== PDF page 31 / printed label 5 ===
[p0031-l0001] [10.5pt] 1. First you would look at what spam typically looks like. You might notice that
[p0031-l0002] [10.5pt] some words or phrases (such as “4U,” “credit card,” “free,” and “amazing”) tend to
[p0031-l0003] [10.5pt] come up a lot in the subject. Perhaps you would also notice a few other patterns
[p0031-l0004] [10.5pt] in the sender’s name, the email’s body, and so on.
[p0031-l0005] [10.5pt] 2. You would write a detection algorithm for each of the patterns that you noticed,
[p0031-l0006] [10.5pt] and your program would flag emails as spam if a number of these patterns are
[p0031-l0007] [10.5pt] detected.
[p0031-l0008] [10.5pt] 3. You would test your program, and repeat steps 1 and 2 until it is good enough.
[p0031-l0009] [10.5pt] Figure 1-1. The traditional approach
[p0031-l0010] [10.5pt] Since the problem is not trivial, your program will likely become a long list of com‐
[p0031-l0011] [10.5pt] plex rules—pretty hard to maintain.
[p0031-l0012] [10.5pt] In contrast, a spam filter based on Machine Learning techniques automatically learns
[p0031-l0013] [10.5pt] which words and phrases are good predictors of spam by detecting unusually fre‐
[p0031-l0014] [10.5pt] quent patterns of words in the spam examples compared to the ham examples
[p0031-l0015] [10.5pt] (Figure 1-2). The program is much shorter, easier to maintain, and most likely more
[p0031-l0016] [10.5pt] accurate.
[p0031-l0017] [9.0pt] Why Use Machine Learning?
[p0031-l0018] [9.0pt] |
[p0031-l0019] [9.0pt] 5

=== PDF page 32 / printed label 6 ===
[p0032-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 1-2. Machine Learning approach
[p0032-l0002] [10.5pt] Moreover, if spammers notice that all their emails containing “4U” are blocked, they
[p0032-l0003] [10.5pt] might start writing “For U” instead. A spam filter using traditional programming
[p0032-l0004] [10.5pt] techniques would need to be updated to flag “For U” emails. If spammers keep work‐
[p0032-l0005] [10.5pt] ing around your spam filter, you will need to keep writing new rules forever.
[p0032-l0006] [10.5pt] In contrast, a spam filter based on Machine Learning techniques automatically noti‐
[p0032-l0007] [10.5pt] ces that “For U” has become unusually frequent in spam flagged by users, and it starts
[p0032-l0008] [10.5pt] flagging them without your intervention (Figure 1-3).
[p0032-l0009] [10.5pt] Figure 1-3. Automatically adapting to change
[p0032-l0010] [10.5pt] Another area where Machine Learning shines is for problems that either are too com‐
[p0032-l0011] [10.5pt] plex for traditional approaches or have no known algorithm. For example, consider
[p0032-l0012] [10.5pt] speech recognition: say you want to start simple and write a program capable of dis‐
[p0032-l0013] [10.5pt] tinguishing the words “one” and “two.” You might notice that the word “two” starts
[p0032-l0014] [10.5pt] with a high-pitch sound (“T”), so you could hardcode an algorithm that measures
[p0032-l0015] [10.5pt] high-pitch sound intensity and use that to distinguish ones and twos. Obviously this
[p0032-l0016] [10.5pt] technique will not scale to thousands of words spoken by millions of very different
[p0032-l0017] [9.0pt] 6
[p0032-l0018] [9.0pt] |
[p0032-l0019] [9.0pt] Chapter 1: The Machine Learning Landscape

=== PDF page 33 / printed label 7 ===
[p0033-l0001] [10.5pt] people in noisy environments and in dozens of languages. The best solution (at least
[p0033-l0002] [10.5pt] today) is to write an algorithm that learns by itself, given many example recordings
[p0033-l0003] [10.5pt] for each word.
[p0033-l0004] [10.5pt] Finally, Machine Learning can help humans learn (Figure 1-4): ML algorithms can be
[p0033-l0005] [10.5pt] inspected to see what they have learned (although for some algorithms this can be
[p0033-l0006] [10.5pt] tricky). For instance, once the spam filter has been trained on enough spam, it can
[p0033-l0007] [10.5pt] easily be inspected to reveal the list of words and combinations of words that it
[p0033-l0008] [10.5pt] believes are the best predictors of spam. Sometimes this will reveal unsuspected cor‐
[p0033-l0009] [10.5pt] relations or new trends, and thereby lead to a better understanding of the problem.
[p0033-l0010] [10.5pt] Applying ML techniques to dig into large amounts of data can help discover patterns
[p0033-l0011] [10.5pt] that were not immediately apparent. This is called data mining.
[p0033-l0012] [10.5pt] Figure 1-4. Machine Learning can help humans learn
[p0033-l0013] [10.5pt] To summarize, Machine Learning is great for:
[p0033-l0014] [10.5pt] • Problems for which existing solutions require a lot of hand-tuning or long lists of
[p0033-l0015] [10.5pt] rules: one Machine Learning algorithm can often simplify code and perform bet‐
[p0033-l0016] [10.5pt] ter.
[p0033-l0017] [10.5pt] • Complex problems for which there is no good solution at all using a traditional
[p0033-l0018] [10.5pt] approach: the best Machine Learning techniques can find a solution.
[p0033-l0019] [10.5pt] • Fluctuating environments: a Machine Learning system can adapt to new data.
[p0033-l0020] [10.5pt] • Getting insights about complex problems and large amounts of data.
[p0033-l0021] [9.0pt] Why Use Machine Learning?

[p0034-l0001] [18.92pt] Types of Machine Learning Systems
[p0034-l0002] [10.5pt] There are so many different types of Machine Learning systems that it is useful to
[p0034-l0003] [10.5pt] classify them in broad categories based on:
[p0034-l0004] [10.5pt] • Whether or not they are trained with human supervision (supervised, unsuper‐
[p0034-l0005] [10.5pt] vised, semisupervised, and Reinforcement Learning)
[p0034-l0006] [10.5pt] • Whether or not they can learn incrementally on the fly (online versus batch
[p0034-l0007] [10.5pt] learning)
[p0034-l0008] [10.5pt] • Whether they work by simply comparing new data points to known data points,
[p0034-l0009] [10.5pt] or instead detect patterns in the training data and build a predictive model, much
[p0034-l0010] [10.5pt] like scientists do (instance-based versus model-based learning)
[p0034-l0011] [10.5pt] These criteria are not exclusive; you can combine them in any way you like. For
[p0034-l0012] [10.5pt] example, a state-of-the-art spam filter may learn on the fly using a deep neural net‐
[p0034-l0013] [10.5pt] work model trained using examples of spam and ham; this makes it an online, model-
[p0034-l0014] [10.5pt] based, supervised learning system.
[p0034-l0015] [10.5pt] Let’s look at each of these criteria a bit more closely.
[p0034-l0016] [15.77pt] Supervised/Unsupervised Learning
[p0034-l0017] [10.5pt] Machine Learning systems can be classified according to the amount and type of
[p0034-l0018] [10.5pt] supervision they get during training. There are four major categories: supervised
[p0034-l0019] [10.5pt] learning, unsupervised learning, semisupervised learning, and Reinforcement Learn‐
[p0034-l0020] [10.5pt] ing.
[p0034-l0021] [11.56pt] Supervised learning
[p0034-l0022] [10.5pt] In supervised learning, the training data you feed to the algorithm includes the desired
[p0034-l0023] [10.5pt] solutions, called labels (Figure 1-5).
[p0034-l0024] [10.5pt] Figure 1-5. A labeled training set for supervised learning (e.g., spam classification)
[p0034-l0025] [9.0pt] 8
[p0034-l0026] [9.0pt] |
[p0034-l0027] [9.0pt] Chapter 1: The Machine Learning Landscape

=== PDF page 35 / printed label 9 ===
[p0035-l0001] [10.5pt] A typical supervised learning task is classification. The spam filter is a good example
[p0035-l0002] [10.5pt] of this: it is trained with many example emails along with their class (spam or ham),
[p0035-l0003] [10.5pt] and it must learn how to classify new emails.
[p0035-l0004] [10.5pt] Another typical task is to predict a target numeric value, such as the price of a car,
[p0035-l0005] [10.5pt] given a set of features (mileage, age, brand, etc.) called predictors. This sort of task is
[p0035-l0006] [10.5pt] called regression (Figure 1-6).1 To train the system, you need to give it many examples
[p0035-l0007] [10.5pt] of cars, including both their predictors and their labels (i.e., their prices).
[p0035-l0008] [9.6pt] In Machine Learning an attribute is a data type (e.g., “Mileage”),
[p0035-l0009] [9.6pt] while a feature has several meanings depending on the context, but
[p0035-l0010] [9.6pt] generally means an attribute plus its value (e.g., “Mileage =
[p0035-l0011] [9.6pt] 15,000”). Many people use the words attribute and feature inter‐
[p0035-l0012] [9.6pt] changeably, though.
[p0035-l0013] [10.5pt] Figure 1-6. Regression
[p0035-l0014] [10.5pt] Note that some regression algorithms can be used for classification as well, and vice
[p0035-l0015] [10.5pt] versa. For example, Logistic Regression is commonly used for classification, as it can
[p0035-l0016] [10.5pt] output a value that corresponds to the probability of belonging to a given class (e.g.,
[p0035-l0017] [10.5pt] 20% chance of being spam).
[p0035-l0018] [8.0pt] 1 Fun fact: this odd-sounding name is a statistics term introduced by Francis Galton while he was studying the
[p0035-l0019] [8.0pt] fact that the children of tall people tend to be shorter than their parents. Since children were shorter, he called
[p0035-l0020] [8.0pt] this regression to the mean. This name was then applied to the methods he used to analyze correlations
[p0035-l0021] [8.0pt] between variables.

[p0037-l0001] [10.5pt] • Visualization and dimensionality reduction

[p0037-l0008] [10.5pt] — Eclat
[p0037-l0009] [10.5pt] For example, say you have a lot of data about your blog’s visitors. You may want to
[p0037-l0010] [10.5pt] run a clustering algorithm to try to detect groups of similar visitors (Figure 1-8). At
[p0037-l0011] [10.5pt] no point do you tell the algorithm which group a visitor belongs to: it finds those
[p0037-l0012] [10.5pt] connections without your help. For example, it might notice that 40% of your visitors
[p0037-l0013] [10.5pt] are males who love comic books and generally read your blog in the evening, while
[p0037-l0014] [10.5pt] 20% are young sci-fi lovers who visit during the weekends, and so on. If you use a
[p0037-l0015] [10.5pt] hierarchical clustering algorithm, it may also subdivide each group into smaller
[p0037-l0016] [10.5pt] groups. This may help you target your posts for each group.
[p0037-l0017] [10.5pt] Figure 1-8. Clustering
[p0037-l0018] [10.5pt] Visualization algorithms are also good examples of unsupervised learning algorithms:
[p0037-l0019] [10.5pt] you feed them a lot of complex and unlabeled data, and they output a 2D or 3D rep‐
[p0037-l0020] [10.5pt] resentation of your data that can easily be plotted (Figure 1-9). These algorithms try
[p0037-l0021] [10.5pt] to preserve as much structure as they can (e.g., trying to keep separate clusters in the
[p0037-l0022] [10.5pt] input space from overlapping in the visualization), so you can understand how the
[p0037-l0023] [10.5pt] data is organized and perhaps identify unsuspected patterns.

[p0038-l0002] [10.5pt] A related task is dimensionality reduction, in which the goal is to simplify the data
[p0038-l0003] [10.5pt] without losing too much information. One way to do this is to merge several correla‐
[p0038-l0004] [10.5pt] ted features into one. For example, a car’s mileage may be very correlated with its age,
[p0038-l0005] [10.5pt] so the dimensionality reduction algorithm will merge them into one feature that rep‐
[p0038-l0006] [10.5pt] resents the car’s wear and tear. This is called feature extraction.
[p0038-l0007] [9.6pt] It is often a good idea to try to reduce the dimension of your train‐
[p0038-l0008] [9.6pt] ing data using a dimensionality reduction algorithm before you
[p0038-l0009] [9.6pt] feed it to another Machine Learning algorithm (such as a super‐
[p0038-l0010] [9.6pt] vised learning algorithm). It will run much faster, the data will take
[p0038-l0011] [9.6pt] up less disk and memory space, and in some cases it may also per‐
[p0038-l0012] [9.6pt] form better.
[p0038-l0013] [10.5pt] Yet another important unsupervised task is anomaly detection—for example, detect‐
[p0038-l0014] [10.5pt] ing unusual credit card transactions to prevent fraud, catching manufacturing defects,
[p0038-l0015] [10.5pt] or automatically removing outliers from a dataset before feeding it to another learn‐
[p0038-l0016] [10.5pt] ing algorithm. The system is shown mostly normal instances during training, so it
[p0038-l0017] [10.5pt] learns to recognize them and when it sees a new instance it can tell whether it looks
[p0038-l0018] [8.0pt] 3 Notice how animals are rather well separated from vehicles, how horses are close to deer but far from birds,
[p0038-l0019] [8.0pt] and so on. Figure reproduced with permission from Socher, Ganjoo, Manning, and Ng (2013), “T-SNE visual‐
[p0038-l0020] [8.0pt] ization of the semantic word space.”

[p0039-l0001] [10.5pt] like a normal one or whether it is likely an anomaly (see Figure 1-10). A very similar
[p0039-l0002] [10.5pt] task is novelty detection: the difference is that novelty detection algorithms expect to
[p0039-l0003] [10.5pt] see only normal data during training, while anomaly detection algorithms are usually
[p0039-l0004] [10.5pt] more tolerant, they can often perform well even with a small percentage of outliers in
[p0039-l0005] [10.5pt] the training set.
[p0039-l0006] [10.5pt] Figure 1-10. Anomaly detection
[p0039-l0007] [10.5pt] Finally, another common unsupervised task is association rule learning, in which the
[p0039-l0008] [10.5pt] goal is to dig into large amounts of data and discover interesting relations between
[p0039-l0009] [10.5pt] attributes. For example, suppose you own a supermarket. Running an association rule
[p0039-l0010] [10.5pt] on your sales logs may reveal that people who purchase barbecue sauce and potato
[p0039-l0011] [10.5pt] chips also tend to buy steak. Thus, you may want to place these items close to each
[p0039-l0012] [10.5pt] other.
[p0039-l0013] [11.56pt] Semisupervised learning
[p0039-l0014] [10.5pt] Some algorithms can deal with partially labeled training data, usually a lot of unla‐
[p0039-l0015] [10.5pt] beled data and a little bit of labeled data. This is called semisupervised learning
[p0039-l0016] [10.5pt] (Figure 1-11).
[p0039-l0017] [10.5pt] Some photo-hosting services, such as Google Photos, are good examples of this. Once
[p0039-l0018] [10.5pt] you upload all your family photos to the service, it automatically recognizes that the
[p0039-l0019] [10.5pt] same person A shows up in photos 1, 5, and 11, while another person B shows up in
[p0039-l0020] [10.5pt] photos 2, 5, and 7. This is the unsupervised part of the algorithm (clustering). Now all
[p0039-l0021] [10.5pt] the system needs is for you to tell it who these people are. Just one label per person,4
[p0039-l0022] [10.5pt] and it is able to name everyone in every photo, which is useful for searching photos.
[p0039-l0023] [8.0pt] 4 That’s when the system works perfectly. In practice it often creates a few clusters per person, and sometimes
[p0039-l0024] [8.0pt] mixes up two people who look alike, so you need to provide a few labels per person and manually clean up
[p0039-l0025] [8.0pt] some clusters.
[p0039-l0026] [9.0pt] Types of Machine Learning Systems
[p0039-l0027] [9.0pt] |

=== PDF page 40 / printed label 14 ===
[p0040-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 1-11. Semisupervised learning
[p0040-l0002] [10.5pt] Most semisupervised learning algorithms are combinations of unsupervised and
[p0040-l0003] [10.5pt] supervised algorithms. For example, deep belief networks (DBNs) are based on unsu‐
[p0040-l0004] [10.5pt] pervised components called restricted Boltzmann machines (RBMs) stacked on top of
[p0040-l0005] [10.5pt] one another. RBMs are trained sequentially in an unsupervised manner, and then the
[p0040-l0006] [10.5pt] whole system is fine-tuned using supervised learning techniques.
[p0040-l0007] [11.56pt] Reinforcement Learning
[p0040-l0008] [10.5pt] Reinforcement Learning is a very different beast. The learning system, called an agent
[p0040-l0009] [10.5pt] in this context, can observe the environment, select and perform actions, and get
[p0040-l0010] [10.5pt] rewards in return (or penalties in the form of negative rewards, as in Figure 1-12). It
[p0040-l0011] [10.5pt] must then learn by itself what is the best strategy, called a policy, to get the most
[p0040-l0012] [10.5pt] reward over time. A policy defines what action the agent should choose when it is in a
[p0040-l0013] [10.5pt] given situation.
[p0040-l0014] [9.0pt] 14
[p0040-l0015] [9.0pt] |
[p0040-l0016] [9.0pt] Chapter 1: The Machine Learning Landscape

=== PDF page 41 / printed label 15 ===
[p0041-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 1-12. Reinforcement Learning
[p0041-l0002] [10.5pt] For example, many robots implement Reinforcement Learning algorithms to learn
[p0041-l0003] [10.5pt] how to walk. DeepMind’s AlphaGo program is also a good example of Reinforcement
[p0041-l0004] [10.5pt] Learning: it made the headlines in May 2017 when it beat the world champion Ke Jie
[p0041-l0005] [10.5pt] at the game of Go. It learned its winning policy by analyzing millions of games, and
[p0041-l0006] [10.5pt] then playing many games against itself. Note that learning was turned off during the
[p0041-l0007] [10.5pt] games against the champion; AlphaGo was just applying the policy it had learned.
[p0041-l0008] [15.77pt] Batch and Online Learning
[p0041-l0009] [10.5pt] Another criterion used to classify Machine Learning systems is whether or not the
[p0041-l0010] [10.5pt] system can learn incrementally from a stream of incoming data.
[p0041-l0011] [11.56pt] Batch learning
[p0041-l0012] [10.5pt] In batch learning, the system is incapable of learning incrementally: it must be trained
[p0041-l0013] [10.5pt] using all the available data. This will generally take a lot of time and computing
[p0041-l0014] [10.5pt] resources, so it is typically done offline. First the system is trained, and then it is
[p0041-l0015] [10.5pt] launched into production and runs without learning anymore; it just applies what it
[p0041-l0016] [10.5pt] has learned. This is called offline learning.
[p0041-l0017] [10.5pt] If you want a batch learning system to know about new data (such as a new type of
[p0041-l0018] [10.5pt] spam), you need to train a new version of the system from scratch on the full dataset
[p0041-l0019] [10.5pt] (not just the new data, but also the old data), then stop the old system and replace it
[p0041-l0020] [10.5pt] with the new one.
[p0041-l0021] [10.5pt] Fortunately, the whole process of training, evaluating, and launching a Machine
[p0041-l0022] [10.5pt] Learning system can be automated fairly easily (as shown in Figure 1-3), so even a
[p0041-l0023] [9.0pt] Types of Machine Learning Systems
[p0041-l0024] [9.0pt] |
[p0041-l0025] [9.0pt] 15

=== PDF page 42 / printed label 16 ===
[p0042-l0001] [10.5pt] batch learning system can adapt to change. Simply update the data and train a new
[p0042-l0002] [10.5pt] version of the system from scratch as often as needed.
[p0042-l0003] [10.5pt] This solution is simple and often works fine, but training using the full set of data can
[p0042-l0004] [10.5pt] take many hours, so you would typically train a new system only every 24 hours or
[p0042-l0005] [10.5pt] even just weekly. If your system needs to adapt to rapidly changing data (e.g., to pre‐
[p0042-l0006] [10.5pt] dict stock prices), then you need a more reactive solution.
[p0042-l0007] [10.5pt] Also, training on the full set of data requires a lot of computing resources (CPU,
[p0042-l0008] [10.5pt] memory space, disk space, disk I/O, network I/O, etc.). If you have a lot of data and
[p0042-l0009] [10.5pt] you automate your system to train from scratch every day, it will end up costing you a
[p0042-l0010] [10.5pt] lot of money. If the amount of data is huge, it may even be impossible to use a batch
[p0042-l0011] [10.5pt] learning algorithm.
[p0042-l0012] [10.5pt] Finally, if your system needs to be able to learn autonomously and it has limited
[p0042-l0013] [10.5pt] resources (e.g., a smartphone application or a rover on Mars), then carrying around
[p0042-l0014] [10.5pt] large amounts of training data and taking up a lot of resources to train for hours
[p0042-l0015] [10.5pt] every day is a showstopper.
[p0042-l0016] [10.5pt] Fortunately, a better option in all these cases is to use algorithms that are capable of
[p0042-l0017] [10.5pt] learning incrementally.
[p0042-l0018] [11.56pt] Online learning
[p0042-l0019] [10.5pt] In online learning, you train the system incrementally by feeding it data instances
[p0042-l0020] [10.5pt] sequentially, either individually or by small groups called mini-batches. Each learning
[p0042-l0021] [10.5pt] step is fast and cheap, so the system can learn about new data on the fly, as it arrives
[p0042-l0022] [10.5pt] (see Figure 1-13).
[p0042-l0023] [10.5pt] Figure 1-13. Online learning
[p0042-l0024] [10.5pt] Online learning is great for systems that receive data as a continuous flow (e.g., stock
[p0042-l0025] [10.5pt] prices) and need to adapt to change rapidly or autonomously. It is also a good option
[p0042-l0026] [9.0pt] 16
[p0042-l0027] [9.0pt] |
[p0042-l0028] [9.0pt] Chapter 1: The Machine Learning Landscape

=== PDF page 43 / printed label 17 ===
[p0043-l0001] [10.5pt] if you have limited computing resources: once an online learning system has learned
[p0043-l0002] [10.5pt] about new data instances, it does not need them anymore, so you can discard them
[p0043-l0003] [10.5pt] (unless you want to be able to roll back to a previous state and “replay” the data). This
[p0043-l0004] [10.5pt] can save a huge amount of space.
[p0043-l0005] [10.5pt] Online learning algorithms can also be used to train systems on huge datasets that
[p0043-l0006] [10.5pt] cannot fit in one machine’s main memory (this is called out-of-core learning). The
[p0043-l0007] [10.5pt] algorithm loads part of the data, runs a training step on that data, and repeats the
[p0043-l0008] [10.5pt] process until it has run on all of the data (see Figure 1-14).
[p0043-l0009] [9.6pt] Out-of-core learning is usually done offline (i.e., not on the live
[p0043-l0010] [9.6pt] system), so online learning can be a confusing name. Think of it as
[p0043-l0011] [9.6pt] incremental learning.
[p0043-l0012] [10.5pt] Figure 1-14. Using online learning to handle huge datasets
[p0043-l0013] [10.5pt] One important parameter of online learning systems is how fast they should adapt to
[p0043-l0014] [10.5pt] changing data: this is called the learning rate. If you set a high learning rate, then your
[p0043-l0015] [10.5pt] system will rapidly adapt to new data, but it will also tend to quickly forget the old
[p0043-l0016] [10.5pt] data (you don’t want a spam filter to flag only the latest kinds of spam it was shown).
[p0043-l0017] [10.5pt] Conversely, if you set a low learning rate, the system will have more inertia; that is, it
[p0043-l0018] [10.5pt] will learn more slowly, but it will also be less sensitive to noise in the new data or to
[p0043-l0019] [10.5pt] sequences of nonrepresentative data points (outliers).
[p0043-l0020] [10.5pt] A big challenge with online learning is that if bad data is fed to the system, the sys‐
[p0043-l0021] [10.5pt] tem’s performance will gradually decline. If we are talking about a live system, your
[p0043-l0022] [10.5pt] clients will notice. For example, bad data could come from a malfunctioning sensor
[p0043-l0023] [10.5pt] on a robot, or from someone spamming a search engine to try to rank high in search
[p0043-l0024] [9.0pt] Types of Machine Learning Systems
[p0043-l0025] [9.0pt] |
[p0043-l0026] [9.0pt] 17

=== PDF page 44 / printed label 18 ===
[p0044-l0001] [10.5pt] results. To reduce this risk, you need to monitor your system closely and promptly
[p0044-l0002] [10.5pt] switch learning off (and possibly revert to a previously working state) if you detect a
[p0044-l0003] [10.5pt] drop in performance. You may also want to monitor the input data and react to
[p0044-l0004] [10.5pt] abnormal data (e.g., using an anomaly detection algorithm).
[p0044-l0005] [15.77pt] Instance-Based Versus Model-Based Learning
[p0044-l0006] [10.5pt] One more way to categorize Machine Learning systems is by how they generalize.
[p0044-l0007] [10.5pt] Most Machine Learning tasks are about making predictions. This means that given a
[p0044-l0008] [10.5pt] number of training examples, the system needs to be able to generalize to examples it
[p0044-l0009] [10.5pt] has never seen before. Having a good performance measure on the training data is
[p0044-l0010] [10.5pt] good, but insufficient; the true goal is to perform well on new instances.
[p0044-l0011] [10.5pt] There are two main approaches to generalization: instance-based learning and
[p0044-l0012] [10.5pt] model-based learning.
[p0044-l0013] [11.56pt] Instance-based learning
[p0044-l0014] [10.5pt] Possibly the most trivial form of learning is simply to learn by heart. If you were to
[p0044-l0015] [10.5pt] create a spam filter this way, it would just flag all emails that are identical to emails
[p0044-l0016] [10.5pt] that have already been flagged by users—not the worst solution, but certainly not the
[p0044-l0017] [10.5pt] best.
[p0044-l0018] [10.5pt] Instead of just flagging emails that are identical to known spam emails, your spam
[p0044-l0019] [10.5pt] filter could be programmed to also flag emails that are very similar to known spam
[p0044-l0020] [10.5pt] emails. This requires a measure of similarity between two emails. A (very basic) simi‐
[p0044-l0021] [10.5pt] larity measure between two emails could be to count the number of words they have
[p0044-l0022] [10.5pt] in common. The system would flag an email as spam if it has many words in com‐
[p0044-l0023] [10.5pt] mon with a known spam email.
[p0044-l0024] [10.5pt] This is called instance-based learning: the system learns the examples by heart, then
[p0044-l0025] [10.5pt] generalizes to new cases by comparing them to the learned examples (or a subset of
[p0044-l0026] [10.5pt] them), using a similarity measure. For example, in Figure 1-15 the new instance
[p0044-l0027] [10.5pt] would be classified as a triangle because the majority of the most similar instances
[p0044-l0028] [10.5pt] belong to that class.
[p0044-l0029] [9.0pt] 18
[p0044-l0030] [9.0pt] |
[p0044-l0031] [9.0pt] Chapter 1: The Machine Learning Landscape

=== PDF page 45 / printed label 19 ===
[p0045-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 1-15. Instance-based learning
[p0045-l0002] [11.56pt] Model-based learning
[p0045-l0003] [10.5pt] Another way to generalize from a set of examples is to build a model of these exam‐
[p0045-l0004] [10.5pt] ples, then use that model to make predictions. This is called model-based learning
[p0045-l0005] [10.5pt] (Figure 1-16).
[p0045-l0006] [10.5pt] Figure 1-16. Model-based learning
[p0045-l0007] [10.5pt] For example, suppose you want to know if money makes people happy, so you down‐
[p0045-l0008] [10.5pt] load the Better Life Index data from the OECD’s website as well as stats about GDP
[p0045-l0009] [10.5pt] per capita from the IMF’s website. Then you join the tables and sort by GDP per cap‐
[p0045-l0010] [10.5pt] ita. Table 1-1 shows an excerpt of what you get.

[p0047-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 1-18. A few possible linear models
[p0047-l0002] [10.5pt] Before you can use your model, you need to define the parameter values θ0 and θ1.
[p0047-l0003] [10.5pt] How can you know which values will make your model perform best? To answer this
[p0047-l0004] [10.5pt] question, you need to specify a performance measure. You can either define a utility
[p0047-l0005] [10.5pt] function (or fitness function) that measures how good your model is, or you can define
[p0047-l0006] [10.5pt] a cost function that measures how bad it is. For linear regression problems, people
[p0047-l0007] [10.5pt] typically use a cost function that measures the distance between the linear model’s
[p0047-l0008] [10.5pt] predictions and the training examples; the objective is to minimize this distance.
[p0047-l0009] [10.5pt] This is where the Linear Regression algorithm comes in: you feed it your training
[p0047-l0010] [10.5pt] examples and it finds the parameters that make the linear model fit best to your data.
[p0047-l0011] [10.5pt] This is called training the model. In our case the algorithm finds that the optimal
[p0047-l0012] [10.5pt] parameter values are θ0 = 4.85 and θ1 = 4.91 × 10–5.
[p0047-l0013] [10.5pt] Now the model fits the training data as closely as possible (for a linear model), as you
[p0047-l0014] [10.5pt] can see in Figure 1-19.
[p0047-l0015] [10.5pt] Figure 1-19. The linear model that fits the training data best

[p0048-l0002] [10.5pt] want to know how happy Cypriots are, and the OECD data does not have the answer.
[p0048-l0003] [10.5pt] Fortunately, you can use your model to make a good prediction: you look up Cyprus’s
[p0048-l0004] [10.5pt] GDP per capita, find $22,587, and then apply your model and find that life satisfac‐
[p0048-l0005] [10.5pt] tion is likely to be somewhere around 4.85 + 22,587 × 4.91 × 10-5 = 5.96.
[p0048-l0006] [10.5pt] To whet your appetite, Example 1-1 shows the Python code that loads the data, pre‐

[p0049-l0001] [9.6pt] If you had used an instance-based learning algorithm instead, you
[p0049-l0002] [9.6pt] would have found that Slovenia has the closest GDP per capita to
[p0049-l0003] [9.6pt] that of Cyprus ($20,732), and since the OECD data tells us that
[p0049-l0004] [9.6pt] Slovenians’ life satisfaction is 5.7, you would have predicted a life
[p0049-l0005] [9.6pt] satisfaction of 5.7 for Cyprus. If you zoom out a bit and look at the
[p0049-l0006] [9.6pt] two next closest countries, you will find Portugal and Spain with
[p0049-l0007] [9.6pt] life satisfactions of 5.1 and 6.5, respectively. Averaging these three
[p0049-l0008] [9.6pt] values, you get 5.77, which is pretty close to your model-based pre‐

[p0049-l0019] [10.5pt] If all went well, your model will make good predictions. If not, you may need to use
[p0049-l0020] [10.5pt] more attributes (employment rate, health, air pollution, etc.), get more or better qual‐
[p0049-l0021] [10.5pt] ity training data, or perhaps select a more powerful model (e.g., a Polynomial Regres‐
[p0049-l0022] [10.5pt] sion model).
[p0049-l0023] [10.5pt] In summary:
[p0049-l0024] [10.5pt] • You studied the data.
[p0049-l0025] [10.5pt] • You selected a model.
[p0049-l0026] [10.5pt] • You trained it on the training data (i.e., the learning algorithm searched for the
[p0049-l0027] [10.5pt] model parameter values that minimize a cost function).
[p0049-l0028] [10.5pt] • Finally, you applied the model to make predictions on new cases (this is called
[p0049-l0029] [10.5pt] inference), hoping that this model will generalize well.
[p0049-l0030] [10.5pt] This is what a typical Machine Learning project looks like. In Chapter 2 you will

[p0050-l0001] [18.92pt] Main Challenges of Machine Learning
[p0050-l0002] [10.5pt] In short, since your main task is to select a learning algorithm and train it on some
[p0050-l0003] [10.5pt] data, the two things that can go wrong are “bad algorithm” and “bad data.” Let’s start
[p0050-l0004] [10.5pt] with examples of bad data.
[p0050-l0005] [15.77pt] Insufficient Quantity of Training Data
[p0050-l0006] [10.5pt] For a toddler to learn what an apple is, all it takes is for you to point to an apple and
[p0050-l0007] [10.5pt] say “apple” (possibly repeating this procedure a few times). Now the child is able to
[p0050-l0008] [10.5pt] recognize apples in all sorts of colors and shapes. Genius.
[p0050-l0009] [10.5pt] Machine Learning is not quite there yet; it takes a lot of data for most Machine Learn‐
[p0050-l0010] [10.5pt] ing algorithms to work properly. Even for very simple problems you typically need
[p0050-l0011] [10.5pt] thousands of examples, and for complex problems such as image or speech recogni‐
[p0050-l0012] [10.5pt] tion you may need millions of examples (unless you can reuse parts of an existing
[p0050-l0013] [10.5pt] model).
[p0050-l0014] [9.0pt] 24
[p0050-l0015] [9.0pt] |
[p0050-l0016] [9.0pt] Chapter 1: The Machine Learning Landscape

=== PDF page 51 / printed label 25 ===
[p0051-l0001] [15.0pt] The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Data
[p0051-l0002] [10.0pt] In a famous paper published in 2001, Microsoft researchers Michele Banko and Eric
[p0051-l0003] [10.0pt] Brill showed that very different Machine Learning algorithms, including fairly simple
[p0051-l0004] [10.0pt] ones, performed almost identically well on a complex problem of natural language
[p0051-l0005] [10.0pt] disambiguation8 once they were given enough data (as you can see in Figure 1-20).
[p0051-l0006] [10.0pt] Figure 1-20. The importance of data versus algorithms9
[p0051-l0007] [10.0pt] As the authors put it: “these results suggest that we may want to reconsider the trade-
[p0051-l0008] [10.0pt] off between spending time and money on algorithm development versus spending it
[p0051-l0009] [10.0pt] on corpus development.”
[p0051-l0010] [10.0pt] The idea that data matters more than algorithms for complex problems was further
[p0051-l0011] [10.0pt] popularized by Peter Norvig et al. in a paper titled “The Unreasonable Effectiveness
[p0051-l0012] [10.0pt] of Data” published in 2009.10 It should be noted, however, that small- and medium-
[p0051-l0013] [10.0pt] sized datasets are still very common, and it is not always easy or cheap to get extra
[p0051-l0014] [10.0pt] training data, so don’t abandon algorithms just yet.
[p0051-l0015] [8.0pt] 8 For example, knowing whether to write “to,” “two,” or “too” depending on the context.
[p0051-l0016] [8.0pt] 9 Figure reproduced with permission from Banko and Brill (2001), “Learning Curves for Confusion Set Disam‐
[p0051-l0017] [8.0pt] biguation.”
[p0051-l0018] [8.0pt] 10 “The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Data,” Peter Norvig et al. (2009).
[p0051-l0019] [9.0pt] Main Challenges of Machine Learning
[p0051-l0020] [9.0pt] |
[p0051-l0021] [9.0pt] 25

=== PDF page 52 / printed label 26 ===
[p0052-l0001] [15.77pt] Nonrepresentative Training Data
[p0052-l0002] [10.5pt] In order to generalize well, it is crucial that your training data be representative of the
[p0052-l0003] [10.5pt] new cases you want to generalize to. This is true whether you use instance-based
[p0052-l0004] [10.5pt] learning or model-based learning.
[p0052-l0005] [10.5pt] For example, the set of countries we used earlier for training the linear model was not
[p0052-l0006] [10.5pt] perfectly representative; a few countries were missing. Figure 1-21 shows what the
[p0052-l0007] [10.5pt] data looks like when you add the missing countries.
[p0052-l0008] [10.5pt] Figure 1-21. A more representative training sample
[p0052-l0009] [10.5pt] If you train a linear model on this data, you get the solid line, while the old model is
[p0052-l0010] [10.5pt] represented by the dotted line. As you can see, not only does adding a few missing
[p0052-l0011] [10.5pt] countries significantly alter the model, but it makes it clear that such a simple linear
[p0052-l0012] [10.5pt] model is probably never going to work well. It seems that very rich countries are not
[p0052-l0013] [10.5pt] happier than moderately rich countries (in fact they seem unhappier), and conversely
[p0052-l0014] [10.5pt] some poor countries seem happier than many rich countries.
[p0052-l0015] [10.5pt] By using a nonrepresentative training set, we trained a model that is unlikely to make
[p0052-l0016] [10.5pt] accurate predictions, especially for very poor and very rich countries.
[p0052-l0017] [10.5pt] It is crucial to use a training set that is representative of the cases you want to general‐
[p0052-l0018] [10.5pt] ize to. This is often harder than it sounds: if the sample is too small, you will have
[p0052-l0019] [10.5pt] sampling noise (i.e., nonrepresentative data as a result of chance), but even very large
[p0052-l0020] [10.5pt] samples can be nonrepresentative if the sampling method is flawed. This is called
[p0052-l0021] [10.5pt] sampling bias.
[p0052-l0022] [15.0pt] A Famous Example of Sampling Bias
[p0052-l0023] [10.0pt] Perhaps the most famous example of sampling bias happened during the US presi‐
[p0052-l0024] [10.0pt] dential election in 1936, which pitted Landon against Roosevelt: the Literary Digest
[p0052-l0025] [10.0pt] conducted a very large poll, sending mail to about 10 million people. It got 2.4 million
[p0052-l0026] [10.0pt] answers, and predicted with high confidence that Landon would get 57% of the votes.
[p0052-l0027] [9.0pt] 26
[p0052-l0028] [9.0pt] |
[p0052-l0029] [9.0pt] Chapter 1: The Machine Learning Landscape

=== PDF page 53 / printed label 27 ===
[p0053-l0001] [10.0pt] Instead, Roosevelt won with 62% of the votes. The flaw was in the Literary Digest’s
[p0053-l0002] [10.0pt] sampling method:
[p0053-l0003] [10.0pt] • First, to obtain the addresses to send the polls to, the Literary Digest used tele‐
[p0053-l0004] [10.0pt] phone directories, lists of magazine subscribers, club membership lists, and the
[p0053-l0005] [10.0pt] like. All of these lists tend to favor wealthier people, who are more likely to vote
[p0053-l0006] [10.0pt] Republican (hence Landon).
[p0053-l0007] [10.0pt] • Second, less than 25% of the people who received the poll answered. Again, this
[p0053-l0008] [10.0pt] introduces a sampling bias, by ruling out people who don’t care much about poli‐
[p0053-l0009] [10.0pt] tics, people who don’t like the Literary Digest, and other key groups. This is a spe‐
[p0053-l0010] [10.0pt] cial type of sampling bias called nonresponse bias.
[p0053-l0011] [10.0pt] Here is another example: say you want to build a system to recognize funk music vid‐
[p0053-l0012] [10.0pt] eos. One way to build your training set is to search “funk music” on YouTube and use
[p0053-l0013] [10.0pt] the resulting videos. But this assumes that YouTube’s search engine returns a set of
[p0053-l0014] [10.0pt] videos that are representative of all the funk music videos on YouTube. In reality, the
[p0053-l0015] [10.0pt] search results are likely to be biased toward popular artists (and if you live in Brazil
[p0053-l0016] [10.0pt] you will get a lot of “funk carioca” videos, which sound nothing like James Brown).
[p0053-l0017] [10.0pt] On the other hand, how else can you get a large training set?
[p0053-l0018] [15.77pt] Poor-Quality Data
[p0053-l0019] [10.5pt] Obviously, if your training data is full of errors, outliers, and noise (e.g., due to poor-
[p0053-l0020] [10.5pt] quality measurements), it will make it harder for the system to detect the underlying
[p0053-l0021] [10.5pt] patterns, so your system is less likely to perform well. It is often well worth the effort
[p0053-l0022] [10.5pt] to spend time cleaning up your training data. The truth is, most data scientists spend
[p0053-l0023] [10.5pt] a significant part of their time doing just that. For example:
[p0053-l0024] [10.5pt] • If some instances are clearly outliers, it may help to simply discard them or try to
[p0053-l0025] [10.5pt] fix the errors manually.
[p0053-l0026] [10.5pt] • If some instances are missing a few features (e.g., 5% of your customers did not
[p0053-l0027] [10.5pt] specify their age), you must decide whether you want to ignore this attribute alto‐
[p0053-l0028] [10.5pt] gether, ignore these instances, fill in the missing values (e.g., with the median
[p0053-l0029] [10.5pt] age), or train one model with the feature and one model without it, and so on.
[p0053-l0030] [15.77pt] Irrelevant Features
[p0053-l0031] [10.5pt] As the saying goes: garbage in, garbage out. Your system will only be capable of learn‐
[p0053-l0032] [10.5pt] ing if the training data contains enough relevant features and not too many irrelevant
[p0053-l0033] [10.5pt] ones. A critical part of the success of a Machine Learning project is coming up with a
[p0053-l0034] [10.5pt] good set of features to train on. This process, called feature engineering, involves:
[p0053-l0035] [9.0pt] Main Challenges of Machine Learning
[p0053-l0036] [9.0pt] |
[p0053-l0037] [9.0pt] 27

=== PDF page 54 / printed label 28 ===
[p0054-l0001] [10.5pt] • Feature selection: selecting the most useful features to train on among existing
[p0054-l0002] [10.5pt] features.
[p0054-l0003] [10.5pt] • Feature extraction: combining existing features to produce a more useful one (as
[p0054-l0004] [10.5pt] we saw earlier, dimensionality reduction algorithms can help).
[p0054-l0005] [10.5pt] • Creating new features by gathering new data.
[p0054-l0006] [10.5pt] Now that we have looked at many examples of bad data, let’s look at a couple of exam‐
[p0054-l0007] [10.5pt] ples of bad algorithms.
[p0054-l0008] [15.77pt] Overfitting the Training Data
[p0054-l0009] [10.5pt] Say you are visiting a foreign country and the taxi driver rips you off. You might be
[p0054-l0010] [10.5pt] tempted to say that all taxi drivers in that country are thieves. Overgeneralizing is
[p0054-l0011] [10.5pt] something that we humans do all too often, and unfortunately machines can fall into
[p0054-l0012] [10.5pt] the same trap if we are not careful. In Machine Learning this is called overfitting: it
[p0054-l0013] [10.5pt] means that the model performs well on the training data, but it does not generalize
[p0054-l0014] [10.5pt] well.
[p0054-l0015] [10.5pt] Figure 1-22 shows an example of a high-degree polynomial life satisfaction model
[p0054-l0016] [10.5pt] that strongly overfits the training data. Even though it performs much better on the
[p0054-l0017] [10.5pt] training data than the simple linear model, would you really trust its predictions?
[p0054-l0018] [10.5pt] Figure 1-22. Overfitting the training data
[p0054-l0019] [10.5pt] Complex models such as deep neural networks can detect subtle patterns in the data,
[p0054-l0020] [10.5pt] but if the training set is noisy, or if it is too small (which introduces sampling noise),
[p0054-l0021] [10.5pt] then the model is likely to detect patterns in the noise itself. Obviously these patterns
[p0054-l0022] [10.5pt] will not generalize to new instances. For example, say you feed your life satisfaction
[p0054-l0023] [10.5pt] model many more attributes, including uninformative ones such as the country’s
[p0054-l0024] [10.5pt] name. In that case, a complex model may detect patterns like the fact that all coun‐
[p0054-l0025] [10.5pt] tries in the training data with a w in their name have a life satisfaction greater than 7:
[p0054-l0026] [10.5pt] New Zealand (7.3), Norway (7.4), Sweden (7.2), and Switzerland (7.5). How confident
[p0054-l0027] [9.0pt] 28
[p0054-l0028] [9.0pt] |
[p0054-l0029] [9.0pt] Chapter 1: The Machine Learning Landscape

=== PDF page 55 / printed label 29 ===
[p0055-l0001] [10.5pt] are you that the W-satisfaction rule generalizes to Rwanda or Zimbabwe? Obviously
[p0055-l0002] [10.5pt] this pattern occurred in the training data by pure chance, but the model has no way
[p0055-l0003] [10.5pt] to tell whether a pattern is real or simply the result of noise in the data.
[p0055-l0004] [9.6pt] Overfitting happens when the model is too complex relative to the
[p0055-l0005] [9.6pt] amount and noisiness of the training data. The possible solutions
[p0055-l0006] [9.6pt] are:
[p0055-l0007] [9.6pt] • To simplify the model by selecting one with fewer parameters
[p0055-l0008] [9.6pt] (e.g., a linear model rather than a high-degree polynomial
[p0055-l0009] [9.6pt] model), by reducing the number of attributes in the training
[p0055-l0010] [9.6pt] data or by constraining the model
[p0055-l0011] [9.6pt] • To gather more training data
[p0055-l0012] [9.6pt] • To reduce the noise in the training data (e.g., fix data errors
[p0055-l0013] [9.6pt] and remove outliers)
[p0055-l0014] [10.5pt] Constraining a model to make it simpler and reduce the risk of overfitting is called
[p0055-l0015] [10.5pt] regularization. For example, the linear model we defined earlier has two parameters,
[p0055-l0016] [10.5pt] θ0 and θ1. This gives the learning algorithm two degrees of freedom to adapt the model
[p0055-l0017] [10.5pt] to the training data: it can tweak both the height (θ0) and the slope (θ1) of the line. If
[p0055-l0018] [10.5pt] we forced θ1 = 0, the algorithm would have only one degree of freedom and would
[p0055-l0019] [10.5pt] have a much harder time fitting the data properly: all it could do is move the line up
[p0055-l0020] [10.5pt] or down to get as close as possible to the training instances, so it would end up
[p0055-l0021] [10.5pt] around the mean. A very simple model indeed! If we allow the algorithm to modify θ1
[p0055-l0022] [10.5pt] but we force it to keep it small, then the learning algorithm will effectively have some‐
[p0055-l0023] [10.5pt] where in between one and two degrees of freedom. It will produce a simpler model
[p0055-l0024] [10.5pt] than with two degrees of freedom, but more complex than with just one. You want to
[p0055-l0025] [10.5pt] find the right balance between fitting the training data perfectly and keeping the
[p0055-l0026] [10.5pt] model simple enough to ensure that it will generalize well.
[p0055-l0027] [10.5pt] Figure 1-23 shows three models: the dotted line represents the original model that
[p0055-l0028] [10.5pt] was trained with a few countries missing, the dashed line is our second model trained
[p0055-l0029] [10.5pt] with all countries, and the solid line is a linear model trained with the same data as
[p0055-l0030] [10.5pt] the first model but with a regularization constraint. You can see that regularization
[p0055-l0031] [10.5pt] forced the model to have a smaller slope, which fits a bit less the training data that the
[p0055-l0032] [10.5pt] model was trained on, but actually allows it to generalize better to new examples.

[p0055-l0034] [9.0pt] |

=== PDF page 56 / printed label 30 ===
[p0056-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 1-23. Regularization reduces the risk of overfitting
[p0056-l0002] [10.5pt] The amount of regularization to apply during learning can be controlled by a hyper‐
[p0056-l0003] [10.5pt] parameter. A hyperparameter is a parameter of a learning algorithm (not of the
[p0056-l0004] [10.5pt] model). As such, it is not affected by the learning algorithm itself; it must be set prior
[p0056-l0005] [10.5pt] to training and remains constant during training. If you set the regularization hyper‐
[p0056-l0006] [10.5pt] parameter to a very large value, you will get an almost flat model (a slope close to
[p0056-l0007] [10.5pt] zero); the learning algorithm will almost certainly not overfit the training data, but it
[p0056-l0008] [10.5pt] will be less likely to find a good solution. Tuning hyperparameters is an important
[p0056-l0009] [10.5pt] part of building a Machine Learning system (you will see a detailed example in the
[p0056-l0010] [10.5pt] next chapter).
[p0056-l0011] [15.77pt] Underfitting the Training Data
[p0056-l0012] [10.5pt] As you might guess, underfitting is the opposite of overfitting: it occurs when your
[p0056-l0013] [10.5pt] model is too simple to learn the underlying structure of the data. For example, a lin‐
[p0056-l0014] [10.5pt] ear model of life satisfaction is prone to underfit; reality is just more complex than
[p0056-l0015] [10.5pt] the model, so its predictions are bound to be inaccurate, even on the training exam‐
[p0056-l0016] [10.5pt] ples.
[p0056-l0017] [10.5pt] The main options to fix this problem are:
[p0056-l0018] [10.5pt] • Selecting a more powerful model, with more parameters
[p0056-l0019] [10.5pt] • Feeding better features to the learning algorithm (feature engineering)
[p0056-l0020] [10.5pt] • Reducing the constraints on the model (e.g., reducing the regularization hyper‐
[p0056-l0021] [10.5pt] parameter)
[p0056-l0022] [15.77pt] Stepping Back
[p0056-l0023] [10.5pt] By now you already know a lot about Machine Learning. However, we went through
[p0056-l0024] [10.5pt] so many concepts that you may be feeling a little lost, so let’s step back and look at the
[p0056-l0025] [10.5pt] big picture:
[p0056-l0026] [9.0pt] 30
[p0056-l0027] [9.0pt] |
[p0056-l0028] [9.0pt] Chapter 1: The Machine Learning Landscape

=== PDF page 57 / printed label 31 ===
[p0057-l0001] [10.5pt] • Machine Learning is about making machines get better at some task by learning
[p0057-l0002] [10.5pt] from data, instead of having to explicitly code rules.
[p0057-l0003] [10.5pt] • There are many different types of ML systems: supervised or not, batch or online,
[p0057-l0004] [10.5pt] instance-based or model-based, and so on.
[p0057-l0005] [10.5pt] • In a ML project you gather data in a training set, and you feed the training set to
[p0057-l0006] [10.5pt] a learning algorithm. If the algorithm is model-based it tunes some parameters to
[p0057-l0007] [10.5pt] fit the model to the training set (i.e., to make good predictions on the training set
[p0057-l0008] [10.5pt] itself), and then hopefully it will be able to make good predictions on new cases
[p0057-l0009] [10.5pt] as well. If the algorithm is instance-based, it just learns the examples by heart and
[p0057-l0010] [10.5pt] generalizes to new instances by comparing them to the learned instances using a
[p0057-l0011] [10.5pt] similarity measure.
[p0057-l0012] [10.5pt] • The system will not perform well if your training set is too small, or if the data is
[p0057-l0013] [10.5pt] not representative, noisy, or polluted with irrelevant features (garbage in, garbage
[p0057-l0014] [10.5pt] out). Lastly, your model needs to be neither too simple (in which case it will
[p0057-l0015] [10.5pt] underfit) nor too complex (in which case it will overfit).
[p0057-l0016] [10.5pt] There’s just one last important topic to cover: once you have trained a model, you
[p0057-l0017] [10.5pt] don’t want to just “hope” it generalizes to new cases. You want to evaluate it, and fine-
[p0057-l0018] [10.5pt] tune it if necessary. Let’s see how.
[p0057-l0019] [18.92pt] Testing and Validating
[p0057-l0020] [10.5pt] The only way to know how well a model will generalize to new cases is to actually try
[p0057-l0021] [10.5pt] it out on new cases. One way to do that is to put your model in production and moni‐
[p0057-l0022] [10.5pt] tor how well it performs. This works well, but if your model is horribly bad, your
[p0057-l0023] [10.5pt] users will complain—not the best idea.
[p0057-l0024] [10.5pt] A better option is to split your data into two sets: the training set and the test set. As
[p0057-l0025] [10.5pt] these names imply, you train your model using the training set, and you test it using
[p0057-l0026] [10.5pt] the test set. The error rate on new cases is called the generalization error (or out-of-
[p0057-l0027] [10.5pt] sample error), and by evaluating your model on the test set, you get an estimate of this
[p0057-l0028] [10.5pt] error. This value tells you how well your model will perform on instances it has never
[p0057-l0029] [10.5pt] seen before.
[p0057-l0030] [10.5pt] If the training error is low (i.e., your model makes few mistakes on the training set)
[p0057-l0031] [10.5pt] but the generalization error is high, it means that your model is overfitting the train‐
[p0057-l0032] [10.5pt] ing data.
[p0057-l0033] [9.6pt] It is common to use 80% of the data for training and hold out 20%
[p0057-l0034] [9.6pt] for testing. However, this depends on the size of the dataset: if it
[p0057-l0035] [9.6pt] contains 10 million instances, then holding out 1% means your test
[p0057-l0036] [9.6pt] set will contain 100,000 instances: that’s probably more than
[p0057-l0037] [9.6pt] enough to get a good estimate of the generalization error.
[p0057-l0038] [9.0pt] Testing and Validating
[p0057-l0039] [9.0pt] |
[p0057-l0040] [9.0pt] 31

=== PDF page 58 / printed label 32 ===
[p0058-l0001] [15.77pt] Hyperparameter Tuning and Model Selection
[p0058-l0002] [10.5pt] So evaluating a model is simple enough: just use a test set. Now suppose you are hesi‐
[p0058-l0003] [10.5pt] tating between two models (say a linear model and a polynomial model): how can
[p0058-l0004] [10.5pt] you decide? One option is to train both and compare how well they generalize using
[p0058-l0005] [10.5pt] the test set.
[p0058-l0006] [10.5pt] Now suppose that the linear model generalizes better, but you want to apply some
[p0058-l0007] [10.5pt] regularization to avoid overfitting. The question is: how do you choose the value of
[p0058-l0008] [10.5pt] the regularization hyperparameter? One option is to train 100 different models using
[p0058-l0009] [10.5pt] 100 different values for this hyperparameter. Suppose you find the best hyperparame‐
[p0058-l0010] [10.5pt] ter value that produces a model with the lowest generalization error, say just 5% error.
[p0058-l0011] [10.5pt] So you launch this model into production, but unfortunately it does not perform as
[p0058-l0012] [10.5pt] well as expected and produces 15% errors. What just happened?
[p0058-l0013] [10.5pt] The problem is that you measured the generalization error multiple times on the test
[p0058-l0014] [10.5pt] set, and you adapted the model and hyperparameters to produce the best model for
[p0058-l0015] [10.5pt] that particular set. This means that the model is unlikely to perform as well on new
[p0058-l0016] [10.5pt] data.
[p0058-l0017] [10.5pt] A common solution to this problem is called holdout validation: you simply hold out
[p0058-l0018] [10.5pt] part of the training set to evaluate several candidate models and select the best one.
[p0058-l0019] [10.5pt] The new heldout set is called the validation set (or sometimes the development set, or
[p0058-l0020] [10.5pt] dev set). More specifically, you train multiple models with various hyperparameters
[p0058-l0021] [10.5pt] on the reduced training set (i.e., the full training set minus the validation set), and
[p0058-l0022] [10.5pt] you select the model that performs best on the validation set. After this holdout vali‐
[p0058-l0023] [10.5pt] dation process, you train the best model on the full training set (including the valida‐
[p0058-l0024] [10.5pt] tion set), and this gives you the final model. Lastly, you evaluate this final model on
[p0058-l0025] [10.5pt] the test set to get an estimate of the generalization error.
[p0058-l0026] [10.5pt] This solution usually works quite well. However, if the validation set is too small, then
[p0058-l0027] [10.5pt] model evaluations will be imprecise: you may end up selecting a suboptimal model by
[p0058-l0028] [10.5pt] mistake. Conversely, if the validation set is too large, then the remaining training set
[p0058-l0029] [10.5pt] will be much smaller than the full training set. Why is this bad? Well, since the final
[p0058-l0030] [10.5pt] model will be trained on the full training set, it is not ideal to compare candidate
[p0058-l0031] [10.5pt] models trained on a much smaller training set. It would be like selecting the fastest
[p0058-l0032] [10.5pt] sprinter to participate in a marathon. One way to solve this problem is to perform
[p0058-l0033] [10.5pt] repeated cross-validation, using many small validation sets. Each model is evaluated
[p0058-l0034] [10.5pt] once per validation set, after it is trained on the rest of the data. By averaging out all
[p0058-l0035] [10.5pt] the evaluations of a model, we get a much more accurate measure of its performance.
[p0058-l0036] [10.5pt] However, there is a drawback: the training time is multiplied by the number of valida‐
[p0058-l0037] [10.5pt] tion sets.
[p0058-l0038] [9.0pt] 32
[p0058-l0039] [9.0pt] |
[p0058-l0040] [9.0pt] Chapter 1: The Machine Learning Landscape

=== PDF page 59 / printed label 33 ===
[p0059-l0001] [15.77pt] Data Mismatch
[p0059-l0002] [10.5pt] In some cases, it is easy to get a large amount of data for training, but it is not per‐
[p0059-l0003] [10.5pt] fectly representative of the data that will be used in production. For example, suppose
[p0059-l0004] [10.5pt] you want to create a mobile app to take pictures of flowers and automatically deter‐
[p0059-l0005] [10.5pt] mine their species. You can easily download millions of pictures of flowers on the
[p0059-l0006] [10.5pt] web, but they won’t be perfectly representative of the pictures that will actually be
[p0059-l0007] [10.5pt] taken using the app on a mobile device. Perhaps you only have 10,000 representative
[p0059-l0008] [10.5pt] pictures (i.e., actually taken with the app). In this case, the most important rule to
[p0059-l0009] [10.5pt] remember is that the validation set and the test must be as representative as possible
[p0059-l0010] [10.5pt] of the data you expect to use in production, so they should be composed exclusively
[p0059-l0011] [10.5pt] of representative pictures: you can shuffle them and put half in the validation set, and
[p0059-l0012] [10.5pt] half in the test set (making sure that no duplicates or near-duplicates end up in both
[p0059-l0013] [10.5pt] sets). After training your model on the web pictures, if you observe that the perfor‐
[p0059-l0014] [10.5pt] mance of your model on the validation set is disappointing, you will not know
[p0059-l0015] [10.5pt] whether this is because your model has overfit the training set, or whether this is just
[p0059-l0016] [10.5pt] due to the mismatch between the web pictures and the mobile app pictures. One sol‐
[p0059-l0017] [10.5pt] ution is to hold out part of the training pictures (from the web) in yet another set that
[p0059-l0018] [10.5pt] Andrew Ng calls the train-dev set. After the model is trained (on the training set, not
[p0059-l0019] [10.5pt] on the train-dev set), you can evaluate it on the train-dev set: if it performs well, then
[p0059-l0020] [10.5pt] the model is not overfitting the training set, so if performs poorly on the validation
[p0059-l0021] [10.5pt] set, the problem must come from the data mismatch. You can try to tackle this prob‐
[p0059-l0022] [10.5pt] lem by preprocessing the web images to make them look more like the pictures that
[p0059-l0023] [10.5pt] will be taken by the mobile app, and then retraining the model. Conversely, if the
[p0059-l0024] [10.5pt] model performs poorly on the train-dev set, then the model must have overfit the
[p0059-l0025] [10.5pt] training set, so you should try to simplify or regularize the model, get more training
[p0059-l0026] [10.5pt] data and clean up the training data, as discussed earlier.
[p0059-l0027] [15.0pt] No Free Lunch Theorem
[p0059-l0028] [10.0pt] A model is a simplified version of the observations. The simplifications are meant to
[p0059-l0029] [10.0pt] discard the superfluous details that are unlikely to generalize to new instances. How‐
[p0059-l0030] [10.0pt] ever, to decide what data to discard and what data to keep, you must make assump‐
[p0059-l0031] [10.0pt] tions. For example, a linear model makes the assumption that the data is
[p0059-l0032] [10.0pt] fundamentally linear and that the distance between the instances and the straight line
[p0059-l0033] [10.0pt] is just noise, which can safely be ignored.
[p0059-l0034] [10.0pt] In a famous 1996 paper,11 David Wolpert demonstrated that if you make absolutely
[p0059-l0035] [10.0pt] no assumption about the data, then there is no reason to prefer one model over any
[p0059-l0036] [10.0pt] other. This is called the No Free Lunch (NFL) theorem. For some datasets the best
[p0059-l0037] [8.0pt] 11 “The Lack of A Priori Distinctions Between Learning Algorithms,” D. Wolpert (1996).
[p0059-l0038] [9.0pt] Testing and Validating
[p0059-l0039] [9.0pt] |
[p0059-l0040] [9.0pt] 33

=== PDF page 60 / printed label 34 ===
[p0060-l0001] [10.0pt] model is a linear model, while for other datasets it is a neural network. There is no
[p0060-l0002] [10.0pt] model that is a priori guaranteed to work better (hence the name of the theorem). The
[p0060-l0003] [10.0pt] only way to know for sure which model is best is to evaluate them all. Since this is not
[p0060-l0004] [10.0pt] possible, in practice you make some reasonable assumptions about the data and you
[p0060-l0005] [10.0pt] evaluate only a few reasonable models. For example, for simple tasks you may evalu‐
[p0060-l0006] [10.0pt] ate linear models with various levels of regularization, and for a complex problem you
[p0060-l0007] [10.0pt] may evaluate various neural networks.
[p0060-l0008] [18.92pt] Exercises
[p0060-l0009] [10.5pt] In this chapter we have covered some of the most important concepts in Machine

[p0060-l0017] [10.5pt] 6. What type of Machine Learning algorithm would you use to allow a robot to
[p0060-l0018] [10.5pt] walk in various unknown terrains?
[p0060-l0019] [10.5pt] 7. What type of algorithm would you use to segment your customers into multiple
