[p0065-l0002] [18.92pt] Look at the Big Picture
[p0065-l0003] [10.5pt] Welcome to Machine Learning Housing Corporation! The first task you are asked to
[p0065-l0004] [10.5pt] perform is to build a model of housing prices in California using the California cen‐
[p0065-l0005] [10.5pt] sus data. This data has metrics such as the population, median income, median hous‐
[p0065-l0006] [10.5pt] ing price, and so on for each block group in California. Block groups are the smallest
[p0065-l0007] [10.5pt] geographical unit for which the US Census Bureau publishes sample data (a block
[p0065-l0008] [10.5pt] group typically has a population of 600 to 3,000 people). We will just call them “dis‐
[p0065-l0009] [10.5pt] tricts” for short.
[p0065-l0010] [10.5pt] Your model should learn from this data and be able to predict the median housing
[p0065-l0011] [10.5pt] price in any district, given all the other metrics.
[p0065-l0012] [9.6pt] Since you are a well-organized data scientist, the first thing you do
[p0065-l0013] [9.6pt] is to pull out your Machine Learning project checklist. You can
[p0065-l0014] [9.6pt] start with the one in ???; it should work reasonably well for most
[p0065-l0015] [9.6pt] Machine Learning projects but make sure to adapt it to your needs.
[p0065-l0016] [9.6pt] In this chapter we will go through many checklist items, but we will
[p0065-l0017] [9.6pt] also skip a few, either because they are self-explanatory or because
[p0065-l0018] [9.6pt] they will be discussed in later chapters.
[p0065-l0019] [15.77pt] Frame the Problem
[p0065-l0020] [10.5pt] The first question to ask your boss is what exactly is the business objective; building a
[p0065-l0021] [10.5pt] model is probably not the end goal. How does the company expect to use and benefit
[p0065-l0022] [9.0pt] Look at the Big Picture
[p0065-l0023] [9.0pt] |
[p0065-l0024] [9.0pt] 39

=== PDF page 66 / printed label 40 ===
[p0066-l0001] [10.5pt] from this model? This is important because it will determine how you frame the
[p0066-l0002] [10.5pt] problem, what algorithms you will select, what performance measure you will use to
[p0066-l0003] [10.5pt] evaluate your model, and how much effort you should spend tweaking it.
[p0066-l0004] [10.5pt] Your boss answers that your model’s output (a prediction of a district’s median hous‐
[p0066-l0005] [10.5pt] ing price) will be fed to another Machine Learning system (see Figure 2-2), along
[p0066-l0006] [10.5pt] with many other signals.3 This downstream system will determine whether it is worth
[p0066-l0007] [10.5pt] investing in a given area or not. Getting this right is critical, as it directly affects reve‐
[p0066-l0008] [10.5pt] nue.
[p0066-l0009] [10.5pt] Figure 2-2. A Machine Learning pipeline for real estate investments
[p0066-l0010] [15.0pt] Pipelines
[p0066-l0011] [10.0pt] A sequence of data processing components is called a data pipeline. Pipelines are very
[p0066-l0012] [10.0pt] common in Machine Learning systems, since there is a lot of data to manipulate and
[p0066-l0013] [10.0pt] many data transformations to apply.
[p0066-l0014] [10.0pt] Components typically run asynchronously. Each component pulls in a large amount
[p0066-l0015] [10.0pt] of data, processes it, and spits out the result in another data store, and then some time
[p0066-l0016] [10.0pt] later the next component in the pipeline pulls this data and spits out its own output,
[p0066-l0017] [10.0pt] and so on. Each component is fairly self-contained: the interface between components
[p0066-l0018] [10.0pt] is simply the data store. This makes the system quite simple to grasp (with the help of
[p0066-l0019] [10.0pt] a data flow graph), and different teams can focus on different components. Moreover,
[p0066-l0020] [10.0pt] if a component breaks down, the downstream components can often continue to run
[p0066-l0021] [10.0pt] normally (at least for a while) by just using the last output from the broken compo‐
[p0066-l0022] [10.0pt] nent. This makes the architecture quite robust.
[p0066-l0023] [8.0pt] 3 A piece of information fed to a Machine Learning system is often called a signal in reference to Shannon’s
[p0066-l0024] [8.0pt] information theory: you want a high signal/noise ratio.
[p0066-l0025] [9.0pt] 40
[p0066-l0026] [9.0pt] |
[p0066-l0027] [9.0pt] Chapter 2: End-to-End Machine Learning Project

=== PDF page 67 / printed label 41 ===
[p0067-l0001] [10.0pt] On the other hand, a broken component can go unnoticed for some time if proper
[p0067-l0002] [10.0pt] monitoring is not implemented. The data gets stale and the overall system’s perfor‐
[p0067-l0003] [10.0pt] mance drops.
[p0067-l0004] [10.5pt] The next question to ask is what the current solution looks like (if any). It will often
[p0067-l0005] [10.5pt] give you a reference performance, as well as insights on how to solve the problem.
[p0067-l0006] [10.5pt] Your boss answers that the district housing prices are currently estimated manually
[p0067-l0007] [10.5pt] by experts: a team gathers up-to-date information about a district, and when they
[p0067-l0008] [10.5pt] cannot get the median housing price, they estimate it using complex rules.
[p0067-l0009] [10.5pt] This is costly and time-consuming, and their estimates are not great; in cases where
[p0067-l0010] [10.5pt] they manage to find out the actual median housing price, they often realize that their
[p0067-l0011] [10.5pt] estimates were off by more than 20%. This is why the company thinks that it would
[p0067-l0012] [10.5pt] be useful to train a model to predict a district’s median housing price given other data
[p0067-l0013] [10.5pt] about that district. The census data looks like a great dataset to exploit for this pur‐
[p0067-l0014] [10.5pt] pose, since it includes the median housing prices of thousands of districts, as well as
[p0067-l0015] [10.5pt] other data.
[p0067-l0016] [10.5pt] Okay, with all this information you are now ready to start designing your system.
[p0067-l0017] [10.5pt] First, you need to frame the problem: is it supervised, unsupervised, or Reinforce‐
[p0067-l0018] [10.5pt] ment Learning? Is it a classification task, a regression task, or something else? Should
[p0067-l0019] [10.5pt] you use batch learning or online learning techniques? Before you read on, pause and
[p0067-l0020] [10.5pt] try to answer these questions for yourself.
[p0067-l0021] [10.5pt] Have you found the answers? Let’s see: it is clearly a typical supervised learning task
[p0067-l0022] [10.5pt] since you are given labeled training examples (each instance comes with the expected
[p0067-l0023] [10.5pt] output, i.e., the district’s median housing price). Moreover, it is also a typical regres‐
[p0067-l0024] [10.5pt] sion task, since you are asked to predict a value. More specifically, this is a multiple
[p0067-l0025] [10.5pt] regression problem since the system will use multiple features to make a prediction (it
[p0067-l0026] [10.5pt] will use the district’s population, the median income, etc.). It is also a univariate
[p0067-l0027] [10.5pt] regression problem since we are only trying to predict a single value for each district.
[p0067-l0028] [10.5pt] If we were trying to predict multiple values per district, it would be a multivariate
[p0067-l0029] [10.5pt] regression problem. Finally, there is no continuous flow of data coming in the system,
[p0067-l0030] [10.5pt] there is no particular need to adjust to changing data rapidly, and the data is small
[p0067-l0031] [10.5pt] enough to fit in memory, so plain batch learning should do just fine.
[p0067-l0032] [9.6pt] If the data was huge, you could either split your batch learning
[p0067-l0033] [9.6pt] work across multiple servers (using the MapReduce technique), or
[p0067-l0034] [9.6pt] you could use an online learning technique instead.

[p0068-l0001] [15.77pt] Select a Performance Measure
[p0068-l0002] [10.5pt] Your next step is to select a performance measure. A typical performance measure for
[p0068-l0003] [10.5pt] regression problems is the Root Mean Square Error (RMSE). It gives an idea of how
[p0068-l0004] [10.5pt] much error the system typically makes in its predictions, with a higher weight for
[p0068-l0005] [10.5pt] large errors. Equation 2-1 shows the mathematical formula to compute the RMSE.

[p0069-l0009] [10.0pt] — For example, if the first district in the dataset is located at longitude –118.29°,
[p0069-l0010] [10.0pt] latitude 33.91°, and it has 1,416 inhabitants with a median income of $38,372,

[p0069-l0018] [10.0pt] and:
[p0069-l0019] [10.0pt] y 1 = 156, 400

[p0070-l0001] [10.0pt] • h is your system’s prediction function, also called a hypothesis. When your system
[p0070-l0002] [10.0pt] is given an instance’s feature vector x(i), it outputs a predicted value ŷ(i) = h(x(i))
[p0070-l0003] [10.0pt] for that instance (ŷ is pronounced “y-hat”).
[p0070-l0004] [10.0pt] — For example, if your system predicts that the median housing price in the first
[p0070-l0005] [10.0pt] district is $158,400, then ŷ(1) = h(x(1)) = 158,400. The prediction error for this
[p0070-l0006] [10.0pt] district is ŷ(1) – y(1) = 2,000.
[p0070-l0007] [10.0pt] • RMSE(X,h) is the cost function measured on the set of examples using your
[p0070-l0008] [10.0pt] hypothesis h.
[p0070-l0009] [10.0pt] We use lowercase italic font for scalar values (such as m or y(i)) and function names
[p0070-l0010] [10.0pt] (such as h), lowercase bold font for vectors (such as x(i)), and uppercase bold font for
[p0070-l0011] [10.0pt] matrices (such as X).
[p0070-l0012] [10.5pt] Even though the RMSE is generally the preferred performance measure for regression
[p0070-l0013] [10.5pt] tasks, in some contexts you may prefer to use another function. For example, suppose
[p0070-l0014] [10.5pt] that there are many outlier districts. In that case, you may consider using the Mean
[p0070-l0015] [10.5pt] Absolute Error (also called the Average Absolute Deviation; see Equation 2-2):
[p0070-l0016] [10.5pt] Equation 2-2. Mean Absolute Error
[p0070-l0017] [8.0pt] m
[p0070-l0018] [10.0pt] MAE X, h = 1
[p0070-l0019] [10.0pt] h x i
[p0070-l0020] [10.0pt] −y i
[p0070-l0021] [8.0pt] i = 1
[p0070-l0022] [14.14pt] m ∑
[p0070-l0023] [10.5pt] Both the RMSE and the MAE are ways to measure the distance between two vectors:
[p0070-l0024] [10.5pt] the vector of predictions and the vector of target values. Various distance measures,
[p0070-l0025] [10.5pt] or norms, are possible:
[p0070-l0026] [10.5pt] • Computing the root of a sum of squares (RMSE) corresponds to the Euclidean
[p0070-l0027] [10.5pt] norm: it is the notion of distance you are familiar with. It is also called the ℓ2
[p0070-l0028] [10.5pt] norm, noted ∥ · ∥2 (or just ∥ · ∥).
[p0070-l0029] [10.5pt] • Computing the sum of absolutes (MAE) corresponds to the ℓ1 norm, noted ∥ · ∥1.
[p0070-l0030] [10.5pt] It is sometimes called the Manhattan norm because it measures the distance
[p0070-l0031] [10.5pt] between two points in a city if you can only travel along orthogonal city blocks.
[p0070-l0032] [10.5pt] • More generally, the ℓk norm of a vector v containing n elements is defined as
[p0070-l0033] [8.0pt] k
[p0070-l0034] [10.5pt] k + v1
[p0070-l0035] [10.5pt] k + ⋯+ vn
[p0070-l0036] [10.5pt] ∥�∥k =
[p0070-l0037] [10.5pt] v0
[p0070-l0038] [8.0pt] 1
[p0070-l0039] [10.5pt] k. ℓ0 just gives the number of non-zero ele‐
[p0070-l0040] [10.5pt] ments in the vector, and ℓ∞ gives the maximum absolute value in the vector.
[p0070-l0041] [10.5pt] • The higher the norm index, the more it focuses on large values and neglects small
[p0070-l0042] [10.5pt] ones. This is why the RMSE is more sensitive to outliers than the MAE. But when
[p0070-l0043] [9.0pt] 44
[p0070-l0044] [9.0pt] |
[p0070-l0045] [9.0pt] Chapter 2: End-to-End Machine Learning Project

=== PDF page 71 / printed label 45 ===
[p0071-l0001] [10.5pt] outliers are exponentially rare (like in a bell-shaped curve), the RMSE performs
[p0071-l0002] [10.5pt] very well and is generally preferred.
[p0071-l0003] [15.77pt] Check the Assumptions
[p0071-l0004] [10.5pt] Lastly, it is good practice to list and verify the assumptions that were made so far (by
[p0071-l0005] [10.5pt] you or others); this can catch serious issues early on. For example, the district prices
[p0071-l0006] [10.5pt] that your system outputs are going to be fed into a downstream Machine Learning
[p0071-l0007] [10.5pt] system, and we assume that these prices are going to be used as such. But what if the
[p0071-l0008] [10.5pt] downstream system actually converts the prices into categories (e.g., “cheap,”
[p0071-l0009] [10.5pt] “medium,” or “expensive”) and then uses those categories instead of the prices them‐
[p0071-l0010] [10.5pt] selves? In this case, getting the price perfectly right is not important at all; your sys‐
[p0071-l0011] [10.5pt] tem just needs to get the category right. If that’s so, then the problem should have
[p0071-l0012] [10.5pt] been framed as a classification task, not a regression task. You don’t want to find this
[p0071-l0013] [10.5pt] out after working on a regression system for months.
[p0071-l0014] [10.5pt] Fortunately, after talking with the team in charge of the downstream system, you are
[p0071-l0015] [10.5pt] confident that they do indeed need the actual prices, not just categories. Great! You’re
[p0071-l0016] [10.5pt] all set, the lights are green, and you can start coding now!
[p0071-l0017] [18.92pt] Get the Data
[p0071-l0018] [10.5pt] It’s time to get your hands dirty. Don’t hesitate to pick up your laptop and walk
[p0071-l0019] [10.5pt] through the following code examples in a Jupyter notebook. The full Jupyter note‐
[p0071-l0020] [10.5pt] book is available at https://github.com/ageron/handson-ml2.
[p0071-l0021] [15.77pt] Create the Workspace
[p0071-l0022] [10.5pt] First you will need to have Python installed. It is probably already installed on your
[p0071-l0023] [10.5pt] system. If not, you can get it at https://www.python.org/.5
[p0071-l0024] [10.5pt] Next you need to create a workspace directory for your Machine Learning code and
[p0071-l0025] [10.5pt] datasets. Open a terminal and type the following commands (after the $ prompts):
[p0071-l0026] [8.5pt] $ export ML_PATH="$HOME/ml"      # You can change the path if you prefer
[p0071-l0027] [8.5pt] $ mkdir -p $ML_PATH

[p0075-l0001] [15.77pt] Download the Data
[p0075-l0002] [10.5pt] In typical environments your data would be available in a relational database (or
[p0075-l0003] [10.5pt] some other common datastore) and spread across multiple tables/documents/files. To
[p0075-l0004] [10.5pt] access it, you would first need to get your credentials and access authorizations,10 and
[p0075-l0005] [10.5pt] familiarize yourself with the data schema. In this project, however, things are much
[p0075-l0006] [10.5pt] simpler: you will just download a single compressed file, housing.tgz, which contains a
[p0075-l0007] [10.5pt] comma-separated value (CSV) file called housing.csv with all the data.
[p0075-l0008] [10.5pt] You could use your web browser to download it, and run tar xzf housing.tgz to
[p0075-l0009] [10.5pt] decompress the file and extract the CSV file, but it is preferable to create a small func‐
[p0075-l0010] [10.5pt] tion to do that. It is useful in particular if data changes regularly, as it allows you to
[p0075-l0011] [10.5pt] write a small script that you can run whenever you need to fetch the latest data (or
[p0075-l0012] [10.5pt] you can set up a scheduled job to do that automatically at regular intervals). Auto‐
[p0075-l0013] [10.5pt] mating the process of fetching the data is also useful if you need to install the dataset
[p0075-l0014] [10.5pt] on multiple machines.
[p0075-l0015] [10.5pt] Here is the function to fetch the data:11

[p0075-l0023] [8.5pt]     if not os.path.isdir(housing_path):
[p0075-l0024] [8.5pt]         os.makedirs(housing_path)

[p0078-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 2-7. Summary of each numerical attribute
[p0078-l0002] [10.5pt] The count, mean, min, and max rows are self-explanatory. Note that the null values are
[p0078-l0003] [10.5pt] ignored (so, for example, count of total_bedrooms is 20,433, not 20,640). The std
[p0078-l0004] [10.5pt] row shows the standard deviation, which measures how dispersed the values are.12
[p0078-l0005] [10.5pt] The 25%, 50%, and 75% rows show the corresponding percentiles: a percentile indi‐
[p0078-l0006] [10.5pt] cates the value below which a given percentage of observations in a group of observa‐
[p0078-l0007] [10.5pt] tions falls. For example, 25% of the districts have a housing_median_age lower than
[p0078-l0008] [10.5pt] 18, while 50% are lower than 29 and 75% are lower than 37. These are often called the
[p0078-l0009] [10.5pt] 25th percentile (or 1st quartile), the median, and the 75th percentile (or 3rd quartile).
[p0078-l0010] [10.5pt] Another quick way to get a feel of the type of data you are dealing with is to plot a
[p0078-l0011] [10.5pt] histogram for each numerical attribute. A histogram shows the number of instances
[p0078-l0012] [10.5pt] (on the vertical axis) that have a given value range (on the horizontal axis). You can
[p0078-l0013] [10.5pt] either plot this one attribute at a time, or you can call the hist() method on the
[p0078-l0014] [10.5pt] whole dataset, and it will plot a histogram for each numerical attribute (see
[p0078-l0015] [10.5pt] Figure 2-8). For example, you can see that slightly over 800 districts have a
[p0078-l0016] [10.5pt] median_house_value equal to about $100,000.

[p0078-l0021] [8.0pt] 12 The standard deviation is generally denoted σ (the Greek letter sigma), and it is the square root of the var‐
[p0078-l0022] [8.0pt] iance, which is the average of the squared deviation from the mean. When a feature has a bell-shaped normal
[p0078-l0023] [8.0pt] distribution (also called a Gaussian distribution), which is very common, the “68-95-99.7” rule applies: about
[p0078-l0024] [8.0pt] 68% of the values fall within 1σ of the mean, 95% within 2σ, and 99.7% within 3σ.

[p0079-l0001] [9.6pt] The hist() method relies on Matplotlib, which in turn relies on a
[p0079-l0002] [9.6pt] user-specified graphical backend to draw on your screen. So before
[p0079-l0003] [9.6pt] you can plot anything, you need to specify which backend Matplot‐
[p0079-l0004] [9.6pt] lib should use. The simplest option is to use Jupyter’s magic com‐
[p0079-l0005] [9.6pt] mand %matplotlib inline. This tells Jupyter to set up Matplotlib
[p0079-l0006] [9.6pt] so it uses Jupyter’s own backend. Plots are then rendered within the
[p0079-l0007] [9.6pt] notebook itself. Note that calling show() is optional in a Jupyter
[p0079-l0008] [9.6pt] notebook, as Jupyter will automatically display plots when a cell is
[p0079-l0009] [9.6pt] executed.
[p0079-l0010] [10.5pt] Figure 2-8. A histogram for each numerical attribute
[p0079-l0011] [10.5pt] Notice a few things in these histograms:
[p0079-l0012] [10.5pt] 1. First, the median income attribute does not look like it is expressed in US dollars
[p0079-l0013] [10.5pt] (USD). After checking with the team that collected the data, you are told that the
[p0079-l0014] [10.5pt] data has been scaled and capped at 15 (actually 15.0001) for higher median
[p0079-l0015] [10.5pt] incomes, and at 0.5 (actually 0.4999) for lower median incomes. The numbers
[p0079-l0016] [10.5pt] represent roughly tens of thousands of dollars (e.g., 3 actually means about
[p0079-l0017] [10.5pt] $30,000). Working with preprocessed attributes is common in Machine Learning,
[p0079-l0018] [9.0pt] Get the Data
[p0079-l0019] [9.0pt] |
[p0079-l0020] [9.0pt] 53

=== PDF page 80 / printed label 54 ===
[p0080-l0001] [10.5pt] and it is not necessarily a problem, but you should try to understand how the
[p0080-l0002] [10.5pt] data was computed.
[p0080-l0003] [10.5pt] 2. The housing median age and the median house value were also capped. The lat‐
[p0080-l0004] [10.5pt] ter may be a serious problem since it is your target attribute (your labels). Your
[p0080-l0005] [10.5pt] Machine Learning algorithms may learn that prices never go beyond that limit.
[p0080-l0006] [10.5pt] You need to check with your client team (the team that will use your system’s out‐
[p0080-l0007] [10.5pt] put) to see if this is a problem or not. If they tell you that they need precise pre‐
[p0080-l0008] [10.5pt] dictions even beyond $500,000, then you have mainly two options:
[p0080-l0009] [10.5pt] a. Collect proper labels for the districts whose labels were capped.
[p0080-l0010] [10.5pt] b. Remove those districts from the training set (and also from the test set, since
[p0080-l0011] [10.5pt] your system should not be evaluated poorly if it predicts values beyond
[p0080-l0012] [10.5pt] $500,000).
[p0080-l0013] [10.5pt] 3. These attributes have very different scales. We will discuss this later in this chap‐
[p0080-l0014] [10.5pt] ter when we explore feature scaling.
[p0080-l0015] [10.5pt] 4. Finally, many histograms are tail heavy: they extend much farther to the right of
[p0080-l0016] [10.5pt] the median than to the left. This may make it a bit harder for some Machine
[p0080-l0017] [10.5pt] Learning algorithms to detect patterns. We will try transforming these attributes
[p0080-l0018] [10.5pt] later on to have more bell-shaped distributions.
[p0080-l0019] [10.5pt] Hopefully you now have a better understanding of the kind of data you are dealing
[p0080-l0020] [10.5pt] with.
[p0080-l0021] [9.6pt] Wait! Before you look at the data any further, you need to create a
[p0080-l0022] [9.6pt] test set, put it aside, and never look at it.
[p0080-l0023] [15.77pt] Create a Test Set
[p0080-l0024] [10.5pt] It may sound strange to voluntarily set aside part of the data at this stage. After all,
[p0080-l0025] [10.5pt] you have only taken a quick glance at the data, and surely you should learn a whole
[p0080-l0026] [10.5pt] lot more about it before you decide what algorithms to use, right? This is true, but
[p0080-l0027] [10.5pt] your brain is an amazing pattern detection system, which means that it is highly
[p0080-l0028] [10.5pt] prone to overfitting: if you look at the test set, you may stumble upon some seemingly
[p0080-l0029] [10.5pt] interesting pattern in the test data that leads you to select a particular kind of
[p0080-l0030] [10.5pt] Machine Learning model. When you estimate the generalization error using the test
[p0080-l0031] [10.5pt] set, your estimate will be too optimistic and you will launch a system that will not
[p0080-l0032] [10.5pt] perform as well as expected. This is called data snooping bias.
[p0080-l0033] [10.5pt] Creating a test set is theoretically quite simple: just pick some instances randomly,
[p0080-l0034] [10.5pt] typically 20% of the dataset (or less if your dataset is very large), and set them aside:
[p0080-l0035] [9.0pt] 54
[p0080-l0036] [9.0pt] |
[p0080-l0037] [9.0pt] Chapter 2: End-to-End Machine Learning Project

=== PDF page 81 / printed label 55 ===
[p0081-l0001] [8.5pt] import numpy as np
[p0081-l0002] [8.5pt] def split_train_test(data, test_ratio):
[p0081-l0003] [8.5pt]     shuffled_indices = np.random.permutation(len(data))
[p0081-l0004] [8.5pt]     test_set_size = int(len(data) * test_ratio)
[p0081-l0005] [8.5pt]     test_indices = shuffled_indices[:test_set_size]
[p0081-l0006] [8.5pt]     train_indices = shuffled_indices[test_set_size:]
[p0081-l0007] [8.5pt]     return data.iloc[train_indices], data.iloc[test_indices]
[p0081-l0008] [10.5pt] You can then use this function like this:13
[p0081-l0009] [8.5pt] >>> train_set, test_set = split_train_test(housing, 0.2)
[p0081-l0010] [8.5pt] >>> len(train_set)
[p0081-l0011] [8.5pt] 16512
[p0081-l0012] [8.5pt] >>> len(test_set)
[p0081-l0013] [8.5pt] 4128
[p0081-l0014] [10.5pt] Well, this works, but it is not perfect: if you run the program again, it will generate a
[p0081-l0015] [10.5pt] different test set! Over time, you (or your Machine Learning algorithms) will get to
[p0081-l0016] [10.5pt] see the whole dataset, which is what you want to avoid.
[p0081-l0017] [10.5pt] One solution is to save the test set on the first run and then load it in subsequent
[p0081-l0018] [10.5pt] runs. Another option is to set the random number generator’s seed (e.g., np.ran
[p0081-l0019] [10.5pt] dom.seed(42))14 before calling np.random.permutation(), so that it always generates
[p0081-l0020] [10.5pt] the same shuffled indices.
[p0081-l0021] [10.5pt] But both these solutions will break next time you fetch an updated dataset. A com‐
[p0081-l0022] [10.5pt] mon solution is to use each instance’s identifier to decide whether or not it should go
[p0081-l0023] [10.5pt] in the test set (assuming instances have a unique and immutable identifier). For
[p0081-l0024] [10.5pt] example, you could compute a hash of each instance’s identifier and put that instance
[p0081-l0025] [10.5pt] in the test set if the hash is lower or equal to 20% of the maximum hash value. This
[p0081-l0026] [10.5pt] ensures that the test set will remain consistent across multiple runs, even if you
[p0081-l0027] [10.5pt] refresh the dataset. The new test set will contain 20% of the new instances, but it will
[p0081-l0028] [10.5pt] not contain any instance that was previously in the training set. Here is a possible
[p0081-l0029] [10.5pt] implementation:
[p0081-l0030] [8.5pt] from zlib import crc32
[p0081-l0031] [8.5pt] def test_set_check(identifier, test_ratio):
[p0081-l0032] [8.5pt]     return crc32(np.int64(identifier)) & 0xffffffff < test_ratio * 2**32
[p0081-l0033] [8.5pt] def split_train_test_by_id(data, test_ratio, id_column):
[p0081-l0034] [8.5pt]     ids = data[id_column]
[p0081-l0035] [8.0pt] 13 In this book, when a code example contains a mix of code and outputs, as is the case here, it is formatted like
[p0081-l0036] [8.0pt] in the Python interpreter, for better readability: the code lines are prefixed with >>> (or ... for indented
[p0081-l0037] [8.0pt] blocks), and the outputs have no prefix.
[p0081-l0038] [8.0pt] 14 You will often see people set the random seed to 42. This number has no special property, other than to be
[p0081-l0039] [8.0pt] The Answer to the Ultimate Question of Life, the Universe, and Everything.
[p0081-l0040] [9.0pt] Get the Data
[p0081-l0041] [9.0pt] |
[p0081-l0042] [9.0pt] 55

=== PDF page 82 / printed label 56 ===
[p0082-l0001] [8.5pt]     in_test_set = ids.apply(lambda id_: test_set_check(id_, test_ratio))
[p0082-l0002] [8.5pt]     return data.loc[~in_test_set], data.loc[in_test_set]
[p0082-l0003] [10.5pt] Unfortunately, the housing dataset does not have an identifier column. The simplest
[p0082-l0004] [10.5pt] solution is to use the row index as the ID:
[p0082-l0005] [8.5pt] housing_with_id = housing.reset_index()   # adds an `index` column
[p0082-l0006] [8.5pt] train_set, test_set = split_train_test_by_id(housing_with_id, 0.2, "index")
[p0082-l0007] [10.5pt] If you use the row index as a unique identifier, you need to make sure that new data
[p0082-l0008] [10.5pt] gets appended to the end of the dataset, and no row ever gets deleted. If this is not
[p0082-l0009] [10.5pt] possible, then you can try to use the most stable features to build a unique identifier.
[p0082-l0010] [10.5pt] For example, a district’s latitude and longitude are guaranteed to be stable for a few
[p0082-l0011] [10.5pt] million years, so you could combine them into an ID like so:15
[p0082-l0012] [8.5pt] housing_with_id["id"] = housing["longitude"] * 1000 + housing["latitude"]
[p0082-l0013] [8.5pt] train_set, test_set = split_train_test_by_id(housing_with_id, 0.2, "id")
[p0082-l0014] [10.5pt] Scikit-Learn provides a few functions to split datasets into multiple subsets in various
[p0082-l0015] [10.5pt] ways. The simplest function is train_test_split, which does pretty much the same
[p0082-l0016] [10.5pt] thing as the function split_train_test defined earlier, with a couple of additional
[p0082-l0017] [10.5pt] features. First there is a random_state parameter that allows you to set the random
[p0082-l0018] [10.5pt] generator seed as explained previously, and second you can pass it multiple datasets
[p0082-l0019] [10.5pt] with an identical number of rows, and it will split them on the same indices (this is
[p0082-l0020] [10.5pt] very useful, for example, if you have a separate DataFrame for labels):
[p0082-l0021] [8.5pt] from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
[p0082-l0022] [8.5pt] train_set, test_set = train_test_split(housing, test_size=0.2, random_state=42)
[p0082-l0023] [10.5pt] So far we have considered purely random sampling methods. This is generally fine if
[p0082-l0024] [10.5pt] your dataset is large enough (especially relative to the number of attributes), but if it
[p0082-l0025] [10.5pt] is not, you run the risk of introducing a significant sampling bias. When a survey
[p0082-l0026] [10.5pt] company decides to call 1,000 people to ask them a few questions, they don’t just pick
[p0082-l0027] [10.5pt] 1,000 people randomly in a phone book. They try to ensure that these 1,000 people
[p0082-l0028] [10.5pt] are representative of the whole population. For example, the US population is com‐
[p0082-l0029] [10.5pt] posed of 51.3% female and 48.7% male, so a well-conducted survey in the US would
[p0082-l0030] [10.5pt] try to maintain this ratio in the sample: 513 female and 487 male. This is called strati‐
[p0082-l0031] [10.5pt] fied sampling: the population is divided into homogeneous subgroups called strata,
[p0082-l0032] [10.5pt] and the right number of instances is sampled from each stratum to guarantee that the
[p0082-l0033] [10.5pt] test set is representative of the overall population. If they used purely random sam‐
[p0082-l0034] [10.5pt] pling, there would be about 12% chance of sampling a skewed test set with either less
[p0082-l0035] [10.5pt] than 49% female or more than 54% female. Either way, the survey results would be
[p0082-l0036] [10.5pt] significantly biased.
[p0082-l0037] [8.0pt] 15 The location information is actually quite coarse, and as a result many districts will have the exact same ID, so
[p0082-l0038] [8.0pt] they will end up in the same set (test or train). This introduces some unfortunate sampling bias.
[p0082-l0039] [9.0pt] 56
[p0082-l0040] [9.0pt] |

[p0083-l0001] [10.5pt] Suppose you chatted with experts who told you that the median income is a very
[p0083-l0002] [10.5pt] important attribute to predict median housing prices. You may want to ensure that
[p0083-l0003] [10.5pt] the test set is representative of the various categories of incomes in the whole dataset.
[p0083-l0004] [10.5pt] Since the median income is a continuous numerical attribute, you first need to create
[p0083-l0005] [10.5pt] an income category attribute. Let’s look at the median income histogram more closely
[p0083-l0006] [10.5pt] (back in Figure 2-8): most median income values are clustered around 1.5 to 6 (i.e.,
[p0083-l0007] [10.5pt] $15,000–$60,000), but some median incomes go far beyond 6. It is important to have
[p0083-l0008] [10.5pt] a sufficient number of instances in your dataset for each stratum, or else the estimate
[p0083-l0009] [10.5pt] of the stratum’s importance may be biased. This means that you should not have too
[p0083-l0010] [10.5pt] many strata, and each stratum should be large enough. The following code uses the
[p0083-l0011] [10.5pt] pd.cut() function to create an income category attribute with 5 categories (labeled
[p0083-l0012] [10.5pt] from 1 to 5): category 1 ranges from 0 to 1.5 (i.e., less than $15,000), category 2 from
[p0083-l0013] [10.5pt] 1.5 to 3, and so on:
[p0083-l0014] [8.5pt] housing["income_cat"] = pd.cut(housing["median_income"],
[p0083-l0015] [8.5pt]                                bins=[0., 1.5, 3.0, 4.5, 6., np.inf],
[p0083-l0016] [8.5pt]                                labels=[1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
[p0083-l0017] [10.5pt] These income categories are represented in Figure 2-9:
[p0083-l0018] [8.5pt] housing["income_cat"].hist()
[p0083-l0019] [10.5pt] Figure 2-9. Histogram of income categories
[p0083-l0020] [10.5pt] Now you are ready to do stratified sampling based on the income category. For this
[p0083-l0021] [10.5pt] you can use Scikit-Learn’s StratifiedShuffleSplit class:
[p0083-l0022] [8.5pt] from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedShuffleSplit
[p0083-l0023] [8.5pt] split = StratifiedShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, test_size=0.2, random_state=42)
[p0083-l0024] [8.5pt] for train_index, test_index in split.split(housing, housing["income_cat"]):
[p0083-l0025] [8.5pt]     strat_train_set = housing.loc[train_index]
[p0083-l0026] [8.5pt]     strat_test_set = housing.loc[test_index]

[p0089-l0003] [9.6pt] The correlation coefficient only measures linear correlations (“if x
[p0089-l0004] [9.6pt] goes up, then y generally goes up/down”). It may completely miss
[p0089-l0005] [9.6pt] out on nonlinear relationships (e.g., “if x is close to zero then y gen‐
[p0089-l0006] [9.6pt] erally goes up”). Note how all the plots of the bottom row have a
[p0089-l0007] [9.6pt] correlation coefficient equal to zero despite the fact that their axes
[p0089-l0008] [9.6pt] are clearly not independent: these are examples of nonlinear rela‐
[p0089-l0009] [9.6pt] tionships. Also, the second row shows examples where the correla‐
[p0089-l0010] [9.6pt] tion coefficient is equal to 1 or –1; notice that this has nothing to
[p0089-l0011] [9.6pt] do with the slope. For example, your height in inches has a correla‐
[p0089-l0012] [9.6pt] tion coefficient of 1 with your height in feet or in nanometers.

[p0091-l0002] [15.77pt] Experimenting with Attribute Combinations
[p0091-l0003] [10.5pt] Hopefully the previous sections gave you an idea of a few ways you can explore the
[p0091-l0004] [10.5pt] data and gain insights. You identified a few data quirks that you may want to clean up
[p0091-l0005] [10.5pt] before feeding the data to a Machine Learning algorithm, and you found interesting
[p0091-l0006] [10.5pt] correlations between attributes, in particular with the target attribute. You also
[p0091-l0007] [10.5pt] noticed that some attributes have a tail-heavy distribution, so you may want to trans‐
[p0091-l0008] [10.5pt] form them (e.g., by computing their logarithm). Of course, your mileage will vary
[p0091-l0009] [10.5pt] considerably with each project, but the general ideas are similar.
[p0091-l0010] [10.5pt] One last thing you may want to do before actually preparing the data for Machine
[p0091-l0011] [10.5pt] Learning algorithms is to try out various attribute combinations. For example, the
[p0091-l0012] [10.5pt] total number of rooms in a district is not very useful if you don’t know how many
[p0091-l0013] [10.5pt] households there are. What you really want is the number of rooms per household.
[p0091-l0014] [10.5pt] Similarly, the total number of bedrooms by itself is not very useful: you probably
[p0091-l0015] [10.5pt] want to compare it to the number of rooms. And the population per household also
[p0091-l0016] [10.5pt] seems like an interesting attribute combination to look at. Let’s create these new
[p0091-l0017] [10.5pt] attributes:
[p0091-l0018] [8.5pt] housing["rooms_per_household"] = housing["total_rooms"]/housing["households"]
[p0091-l0019] [8.5pt] housing["bedrooms_per_room"] = housing["total_bedrooms"]/housing["total_rooms"]
[p0091-l0020] [8.5pt] housing["population_per_household"]=housing["population"]/housing["households"]
[p0091-l0021] [10.5pt] And now let’s look at the correlation matrix again:
[p0091-l0022] [8.5pt] >>> corr_matrix = housing.corr()
[p0091-l0023] [8.5pt] >>> corr_matrix["median_house_value"].sort_values(ascending=False)
[p0091-l0024] [8.5pt] median_house_value          1.000000

[p0092-l0023] [18.92pt] Prepare the Data for Machine Learning Algorithms
[p0092-l0024] [10.5pt] It’s time to prepare the data for your Machine Learning algorithms. Instead of just
[p0092-l0025] [10.5pt] doing this manually, you should write functions to do that, for several good reasons:
[p0092-l0026] [10.5pt] • This will allow you to reproduce these transformations easily on any dataset (e.g.,
[p0092-l0027] [10.5pt] the next time you get a fresh dataset).
[p0092-l0028] [10.5pt] • You will gradually build a library of transformation functions that you can reuse
[p0092-l0029] [10.5pt] in future projects.
[p0092-l0030] [10.5pt] • You can use these functions in your live system to transform the new data before
[p0092-l0031] [10.5pt] feeding it to your algorithms.
[p0092-l0032] [10.5pt] • This will make it possible for you to easily try various transformations and see
[p0092-l0033] [10.5pt] which combination of transformations works best.
[p0092-l0034] [10.5pt] But first let’s revert to a clean training set (by copying strat_train_set once again),
[p0092-l0035] [10.5pt] and let’s separate the predictors and the labels since we don’t necessarily want to apply
[p0092-l0036] [10.5pt] the same transformations to the predictors and the target values (note that drop()
[p0092-l0037] [10.5pt] creates a copy of the data and does not affect strat_train_set):
[p0092-l0038] [8.5pt] housing = strat_train_set.drop("median_house_value", axis=1)
[p0092-l0039] [8.5pt] housing_labels = strat_train_set["median_house_value"].copy()

[p0093-l0001] [15.77pt] Data Cleaning
[p0093-l0002] [10.5pt] Most Machine Learning algorithms cannot work with missing features, so let’s create
[p0093-l0003] [10.5pt] a few functions to take care of them. You noticed earlier that the total_bedrooms
[p0093-l0004] [10.5pt] attribute has some missing values, so let’s fix this. You have three options:
[p0093-l0005] [10.5pt] • Get rid of the corresponding districts.
[p0093-l0006] [10.5pt] • Get rid of the whole attribute.
[p0093-l0007] [10.5pt] • Set the values to some value (zero, the mean, the median, etc.).
[p0093-l0008] [10.5pt] You can accomplish these easily using DataFrame’s dropna(), drop(), and fillna()
[p0093-l0009] [10.5pt] methods:
[p0093-l0010] [8.5pt] housing.dropna(subset=["total_bedrooms"])    # option 1
[p0093-l0011] [8.5pt] housing.drop("total_bedrooms", axis=1)       # option 2
[p0093-l0012] [8.5pt] median = housing["total_bedrooms"].median()  # option 3
[p0093-l0013] [8.5pt] housing["total_bedrooms"].fillna(median, inplace=True)
[p0093-l0014] [10.5pt] If you choose option 3, you should compute the median value on the training set, and
[p0093-l0015] [10.5pt] use it to fill the missing values in the training set, but also don’t forget to save the
[p0093-l0016] [10.5pt] median value that you have computed. You will need it later to replace missing values
[p0093-l0017] [10.5pt] in the test set when you want to evaluate your system, and also once the system goes
[p0093-l0018] [10.5pt] live to replace missing values in new data.
[p0093-l0019] [10.5pt] Scikit-Learn provides a handy class to take care of missing values: SimpleImputer.
[p0093-l0020] [10.5pt] Here is how to use it. First, you need to create a SimpleImputer instance, specifying
[p0093-l0021] [10.5pt] that you want to replace each attribute’s missing values with the median of that
[p0093-l0022] [10.5pt] attribute:
[p0093-l0023] [8.5pt] from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
[p0093-l0024] [8.5pt] imputer = SimpleImputer(strategy="median")
[p0093-l0025] [10.5pt] Since the median can only be computed on numerical attributes, we need to create a
[p0093-l0026] [10.5pt] copy of the data without the text attribute ocean_proximity:
[p0093-l0027] [8.5pt] housing_num = housing.drop("ocean_proximity", axis=1)
[p0093-l0028] [10.5pt] Now you can fit the imputer instance to the training data using the fit() method:
[p0093-l0029] [8.5pt] imputer.fit(housing_num)
[p0093-l0030] [10.5pt] The imputer has simply computed the median of each attribute and stored the result
[p0093-l0031] [10.5pt] in its statistics_ instance variable. Only the total_bedrooms attribute had missing
[p0093-l0032] [10.5pt] values, but we cannot be sure that there won’t be any missing values in new data after
[p0093-l0033] [10.5pt] the system goes live, so it is safer to apply the imputer to all the numerical attributes:
[p0093-l0034] [8.5pt] >>> imputer.statistics_
[p0093-l0035] [8.5pt] array([ -118.51 , 34.26 , 29. , 2119.5 , 433. , 1164. , 408. , 3.5409])
[p0093-l0036] [9.0pt] Prepare the Data for Machine Learning Algorithms
[p0093-l0037] [9.0pt] |
[p0093-l0038] [9.0pt] 67

[p0094-l0001] [8.5pt] >>> housing_num.median().values
[p0094-l0002] [8.5pt] array([ -118.51 , 34.26 , 29. , 2119.5 , 433. , 1164. , 408. , 3.5409])
[p0094-l0003] [10.5pt] Now you can use this “trained” imputer to transform the training set by replacing
[p0094-l0004] [10.5pt] missing values by the learned medians:
[p0094-l0005] [8.5pt] X = imputer.transform(housing_num)
[p0094-l0006] [10.5pt] The result is a plain NumPy array containing the transformed features. If you want to
[p0094-l0007] [10.5pt] put it back into a Pandas DataFrame, it’s simple:
[p0094-l0008] [8.5pt] housing_tr = pd.DataFrame(X, columns=housing_num.columns)
[p0094-l0009] [15.0pt] Scikit-Learn Design
[p0094-l0010] [10.0pt] Scikit-Learn’s API is remarkably well designed. The main design principles are:17
[p0094-l0011] [10.0pt] • Consistency. All objects share a consistent and simple interface:
[p0094-l0012] [10.0pt] — Estimators. Any object that can estimate some parameters based on a dataset
[p0094-l0013] [10.0pt] is called an estimator (e.g., an imputer is an estimator). The estimation itself is
[p0094-l0014] [10.0pt] performed by the fit() method, and it takes only a dataset as a parameter (or
[p0094-l0015] [10.0pt] two for supervised learning algorithms; the second dataset contains the
[p0094-l0016] [10.0pt] labels). Any other parameter needed to guide the estimation process is con‐
[p0094-l0017] [10.0pt] sidered a hyperparameter (such as an imputer’s strategy), and it must be set
[p0094-l0018] [10.0pt] as an instance variable (generally via a constructor parameter).
[p0094-l0019] [10.0pt] — Transformers. Some estimators (such as an imputer) can also transform a
[p0094-l0020] [10.0pt] dataset; these are called transformers. Once again, the API is quite simple: the
[p0094-l0021] [10.0pt] transformation is performed by the transform() method with the dataset to
[p0094-l0022] [10.0pt] transform as a parameter. It returns the transformed dataset. This transforma‐
[p0094-l0023] [10.0pt] tion generally relies on the learned parameters, as is the case for an imputer.
[p0094-l0024] [10.0pt] All transformers also have a convenience method called fit_transform()
[p0094-l0025] [10.0pt] that is equivalent to calling fit() and then transform() (but sometimes
[p0094-l0026] [10.0pt] fit_transform() is optimized and runs much faster).
[p0094-l0027] [10.0pt] — Predictors. Finally, some estimators are capable of making predictions given a
[p0094-l0028] [10.0pt] dataset; they are called predictors. For example, the LinearRegression model
[p0094-l0029] [10.0pt] in the previous chapter was a predictor: it predicted life satisfaction given a
[p0094-l0030] [10.0pt] country’s GDP per capita. A predictor has a predict() method that takes a
[p0094-l0031] [10.0pt] dataset of new instances and returns a dataset of corresponding predictions. It
[p0094-l0032] [10.0pt] also has a score() method that measures the quality of the predictions given
[p0094-l0033] [8.0pt] 17 For more details on the design principles, see “API design for machine learning software: experiences from
[p0094-l0034] [8.0pt] the scikit-learn project,” L. Buitinck, G. Louppe, M. Blondel, F. Pedregosa, A. Müller, et al. (2013).
[p0094-l0035] [9.0pt] 68
[p0094-l0036] [9.0pt] |
[p0094-l0037] [9.0pt] Chapter 2: End-to-End Machine Learning Project

=== PDF page 95 / printed label 69 ===
[p0095-l0001] [10.0pt] a test set (and the corresponding labels in the case of supervised learning
[p0095-l0002] [10.0pt] algorithms).18
[p0095-l0003] [10.0pt] • Inspection. All the estimator’s hyperparameters are accessible directly via public
[p0095-l0004] [10.0pt] instance variables (e.g., imputer.strategy), and all the estimator’s learned
[p0095-l0005] [10.0pt] parameters are also accessible via public instance variables with an underscore
[p0095-l0006] [10.0pt] suffix (e.g., imputer.statistics_).
[p0095-l0007] [10.0pt] • Nonproliferation of classes. Datasets are represented as NumPy arrays or SciPy
[p0095-l0008] [10.0pt] sparse matrices, instead of homemade classes. Hyperparameters are just regular
[p0095-l0009] [10.0pt] Python strings or numbers.
[p0095-l0010] [10.0pt] • Composition. Existing building blocks are reused as much as possible. For
[p0095-l0011] [10.0pt] example, it is easy to create a Pipeline estimator from an arbitrary sequence of
[p0095-l0012] [10.0pt] transformers followed by a final estimator, as we will see.
[p0095-l0013] [10.0pt] • Sensible defaults. Scikit-Learn provides reasonable default values for most
[p0095-l0014] [10.0pt] parameters, making it easy to create a baseline working system quickly.

[p0096-l0013] [10.5pt] You can get the list of categories using the categories_ instance variable. It is a list
[p0096-l0014] [10.5pt] containing a 1D array of categories for each categorical attribute (in this case, a list
[p0096-l0015] [10.5pt] containing a single array since there is just one categorical attribute):
[p0096-l0016] [8.5pt] >>> ordinal_encoder.categories_
[p0096-l0017] [8.5pt] [array(['<1H OCEAN', 'INLAND', 'ISLAND', 'NEAR BAY', 'NEAR OCEAN'],
[p0096-l0018] [8.5pt]        dtype=object)]
[p0096-l0019] [10.5pt] One issue with this representation is that ML algorithms will assume that two nearby
[p0096-l0020] [10.5pt] values are more similar than two distant values. This may be fine in some cases (e.g.,
[p0096-l0021] [10.5pt] for ordered categories such as “bad”, “average”, “good”, “excellent”), but it is obviously
[p0096-l0022] [10.5pt] not the case for the ocean_proximity column (for example, categories 0 and 4 are
[p0096-l0023] [10.5pt] clearly more similar than categories 0 and 1). To fix this issue, a common solution is
[p0096-l0024] [10.5pt] to create one binary attribute per category: one attribute equal to 1 when the category
[p0096-l0025] [10.5pt] is “<1H OCEAN” (and 0 otherwise), another attribute equal to 1 when the category is
[p0096-l0026] [10.5pt] “INLAND” (and 0 otherwise), and so on. This is called one-hot encoding, because
[p0096-l0027] [10.5pt] only one attribute will be equal to 1 (hot), while the others will be 0 (cold). The new
[p0096-l0028] [10.5pt] attributes are sometimes called dummy attributes. Scikit-Learn provides a OneHotEn
[p0096-l0029] [10.5pt] coder class to convert categorical values into one-hot vectors20:
[p0096-l0030] [8.5pt] >>> from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder
[p0096-l0031] [8.5pt] >>> cat_encoder = OneHotEncoder()
[p0096-l0032] [8.5pt] >>> housing_cat_1hot = cat_encoder.fit_transform(housing_cat)
[p0096-l0033] [8.5pt] >>> housing_cat_1hot
[p0096-l0034] [8.5pt] <16512x5 sparse matrix of type '<class 'numpy.float64'>'
[p0096-l0035] [8.5pt]   with 16512 stored elements in Compressed Sparse Row format>
[p0096-l0036] [10.5pt] Notice that the output is a SciPy sparse matrix, instead of a NumPy array. This is very
[p0096-l0037] [10.5pt] useful when you have categorical attributes with thousands of categories. After one-
[p0096-l0038] [10.5pt] hot encoding we get a matrix with thousands of columns, and the matrix is full of
[p0096-l0039] [10.5pt] zeros except for a single 1 per row. Using up tons of memory mostly to store zeros
[p0096-l0040] [10.5pt] would be very wasteful, so instead a sparse matrix only stores the location of the non‐
[p0096-l0041] [8.0pt] 20 Before Scikit-Learn 0.20, it could only encode integer categorical values, but since 0.20 it can also handle
[p0096-l0042] [8.0pt] other types of inputs, including text categorical inputs.

[p0097-l0016] [9.6pt] If a categorical attribute has a large number of possible categories
[p0097-l0017] [9.6pt] (e.g., country code, profession, species, etc.), then one-hot encod‐
[p0097-l0018] [9.6pt] ing will result in a large number of input features. This may slow
[p0097-l0019] [9.6pt] down training and degrade performance. If this happens, you may
[p0097-l0020] [9.6pt] want to replace the categorical input with useful numerical features
[p0097-l0021] [9.6pt] related to the categories: for example, you could replace the
[p0097-l0022] [9.6pt] ocean_proximity feature with the distance to the ocean (similarly,
[p0097-l0023] [9.6pt] a country code could be replaced with the country’s population and
[p0097-l0024] [9.6pt] GDP per capita). Alternatively, you could replace each category
[p0097-l0025] [9.6pt] with a learnable low dimensional vector called an embedding. Each
[p0097-l0026] [9.6pt] category’s representation would be learned during training: this is
[p0097-l0027] [9.6pt] an example of representation learning (see Chapter 13 and ??? for
[p0097-l0028] [9.6pt] more details).
[p0097-l0029] [15.77pt] Custom Transformers
[p0097-l0030] [10.5pt] Although Scikit-Learn provides many useful transformers, you will need to write
[p0097-l0031] [10.5pt] your own for tasks such as custom cleanup operations or combining specific
[p0097-l0032] [10.5pt] attributes. You will want your transformer to work seamlessly with Scikit-Learn func‐
[p0097-l0033] [10.5pt] tionalities (such as pipelines), and since Scikit-Learn relies on duck typing (not inher‐
[p0097-l0034] [10.5pt] itance), all you need is to create a class and implement three methods: fit()
[p0097-l0035] [10.5pt] (returning self), transform(), and fit_transform(). You can get the last one for
[p0097-l0036] [10.5pt] free by simply adding TransformerMixin as a base class. Also, if you add BaseEstima
[p0097-l0037] [10.5pt] tor as a base class (and avoid *args and **kargs in your constructor) you will get
[p0097-l0038] [10.5pt] two extra methods (get_params() and set_params()) that will be useful for auto‐
[p0097-l0039] [8.0pt] 21 See SciPy’s documentation for more details.
[p0097-l0040] [9.0pt] Prepare the Data for Machine Learning Algorithms

[p0098-l0001] [10.5pt] matic hyperparameter tuning. For example, here is a small transformer class that adds
[p0098-l0002] [10.5pt] the combined attributes we discussed earlier:
[p0098-l0003] [8.5pt] from sklearn.base import BaseEstimator, TransformerMixin
[p0098-l0004] [8.5pt] rooms_ix, bedrooms_ix, population_ix, households_ix = 3, 4, 5, 6
[p0098-l0005] [8.5pt] class CombinedAttributesAdder(BaseEstimator, TransformerMixin):
[p0098-l0006] [8.5pt]     def __init__(self, add_bedrooms_per_room = True): # no *args or **kargs
[p0098-l0007] [8.5pt]         self.add_bedrooms_per_room = add_bedrooms_per_room
[p0098-l0008] [8.5pt]     def fit(self, X, y=None):
[p0098-l0009] [8.5pt]         return self  # nothing else to do
[p0098-l0010] [8.5pt]     def transform(self, X, y=None):
[p0098-l0011] [8.5pt]         rooms_per_household = X[:, rooms_ix] / X[:, households_ix]
[p0098-l0012] [8.5pt]         population_per_household = X[:, population_ix] / X[:, households_ix]
[p0098-l0013] [8.5pt]         if self.add_bedrooms_per_room:
[p0098-l0014] [8.5pt]             bedrooms_per_room = X[:, bedrooms_ix] / X[:, rooms_ix]
[p0098-l0015] [8.5pt]             return np.c_[X, rooms_per_household, population_per_household,
[p0098-l0016] [8.5pt]                          bedrooms_per_room]
[p0098-l0017] [8.5pt]         else:
[p0098-l0018] [8.5pt]             return np.c_[X, rooms_per_household, population_per_household]
[p0098-l0019] [8.5pt] attr_adder = CombinedAttributesAdder(add_bedrooms_per_room=False)
[p0098-l0020] [8.5pt] housing_extra_attribs = attr_adder.transform(housing.values)
[p0098-l0021] [10.5pt] In this example the transformer has one hyperparameter, add_bedrooms_per_room,
[p0098-l0022] [10.5pt] set to True by default (it is often helpful to provide sensible defaults). This hyperpara‐
[p0098-l0023] [10.5pt] meter will allow you to easily find out whether adding this attribute helps the
[p0098-l0024] [10.5pt] Machine Learning algorithms or not. More generally, you can add a hyperparameter
[p0098-l0025] [10.5pt] to gate any data preparation step that you are not 100% sure about. The more you
[p0098-l0026] [10.5pt] automate these data preparation steps, the more combinations you can automatically
[p0098-l0027] [10.5pt] try out, making it much more likely that you will find a great combination (and sav‐
[p0098-l0028] [10.5pt] ing you a lot of time).
[p0098-l0029] [15.77pt] Feature Scaling
[p0098-l0030] [10.5pt] One of the most important transformations you need to apply to your data is feature
[p0098-l0031] [10.5pt] scaling. With few exceptions, Machine Learning algorithms don’t perform well when
[p0098-l0032] [10.5pt] the input numerical attributes have very different scales. This is the case for the hous‐
[p0098-l0033] [10.5pt] ing data: the total number of rooms ranges from about 6 to 39,320, while the median
[p0098-l0034] [10.5pt] incomes only range from 0 to 15. Note that scaling the target values is generally not
[p0098-l0035] [10.5pt] required.
[p0098-l0036] [10.5pt] There are two common ways to get all attributes to have the same scale: min-max
[p0098-l0037] [10.5pt] scaling and standardization.
[p0098-l0038] [10.5pt] Min-max scaling (many people call this normalization) is quite simple: values are
[p0098-l0039] [10.5pt] shifted and rescaled so that they end up ranging from 0 to 1. We do this by subtract‐
[p0098-l0040] [10.5pt] ing the min value and dividing by the max minus the min. Scikit-Learn provides a
[p0098-l0041] [9.0pt] 72
[p0098-l0042] [9.0pt] |
[p0098-l0043] [9.0pt] Chapter 2: End-to-End Machine Learning Project

=== PDF page 99 / printed label 73 ===
[p0099-l0001] [10.5pt] transformer called MinMaxScaler for this. It has a feature_range hyperparameter
[p0099-l0002] [10.5pt] that lets you change the range if you don’t want 0–1 for some reason.
[p0099-l0003] [10.5pt] Standardization is quite different: first it subtracts the mean value (so standardized
[p0099-l0004] [10.5pt] values always have a zero mean), and then it divides by the standard deviation so that
[p0099-l0005] [10.5pt] the resulting distribution has unit variance. Unlike min-max scaling, standardization
[p0099-l0006] [10.5pt] does not bound values to a specific range, which may be a problem for some algo‐
[p0099-l0007] [10.5pt] rithms (e.g., neural networks often expect an input value ranging from 0 to 1). How‐
[p0099-l0008] [10.5pt] ever, standardization is much less affected by outliers. For example, suppose a district
[p0099-l0009] [10.5pt] had a median income equal to 100 (by mistake). Min-max scaling would then crush
[p0099-l0010] [10.5pt] all the other values from 0–15 down to 0–0.15, whereas standardization would not be
[p0099-l0011] [10.5pt] much affected. Scikit-Learn provides a transformer called StandardScaler for stand‐
[p0099-l0012] [10.5pt] ardization.
[p0099-l0013] [9.6pt] As with all the transformations, it is important to fit the scalers to
[p0099-l0014] [9.6pt] the training data only, not to the full dataset (including the test set).
[p0099-l0015] [9.6pt] Only then can you use them to transform the training set and the
[p0099-l0016] [9.6pt] test set (and new data).
[p0099-l0017] [15.77pt] Transformation Pipelines
[p0099-l0018] [10.5pt] As you can see, there are many data transformation steps that need to be executed in
[p0099-l0019] [10.5pt] the right order. Fortunately, Scikit-Learn provides the Pipeline class to help with
[p0099-l0020] [10.5pt] such sequences of transformations. Here is a small pipeline for the numerical
[p0099-l0021] [10.5pt] attributes:
[p0099-l0022] [8.5pt] from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
[p0099-l0023] [8.5pt] from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
[p0099-l0024] [8.5pt] num_pipeline = Pipeline([
[p0099-l0025] [8.5pt]         ('imputer', SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
[p0099-l0026] [8.5pt]         ('attribs_adder', CombinedAttributesAdder()),
[p0099-l0027] [8.5pt]         ('std_scaler', StandardScaler()),
[p0099-l0028] [8.5pt]     ])
[p0099-l0029] [8.5pt] housing_num_tr = num_pipeline.fit_transform(housing_num)
[p0099-l0030] [10.5pt] The Pipeline constructor takes a list of name/estimator pairs defining a sequence of
[p0099-l0031] [10.5pt] steps. All but the last estimator must be transformers (i.e., they must have a
[p0099-l0032] [10.5pt] fit_transform() method). The names can be anything you like (as long as they are
[p0099-l0033] [10.5pt] unique and don’t contain double underscores “__”): they will come in handy later for
[p0099-l0034] [10.5pt] hyperparameter tuning.
[p0099-l0035] [10.5pt] When you call the pipeline’s fit() method, it calls fit_transform() sequentially on
[p0099-l0036] [10.5pt] all transformers, passing the output of each call as the parameter to the next call, until
[p0099-l0037] [10.5pt] it reaches the final estimator, for which it just calls the fit() method.
[p0099-l0038] [9.0pt] Prepare the Data for Machine Learning Algorithms
[p0099-l0039] [9.0pt] |
[p0099-l0040] [9.0pt] 73

=== PDF page 100 / printed label 74 ===
[p0100-l0001] [10.5pt] The pipeline exposes the same methods as the final estimator. In this example, the last
[p0100-l0002] [10.5pt] estimator is a StandardScaler, which is a transformer, so the pipeline has a trans
[p0100-l0003] [10.5pt] form() method that applies all the transforms to the data in sequence (and of course
[p0100-l0004] [10.5pt] also a fit_transform() method, which is the one we used).
[p0100-l0005] [10.5pt] So far, we have handled the categorical columns and the numerical columns sepa‐
[p0100-l0006] [10.5pt] rately. It would be more convenient to have a single transformer able to handle all col‐
[p0100-l0007] [10.5pt] umns, applying the appropriate transformations to each column. In version 0.20,
[p0100-l0008] [10.5pt] Scikit-Learn introduced the ColumnTransformer for this purpose, and the good news
[p0100-l0009] [10.5pt] is that it works great with Pandas DataFrames. Let’s use it to apply all the transforma‐
[p0100-l0010] [10.5pt] tions to the housing data:
[p0100-l0011] [8.5pt] from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
[p0100-l0012] [8.5pt] num_attribs = list(housing_num)
[p0100-l0013] [8.5pt] cat_attribs = ["ocean_proximity"]
[p0100-l0014] [8.5pt] full_pipeline = ColumnTransformer([
[p0100-l0015] [8.5pt]         ("num", num_pipeline, num_attribs),
[p0100-l0016] [8.5pt]         ("cat", OneHotEncoder(), cat_attribs),
[p0100-l0017] [8.5pt]     ])
[p0100-l0018] [8.5pt] housing_prepared = full_pipeline.fit_transform(housing)
[p0100-l0019] [10.5pt] Here is how this works: first we import the ColumnTransformer class, next we get the
[p0100-l0020] [10.5pt] list of numerical column names and the list of categorical column names, and we
[p0100-l0021] [10.5pt] construct a ColumnTransformer. The constructor requires a list of tuples, where each
[p0100-l0022] [10.5pt] tuple contains a name22, a transformer and a list of names (or indices) of columns
[p0100-l0023] [10.5pt] that the transformer should be applied to. In this example, we specify that the numer‐
[p0100-l0024] [10.5pt] ical columns should be transformed using the num_pipeline that we defined earlier,
[p0100-l0025] [10.5pt] and the categorical columns should be transformed using a OneHotEncoder. Finally,
[p0100-l0026] [10.5pt] we apply this ColumnTransformer to the housing data: it applies each transformer to
[p0100-l0027] [10.5pt] the appropriate columns and concatenates the outputs along the second axis (the
[p0100-l0028] [10.5pt] transformers must return the same number of rows).
[p0100-l0029] [10.5pt] Note that the OneHotEncoder returns a sparse matrix, while the num_pipeline returns
[p0100-l0030] [10.5pt] a dense matrix. When there is such a mix of sparse and dense matrices, the Colum
[p0100-l0031] [10.5pt] nTransformer estimates the density of the final matrix (i.e., the ratio of non-zero
[p0100-l0032] [10.5pt] cells), and it returns a sparse matrix if the density is lower than a given threshold (by
[p0100-l0033] [10.5pt] default, sparse_threshold=0.3). In this example, it returns a dense matrix. And
[p0100-l0034] [10.5pt] that’s it! We have a preprocessing pipeline that takes the full housing data and applies
[p0100-l0035] [10.5pt] the appropriate transformations to each column.
[p0100-l0036] [8.0pt] 22 Just like for pipelines, the name can be anything as long as it does not contain double underscores.
[p0100-l0037] [9.0pt] 74
[p0100-l0038] [9.0pt] |
[p0100-l0039] [9.0pt] Chapter 2: End-to-End Machine Learning Project

[p0101-l0001] [9.6pt] Instead of a transformer, you can specify the string "drop" if you
[p0101-l0002] [9.6pt] want the columns to be dropped. Or you can specify "pass
[p0101-l0003] [9.6pt] through" if you want the columns to be left untouched. By default,
[p0101-l0004] [9.6pt] the remaining columns (i.e., the ones that were not listed) will be
[p0101-l0005] [9.6pt] dropped, but you can set the remainder hyperparameter to any
[p0101-l0006] [9.6pt] transformer (or to "passthrough") if you want these columns to be
[p0101-l0007] [9.6pt] handled differently.
[p0101-l0008] [10.5pt] If you are using Scikit-Learn 0.19 or earlier, you can use a third-party library such as
[p0101-l0009] [10.5pt] sklearn-pandas, or roll out your own custom transformer to get the same function‐
[p0101-l0010] [10.5pt] ality as the ColumnTransformer. Alternatively, you can use the FeatureUnion class
[p0101-l0011] [10.5pt] which can also apply different transformers and concatenate their outputs, but you
[p0101-l0012] [10.5pt] cannot specify different columns for each transformer, they all apply to the whole
[p0101-l0013] [10.5pt] data. It is possible to work around this limitation using a custom transformer for col‐
[p0101-l0014] [10.5pt] umn selection (see the Jupyter notebook for an example).
[p0101-l0015] [18.92pt] Select and Train a Model
[p0101-l0016] [10.5pt] At last! You framed the problem, you got the data and explored it, you sampled a
[p0101-l0017] [10.5pt] training set and a test set, and you wrote transformation pipelines to clean up and
[p0101-l0018] [10.5pt] prepare your data for Machine Learning algorithms automatically. You are now ready
[p0101-l0019] [10.5pt] to select and train a Machine Learning model.
[p0101-l0020] [15.77pt] Training and Evaluating on the Training Set

[p0102-l0010] [10.5pt] Okay, this is better than nothing but clearly not a great score: most districts’
[p0102-l0011] [10.5pt] median_housing_values range between $120,000 and $265,000, so a typical predic‐
[p0102-l0012] [10.5pt] tion error of $68,628 is not very satisfying. This is an example of a model underfitting
[p0102-l0013] [10.5pt] the training data. When this happens it can mean that the features do not provide
[p0102-l0014] [10.5pt] enough information to make good predictions, or that the model is not powerful
[p0102-l0015] [10.5pt] enough. As we saw in the previous chapter, the main ways to fix underfitting are to
[p0102-l0016] [10.5pt] select a more powerful model, to feed the training algorithm with better features, or
[p0102-l0017] [10.5pt] to reduce the constraints on the model. This model is not regularized, so this rules
[p0102-l0018] [10.5pt] out the last option. You could try to add more features (e.g., the log of the popula‐

[p0102-l0034] [10.5pt] As we saw earlier, you don’t want to touch the test set until you are ready to launch a

[p0102-l0037] [15.77pt] Better Evaluation Using Cross-Validation
[p0102-l0038] [10.5pt] One way to evaluate the Decision Tree model would be to use the train_test_split
[p0102-l0039] [10.5pt] function to split the training set into a smaller training set and a validation set, then
[p0102-l0040] [9.0pt] 76

[p0103-l0001] [10.5pt] train your models against the smaller training set and evaluate them against the vali‐
[p0103-l0002] [10.5pt] dation set. It’s a bit of work, but nothing too difficult and it would work fairly well.
[p0103-l0003] [10.5pt] A great alternative is to use Scikit-Learn’s K-fold cross-validation feature. The follow‐
[p0103-l0004] [10.5pt] ing code randomly splits the training set into 10 distinct subsets called folds, then it
[p0103-l0005] [10.5pt] trains and evaluates the Decision Tree model 10 times, picking a different fold for

[p0103-l0007] [10.5pt] taining the 10 evaluation scores:
[p0103-l0008] [8.5pt] from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score

[p0103-l0012] [9.6pt] Scikit-Learn’s cross-validation features expect a utility function
[p0103-l0013] [9.6pt] (greater is better) rather than a cost function (lower is better), so
[p0103-l0014] [9.6pt] the scoring function is actually the opposite of the MSE (i.e., a neg‐
[p0103-l0015] [9.6pt] ative value), which is why the preceding code computes -scores
[p0103-l0016] [9.6pt] before calculating the square root.

[p0105-l0001] [9.6pt] You should save every model you experiment with, so you can
[p0105-l0002] [9.6pt] come back easily to any model you want. Make sure you save both
[p0105-l0003] [9.6pt] the hyperparameters and the trained parameters, as well as the
[p0105-l0004] [9.6pt] cross-validation scores and perhaps the actual predictions as well.
[p0105-l0005] [9.6pt] This will allow you to easily compare scores across model types,
[p0105-l0006] [9.6pt] and compare the types of errors they make. You can easily save
[p0105-l0007] [9.6pt] Scikit-Learn models by using Python’s pickle module, or using
[p0105-l0008] [9.6pt] sklearn.externals.joblib, which is more efficient at serializing
[p0105-l0009] [9.6pt] large NumPy arrays:
[p0105-l0010] [8.5pt] from sklearn.externals import joblib
[p0105-l0011] [8.5pt] joblib.dump(my_model, "my_model.pkl")
[p0105-l0012] [8.5pt] # and later...
[p0105-l0013] [8.5pt] my_model_loaded = joblib.load("my_model.pkl")
[p0105-l0014] [18.92pt] Fine-Tune Your Model
[p0105-l0015] [10.5pt] Let’s assume that you now have a shortlist of promising models. You now need to
[p0105-l0016] [10.5pt] fine-tune them. Let’s look at a few ways you can do that.
[p0105-l0017] [15.77pt] Grid Search
[p0105-l0018] [10.5pt] One way to do that would be to fiddle with the hyperparameters manually, until you
[p0105-l0019] [10.5pt] find a great combination of hyperparameter values. This would be very tedious work,
[p0105-l0020] [10.5pt] and you may not have time to explore many combinations.
[p0105-l0021] [10.5pt] Instead you should get Scikit-Learn’s GridSearchCV to search for you. All you need to
[p0105-l0022] [10.5pt] do is tell it which hyperparameters you want it to experiment with, and what values to
[p0105-l0023] [10.5pt] try out, and it will evaluate all the possible combinations of hyperparameter values,
[p0105-l0024] [10.5pt] using cross-validation. For example, the following code searches for the best combi‐
[p0105-l0025] [10.5pt] nation of hyperparameter values for the RandomForestRegressor:
[p0105-l0026] [8.5pt] from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV
[p0105-l0027] [8.5pt] param_grid = [
[p0105-l0028] [8.5pt]     {'n_estimators': [3, 10, 30], 'max_features': [2, 4, 6, 8]},
[p0105-l0029] [8.5pt]     {'bootstrap': [False], 'n_estimators': [3, 10], 'max_features': [2, 3, 4]},
[p0105-l0030] [8.5pt]   ]
[p0105-l0031] [8.5pt] forest_reg = RandomForestRegressor()
[p0105-l0032] [8.5pt] grid_search = GridSearchCV(forest_reg, param_grid, cv=5,
[p0105-l0033] [8.5pt]                            scoring='neg_mean_squared_error',
[p0105-l0034] [8.5pt]                            return_train_score=True)
[p0105-l0035] [8.5pt] grid_search.fit(housing_prepared, housing_labels)
[p0105-l0036] [9.0pt] Fine-Tune Your Model
[p0105-l0037] [9.0pt] |
[p0105-l0038] [9.0pt] 79

=== PDF page 106 / printed label 80 ===
[p0106-l0001] [9.6pt] When you have no idea what value a hyperparameter should have,
[p0106-l0002] [9.6pt] a simple approach is to try out consecutive powers of 10 (or a
[p0106-l0003] [9.6pt] smaller number if you want a more fine-grained search, as shown
[p0106-l0004] [9.6pt] in this example with the n_estimators hyperparameter).
[p0106-l0005] [10.5pt] This param_grid tells Scikit-Learn to first evaluate all 3 × 4 = 12 combinations of
[p0106-l0006] [10.5pt] n_estimators and max_features hyperparameter values specified in the first dict
[p0106-l0007] [10.5pt] (don’t worry about what these hyperparameters mean for now; they will be explained
[p0106-l0008] [10.5pt] in Chapter 7), then try all 2 × 3 = 6 combinations of hyperparameter values in the
[p0106-l0009] [10.5pt] second dict, but this time with the bootstrap hyperparameter set to False instead of
[p0106-l0010] [10.5pt] True (which is the default value for this hyperparameter).
[p0106-l0011] [10.5pt] All in all, the grid search will explore 12 + 6 = 18 combinations of RandomForestRe
[p0106-l0012] [10.5pt] gressor hyperparameter values, and it will train each model five times (since we are
[p0106-l0013] [10.5pt] using five-fold cross validation). In other words, all in all, there will be 18 × 5 = 90
[p0106-l0014] [10.5pt] rounds of training! It may take quite a long time, but when it is done you can get the
[p0106-l0015] [10.5pt] best combination of parameters like this:
[p0106-l0016] [8.5pt] >>> grid_search.best_params_
[p0106-l0017] [8.5pt] {'max_features': 8, 'n_estimators': 30}
[p0106-l0018] [9.6pt] Since 8 and 30 are the maximum values that were evaluated, you
[p0106-l0019] [9.6pt] should probably try searching again with higher values, since the
[p0106-l0020] [9.6pt] score may continue to improve.
[p0106-l0021] [10.5pt] You can also get the best estimator directly:
[p0106-l0022] [8.5pt] >>> grid_search.best_estimator_
[p0106-l0023] [8.5pt] RandomForestRegressor(bootstrap=True, criterion='mse', max_depth=None,
[p0106-l0024] [8.5pt]            max_features=8, max_leaf_nodes=None, min_impurity_decrease=0.0,
[p0106-l0025] [8.5pt]            min_impurity_split=None, min_samples_leaf=1,
[p0106-l0026] [8.5pt]            min_samples_split=2, min_weight_fraction_leaf=0.0,
[p0106-l0027] [8.5pt]            n_estimators=30, n_jobs=None, oob_score=False, random_state=None,
[p0106-l0028] [8.5pt]            verbose=0, warm_start=False)
[p0106-l0029] [9.6pt] If GridSearchCV is initialized with refit=True (which is the
[p0106-l0030] [9.6pt] default), then once it finds the best estimator using cross-
[p0106-l0031] [9.6pt] validation, it retrains it on the whole training set. This is usually a
[p0106-l0032] [9.6pt] good idea since feeding it more data will likely improve its perfor‐
[p0106-l0033] [9.6pt] mance.
[p0106-l0034] [10.5pt] And of course the evaluation scores are also available:
[p0106-l0035] [8.5pt] >>> cvres = grid_search.cv_results_
[p0106-l0036] [8.5pt] >>> for mean_score, params in zip(cvres["mean_test_score"], cvres["params"]):

[p0107-l0033] [15.77pt] Randomized Search
[p0107-l0034] [10.5pt] The grid search approach is fine when you are exploring relatively few combinations,
[p0107-l0035] [10.5pt] like in the previous example, but when the hyperparameter search space is large, it is
[p0107-l0036] [10.5pt] often preferable to use RandomizedSearchCV instead. This class can be used in much
[p0107-l0037] [10.5pt] the same way as the GridSearchCV class, but instead of trying out all possible combi‐
[p0107-l0038] [10.5pt] nations, it evaluates a given number of random combinations by selecting a random
[p0107-l0039] [10.5pt] value for each hyperparameter at every iteration. This approach has two main bene‐
[p0107-l0040] [10.5pt] fits:
[p0107-l0041] [9.0pt] Fine-Tune Your Model
[p0107-l0042] [9.0pt] |
[p0107-l0043] [9.0pt] 81

=== PDF page 108 / printed label 82 ===
[p0108-l0001] [10.5pt] • If you let the randomized search run for, say, 1,000 iterations, this approach will
[p0108-l0002] [10.5pt] explore 1,000 different values for each hyperparameter (instead of just a few val‐
[p0108-l0003] [10.5pt] ues per hyperparameter with the grid search approach).
[p0108-l0004] [10.5pt] • You have more control over the computing budget you want to allocate to hyper‐
[p0108-l0005] [10.5pt] parameter search, simply by setting the number of iterations.
[p0108-l0006] [15.77pt] Ensemble Methods
[p0108-l0007] [10.5pt] Another way to fine-tune your system is to try to combine the models that perform
[p0108-l0008] [10.5pt] best. The group (or “ensemble”) will often perform better than the best individual
[p0108-l0009] [10.5pt] model (just like Random Forests perform better than the individual Decision Trees
[p0108-l0010] [10.5pt] they rely on), especially if the individual models make very different types of errors.
[p0108-l0011] [10.5pt] We will cover this topic in more detail in Chapter 7.
[p0108-l0012] [15.77pt] Analyze the Best Models and Their Errors

[p0109-l0009] [15.77pt] Evaluate Your System on the Test Set
[p0109-l0010] [10.5pt] After tweaking your models for a while, you eventually have a system that performs
[p0109-l0011] [10.5pt] sufficiently well. Now is the time to evaluate the final model on the test set. There is
[p0109-l0012] [10.5pt] nothing special about this process; just get the predictors and the labels from your
[p0109-l0013] [10.5pt] test set, run your full_pipeline to transform the data (call transform(), not
[p0109-l0014] [10.5pt] fit_transform(), you do not want to fit the test set!), and evaluate the final model
[p0109-l0015] [10.5pt] on the test set:
[p0109-l0016] [8.5pt] final_model = grid_search.best_estimator_
[p0109-l0017] [8.5pt] X_test = strat_test_set.drop("median_house_value", axis=1)
[p0109-l0018] [8.5pt] y_test = strat_test_set["median_house_value"].copy()
[p0109-l0019] [8.5pt] X_test_prepared = full_pipeline.transform(X_test)
[p0109-l0020] [8.5pt] final_predictions = final_model.predict(X_test_prepared)
[p0109-l0021] [8.5pt] final_mse = mean_squared_error(y_test, final_predictions)
[p0109-l0022] [8.5pt] final_rmse = np.sqrt(final_mse)   # => evaluates to 47,730.2
[p0109-l0023] [10.5pt] In some cases, such a point estimate of the generalization error will not be quite
[p0109-l0024] [10.5pt] enough to convince you to launch: what if it is just 0.1% better than the model cur‐
[p0109-l0025] [10.5pt] rently in production? You might want to have an idea of how precise this estimate is.
[p0109-l0026] [10.5pt] For this, you can compute a 95% confidence interval for the generalization error using
[p0109-l0027] [10.5pt] scipy.stats.t.interval():
[p0109-l0028] [8.5pt] >>> from scipy import stats
[p0109-l0029] [8.5pt] >>> confidence = 0.95
[p0109-l0030] [8.5pt] >>> squared_errors = (final_predictions - y_test) ** 2
[p0109-l0031] [8.5pt] >>> np.sqrt(stats.t.interval(confidence, len(squared_errors) - 1,
[p0109-l0032] [8.5pt] ...                          loc=squared_errors.mean(),
[p0109-l0033] [8.5pt] ...                          scale=stats.sem(squared_errors)))
[p0109-l0034] [8.5pt] ...
[p0109-l0035] [8.5pt] array([45685.10470776, 49691.25001878])
[p0109-l0036] [10.5pt] The performance will usually be slightly worse than what you measured using cross-
[p0109-l0037] [10.5pt] validation if you did a lot of hyperparameter tuning (because your system ends up
[p0109-l0038] [10.5pt] fine-tuned to perform well on the validation data, and will likely not perform as well
[p0109-l0039] [9.0pt] Fine-Tune Your Model
[p0109-l0040] [9.0pt] |
[p0109-l0041] [9.0pt] 83

[p0110-l0001] [10.5pt] on unknown datasets). It is not the case in this example, but when this happens you
[p0110-l0002] [10.5pt] must resist the temptation to tweak the hyperparameters to make the numbers look
[p0110-l0003] [10.5pt] good on the test set; the improvements would be unlikely to generalize to new data.
[p0110-l0004] [10.5pt] Now comes the project prelaunch phase: you need to present your solution (high‐
[p0110-l0005] [10.5pt] lighting what you have learned, what worked and what did not, what assumptions
[p0110-l0006] [10.5pt] were made, and what your system’s limitations are), document everything, and create
[p0110-l0007] [10.5pt] nice presentations with clear visualizations and easy-to-remember statements (e.g.,
[p0110-l0008] [10.5pt] “the median income is the number one predictor of housing prices”). In this Califor‐
[p0110-l0009] [10.5pt] nia housing example, the final performance of the system is not better than the
[p0110-l0010] [10.5pt] experts’, but it may still be a good idea to launch it, especially if this frees up some
[p0110-l0011] [10.5pt] time for the experts so they can work on more interesting and productive tasks.
[p0110-l0012] [18.92pt] Launch, Monitor, and Maintain Your System
[p0110-l0013] [10.5pt] Perfect, you got approval to launch! You need to get your solution ready for produc‐
[p0110-l0014] [10.5pt] tion, in particular by plugging the production input data sources into your system
[p0110-l0015] [10.5pt] and writing tests.
[p0110-l0016] [10.5pt] You also need to write monitoring code to check your system’s live performance at
[p0110-l0017] [10.5pt] regular intervals and trigger alerts when it drops. This is important to catch not only
[p0110-l0018] [10.5pt] sudden breakage, but also performance degradation. This is quite common because
[p0110-l0019] [10.5pt] models tend to “rot” as data evolves over time, unless the models are regularly trained
[p0110-l0020] [10.5pt] on fresh data.
[p0110-l0021] [10.5pt] Evaluating your system’s performance will require sampling the system’s predictions
[p0110-l0022] [10.5pt] and evaluating them. This will generally require a human analysis. These analysts
[p0110-l0023] [10.5pt] may be field experts, or workers on a crowdsourcing platform (such as Amazon
[p0110-l0024] [10.5pt] Mechanical Turk or CrowdFlower). Either way, you need to plug the human evalua‐
[p0110-l0025] [10.5pt] tion pipeline into your system.
[p0110-l0026] [10.5pt] You should also make sure you evaluate the system’s input data quality. Sometimes
[p0110-l0027] [10.5pt] performance will degrade slightly because of a poor quality signal (e.g., a malfunc‐
[p0110-l0028] [10.5pt] tioning sensor sending random values, or another team’s output becoming stale), but
[p0110-l0029] [10.5pt] it may take a while before your system’s performance degrades enough to trigger an
[p0110-l0030] [10.5pt] alert. If you monitor your system’s inputs, you may catch this earlier. Monitoring the
[p0110-l0031] [10.5pt] inputs is particularly important for online learning systems.
[p0110-l0032] [10.5pt] Finally, you will generally want to train your models on a regular basis using fresh
[p0110-l0033] [10.5pt] data. You should automate this process as much as possible. If you don’t, you are very
[p0110-l0034] [10.5pt] likely to refresh your model only every six months (at best), and your system’s perfor‐
[p0110-l0035] [10.5pt] mance may fluctuate severely over time. If your system is an online learning system,
[p0110-l0036] [10.5pt] you should make sure you save snapshots of its state at regular intervals so you can
[p0110-l0037] [10.5pt] easily roll back to a previously working state.
