[p0152-l0001] [15.0pt] Convergence Rate
[p0152-l0002] [10.0pt] When the cost function is convex and its slope does not change abruptly (as is the
[p0152-l0003] [10.0pt] case for the MSE cost function), Batch Gradient Descent with a fixed learning rate
[p0152-l0004] [10.0pt] will eventually converge to the optimal solution, but you may have to wait a while: it
[p0152-l0005] [10.0pt] can take O(1/ϵ) iterations to reach the optimum within a range of ϵ depending on the
[p0152-l0006] [10.0pt] shape of the cost function. If you divide the tolerance by 10 to have a more precise
[p0152-l0007] [10.0pt] solution, then the algorithm may have to run about 10 times longer.
[p0152-l0008] [15.77pt] Stochastic Gradient Descent
[p0152-l0009] [10.5pt] The main problem with Batch Gradient Descent is the fact that it uses the whole
[p0152-l0010] [10.5pt] training set to compute the gradients at every step, which makes it very slow when
[p0152-l0011] [10.5pt] the training set is large. At the opposite extreme, Stochastic Gradient Descent just
[p0152-l0012] [10.5pt] picks a random instance in the training set at every step and computes the gradients
[p0152-l0013] [10.5pt] based only on that single instance. Obviously this makes the algorithm much faster
[p0152-l0014] [10.5pt] since it has very little data to manipulate at every iteration. It also makes it possible to
[p0152-l0015] [10.5pt] train on huge training sets, since only one instance needs to be in memory at each
[p0152-l0016] [10.5pt] iteration (SGD can be implemented as an out-of-core algorithm.7)
[p0152-l0017] [10.5pt] On the other hand, due to its stochastic (i.e., random) nature, this algorithm is much
[p0152-l0018] [10.5pt] less regular than Batch Gradient Descent: instead of gently decreasing until it reaches
[p0152-l0019] [10.5pt] the minimum, the cost function will bounce up and down, decreasing only on aver‐
[p0152-l0020] [10.5pt] age. Over time it will end up very close to the minimum, but once it gets there it will
[p0152-l0021] [10.5pt] continue to bounce around, never settling down (see Figure 4-9). So once the algo‐
[p0152-l0022] [10.5pt] rithm stops, the final parameter values are good, but not optimal.
[p0152-l0023] [10.5pt] Figure 4-9. Stochastic Gradient Descent
[p0152-l0024] [8.0pt] 7 Out-of-core algorithms are discussed in Chapter 1.
[p0152-l0025] [9.0pt] 126
[p0152-l0026] [9.0pt] |
[p0152-l0027] [9.0pt] Chapter 4: Training Models

=== PDF page 153 / printed label 127 ===
[p0153-l0001] [10.5pt] When the cost function is very irregular (as in Figure 4-6), this can actually help the
[p0153-l0002] [10.5pt] algorithm jump out of local minima, so Stochastic Gradient Descent has a better
[p0153-l0003] [10.5pt] chance of finding the global minimum than Batch Gradient Descent does.
[p0153-l0004] [10.5pt] Therefore randomness is good to escape from local optima, but bad because it means
[p0153-l0005] [10.5pt] that the algorithm can never settle at the minimum. One solution to this dilemma is
[p0153-l0006] [10.5pt] to gradually reduce the learning rate. The steps start out large (which helps make
[p0153-l0007] [10.5pt] quick progress and escape local minima), then get smaller and smaller, allowing the
[p0153-l0008] [10.5pt] algorithm to settle at the global minimum. This process is akin to simulated anneal‐
[p0153-l0009] [10.5pt] ing, an algorithm inspired from the process of annealing in metallurgy where molten
[p0153-l0010] [10.5pt] metal is slowly cooled down. The function that determines the learning rate at each
[p0153-l0011] [10.5pt] iteration is called the learning schedule. If the learning rate is reduced too quickly, you
[p0153-l0012] [10.5pt] may get stuck in a local minimum, or even end up frozen halfway to the minimum. If
[p0153-l0013] [10.5pt] the learning rate is reduced too slowly, you may jump around the minimum for a
[p0153-l0014] [10.5pt] long time and end up with a suboptimal solution if you halt training too early.
[p0153-l0015] [10.5pt] This code implements Stochastic Gradient Descent using a simple learning schedule:
[p0153-l0016] [8.5pt] n_epochs = 50
[p0153-l0017] [8.5pt] t0, t1 = 5, 50  # learning schedule hyperparameters
[p0153-l0018] [8.5pt] def learning_schedule(t):
[p0153-l0019] [8.5pt]     return t0 / (t + t1)
[p0153-l0020] [8.5pt] theta = np.random.randn(2,1)  # random initialization
[p0153-l0021] [8.5pt] for epoch in range(n_epochs):
[p0153-l0022] [8.5pt]     for i in range(m):
[p0153-l0023] [8.5pt]         random_index = np.random.randint(m)
[p0153-l0024] [8.5pt]         xi = X_b[random_index:random_index+1]
[p0153-l0025] [8.5pt]         yi = y[random_index:random_index+1]
[p0153-l0026] [8.5pt]         gradients = 2 * xi.T.dot(xi.dot(theta) - yi)
[p0153-l0027] [8.5pt]         eta = learning_schedule(epoch * m + i)
[p0153-l0028] [8.5pt]         theta = theta - eta * gradients
[p0153-l0029] [10.5pt] By convention we iterate by rounds of m iterations; each round is called an epoch.
[p0153-l0030] [10.5pt] While the Batch Gradient Descent code iterated 1,000 times through the whole train‐
[p0153-l0031] [10.5pt] ing set, this code goes through the training set only 50 times and reaches a fairly good
[p0153-l0032] [10.5pt] solution:
[p0153-l0033] [8.5pt] >>> theta
[p0153-l0034] [8.5pt] array([[4.21076011],
[p0153-l0035] [8.5pt]        [2.74856079]])
[p0153-l0036] [10.5pt] Figure 4-10 shows the first 20 steps of training (notice how irregular the steps are).
[p0153-l0037] [9.0pt] Gradient Descent
[p0153-l0038] [9.0pt] |
[p0153-l0039] [9.0pt] 127

=== PDF page 154 / printed label 128 ===
[p0154-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 4-10. Stochastic Gradient Descent first 20 steps
[p0154-l0002] [10.5pt] Note that since instances are picked randomly, some instances may be picked several
[p0154-l0003] [10.5pt] times per epoch while others may not be picked at all. If you want to be sure that the
[p0154-l0004] [10.5pt] algorithm goes through every instance at each epoch, another approach is to shuffle
[p0154-l0005] [10.5pt] the training set (making sure to shuffle the input features and the labels jointly), then
[p0154-l0006] [10.5pt] go through it instance by instance, then shuffle it again, and so on. However, this gen‐
[p0154-l0007] [10.5pt] erally converges more slowly.
[p0154-l0008] [9.6pt] When using Stochastic Gradient Descent, the training instances
[p0154-l0009] [9.6pt] must be independent and identically distributed (IID), to ensure
[p0154-l0010] [9.6pt] that the parameters get pulled towards the global optimum, on
[p0154-l0011] [9.6pt] average. A simple way to ensure this is to shuffle the instances dur‐
[p0154-l0012] [9.6pt] ing training (e.g., pick each instance randomly, or shuffle the train‐
[p0154-l0013] [9.6pt] ing set at the beginning of each epoch). If you do not do this, for
[p0154-l0014] [9.6pt] example if the instances are sorted by label, then SGD will start by
[p0154-l0015] [9.6pt] optimizing for one label, then the next, and so on, and it will not
[p0154-l0016] [9.6pt] settle close to the global minimum.
[p0154-l0017] [10.5pt] To perform Linear Regression using SGD with Scikit-Learn, you can use the SGDRe
[p0154-l0018] [10.5pt] gressor class, which defaults to optimizing the squared error cost function. The fol‐
[p0154-l0019] [10.5pt] lowing code runs for maximum 1000 epochs (max_iter=1000) or until the loss drops
[p0154-l0020] [10.5pt] by less than 1e-3 during one epoch (tol=1e-3), starting with a learning rate of 0.1
[p0154-l0021] [10.5pt] (eta0=0.1), using the default learning schedule (different from the preceding one),
[p0154-l0022] [10.5pt] and it does not use any regularization (penalty=None; more details on this shortly):
[p0154-l0023] [8.5pt] from sklearn.linear_model import SGDRegressor
[p0154-l0024] [8.5pt] sgd_reg = SGDRegressor(max_iter=1000, tol=1e-3, penalty=None, eta0=0.1)
[p0154-l0025] [8.5pt] sgd_reg.fit(X, y.ravel())
[p0154-l0026] [9.0pt] 128
[p0154-l0027] [9.0pt] |
[p0154-l0028] [9.0pt] Chapter 4: Training Models

=== PDF page 155 / printed label 129 ===
[p0155-l0001] [10.5pt] Once again, you find a solution quite close to the one returned by the Normal Equa‐
[p0155-l0002] [10.5pt] tion:
[p0155-l0003] [8.5pt] >>> sgd_reg.intercept_, sgd_reg.coef_
[p0155-l0004] [8.5pt] (array([4.24365286]), array([2.8250878]))
[p0155-l0005] [15.77pt] Mini-batch Gradient Descent
[p0155-l0006] [10.5pt] The last Gradient Descent algorithm we will look at is called Mini-batch Gradient
[p0155-l0007] [10.5pt] Descent. It is quite simple to understand once you know Batch and Stochastic Gradi‐
[p0155-l0008] [10.5pt] ent Descent: at each step, instead of computing the gradients based on the full train‐
[p0155-l0009] [10.5pt] ing set (as in Batch GD) or based on just one instance (as in Stochastic GD), Mini-
[p0155-l0010] [10.5pt] batch GD computes the gradients on small random sets of instances called mini-
[p0155-l0011] [10.5pt] batches. The main advantage of Mini-batch GD over Stochastic GD is that you can
[p0155-l0012] [10.5pt] get a performance boost from hardware optimization of matrix operations, especially
[p0155-l0013] [10.5pt] when using GPUs.
[p0155-l0014] [10.5pt] The algorithm’s progress in parameter space is less erratic than with SGD, especially
[p0155-l0015] [10.5pt] with fairly large mini-batches. As a result, Mini-batch GD will end up walking
[p0155-l0016] [10.5pt] around a bit closer to the minimum than SGD. But, on the other hand, it may be
[p0155-l0017] [10.5pt] harder for it to escape from local minima (in the case of problems that suffer from
[p0155-l0018] [10.5pt] local minima, unlike Linear Regression as we saw earlier). Figure 4-11 shows the
[p0155-l0019] [10.5pt] paths taken by the three Gradient Descent algorithms in parameter space during
[p0155-l0020] [10.5pt] training. They all end up near the minimum, but Batch GD’s path actually stops at the
[p0155-l0021] [10.5pt] minimum, while both Stochastic GD and Mini-batch GD continue to walk around.
[p0155-l0022] [10.5pt] However, don’t forget that Batch GD takes a lot of time to take each step, and Stochas‐
[p0155-l0023] [10.5pt] tic GD and Mini-batch GD would also reach the minimum if you used a good learn‐
[p0155-l0024] [10.5pt] ing schedule.
[p0155-l0025] [10.5pt] Figure 4-11. Gradient Descent paths in parameter space
[p0155-l0026] [9.0pt] Gradient Descent

[p0156-l0049] [18.92pt] Polynomial Regression
[p0156-l0050] [10.5pt] What if your data is actually more complex than a simple straight line? Surprisingly,
[p0156-l0051] [10.5pt] you can actually use a linear model to fit nonlinear data. A simple way to do this is to
[p0156-l0052] [10.5pt] add powers of each feature as new features, then train a linear model on this extended
[p0156-l0053] [10.5pt] set of features. This technique is called Polynomial Regression.
[p0156-l0054] [10.5pt] Let’s look at an example. First, let’s generate some nonlinear data, based on a simple
[p0156-l0055] [10.5pt] quadratic equation9 (plus some noise; see Figure 4-12):
[p0156-l0056] [8.5pt] m = 100
[p0156-l0057] [8.5pt] X = 6 * np.random.rand(m, 1) - 3
[p0156-l0058] [8.5pt] y = 0.5 * X**2 + X + 2 + np.random.randn(m, 1)
[p0156-l0059] [8.0pt] 8 While the Normal Equation can only perform Linear Regression, the Gradient Descent algorithms can be
[p0156-l0060] [8.0pt] used to train many other models, as we will see.
[p0156-l0061] [8.0pt] 9 A quadratic equation is of the form y = ax2 + bx + c.
[p0156-l0062] [9.0pt] 130
[p0156-l0063] [9.0pt] |
[p0156-l0064] [9.0pt] Chapter 4: Training Models

=== PDF page 157 / printed label 131 ===
[p0157-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 4-12. Generated nonlinear and noisy dataset
[p0157-l0002] [10.5pt] Clearly, a straight line will never fit this data properly. So let’s use Scikit-Learn’s Poly
[p0157-l0003] [10.5pt] nomialFeatures class to transform our training data, adding the square (2nd-degree
[p0157-l0004] [10.5pt] polynomial) of each feature in the training set as new features (in this case there is
[p0157-l0005] [10.5pt] just one feature):
[p0157-l0006] [8.5pt] >>> from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures
[p0157-l0007] [8.5pt] >>> poly_features = PolynomialFeatures(degree=2, include_bias=False)
[p0157-l0008] [8.5pt] >>> X_poly = poly_features.fit_transform(X)
[p0157-l0009] [8.5pt] >>> X[0]
[p0157-l0010] [8.5pt] array([-0.75275929])
[p0157-l0011] [8.5pt] >>> X_poly[0]
[p0157-l0012] [8.5pt] array([-0.75275929, 0.56664654])
[p0157-l0013] [10.5pt] X_poly now contains the original feature of X plus the square of this feature. Now you
[p0157-l0014] [10.5pt] can fit a LinearRegression model to this extended training data (Figure 4-13):
[p0157-l0015] [8.5pt] >>> lin_reg = LinearRegression()
[p0157-l0016] [8.5pt] >>> lin_reg.fit(X_poly, y)
[p0157-l0017] [8.5pt] >>> lin_reg.intercept_, lin_reg.coef_
[p0157-l0018] [8.5pt] (array([1.78134581]), array([[0.93366893, 0.56456263]]))
[p0157-l0019] [9.0pt] Polynomial Regression
[p0157-l0020] [9.0pt] |
[p0157-l0021] [9.0pt] 131

=== PDF page 158 / printed label 132 ===
[p0158-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 4-13. Polynomial Regression model predictions
[p0158-l0002] [10.5pt] Not bad: the model estimates y = 0 . 56x1
[p0158-l0003] [10.5pt] 2 + 0 . 93x1 + 1 . 78 when in fact the original
[p0158-l0004] [10.5pt] function was y = 0 . 5x1
[p0158-l0005] [10.5pt] 2 + 1 . 0x1 + 2 . 0 + Gaussian noise.
[p0158-l0006] [10.5pt] Note that when there are multiple features, Polynomial Regression is capable of find‐
[p0158-l0007] [10.5pt] ing relationships between features (which is something a plain Linear Regression
[p0158-l0008] [10.5pt] model cannot do). This is made possible by the fact that PolynomialFeatures also
[p0158-l0009] [10.5pt] adds all combinations of features up to the given degree. For example, if there were
[p0158-l0010] [10.5pt] two features a and b, PolynomialFeatures with degree=3 would not only add the
[p0158-l0011] [10.5pt] features a2, a3, b2, and b3, but also the combinations ab, a2b, and ab2.
[p0158-l0012] [9.6pt] PolynomialFeatures(degree=d) transforms an array containing n
[p0158-l0013] [9.6pt] features into an array containing n + d !
[p0158-l0014] [9.6pt] d! n! features, where n! is the
[p0158-l0015] [9.6pt] factorial of n, equal to 1 × 2 × 3 × ⋯ × n. Beware of the combinato‐
[p0158-l0016] [9.6pt] rial explosion of the number of features!
[p0158-l0017] [18.92pt] Learning Curves
[p0158-l0018] [10.5pt] If you perform high-degree Polynomial Regression, you will likely fit the training
[p0158-l0019] [10.5pt] data much better than with plain Linear Regression. For example, Figure 4-14 applies
[p0158-l0020] [10.5pt] a 300-degree polynomial model to the preceding training data, and compares the
[p0158-l0021] [10.5pt] result with a pure linear model and a quadratic model (2nd-degree polynomial).
[p0158-l0022] [10.5pt] Notice how the 300-degree polynomial model wiggles around to get as close as possi‐
[p0158-l0023] [10.5pt] ble to the training instances.
[p0158-l0024] [9.0pt] 132
[p0158-l0025] [9.0pt] |
[p0158-l0026] [9.0pt] Chapter 4: Training Models

=== PDF page 159 / printed label 133 ===
[p0159-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 4-14. High-degree Polynomial Regression
[p0159-l0002] [10.5pt] Of course, this high-degree Polynomial Regression model is severely overfitting the
[p0159-l0003] [10.5pt] training data, while the linear model is underfitting it. The model that will generalize
[p0159-l0004] [10.5pt] best in this case is the quadratic model. It makes sense since the data was generated
[p0159-l0005] [10.5pt] using a quadratic model, but in general you won’t know what function generated the
[p0159-l0006] [10.5pt] data, so how can you decide how complex your model should be? How can you tell
[p0159-l0007] [10.5pt] that your model is overfitting or underfitting the data?
[p0159-l0008] [10.5pt] In Chapter 2 you used cross-validation to get an estimate of a model’s generalization
[p0159-l0009] [10.5pt] performance. If a model performs well on the training data but generalizes poorly
[p0159-l0010] [10.5pt] according to the cross-validation metrics, then your model is overfitting. If it per‐
[p0159-l0011] [10.5pt] forms poorly on both, then it is underfitting. This is one way to tell when a model is
[p0159-l0012] [10.5pt] too simple or too complex.
[p0159-l0013] [10.5pt] Another way is to look at the learning curves: these are plots of the model’s perfor‐
[p0159-l0014] [10.5pt] mance on the training set and the validation set as a function of the training set size
[p0159-l0015] [10.5pt] (or the training iteration). To generate the plots, simply train the model several times
[p0159-l0016] [10.5pt] on different sized subsets of the training set. The following code defines a function
[p0159-l0017] [10.5pt] that plots the learning curves of a model given some training data:
[p0159-l0018] [8.5pt] from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error
[p0159-l0019] [8.5pt] from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
[p0159-l0020] [8.5pt] def plot_learning_curves(model, X, y):
[p0159-l0021] [8.5pt]     X_train, X_val, y_train, y_val = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2)
[p0159-l0022] [8.5pt]     train_errors, val_errors = [], []
[p0159-l0023] [8.5pt]     for m in range(1, len(X_train)):
[p0159-l0024] [8.5pt]         model.fit(X_train[:m], y_train[:m])
[p0159-l0025] [8.5pt]         y_train_predict = model.predict(X_train[:m])
[p0159-l0026] [9.0pt] Learning Curves
[p0159-l0027] [9.0pt] |
[p0159-l0028] [9.0pt] 133

=== PDF page 160 / printed label 134 ===
[p0160-l0001] [8.5pt]         y_val_predict = model.predict(X_val)
[p0160-l0002] [8.5pt]         train_errors.append(mean_squared_error(y_train[:m], y_train_predict))
[p0160-l0003] [8.5pt]         val_errors.append(mean_squared_error(y_val, y_val_predict))
[p0160-l0004] [8.5pt]     plt.plot(np.sqrt(train_errors), "r-+", linewidth=2, label="train")
[p0160-l0005] [8.5pt]     plt.plot(np.sqrt(val_errors), "b-", linewidth=3, label="val")
[p0160-l0006] [10.5pt] Let’s look at the learning curves of the plain Linear Regression model (a straight line;
[p0160-l0007] [10.5pt] Figure 4-15):
[p0160-l0008] [8.5pt] lin_reg = LinearRegression()
[p0160-l0009] [8.5pt] plot_learning_curves(lin_reg, X, y)
[p0160-l0010] [10.5pt] Figure 4-15. Learning curves
[p0160-l0011] [10.5pt] This deserves a bit of explanation. First, let’s look at the performance on the training
[p0160-l0012] [10.5pt] data: when there are just one or two instances in the training set, the model can fit
[p0160-l0013] [10.5pt] them perfectly, which is why the curve starts at zero. But as new instances are added
[p0160-l0014] [10.5pt] to the training set, it becomes impossible for the model to fit the training data per‐
[p0160-l0015] [10.5pt] fectly, both because the data is noisy and because it is not linear at all. So the error on
[p0160-l0016] [10.5pt] the training data goes up until it reaches a plateau, at which point adding new instan‐
[p0160-l0017] [10.5pt] ces to the training set doesn’t make the average error much better or worse. Now let’s
[p0160-l0018] [10.5pt] look at the performance of the model on the validation data. When the model is
[p0160-l0019] [10.5pt] trained on very few training instances, it is incapable of generalizing properly, which
[p0160-l0020] [10.5pt] is why the validation error is initially quite big. Then as the model is shown more
[p0160-l0021] [10.5pt] training examples, it learns and thus the validation error slowly goes down. However,
[p0160-l0022] [10.5pt] once again a straight line cannot do a good job modeling the data, so the error ends
[p0160-l0023] [10.5pt] up at a plateau, very close to the other curve.
[p0160-l0024] [10.5pt] These learning curves are typical of an underfitting model. Both curves have reached
[p0160-l0025] [10.5pt] a plateau; they are close and fairly high.
[p0160-l0026] [9.0pt] 134
[p0160-l0027] [9.0pt] |
[p0160-l0028] [9.0pt] Chapter 4: Training Models

[p0161-l0001] [9.6pt] If your model is underfitting the training data, adding more train‐
[p0161-l0002] [9.6pt] ing examples will not help. You need to use a more complex model
[p0161-l0003] [9.6pt] or come up with better features.
[p0161-l0004] [10.5pt] Now let’s look at the learning curves of a 10th-degree polynomial model on the same
[p0161-l0005] [10.5pt] data (Figure 4-16):
[p0161-l0006] [8.5pt] from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
[p0161-l0007] [8.5pt] polynomial_regression = Pipeline([
[p0161-l0008] [8.5pt]         ("poly_features", PolynomialFeatures(degree=10, include_bias=False)),
[p0161-l0009] [8.5pt]         ("lin_reg", LinearRegression()),
[p0161-l0010] [8.5pt]     ])
[p0161-l0011] [8.5pt] plot_learning_curves(polynomial_regression, X, y)
[p0161-l0012] [10.5pt] These learning curves look a bit like the previous ones, but there are two very impor‐
[p0161-l0013] [10.5pt] tant differences:
[p0161-l0014] [10.5pt] • The error on the training data is much lower than with the Linear Regression
[p0161-l0015] [10.5pt] model.
[p0161-l0016] [10.5pt] • There is a gap between the curves. This means that the model performs signifi‐
[p0161-l0017] [10.5pt] cantly better on the training data than on the validation data, which is the hall‐
[p0161-l0018] [10.5pt] mark of an overfitting model. However, if you used a much larger training set,
[p0161-l0019] [10.5pt] the two curves would continue to get closer.
[p0161-l0020] [10.5pt] Figure 4-16. Learning curves for the polynomial model

[p0162-l0001] [9.6pt] One way to improve an overfitting model is to feed it more training
[p0162-l0002] [9.6pt] data until the validation error reaches the training error.
[p0162-l0003] [15.0pt] The Bias/Variance Tradeoff
[p0162-l0004] [10.0pt] An important theoretical result of statistics and Machine Learning is the fact that a
[p0162-l0005] [10.0pt] model’s generalization error can be expressed as the sum of three very different
[p0162-l0006] [10.0pt] errors:
[p0162-l0007] [10.0pt] Bias
[p0162-l0008] [10.0pt] This part of the generalization error is due to wrong assumptions, such as assum‐
[p0162-l0009] [10.0pt] ing that the data is linear when it is actually quadratic. A high-bias model is most
[p0162-l0010] [10.0pt] likely to underfit the training data.10
[p0162-l0011] [10.0pt] Variance
[p0162-l0012] [10.0pt] This part is due to the model’s excessive sensitivity to small variations in the
[p0162-l0013] [10.0pt] training data. A model with many degrees of freedom (such as a high-degree pol‐
[p0162-l0014] [10.0pt] ynomial model) is likely to have high variance, and thus to overfit the training
[p0162-l0015] [10.0pt] data.
[p0162-l0016] [10.0pt] Irreducible error
[p0162-l0017] [10.0pt] This part is due to the noisiness of the data itself. The only way to reduce this
[p0162-l0018] [10.0pt] part of the error is to clean up the data (e.g., fix the data sources, such as broken
[p0162-l0019] [10.0pt] sensors, or detect and remove outliers).
[p0162-l0020] [10.0pt] Increasing a model’s complexity will typically increase its variance and reduce its bias.
[p0162-l0021] [10.0pt] Conversely, reducing a model’s complexity increases its bias and reduces its variance.
[p0162-l0022] [10.0pt] This is why it is called a tradeoff.
[p0162-l0023] [18.92pt] Regularized Linear Models
[p0162-l0024] [10.5pt] As we saw in Chapters 1 and 2, a good way to reduce overfitting is to regularize the
[p0162-l0025] [10.5pt] model (i.e., to constrain it): the fewer degrees of freedom it has, the harder it will be
[p0162-l0026] [10.5pt] for it to overfit the data. For example, a simple way to regularize a polynomial model
[p0162-l0027] [10.5pt] is to reduce the number of polynomial degrees.
[p0162-l0028] [10.5pt] For a linear model, regularization is typically achieved by constraining the weights of
[p0162-l0029] [10.5pt] the model. We will now look at Ridge Regression, Lasso Regression, and Elastic Net,
[p0162-l0030] [10.5pt] which implement three different ways to constrain the weights.
[p0162-l0031] [8.0pt] 10 This notion of bias is not to be confused with the bias term of linear models.
[p0162-l0032] [9.0pt] 136
[p0162-l0033] [9.0pt] |
[p0162-l0034] [9.0pt] Chapter 4: Training Models

=== PDF page 163 / printed label 137 ===
[p0163-l0001] [15.77pt] Ridge Regression
[p0163-l0002] [10.5pt] Ridge Regression (also called Tikhonov regularization) is a regularized version of Lin‐
[p0163-l0003] [10.5pt] ear Regression: a regularization term equal to α∑i = 1
[p0163-l0004] [8.0pt] n
[p0163-l0005] [10.5pt] θi
[p0163-l0006] [10.5pt] 2 is added to the cost function.
[p0163-l0007] [10.5pt] This forces the learning algorithm to not only fit the data but also keep the model
[p0163-l0008] [10.5pt] weights as small as possible. Note that the regularization term should only be added
[p0163-l0009] [10.5pt] to the cost function during training. Once the model is trained, you want to evaluate
[p0163-l0010] [10.5pt] the model’s performance using the unregularized performance measure.
[p0163-l0011] [9.6pt] It is quite common for the cost function used during training to be
[p0163-l0012] [9.6pt] different from the performance measure used for testing. Apart
[p0163-l0013] [9.6pt] from regularization, another reason why they might be different is
[p0163-l0014] [9.6pt] that a good training cost function should have optimization-
[p0163-l0015] [9.6pt] friendly derivatives, while the performance measure used for test‐
[p0163-l0016] [9.6pt] ing should be as close as possible to the final objective. A good
[p0163-l0017] [9.6pt] example of this is a classifier trained using a cost function such as
[p0163-l0018] [9.6pt] the log loss (discussed in a moment) but evaluated using precision/
[p0163-l0019] [9.6pt] recall.
[p0163-l0020] [10.5pt] The hyperparameter α controls how much you want to regularize the model. If α = 0
[p0163-l0021] [10.5pt] then Ridge Regression is just Linear Regression. If α is very large, then all weights end
[p0163-l0022] [10.5pt] up very close to zero and the result is a flat line going through the data’s mean. Equa‐
[p0163-l0023] [10.5pt] tion 4-8 presents the Ridge Regression cost function.11
[p0163-l0024] [10.5pt] Equation 4-8. Ridge Regression cost function
[p0163-l0025] [8.0pt] 2
[p0163-l0026] [10.0pt] J θ = MSE θ + α1
[p0163-l0027] [10.0pt] 2 ∑i = 1
[p0163-l0028] [8.0pt] n
[p0163-l0029] [10.0pt] θi
[p0163-l0030] [10.5pt] Note that the bias term θ0 is not regularized (the sum starts at i = 1, not 0). If we
[p0163-l0031] [10.5pt] define w as the vector of feature weights (θ1 to θn), then the regularization term is
[p0163-l0032] [10.5pt] simply equal to ½(∥ w ∥2)2, where ∥ w ∥2 represents the ℓ2 norm of the weight vector.12
[p0163-l0033] [10.5pt] For Gradient Descent, just add αw to the MSE gradient vector (Equation 4-6).
[p0163-l0034] [9.6pt] It is important to scale the data (e.g., using a StandardScaler)
[p0163-l0035] [9.6pt] before performing Ridge Regression, as it is sensitive to the scale of
[p0163-l0036] [9.6pt] the input features. This is true of most regularized models.
[p0163-l0037] [8.0pt] 11 It is common to use the notation J(θ) for cost functions that don’t have a short name; we will often use this
[p0163-l0038] [8.0pt] notation throughout the rest of this book. The context will make it clear which cost function is being dis‐
[p0163-l0039] [8.0pt] cussed.
[p0163-l0040] [8.0pt] 12 Norms are discussed in Chapter 2.
[p0163-l0041] [9.0pt] Regularized Linear Models
[p0163-l0042] [9.0pt] |
[p0163-l0043] [9.0pt] 137

=== PDF page 164 / printed label 138 ===
[p0164-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 4-17 shows several Ridge models trained on some linear data using different α
[p0164-l0002] [10.5pt] value. On the left, plain Ridge models are used, leading to linear predictions. On the
[p0164-l0003] [10.5pt] right, the data is first expanded using PolynomialFeatures(degree=10), then it is
[p0164-l0004] [10.5pt] scaled using a StandardScaler, and finally the Ridge models are applied to the result‐
[p0164-l0005] [10.5pt] ing features: this is Polynomial Regression with Ridge regularization. Note how
[p0164-l0006] [10.5pt] increasing α leads to flatter (i.e., less extreme, more reasonable) predictions; this
[p0164-l0007] [10.5pt] reduces the model’s variance but increases its bias.
[p0164-l0008] [10.5pt] As with Linear Regression, we can perform Ridge Regression either by computing a
[p0164-l0009] [10.5pt] closed-form equation or by performing Gradient Descent. The pros and cons are the
[p0164-l0010] [10.5pt] same. Equation 4-9 shows the closed-form solution (where A is the (n + 1) × (n + 1)
[p0164-l0011] [10.5pt] identity matrix13 except with a 0 in the top-left cell, corresponding to the bias term).
[p0164-l0012] [10.5pt] Figure 4-17. Ridge Regression
[p0164-l0013] [10.5pt] Equation 4-9. Ridge Regression closed-form solution
[p0164-l0014] [10.0pt] θ = XTX + αA
[p0164-l0015] [10.0pt] −1   XT   y
[p0164-l0016] [10.5pt] Here is how to perform Ridge Regression with Scikit-Learn using a closed-form solu‐
[p0164-l0017] [10.5pt] tion (a variant of Equation 4-9 using a matrix factorization technique by André-Louis
[p0164-l0018] [10.5pt] Cholesky):
[p0164-l0019] [8.5pt] >>> from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge
[p0164-l0020] [8.5pt] >>> ridge_reg = Ridge(alpha=1, solver="cholesky")
[p0164-l0021] [8.5pt] >>> ridge_reg.fit(X, y)
[p0164-l0022] [8.0pt] 13 A square matrix full of 0s except for 1s on the main diagonal (top-left to bottom-right).

[p0165-l0008] [10.5pt] The penalty hyperparameter sets the type of regularization term to use. Specifying
[p0165-l0009] [10.5pt] "l2" indicates that you want SGD to add a regularization term to the cost function
[p0165-l0010] [10.5pt] equal to half the square of the ℓ2 norm of the weight vector: this is simply Ridge
[p0165-l0011] [10.5pt] Regression.
[p0165-l0012] [15.77pt] Lasso Regression
[p0165-l0013] [10.5pt] Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator Regression (simply called Lasso
[p0165-l0014] [10.5pt] Regression) is another regularized version of Linear Regression: just like Ridge
[p0165-l0015] [10.5pt] Regression, it adds a regularization term to the cost function, but it uses the ℓ1 norm
[p0165-l0016] [10.5pt] of the weight vector instead of half the square of the ℓ2 norm (see Equation 4-10).
[p0165-l0017] [10.5pt] Equation 4-10. Lasso Regression cost function
[p0165-l0018] [10.0pt] J θ = MSE θ + α∑i = 1
[p0165-l0019] [8.0pt] n
[p0165-l0020] [10.0pt] θi
[p0165-l0021] [10.5pt] Figure 4-18 shows the same thing as Figure 4-17 but replaces Ridge models with
[p0165-l0022] [10.5pt] Lasso models and uses smaller α values.
[p0165-l0023] [8.0pt] 14 Alternatively you can use the Ridge class with the "sag" solver. Stochastic Average GD is a variant of SGD.
[p0165-l0024] [8.0pt] For more details, see the presentation “Minimizing Finite Sums with the Stochastic Average Gradient Algo‐
[p0165-l0025] [8.0pt] rithm” by Mark Schmidt et al. from the University of British Columbia.
[p0165-l0026] [9.0pt] Regularized Linear Models
[p0165-l0027] [9.0pt] |
[p0165-l0028] [9.0pt] 139

=== PDF page 166 / printed label 140 ===
[p0166-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 4-18. Lasso Regression
[p0166-l0002] [10.5pt] An important characteristic of Lasso Regression is that it tends to completely elimi‐
[p0166-l0003] [10.5pt] nate the weights of the least important features (i.e., set them to zero). For example,
[p0166-l0004] [10.5pt] the dashed line in the right plot on Figure 4-18 (with α = 10-7) looks quadratic, almost
[p0166-l0005] [10.5pt] linear: all the weights for the high-degree polynomial features are equal to zero. In
[p0166-l0006] [10.5pt] other words, Lasso Regression automatically performs feature selection and outputs a
[p0166-l0007] [10.5pt] sparse model (i.e., with few nonzero feature weights).
[p0166-l0008] [10.5pt] You can get a sense of why this is the case by looking at Figure 4-19: on the top-left
[p0166-l0009] [10.5pt] plot, the background contours (ellipses) represent an unregularized MSE cost func‐
[p0166-l0010] [10.5pt] tion (α = 0), and the white circles show the Batch Gradient Descent path with that
[p0166-l0011] [10.5pt] cost function. The foreground contours (diamonds) represent the ℓ1 penalty, and the
[p0166-l0012] [10.5pt] triangles show the BGD path for this penalty only (α → ∞). Notice how the path first
[p0166-l0013] [10.5pt] reaches θ1 = 0, then rolls down a gutter until it reaches θ2 = 0. On the top-right plot,
[p0166-l0014] [10.5pt] the contours represent the same cost function plus an ℓ1 penalty with α = 0.5. The
[p0166-l0015] [10.5pt] global minimum is on the θ2 = 0 axis. BGD first reaches θ2 = 0, then rolls down the
[p0166-l0016] [10.5pt] gutter until it reaches the global minimum. The two bottom plots show the same
[p0166-l0017] [10.5pt] thing but uses an ℓ2 penalty instead. The regularized minimum is closer to θ = 0 than
[p0166-l0018] [10.5pt] the unregularized minimum, but the weights do not get fully eliminated.
[p0166-l0019] [9.0pt] 140
[p0166-l0020] [9.0pt] |
[p0166-l0021] [9.0pt] Chapter 4: Training Models

=== PDF page 167 / printed label 141 ===
[p0167-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 4-19. Lasso versus Ridge regularization
[p0167-l0002] [9.6pt] On the Lasso cost function, the BGD path tends to bounce across
[p0167-l0003] [9.6pt] the gutter toward the end. This is because the slope changes
[p0167-l0004] [9.6pt] abruptly at θ2 = 0. You need to gradually reduce the learning rate in
[p0167-l0005] [9.6pt] order to actually converge to the global minimum.
[p0167-l0006] [10.5pt] The Lasso cost function is not differentiable at θi = 0 (for i = 1, 2, ⋯, n), but Gradient
[p0167-l0007] [10.5pt] Descent still works fine if you use a subgradient vector g15 instead when any θi = 0.
[p0167-l0008] [10.5pt] Equation 4-11 shows a subgradient vector equation you can use for Gradient Descent
[p0167-l0009] [10.5pt] with the Lasso cost function.
[p0167-l0010] [10.5pt] Equation 4-11. Lasso Regression subgradient vector
[p0167-l0011] [10.0pt] −1 if θi < 0
[p0167-l0012] [10.0pt] sign θ1
[p0167-l0013] [10.0pt] sign θ2
[p0167-l0014] [10.0pt] 0 if θi = 0
[p0167-l0015] [10.0pt] g θ, J = ∇θ MSE θ + α
[p0167-l0016] [10.0pt]    where  sign θi =
[p0167-l0017] [10.0pt] +1 if θi > 0
[p0167-l0018] [10.0pt] ⋮
[p0167-l0019] [10.0pt] sign θn
[p0167-l0020] [8.0pt] 15 You can think of a subgradient vector at a nondifferentiable point as an intermediate vector between the gra‐
[p0167-l0021] [8.0pt] dient vectors around that point.

[p0168-l0008] [15.77pt] Elastic Net
[p0168-l0009] [10.5pt] Elastic Net is a middle ground between Ridge Regression and Lasso Regression. The
[p0168-l0010] [10.5pt] regularization term is a simple mix of both Ridge and Lasso’s regularization terms,
[p0168-l0011] [10.5pt] and you can control the mix ratio r. When r = 0, Elastic Net is equivalent to Ridge
[p0168-l0012] [10.5pt] Regression, and when r = 1, it is equivalent to Lasso Regression (see Equation 4-12).
[p0168-l0013] [10.5pt] Equation 4-12. Elastic Net cost function
[p0168-l0014] [8.0pt] 2
[p0168-l0015] [10.0pt] J θ = MSE θ + rα∑i = 1
[p0168-l0016] [8.0pt] n
[p0168-l0017] [10.0pt] θi + 1 −r
[p0168-l0018] [10.0pt] 2 α∑i = 1
[p0168-l0019] [8.0pt] n
[p0168-l0020] [10.0pt] θi
[p0168-l0021] [10.5pt] So when should you use plain Linear Regression (i.e., without any regularization),
[p0168-l0022] [10.5pt] Ridge, Lasso, or Elastic Net? It is almost always preferable to have at least a little bit of
[p0168-l0023] [10.5pt] regularization, so generally you should avoid plain Linear Regression. Ridge is a good
[p0168-l0024] [10.5pt] default, but if you suspect that only a few features are actually useful, you should pre‐
[p0168-l0025] [10.5pt] fer Lasso or Elastic Net since they tend to reduce the useless features’ weights down to
[p0168-l0026] [10.5pt] zero as we have discussed. In general, Elastic Net is preferred over Lasso since Lasso
[p0168-l0027] [10.5pt] may behave erratically when the number of features is greater than the number of
[p0168-l0028] [10.5pt] training instances or when several features are strongly correlated.
[p0168-l0029] [10.5pt] Here is a short example using Scikit-Learn’s ElasticNet (l1_ratio corresponds to
[p0168-l0030] [10.5pt] the mix ratio r):
[p0168-l0031] [8.5pt] >>> from sklearn.linear_model import ElasticNet
[p0168-l0032] [8.5pt] >>> elastic_net = ElasticNet(alpha=0.1, l1_ratio=0.5)
[p0168-l0033] [8.5pt] >>> elastic_net.fit(X, y)
[p0168-l0034] [8.5pt] >>> elastic_net.predict([[1.5]])
[p0168-l0035] [8.5pt] array([1.54333232])
[p0168-l0036] [15.77pt] Early Stopping
[p0168-l0037] [10.5pt] A very different way to regularize iterative learning algorithms such as Gradient
[p0168-l0038] [10.5pt] Descent is to stop training as soon as the validation error reaches a minimum. This is
[p0168-l0039] [10.5pt] called early stopping. Figure 4-20 shows a complex model (in this case a high-degree
[p0168-l0040] [10.5pt] Polynomial Regression model) being trained using Batch Gradient Descent. As the
[p0168-l0041] [10.5pt] epochs go by, the algorithm learns and its prediction error (RMSE) on the training set
[p0168-l0042] [10.5pt] naturally goes down, and so does its prediction error on the validation set. However,
[p0168-l0043] [9.0pt] 142
[p0168-l0044] [9.0pt] |
[p0168-l0045] [9.0pt] Chapter 4: Training Models

=== PDF page 169 / printed label 143 ===
[p0169-l0001] [10.5pt] after a while the validation error stops decreasing and actually starts to go back up.
[p0169-l0002] [10.5pt] This indicates that the model has started to overfit the training data. With early stop‐
[p0169-l0003] [10.5pt] ping you just stop training as soon as the validation error reaches the minimum. It is
[p0169-l0004] [10.5pt] such a simple and efficient regularization technique that Geoffrey Hinton called it a
[p0169-l0005] [10.5pt] “beautiful free lunch.”
[p0169-l0006] [10.5pt] Figure 4-20. Early stopping regularization
[p0169-l0007] [9.6pt] With Stochastic and Mini-batch Gradient Descent, the curves are
[p0169-l0008] [9.6pt] not so smooth, and it may be hard to know whether you have
[p0169-l0009] [9.6pt] reached the minimum or not. One solution is to stop only after the
[p0169-l0010] [9.6pt] validation error has been above the minimum for some time (when
[p0169-l0011] [9.6pt] you are confident that the model will not do any better), then roll
[p0169-l0012] [9.6pt] back the model parameters to the point where the validation error
[p0169-l0013] [9.6pt] was at a minimum.
[p0169-l0014] [10.5pt] Here is a basic implementation of early stopping:
[p0169-l0015] [8.5pt] from sklearn.base import clone
[p0169-l0016] [8.5pt] # prepare the data
[p0169-l0017] [8.5pt] poly_scaler = Pipeline([
[p0169-l0018] [8.5pt]         ("poly_features", PolynomialFeatures(degree=90, include_bias=False)),
[p0169-l0019] [8.5pt]         ("std_scaler", StandardScaler())
[p0169-l0020] [8.5pt]     ])
[p0169-l0021] [8.5pt] X_train_poly_scaled = poly_scaler.fit_transform(X_train)
[p0169-l0022] [8.5pt] X_val_poly_scaled = poly_scaler.transform(X_val)
[p0169-l0023] [8.5pt] sgd_reg = SGDRegressor(max_iter=1, tol=-np.infty, warm_start=True,
[p0169-l0024] [8.5pt]                        penalty=None, learning_rate="constant", eta0=0.0005)
[p0169-l0025] [9.0pt] Regularized Linear Models
[p0169-l0026] [9.0pt] |
[p0169-l0027] [9.0pt] 143

=== PDF page 170 / printed label 144 ===
[p0170-l0001] [8.5pt] minimum_val_error = float("inf")
[p0170-l0002] [8.5pt] best_epoch = None
[p0170-l0003] [8.5pt] best_model = None
[p0170-l0004] [8.5pt] for epoch in range(1000):
[p0170-l0005] [8.5pt]     sgd_reg.fit(X_train_poly_scaled, y_train)  # continues where it left off
[p0170-l0006] [8.5pt]     y_val_predict = sgd_reg.predict(X_val_poly_scaled)
[p0170-l0007] [8.5pt]     val_error = mean_squared_error(y_val, y_val_predict)
[p0170-l0008] [8.5pt]     if val_error < minimum_val_error:
[p0170-l0009] [8.5pt]         minimum_val_error = val_error
[p0170-l0010] [8.5pt]         best_epoch = epoch
[p0170-l0011] [8.5pt]         best_model = clone(sgd_reg)
[p0170-l0012] [10.5pt] Note that with warm_start=True, when the fit() method is called, it just continues
[p0170-l0013] [10.5pt] training where it left off instead of restarting from scratch.
[p0170-l0014] [18.92pt] Logistic Regression
[p0170-l0015] [10.5pt] As we discussed in Chapter 1, some regression algorithms can be used for classifica‐
[p0170-l0016] [10.5pt] tion as well (and vice versa). Logistic Regression (also called Logit Regression) is com‐
[p0170-l0017] [10.5pt] monly used to estimate the probability that an instance belongs to a particular class
[p0170-l0018] [10.5pt] (e.g., what is the probability that this email is spam?). If the estimated probability is
[p0170-l0019] [10.5pt] greater than 50%, then the model predicts that the instance belongs to that class
[p0170-l0020] [10.5pt] (called the positive class, labeled “1”), or else it predicts that it does not (i.e., it
[p0170-l0021] [10.5pt] belongs to the negative class, labeled “0”). This makes it a binary classifier.
[p0170-l0022] [15.77pt] Estimating Probabilities
[p0170-l0023] [10.5pt] So how does it work? Just like a Linear Regression model, a Logistic Regression
[p0170-l0024] [10.5pt] model computes a weighted sum of the input features (plus a bias term), but instead
[p0170-l0025] [10.5pt] of outputting the result directly like the Linear Regression model does, it outputs the
[p0170-l0026] [10.5pt] logistic of this result (see Equation 4-13).
[p0170-l0027] [10.5pt] Equation 4-13. Logistic Regression model estimated probability (vectorized form)
[p0170-l0028] [10.0pt] p = hθ x = σ xTθ
[p0170-l0029] [10.5pt] The logistic—noted σ(·)—is a sigmoid function (i.e., S-shaped) that outputs a number
[p0170-l0030] [10.5pt] between 0 and 1. It is defined as shown in Equation 4-14 and Figure 4-21.
[p0170-l0031] [10.5pt] Equation 4-14. Logistic function
[p0170-l0032] [10.0pt] σ t =
[p0170-l0033] [10.0pt] 1
[p0170-l0034] [10.0pt] 1 + exp
[p0170-l0035] [10.0pt] −t
[p0170-l0036] [9.0pt] 144
[p0170-l0037] [9.0pt] |
[p0170-l0038] [9.0pt] Chapter 4: Training Models

=== PDF page 171 / printed label 145 ===
[p0171-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 4-21. Logistic function
[p0171-l0002] [10.5pt] Once the Logistic Regression model has estimated the probability p = hθ(x) that an
[p0171-l0003] [10.5pt] instance x belongs to the positive class, it can make its prediction ŷ easily (see Equa‐
[p0171-l0004] [10.5pt] tion 4-15).
[p0171-l0005] [10.5pt] Equation 4-15. Logistic Regression model prediction
[p0171-l0006] [10.0pt] y = 0 if p < 0 . 5
[p0171-l0007] [10.0pt] 1 if p ≥0 . 5
[p0171-l0008] [10.5pt] Notice that σ(t) < 0.5 when t < 0, and σ(t) ≥ 0.5 when t ≥ 0, so a Logistic Regression
[p0171-l0009] [10.5pt] model predicts 1 if xT θ is positive, and 0 if it is negative.
[p0171-l0010] [9.6pt] The score t is often called the logit: this name comes from the fact
[p0171-l0011] [9.6pt] that the logit function, defined as logit(p) = log(p / (1 - p)), is the
[p0171-l0012] [9.6pt] inverse of the logistic function. Indeed, if you compute the logit of
[p0171-l0013] [9.6pt] the estimated probability p, you will find that the result is t. The
[p0171-l0014] [9.6pt] logit is also called the log-odds, since it is the log of the ratio
[p0171-l0015] [9.6pt] between the estimated probability for the positive class and the
[p0171-l0016] [9.6pt] estimated probability for the negative class.
[p0171-l0017] [15.77pt] Training and Cost Function
[p0171-l0018] [10.5pt] Good, now you know how a Logistic Regression model estimates probabilities and
[p0171-l0019] [10.5pt] makes predictions. But how is it trained? The objective of training is to set the param‐
[p0171-l0020] [10.5pt] eter vector θ so that the model estimates high probabilities for positive instances (y =
[p0171-l0021] [10.5pt] 1) and low probabilities for negative instances (y = 0). This idea is captured by the
[p0171-l0022] [10.5pt] cost function shown in Equation 4-16 for a single training instance x.
[p0171-l0023] [10.5pt] Equation 4-16. Cost function of a single training instance
[p0171-l0024] [10.0pt] −log p
[p0171-l0025] [10.0pt] if y = 1
[p0171-l0026] [10.0pt] c θ =
[p0171-l0027] [10.0pt] −log 1 −p if y = 0
[p0171-l0028] [9.0pt] Logistic Regression
[p0171-l0029] [9.0pt] |
[p0171-l0030] [9.0pt] 145

=== PDF page 172 / printed label 146 ===
[p0172-l0001] [10.5pt] This cost function makes sense because – log(t) grows very large when t approaches
[p0172-l0002] [10.5pt] 0, so the cost will be large if the model estimates a probability close to 0 for a positive
[p0172-l0003] [10.5pt] instance, and it will also be very large if the model estimates a probability close to 1
[p0172-l0004] [10.5pt] for a negative instance. On the other hand, – log(t) is close to 0 when t is close to 1, so
[p0172-l0005] [10.5pt] the cost will be close to 0 if the estimated probability is close to 0 for a negative
[p0172-l0006] [10.5pt] instance or close to 1 for a positive instance, which is precisely what we want.
[p0172-l0007] [10.5pt] The cost function over the whole training set is simply the average cost over all train‐
[p0172-l0008] [10.5pt] ing instances. It can be written in a single expression (as you can verify easily), called
[p0172-l0009] [10.5pt] the log loss, shown in Equation 4-17.
[p0172-l0010] [10.5pt] Equation 4-17. Logistic Regression cost function (log loss)
[p0172-l0011] [10.0pt] J θ = −1
[p0172-l0012] [8.0pt] m
[p0172-l0013] [10.0pt] y i log p i
[p0172-l0014] [10.0pt] + 1 −y i log 1 −p i
[p0172-l0015] [10.0pt] m ∑i = 1
[p0172-l0016] [10.5pt] The bad news is that there is no known closed-form equation to compute the value of
[p0172-l0017] [10.5pt] θ that minimizes this cost function (there is no equivalent of the Normal Equation).
[p0172-l0018] [10.5pt] But the good news is that this cost function is convex, so Gradient Descent (or any
[p0172-l0019] [10.5pt] other optimization algorithm) is guaranteed to find the global minimum (if the learn‐
[p0172-l0020] [10.5pt] ing rate is not too large and you wait long enough). The partial derivatives of the cost
[p0172-l0021] [10.5pt] function with regards to the jth model parameter θj is given by Equation 4-18.
[p0172-l0022] [10.5pt] Equation 4-18. Logistic cost function partial derivatives
[p0172-l0023] [8.0pt] m
[p0172-l0024] [8.0pt] i
[p0172-l0025] [10.0pt] J θ = 1
[p0172-l0026] [10.0pt] σ θTx i
[p0172-l0027] [10.0pt] −y i xj
[p0172-l0028] [8.0pt] i = 1
[p0172-l0029] [14.14pt] m ∑
[p0172-l0030] [10.0pt] ∂
[p0172-l0031] [10.0pt] ∂θj
[p0172-l0032] [10.5pt] This equation looks very much like Equation 4-5: for each instance it computes the
[p0172-l0033] [10.5pt] prediction error and multiplies it by the jth feature value, and then it computes the
[p0172-l0034] [10.5pt] average over all training instances. Once you have the gradient vector containing all
[p0172-l0035] [10.5pt] the partial derivatives you can use it in the Batch Gradient Descent algorithm. That’s
[p0172-l0036] [10.5pt] it: you now know how to train a Logistic Regression model. For Stochastic GD you
[p0172-l0037] [10.5pt] would of course just take one instance at a time, and for Mini-batch GD you would
[p0172-l0038] [10.5pt] use a mini-batch at a time.
[p0172-l0039] [15.77pt] Decision Boundaries
[p0172-l0040] [10.5pt] Let’s use the iris dataset to illustrate Logistic Regression. This is a famous dataset that
[p0172-l0041] [10.5pt] contains the sepal and petal length and width of 150 iris flowers of three different
[p0172-l0042] [10.5pt] species: Iris-Setosa, Iris-Versicolor, and Iris-Virginica (see Figure 4-22).
[p0172-l0043] [9.0pt] 146
[p0172-l0044] [9.0pt] |
[p0172-l0045] [9.0pt] Chapter 4: Training Models

=== PDF page 173 / printed label 147 ===
[p0173-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 4-22. Flowers of three iris plant species16
[p0173-l0002] [10.5pt] Let’s try to build a classifier to detect the Iris-Virginica type based only on the petal
[p0173-l0003] [10.5pt] width feature. First let’s load the data:
[p0173-l0004] [8.5pt] >>> from sklearn import datasets
[p0173-l0005] [8.5pt] >>> iris = datasets.load_iris()
[p0173-l0006] [8.5pt] >>> list(iris.keys())
[p0173-l0007] [8.5pt] ['data', 'target', 'target_names', 'DESCR', 'feature_names', 'filename']
[p0173-l0008] [8.5pt] >>> X = iris["data"][:, 3:]  # petal width
[p0173-l0009] [8.5pt] >>> y = (iris["target"] == 2).astype(np.int)  # 1 if Iris-Virginica, else 0
[p0173-l0010] [10.5pt] Now let’s train a Logistic Regression model:
[p0173-l0011] [8.5pt] from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
[p0173-l0012] [8.5pt] log_reg = LogisticRegression()
[p0173-l0013] [8.5pt] log_reg.fit(X, y)

[p0174-l0003] [10.5pt] Figure 4-23. Estimated probabilities and decision boundary
[p0174-l0004] [10.5pt] The petal width of Iris-Virginica flowers (represented by triangles) ranges from 1.4
[p0174-l0005] [10.5pt] cm to 2.5 cm, while the other iris flowers (represented by squares) generally have a
[p0174-l0006] [10.5pt] smaller petal width, ranging from 0.1 cm to 1.8 cm. Notice that there is a bit of over‐
[p0174-l0007] [10.5pt] lap. Above about 2 cm the classifier is highly confident that the flower is an Iris-
[p0174-l0008] [10.5pt] Virginica (it outputs a high probability to that class), while below 1 cm it is highly
[p0174-l0009] [10.5pt] confident that it is not an Iris-Virginica (high probability for the “Not Iris-Virginica”
[p0174-l0010] [10.5pt] class). In between these extremes, the classifier is unsure. However, if you ask it to
[p0174-l0011] [10.5pt] predict the class (using the predict() method rather than the predict_proba()
[p0174-l0012] [10.5pt] method), it will return whichever class is the most likely. Therefore, there is a decision
[p0174-l0013] [10.5pt] boundary at around 1.6 cm where both probabilities are equal to 50%: if the petal
[p0174-l0014] [10.5pt] width is higher than 1.6 cm, the classifier will predict that the flower is an Iris-
[p0174-l0015] [10.5pt] Virginica, or else it will predict that it is not (even if it is not very confident):
[p0174-l0016] [8.5pt] >>> log_reg.predict([[1.7], [1.5]])
[p0174-l0017] [8.5pt] array([1, 0])
[p0174-l0018] [10.5pt] Figure 4-24 shows the same dataset but this time displaying two features: petal width
[p0174-l0019] [10.5pt] and length. Once trained, the Logistic Regression classifier can estimate the probabil‐
[p0174-l0020] [10.5pt] ity that a new flower is an Iris-Virginica based on these two features. The dashed line
[p0174-l0021] [10.5pt] represents the points where the model estimates a 50% probability: this is the model’s
[p0174-l0022] [10.5pt] decision boundary. Note that it is a linear boundary.18 Each parallel line represents the
[p0174-l0023] [10.5pt] points where the model outputs a specific probability, from 15% (bottom left) to 90%
[p0174-l0024] [10.5pt] (top right). All the flowers beyond the top-right line have an over 90% chance of
[p0174-l0025] [10.5pt] being Iris-Virginica according to the model.
[p0174-l0026] [8.0pt] 18 It is the the set of points x such that θ0 + θ1x1 + θ2x2 = 0, which defines a straight line.

[p0175-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 4-24. Linear decision boundary
[p0175-l0002] [10.5pt] Just like the other linear models, Logistic Regression models can be regularized using
[p0175-l0003] [10.5pt] ℓ1 or ℓ2 penalties. Scitkit-Learn actually adds an ℓ2 penalty by default.
[p0175-l0004] [9.6pt] The hyperparameter controlling the regularization strength of a
[p0175-l0005] [9.6pt] Scikit-Learn LogisticRegression model is not alpha (as in other
[p0175-l0006] [9.6pt] linear models), but its inverse: C. The higher the value of C, the less
[p0175-l0007] [9.6pt] the model is regularized.
[p0175-l0008] [15.77pt] Softmax Regression
[p0175-l0009] [10.5pt] The Logistic Regression model can be generalized to support multiple classes directly,
[p0175-l0010] [10.5pt] without having to train and combine multiple binary classifiers (as discussed in
[p0175-l0011] [10.5pt] Chapter 3). This is called Softmax Regression, or Multinomial Logistic Regression.
[p0175-l0012] [10.5pt] The idea is quite simple: when given an instance x, the Softmax Regression model
[p0175-l0013] [10.5pt] first computes a score sk(x) for each class k, then estimates the probability of each
[p0175-l0014] [10.5pt] class by applying the softmax function (also called the normalized exponential) to the
[p0175-l0015] [10.5pt] scores. The equation to compute sk(x) should look familiar, as it is just like the equa‐
[p0175-l0016] [10.5pt] tion for Linear Regression prediction (see Equation 4-19).
[p0175-l0017] [10.5pt] Equation 4-19. Softmax score for class k
[p0175-l0018] [10.0pt] sk x = xTθ k
[p0175-l0019] [10.5pt] Note that each class has its own dedicated parameter vector θ(k). All these vectors are
[p0175-l0020] [10.5pt] typically stored as rows in a parameter matrix Θ.
[p0175-l0021] [10.5pt] Once you have computed the score of every class for the instance x, you can estimate
[p0175-l0022] [10.5pt] the probability pk that the instance belongs to class k by running the scores through
[p0175-l0023] [10.5pt] the softmax function (Equation 4-20): it computes the exponential of every score,
[p0175-l0024] [9.0pt] Logistic Regression
[p0175-l0025] [9.0pt] |
[p0175-l0026] [9.0pt] 149

=== PDF page 176 / printed label 150 ===
[p0176-l0001] [10.5pt] then normalizes them (dividing by the sum of all the exponentials). The scores are
[p0176-l0002] [10.5pt] generally called logits or log-odds (although they are actually unnormalized log-
[p0176-l0003] [10.5pt] odds).
[p0176-l0004] [10.5pt] Equation 4-20. Softmax function
[p0176-l0005] [10.0pt] exp sk x
[p0176-l0006] [10.0pt] pk = σ s x
[p0176-l0007] [10.0pt] k =
[p0176-l0008] [10.0pt] ∑j = 1
[p0176-l0009] [8.0pt] K
[p0176-l0010] [10.0pt] exp sj x
[p0176-l0011] [10.5pt] • K is the number of classes.
[p0176-l0012] [10.5pt] • s(x) is a vector containing the scores of each class for the instance x.
[p0176-l0013] [10.5pt] • σ(s(x))k is the estimated probability that the instance x belongs to class k given
[p0176-l0014] [10.5pt] the scores of each class for that instance.
[p0176-l0015] [10.5pt] Just like the Logistic Regression classifier, the Softmax Regression classifier predicts
[p0176-l0016] [10.5pt] the class with the highest estimated probability (which is simply the class with the
[p0176-l0017] [10.5pt] highest score), as shown in Equation 4-21.
[p0176-l0018] [10.5pt] Equation 4-21. Softmax Regression classifier prediction
[p0176-l0019] [10.0pt] y = argmax
[p0176-l0020] [10.0pt] θ k Tx
[p0176-l0021] [10.0pt] σ s x
[p0176-l0022] [10.0pt] k = argmax
[p0176-l0023] [10.0pt] sk x = argmax
[p0176-l0024] [8.0pt] k
[p0176-l0025] [8.0pt] k
[p0176-l0026] [8.0pt] k
[p0176-l0027] [10.5pt] • The argmax operator returns the value of a variable that maximizes a function. In
[p0176-l0028] [10.5pt] this equation, it returns the value of k that maximizes the estimated probability
[p0176-l0029] [10.5pt] σ(s(x))k.
[p0176-l0030] [9.6pt] The Softmax Regression classifier predicts only one class at a time
[p0176-l0031] [9.6pt] (i.e., it is multiclass, not multioutput) so it should be used only with
[p0176-l0032] [9.6pt] mutually exclusive classes such as different types of plants. You
[p0176-l0033] [9.6pt] cannot use it to recognize multiple people in one picture.
[p0176-l0034] [10.5pt] Now that you know how the model estimates probabilities and makes predictions,
[p0176-l0035] [10.5pt] let’s take a look at training. The objective is to have a model that estimates a high
[p0176-l0036] [10.5pt] probability for the target class (and consequently a low probability for the other
[p0176-l0037] [10.5pt] classes). Minimizing the cost function shown in Equation 4-22, called the cross
[p0176-l0038] [10.5pt] entropy, should lead to this objective because it penalizes the model when it estimates
[p0176-l0039] [10.5pt] a low probability for a target class. Cross entropy is frequently used to measure how
[p0176-l0040] [9.0pt] 150
[p0176-l0041] [9.0pt] |
[p0176-l0042] [9.0pt] Chapter 4: Training Models

[p0177-l0001] [10.5pt] well a set of estimated class probabilities match the target classes (we will use it again
[p0177-l0002] [10.5pt] several times in the following chapters).
[p0177-l0003] [10.5pt] Equation 4-22. Cross entropy cost function
[p0177-l0004] [8.0pt] i
[p0177-l0005] [10.0pt] J Θ = −1
[p0177-l0006] [10.0pt] i log pk
[p0177-l0007] [8.0pt] m
[p0177-l0008] [10.0pt] ∑k = 1
[p0177-l0009] [8.0pt] K
[p0177-l0010] [10.0pt] yk
[p0177-l0011] [10.0pt] m ∑i = 1
[p0177-l0012] [10.5pt] • yk
[p0177-l0013] [10.5pt] i is the target probability that the ith instance belongs to class k. In general, it is
[p0177-l0014] [10.5pt] either equal to 1 or 0, depending on whether the instance belongs to the class or
[p0177-l0015] [10.5pt] not.
[p0177-l0016] [10.5pt] Notice that when there are just two classes (K = 2), this cost function is equivalent to
[p0177-l0017] [10.5pt] the Logistic Regression’s cost function (log loss; see Equation 4-17).
[p0177-l0018] [15.0pt] Cross Entropy
[p0177-l0019] [10.0pt] Cross entropy originated from information theory. Suppose you want to efficiently
[p0177-l0020] [10.0pt] transmit information about the weather every day. If there are eight options (sunny,
[p0177-l0021] [10.0pt] rainy, etc.), you could encode each option using 3 bits since 23 = 8. However, if you
[p0177-l0022] [10.0pt] think it will be sunny almost every day, it would be much more efficient to code
[p0177-l0023] [10.0pt] “sunny” on just one bit (0) and the other seven options on 4 bits (starting with a 1).
[p0177-l0024] [10.0pt] Cross entropy measures the average number of bits you actually send per option. If
[p0177-l0025] [10.0pt] your assumption about the weather is perfect, cross entropy will just be equal to the
[p0177-l0026] [10.0pt] entropy of the weather itself (i.e., its intrinsic unpredictability). But if your assump‐
[p0177-l0027] [10.0pt] tions are wrong (e.g., if it rains often), cross entropy will be greater by an amount
[p0177-l0028] [10.0pt] called the Kullback–Leibler divergence.
[p0177-l0029] [10.0pt] The cross entropy between two probability distributions p and q is defined as
[p0177-l0030] [10.0pt] H p, q = −∑x p x log q x (at least when the distributions are discrete). For more
[p0177-l0031] [10.0pt] details, check out this video.
[p0177-l0032] [10.5pt] The gradient vector of this cost function with regards to θ(k) is given by Equation
[p0177-l0033] [10.5pt] 4-23:
[p0177-l0034] [10.5pt] Equation 4-23. Cross entropy gradient vector for class k
[p0177-l0035] [8.0pt] m
[p0177-l0036] [10.0pt] ∇
[p0177-l0037] [10.0pt] i x i
[p0177-l0038] [10.0pt] pk
[p0177-l0039] [10.0pt] i −yk
[p0177-l0040] [10.0pt] θ k J Θ = 1
[p0177-l0041] [8.0pt] i = 1
[p0177-l0042] [14.14pt] m ∑
[p0177-l0043] [10.5pt] Now you can compute the gradient vector for every class, then use Gradient Descent
[p0177-l0044] [10.5pt] (or any other optimization algorithm) to find the parameter matrix Θ that minimizes
[p0177-l0045] [10.5pt] the cost function.

[p0178-l0001] [10.5pt] Let’s use Softmax Regression to classify the iris flowers into all three classes. Scikit-
[p0178-l0002] [10.5pt] Learn’s LogisticRegression uses one-versus-all by default when you train it on more
[p0178-l0003] [10.5pt] than two classes, but you can set the multi_class hyperparameter to "multinomial"
[p0178-l0004] [10.5pt] to switch it to Softmax Regression instead. You must also specify a solver that sup‐
[p0178-l0005] [10.5pt] ports Softmax Regression, such as the "lbfgs" solver (see Scikit-Learn’s documenta‐
[p0178-l0006] [10.5pt] tion for more details). It also applies ℓ2 regularization by default, which you can
[p0178-l0007] [10.5pt] control using the hyperparameter C.
[p0178-l0008] [8.5pt] X = iris["data"][:, (2, 3)]  # petal length, petal width
[p0178-l0009] [8.5pt] y = iris["target"]
[p0178-l0010] [8.5pt] softmax_reg = LogisticRegression(multi_class="multinomial",solver="lbfgs", C=10)
[p0178-l0011] [8.5pt] softmax_reg.fit(X, y)
[p0178-l0012] [10.5pt] So the next time you find an iris with 5 cm long and 2 cm wide petals, you can ask
[p0178-l0013] [10.5pt] your model to tell you what type of iris it is, and it will answer Iris-Virginica (class 2)
[p0178-l0014] [10.5pt] with 94.2% probability (or Iris-Versicolor with 5.8% probability):
[p0178-l0015] [8.5pt] >>> softmax_reg.predict([[5, 2]])
[p0178-l0016] [8.5pt] array([2])
[p0178-l0017] [8.5pt] >>> softmax_reg.predict_proba([[5, 2]])
[p0178-l0018] [8.5pt] array([[6.38014896e-07, 5.74929995e-02, 9.42506362e-01]])
[p0178-l0019] [10.5pt] Figure 4-25 shows the resulting decision boundaries, represented by the background
[p0178-l0020] [10.5pt] colors. Notice that the decision boundaries between any two classes are linear. The
[p0178-l0021] [10.5pt] figure also shows the probabilities for the Iris-Versicolor class, represented by the
[p0178-l0022] [10.5pt] curved lines (e.g., the line labeled with 0.450 represents the 45% probability bound‐
[p0178-l0023] [10.5pt] ary). Notice that the model can predict a class that has an estimated probability below
[p0178-l0024] [10.5pt] 50%. For example, at the point where all decision boundaries meet, all classes have an

[p0181-l0001] [16.82pt] CHAPTER 5
[p0181-l0002] [25.22pt] Support Vector Machines
[p0181-l0003] [9.6pt] With Early Release ebooks, you get books in their earliest form—
[p0181-l0004] [9.6pt] the author’s raw and unedited content as he or she writes—so you
[p0181-l0005] [9.6pt] can take advantage of these technologies long before the official
[p0181-l0006] [9.6pt] release of these titles. The following will be Chapter 5 in the final
[p0181-l0007] [9.6pt] release of the book.
[p0181-l0008] [10.5pt] A Support Vector Machine (SVM) is a very powerful and versatile Machine Learning
[p0181-l0009] [10.5pt] model, capable of performing linear or nonlinear classification, regression, and even
[p0181-l0010] [10.5pt] outlier detection. It is one of the most popular models in Machine Learning, and any‐
[p0181-l0011] [10.5pt] one interested in Machine Learning should have it in their toolbox. SVMs are partic‐
[p0181-l0012] [10.5pt] ularly well suited for classification of complex but small- or medium-sized datasets.
[p0181-l0013] [10.5pt] This chapter will explain the core concepts of SVMs, how to use them, and how they
[p0181-l0014] [10.5pt] work.
[p0181-l0015] [18.92pt] Linear SVM Classification
[p0181-l0016] [10.5pt] The fundamental idea behind SVMs is best explained with some pictures. Figure 5-1
[p0181-l0017] [10.5pt] shows part of the iris dataset that was introduced at the end of Chapter 4. The two
[p0181-l0018] [10.5pt] classes can clearly be separated easily with a straight line (they are linearly separable).
[p0181-l0019] [10.5pt] The left plot shows the decision boundaries of three possible linear classifiers. The
[p0181-l0020] [10.5pt] model whose decision boundary is represented by the dashed line is so bad that it
[p0181-l0021] [10.5pt] does not even separate the classes properly. The other two models work perfectly on
[p0181-l0022] [10.5pt] this training set, but their decision boundaries come so close to the instances that
[p0181-l0023] [10.5pt] these models will probably not perform as well on new instances. In contrast, the
[p0181-l0024] [10.5pt] solid line in the plot on the right represents the decision boundary of an SVM classi‐
[p0181-l0025] [10.5pt] fier; this line not only separates the two classes but also stays as far away from the
[p0181-l0026] [10.5pt] closest training instances as possible. You can think of an SVM classifier as fitting the
[p0181-l0027] [9.0pt] 155

=== PDF page 182 / printed label 156 ===
[p0182-l0001] [10.5pt] widest possible street (represented by the parallel dashed lines) between the classes.
[p0182-l0002] [10.5pt] This is called large margin classification.
[p0182-l0003] [10.5pt] Figure 5-1. Large margin classification
[p0182-l0004] [10.5pt] Notice that adding more training instances “off the street” will not affect the decision
[p0182-l0005] [10.5pt] boundary at all: it is fully determined (or “supported”) by the instances located on the
[p0182-l0006] [10.5pt] edge of the street. These instances are called the support vectors (they are circled in
[p0182-l0007] [10.5pt] Figure 5-1).
[p0182-l0008] [9.6pt] SVMs are sensitive to the feature scales, as you can see in
[p0182-l0009] [9.6pt] Figure 5-2: on the left plot, the vertical scale is much larger than the
[p0182-l0010] [9.6pt] horizontal scale, so the widest possible street is close to horizontal.
[p0182-l0011] [9.6pt] After feature scaling (e.g., using Scikit-Learn’s StandardScaler),
[p0182-l0012] [9.6pt] the decision boundary looks much better (on the right plot).
[p0182-l0013] [10.5pt] Figure 5-2. Sensitivity to feature scales
[p0182-l0014] [15.77pt] Soft Margin Classification
[p0182-l0015] [10.5pt] If we strictly impose that all instances be off the street and on the right side, this is
[p0182-l0016] [10.5pt] called hard margin classification. There are two main issues with hard margin classifi‐
[p0182-l0017] [10.5pt] cation. First, it only works if the data is linearly separable, and second it is quite sensi‐
[p0182-l0018] [10.5pt] tive to outliers. Figure 5-3 shows the iris dataset with just one additional outlier: on
[p0182-l0019] [10.5pt] the left, it is impossible to find a hard margin, and on the right the decision boundary
[p0182-l0020] [10.5pt] ends up very different from the one we saw in Figure 5-1 without the outlier, and it
[p0182-l0021] [10.5pt] will probably not generalize as well.
[p0182-l0022] [9.0pt] 156
[p0182-l0023] [9.0pt] |
[p0182-l0024] [9.0pt] Chapter 5: Support Vector Machines

=== PDF page 183 / printed label 157 ===
[p0183-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 5-3. Hard margin sensitivity to outliers
[p0183-l0002] [10.5pt] To avoid these issues it is preferable to use a more flexible model. The objective is to
[p0183-l0003] [10.5pt] find a good balance between keeping the street as large as possible and limiting the
[p0183-l0004] [10.5pt] margin violations (i.e., instances that end up in the middle of the street or even on the
[p0183-l0005] [10.5pt] wrong side). This is called soft margin classification.
[p0183-l0006] [10.5pt] In Scikit-Learn’s SVM classes, you can control this balance using the C hyperparame‐
[p0183-l0007] [10.5pt] ter: a smaller C value leads to a wider street but more margin violations. Figure 5-4
[p0183-l0008] [10.5pt] shows the decision boundaries and margins of two soft margin SVM classifiers on a
[p0183-l0009] [10.5pt] nonlinearly separable dataset. On the left, using a low C value the margin is quite
[p0183-l0010] [10.5pt] large, but many instances end up on the street. On the right, using a high C value the
[p0183-l0011] [10.5pt] classifier makes fewer margin violations but ends up with a smaller margin. However,
[p0183-l0012] [10.5pt] it seems likely that the first classifier will generalize better: in fact even on this train‐
[p0183-l0013] [10.5pt] ing set it makes fewer prediction errors, since most of the margin violations are
[p0183-l0014] [10.5pt] actually on the correct side of the decision boundary.
[p0183-l0015] [10.5pt] Figure 5-4. Large margin (left) versus fewer margin violations (right)
[p0183-l0016] [9.6pt] If your SVM model is overfitting, you can try regularizing it by
[p0183-l0017] [9.6pt] reducing C.
[p0183-l0018] [10.5pt] The following Scikit-Learn code loads the iris dataset, scales the features, and then
[p0183-l0019] [10.5pt] trains a linear SVM model (using the LinearSVC class with C = 1 and the hinge loss
[p0183-l0020] [10.5pt] function, described shortly) to detect Iris-Virginica flowers. The resulting model is
[p0183-l0021] [10.5pt] represented on the left of Figure 5-4.
[p0183-l0022] [9.0pt] Linear SVM Classification
[p0183-l0023] [9.0pt] |
[p0183-l0024] [9.0pt] 157

[p0184-l0001] [8.5pt] import numpy as np
[p0184-l0002] [8.5pt] from sklearn import datasets
[p0184-l0003] [8.5pt] from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
[p0184-l0004] [8.5pt] from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
[p0184-l0005] [8.5pt] from sklearn.svm import LinearSVC
[p0184-l0006] [8.5pt] iris = datasets.load_iris()
[p0184-l0007] [8.5pt] X = iris["data"][:, (2, 3)]  # petal length, petal width
[p0184-l0008] [8.5pt] y = (iris["target"] == 2).astype(np.float64)  # Iris-Virginica
[p0184-l0009] [8.5pt] svm_clf = Pipeline([
[p0184-l0010] [8.5pt]         ("scaler", StandardScaler()),
[p0184-l0011] [8.5pt]         ("linear_svc", LinearSVC(C=1, loss="hinge")),
[p0184-l0012] [8.5pt]     ])
[p0184-l0013] [8.5pt] svm_clf.fit(X, y)
[p0184-l0014] [10.5pt] Then, as usual, you can use the model to make predictions:
[p0184-l0015] [8.5pt] >>> svm_clf.predict([[5.5, 1.7]])
[p0184-l0016] [8.5pt] array([1.])
[p0184-l0017] [9.6pt] Unlike Logistic Regression classifiers, SVM classifiers do not out‐
[p0184-l0018] [9.6pt] put probabilities for each class.
[p0184-l0019] [10.5pt] Alternatively, you could use the SVC class, using SVC(kernel="linear", C=1), but it
[p0184-l0020] [10.5pt] is much slower, especially with large training sets, so it is not recommended. Another
[p0184-l0021] [10.5pt] option is to use the SGDClassifier class, with SGDClassifier(loss="hinge",
[p0184-l0022] [10.5pt] alpha=1/(m*C)). This applies regular Stochastic Gradient Descent (see Chapter 4) to
[p0184-l0023] [10.5pt] train a linear SVM classifier. It does not converge as fast as the LinearSVC class, but it
[p0184-l0024] [10.5pt] can be useful to handle huge datasets that do not fit in memory (out-of-core train‐
[p0184-l0025] [10.5pt] ing), or to handle online classification tasks.
[p0184-l0026] [9.6pt] The LinearSVC class regularizes the bias term, so you should center
[p0184-l0027] [9.6pt] the training set first by subtracting its mean. This is automatic if
[p0184-l0028] [9.6pt] you scale the data using the StandardScaler. Moreover, make sure
[p0184-l0029] [9.6pt] you set the loss hyperparameter to "hinge", as it is not the default
[p0184-l0030] [9.6pt] value. Finally, for better performance you should set the dual
[p0184-l0031] [9.6pt] hyperparameter to False, unless there are more features than
[p0184-l0032] [9.6pt] training instances (we will discuss duality later in the chapter).
