[p0185-l0001] [18.92pt] Nonlinear SVM Classification
[p0185-l0002] [10.5pt] Although linear SVM classifiers are efficient and work surprisingly well in many
[p0185-l0003] [10.5pt] cases, many datasets are not even close to being linearly separable. One approach to
[p0185-l0004] [10.5pt] handling nonlinear datasets is to add more features, such as polynomial features (as
[p0185-l0005] [10.5pt] you did in Chapter 4); in some cases this can result in a linearly separable dataset.
[p0185-l0006] [10.5pt] Consider the left plot in Figure 5-5: it represents a simple dataset with just one feature
[p0185-l0007] [10.5pt] x1. This dataset is not linearly separable, as you can see. But if you add a second fea‐
[p0185-l0008] [10.5pt] ture x2 = (x1)2, the resulting 2D dataset is perfectly linearly separable.
[p0185-l0009] [10.5pt] Figure 5-5. Adding features to make a dataset linearly separable
[p0185-l0010] [10.5pt] To implement this idea using Scikit-Learn, you can create a Pipeline containing a
[p0185-l0011] [10.5pt] PolynomialFeatures transformer (discussed in “Polynomial Regression” on page
[p0185-l0012] [10.5pt] 130), followed by a StandardScaler and a LinearSVC. Let’s test this on the moons
[p0185-l0013] [10.5pt] dataset: this is a toy dataset for binary classification in which the data points are sha‐
[p0185-l0014] [10.5pt] ped as two interleaving half circles (see Figure 5-6). You can generate this dataset
[p0185-l0015] [10.5pt] using the make_moons() function:
[p0185-l0016] [8.5pt] from sklearn.datasets import make_moons
[p0185-l0017] [8.5pt] from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
[p0185-l0018] [8.5pt] from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures
[p0185-l0019] [8.5pt] polynomial_svm_clf = Pipeline([
[p0185-l0020] [8.5pt]         ("poly_features", PolynomialFeatures(degree=3)),
[p0185-l0021] [8.5pt]         ("scaler", StandardScaler()),
[p0185-l0022] [8.5pt]         ("svm_clf", LinearSVC(C=10, loss="hinge"))
[p0185-l0023] [8.5pt]     ])
[p0185-l0024] [8.5pt] polynomial_svm_clf.fit(X, y)
[p0185-l0025] [9.0pt] Nonlinear SVM Classification
[p0185-l0026] [9.0pt] |
[p0185-l0027] [9.0pt] 159

=== PDF page 186 / printed label 160 ===
[p0186-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 5-6. Linear SVM classifier using polynomial features
[p0186-l0002] [15.77pt] Polynomial Kernel
[p0186-l0003] [10.5pt] Adding polynomial features is simple to implement and can work great with all sorts
[p0186-l0004] [10.5pt] of Machine Learning algorithms (not just SVMs), but at a low polynomial degree it
[p0186-l0005] [10.5pt] cannot deal with very complex datasets, and with a high polynomial degree it creates
[p0186-l0006] [10.5pt] a huge number of features, making the model too slow.
[p0186-l0007] [10.5pt] Fortunately, when using SVMs you can apply an almost miraculous mathematical
[p0186-l0008] [10.5pt] technique called the kernel trick (it is explained in a moment). It makes it possible to
[p0186-l0009] [10.5pt] get the same result as if you added many polynomial features, even with very high-
[p0186-l0010] [10.5pt] degree polynomials, without actually having to add them. So there is no combinato‐
[p0186-l0011] [10.5pt] rial explosion of the number of features since you don’t actually add any features. This
[p0186-l0012] [10.5pt] trick is implemented by the SVC class. Let’s test it on the moons dataset:
[p0186-l0013] [8.5pt] from sklearn.svm import SVC
[p0186-l0014] [8.5pt] poly_kernel_svm_clf = Pipeline([
[p0186-l0015] [8.5pt]         ("scaler", StandardScaler()),
[p0186-l0016] [8.5pt]         ("svm_clf", SVC(kernel="poly", degree=3, coef0=1, C=5))
[p0186-l0017] [8.5pt]     ])
[p0186-l0018] [8.5pt] poly_kernel_svm_clf.fit(X, y)
[p0186-l0019] [10.5pt] This code trains an SVM classifier using a 3rd-degree polynomial kernel. It is repre‐
[p0186-l0020] [10.5pt] sented on the left of Figure 5-7. On the right is another SVM classifier using a 10th-
[p0186-l0021] [10.5pt] degree polynomial kernel. Obviously, if your model is overfitting, you might want to
[p0186-l0022] [9.0pt] 160
[p0186-l0023] [9.0pt] |
[p0186-l0024] [9.0pt] Chapter 5: Support Vector Machines

=== PDF page 187 / printed label 161 ===
[p0187-l0001] [10.5pt] reduce the polynomial degree. Conversely, if it is underfitting, you can try increasing
[p0187-l0002] [10.5pt] it. The hyperparameter coef0 controls how much the model is influenced by high-
[p0187-l0003] [10.5pt] degree polynomials versus low-degree polynomials.
[p0187-l0004] [10.5pt] Figure 5-7. SVM classifiers with a polynomial kernel
[p0187-l0005] [9.6pt] A common approach to find the right hyperparameter values is to
[p0187-l0006] [9.6pt] use grid search (see Chapter 2). It is often faster to first do a very
[p0187-l0007] [9.6pt] coarse grid search, then a finer grid search around the best values
[p0187-l0008] [9.6pt] found. Having a good sense of what each hyperparameter actually
[p0187-l0009] [9.6pt] does can also help you search in the right part of the hyperparame‐
[p0187-l0010] [9.6pt] ter space.
[p0187-l0011] [15.77pt] Adding Similarity Features
[p0187-l0012] [10.5pt] Another technique to tackle nonlinear problems is to add features computed using a
[p0187-l0013] [10.5pt] similarity function that measures how much each instance resembles a particular
[p0187-l0014] [10.5pt] landmark. For example, let’s take the one-dimensional dataset discussed earlier and
[p0187-l0015] [10.5pt] add two landmarks to it at x1 = –2 and x1 = 1 (see the left plot in Figure 5-8). Next,
[p0187-l0016] [10.5pt] let’s define the similarity function to be the Gaussian Radial Basis Function (RBF)
[p0187-l0017] [10.5pt] with γ = 0.3 (see Equation 5-1).
[p0187-l0018] [10.5pt] Equation 5-1. Gaussian RBF
[p0187-l0019] [10.0pt] ϕγ x, ℓ= exp −γ∥x −ℓ∥2
[p0187-l0020] [10.5pt] It is a bell-shaped function varying from 0 (very far away from the landmark) to 1 (at
[p0187-l0021] [10.5pt] the landmark). Now we are ready to compute the new features. For example, let’s look
[p0187-l0022] [10.5pt] at the instance x1 = –1: it is located at a distance of 1 from the first landmark, and 2
[p0187-l0023] [10.5pt] from the second landmark. Therefore its new features are x2 = exp (–0.3 × 12) ≈ 0.74
[p0187-l0024] [10.5pt] and x3 = exp (–0.3 × 22) ≈ 0.30. The plot on the right of Figure 5-8 shows the trans‐
[p0187-l0025] [10.5pt] formed dataset (dropping the original features). As you can see, it is now linearly
[p0187-l0026] [10.5pt] separable.
[p0187-l0027] [9.0pt] Nonlinear SVM Classification
[p0187-l0028] [9.0pt] |
[p0187-l0029] [9.0pt] 161

=== PDF page 188 / printed label 162 ===
[p0188-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 5-8. Similarity features using the Gaussian RBF
[p0188-l0002] [10.5pt] You may wonder how to select the landmarks. The simplest approach is to create a
[p0188-l0003] [10.5pt] landmark at the location of each and every instance in the dataset. This creates many
[p0188-l0004] [10.5pt] dimensions and thus increases the chances that the transformed training set will be
[p0188-l0005] [10.5pt] linearly separable. The downside is that a training set with m instances and n features
[p0188-l0006] [10.5pt] gets transformed into a training set with m instances and m features (assuming you
[p0188-l0007] [10.5pt] drop the original features). If your training set is very large, you end up with an
[p0188-l0008] [10.5pt] equally large number of features.
[p0188-l0009] [15.77pt] Gaussian RBF Kernel
[p0188-l0010] [10.5pt] Just like the polynomial features method, the similarity features method can be useful
[p0188-l0011] [10.5pt] with any Machine Learning algorithm, but it may be computationally expensive to
[p0188-l0012] [10.5pt] compute all the additional features, especially on large training sets. However, once
[p0188-l0013] [10.5pt] again the kernel trick does its SVM magic: it makes it possible to obtain a similar
[p0188-l0014] [10.5pt] result as if you had added many similarity features, without actually having to add
[p0188-l0015] [10.5pt] them. Let’s try the Gaussian RBF kernel using the SVC class:
[p0188-l0016] [8.5pt] rbf_kernel_svm_clf = Pipeline([
[p0188-l0017] [8.5pt]         ("scaler", StandardScaler()),
[p0188-l0018] [8.5pt]         ("svm_clf", SVC(kernel="rbf", gamma=5, C=0.001))
[p0188-l0019] [8.5pt]     ])
[p0188-l0020] [8.5pt] rbf_kernel_svm_clf.fit(X, y)
[p0188-l0021] [10.5pt] This model is represented on the bottom left of Figure 5-9. The other plots show
[p0188-l0022] [10.5pt] models trained with different values of hyperparameters gamma (γ) and C. Increasing
[p0188-l0023] [10.5pt] gamma makes the bell-shape curve narrower (see the left plot of Figure 5-8), and as a
[p0188-l0024] [10.5pt] result each instance’s range of influence is smaller: the decision boundary ends up
[p0188-l0025] [10.5pt] being more irregular, wiggling around individual instances. Conversely, a small gamma
[p0188-l0026] [10.5pt] value makes the bell-shaped curve wider, so instances have a larger range of influ‐
[p0188-l0027] [10.5pt] ence, and the decision boundary ends up smoother. So γ acts like a regularization
[p0188-l0028] [10.5pt] hyperparameter: if your model is overfitting, you should reduce it, and if it is under‐
[p0188-l0029] [10.5pt] fitting, you should increase it (similar to the C hyperparameter).
[p0188-l0030] [9.0pt] 162
[p0188-l0031] [9.0pt] |
[p0188-l0032] [9.0pt] Chapter 5: Support Vector Machines

=== PDF page 189 / printed label 163 ===
[p0189-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 5-9. SVM classifiers using an RBF kernel
[p0189-l0002] [10.5pt] Other kernels exist but are used much more rarely. For example, some kernels are
[p0189-l0003] [10.5pt] specialized for specific data structures. String kernels are sometimes used when classi‐
[p0189-l0004] [10.5pt] fying text documents or DNA sequences (e.g., using the string subsequence kernel or
[p0189-l0005] [10.5pt] kernels based on the Levenshtein distance).
[p0189-l0006] [9.6pt] With so many kernels to choose from, how can you decide which
[p0189-l0007] [9.6pt] one to use? As a rule of thumb, you should always try the linear
[p0189-l0008] [9.6pt] kernel first (remember that LinearSVC is much faster than SVC(ker
[p0189-l0009] [9.6pt] nel="linear")), especially if the training set is very large or if it
[p0189-l0010] [9.6pt] has plenty of features. If the training set is not too large, you should
[p0189-l0011] [9.6pt] try the Gaussian RBF kernel as well; it works well in most cases.
[p0189-l0012] [9.6pt] Then if you have spare time and computing power, you can also
[p0189-l0013] [9.6pt] experiment with a few other kernels using cross-validation and grid
[p0189-l0014] [9.6pt] search, especially if there are kernels specialized for your training
[p0189-l0015] [9.6pt] set’s data structure.
[p0189-l0016] [15.77pt] Computational Complexity
[p0189-l0017] [10.5pt] The LinearSVC class is based on the liblinear library, which implements an optimized
[p0189-l0018] [10.5pt] algorithm for linear SVMs.1 It does not support the kernel trick, but it scales almost
[p0189-l0019] [8.0pt] 1 “A Dual Coordinate Descent Method for Large-scale Linear SVM,” Lin et al. (2008).
[p0189-l0020] [9.0pt] Nonlinear SVM Classification
[p0189-l0021] [9.0pt] |
[p0189-l0022] [9.0pt] 163

=== PDF page 190 / printed label 164 ===
[p0190-l0001] [10.5pt] linearly with the number of training instances and the number of features: its training
[p0190-l0002] [10.5pt] time complexity is roughly O(m × n).
[p0190-l0003] [10.5pt] The algorithm takes longer if you require a very high precision. This is controlled by
[p0190-l0004] [10.5pt] the tolerance hyperparameter ϵ (called tol in Scikit-Learn). In most classification
[p0190-l0005] [10.5pt] tasks, the default tolerance is fine.
[p0190-l0006] [10.5pt] The SVC class is based on the libsvm library, which implements an algorithm that sup‐
[p0190-l0007] [10.5pt] ports the kernel trick.2 The training time complexity is usually between O(m2 × n)
[p0190-l0008] [10.5pt] and O(m3 × n). Unfortunately, this means that it gets dreadfully slow when the num‐
[p0190-l0009] [10.5pt] ber of training instances gets large (e.g., hundreds of thousands of instances). This
[p0190-l0010] [10.5pt] algorithm is perfect for complex but small or medium training sets. However, it scales
[p0190-l0011] [10.5pt] well with the number of features, especially with sparse features (i.e., when each
[p0190-l0012] [10.5pt] instance has few nonzero features). In this case, the algorithm scales roughly with the
[p0190-l0013] [10.5pt] average number of nonzero features per instance. Table 5-1 compares Scikit-Learn’s
[p0190-l0014] [10.5pt] SVM classification classes.

[p0190-l0034] [18.92pt] SVM Regression
[p0190-l0035] [10.5pt] As we mentioned earlier, the SVM algorithm is quite versatile: not only does it sup‐
[p0190-l0036] [10.5pt] port linear and nonlinear classification, but it also supports linear and nonlinear
[p0190-l0037] [10.5pt] regression. The trick is to reverse the objective: instead of trying to fit the largest pos‐
[p0190-l0038] [10.5pt] sible street between two classes while limiting margin violations, SVM Regression
[p0190-l0039] [10.5pt] tries to fit as many instances as possible on the street while limiting margin violations
[p0190-l0040] [10.5pt] (i.e., instances off the street). The width of the street is controlled by a hyperparame‐
[p0190-l0041] [10.5pt] ter ϵ. Figure 5-10 shows two linear SVM Regression models trained on some random
[p0190-l0042] [10.5pt] linear data, one with a large margin (ϵ = 1.5) and the other with a small margin (ϵ =
[p0190-l0043] [10.5pt] 0.5).
[p0190-l0044] [8.0pt] 2 “Sequential Minimal Optimization (SMO),” J. Platt (1998).
[p0190-l0045] [9.0pt] 164
[p0190-l0046] [9.0pt] |
[p0190-l0047] [9.0pt] Chapter 5: Support Vector Machines

=== PDF page 191 / printed label 165 ===
[p0191-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 5-10. SVM Regression
[p0191-l0002] [10.5pt] Adding more training instances within the margin does not affect the model’s predic‐
[p0191-l0003] [10.5pt] tions; thus, the model is said to be ϵ-insensitive.
[p0191-l0004] [10.5pt] You can use Scikit-Learn’s LinearSVR class to perform linear SVM Regression. The
[p0191-l0005] [10.5pt] following code produces the model represented on the left of Figure 5-10 (the train‐
[p0191-l0006] [10.5pt] ing data should be scaled and centered first):
[p0191-l0007] [8.5pt] from sklearn.svm import LinearSVR
[p0191-l0008] [8.5pt] svm_reg = LinearSVR(epsilon=1.5)
[p0191-l0009] [8.5pt] svm_reg.fit(X, y)
[p0191-l0010] [10.5pt] To tackle nonlinear regression tasks, you can use a kernelized SVM model. For exam‐
[p0191-l0011] [10.5pt] ple, Figure 5-11 shows SVM Regression on a random quadratic training set, using a
[p0191-l0012] [10.5pt] 2nd-degree polynomial kernel. There is little regularization on the left plot (i.e., a large
[p0191-l0013] [10.5pt] C value), and much more regularization on the right plot (i.e., a small C value).
[p0191-l0014] [10.5pt] Figure 5-11. SVM regression using a 2nd-degree polynomial kernel

[p0191-l0016] [9.0pt] |

[p0192-l0001] [10.5pt] The following code produces the model represented on the left of Figure 5-11 using
[p0192-l0002] [10.5pt] Scikit-Learn’s SVR class (which supports the kernel trick). The SVR class is the regres‐
[p0192-l0003] [10.5pt] sion equivalent of the SVC class, and the LinearSVR class is the regression equivalent
[p0192-l0004] [10.5pt] of the LinearSVC class. The LinearSVR class scales linearly with the size of the train‐
[p0192-l0005] [10.5pt] ing set (just like the LinearSVC class), while the SVR class gets much too slow when
[p0192-l0006] [10.5pt] the training set grows large (just like the SVC class).
[p0192-l0007] [8.5pt] from sklearn.svm import SVR
[p0192-l0008] [8.5pt] svm_poly_reg = SVR(kernel="poly", degree=2, C=100, epsilon=0.1)
[p0192-l0009] [8.5pt] svm_poly_reg.fit(X, y)
[p0192-l0010] [9.6pt] SVMs can also be used for outlier detection; see Scikit-Learn’s doc‐
[p0192-l0011] [9.6pt] umentation for more details.
[p0192-l0012] [18.92pt] Under the Hood
[p0192-l0013] [10.5pt] This section explains how SVMs make predictions and how their training algorithms
[p0192-l0014] [10.5pt] work, starting with linear SVM classifiers. You can safely skip it and go straight to the
[p0192-l0015] [10.5pt] exercises at the end of this chapter if you are just getting started with Machine Learn‐
[p0192-l0016] [10.5pt] ing, and come back later when you want to get a deeper understanding of SVMs.
[p0192-l0017] [10.5pt] First, a word about notations: in Chapter 4 we used the convention of putting all the
[p0192-l0018] [10.5pt] model parameters in one vector θ, including the bias term θ0 and the input feature
[p0192-l0019] [10.5pt] weights θ1 to θn, and adding a bias input x0 = 1 to all instances. In this chapter, we will
[p0192-l0020] [10.5pt] use a different convention, which is more convenient (and more common) when you
[p0192-l0021] [10.5pt] are dealing with SVMs: the bias term will be called b and the feature weights vector
[p0192-l0022] [10.5pt] will be called w. No bias feature will be added to the input feature vectors.
[p0192-l0023] [15.77pt] Decision Function and Predictions
[p0192-l0024] [10.5pt] The linear SVM classifier model predicts the class of a new instance x by simply com‐
[p0192-l0025] [10.5pt] puting the decision function wT x + b = w1 x1 + ⋯ + wn xn + b: if the result is positive,
[p0192-l0026] [10.5pt] the predicted class ŷ is the positive class (1), or else it is the negative class (0); see
[p0192-l0027] [10.5pt] Equation 5-2.
[p0192-l0028] [10.5pt] Equation 5-2. Linear SVM classifier prediction
[p0192-l0029] [10.0pt] y = 0 if wTx + b < 0,
[p0192-l0030] [10.0pt] 1 if wTx + b ≥0
[p0192-l0031] [9.0pt] 166
[p0192-l0032] [9.0pt] |
[p0192-l0033] [9.0pt] Chapter 5: Support Vector Machines

[p0193-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 5-12 shows the decision function that corresponds to the model on the left of
[p0193-l0002] [10.5pt] Figure 5-4: it is a two-dimensional plane since this dataset has two features (petal
[p0193-l0003] [10.5pt] width and petal length). The decision boundary is the set of points where the decision
[p0193-l0004] [10.5pt] function is equal to 0: it is the intersection of two planes, which is a straight line (rep‐
[p0193-l0005] [10.5pt] resented by the thick solid line).3
[p0193-l0006] [10.5pt] Figure 5-12. Decision function for the iris dataset
[p0193-l0007] [10.5pt] The dashed lines represent the points where the decision function is equal to 1 or –1:
[p0193-l0008] [10.5pt] they are parallel and at equal distance to the decision boundary, forming a margin
[p0193-l0009] [10.5pt] around it. Training a linear SVM classifier means finding the value of w and b that
[p0193-l0010] [10.5pt] make this margin as wide as possible while avoiding margin violations (hard margin)
[p0193-l0011] [10.5pt] or limiting them (soft margin).
[p0193-l0012] [15.77pt] Training Objective
[p0193-l0013] [10.5pt] Consider the slope of the decision function: it is equal to the norm of the weight vec‐
[p0193-l0014] [10.5pt] tor, ∥ w ∥. If we divide this slope by 2, the points where the decision function is equal
[p0193-l0015] [10.5pt] to ±1 are going to be twice as far away from the decision boundary. In other words,
[p0193-l0016] [10.5pt] dividing the slope by 2 will multiply the margin by 2. Perhaps this is easier to visual‐
[p0193-l0017] [10.5pt] ize in 2D in Figure 5-13. The smaller the weight vector w, the larger the margin.
[p0193-l0018] [8.0pt] 3 More generally, when there are n features, the decision function is an n-dimensional hyperplane, and the deci‐
[p0193-l0019] [8.0pt] sion boundary is an (n – 1)-dimensional hyperplane.

[p0194-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 5-13. A smaller weight vector results in a larger margin
[p0194-l0002] [10.5pt] So we want to minimize ∥ w ∥ to get a large margin. However, if we also want to avoid
[p0194-l0003] [10.5pt] any margin violation (hard margin), then we need the decision function to be greater
[p0194-l0004] [10.5pt] than 1 for all positive training instances, and lower than –1 for negative training
[p0194-l0005] [10.5pt] instances. If we define t(i) = –1 for negative instances (if y(i) = 0) and t(i) = 1 for positive
[p0194-l0006] [10.5pt] instances (if y(i) = 1), then we can express this constraint as t(i)(wT x(i) + b) ≥ 1 for all
[p0194-l0007] [10.5pt] instances.
[p0194-l0008] [10.5pt] We can therefore express the hard margin linear SVM classifier objective as the con‐
[p0194-l0009] [10.5pt] strained optimization problem in Equation 5-3.
[p0194-l0010] [10.5pt] Equation 5-3. Hard margin linear SVM classifier objective

[p0194-l0012] [8.0pt] w, b
[p0194-l0013] [10.0pt] 1
[p0194-l0014] [10.0pt] 2wTw
[p0194-l0015] [10.0pt] subject to
[p0194-l0016] [10.0pt] t i wTx i + b ≥1
[p0194-l0017] [10.0pt] for i = 1, 2, ⋯, m
[p0194-l0018] [9.6pt] We are minimizing 1
[p0194-l0019] [9.6pt] 2wT w, which is equal to 1
[p0194-l0020] [9.6pt] 2∥ w ∥2, rather than
[p0194-l0021] [9.6pt] minimizing ∥ w ∥. Indeed, 1
[p0194-l0022] [9.6pt] 2∥ w ∥2 has a nice and simple derivative
[p0194-l0023] [9.6pt] (it is just w) while ∥ w ∥ is not differentiable at w = 0. Optimization
[p0194-l0024] [9.6pt] algorithms work much better on differentiable functions.
[p0194-l0025] [10.5pt] To get the soft margin objective, we need to introduce a slack variable ζ(i) ≥ 0 for each
[p0194-l0026] [10.5pt] instance:4 ζ(i) measures how much the ith instance is allowed to violate the margin. We
[p0194-l0027] [10.5pt] now have two conflicting objectives: making the slack variables as small as possible to
[p0194-l0028] [10.5pt] reduce the margin violations, and making 1
[p0194-l0029] [10.5pt] 2wT w as small as possible to increase the
[p0194-l0030] [10.5pt] margin. This is where the C hyperparameter comes in: it allows us to define the trade‐
[p0194-l0031] [8.0pt] 4 Zeta (ζ) is the 6th letter of the Greek alphabet.

[p0195-l0016] [15.77pt] Quadratic Programming
[p0195-l0017] [10.5pt] The hard margin and soft margin problems are both convex quadratic optimization
[p0195-l0018] [10.5pt] problems with linear constraints. Such problems are known as Quadratic Program‐
[p0195-l0019] [10.5pt] ming (QP) problems. Many off-the-shelf solvers are available to solve QP problems
[p0195-l0020] [10.5pt] using a variety of techniques that are outside the scope of this book.5 The general
[p0195-l0021] [10.5pt] problem formulation is given by Equation 5-5.
[p0195-l0022] [10.5pt] Equation 5-5. Quadratic Programming problem
[p0195-l0023] [10.0pt] Minimize
[p0195-l0024] [10.0pt] 1
[p0195-l0025] [10.0pt] 2pTHp
[p0195-l0026] [10.0pt] +
[p0195-l0027] [10.0pt] fTp
[p0195-l0028] [8.0pt] p
[p0195-l0029] [10.0pt] subject to
[p0195-l0030] [10.0pt] Ap ≤b
[p0195-l0031] [10.0pt] p
[p0195-l0032] [10.0pt] is an np‐dimensional vector (np = number of parameters),
[p0195-l0033] [10.0pt] H
[p0195-l0034] [10.0pt] is an np × np matrix,
[p0195-l0035] [10.0pt] where
[p0195-l0036] [10.0pt] f
[p0195-l0037] [10.0pt] is an np‐dimensional vector,
[p0195-l0038] [10.0pt] A
[p0195-l0039] [10.0pt] is an nc × np matrix (nc = number of constraints),
[p0195-l0040] [10.0pt] b
[p0195-l0041] [10.0pt] is an nc‐dimensional vector.
[p0195-l0042] [10.5pt] Note that the expression A p ≤ b actually defines nc constraints: pT a(i) ≤ b(i) for i = 1,
[p0195-l0043] [10.5pt] 2, ⋯, nc, where a(i) is the vector containing the elements of the ith row of A and b(i) is
[p0195-l0044] [10.5pt] the ith element of b.
[p0195-l0045] [10.5pt] You can easily verify that if you set the QP parameters in the following way, you get
[p0195-l0046] [10.5pt] the hard margin linear SVM classifier objective:
[p0195-l0047] [10.5pt] • np = n + 1, where n is the number of features (the +1 is for the bias term).
[p0195-l0048] [8.0pt] 5 To learn more about Quadratic Programming, you can start by reading Stephen Boyd and Lieven Vanden‐

[p0195-l0050] [8.0pt] series of video lectures.

[p0196-l0001] [10.5pt] • nc = m, where m is the number of training instances.
[p0196-l0002] [10.5pt] • H is the np × np identity matrix, except with a zero in the top-left cell (to ignore
[p0196-l0003] [10.5pt] the bias term).
[p0196-l0004] [10.5pt] • f = 0, an np-dimensional vector full of 0s.
[p0196-l0005] [10.5pt] • b = –1, an nc-dimensional vector full of –1s.
[p0196-l0006] [10.5pt] • a(i) = –t(i) x˙ (i), where x˙ (i) is equal to x(i) with an extra bias feature x˙ 0 = 1.
[p0196-l0007] [10.5pt] So one way to train a hard margin linear SVM classifier is just to use an off-the-shelf
[p0196-l0008] [10.5pt] QP solver by passing it the preceding parameters. The resulting vector p will contain
[p0196-l0009] [10.5pt] the bias term b = p0 and the feature weights wi = pi for i = 1, 2, ⋯, n. Similarly, you
[p0196-l0010] [10.5pt] can use a QP solver to solve the soft margin problem (see the exercises at the end of
[p0196-l0011] [10.5pt] the chapter).
[p0196-l0012] [10.5pt] However, to use the kernel trick we are going to look at a different constrained opti‐
[p0196-l0013] [10.5pt] mization problem.
[p0196-l0014] [15.77pt] The Dual Problem
[p0196-l0015] [10.5pt] Given a constrained optimization problem, known as the primal problem, it is possi‐
[p0196-l0016] [10.5pt] ble to express a different but closely related problem, called its dual problem. The sol‐
[p0196-l0017] [10.5pt] ution to the dual problem typically gives a lower bound to the solution of the primal
[p0196-l0018] [10.5pt] problem, but under some conditions it can even have the same solutions as the pri‐
[p0196-l0019] [10.5pt] mal problem. Luckily, the SVM problem happens to meet these conditions,6 so you
[p0196-l0020] [10.5pt] can choose to solve the primal problem or the dual problem; both will have the same
[p0196-l0021] [10.5pt] solution. Equation 5-6 shows the dual form of the linear SVM objective (if you are
[p0196-l0022] [10.5pt] interested in knowing how to derive the dual problem from the primal problem,
[p0196-l0023] [10.5pt] see ???).

[p0197-l0014] [10.5pt] The dual problem is faster to solve than the primal when the number of training
[p0197-l0015] [10.5pt] instances is smaller than the number of features. More importantly, it makes the ker‐
[p0197-l0016] [10.5pt] nel trick possible, while the primal does not. So what is this kernel trick anyway?
[p0197-l0017] [15.77pt] Kernelized SVM
[p0197-l0018] [10.5pt] Suppose you want to apply a 2nd-degree polynomial transformation to a two-
[p0197-l0019] [10.5pt] dimensional training set (such as the moons training set), then train a linear SVM
[p0197-l0020] [10.5pt] classifier on the transformed training set. Equation 5-8 shows the 2nd-degree polyno‐
[p0197-l0021] [10.5pt] mial mapping function ϕ that you want to apply.
[p0197-l0022] [10.5pt] Equation 5-8. Second-degree polynomial mapping
[p0197-l0023] [8.0pt] 2

[p0197-l0026] [10.0pt] =
[p0197-l0027] [10.0pt] 2 x1x2

[p0197-l0029] [10.0pt] x2
[p0197-l0030] [8.0pt] 2
[p0197-l0031] [10.0pt] x2
[p0197-l0032] [10.5pt] Notice that the transformed vector is three-dimensional instead of two-dimensional.
[p0197-l0033] [10.5pt] Now let’s look at what happens to a couple of two-dimensional vectors, a and b, if we
[p0197-l0034] [10.5pt] apply this 2nd-degree polynomial mapping and then compute the dot product7 of the
[p0197-l0035] [10.5pt] transformed vectors (See Equation 5-9).
[p0197-l0036] [8.0pt] 7 As explained in Chapter 4, the dot product of two vectors a and b is normally noted a · b. However, in
[p0197-l0037] [8.0pt] Machine Learning, vectors are frequently represented as column vectors (i.e., single-column matrices), so the
[p0197-l0038] [8.0pt] dot product is achieved by computing aTb. To remain consistent with the rest of the book, we will use this
[p0197-l0039] [8.0pt] notation here, ignoring the fact that this technically results in a single-cell matrix rather than a scalar value.

[p0198-l0029] [10.5pt] How about that? The dot product of the transformed vectors is equal to the square of
[p0198-l0030] [10.5pt] the dot product of the original vectors: ϕ(a)T ϕ(b) = (aT b)2.
[p0198-l0031] [10.5pt] Now here is the key insight: if you apply the transformation ϕ to all training instan‐
[p0198-l0032] [10.5pt] ces, then the dual problem (see Equation 5-6) will contain the dot product ϕ(x(i))T
[p0198-l0033] [10.5pt] ϕ(x(j)). But if ϕ is the 2nd-degree polynomial transformation defined in Equation 5-8,
[p0198-l0034] [10.5pt] then you can replace this dot product of transformed vectors simply by x i Tx j
[p0198-l0035] [8.0pt] 2
[p0198-l0036] [10.5pt] . So
[p0198-l0037] [10.5pt] you don’t actually need to transform the training instances at all: just replace the dot
[p0198-l0038] [10.5pt] product by its square in Equation 5-6. The result will be strictly the same as if you
[p0198-l0039] [10.5pt] went through the trouble of actually transforming the training set then fitting a linear
[p0198-l0040] [10.5pt] SVM algorithm, but this trick makes the whole process much more computationally
[p0198-l0041] [10.5pt] efficient. This is the essence of the kernel trick.
[p0198-l0042] [10.5pt] The function K(a, b) = (aT b)2 is called a 2nd-degree polynomial kernel. In Machine
[p0198-l0043] [10.5pt] Learning, a kernel is a function capable of computing the dot product ϕ(a)T ϕ(b)
[p0198-l0044] [10.5pt] based only on the original vectors a and b, without having to compute (or even to
[p0198-l0045] [10.5pt] know about) the transformation ϕ. Equation 5-10 lists some of the most commonly
[p0198-l0046] [10.5pt] used kernels.
[p0198-l0047] [10.5pt] Equation 5-10. Common kernels
[p0198-l0048] [10.0pt] Linear:
[p0198-l0049] [10.0pt] K a, b = aTb
[p0198-l0050] [8.0pt] d
[p0198-l0051] [10.0pt] Polynomial:
[p0198-l0052] [10.0pt] K a, b = γaTb + r
[p0198-l0053] [10.0pt] Gaussian RBF:
[p0198-l0054] [10.0pt] K a, b = exp −γ∥a −b ∥2
[p0198-l0055] [10.0pt] Sigmoid:
[p0198-l0056] [10.0pt] K a, b = tanh γaTb + r

[p0199-l0001] [15.0pt] Mercer’s Theorem
[p0199-l0002] [10.0pt] According to Mercer’s theorem, if a function K(a, b) respects a few mathematical con‐
[p0199-l0003] [10.0pt] ditions called Mercer’s conditions (K must be continuous, symmetric in its arguments
[p0199-l0004] [10.0pt] so K(a, b) = K(b, a), etc.), then there exists a function ϕ that maps a and b into
[p0199-l0005] [10.0pt] another space (possibly with much higher dimensions) such that K(a, b) = ϕ(a)T ϕ(b).
[p0199-l0006] [10.0pt] So you can use K as a kernel since you know ϕ exists, even if you don’t know what ϕ
[p0199-l0007] [10.0pt] is. In the case of the Gaussian RBF kernel, it can be shown that ϕ actually maps each
[p0199-l0008] [10.0pt] training instance to an infinite-dimensional space, so it’s a good thing you don’t need
[p0199-l0009] [10.0pt] to actually perform the mapping!
[p0199-l0010] [10.0pt] Note that some frequently used kernels (such as the Sigmoid kernel) don’t respect all
[p0199-l0011] [10.0pt] of Mercer’s conditions, yet they generally work well in practice.
[p0199-l0012] [10.5pt] There is still one loose end we must tie. Equation 5-7 shows how to go from the dual
[p0199-l0013] [10.5pt] solution to the primal solution in the case of a linear SVM classifier, but if you apply
[p0199-l0014] [10.5pt] the kernel trick you end up with equations that include ϕ(x(i)). In fact, w must have
[p0199-l0015] [10.5pt] the same number of dimensions as ϕ(x(i)), which may be huge or even infinite, so you
[p0199-l0016] [10.5pt] can’t compute it. But how can you make predictions without knowing w? Well, the
[p0199-l0017] [10.5pt] good news is that you can plug in the formula for w from Equation 5-7 into the deci‐
[p0199-l0018] [10.5pt] sion function for a new instance x(n), and you get an equation with only dot products
[p0199-l0019] [10.5pt] between input vectors. This makes it possible to use the kernel trick, once again
[p0199-l0020] [10.5pt] (Equation 5-11).
[p0199-l0021] [10.5pt] Equation 5-11. Making predictions with a kernelized SVM
[p0199-l0022] [8.0pt] T
[p0199-l0023] [8.0pt] m
[p0199-l0024] [10.0pt] α i t i ϕ x i
[p0199-l0025] [10.0pt] ϕ x n
[p0199-l0026] [10.0pt] + b
[p0199-l0027] [10.0pt] hw, b ϕ x n
[p0199-l0028] [10.0pt] = wTϕ x n
[p0199-l0029] [14.14pt] + b = ∑
[p0199-l0030] [8.0pt] i = 1
[p0199-l0031] [8.0pt] m
[p0199-l0032] [10.0pt] α i t i ϕ x i Tϕ x n

[p0200-l0032] [15.77pt] Online SVMs
[p0200-l0033] [10.5pt] Before concluding this chapter, let’s take a quick look at online SVM classifiers (recall
[p0200-l0034] [10.5pt] that online learning means learning incrementally, typically as new instances arrive).
[p0200-l0035] [10.5pt] For linear SVM classifiers, one method is to use Gradient Descent (e.g., using
[p0200-l0036] [10.5pt] SGDClassifier) to minimize the cost function in Equation 5-13, which is derived
[p0200-l0037] [10.5pt] from the primal problem. Unfortunately it converges much more slowly than the
[p0200-l0038] [10.5pt] methods based on QP.
[p0200-l0039] [10.5pt] Equation 5-13. Linear SVM classifier cost function
[p0200-l0040] [8.0pt] m
[p0200-l0041] [10.0pt] J w, b = 1
[p0200-l0042] [10.0pt] max 0, 1 −t i wTx i + b
[p0200-l0043] [10.0pt] 2wTw
[p0200-l0044] [10.0pt] +
[p0200-l0045] [14.14pt] C ∑
[p0200-l0046] [8.0pt] i = 1
[p0200-l0047] [10.5pt] The first sum in the cost function will push the model to have a small weight vector
[p0200-l0048] [10.5pt] w, leading to a larger margin. The second sum computes the total of all margin viola‐
[p0200-l0049] [10.5pt] tions. An instance’s margin violation is equal to 0 if it is located off the street and on
[p0200-l0050] [10.5pt] the correct side, or else it is proportional to the distance to the correct side of the
[p0200-l0051] [10.5pt] street. Minimizing this term ensures that the model makes the margin violations as
[p0200-l0052] [10.5pt] small and as few as possible
[p0200-l0053] [15.0pt] Hinge Loss
[p0200-l0054] [10.0pt] The function max(0, 1 – t) is called the hinge loss function (represented below). It is
[p0200-l0055] [10.0pt] equal to 0 when t ≥ 1. Its derivative (slope) is equal to –1 if t < 1 and 0 if t > 1. It is not
[p0200-l0056] [10.0pt] differentiable at t = 1, but just like for Lasso Regression (see “Lasso Regression” on
[p0200-l0057] [10.0pt] page 139) you can still use Gradient Descent using any subderivative at t = 1 (i.e., any
[p0200-l0058] [10.0pt] value between –1 and 0).

[p0203-l0001] [16.82pt] CHAPTER 6
[p0203-l0002] [25.22pt] Decision Trees
[p0203-l0003] [9.6pt] With Early Release ebooks, you get books in their earliest form—
[p0203-l0004] [9.6pt] the author’s raw and unedited content as he or she writes—so you
[p0203-l0005] [9.6pt] can take advantage of these technologies long before the official
[p0203-l0006] [9.6pt] release of these titles. The following will be Chapter 6 in the final
[p0203-l0007] [9.6pt] release of the book.
[p0203-l0008] [10.5pt] Like SVMs, Decision Trees are versatile Machine Learning algorithms that can per‐
[p0203-l0009] [10.5pt] form both classification and regression tasks, and even multioutput tasks. They are
[p0203-l0010] [10.5pt] very powerful algorithms, capable of fitting complex datasets. For example, in Chap‐
[p0203-l0011] [10.5pt] ter 2 you trained a DecisionTreeRegressor model on the California housing dataset,
[p0203-l0012] [10.5pt] fitting it perfectly (actually overfitting it).
[p0203-l0013] [10.5pt] Decision Trees are also the fundamental components of Random Forests (see Chap‐
[p0203-l0014] [10.5pt] ter 7), which are among the most powerful Machine Learning algorithms available
[p0203-l0015] [10.5pt] today.
[p0203-l0016] [10.5pt] In this chapter we will start by discussing how to train, visualize, and make predic‐
[p0203-l0017] [10.5pt] tions with Decision Trees. Then we will go through the CART training algorithm
[p0203-l0018] [10.5pt] used by Scikit-Learn, and we will discuss how to regularize trees and use them for
[p0203-l0019] [10.5pt] regression tasks. Finally, we will discuss some of the limitations of Decision Trees.
[p0203-l0020] [18.92pt] Training and Visualizing a Decision Tree
[p0203-l0021] [10.5pt] To understand Decision Trees, let’s just build one and take a look at how it makes pre‐
[p0203-l0022] [10.5pt] dictions. The following code trains a DecisionTreeClassifier on the iris dataset
[p0203-l0023] [10.5pt] (see Chapter 4):
[p0203-l0024] [8.5pt] from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
[p0203-l0025] [8.5pt] from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
[p0203-l0026] [9.0pt] 177

=== PDF page 204 / printed label 178 ===
[p0204-l0001] [8.5pt] iris = load_iris()
[p0204-l0002] [8.5pt] X = iris.data[:, 2:] # petal length and width
[p0204-l0003] [8.5pt] y = iris.target
[p0204-l0004] [8.5pt] tree_clf = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=2)
[p0204-l0005] [8.5pt] tree_clf.fit(X, y)
[p0204-l0006] [10.5pt] You can visualize the trained Decision Tree by first using the export_graphviz()
[p0204-l0007] [10.5pt] method to output a graph definition file called iris_tree.dot:
[p0204-l0008] [8.5pt] from sklearn.tree import export_graphviz
[p0204-l0009] [8.5pt] export_graphviz(
[p0204-l0010] [8.5pt]         tree_clf,

[p0204-l0019] [10.5pt] the .dot file to a .png image file:
[p0204-l0020] [8.5pt] $ dot -Tpng iris_tree.dot -o iris_tree.png
[p0204-l0021] [10.5pt] Your first decision tree looks like Figure 6-1.

[p0205-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 6-1. Iris Decision Tree
[p0205-l0002] [18.92pt] Making Predictions
[p0205-l0003] [10.5pt] Let’s see how the tree represented in Figure 6-1 makes predictions. Suppose you find
[p0205-l0004] [10.5pt] an iris flower and you want to classify it. You start at the root node (depth 0, at the
[p0205-l0005] [10.5pt] top): this node asks whether the flower’s petal length is smaller than 2.45 cm. If it is,
[p0205-l0006] [10.5pt] then you move down to the root’s left child node (depth 1, left). In this case, it is a leaf
[p0205-l0007] [10.5pt] node (i.e., it does not have any children nodes), so it does not ask any questions: you
[p0205-l0008] [10.5pt] can simply look at the predicted class for that node and the Decision Tree predicts
[p0205-l0009] [10.5pt] that your flower is an Iris-Setosa (class=setosa).
[p0205-l0010] [10.5pt] Now suppose you find another flower, but this time the petal length is greater than
[p0205-l0011] [10.5pt] 2.45 cm. You must move down to the root’s right child node (depth 1, right), which is
[p0205-l0012] [10.5pt] not a leaf node, so it asks another question: is the petal width smaller than 1.75 cm? If
[p0205-l0013] [10.5pt] it is, then your flower is most likely an Iris-Versicolor (depth 2, left). If not, it is likely
[p0205-l0014] [10.5pt] an Iris-Virginica (depth 2, right). It’s really that simple.
[p0205-l0015] [9.6pt] One of the many qualities of Decision Trees is that they require
[p0205-l0016] [9.6pt] very little data preparation. In particular, they don’t require feature
[p0205-l0017] [9.6pt] scaling or centering at all.
[p0205-l0018] [9.0pt] Making Predictions
[p0205-l0019] [9.0pt] |
[p0205-l0020] [9.0pt] 179

=== PDF page 206 / printed label 180 ===
[p0206-l0001] [10.5pt] A node’s samples attribute counts how many training instances it applies to. For
[p0206-l0002] [10.5pt] example, 100 training instances have a petal length greater than 2.45 cm (depth 1,
[p0206-l0003] [10.5pt] right), among which 54 have a petal width smaller than 1.75 cm (depth 2, left). A
[p0206-l0004] [10.5pt] node’s value attribute tells you how many training instances of each class this node
[p0206-l0005] [10.5pt] applies to: for example, the bottom-right node applies to 0 Iris-Setosa, 1 Iris-
[p0206-l0006] [10.5pt] Versicolor, and 45 Iris-Virginica. Finally, a node’s gini attribute measures its impur‐
[p0206-l0007] [10.5pt] ity: a node is “pure” (gini=0) if all training instances it applies to belong to the same
[p0206-l0008] [10.5pt] class. For example, since the depth-1 left node applies only to Iris-Setosa training
[p0206-l0009] [10.5pt] instances, it is pure and its gini score is 0. Equation 6-1 shows how the training algo‐
[p0206-l0010] [10.5pt] rithm computes the gini score Gi of the ith node. For example, the depth-2 left node
[p0206-l0011] [10.5pt] has a gini score equal to 1 – (0/54)2 – (49/54)2 – (5/54)2 ≈ 0.168. Another impurity
[p0206-l0012] [10.5pt] measure is discussed shortly.
[p0206-l0013] [10.5pt] Equation 6-1. Gini impurity
[p0206-l0014] [8.0pt] n
[p0206-l0015] [8.0pt] 2
[p0206-l0016] [10.0pt] pi, k
[p0206-l0017] [14.14pt] Gi = 1 −∑
[p0206-l0018] [8.0pt] k = 1
[p0206-l0019] [10.5pt] • pi,k is the ratio of class k instances among the training instances in the ith node.
[p0206-l0020] [9.6pt] Scikit-Learn uses the CART algorithm, which produces only binary
[p0206-l0021] [9.6pt] trees: nonleaf nodes always have two children (i.e., questions only
[p0206-l0022] [9.6pt] have yes/no answers). However, other algorithms such as ID3 can
[p0206-l0023] [9.6pt] produce Decision Trees with nodes that have more than two chil‐
[p0206-l0024] [9.6pt] dren.
[p0206-l0025] [10.5pt] Figure 6-2 shows this Decision Tree’s decision boundaries. The thick vertical line rep‐
[p0206-l0026] [10.5pt] resents the decision boundary of the root node (depth 0): petal length = 2.45 cm.
[p0206-l0027] [10.5pt] Since the left area is pure (only Iris-Setosa), it cannot be split any further. However,
[p0206-l0028] [10.5pt] the right area is impure, so the depth-1 right node splits it at petal width = 1.75 cm
[p0206-l0029] [10.5pt] (represented by the dashed line). Since max_depth was set to 2, the Decision Tree
[p0206-l0030] [10.5pt] stops right there. However, if you set max_depth to 3, then the two depth-2 nodes
[p0206-l0031] [10.5pt] would each add another decision boundary (represented by the dotted lines).

[p0207-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 6-2. Decision Tree decision boundaries
[p0207-l0002] [15.0pt] Model Interpretation: White Box Versus Black Box
[p0207-l0003] [10.0pt] As you can see Decision Trees are fairly intuitive and their decisions are easy to inter‐
[p0207-l0004] [10.0pt] pret. Such models are often called white box models. In contrast, as we will see, Ran‐
[p0207-l0005] [10.0pt] dom Forests or neural networks are generally considered black box models. They
[p0207-l0006] [10.0pt] make great predictions, and you can easily check the calculations that they performed
[p0207-l0007] [10.0pt] to make these predictions; nevertheless, it is usually hard to explain in simple terms
[p0207-l0008] [10.0pt] why the predictions were made. For example, if a neural network says that a particu‐
[p0207-l0009] [10.0pt] lar person appears on a picture, it is hard to know what actually contributed to this
[p0207-l0010] [10.0pt] prediction: did the model recognize that person’s eyes? Her mouth? Her nose? Her
[p0207-l0011] [10.0pt] shoes? Or even the couch that she was sitting on? Conversely, Decision Trees provide
[p0207-l0012] [10.0pt] nice and simple classification rules that can even be applied manually if need be (e.g.,
[p0207-l0013] [10.0pt] for flower classification).
[p0207-l0014] [18.92pt] Estimating Class Probabilities
[p0207-l0015] [10.5pt] A Decision Tree can also estimate the probability that an instance belongs to a partic‐
[p0207-l0016] [10.5pt] ular class k: first it traverses the tree to find the leaf node for this instance, and then it
[p0207-l0017] [10.5pt] returns the ratio of training instances of class k in this node. For example, suppose
[p0207-l0018] [10.5pt] you have found a flower whose petals are 5 cm long and 1.5 cm wide. The corre‐
[p0207-l0019] [10.5pt] sponding leaf node is the depth-2 left node, so the Decision Tree should output the
[p0207-l0020] [10.5pt] following probabilities: 0% for Iris-Setosa (0/54), 90.7% for Iris-Versicolor (49/54),
[p0207-l0021] [10.5pt] and 9.3% for Iris-Virginica (5/54). And of course if you ask it to predict the class, it
[p0207-l0022] [10.5pt] should output Iris-Versicolor (class 1) since it has the highest probability. Let’s check
[p0207-l0023] [10.5pt] this:
[p0207-l0024] [8.5pt] >>> tree_clf.predict_proba([[5, 1.5]])
[p0207-l0025] [8.5pt] array([[0.        , 0.90740741, 0.09259259]])
[p0207-l0026] [9.0pt] Estimating Class Probabilities
[p0207-l0027] [9.0pt] |
[p0207-l0028] [9.0pt] 181

=== PDF page 208 / printed label 182 ===
[p0208-l0001] [8.5pt] >>> tree_clf.predict([[5, 1.5]])
[p0208-l0002] [8.5pt] array([1])
[p0208-l0003] [10.5pt] Perfect! Notice that the estimated probabilities would be identical anywhere else in
[p0208-l0004] [10.5pt] the bottom-right rectangle of Figure 6-2—for example, if the petals were 6 cm long
[p0208-l0005] [10.5pt] and 1.5 cm wide (even though it seems obvious that it would most likely be an Iris-
[p0208-l0006] [10.5pt] Virginica in this case).
[p0208-l0007] [18.92pt] The CART Training Algorithm
[p0208-l0008] [10.5pt] Scikit-Learn uses the Classification And Regression Tree (CART) algorithm to train
[p0208-l0009] [10.5pt] Decision Trees (also called “growing” trees). The idea is really quite simple: the algo‐
[p0208-l0010] [10.5pt] rithm first splits the training set in two subsets using a single feature k and a thres‐
[p0208-l0011] [10.5pt] hold tk (e.g., “petal length ≤ 2.45 cm”). How does it choose k and tk? It searches for the
[p0208-l0012] [10.5pt] pair (k, tk) that produces the purest subsets (weighted by their size). The cost function
[p0208-l0013] [10.5pt] that the algorithm tries to minimize is given by Equation 6-2.
[p0208-l0014] [10.5pt] Equation 6-2. CART cost function for classification
[p0208-l0015] [10.0pt] mleft
[p0208-l0016] [10.0pt] mright
[p0208-l0017] [10.0pt] J k, tk =
[p0208-l0018] [10.0pt] m Gleft +
[p0208-l0019] [10.0pt] m
[p0208-l0020] [10.0pt] Gright
[p0208-l0021] [10.0pt] Gleft/right measures the impurity of the left/right subset,
[p0208-l0022] [10.0pt] where
[p0208-l0023] [10.0pt] mleft/right is the number of instances in the left/right subset.
[p0208-l0024] [10.5pt] Once it has successfully split the training set in two, it splits the subsets using the
[p0208-l0025] [10.5pt] same logic, then the sub-subsets and so on, recursively. It stops recursing once it rea‐
[p0208-l0026] [10.5pt] ches the maximum depth (defined by the max_depth hyperparameter), or if it cannot
[p0208-l0027] [10.5pt] find a split that will reduce impurity. A few other hyperparameters (described in a
[p0208-l0028] [10.5pt] moment) control additional stopping conditions (min_samples_split, min_sam
[p0208-l0029] [10.5pt] ples_leaf, min_weight_fraction_leaf, and max_leaf_nodes).
[p0208-l0030] [9.0pt] 182
[p0208-l0031] [9.0pt] |
[p0208-l0032] [9.0pt] Chapter 6: Decision Trees

=== PDF page 209 / printed label 183 ===
[p0209-l0001] [9.6pt] As you can see, the CART algorithm is a greedy algorithm: it greed‐
[p0209-l0002] [9.6pt] ily searches for an optimum split at the top level, then repeats the
[p0209-l0003] [9.6pt] process at each level. It does not check whether or not the split will
[p0209-l0004] [9.6pt] lead to the lowest possible impurity several levels down. A greedy
[p0209-l0005] [9.6pt] algorithm often produces a reasonably good solution, but it is not
[p0209-l0006] [9.6pt] guaranteed to be the optimal solution.
[p0209-l0007] [9.6pt] Unfortunately, finding the optimal tree is known to be an NP-
[p0209-l0008] [9.6pt] Complete problem:2 it requires O(exp(m)) time, making the prob‐
[p0209-l0009] [9.6pt] lem intractable even for fairly small training sets. This is why we
[p0209-l0010] [9.6pt] must settle for a “reasonably good” solution.
[p0209-l0011] [18.92pt] Computational Complexity
[p0209-l0012] [10.5pt] Making predictions requires traversing the Decision Tree from the root to a leaf.
[p0209-l0013] [10.5pt] Decision Trees are generally approximately balanced, so traversing the Decision Tree
[p0209-l0014] [10.5pt] requires going through roughly O(log2(m)) nodes.3 Since each node only requires
[p0209-l0015] [10.5pt] checking the value of one feature, the overall prediction complexity is just O(log2(m)),
[p0209-l0016] [10.5pt] independent of the number of features. So predictions are very fast, even when deal‐
[p0209-l0017] [10.5pt] ing with large training sets.
[p0209-l0018] [10.5pt] However, the training algorithm compares all features (or less if max_features is set)
[p0209-l0019] [10.5pt] on all samples at each node. This results in a training complexity of O(n × m log(m)).
[p0209-l0020] [10.5pt] For small training sets (less than a few thousand instances), Scikit-Learn can speed up
[p0209-l0021] [10.5pt] training by presorting the data (set presort=True), but this slows down training con‐
[p0209-l0022] [10.5pt] siderably for larger training sets.
[p0209-l0023] [18.92pt] Gini Impurity or Entropy?
[p0209-l0024] [10.5pt] By default, the Gini impurity measure is used, but you can select the entropy impurity
[p0209-l0025] [10.5pt] measure instead by setting the criterion hyperparameter to "entropy". The concept
[p0209-l0026] [10.5pt] of entropy originated in thermodynamics as a measure of molecular disorder:
[p0209-l0027] [10.5pt] entropy approaches zero when molecules are still and well ordered. It later spread to a
[p0209-l0028] [10.5pt] wide variety of domains, including Shannon’s information theory, where it measures
[p0209-l0029] [10.5pt] the average information content of a message:4 entropy is zero when all messages are
[p0209-l0030] [10.5pt] identical. In Machine Learning, it is frequently used as an impurity measure: a set’s
[p0209-l0031] [8.0pt] 2 P is the set of problems that can be solved in polynomial time. NP is the set of problems whose solutions can
[p0209-l0032] [8.0pt] be verified in polynomial time. An NP-Hard problem is a problem to which any NP problem can be reduced
[p0209-l0033] [8.0pt] in polynomial time. An NP-Complete problem is both NP and NP-Hard. A major open mathematical ques‐
[p0209-l0034] [8.0pt] tion is whether or not P = NP. If P ≠ NP (which seems likely), then no polynomial algorithm will ever be
[p0209-l0035] [8.0pt] found for any NP-Complete problem (except perhaps on a quantum computer).
[p0209-l0036] [8.0pt] 3 log2 is the binary logarithm. It is equal to log2(m) = log(m) / log(2).
[p0209-l0037] [8.0pt] 4 A reduction of entropy is often called an information gain.
[p0209-l0038] [9.0pt] Computational Complexity
[p0209-l0039] [9.0pt] |

[p0210-l0017] [10.5pt] So should you use Gini impurity or entropy? The truth is, most of the time it does not
[p0210-l0018] [10.5pt] make a big difference: they lead to similar trees. Gini impurity is slightly faster to
[p0210-l0019] [10.5pt] compute, so it is a good default. However, when they differ, Gini impurity tends to
[p0210-l0020] [10.5pt] isolate the most frequent class in its own branch of the tree, while entropy tends to
[p0210-l0021] [10.5pt] produce slightly more balanced trees.5
[p0210-l0022] [18.92pt] Regularization Hyperparameters
[p0210-l0023] [10.5pt] Decision Trees make very few assumptions about the training data (as opposed to lin‐
[p0210-l0024] [10.5pt] ear models, which obviously assume that the data is linear, for example). If left
[p0210-l0025] [10.5pt] unconstrained, the tree structure will adapt itself to the training data, fitting it very
[p0210-l0026] [10.5pt] closely, and most likely overfitting it. Such a model is often called a nonparametric
[p0210-l0027] [10.5pt] model, not because it does not have any parameters (it often has a lot) but because the
[p0210-l0028] [10.5pt] number of parameters is not determined prior to training, so the model structure is
[p0210-l0029] [10.5pt] free to stick closely to the data. In contrast, a parametric model such as a linear model
[p0210-l0030] [10.5pt] has a predetermined number of parameters, so its degree of freedom is limited,
[p0210-l0031] [10.5pt] reducing the risk of overfitting (but increasing the risk of underfitting).
[p0210-l0032] [10.5pt] To avoid overfitting the training data, you need to restrict the Decision Tree’s freedom
[p0210-l0033] [10.5pt] during training. As you know by now, this is called regularization. The regularization
[p0210-l0034] [10.5pt] hyperparameters depend on the algorithm used, but generally you can at least restrict
[p0210-l0035] [10.5pt] the maximum depth of the Decision Tree. In Scikit-Learn, this is controlled by the
[p0210-l0036] [10.5pt] max_depth hyperparameter (the default value is None, which means unlimited).
[p0210-l0037] [10.5pt] Reducing max_depth will regularize the model and thus reduce the risk of overfitting.
[p0210-l0038] [10.5pt] The DecisionTreeClassifier class has a few other parameters that similarly restrict
[p0210-l0039] [10.5pt] the shape of the Decision Tree: min_samples_split (the minimum number of sam‐
[p0210-l0040] [10.5pt] ples a node must have before it can be split), min_samples_leaf (the minimum num‐
[p0210-l0041] [10.5pt] ber of samples a leaf node must have), min_weight_fraction_leaf (same as
[p0210-l0042] [10.5pt] min_samples_leaf but expressed as a fraction of the total number of weighted
[p0210-l0043] [8.0pt] 5 See Sebastian Raschka’s interesting analysis for more details.
[p0210-l0044] [9.0pt] 184
[p0210-l0045] [9.0pt] |
[p0210-l0046] [9.0pt] Chapter 6: Decision Trees

=== PDF page 211 / printed label 185 ===
[p0211-l0001] [10.5pt] instances), max_leaf_nodes (maximum number of leaf nodes), and max_features
[p0211-l0002] [10.5pt] (maximum number of features that are evaluated for splitting at each node). Increas‐
[p0211-l0003] [10.5pt] ing min_* hyperparameters or reducing max_* hyperparameters will regularize the
[p0211-l0004] [10.5pt] model.
[p0211-l0005] [9.6pt] Other algorithms work by first training the Decision Tree without
[p0211-l0006] [9.6pt] restrictions, then pruning (deleting) unnecessary nodes. A node
[p0211-l0007] [9.6pt] whose children are all leaf nodes is considered unnecessary if the
[p0211-l0008] [9.6pt] purity improvement it provides is not statistically significant. Stan‐
[p0211-l0009] [9.6pt] dard statistical tests, such as the χ2 test, are used to estimate the
[p0211-l0010] [9.6pt] probability that the improvement is purely the result of chance
[p0211-l0011] [9.6pt] (which is called the null hypothesis). If this probability, called the p-
[p0211-l0012] [9.6pt] value, is higher than a given threshold (typically 5%, controlled by
[p0211-l0013] [9.6pt] a hyperparameter), then the node is considered unnecessary and its
[p0211-l0014] [9.6pt] children are deleted. The pruning continues until all unnecessary
[p0211-l0015] [9.6pt] nodes have been pruned.
[p0211-l0016] [10.5pt] Figure 6-3 shows two Decision Trees trained on the moons dataset (introduced in
[p0211-l0017] [10.5pt] Chapter 5). On the left, the Decision Tree is trained with the default hyperparameters
[p0211-l0018] [10.5pt] (i.e., no restrictions), and on the right the Decision Tree is trained with min_sam
[p0211-l0019] [10.5pt] ples_leaf=4. It is quite obvious that the model on the left is overfitting, and the
[p0211-l0020] [10.5pt] model on the right will probably generalize better.
[p0211-l0021] [10.5pt] Figure 6-3. Regularization using min_samples_leaf

[p0212-l0004] [10.5pt] Figure 6-4. A Decision Tree for regression
[p0212-l0005] [10.5pt] This tree looks very similar to the classification tree you built earlier. The main differ‐
[p0212-l0006] [10.5pt] ence is that instead of predicting a class in each node, it predicts a value. For example,
[p0212-l0007] [10.5pt] suppose you want to make a prediction for a new instance with x1 = 0.6. You traverse
[p0212-l0008] [10.5pt] the tree starting at the root, and you eventually reach the leaf node that predicts
[p0212-l0009] [10.5pt] value=0.1106. This prediction is simply the average target value of the 110 training
[p0212-l0010] [10.5pt] instances associated to this leaf node. This prediction results in a Mean Squared Error
[p0212-l0011] [10.5pt] (MSE) equal to 0.0151 over these 110 instances.
[p0212-l0012] [10.5pt] This model’s predictions are represented on the left of Figure 6-5. If you set
[p0212-l0013] [10.5pt] max_depth=3, you get the predictions represented on the right. Notice how the pre‐
[p0212-l0014] [10.5pt] dicted value for each region is always the average target value of the instances in that
[p0212-l0015] [10.5pt] region. The algorithm splits each region in a way that makes most training instances
[p0212-l0016] [10.5pt] as close as possible to that predicted value.

[p0214-l0001] [18.92pt] Instability
[p0214-l0002] [10.5pt] Hopefully by now you are convinced that Decision Trees have a lot going for them:
[p0214-l0003] [10.5pt] they are simple to understand and interpret, easy to use, versatile, and powerful.
[p0214-l0004] [10.5pt] However they do have a few limitations. First, as you may have noticed, Decision
[p0214-l0005] [10.5pt] Trees love orthogonal decision boundaries (all splits are perpendicular to an axis),
[p0214-l0006] [10.5pt] which makes them sensitive to training set rotation. For example, Figure 6-7 shows a
[p0214-l0007] [10.5pt] simple linearly separable dataset: on the left, a Decision Tree can split it easily, while
[p0214-l0008] [10.5pt] on the right, after the dataset is rotated by 45°, the decision boundary looks unneces‐
[p0214-l0009] [10.5pt] sarily convoluted. Although both Decision Trees fit the training set perfectly, it is very
[p0214-l0010] [10.5pt] likely that the model on the right will not generalize well. One way to limit this prob‐
[p0214-l0011] [10.5pt] lem is to use PCA (see Chapter 8), which often results in a better orientation of the
[p0214-l0012] [10.5pt] training data.
[p0214-l0013] [10.5pt] Figure 6-7. Sensitivity to training set rotation
[p0214-l0014] [10.5pt] More generally, the main issue with Decision Trees is that they are very sensitive to
[p0214-l0015] [10.5pt] small variations in the training data. For example, if you just remove the widest Iris-
[p0214-l0016] [10.5pt] Versicolor from the iris training set (the one with petals 4.8 cm long and 1.8 cm wide)
[p0214-l0017] [10.5pt] and train a new Decision Tree, you may get the model represented in Figure 6-8. As
[p0214-l0018] [10.5pt] you can see, it looks very different from the previous Decision Tree (Figure 6-2).
[p0214-l0019] [10.5pt] Actually, since the training algorithm used by Scikit-Learn is stochastic6 you may
[p0214-l0020] [10.5pt] get very different models even on the same training data (unless you set the
[p0214-l0021] [10.5pt] random_state hyperparameter).
[p0214-l0022] [8.0pt] 6 It randomly selects the set of features to evaluate at each node.
[p0214-l0023] [9.0pt] 188
[p0214-l0024] [9.0pt] |
[p0214-l0025] [9.0pt] Chapter 6: Decision Trees

=== PDF page 215 / printed label 189 ===
[p0215-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 6-8. Sensitivity to training set details
[p0215-l0002] [10.5pt] Random Forests can limit this instability by averaging predictions over many trees, as
[p0215-l0003] [10.5pt] we will see in the next chapter.

[p0216-l0001] [10.5pt] c. Use grid search with cross-validation (with the help of the GridSearchCV

[p0216-l0006] [10.5pt] accuracy.
[p0216-l0007] [10.5pt] 8. Grow a forest.
[p0216-l0008] [10.5pt] a. Continuing the previous exercise, generate 1,000 subsets of the training set,

[p0217-l0001] [16.82pt] CHAPTER 7
[p0217-l0002] [25.22pt] Ensemble Learning and Random Forests
[p0217-l0003] [9.6pt] With Early Release ebooks, you get books in their earliest form—
[p0217-l0004] [9.6pt] the author’s raw and unedited content as he or she writes—so you
[p0217-l0005] [9.6pt] can take advantage of these technologies long before the official
[p0217-l0006] [9.6pt] release of these titles. The following will be Chapter 7 in the final
[p0217-l0007] [9.6pt] release of the book.
[p0217-l0008] [10.5pt] Suppose you ask a complex question to thousands of random people, then aggregate
[p0217-l0009] [10.5pt] their answers. In many cases you will find that this aggregated answer is better than
[p0217-l0010] [10.5pt] an expert’s answer. This is called the wisdom of the crowd. Similarly, if you aggregate
[p0217-l0011] [10.5pt] the predictions of a group of predictors (such as classifiers or regressors), you will
[p0217-l0012] [10.5pt] often get better predictions than with the best individual predictor. A group of pre‐
[p0217-l0013] [10.5pt] dictors is called an ensemble; thus, this technique is called Ensemble Learning, and an
[p0217-l0014] [10.5pt] Ensemble Learning algorithm is called an Ensemble method.
[p0217-l0015] [10.5pt] For example, you can train a group of Decision Tree classifiers, each on a different
[p0217-l0016] [10.5pt] random subset of the training set. To make predictions, you just obtain the predic‐
[p0217-l0017] [10.5pt] tions of all individual trees, then predict the class that gets the most votes (see the last
[p0217-l0018] [10.5pt] exercise in Chapter 6). Such an ensemble of Decision Trees is called a Random Forest,
[p0217-l0019] [10.5pt] and despite its simplicity, this is one of the most powerful Machine Learning algo‐
[p0217-l0020] [10.5pt] rithms available today.
[p0217-l0021] [10.5pt] Moreover, as we discussed in Chapter 2, you will often use Ensemble methods near
[p0217-l0022] [10.5pt] the end of a project, once you have already built a few good predictors, to combine
[p0217-l0023] [10.5pt] them into an even better predictor. In fact, the winning solutions in Machine Learn‐
[p0217-l0024] [10.5pt] ing competitions often involve several Ensemble methods (most famously in the Net‐
[p0217-l0025] [10.5pt] flix Prize competition).
[p0217-l0026] [10.5pt] In this chapter we will discuss the most popular Ensemble methods, including bag‐
[p0217-l0027] [10.5pt] ging, boosting, stacking, and a few others. We will also explore Random Forests.
[p0217-l0028] [9.0pt] 191

=== PDF page 218 / printed label 192 ===
[p0218-l0001] [18.92pt] Voting Classifiers
[p0218-l0002] [10.5pt] Suppose you have trained a few classifiers, each one achieving about 80% accuracy.
[p0218-l0003] [10.5pt] You may have a Logistic Regression classifier, an SVM classifier, a Random Forest
[p0218-l0004] [10.5pt] classifier, a K-Nearest Neighbors classifier, and perhaps a few more (see Figure 7-1).
[p0218-l0005] [10.5pt] Figure 7-1. Training diverse classifiers
[p0218-l0006] [10.5pt] A very simple way to create an even better classifier is to aggregate the predictions of
[p0218-l0007] [10.5pt] each classifier and predict the class that gets the most votes. This majority-vote classi‐
[p0218-l0008] [10.5pt] fier is called a hard voting classifier (see Figure 7-2).
[p0218-l0009] [10.5pt] Figure 7-2. Hard voting classifier predictions
[p0218-l0010] [9.0pt] 192
[p0218-l0011] [9.0pt] |
[p0218-l0012] [9.0pt] Chapter 7: Ensemble Learning and Random Forests

=== PDF page 219 / printed label 193 ===
[p0219-l0001] [10.5pt] Somewhat surprisingly, this voting classifier often achieves a higher accuracy than the
[p0219-l0002] [10.5pt] best classifier in the ensemble. In fact, even if each classifier is a weak learner (mean‐
[p0219-l0003] [10.5pt] ing it does only slightly better than random guessing), the ensemble can still be a
[p0219-l0004] [10.5pt] strong learner (achieving high accuracy), provided there are a sufficient number of
[p0219-l0005] [10.5pt] weak learners and they are sufficiently diverse.
[p0219-l0006] [10.5pt] How is this possible? The following analogy can help shed some light on this mystery.
[p0219-l0007] [10.5pt] Suppose you have a slightly biased coin that has a 51% chance of coming up heads,
[p0219-l0008] [10.5pt] and 49% chance of coming up tails. If you toss it 1,000 times, you will generally get
[p0219-l0009] [10.5pt] more or less 510 heads and 490 tails, and hence a majority of heads. If you do the
[p0219-l0010] [10.5pt] math, you will find that the probability of obtaining a majority of heads after 1,000
[p0219-l0011] [10.5pt] tosses is close to 75%. The more you toss the coin, the higher the probability (e.g.,
[p0219-l0012] [10.5pt] with 10,000 tosses, the probability climbs over 97%). This is due to the law of large
[p0219-l0013] [10.5pt] numbers: as you keep tossing the coin, the ratio of heads gets closer and closer to the
[p0219-l0014] [10.5pt] probability of heads (51%). Figure 7-3 shows 10 series of biased coin tosses. You can
[p0219-l0015] [10.5pt] see that as the number of tosses increases, the ratio of heads approaches 51%. Eventu‐
[p0219-l0016] [10.5pt] ally all 10 series end up so close to 51% that they are consistently above 50%.
[p0219-l0017] [10.5pt] Figure 7-3. The law of large numbers
[p0219-l0018] [10.5pt] Similarly, suppose you build an ensemble containing 1,000 classifiers that are individ‐
[p0219-l0019] [10.5pt] ually correct only 51% of the time (barely better than random guessing). If you pre‐
[p0219-l0020] [10.5pt] dict the majority voted class, you can hope for up to 75% accuracy! However, this is
[p0219-l0021] [10.5pt] only true if all classifiers are perfectly independent, making uncorrelated errors,
[p0219-l0022] [10.5pt] which is clearly not the case since they are trained on the same data. They are likely to
[p0219-l0023] [10.5pt] make the same types of errors, so there will be many majority votes for the wrong
[p0219-l0024] [10.5pt] class, reducing the ensemble’s accuracy.
[p0219-l0025] [9.0pt] Voting Classifiers
[p0219-l0026] [9.0pt] |
[p0219-l0027] [9.0pt] 193

=== PDF page 220 / printed label 194 ===
[p0220-l0001] [9.6pt] Ensemble methods work best when the predictors are as independ‐
[p0220-l0002] [9.6pt] ent from one another as possible. One way to get diverse classifiers
[p0220-l0003] [9.6pt] is to train them using very different algorithms. This increases the
[p0220-l0004] [9.6pt] chance that they will make very different types of errors, improving
[p0220-l0005] [9.6pt] the ensemble’s accuracy.
[p0220-l0006] [10.5pt] The following code creates and trains a voting classifier in Scikit-Learn, composed of
[p0220-l0007] [10.5pt] three diverse classifiers (the training set is the moons dataset, introduced in Chap‐
[p0220-l0008] [10.5pt] ter 5):
[p0220-l0009] [8.5pt] from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
[p0220-l0010] [8.5pt] from sklearn.ensemble import VotingClassifier
[p0220-l0011] [8.5pt] from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
[p0220-l0012] [8.5pt] from sklearn.svm import SVC
[p0220-l0013] [8.5pt] log_clf = LogisticRegression()
[p0220-l0014] [8.5pt] rnd_clf = RandomForestClassifier()
[p0220-l0015] [8.5pt] svm_clf = SVC()
[p0220-l0016] [8.5pt] voting_clf = VotingClassifier(
[p0220-l0017] [8.5pt]     estimators=[('lr', log_clf), ('rf', rnd_clf), ('svc', svm_clf)],
[p0220-l0018] [8.5pt]     voting='hard')
[p0220-l0019] [8.5pt] voting_clf.fit(X_train, y_train)
[p0220-l0020] [10.5pt] Let’s look at each classifier’s accuracy on the test set:
[p0220-l0021] [8.5pt] >>> from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score
[p0220-l0022] [8.5pt] >>> for clf in (log_clf, rnd_clf, svm_clf, voting_clf):
[p0220-l0023] [8.5pt] ...     clf.fit(X_train, y_train)
[p0220-l0024] [8.5pt] ...     y_pred = clf.predict(X_test)
[p0220-l0025] [8.5pt] ...     print(clf.__class__.__name__, accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred))
[p0220-l0026] [8.5pt] ...
[p0220-l0027] [8.5pt] LogisticRegression 0.864
[p0220-l0028] [8.5pt] RandomForestClassifier 0.896
[p0220-l0029] [8.5pt] SVC 0.888
[p0220-l0030] [8.5pt] VotingClassifier 0.904
[p0220-l0031] [10.5pt] There you have it! The voting classifier slightly outperforms all the individual classifi‐
[p0220-l0032] [10.5pt] ers.
[p0220-l0033] [10.5pt] If all classifiers are able to estimate class probabilities (i.e., they have a pre
[p0220-l0034] [10.5pt] dict_proba() method), then you can tell Scikit-Learn to predict the class with the
[p0220-l0035] [10.5pt] highest class probability, averaged over all the individual classifiers. This is called soft
[p0220-l0036] [10.5pt] voting. It often achieves higher performance than hard voting because it gives more
[p0220-l0037] [10.5pt] weight to highly confident votes. All you need to do is replace voting="hard" with
[p0220-l0038] [10.5pt] voting="soft" and ensure that all classifiers can estimate class probabilities. This is
[p0220-l0039] [10.5pt] not the case of the SVC class by default, so you need to set its probability hyperpara‐
[p0220-l0040] [10.5pt] meter to True (this will make the SVC class use cross-validation to estimate class prob‐
[p0220-l0041] [10.5pt] abilities, slowing down training, and it will add a predict_proba() method). If you
[p0220-l0042] [9.0pt] 194
[p0220-l0043] [9.0pt] |
[p0220-l0044] [9.0pt] Chapter 7: Ensemble Learning and Random Forests

[p0221-l0001] [10.5pt] modify the preceding code to use soft voting, you will find that the voting classifier
[p0221-l0002] [10.5pt] achieves over 91.2% accuracy!
[p0221-l0003] [18.92pt] Bagging and Pasting
[p0221-l0004] [10.5pt] One way to get a diverse set of classifiers is to use very different training algorithms,
[p0221-l0005] [10.5pt] as just discussed. Another approach is to use the same training algorithm for every
[p0221-l0006] [10.5pt] predictor, but to train them on different random subsets of the training set. When
[p0221-l0007] [10.5pt] sampling is performed with replacement, this method is called bagging1 (short for
[p0221-l0008] [10.5pt] bootstrap aggregating2). When sampling is performed without replacement, it is called
[p0221-l0009] [10.5pt] pasting.3
[p0221-l0010] [10.5pt] In other words, both bagging and pasting allow training instances to be sampled sev‐
[p0221-l0011] [10.5pt] eral times across multiple predictors, but only bagging allows training instances to be
[p0221-l0012] [10.5pt] sampled several times for the same predictor. This sampling and training process is
[p0221-l0013] [10.5pt] represented in Figure 7-4.
[p0221-l0014] [10.5pt] Figure 7-4. Pasting/bagging training set sampling and training
[p0221-l0015] [10.5pt] Once all predictors are trained, the ensemble can make a prediction for a new
[p0221-l0016] [10.5pt] instance by simply aggregating the predictions of all predictors. The aggregation
[p0221-l0017] [10.5pt] function is typically the statistical mode (i.e., the most frequent prediction, just like a
[p0221-l0018] [10.5pt] hard voting classifier) for classification, or the average for regression. Each individual
[p0221-l0019] [8.0pt] 1 “Bagging Predictors,” L. Breiman (1996).
[p0221-l0020] [8.0pt] 2 In statistics, resampling with replacement is called bootstrapping.
[p0221-l0021] [8.0pt] 3 “Pasting small votes for classification in large databases and on-line,” L. Breiman (1999).
[p0221-l0022] [9.0pt] Bagging and Pasting
[p0221-l0023] [9.0pt] |
[p0221-l0024] [9.0pt] 195

=== PDF page 222 / printed label 196 ===
[p0222-l0001] [10.5pt] predictor has a higher bias than if it were trained on the original training set, but
[p0222-l0002] [10.5pt] aggregation reduces both bias and variance.4 Generally, the net result is that the
[p0222-l0003] [10.5pt] ensemble has a similar bias but a lower variance than a single predictor trained on the
[p0222-l0004] [10.5pt] original training set.
[p0222-l0005] [10.5pt] As you can see in Figure 7-4, predictors can all be trained in parallel, via different
[p0222-l0006] [10.5pt] CPU cores or even different servers. Similarly, predictions can be made in parallel.
[p0222-l0007] [10.5pt] This is one of the reasons why bagging and pasting are such popular methods: they
[p0222-l0008] [10.5pt] scale very well.
[p0222-l0009] [15.77pt] Bagging and Pasting in Scikit-Learn
[p0222-l0010] [10.5pt] Scikit-Learn offers a simple API for both bagging and pasting with the BaggingClas
[p0222-l0011] [10.5pt] sifier class (or BaggingRegressor for regression). The following code trains an
[p0222-l0012] [10.5pt] ensemble of 500 Decision Tree classifiers,5 each trained on 100 training instances ran‐
[p0222-l0013] [10.5pt] domly sampled from the training set with replacement (this is an example of bagging,
[p0222-l0014] [10.5pt] but if you want to use pasting instead, just set bootstrap=False). The n_jobs param‐
[p0222-l0015] [10.5pt] eter tells Scikit-Learn the number of CPU cores to use for training and predictions
[p0222-l0016] [10.5pt] (–1 tells Scikit-Learn to use all available cores):
[p0222-l0017] [8.5pt] from sklearn.ensemble import BaggingClassifier
[p0222-l0018] [8.5pt] from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
[p0222-l0019] [8.5pt] bag_clf = BaggingClassifier(
[p0222-l0020] [8.5pt]     DecisionTreeClassifier(), n_estimators=500,
[p0222-l0021] [8.5pt]     max_samples=100, bootstrap=True, n_jobs=-1)
[p0222-l0022] [8.5pt] bag_clf.fit(X_train, y_train)
[p0222-l0023] [8.5pt] y_pred = bag_clf.predict(X_test)
[p0222-l0024] [9.6pt] The BaggingClassifier automatically performs soft voting
[p0222-l0025] [9.6pt] instead of hard voting if the base classifier can estimate class proba‐
[p0222-l0026] [9.6pt] bilities (i.e., if it has a predict_proba() method), which is the case
[p0222-l0027] [9.6pt] with Decision Trees classifiers.
[p0222-l0028] [10.5pt] Figure 7-5 compares the decision boundary of a single Decision Tree with the deci‐
[p0222-l0029] [10.5pt] sion boundary of a bagging ensemble of 500 trees (from the preceding code), both
[p0222-l0030] [10.5pt] trained on the moons dataset. As you can see, the ensemble’s predictions will likely
[p0222-l0031] [10.5pt] generalize much better than the single Decision Tree’s predictions: the ensemble has a
[p0222-l0032] [10.5pt] comparable bias but a smaller variance (it makes roughly the same number of errors
[p0222-l0033] [10.5pt] on the training set, but the decision boundary is less irregular).
[p0222-l0034] [8.0pt] 4 Bias and variance were introduced in Chapter 4.
[p0222-l0035] [8.0pt] 5 max_samples can alternatively be set to a float between 0.0 and 1.0, in which case the max number of instances
[p0222-l0036] [8.0pt] to sample is equal to the size of the training set times max_samples.

[p0222-l0039] [9.0pt] Chapter 7: Ensemble Learning and Random Forests

[p0223-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 7-5. A single Decision Tree versus a bagging ensemble of 500 trees
[p0223-l0002] [10.5pt] Bootstrapping introduces a bit more diversity in the subsets that each predictor is
[p0223-l0003] [10.5pt] trained on, so bagging ends up with a slightly higher bias than pasting, but this also
[p0223-l0004] [10.5pt] means that predictors end up being less correlated so the ensemble’s variance is
[p0223-l0005] [10.5pt] reduced. Overall, bagging often results in better models, which explains why it is gen‐
[p0223-l0006] [10.5pt] erally preferred. However, if you have spare time and CPU power you can use cross-
[p0223-l0007] [10.5pt] validation to evaluate both bagging and pasting and select the one that works best.
[p0223-l0008] [15.77pt] Out-of-Bag Evaluation
[p0223-l0009] [10.5pt] With bagging, some instances may be sampled several times for any given predictor,
[p0223-l0010] [10.5pt] while others may not be sampled at all. By default a BaggingClassifier samples m
[p0223-l0011] [10.5pt] training instances with replacement (bootstrap=True), where m is the size of the
[p0223-l0012] [10.5pt] training set. This means that only about 63% of the training instances are sampled on
[p0223-l0013] [10.5pt] average for each predictor.6 The remaining 37% of the training instances that are not
[p0223-l0014] [10.5pt] sampled are called out-of-bag (oob) instances. Note that they are not the same 37%
[p0223-l0015] [10.5pt] for all predictors.
[p0223-l0016] [10.5pt] Since a predictor never sees the oob instances during training, it can be evaluated on
[p0223-l0017] [10.5pt] these instances, without the need for a separate validation set. You can evaluate the
[p0223-l0018] [10.5pt] ensemble itself by averaging out the oob evaluations of each predictor.
[p0223-l0019] [10.5pt] In Scikit-Learn, you can set oob_score=True when creating a BaggingClassifier to
[p0223-l0020] [10.5pt] request an automatic oob evaluation after training. The following code demonstrates
[p0223-l0021] [10.5pt] this. The resulting evaluation score is available through the oob_score_ variable:
[p0223-l0022] [8.5pt] >>> bag_clf = BaggingClassifier(
[p0223-l0023] [8.5pt] ...     DecisionTreeClassifier(), n_estimators=500,
[p0223-l0024] [8.5pt] ...     bootstrap=True, n_jobs=-1, oob_score=True)
[p0223-l0025] [8.5pt] ...
[p0223-l0026] [8.5pt] >>> bag_clf.fit(X_train, y_train)
[p0223-l0027] [8.0pt] 6 As m grows, this ratio approaches 1 – exp(–1) ≈ 63.212%.
[p0223-l0028] [9.0pt] Bagging and Pasting

[p0224-l0002] [8.5pt] 0.90133333333333332
[p0224-l0003] [10.5pt] According to this oob evaluation, this BaggingClassifier is likely to achieve about
[p0224-l0004] [10.5pt] 90.1% accuracy on the test set. Let’s verify this:
[p0224-l0005] [8.5pt] >>> from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score

[p0224-l0007] [8.5pt] >>> accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred)
[p0224-l0008] [8.5pt] 0.91200000000000003
[p0224-l0009] [10.5pt] We get 91.2% accuracy on the test set—close enough!
[p0224-l0010] [10.5pt] The oob decision function for each training instance is also available through the

[p0224-l0012] [10.5pt] dict_proba() method) the decision function returns the class probabilities for each
[p0224-l0013] [10.5pt] training instance. For example, the oob evaluation estimates that the first training
[p0224-l0014] [10.5pt] instance has a 68.25% probability of belonging to the positive class (and 31.75% of
