[p0224-l0024] [18.92pt] Random Patches and Random Subspaces
[p0224-l0025] [10.5pt] The BaggingClassifier class supports sampling the features as well. This is con‐
[p0224-l0026] [10.5pt] trolled by two hyperparameters: max_features and bootstrap_features. They work
[p0224-l0027] [10.5pt] the same way as max_samples and bootstrap, but for feature sampling instead of
[p0224-l0028] [10.5pt] instance sampling. Thus, each predictor will be trained on a random subset of the
[p0224-l0029] [10.5pt] input features.
[p0224-l0030] [10.5pt] This is particularly useful when you are dealing with high-dimensional inputs (such
[p0224-l0031] [10.5pt] as images). Sampling both training instances and features is called the Random
[p0224-l0032] [10.5pt] Patches method.7 Keeping all training instances (i.e., bootstrap=False and max_sam
[p0224-l0033] [10.5pt] ples=1.0) but sampling features (i.e., bootstrap_features=True and/or max_fea
[p0224-l0034] [10.5pt] tures smaller than 1.0) is called the Random Subspaces method.8
[p0224-l0035] [8.0pt] 7 “Ensembles on Random Patches,” G. Louppe and P. Geurts (2012).
[p0224-l0036] [8.0pt] 8 “The random subspace method for constructing decision forests,” Tin Kam Ho (1998).
[p0224-l0037] [9.0pt] 198
[p0224-l0038] [9.0pt] |
[p0224-l0039] [9.0pt] Chapter 7: Ensemble Learning and Random Forests

=== PDF page 225 / printed label 199 ===
[p0225-l0001] [10.5pt] Sampling features results in even more predictor diversity, trading a bit more bias for
[p0225-l0002] [10.5pt] a lower variance.
[p0225-l0003] [18.92pt] Random Forests
[p0225-l0004] [10.5pt] As we have discussed, a Random Forest9 is an ensemble of Decision Trees, generally
[p0225-l0005] [10.5pt] trained via the bagging method (or sometimes pasting), typically with max_samples
[p0225-l0006] [10.5pt] set to the size of the training set. Instead of building a BaggingClassifier and pass‐
[p0225-l0007] [10.5pt] ing it a DecisionTreeClassifier, you can instead use the RandomForestClassifier
[p0225-l0008] [10.5pt] class, which is more convenient and optimized for Decision Trees10 (similarly, there is
[p0225-l0009] [10.5pt] a RandomForestRegressor class for regression tasks). The following code trains a
[p0225-l0010] [10.5pt] Random Forest classifier with 500 trees (each limited to maximum 16 nodes), using
[p0225-l0011] [10.5pt] all available CPU cores:
[p0225-l0012] [8.5pt] from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
[p0225-l0013] [8.5pt] rnd_clf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=500, max_leaf_nodes=16, n_jobs=-1)
[p0225-l0014] [8.5pt] rnd_clf.fit(X_train, y_train)
[p0225-l0015] [8.5pt] y_pred_rf = rnd_clf.predict(X_test)
[p0225-l0016] [10.5pt] With a few exceptions, a RandomForestClassifier has all the hyperparameters of a
[p0225-l0017] [10.5pt] DecisionTreeClassifier (to control how trees are grown), plus all the hyperpara‐
[p0225-l0018] [10.5pt] meters of a BaggingClassifier to control the ensemble itself.11
[p0225-l0019] [10.5pt] The Random Forest algorithm introduces extra randomness when growing trees;
[p0225-l0020] [10.5pt] instead of searching for the very best feature when splitting a node (see Chapter 6), it
[p0225-l0021] [10.5pt] searches for the best feature among a random subset of features. This results in a
[p0225-l0022] [10.5pt] greater tree diversity, which (once again) trades a higher bias for a lower variance,
[p0225-l0023] [10.5pt] generally yielding an overall better model. The following BaggingClassifier is
[p0225-l0024] [10.5pt] roughly equivalent to the previous RandomForestClassifier:
[p0225-l0025] [8.5pt] bag_clf = BaggingClassifier(
[p0225-l0026] [8.5pt]     DecisionTreeClassifier(splitter="random", max_leaf_nodes=16),
[p0225-l0027] [8.5pt]     n_estimators=500, max_samples=1.0, bootstrap=True, n_jobs=-1)
[p0225-l0028] [8.0pt] 9 “Random Decision Forests,” T. Ho (1995).
[p0225-l0029] [8.0pt] 10 The BaggingClassifier class remains useful if you want a bag of something other than Decision Trees.
[p0225-l0030] [8.0pt] 11 There are a few notable exceptions: splitter is absent (forced to "random"), presort is absent (forced to
[p0225-l0031] [8.0pt] False), max_samples is absent (forced to 1.0), and base_estimator is absent (forced to DecisionTreeClassi
[p0225-l0032] [8.0pt] fier with the provided hyperparameters).
[p0225-l0033] [9.0pt] Random Forests
[p0225-l0034] [9.0pt] |
[p0225-l0035] [9.0pt] 199

=== PDF page 226 / printed label 200 ===
[p0226-l0001] [15.77pt] Extra-Trees
[p0226-l0002] [10.5pt] When you are growing a tree in a Random Forest, at each node only a random subset
[p0226-l0003] [10.5pt] of the features is considered for splitting (as discussed earlier). It is possible to make
[p0226-l0004] [10.5pt] trees even more random by also using random thresholds for each feature rather than
[p0226-l0005] [10.5pt] searching for the best possible thresholds (like regular Decision Trees do).
[p0226-l0006] [10.5pt] A forest of such extremely random trees is simply called an Extremely Randomized
[p0226-l0007] [10.5pt] Trees ensemble12 (or Extra-Trees for short). Once again, this trades more bias for a
[p0226-l0008] [10.5pt] lower variance. It also makes Extra-Trees much faster to train than regular Random
[p0226-l0009] [10.5pt] Forests since finding the best possible threshold for each feature at every node is one
[p0226-l0010] [10.5pt] of the most time-consuming tasks of growing a tree.
[p0226-l0011] [10.5pt] You can create an Extra-Trees classifier using Scikit-Learn’s ExtraTreesClassifier
[p0226-l0012] [10.5pt] class. Its API is identical to the RandomForestClassifier class. Similarly, the Extra
[p0226-l0013] [10.5pt] TreesRegressor class has the same API as the RandomForestRegressor class.
[p0226-l0014] [9.6pt] It is hard to tell in advance whether a RandomForestClassifier
[p0226-l0015] [9.6pt] will perform better or worse than an ExtraTreesClassifier. Gen‐
[p0226-l0016] [9.6pt] erally, the only way to know is to try both and compare them using
[p0226-l0017] [9.6pt] cross-validation (and tuning the hyperparameters using grid
[p0226-l0018] [9.6pt] search).
[p0226-l0019] [15.77pt] Feature Importance
[p0226-l0020] [10.5pt] Yet another great quality of Random Forests is that they make it easy to measure the
[p0226-l0021] [10.5pt] relative importance of each feature. Scikit-Learn measures a feature’s importance by
[p0226-l0022] [10.5pt] looking at how much the tree nodes that use that feature reduce impurity on average
[p0226-l0023] [10.5pt] (across all trees in the forest). More precisely, it is a weighted average, where each
[p0226-l0024] [10.5pt] node’s weight is equal to the number of training samples that are associated with it
[p0226-l0025] [10.5pt] (see Chapter 6).
[p0226-l0026] [10.5pt] Scikit-Learn computes this score automatically for each feature after training, then it
[p0226-l0027] [10.5pt] scales the results so that the sum of all importances is equal to 1. You can access the
[p0226-l0028] [10.5pt] result using the feature_importances_ variable. For example, the following code
[p0226-l0029] [10.5pt] trains a RandomForestClassifier on the iris dataset (introduced in Chapter 4) and
[p0226-l0030] [10.5pt] outputs each feature’s importance. It seems that the most important features are the
[p0226-l0031] [10.5pt] petal length (44%) and width (42%), while sepal length and width are rather unim‐
[p0226-l0032] [10.5pt] portant in comparison (11% and 2%, respectively).
[p0226-l0033] [8.0pt] 12 “Extremely randomized trees,” P. Geurts, D. Ernst, L. Wehenkel (2005).
[p0226-l0034] [9.0pt] 200
[p0226-l0035] [9.0pt] |
[p0226-l0036] [9.0pt] Chapter 7: Ensemble Learning and Random Forests

[p0227-l0003] [8.5pt] >>> rnd_clf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=500, n_jobs=-1)
[p0227-l0004] [8.5pt] >>> rnd_clf.fit(iris["data"], iris["target"])

[p0227-l0006] [8.5pt] ...     print(name, score)
[p0227-l0007] [8.5pt] ...
[p0227-l0008] [8.5pt] sepal length (cm) 0.112492250999
[p0227-l0009] [8.5pt] sepal width (cm) 0.0231192882825
[p0227-l0010] [8.5pt] petal length (cm) 0.441030464364

[p0227-l0012] [10.5pt] Similarly, if you train a Random Forest classifier on the MNIST dataset (introduced
[p0227-l0013] [10.5pt] in Chapter 3) and plot each pixel’s importance, you get the image represented in
[p0227-l0014] [10.5pt] Figure 7-6.
[p0227-l0015] [10.5pt] Figure 7-6. MNIST pixel importance (according to a Random Forest classifier)
[p0227-l0016] [10.5pt] Random Forests are very handy to get a quick understanding of what features
[p0227-l0017] [10.5pt] actually matter, in particular if you need to perform feature selection.
[p0227-l0018] [18.92pt] Boosting
[p0227-l0019] [10.5pt] Boosting (originally called hypothesis boosting) refers to any Ensemble method that
[p0227-l0020] [10.5pt] can combine several weak learners into a strong learner. The general idea of most
[p0227-l0021] [10.5pt] boosting methods is to train predictors sequentially, each trying to correct its prede‐
[p0227-l0022] [10.5pt] cessor. There are many boosting methods available, but by far the most popular are
[p0227-l0023] [9.0pt] Boosting
[p0227-l0024] [9.0pt] |
[p0227-l0025] [9.0pt] 201

=== PDF page 228 / printed label 202 ===
[p0228-l0001] [10.5pt] AdaBoost13 (short for Adaptive Boosting) and Gradient Boosting. Let’s start with Ada‐
[p0228-l0002] [10.5pt] Boost.
[p0228-l0003] [15.77pt] AdaBoost
[p0228-l0004] [10.5pt] One way for a new predictor to correct its predecessor is to pay a bit more attention
[p0228-l0005] [10.5pt] to the training instances that the predecessor underfitted. This results in new predic‐
[p0228-l0006] [10.5pt] tors focusing more and more on the hard cases. This is the technique used by Ada‐
[p0228-l0007] [10.5pt] Boost.
[p0228-l0008] [10.5pt] For example, to build an AdaBoost classifier, a first base classifier (such as a Decision
[p0228-l0009] [10.5pt] Tree) is trained and used to make predictions on the training set. The relative weight
[p0228-l0010] [10.5pt] of misclassified training instances is then increased. A second classifier is trained
[p0228-l0011] [10.5pt] using the updated weights and again it makes predictions on the training set, weights
[p0228-l0012] [10.5pt] are updated, and so on (see Figure 7-7).
[p0228-l0013] [10.5pt] Figure 7-7. AdaBoost sequential training with instance weight updates
[p0228-l0014] [10.5pt] Figure 7-8 shows the decision boundaries of five consecutive predictors on the
[p0228-l0015] [10.5pt] moons dataset (in this example, each predictor is a highly regularized SVM classifier
[p0228-l0016] [10.5pt] with an RBF kernel14). The first classifier gets many instances wrong, so their weights
[p0228-l0017] [8.0pt] 13 “A Decision-Theoretic Generalization of On-Line Learning and an Application to Boosting,” Yoav Freund,
[p0228-l0018] [8.0pt] Robert E. Schapire (1997).
[p0228-l0019] [8.0pt] 14 This is just for illustrative purposes. SVMs are generally not good base predictors for AdaBoost, because they
[p0228-l0020] [8.0pt] are slow and tend to be unstable with AdaBoost.
[p0228-l0021] [9.0pt] 202
[p0228-l0022] [9.0pt] |
[p0228-l0023] [9.0pt] Chapter 7: Ensemble Learning and Random Forests

=== PDF page 229 / printed label 203 ===
[p0229-l0001] [10.5pt] get boosted. The second classifier therefore does a better job on these instances, and
[p0229-l0002] [10.5pt] so on. The plot on the right represents the same sequence of predictors except that
[p0229-l0003] [10.5pt] the learning rate is halved (i.e., the misclassified instance weights are boosted half as
[p0229-l0004] [10.5pt] much at every iteration). As you can see, this sequential learning technique has some
[p0229-l0005] [10.5pt] similarities with Gradient Descent, except that instead of tweaking a single predictor’s
[p0229-l0006] [10.5pt] parameters to minimize a cost function, AdaBoost adds predictors to the ensemble,
[p0229-l0007] [10.5pt] gradually making it better.
[p0229-l0008] [10.5pt] Figure 7-8. Decision boundaries of consecutive predictors
[p0229-l0009] [10.5pt] Once all predictors are trained, the ensemble makes predictions very much like bag‐
[p0229-l0010] [10.5pt] ging or pasting, except that predictors have different weights depending on their
[p0229-l0011] [10.5pt] overall accuracy on the weighted training set.
[p0229-l0012] [9.6pt] There is one important drawback to this sequential learning techni‐
[p0229-l0013] [9.6pt] que: it cannot be parallelized (or only partially), since each predic‐
[p0229-l0014] [9.6pt] tor can only be trained after the previous predictor has been
[p0229-l0015] [9.6pt] trained and evaluated. As a result, it does not scale as well as bag‐
[p0229-l0016] [9.6pt] ging or pasting.
[p0229-l0017] [10.5pt] Let’s take a closer look at the AdaBoost algorithm. Each instance weight w(i) is initially
[p0229-l0018] [10.5pt] set to 1

[p0230-l0023] [10.5pt] Finally, a new predictor is trained using the updated weights, and the whole process is

[p0231-l0001] [10.5pt] Scikit-Learn actually uses a multiclass version of AdaBoost called SAMME16 (which
[p0231-l0002] [10.5pt] stands for Stagewise Additive Modeling using a Multiclass Exponential loss function).
[p0231-l0003] [10.5pt] When there are just two classes, SAMME is equivalent to AdaBoost. Moreover, if the
[p0231-l0004] [10.5pt] predictors can estimate class probabilities (i.e., if they have a predict_proba()
[p0231-l0005] [10.5pt] method), Scikit-Learn can use a variant of SAMME called SAMME.R (the R stands
[p0231-l0006] [10.5pt] for “Real”), which relies on class probabilities rather than predictions and generally
[p0231-l0007] [10.5pt] performs better.
[p0231-l0008] [10.5pt] The following code trains an AdaBoost classifier based on 200 Decision Stumps using
[p0231-l0009] [10.5pt] Scikit-Learn’s AdaBoostClassifier class (as you might expect, there is also an Ada
[p0231-l0010] [10.5pt] BoostRegressor class). A Decision Stump is a Decision Tree with max_depth=1—in
[p0231-l0011] [10.5pt] other words, a tree composed of a single decision node plus two leaf nodes. This is
[p0231-l0012] [10.5pt] the default base estimator for the AdaBoostClassifier class:
[p0231-l0013] [8.5pt] from sklearn.ensemble import AdaBoostClassifier
[p0231-l0014] [8.5pt] ada_clf = AdaBoostClassifier(
[p0231-l0015] [8.5pt]     DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=1), n_estimators=200,
[p0231-l0016] [8.5pt]     algorithm="SAMME.R", learning_rate=0.5)
[p0231-l0017] [8.5pt] ada_clf.fit(X_train, y_train)
[p0231-l0018] [9.6pt] If your AdaBoost ensemble is overfitting the training set, you can
[p0231-l0019] [9.6pt] try reducing the number of estimators or more strongly regulariz‐
[p0231-l0020] [9.6pt] ing the base estimator.
[p0231-l0021] [15.77pt] Gradient Boosting
[p0231-l0022] [10.5pt] Another very popular Boosting algorithm is Gradient Boosting.17 Just like AdaBoost,
[p0231-l0023] [10.5pt] Gradient Boosting works by sequentially adding predictors to an ensemble, each one
[p0231-l0024] [10.5pt] correcting its predecessor. However, instead of tweaking the instance weights at every
[p0231-l0025] [10.5pt] iteration like AdaBoost does, this method tries to fit the new predictor to the residual
[p0231-l0026] [10.5pt] errors made by the previous predictor.
[p0231-l0027] [10.5pt] Let’s go through a simple regression example using Decision Trees as the base predic‐
[p0231-l0028] [10.5pt] tors (of course Gradient Boosting also works great with regression tasks). This is
[p0231-l0029] [10.5pt] called Gradient Tree Boosting, or Gradient Boosted Regression Trees (GBRT). First, let’s
[p0231-l0030] [10.5pt] fit a DecisionTreeRegressor to the training set (for example, a noisy quadratic train‐
[p0231-l0031] [10.5pt] ing set):
[p0231-l0032] [8.0pt] 16 For more details, see “Multi-Class AdaBoost,” J. Zhu et al. (2006).
[p0231-l0033] [8.0pt] 17 First introduced in “Arcing the Edge,” L. Breiman (1997), and further developed in the paper “Greedy Func‐
[p0231-l0034] [8.0pt] tion Approximation: A Gradient Boosting Machine,” Jerome H. Friedman (1999).
[p0231-l0035] [9.0pt] Boosting
[p0231-l0036] [9.0pt] |
[p0231-l0037] [9.0pt] 205

=== PDF page 232 / printed label 206 ===
[p0232-l0001] [8.5pt] from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor
[p0232-l0002] [8.5pt] tree_reg1 = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=2)
[p0232-l0003] [8.5pt] tree_reg1.fit(X, y)
[p0232-l0004] [10.5pt] Now train a second DecisionTreeRegressor on the residual errors made by the first
[p0232-l0005] [10.5pt] predictor:
[p0232-l0006] [8.5pt] y2 = y - tree_reg1.predict(X)
[p0232-l0007] [8.5pt] tree_reg2 = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=2)
[p0232-l0008] [8.5pt] tree_reg2.fit(X, y2)
[p0232-l0009] [10.5pt] Then we train a third regressor on the residual errors made by the second predictor:
[p0232-l0010] [8.5pt] y3 = y2 - tree_reg2.predict(X)
[p0232-l0011] [8.5pt] tree_reg3 = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=2)
[p0232-l0012] [8.5pt] tree_reg3.fit(X, y3)
[p0232-l0013] [10.5pt] Now we have an ensemble containing three trees. It can make predictions on a new
[p0232-l0014] [10.5pt] instance simply by adding up the predictions of all the trees:
[p0232-l0015] [8.5pt] y_pred = sum(tree.predict(X_new) for tree in (tree_reg1, tree_reg2, tree_reg3))
[p0232-l0016] [10.5pt] Figure 7-9 represents the predictions of these three trees in the left column, and the
[p0232-l0017] [10.5pt] ensemble’s predictions in the right column. In the first row, the ensemble has just one
[p0232-l0018] [10.5pt] tree, so its predictions are exactly the same as the first tree’s predictions. In the second
[p0232-l0019] [10.5pt] row, a new tree is trained on the residual errors of the first tree. On the right you can
[p0232-l0020] [10.5pt] see that the ensemble’s predictions are equal to the sum of the predictions of the first
[p0232-l0021] [10.5pt] two trees. Similarly, in the third row another tree is trained on the residual errors of
[p0232-l0022] [10.5pt] the second tree. You can see that the ensemble’s predictions gradually get better as
[p0232-l0023] [10.5pt] trees are added to the ensemble.
[p0232-l0024] [10.5pt] A simpler way to train GBRT ensembles is to use Scikit-Learn’s GradientBoostingRe
[p0232-l0025] [10.5pt] gressor class. Much like the RandomForestRegressor class, it has hyperparameters to
[p0232-l0026] [10.5pt] control the growth of Decision Trees (e.g., max_depth, min_samples_leaf, and so on),
[p0232-l0027] [10.5pt] as well as hyperparameters to control the ensemble training, such as the number of
[p0232-l0028] [10.5pt] trees (n_estimators). The following code creates the same ensemble as the previous
[p0232-l0029] [10.5pt] one:
[p0232-l0030] [8.5pt] from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingRegressor
[p0232-l0031] [8.5pt] gbrt = GradientBoostingRegressor(max_depth=2, n_estimators=3, learning_rate=1.0)
[p0232-l0032] [8.5pt] gbrt.fit(X, y)
[p0232-l0033] [9.0pt] 206
[p0232-l0034] [9.0pt] |
[p0232-l0035] [9.0pt] Chapter 7: Ensemble Learning and Random Forests

=== PDF page 233 / printed label 207 ===
[p0233-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 7-9. Gradient Boosting
[p0233-l0002] [10.5pt] The learning_rate hyperparameter scales the contribution of each tree. If you set it
[p0233-l0003] [10.5pt] to a low value, such as 0.1, you will need more trees in the ensemble to fit the train‐
[p0233-l0004] [10.5pt] ing set, but the predictions will usually generalize better. This is a regularization tech‐
[p0233-l0005] [10.5pt] nique called shrinkage. Figure 7-10 shows two GBRT ensembles trained with a low
[p0233-l0006] [10.5pt] learning rate: the one on the left does not have enough trees to fit the training set,
[p0233-l0007] [10.5pt] while the one on the right has too many trees and overfits the training set.
[p0233-l0008] [9.0pt] Boosting
[p0233-l0009] [9.0pt] |
[p0233-l0010] [9.0pt] 207

=== PDF page 234 / printed label 208 ===
[p0234-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 7-10. GBRT ensembles with not enough predictors (left) and too many (right)
[p0234-l0002] [10.5pt] In order to find the optimal number of trees, you can use early stopping (see Chap‐
[p0234-l0003] [10.5pt] ter 4). A simple way to implement this is to use the staged_predict() method: it
[p0234-l0004] [10.5pt] returns an iterator over the predictions made by the ensemble at each stage of train‐
[p0234-l0005] [10.5pt] ing (with one tree, two trees, etc.). The following code trains a GBRT ensemble with
[p0234-l0006] [10.5pt] 120 trees, then measures the validation error at each stage of training to find the opti‐
[p0234-l0007] [10.5pt] mal number of trees, and finally trains another GBRT ensemble using the optimal
[p0234-l0008] [10.5pt] number of trees:
[p0234-l0009] [8.5pt] import numpy as np
[p0234-l0010] [8.5pt] from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
[p0234-l0011] [8.5pt] from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error
[p0234-l0012] [8.5pt] X_train, X_val, y_train, y_val = train_test_split(X, y)
[p0234-l0013] [8.5pt] gbrt = GradientBoostingRegressor(max_depth=2, n_estimators=120)
[p0234-l0014] [8.5pt] gbrt.fit(X_train, y_train)
[p0234-l0015] [8.5pt] errors = [mean_squared_error(y_val, y_pred)
[p0234-l0016] [8.5pt]           for y_pred in gbrt.staged_predict(X_val)]
[p0234-l0017] [8.5pt] bst_n_estimators = np.argmin(errors)
[p0234-l0018] [8.5pt] gbrt_best = GradientBoostingRegressor(max_depth=2,n_estimators=bst_n_estimators)
[p0234-l0019] [8.5pt] gbrt_best.fit(X_train, y_train)
[p0234-l0020] [10.5pt] The validation errors are represented on the left of Figure 7-11, and the best model’s
[p0234-l0021] [10.5pt] predictions are represented on the right.
[p0234-l0022] [9.0pt] 208
[p0234-l0023] [9.0pt] |
[p0234-l0024] [9.0pt] Chapter 7: Ensemble Learning and Random Forests

=== PDF page 235 / printed label 209 ===
[p0235-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 7-11. Tuning the number of trees using early stopping
[p0235-l0002] [10.5pt] It is also possible to implement early stopping by actually stopping training early
[p0235-l0003] [10.5pt] (instead of training a large number of trees first and then looking back to find the
[p0235-l0004] [10.5pt] optimal number). You can do so by setting warm_start=True, which makes Scikit-
[p0235-l0005] [10.5pt] Learn keep existing trees when the fit() method is called, allowing incremental
[p0235-l0006] [10.5pt] training. The following code stops training when the validation error does not
[p0235-l0007] [10.5pt] improve for five iterations in a row:
[p0235-l0008] [8.5pt] gbrt = GradientBoostingRegressor(max_depth=2, warm_start=True)
[p0235-l0009] [8.5pt] min_val_error = float("inf")
[p0235-l0010] [8.5pt] error_going_up = 0
[p0235-l0011] [8.5pt] for n_estimators in range(1, 120):
[p0235-l0012] [8.5pt]     gbrt.n_estimators = n_estimators
[p0235-l0013] [8.5pt]     gbrt.fit(X_train, y_train)
[p0235-l0014] [8.5pt]     y_pred = gbrt.predict(X_val)
[p0235-l0015] [8.5pt]     val_error = mean_squared_error(y_val, y_pred)
[p0235-l0016] [8.5pt]     if val_error < min_val_error:
[p0235-l0017] [8.5pt]         min_val_error = val_error
[p0235-l0018] [8.5pt]         error_going_up = 0
[p0235-l0019] [8.5pt]     else:
[p0235-l0020] [8.5pt]         error_going_up += 1
[p0235-l0021] [8.5pt]         if error_going_up == 5:
[p0235-l0022] [8.5pt]             break  # early stopping
[p0235-l0023] [10.5pt] The GradientBoostingRegressor class also supports a subsample hyperparameter,
[p0235-l0024] [10.5pt] which specifies the fraction of training instances to be used for training each tree. For
[p0235-l0025] [10.5pt] example, if subsample=0.25, then each tree is trained on 25% of the training instan‐
[p0235-l0026] [10.5pt] ces, selected randomly. As you can probably guess by now, this trades a higher bias
[p0235-l0027] [10.5pt] for a lower variance. It also speeds up training considerably. This technique is called
[p0235-l0028] [10.5pt] Stochastic Gradient Boosting.
[p0235-l0029] [9.0pt] Boosting
[p0235-l0030] [9.0pt] |
[p0235-l0031] [9.0pt] 209

=== PDF page 236 / printed label 210 ===
[p0236-l0001] [9.6pt] It is possible to use Gradient Boosting with other cost functions.
[p0236-l0002] [9.6pt] This is controlled by the loss hyperparameter (see Scikit-Learn’s
[p0236-l0003] [9.6pt] documentation for more details).
[p0236-l0004] [10.5pt] It is worth noting that an optimized implementation of Gradient Boosting is available
[p0236-l0005] [10.5pt] in the popular python library XGBoost, which stands for Extreme Gradient Boosting.
[p0236-l0006] [10.5pt] This package was initially developed by Tianqi Chen as part of the Distributed (Deep)
[p0236-l0007] [10.5pt] Machine Learning Community (DMLC), and it aims at being extremely fast, scalable
[p0236-l0008] [10.5pt] and portable. In fact, XGBoost is often an important component of the winning
[p0236-l0009] [10.5pt] entries in ML competitions. XGBoost’s API is quite similar to Scikit-Learn’s:
[p0236-l0010] [8.5pt] import xgboost
[p0236-l0011] [8.5pt] xgb_reg = xgboost.XGBRegressor()
[p0236-l0012] [8.5pt] xgb_reg.fit(X_train, y_train)
[p0236-l0013] [8.5pt] y_pred = xgb_reg.predict(X_val)
[p0236-l0014] [10.5pt] XGBoost also offers several nice features, such as automatically taking care of early
[p0236-l0015] [10.5pt] stopping:
[p0236-l0016] [8.5pt] xgb_reg.fit(X_train, y_train,
[p0236-l0017] [8.5pt]             eval_set=[(X_val, y_val)], early_stopping_rounds=2)
[p0236-l0018] [8.5pt] y_pred = xgb_reg.predict(X_val)
[p0236-l0019] [10.5pt] You should definitely check it out!
[p0236-l0020] [18.92pt] Stacking
[p0236-l0021] [10.5pt] The last Ensemble method we will discuss in this chapter is called stacking (short for
[p0236-l0022] [10.5pt] stacked generalization).18 It is based on a simple idea: instead of using trivial functions
[p0236-l0023] [10.5pt] (such as hard voting) to aggregate the predictions of all predictors in an ensemble,
[p0236-l0024] [10.5pt] why don’t we train a model to perform this aggregation? Figure 7-12 shows such an
[p0236-l0025] [10.5pt] ensemble performing a regression task on a new instance. Each of the bottom three
[p0236-l0026] [10.5pt] predictors predicts a different value (3.1, 2.7, and 2.9), and then the final predictor
[p0236-l0027] [10.5pt] (called a blender, or a meta learner) takes these predictions as inputs and makes the
[p0236-l0028] [10.5pt] final prediction (3.0).
[p0236-l0029] [8.0pt] 18 “Stacked Generalization,” D. Wolpert (1992).
[p0236-l0030] [9.0pt] 210
[p0236-l0031] [9.0pt] |
[p0236-l0032] [9.0pt] Chapter 7: Ensemble Learning and Random Forests

[p0237-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 7-12. Aggregating predictions using a blending predictor
[p0237-l0002] [10.5pt] To train the blender, a common approach is to use a hold-out set.19 Let’s see how it
[p0237-l0003] [10.5pt] works. First, the training set is split in two subsets. The first subset is used to train the
[p0237-l0004] [10.5pt] predictors in the first layer (see Figure 7-13).
[p0237-l0005] [10.5pt] Figure 7-13. Training the first layer
[p0237-l0006] [10.5pt] Next, the first layer predictors are used to make predictions on the second (held-out)
[p0237-l0007] [10.5pt] set (see Figure 7-14). This ensures that the predictions are “clean,” since the predictors
[p0237-l0008] [10.5pt] never saw these instances during training. Now for each instance in the hold-out set
[p0237-l0009] [8.0pt] 19 Alternatively, it is possible to use out-of-fold predictions. In some contexts this is called stacking, while using a
[p0237-l0010] [8.0pt] hold-out set is called blending. However, for many people these terms are synonymous.
[p0237-l0011] [9.0pt] Stacking
[p0237-l0012] [9.0pt] |
[p0237-l0013] [9.0pt] 211

=== PDF page 238 / printed label 212 ===
[p0238-l0001] [10.5pt] there are three predicted values. We can create a new training set using these predic‐
[p0238-l0002] [10.5pt] ted values as input features (which makes this new training set three-dimensional),
[p0238-l0003] [10.5pt] and keeping the target values. The blender is trained on this new training set, so it
[p0238-l0004] [10.5pt] learns to predict the target value given the first layer’s predictions.
[p0238-l0005] [10.5pt] Figure 7-14. Training the blender
[p0238-l0006] [10.5pt] It is actually possible to train several different blenders this way (e.g., one using Lin‐
[p0238-l0007] [10.5pt] ear Regression, another using Random Forest Regression, and so on): we get a whole
[p0238-l0008] [10.5pt] layer of blenders. The trick is to split the training set into three subsets: the first one is
[p0238-l0009] [10.5pt] used to train the first layer, the second one is used to create the training set used to
[p0238-l0010] [10.5pt] train the second layer (using predictions made by the predictors of the first layer),
[p0238-l0011] [10.5pt] and the third one is used to create the training set to train the third layer (using pre‐
[p0238-l0012] [10.5pt] dictions made by the predictors of the second layer). Once this is done, we can make
[p0238-l0013] [10.5pt] a prediction for a new instance by going through each layer sequentially, as shown in
[p0238-l0014] [10.5pt] Figure 7-15.
[p0238-l0015] [9.0pt] 212

[p0241-l0001] [16.82pt] CHAPTER 8
[p0241-l0002] [25.22pt] Dimensionality Reduction
[p0241-l0003] [9.6pt] With Early Release ebooks, you get books in their earliest form—
[p0241-l0004] [9.6pt] the author’s raw and unedited content as he or she writes—so you
[p0241-l0005] [9.6pt] can take advantage of these technologies long before the official
[p0241-l0006] [9.6pt] release of these titles. The following will be Chapter 8 in the final
[p0241-l0007] [9.6pt] release of the book.
[p0241-l0008] [10.5pt] Many Machine Learning problems involve thousands or even millions of features for
[p0241-l0009] [10.5pt] each training instance. Not only does this make training extremely slow, it can also
[p0241-l0010] [10.5pt] make it much harder to find a good solution, as we will see. This problem is often
[p0241-l0011] [10.5pt] referred to as the curse of dimensionality.
[p0241-l0012] [10.5pt] Fortunately, in real-world problems, it is often possible to reduce the number of fea‐
[p0241-l0013] [10.5pt] tures considerably, turning an intractable problem into a tractable one. For example,
[p0241-l0014] [10.5pt] consider the MNIST images (introduced in Chapter 3): the pixels on the image bor‐
[p0241-l0015] [10.5pt] ders are almost always white, so you could completely drop these pixels from the
[p0241-l0016] [10.5pt] training set without losing much information. Figure 7-6 confirms that these pixels
[p0241-l0017] [10.5pt] are utterly unimportant for the classification task. Moreover, two neighboring pixels
[p0241-l0018] [10.5pt] are often highly correlated: if you merge them into a single pixel (e.g., by taking the
[p0241-l0019] [10.5pt] mean of the two pixel intensities), you will not lose much information.
[p0241-l0020] [9.0pt] 215

=== PDF page 242 / printed label 216 ===
[p0242-l0001] [9.6pt] Reducing dimensionality does lose some information (just like
[p0242-l0002] [9.6pt] compressing an image to JPEG can degrade its quality), so even
[p0242-l0003] [9.6pt] though it will speed up training, it may also make your system per‐
[p0242-l0004] [9.6pt] form slightly worse. It also makes your pipelines a bit more com‐
[p0242-l0005] [9.6pt] plex and thus harder to maintain. So you should first try to train
[p0242-l0006] [9.6pt] your system with the original data before considering using dimen‐
[p0242-l0007] [9.6pt] sionality reduction if training is too slow. In some cases, however,
[p0242-l0008] [9.6pt] reducing the dimensionality of the training data may filter out
[p0242-l0009] [9.6pt] some noise and unnecessary details and thus result in higher per‐
[p0242-l0010] [9.6pt] formance (but in general it won’t; it will just speed up training).
[p0242-l0011] [10.5pt] Apart from speeding up training, dimensionality reduction is also extremely useful
[p0242-l0012] [10.5pt] for data visualization (or DataViz). Reducing the number of dimensions down to two
[p0242-l0013] [10.5pt] (or three) makes it possible to plot a condensed view of a high-dimensional training
[p0242-l0014] [10.5pt] set on a graph and often gain some important insights by visually detecting patterns,
[p0242-l0015] [10.5pt] such as clusters. Moreover, DataViz is essential to communicate your conclusions to
[p0242-l0016] [10.5pt] people who are not data scientists, in particular decision makers who will use your
[p0242-l0017] [10.5pt] results.
[p0242-l0018] [10.5pt] In this chapter we will discuss the curse of dimensionality and get a sense of what
[p0242-l0019] [10.5pt] goes on in high-dimensional space. Then, we will present the two main approaches to
[p0242-l0020] [10.5pt] dimensionality reduction (projection and Manifold Learning), and we will go
[p0242-l0021] [10.5pt] through three of the most popular dimensionality reduction techniques: PCA, Kernel
[p0242-l0022] [10.5pt] PCA, and LLE.
[p0242-l0023] [18.92pt] The Curse of Dimensionality
[p0242-l0024] [10.5pt] We are so used to living in three dimensions1 that our intuition fails us when we try
[p0242-l0025] [10.5pt] to imagine a high-dimensional space. Even a basic 4D hypercube is incredibly hard to
[p0242-l0026] [10.5pt] picture in our mind (see Figure 8-1), let alone a 200-dimensional ellipsoid bent in a
[p0242-l0027] [10.5pt] 1,000-dimensional space.
[p0242-l0028] [8.0pt] 1 Well, four dimensions if you count time, and a few more if you are a string theorist.
[p0242-l0029] [9.0pt] 216
[p0242-l0030] [9.0pt] |
[p0242-l0031] [9.0pt] Chapter 8: Dimensionality Reduction

=== PDF page 243 / printed label 217 ===
[p0243-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 8-1. Point, segment, square, cube, and tesseract (0D to 4D hypercubes)2
[p0243-l0002] [10.5pt] It turns out that many things behave very differently in high-dimensional space. For
[p0243-l0003] [10.5pt] example, if you pick a random point in a unit square (a 1 × 1 square), it will have only
[p0243-l0004] [10.5pt] about a 0.4% chance of being located less than 0.001 from a border (in other words, it
[p0243-l0005] [10.5pt] is very unlikely that a random point will be “extreme” along any dimension). But in a
[p0243-l0006] [10.5pt] 10,000-dimensional unit hypercube (a 1 × 1 × ⋯ × 1 cube, with ten thousand 1s), this
[p0243-l0007] [10.5pt] probability is greater than 99.999999%. Most points in a high-dimensional hypercube
[p0243-l0008] [10.5pt] are very close to the border.3
[p0243-l0009] [10.5pt] Here is a more troublesome difference: if you pick two points randomly in a unit
[p0243-l0010] [10.5pt] square, the distance between these two points will be, on average, roughly 0.52. If you
[p0243-l0011] [10.5pt] pick two random points in a unit 3D cube, the average distance will be roughly 0.66.
[p0243-l0012] [10.5pt] But what about two points picked randomly in a 1,000,000-dimensional hypercube?
[p0243-l0013] [10.5pt] Well, the average distance, believe it or not, will be about 408.25 (roughly
[p0243-l0014] [10.5pt] 1, 000, 000/6)! This is quite counterintuitive: how can two points be so far apart
[p0243-l0015] [10.5pt] when they both lie within the same unit hypercube? This fact implies that high-
[p0243-l0016] [10.5pt] dimensional datasets are at risk of being very sparse: most training instances are
[p0243-l0017] [10.5pt] likely to be far away from each other. Of course, this also means that a new instance
[p0243-l0018] [10.5pt] will likely be far away from any training instance, making predictions much less relia‐
[p0243-l0019] [10.5pt] ble than in lower dimensions, since they will be based on much larger extrapolations.
[p0243-l0020] [10.5pt] In short, the more dimensions the training set has, the greater the risk of overfitting
[p0243-l0021] [10.5pt] it.
[p0243-l0022] [10.5pt] In theory, one solution to the curse of dimensionality could be to increase the size of
[p0243-l0023] [10.5pt] the training set to reach a sufficient density of training instances. Unfortunately, in
[p0243-l0024] [10.5pt] practice, the number of training instances required to reach a given density grows
[p0243-l0025] [10.5pt] exponentially with the number of dimensions. With just 100 features (much less than
[p0243-l0026] [8.0pt] 2 Watch a rotating tesseract projected into 3D space at https://homl.info/30. Image by Wikipedia user Nerd‐
[p0243-l0027] [8.0pt] Boy1392 (Creative Commons BY-SA 3.0). Reproduced from https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tesseract.
[p0243-l0028] [8.0pt] 3 Fun fact: anyone you know is probably an extremist in at least one dimension (e.g., how much sugar they put
[p0243-l0029] [8.0pt] in their coffee), if you consider enough dimensions.
[p0243-l0030] [9.0pt] The Curse of Dimensionality
[p0243-l0031] [9.0pt] |
[p0243-l0032] [9.0pt] 217

=== PDF page 244 / printed label 218 ===
[p0244-l0001] [10.5pt] in the MNIST problem), you would need more training instances than atoms in the
[p0244-l0002] [10.5pt] observable universe in order for training instances to be within 0.1 of each other on
[p0244-l0003] [10.5pt] average, assuming they were spread out uniformly across all dimensions.
[p0244-l0004] [18.92pt] Main Approaches for Dimensionality Reduction
[p0244-l0005] [10.5pt] Before we dive into specific dimensionality reduction algorithms, let’s take a look at
[p0244-l0006] [10.5pt] the two main approaches to reducing dimensionality: projection and Manifold
[p0244-l0007] [10.5pt] Learning.
[p0244-l0008] [15.77pt] Projection
[p0244-l0009] [10.5pt] In most real-world problems, training instances are not spread out uniformly across
[p0244-l0010] [10.5pt] all dimensions. Many features are almost constant, while others are highly correlated
[p0244-l0011] [10.5pt] (as discussed earlier for MNIST). As a result, all training instances actually lie within
[p0244-l0012] [10.5pt] (or close to) a much lower-dimensional subspace of the high-dimensional space. This
[p0244-l0013] [10.5pt] sounds very abstract, so let’s look at an example. In Figure 8-2 you can see a 3D data‐
[p0244-l0014] [10.5pt] set represented by the circles.
[p0244-l0015] [10.5pt] Figure 8-2. A 3D dataset lying close to a 2D subspace
[p0244-l0016] [10.5pt] Notice that all training instances lie close to a plane: this is a lower-dimensional (2D)
[p0244-l0017] [10.5pt] subspace of the high-dimensional (3D) space. Now if we project every training
[p0244-l0018] [10.5pt] instance perpendicularly onto this subspace (as represented by the short lines con‐
[p0244-l0019] [10.5pt] necting the instances to the plane), we get the new 2D dataset shown in Figure 8-3.
[p0244-l0020] [10.5pt] Ta-da! We have just reduced the dataset’s dimensionality from 3D to 2D. Note that
[p0244-l0021] [10.5pt] the axes correspond to new features z1 and z2 (the coordinates of the projections on
[p0244-l0022] [10.5pt] the plane).
[p0244-l0023] [9.0pt] 218
[p0244-l0024] [9.0pt] |
[p0244-l0025] [9.0pt] Chapter 8: Dimensionality Reduction

=== PDF page 245 / printed label 219 ===
[p0245-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 8-3. The new 2D dataset after projection
[p0245-l0002] [10.5pt] However, projection is not always the best approach to dimensionality reduction. In
[p0245-l0003] [10.5pt] many cases the subspace may twist and turn, such as in the famous Swiss roll toy data‐
[p0245-l0004] [10.5pt] set represented in Figure 8-4.
[p0245-l0005] [10.5pt] Figure 8-4. Swiss roll dataset
[p0245-l0006] [9.0pt] Main Approaches for Dimensionality Reduction
[p0245-l0007] [9.0pt] |
[p0245-l0008] [9.0pt] 219

=== PDF page 246 / printed label 220 ===
[p0246-l0001] [10.5pt] Simply projecting onto a plane (e.g., by dropping x3) would squash different layers of
[p0246-l0002] [10.5pt] the Swiss roll together, as shown on the left of Figure 8-5. However, what you really
[p0246-l0003] [10.5pt] want is to unroll the Swiss roll to obtain the 2D dataset on the right of Figure 8-5.
[p0246-l0004] [10.5pt] Figure 8-5. Squashing by projecting onto a plane (left) versus unrolling the Swiss roll
[p0246-l0005] [10.5pt] (right)
[p0246-l0006] [15.77pt] Manifold Learning
[p0246-l0007] [10.5pt] The Swiss roll is an example of a 2D manifold. Put simply, a 2D manifold is a 2D
[p0246-l0008] [10.5pt] shape that can be bent and twisted in a higher-dimensional space. More generally, a
[p0246-l0009] [10.5pt] d-dimensional manifold is a part of an n-dimensional space (where d < n) that locally
[p0246-l0010] [10.5pt] resembles a d-dimensional hyperplane. In the case of the Swiss roll, d = 2 and n = 3: it
[p0246-l0011] [10.5pt] locally resembles a 2D plane, but it is rolled in the third dimension.
[p0246-l0012] [10.5pt] Many dimensionality reduction algorithms work by modeling the manifold on which
[p0246-l0013] [10.5pt] the training instances lie; this is called Manifold Learning. It relies on the manifold
[p0246-l0014] [10.5pt] assumption, also called the manifold hypothesis, which holds that most real-world
[p0246-l0015] [10.5pt] high-dimensional datasets lie close to a much lower-dimensional manifold. This
[p0246-l0016] [10.5pt] assumption is very often empirically observed.
[p0246-l0017] [10.5pt] Once again, think about the MNIST dataset: all handwritten digit images have some
[p0246-l0018] [10.5pt] similarities. They are made of connected lines, the borders are white, they are more
[p0246-l0019] [10.5pt] or less centered, and so on. If you randomly generated images, only a ridiculously
[p0246-l0020] [10.5pt] tiny fraction of them would look like handwritten digits. In other words, the degrees
[p0246-l0021] [10.5pt] of freedom available to you if you try to create a digit image are dramatically lower
[p0246-l0022] [10.5pt] than the degrees of freedom you would have if you were allowed to generate any
[p0246-l0023] [10.5pt] image you wanted. These constraints tend to squeeze the dataset into a lower-
[p0246-l0024] [10.5pt] dimensional manifold.
[p0246-l0025] [10.5pt] The manifold assumption is often accompanied by another implicit assumption: that
[p0246-l0026] [10.5pt] the task at hand (e.g., classification or regression) will be simpler if expressed in the
[p0246-l0027] [10.5pt] lower-dimensional space of the manifold. For example, in the top row of Figure 8-6
[p0246-l0028] [10.5pt] the Swiss roll is split into two classes: in the 3D space (on the left), the decision
[p0246-l0029] [9.0pt] 220
[p0246-l0030] [9.0pt] |
[p0246-l0031] [9.0pt] Chapter 8: Dimensionality Reduction

=== PDF page 247 / printed label 221 ===
[p0247-l0001] [10.5pt] boundary would be fairly complex, but in the 2D unrolled manifold space (on the
[p0247-l0002] [10.5pt] right), the decision boundary is a simple straight line.
[p0247-l0003] [10.5pt] However, this assumption does not always hold. For example, in the bottom row of
[p0247-l0004] [10.5pt] Figure 8-6, the decision boundary is located at x1 = 5. This decision boundary looks
[p0247-l0005] [10.5pt] very simple in the original 3D space (a vertical plane), but it looks more complex in
[p0247-l0006] [10.5pt] the unrolled manifold (a collection of four independent line segments).
[p0247-l0007] [10.5pt] In short, if you reduce the dimensionality of your training set before training a
[p0247-l0008] [10.5pt] model, it will usually speed up training, but it may not always lead to a better or sim‐
[p0247-l0009] [10.5pt] pler solution; it all depends on the dataset.
[p0247-l0010] [10.5pt] Hopefully you now have a good sense of what the curse of dimensionality is and how
[p0247-l0011] [10.5pt] dimensionality reduction algorithms can fight it, especially when the manifold
[p0247-l0012] [10.5pt] assumption holds. The rest of this chapter will go through some of the most popular
[p0247-l0013] [10.5pt] algorithms.
[p0247-l0014] [10.5pt] Figure 8-6. The decision boundary may not always be simpler with lower dimensions
[p0247-l0015] [9.0pt] Main Approaches for Dimensionality Reduction
[p0247-l0016] [9.0pt] |
[p0247-l0017] [9.0pt] 221

=== PDF page 248 / printed label 222 ===
[p0248-l0001] [18.92pt] PCA
[p0248-l0002] [10.5pt] Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is by far the most popular dimensionality reduc‐
[p0248-l0003] [10.5pt] tion algorithm. First it identifies the hyperplane that lies closest to the data, and then
[p0248-l0004] [10.5pt] it projects the data onto it, just like in Figure 8-2.
[p0248-l0005] [15.77pt] Preserving the Variance
[p0248-l0006] [10.5pt] Before you can project the training set onto a lower-dimensional hyperplane, you
[p0248-l0007] [10.5pt] first need to choose the right hyperplane. For example, a simple 2D dataset is repre‐
[p0248-l0008] [10.5pt] sented on the left of Figure 8-7, along with three different axes (i.e., one-dimensional
[p0248-l0009] [10.5pt] hyperplanes). On the right is the result of the projection of the dataset onto each of
[p0248-l0010] [10.5pt] these axes. As you can see, the projection onto the solid line preserves the maximum
[p0248-l0011] [10.5pt] variance, while the projection onto the dotted line preserves very little variance, and
[p0248-l0012] [10.5pt] the projection onto the dashed line preserves an intermediate amount of variance.
[p0248-l0013] [10.5pt] Figure 8-7. Selecting the subspace onto which to project
[p0248-l0014] [10.5pt] It seems reasonable to select the axis that preserves the maximum amount of var‐
[p0248-l0015] [10.5pt] iance, as it will most likely lose less information than the other projections. Another
[p0248-l0016] [10.5pt] way to justify this choice is that it is the axis that minimizes the mean squared dis‐
[p0248-l0017] [10.5pt] tance between the original dataset and its projection onto that axis. This is the rather
[p0248-l0018] [10.5pt] simple idea behind PCA.4
[p0248-l0019] [8.0pt] 4 “On Lines and Planes of Closest Fit to Systems of Points in Space,” K. Pearson (1901).
[p0248-l0020] [9.0pt] 222
[p0248-l0021] [9.0pt] |
[p0248-l0022] [9.0pt] Chapter 8: Dimensionality Reduction

[p0249-l0001] [15.77pt] Principal Components
[p0249-l0002] [10.5pt] PCA identifies the axis that accounts for the largest amount of variance in the train‐
[p0249-l0003] [10.5pt] ing set. In Figure 8-7, it is the solid line. It also finds a second axis, orthogonal to the
[p0249-l0004] [10.5pt] first one, that accounts for the largest amount of remaining variance. In this 2D
[p0249-l0005] [10.5pt] example there is no choice: it is the dotted line. If it were a higher-dimensional data‐
[p0249-l0006] [10.5pt] set, PCA would also find a third axis, orthogonal to both previous axes, and a fourth,
[p0249-l0007] [10.5pt] a fifth, and so on—as many axes as the number of dimensions in the dataset.
[p0249-l0008] [10.5pt] The unit vector that defines the ith axis is called the ith principal component (PC). In
[p0249-l0009] [10.5pt] Figure 8-7, the 1st PC is c1 and the 2nd PC is c2. In Figure 8-2 the first two PCs are
[p0249-l0010] [10.5pt] represented by the orthogonal arrows in the plane, and the third PC would be
[p0249-l0011] [10.5pt] orthogonal to the plane (pointing up or down).
[p0249-l0012] [9.6pt] The direction of the principal components is not stable: if you per‐
[p0249-l0013] [9.6pt] turb the training set slightly and run PCA again, some of the new
[p0249-l0014] [9.6pt] PCs may point in the opposite direction of the original PCs. How‐
[p0249-l0015] [9.6pt] ever, they will generally still lie on the same axes. In some cases, a
[p0249-l0016] [9.6pt] pair of PCs may even rotate or swap, but the plane they define will
[p0249-l0017] [9.6pt] generally remain the same.
[p0249-l0018] [10.5pt] So how can you find the principal components of a training set? Luckily, there is a
[p0249-l0019] [10.5pt] standard matrix factorization technique called Singular Value Decomposition (SVD)
[p0249-l0020] [10.5pt] that can decompose the training set matrix X into the matrix multiplication of three
[p0249-l0021] [10.5pt] matrices U Σ VT, where V contains all the principal components that we are looking
[p0249-l0022] [10.5pt] for, as shown in Equation 8-1.
[p0249-l0023] [10.5pt] Equation 8-1. Principal components matrix
[p0249-l0024] [10.0pt] V =
[p0249-l0025] [10.0pt] ∣
[p0249-l0026] [10.0pt] ∣
[p0249-l0027] [10.0pt] ∣
[p0249-l0028] [10.0pt] c1 c2 ⋯cn
[p0249-l0029] [10.0pt] ∣
[p0249-l0030] [10.0pt] ∣
[p0249-l0031] [10.0pt] ∣
[p0249-l0032] [10.5pt] The following Python code uses NumPy’s svd() function to obtain all the principal
[p0249-l0033] [10.5pt] components of the training set, then extracts the first two PCs:
[p0249-l0034] [8.5pt] X_centered = X - X.mean(axis=0)
[p0249-l0035] [8.5pt] U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(X_centered)
[p0249-l0036] [8.5pt] c1 = Vt.T[:, 0]
[p0249-l0037] [8.5pt] c2 = Vt.T[:, 1]
[p0249-l0038] [9.0pt] PCA
[p0249-l0039] [9.0pt] |
[p0249-l0040] [9.0pt] 223

=== PDF page 250 / printed label 224 ===
[p0250-l0001] [9.6pt] PCA assumes that the dataset is centered around the origin. As we
[p0250-l0002] [9.6pt] will see, Scikit-Learn’s PCA classes take care of centering the data
[p0250-l0003] [9.6pt] for you. However, if you implement PCA yourself (as in the pre‐
[p0250-l0004] [9.6pt] ceding example), or if you use other libraries, don’t forget to center
[p0250-l0005] [9.6pt] the data first.
[p0250-l0006] [15.77pt] Projecting Down to d Dimensions
[p0250-l0007] [10.5pt] Once you have identified all the principal components, you can reduce the dimen‐
[p0250-l0008] [10.5pt] sionality of the dataset down to d dimensions by projecting it onto the hyperplane
[p0250-l0009] [10.5pt] defined by the first d principal components. Selecting this hyperplane ensures that the
[p0250-l0010] [10.5pt] projection will preserve as much variance as possible. For example, in Figure 8-2 the
[p0250-l0011] [10.5pt] 3D dataset is projected down to the 2D plane defined by the first two principal com‐
[p0250-l0012] [10.5pt] ponents, preserving a large part of the dataset’s variance. As a result, the 2D projec‐
[p0250-l0013] [10.5pt] tion looks very much like the original 3D dataset.
[p0250-l0014] [10.5pt] To project the training set onto the hyperplane, you can simply compute the matrix
[p0250-l0015] [10.5pt] multiplication of the training set matrix X by the matrix Wd, defined as the matrix
[p0250-l0016] [10.5pt] containing the first d principal components (i.e., the matrix composed of the first d
[p0250-l0017] [10.5pt] columns of V), as shown in Equation 8-2.
[p0250-l0018] [10.5pt] Equation 8-2. Projecting the training set down to d dimensions
[p0250-l0019] [10.0pt] Xd‐proj = XWd
[p0250-l0020] [10.5pt] The following Python code projects the training set onto the plane defined by the first
[p0250-l0021] [10.5pt] two principal components:
[p0250-l0022] [8.5pt] W2 = Vt.T[:, :2]
[p0250-l0023] [8.5pt] X2D = X_centered.dot(W2)
[p0250-l0024] [10.5pt] There you have it! You now know how to reduce the dimensionality of any dataset
[p0250-l0025] [10.5pt] down to any number of dimensions, while preserving as much variance as possible.
[p0250-l0026] [15.77pt] Using Scikit-Learn
[p0250-l0027] [10.5pt] Scikit-Learn’s PCA class implements PCA using SVD decomposition just like we did
[p0250-l0028] [10.5pt] before. The following code applies PCA to reduce the dimensionality of the dataset
[p0250-l0029] [10.5pt] down to two dimensions (note that it automatically takes care of centering the data):
[p0250-l0030] [8.5pt] from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
[p0250-l0031] [8.5pt] pca = PCA(n_components = 2)
[p0250-l0032] [8.5pt] X2D = pca.fit_transform(X)
[p0250-l0033] [10.5pt] After fitting the PCA transformer to the dataset, you can access the principal compo‐
[p0250-l0034] [10.5pt] nents using the components_ variable (note that it contains the PCs as horizontal vec‐
[p0250-l0035] [9.0pt] 224
[p0250-l0036] [9.0pt] |
[p0250-l0037] [9.0pt] Chapter 8: Dimensionality Reduction

=== PDF page 251 / printed label 225 ===
[p0251-l0001] [10.5pt] tors, so, for example, the first principal component is equal to pca.components_.T[:,
[p0251-l0002] [10.5pt] 0]).
[p0251-l0003] [15.77pt] Explained Variance Ratio
[p0251-l0004] [10.5pt] Another very useful piece of information is the explained variance ratio of each prin‐
[p0251-l0005] [10.5pt] cipal component, available via the explained_variance_ratio_ variable. It indicates
[p0251-l0006] [10.5pt] the proportion of the dataset’s variance that lies along the axis of each principal com‐
[p0251-l0007] [10.5pt] ponent. For example, let’s look at the explained variance ratios of the first two compo‐
[p0251-l0008] [10.5pt] nents of the 3D dataset represented in Figure 8-2:
[p0251-l0009] [8.5pt] >>> pca.explained_variance_ratio_
[p0251-l0010] [8.5pt] array([0.84248607, 0.14631839])
[p0251-l0011] [10.5pt] This tells you that 84.2% of the dataset’s variance lies along the first axis, and 14.6%
[p0251-l0012] [10.5pt] lies along the second axis. This leaves less than 1.2% for the third axis, so it is reason‐
[p0251-l0013] [10.5pt] able to assume that it probably carries little information.
[p0251-l0014] [15.77pt] Choosing the Right Number of Dimensions
[p0251-l0015] [10.5pt] Instead of arbitrarily choosing the number of dimensions to reduce down to, it is
[p0251-l0016] [10.5pt] generally preferable to choose the number of dimensions that add up to a sufficiently
[p0251-l0017] [10.5pt] large portion of the variance (e.g., 95%). Unless, of course, you are reducing dimen‐
[p0251-l0018] [10.5pt] sionality for data visualization—in that case you will generally want to reduce the
[p0251-l0019] [10.5pt] dimensionality down to 2 or 3.
[p0251-l0020] [10.5pt] The following code computes PCA without reducing dimensionality, then computes
[p0251-l0021] [10.5pt] the minimum number of dimensions required to preserve 95% of the training set’s
[p0251-l0022] [10.5pt] variance:
[p0251-l0023] [8.5pt] pca = PCA()
[p0251-l0024] [8.5pt] pca.fit(X_train)
[p0251-l0025] [8.5pt] cumsum = np.cumsum(pca.explained_variance_ratio_)
[p0251-l0026] [8.5pt] d = np.argmax(cumsum >= 0.95) + 1
[p0251-l0027] [10.5pt] You could then set n_components=d and run PCA again. However, there is a much
[p0251-l0028] [10.5pt] better option: instead of specifying the number of principal components you want to
[p0251-l0029] [10.5pt] preserve, you can set n_components to be a float between 0.0 and 1.0, indicating the
[p0251-l0030] [10.5pt] ratio of variance you wish to preserve:
[p0251-l0031] [8.5pt] pca = PCA(n_components=0.95)
[p0251-l0032] [8.5pt] X_reduced = pca.fit_transform(X_train)
[p0251-l0033] [10.5pt] Yet another option is to plot the explained variance as a function of the number of
[p0251-l0034] [10.5pt] dimensions (simply plot cumsum; see Figure 8-8). There will usually be an elbow in the
[p0251-l0035] [10.5pt] curve, where the explained variance stops growing fast. You can think of this as the
[p0251-l0036] [10.5pt] intrinsic dimensionality of the dataset. In this case, you can see that reducing the
[p0251-l0037] [9.0pt] PCA
[p0251-l0038] [9.0pt] |
[p0251-l0039] [9.0pt] 225

=== PDF page 252 / printed label 226 ===
[p0252-l0001] [10.5pt] dimensionality down to about 100 dimensions wouldn’t lose too much explained var‐
[p0252-l0002] [10.5pt] iance.
[p0252-l0003] [10.5pt] Figure 8-8. Explained variance as a function of the number of dimensions
[p0252-l0004] [15.77pt] PCA for Compression
[p0252-l0005] [10.5pt] Obviously after dimensionality reduction, the training set takes up much less space.
[p0252-l0006] [10.5pt] For example, try applying PCA to the MNIST dataset while preserving 95% of its var‐
[p0252-l0007] [10.5pt] iance. You should find that each instance will have just over 150 features, instead of
[p0252-l0008] [10.5pt] the original 784 features. So while most of the variance is preserved, the dataset is
[p0252-l0009] [10.5pt] now less than 20% of its original size! This is a reasonable compression ratio, and you
[p0252-l0010] [10.5pt] can see how this can speed up a classification algorithm (such as an SVM classifier)
[p0252-l0011] [10.5pt] tremendously.
[p0252-l0012] [10.5pt] It is also possible to decompress the reduced dataset back to 784 dimensions by
[p0252-l0013] [10.5pt] applying the inverse transformation of the PCA projection. Of course this won’t give
[p0252-l0014] [10.5pt] you back the original data, since the projection lost a bit of information (within the
[p0252-l0015] [10.5pt] 5% variance that was dropped), but it will likely be quite close to the original data.
[p0252-l0016] [10.5pt] The mean squared distance between the original data and the reconstructed data
[p0252-l0017] [10.5pt] (compressed and then decompressed) is called the reconstruction error. For example,
[p0252-l0018] [10.5pt] the following code compresses the MNIST dataset down to 154 dimensions, then uses
[p0252-l0019] [10.5pt] the inverse_transform() method to decompress it back to 784 dimensions.
[p0252-l0020] [10.5pt] Figure 8-9 shows a few digits from the original training set (on the left), and the cor‐
[p0252-l0021] [10.5pt] responding digits after compression and decompression. You can see that there is a
[p0252-l0022] [10.5pt] slight image quality loss, but the digits are still mostly intact.
[p0252-l0023] [8.5pt] pca = PCA(n_components = 154)
[p0252-l0024] [8.5pt] X_reduced = pca.fit_transform(X_train)
[p0252-l0025] [8.5pt] X_recovered = pca.inverse_transform(X_reduced)

[p0253-l0007] [15.77pt] Randomized PCA
[p0253-l0008] [10.5pt] If you set the svd_solver hyperparameter to "randomized", Scikit-Learn uses a sto‐
[p0253-l0009] [10.5pt] chastic algorithm called Randomized PCA that quickly finds an approximation of the
[p0253-l0010] [10.5pt] first d principal components. Its computational complexity is O(m × d2) + O(d3),
[p0253-l0011] [10.5pt] instead of O(m × n2) + O(n3) for the full SVD approach, so it is dramatically faster
[p0253-l0012] [10.5pt] than full SVD when d is much smaller than n:
[p0253-l0013] [8.5pt] rnd_pca = PCA(n_components=154, svd_solver="randomized")
[p0253-l0014] [8.5pt] X_reduced = rnd_pca.fit_transform(X_train)
[p0253-l0015] [10.5pt] By default, svd_solver is actually set to "auto": Scikit-Learn automatically uses the
[p0253-l0016] [10.5pt] randomized PCA algorithm if m or n is greater than 500 and d is less than 80% of m
[p0253-l0017] [10.5pt] or n, or else it uses the full SVD approach. If you want to force Scikit-Learn to use full
[p0253-l0018] [10.5pt] SVD, you can set the svd_solver hyperparameter to "full".
[p0253-l0019] [15.77pt] Incremental PCA
[p0253-l0020] [10.5pt] One problem with the preceding implementations of PCA is that they require the
[p0253-l0021] [10.5pt] whole training set to fit in memory in order for the algorithm to run. Fortunately,
[p0253-l0022] [10.5pt] Incremental PCA (IPCA) algorithms have been developed: you can split the training
[p0253-l0023] [10.5pt] set into mini-batches and feed an IPCA algorithm one mini-batch at a time. This is
[p0253-l0024] [9.0pt] PCA
[p0253-l0025] [9.0pt] |
[p0253-l0026] [9.0pt] 227

=== PDF page 254 / printed label 228 ===
[p0254-l0001] [10.5pt] useful for large training sets, and also to apply PCA online (i.e., on the fly, as new
[p0254-l0002] [10.5pt] instances arrive).
[p0254-l0003] [10.5pt] The following code splits the MNIST dataset into 100 mini-batches (using NumPy’s
[p0254-l0004] [10.5pt] array_split() function) and feeds them to Scikit-Learn’s IncrementalPCA class5 to
[p0254-l0005] [10.5pt] reduce the dimensionality of the MNIST dataset down to 154 dimensions (just like
[p0254-l0006] [10.5pt] before). Note that you must call the partial_fit() method with each mini-batch
[p0254-l0007] [10.5pt] rather than the fit() method with the whole training set:
[p0254-l0008] [8.5pt] from sklearn.decomposition import IncrementalPCA
[p0254-l0009] [8.5pt] n_batches = 100
[p0254-l0010] [8.5pt] inc_pca = IncrementalPCA(n_components=154)
[p0254-l0011] [8.5pt] for X_batch in np.array_split(X_train, n_batches):
[p0254-l0012] [8.5pt]     inc_pca.partial_fit(X_batch)
[p0254-l0013] [8.5pt] X_reduced = inc_pca.transform(X_train)
[p0254-l0014] [10.5pt] Alternatively, you can use NumPy’s memmap class, which allows you to manipulate a
[p0254-l0015] [10.5pt] large array stored in a binary file on disk as if it were entirely in memory; the class
[p0254-l0016] [10.5pt] loads only the data it needs in memory, when it needs it. Since the IncrementalPCA
[p0254-l0017] [10.5pt] class uses only a small part of the array at any given time, the memory usage remains
[p0254-l0018] [10.5pt] under control. This makes it possible to call the usual fit() method, as you can see
[p0254-l0019] [10.5pt] in the following code:
[p0254-l0020] [8.5pt] X_mm = np.memmap(filename, dtype="float32", mode="readonly", shape=(m, n))
[p0254-l0021] [8.5pt] batch_size = m // n_batches
[p0254-l0022] [8.5pt] inc_pca = IncrementalPCA(n_components=154, batch_size=batch_size)
[p0254-l0023] [8.5pt] inc_pca.fit(X_mm)
[p0254-l0024] [18.92pt] Kernel PCA
[p0254-l0025] [10.5pt] In Chapter 5 we discussed the kernel trick, a mathematical technique that implicitly
[p0254-l0026] [10.5pt] maps instances into a very high-dimensional space (called the feature space), enabling
[p0254-l0027] [10.5pt] nonlinear classification and regression with Support Vector Machines. Recall that a
[p0254-l0028] [10.5pt] linear decision boundary in the high-dimensional feature space corresponds to a
[p0254-l0029] [10.5pt] complex nonlinear decision boundary in the original space.
[p0254-l0030] [10.5pt] It turns out that the same trick can be applied to PCA, making it possible to perform
[p0254-l0031] [10.5pt] complex nonlinear projections for dimensionality reduction. This is called Kernel
[p0254-l0032] [8.0pt] 5 Scikit-Learn uses the algorithm described in “Incremental Learning for Robust Visual Tracking,” D. Ross et al.
[p0254-l0033] [8.0pt] (2007).
[p0254-l0034] [9.0pt] 228
[p0254-l0035] [9.0pt] |
[p0254-l0036] [9.0pt] Chapter 8: Dimensionality Reduction

=== PDF page 255 / printed label 229 ===
[p0255-l0001] [10.5pt] PCA (kPCA).6 It is often good at preserving clusters of instances after projection, or
[p0255-l0002] [10.5pt] sometimes even unrolling datasets that lie close to a twisted manifold.
[p0255-l0003] [10.5pt] For example, the following code uses Scikit-Learn’s KernelPCA class to perform kPCA
[p0255-l0004] [10.5pt] with an RBF kernel (see Chapter 5 for more details about the RBF kernel and the
[p0255-l0005] [10.5pt] other kernels):
[p0255-l0006] [8.5pt] from sklearn.decomposition import KernelPCA
[p0255-l0007] [8.5pt] rbf_pca = KernelPCA(n_components = 2, kernel="rbf", gamma=0.04)
[p0255-l0008] [8.5pt] X_reduced = rbf_pca.fit_transform(X)
[p0255-l0009] [10.5pt] Figure 8-10 shows the Swiss roll, reduced to two dimensions using a linear kernel
[p0255-l0010] [10.5pt] (equivalent to simply using the PCA class), an RBF kernel, and a sigmoid kernel
[p0255-l0011] [10.5pt] (Logistic).
[p0255-l0012] [10.5pt] Figure 8-10. Swiss roll reduced to 2D using kPCA with various kernels
[p0255-l0013] [15.77pt] Selecting a Kernel and Tuning Hyperparameters
[p0255-l0014] [10.5pt] As kPCA is an unsupervised learning algorithm, there is no obvious performance
[p0255-l0015] [10.5pt] measure to help you select the best kernel and hyperparameter values. However,
[p0255-l0016] [10.5pt] dimensionality reduction is often a preparation step for a supervised learning task
[p0255-l0017] [10.5pt] (e.g., classification), so you can simply use grid search to select the kernel and hyper‐
[p0255-l0018] [10.5pt] parameters that lead to the best performance on that task. For example, the following
[p0255-l0019] [10.5pt] code creates a two-step pipeline, first reducing dimensionality to two dimensions
[p0255-l0020] [10.5pt] using kPCA, then applying Logistic Regression for classification. Then it uses Grid
[p0255-l0021] [10.5pt] SearchCV to find the best kernel and gamma value for kPCA in order to get the best
[p0255-l0022] [10.5pt] classification accuracy at the end of the pipeline:
[p0255-l0023] [8.5pt] from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV
[p0255-l0024] [8.5pt] from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
[p0255-l0025] [8.5pt] from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
[p0255-l0026] [8.0pt] 6 “Kernel Principal Component Analysis,” B. Schölkopf, A. Smola, K. Müller (1999).
[p0255-l0027] [9.0pt] Kernel PCA
[p0255-l0028] [9.0pt] |
[p0255-l0029] [9.0pt] 229

=== PDF page 256 / printed label 230 ===
[p0256-l0001] [8.5pt] clf = Pipeline([
[p0256-l0002] [8.5pt]         ("kpca", KernelPCA(n_components=2)),
[p0256-l0003] [8.5pt]         ("log_reg", LogisticRegression())
[p0256-l0004] [8.5pt]     ])
[p0256-l0005] [8.5pt] param_grid = [{
[p0256-l0006] [8.5pt]         "kpca__gamma": np.linspace(0.03, 0.05, 10),
[p0256-l0007] [8.5pt]         "kpca__kernel": ["rbf", "sigmoid"]
[p0256-l0008] [8.5pt]     }]
[p0256-l0009] [8.5pt] grid_search = GridSearchCV(clf, param_grid, cv=3)
[p0256-l0010] [8.5pt] grid_search.fit(X, y)
[p0256-l0011] [10.5pt] The best kernel and hyperparameters are then available through the best_params_
[p0256-l0012] [10.5pt] variable:
[p0256-l0013] [8.5pt] >>> print(grid_search.best_params_)
[p0256-l0014] [8.5pt] {'kpca__gamma': 0.043333333333333335, 'kpca__kernel': 'rbf'}
[p0256-l0015] [10.5pt] Another approach, this time entirely unsupervised, is to select the kernel and hyper‐
[p0256-l0016] [10.5pt] parameters that yield the lowest reconstruction error. However, reconstruction is not
[p0256-l0017] [10.5pt] as easy as with linear PCA. Here’s why. Figure 8-11 shows the original Swiss roll 3D
[p0256-l0018] [10.5pt] dataset (top left), and the resulting 2D dataset after kPCA is applied using an RBF
[p0256-l0019] [10.5pt] kernel (top right). Thanks to the kernel trick, this is mathematically equivalent to
[p0256-l0020] [10.5pt] mapping the training set to an infinite-dimensional feature space (bottom right)
[p0256-l0021] [10.5pt] using the feature map φ, then projecting the transformed training set down to 2D
[p0256-l0022] [10.5pt] using linear PCA. Notice that if we could invert the linear PCA step for a given
[p0256-l0023] [10.5pt] instance in the reduced space, the reconstructed point would lie in feature space, not
[p0256-l0024] [10.5pt] in the original space (e.g., like the one represented by an x in the diagram). Since the
[p0256-l0025] [10.5pt] feature space is infinite-dimensional, we cannot compute the reconstructed point,
[p0256-l0026] [10.5pt] and therefore we cannot compute the true reconstruction error. Fortunately, it is pos‐
[p0256-l0027] [10.5pt] sible to find a point in the original space that would map close to the reconstructed
[p0256-l0028] [10.5pt] point. This is called the reconstruction pre-image. Once you have this pre-image, you
[p0256-l0029] [10.5pt] can measure its squared distance to the original instance. You can then select the ker‐
[p0256-l0030] [10.5pt] nel and hyperparameters that minimize this reconstruction pre-image error.
[p0256-l0031] [9.0pt] 230
[p0256-l0032] [9.0pt] |
[p0256-l0033] [9.0pt] Chapter 8: Dimensionality Reduction

=== PDF page 257 / printed label 231 ===
[p0257-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 8-11. Kernel PCA and the reconstruction pre-image error
[p0257-l0002] [10.5pt] You may be wondering how to perform this reconstruction. One solution is to train a
[p0257-l0003] [10.5pt] supervised regression model, with the projected instances as the training set and the
[p0257-l0004] [10.5pt] original instances as the targets. Scikit-Learn will do this automatically if you set
[p0257-l0005] [10.5pt] fit_inverse_transform=True, as shown in the following code:7
[p0257-l0006] [8.5pt] rbf_pca = KernelPCA(n_components = 2, kernel="rbf", gamma=0.0433,
[p0257-l0007] [8.5pt]                     fit_inverse_transform=True)
[p0257-l0008] [8.5pt] X_reduced = rbf_pca.fit_transform(X)
[p0257-l0009] [8.5pt] X_preimage = rbf_pca.inverse_transform(X_reduced)
[p0257-l0010] [9.6pt] By default, fit_inverse_transform=False and KernelPCA has no
[p0257-l0011] [9.6pt] inverse_transform() method. This method only gets created
[p0257-l0012] [9.6pt] when you set fit_inverse_transform=True.
[p0257-l0013] [8.0pt] 7 Scikit-Learn uses the algorithm based on Kernel Ridge Regression described in Gokhan H. Bakır, Jason
[p0257-l0014] [8.0pt] Weston, and Bernhard Scholkopf, “Learning to Find Pre-images” (Tubingen, Germany: Max Planck Institute
[p0257-l0015] [8.0pt] for Biological Cybernetics, 2004).
[p0257-l0016] [9.0pt] Kernel PCA
[p0257-l0017] [9.0pt] |
[p0257-l0018] [9.0pt] 231

=== PDF page 258 / printed label 232 ===
[p0258-l0001] [10.5pt] You can then compute the reconstruction pre-image error:
[p0258-l0002] [8.5pt] >>> from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error
[p0258-l0003] [8.5pt] >>> mean_squared_error(X, X_preimage)
[p0258-l0004] [8.5pt] 32.786308795766132
[p0258-l0005] [10.5pt] Now you can use grid search with cross-validation to find the kernel and hyperpara‐
[p0258-l0006] [10.5pt] meters that minimize this pre-image reconstruction error.
[p0258-l0007] [18.92pt] LLE
[p0258-l0008] [10.5pt] Locally Linear Embedding (LLE)8 is another very powerful nonlinear dimensionality
[p0258-l0009] [10.5pt] reduction (NLDR) technique. It is a Manifold Learning technique that does not rely
[p0258-l0010] [10.5pt] on projections like the previous algorithms. In a nutshell, LLE works by first measur‐
[p0258-l0011] [10.5pt] ing how each training instance linearly relates to its closest neighbors (c.n.), and then
[p0258-l0012] [10.5pt] looking for a low-dimensional representation of the training set where these local
[p0258-l0013] [10.5pt] relationships are best preserved (more details shortly). This makes it particularly
[p0258-l0014] [10.5pt] good at unrolling twisted manifolds, especially when there is not too much noise.
[p0258-l0015] [10.5pt] For example, the following code uses Scikit-Learn’s LocallyLinearEmbedding class to
[p0258-l0016] [10.5pt] unroll the Swiss roll. The resulting 2D dataset is shown in Figure 8-12. As you can
[p0258-l0017] [10.5pt] see, the Swiss roll is completely unrolled and the distances between instances are
[p0258-l0018] [10.5pt] locally well preserved. However, distances are not preserved on a larger scale: the left
[p0258-l0019] [10.5pt] part of the unrolled Swiss roll is stretched, while the right part is squeezed. Neverthe‐
[p0258-l0020] [10.5pt] less, LLE did a pretty good job at modeling the manifold.
[p0258-l0021] [8.5pt] from sklearn.manifold import LocallyLinearEmbedding
[p0258-l0022] [8.5pt] lle = LocallyLinearEmbedding(n_components=2, n_neighbors=10)
[p0258-l0023] [8.5pt] X_reduced = lle.fit_transform(X)
[p0258-l0024] [8.0pt] 8 “Nonlinear Dimensionality Reduction by Locally Linear Embedding,” S. Roweis, L. Saul (2000).
[p0258-l0025] [9.0pt] 232
[p0258-l0026] [9.0pt] |
[p0258-l0027] [9.0pt] Chapter 8: Dimensionality Reduction

=== PDF page 259 / printed label 233 ===
[p0259-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 8-12. Unrolled Swiss roll using LLE
[p0259-l0002] [10.5pt] Here’s how LLE works: first, for each training instance x(i), the algorithm identifies its
[p0259-l0003] [10.5pt] k closest neighbors (in the preceding code k = 10), then tries to reconstruct x(i) as a
[p0259-l0004] [10.5pt] linear function of these neighbors. More specifically, it finds the weights wi,j such that
[p0259-l0005] [10.5pt] the squared distance between x(i) and ∑j = 1
[p0259-l0006] [8.0pt] m
[p0259-l0007] [10.5pt] wi, jx j is as small as possible, assuming wi,j
[p0259-l0008] [10.5pt] = 0 if x(j) is not one of the k closest neighbors of x(i). Thus the first step of LLE is the
[p0259-l0009] [10.5pt] constrained optimization problem described in Equation 8-4, where W is the weight
[p0259-l0010] [10.5pt] matrix containing all the weights wi,j. The second constraint simply normalizes the
[p0259-l0011] [10.5pt] weights for each training instance x(i).
[p0259-l0012] [9.0pt] LLE
[p0259-l0013] [9.0pt] |
[p0259-l0014] [9.0pt] 233

[p0260-l0019] [10.5pt] After this step, the weight matrix W (containing the weights wi, j) encodes the local
[p0260-l0020] [10.5pt] linear relationships between the training instances. Now the second step is to map the
[p0260-l0021] [10.5pt] training instances into a d-dimensional space (where d < n) while preserving these
[p0260-l0022] [10.5pt] local relationships as much as possible. If z(i) is the image of x(i) in this d-dimensional
[p0260-l0023] [10.5pt] space, then we want the squared distance between z(i) and ∑j = 1
[p0260-l0024] [8.0pt] m
[p0260-l0025] [10.5pt] wi, jz j to be as small
[p0260-l0026] [10.5pt] as possible. This idea leads to the unconstrained optimization problem described in
[p0260-l0027] [10.5pt] Equation 8-5. It looks very similar to the first step, but instead of keeping the instan‐
[p0260-l0028] [10.5pt] ces fixed and finding the optimal weights, we are doing the reverse: keeping the
[p0260-l0029] [10.5pt] weights fixed and finding the optimal position of the instances’ images in the low-
[p0260-l0030] [10.5pt] dimensional space. Note that Z is the matrix containing all z(i).
[p0260-l0031] [10.5pt] Equation 8-5. LLE step 2: reducing dimensionality while preserving relationships
[p0260-l0032] [8.0pt] 2
[p0260-l0033] [8.0pt] m
[p0260-l0034] [8.0pt] m
[p0260-l0035] [10.0pt] Z = argmin
[p0260-l0036] [14.14pt] z i −∑
[p0260-l0037] [10.0pt] wi, jz j
[p0260-l0038] [8.0pt] j = 1
[p0260-l0039] [8.0pt] Z
[p0260-l0040] [14.14pt] ∑
[p0260-l0041] [8.0pt] i = 1
[p0260-l0042] [10.5pt] Scikit-Learn’s LLE implementation has the following computational complexity:
[p0260-l0043] [10.5pt] O(m log(m)n log(k)) for finding the k nearest neighbors, O(mnk3) for optimizing the
[p0260-l0044] [10.5pt] weights, and O(dm2) for constructing the low-dimensional representations. Unfortu‐
[p0260-l0045] [10.5pt] nately, the m2 in the last term makes this algorithm scale poorly to very large datasets.
[p0260-l0046] [18.92pt] Other Dimensionality Reduction Techniques
[p0260-l0047] [10.5pt] There are many other dimensionality reduction techniques, several of which are
[p0260-l0048] [10.5pt] available in Scikit-Learn. Here are some of the most popular:
[p0260-l0049] [10.5pt] • Multidimensional Scaling (MDS) reduces dimensionality while trying to preserve
[p0260-l0050] [10.5pt] the distances between the instances (see Figure 8-13).
[p0260-l0051] [9.0pt] 234
[p0260-l0052] [9.0pt] |
[p0260-l0053] [9.0pt] Chapter 8: Dimensionality Reduction

=== PDF page 261 / printed label 235 ===
[p0261-l0001] [10.5pt] • Isomap creates a graph by connecting each instance to its nearest neighbors, then
[p0261-l0002] [10.5pt] reduces dimensionality while trying to preserve the geodesic distances9 between
[p0261-l0003] [10.5pt] the instances.
[p0261-l0004] [10.5pt] • t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE) reduces dimensionality
[p0261-l0005] [10.5pt] while trying to keep similar instances close and dissimilar instances apart. It is
[p0261-l0006] [10.5pt] mostly used for visualization, in particular to visualize clusters of instances in
[p0261-l0007] [10.5pt] high-dimensional space (e.g., to visualize the MNIST images in 2D).
[p0261-l0008] [10.5pt] • Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) is actually a classification algorithm, but dur‐
[p0261-l0009] [10.5pt] ing training it learns the most discriminative axes between the classes, and these
[p0261-l0010] [10.5pt] axes can then be used to define a hyperplane onto which to project the data. The
[p0261-l0011] [10.5pt] benefit is that the projection will keep classes as far apart as possible, so LDA is a
[p0261-l0012] [10.5pt] good technique to reduce dimensionality before running another classification
[p0261-l0013] [10.5pt] algorithm such as an SVM classifier.
[p0261-l0014] [10.5pt] Figure 8-13. Reducing the Swiss roll to 2D using various techniques
