[p0263-l0001] [16.82pt] CHAPTER 9
[p0263-l0002] [25.22pt] Unsupervised Learning Techniques
[p0263-l0003] [9.6pt] With Early Release ebooks, you get books in their earliest form—
[p0263-l0004] [9.6pt] the author’s raw and unedited content as he or she writes—so you
[p0263-l0005] [9.6pt] can take advantage of these technologies long before the official
[p0263-l0006] [9.6pt] release of these titles. The following will be Chapter 9 in the final
[p0263-l0007] [9.6pt] release of the book.
[p0263-l0008] [10.5pt] Although most of the applications of Machine Learning today are based on super‐
[p0263-l0009] [10.5pt] vised learning (and as a result, this is where most of the investments go to), the vast
[p0263-l0010] [10.5pt] majority of the available data is actually unlabeled: we have the input features X, but
[p0263-l0011] [10.5pt] we do not have the labels y. Yann LeCun famously said that “if intelligence was a cake,
[p0263-l0012] [10.5pt] unsupervised learning would be the cake, supervised learning would be the icing on
[p0263-l0013] [10.5pt] the cake, and reinforcement learning would be the cherry on the cake”. In other
[p0263-l0014] [10.5pt] words, there is a huge potential in unsupervised learning that we have only barely
[p0263-l0015] [10.5pt] started to sink our teeth into.
[p0263-l0016] [10.5pt] For example, say you want to create a system that will take a few pictures of each item
[p0263-l0017] [10.5pt] on a manufacturing production line and detect which items are defective. You can
[p0263-l0018] [10.5pt] fairly easily create a system that will take pictures automatically, and this might give
[p0263-l0019] [10.5pt] you thousands of pictures every day. You can then build a reasonably large dataset in
[p0263-l0020] [10.5pt] just a few weeks. But wait, there are no labels! If you want to train a regular binary
[p0263-l0021] [10.5pt] classifier that will predict whether an item is defective or not, you will need to label
[p0263-l0022] [10.5pt] every single picture as “defective” or “normal”. This will generally require human
[p0263-l0023] [10.5pt] experts to sit down and manually go through all the pictures. This is a long, costly
[p0263-l0024] [10.5pt] and tedious task, so it will usually only be done on a small subset of the available pic‐
[p0263-l0025] [10.5pt] tures. As a result, the labeled dataset will be quite small, and the classifier’s perfor‐
[p0263-l0026] [10.5pt] mance will be disappointing. Moreover, every time the company makes any change to
[p0263-l0027] [10.5pt] its products, the whole process will need to be started over from scratch. Wouldn’t it
[p0263-l0028] [9.0pt] 237

=== PDF page 264 / printed label 238 ===
[p0264-l0001] [10.5pt] be great if the algorithm could just exploit the unlabeled data without needing
[p0264-l0002] [10.5pt] humans to label every picture? Enter unsupervised learning.
[p0264-l0003] [10.5pt] In Chapter 8, we looked at the most common unsupervised learning task: dimension‐
[p0264-l0004] [10.5pt] ality reduction. In this chapter, we will look at a few more unsupervised learning tasks
[p0264-l0005] [10.5pt] and algorithms:
[p0264-l0006] [10.5pt] • Clustering: the goal is to group similar instances together into clusters. This is a
[p0264-l0007] [10.5pt] great tool for data analysis, customer segmentation, recommender systems,
[p0264-l0008] [10.5pt] search engines, image segmentation, semi-supervised learning, dimensionality
[p0264-l0009] [10.5pt] reduction, and more.
[p0264-l0010] [10.5pt] • Anomaly detection: the objective is to learn what “normal” data looks like, and
[p0264-l0011] [10.5pt] use this to detect abnormal instances, such as defective items on a production
[p0264-l0012] [10.5pt] line or a new trend in a time series.
[p0264-l0013] [10.5pt] • Density estimation: this is the task of estimating the probability density function
[p0264-l0014] [10.5pt] (PDF) of the random process that generated the dataset. This is commonly used
[p0264-l0015] [10.5pt] for anomaly detection: instances located in very low-density regions are likely to
[p0264-l0016] [10.5pt] be anomalies. It is also useful for data analysis and visualization.
[p0264-l0017] [10.5pt] Ready for some cake? We will start with clustering, using K-Means and DBSCAN,
[p0264-l0018] [10.5pt] and then we will discuss Gaussian mixture models and see how they can be used for
[p0264-l0019] [10.5pt] density estimation, clustering, and anomaly detection.
[p0264-l0020] [18.92pt] Clustering
[p0264-l0021] [10.5pt] As you enjoy a hike in the mountains, you stumble upon a plant you have never seen
[p0264-l0022] [10.5pt] before. You look around and you notice a few more. They are not perfectly identical,
[p0264-l0023] [10.5pt] yet they are sufficiently similar for you to know that they most likely belong to the
[p0264-l0024] [10.5pt] same species (or at least the same genus). You may need a botanist to tell you what
[p0264-l0025] [10.5pt] species that is, but you certainly don’t need an expert to identify groups of similar-
[p0264-l0026] [10.5pt] looking objects. This is called clustering: it is the task of identifying similar instances
[p0264-l0027] [10.5pt] and assigning them to clusters, i.e., groups of similar instances.
[p0264-l0028] [10.5pt] Just like in classification, each instance gets assigned to a group. However, this is an
[p0264-l0029] [10.5pt] unsupervised task. Consider Figure 9-1: on the left is the iris dataset (introduced in
[p0264-l0030] [10.5pt] Chapter 4), where each instance’s species (i.e., its class) is represented with a different
[p0264-l0031] [10.5pt] marker. It is a labeled dataset, for which classification algorithms such as Logistic
[p0264-l0032] [10.5pt] Regression, SVMs or Random Forest classifiers are well suited. On the right is the
[p0264-l0033] [10.5pt] same dataset, but without the labels, so you cannot use a classification algorithm any‐
[p0264-l0034] [10.5pt] more. This is where clustering algorithms step in: many of them can easily detect the
[p0264-l0035] [10.5pt] top left cluster. It is also quite easy to see with our own eyes, but it is not so obvious
[p0264-l0036] [10.5pt] that the lower right cluster is actually composed of two distinct sub-clusters. That
[p0264-l0037] [10.5pt] said, the dataset actually has two additional features (sepal length and width), not
[p0264-l0038] [9.0pt] 238
[p0264-l0039] [9.0pt] |
[p0264-l0040] [9.0pt] Chapter 9: Unsupervised Learning Techniques

=== PDF page 265 / printed label 239 ===
[p0265-l0001] [10.5pt] represented here, and clustering algorithms can make good use of all features, so in
[p0265-l0002] [10.5pt] fact they identify the three clusters fairly well (e.g., using a Gaussian mixture model,
[p0265-l0003] [10.5pt] only 5 instances out of 150 are assigned to the wrong cluster).
[p0265-l0004] [10.5pt] Figure 9-1. Classification (left) versus clustering (right)
[p0265-l0005] [10.5pt] Clustering is used in a wide variety of applications, including:
[p0265-l0006] [10.5pt] • For customer segmentation: you can cluster your customers based on their pur‐
[p0265-l0007] [10.5pt] chases, their activity on your website, and so on. This is useful to understand who
[p0265-l0008] [10.5pt] your customers are and what they need, so you can adapt your products and
[p0265-l0009] [10.5pt] marketing campaigns to each segment. For example, this can be useful in recom‐
[p0265-l0010] [10.5pt] mender systems to suggest content that other users in the same cluster enjoyed.
[p0265-l0011] [10.5pt] • For data analysis: when analyzing a new dataset, it is often useful to first discover
[p0265-l0012] [10.5pt] clusters of similar instances, as it is often easier to analyze clusters separately.
[p0265-l0013] [10.5pt] • As a dimensionality reduction technique: once a dataset has been clustered, it is
[p0265-l0014] [10.5pt] usually possible to measure each instance’s affinity with each cluster (affinity is
[p0265-l0015] [10.5pt] any measure of how well an instance fits into a cluster). Each instance’s feature
[p0265-l0016] [10.5pt] vector x can then be replaced with the vector of its cluster affinities. If there are k
[p0265-l0017] [10.5pt] clusters, then this vector is k dimensional. This is typically much lower dimen‐
[p0265-l0018] [10.5pt] sional than the original feature vector, but it can preserve enough information for
[p0265-l0019] [10.5pt] further processing.
[p0265-l0020] [10.5pt] • For anomaly detection (also called outlier detection): any instance that has a low
[p0265-l0021] [10.5pt] affinity to all the clusters is likely to be an anomaly. For example, if you have clus‐
[p0265-l0022] [10.5pt] tered the users of your website based on their behavior, you can detect users with
[p0265-l0023] [10.5pt] unusual behavior, such as an unusual number of requests per second, and so on.
[p0265-l0024] [10.5pt] Anomaly detection is particularly useful in detecting defects in manufacturing, or
[p0265-l0025] [10.5pt] for fraud detection.
[p0265-l0026] [10.5pt] • For semi-supervised learning: if you only have a few labels, you could perform
[p0265-l0027] [10.5pt] clustering and propagate the labels to all the instances in the same cluster. This
[p0265-l0028] [10.5pt] can greatly increase the amount of labels available for a subsequent supervised
[p0265-l0029] [10.5pt] learning algorithm, and thus improve its performance.
[p0265-l0030] [9.0pt] Clustering
[p0265-l0031] [9.0pt] |
[p0265-l0032] [9.0pt] 239

=== PDF page 266 / printed label 240 ===
[p0266-l0001] [10.5pt] • For search engines: for example, some search engines let you search for images
[p0266-l0002] [10.5pt] that are similar to a reference image. To build such a system, you would first
[p0266-l0003] [10.5pt] apply a clustering algorithm to all the images in your database: similar images
[p0266-l0004] [10.5pt] would end up in the same cluster. Then when a user provides a reference image,
[p0266-l0005] [10.5pt] all you need to do is to find this image’s cluster using the trained clustering
[p0266-l0006] [10.5pt] model, and you can then simply return all the images from this cluster.
[p0266-l0007] [10.5pt] • To segment an image: by clustering pixels according to their color, then replacing
[p0266-l0008] [10.5pt] each pixel’s color with the mean color of its cluster, it is possible to reduce the
[p0266-l0009] [10.5pt] number of different colors in the image considerably. This technique is used in
[p0266-l0010] [10.5pt] many object detection and tracking systems, as it makes it easier to detect the
[p0266-l0011] [10.5pt] contour of each object.
[p0266-l0012] [10.5pt] There is no universal definition of what a cluster is: it really depends on the context,
[p0266-l0013] [10.5pt] and different algorithms will capture different kinds of clusters. For example, some
[p0266-l0014] [10.5pt] algorithms look for instances centered around a particular point, called a centroid.
[p0266-l0015] [10.5pt] Others look for continuous regions of densely packed instances: these clusters can
[p0266-l0016] [10.5pt] take on any shape. Some algorithms are hierarchical, looking for clusters of clusters.
[p0266-l0017] [10.5pt] And the list goes on.
[p0266-l0018] [10.5pt] In this section, we will look at two popular clustering algorithms: K-Means and
[p0266-l0019] [10.5pt] DBSCAN, and we will show some of their applications, such as non-linear dimen‐
[p0266-l0020] [10.5pt] sionality reduction, semi-supervised learning and anomaly detection.
[p0266-l0021] [15.77pt] K-Means
[p0266-l0022] [10.5pt] Consider the unlabeled dataset represented in Figure 9-2: you can clearly see 5 blobs
[p0266-l0023] [10.5pt] of instances. The K-Means algorithm is a simple algorithm capable of clustering this
[p0266-l0024] [10.5pt] kind of dataset very quickly and efficiently, often in just a few iterations. It was pro‐
[p0266-l0025] [10.5pt] posed by Stuart Lloyd at the Bell Labs in 1957 as a technique for pulse-code modula‐
[p0266-l0026] [10.5pt] tion, but it was only published outside of the company in 1982, in a paper titled
[p0266-l0027] [10.5pt] “Least square quantization in PCM”.1 By then, in 1965, Edward W. Forgy had pub‐
[p0266-l0028] [10.5pt] lished virtually the same algorithm, so K-Means is sometimes referred to as Lloyd-
[p0266-l0029] [10.5pt] Forgy.
[p0266-l0030] [8.0pt] 1 “Least square quantization in PCM,” Stuart P. Lloyd. (1982).
[p0266-l0031] [9.0pt] 240
[p0266-l0032] [9.0pt] |
[p0266-l0033] [9.0pt] Chapter 9: Unsupervised Learning Techniques

=== PDF page 267 / printed label 241 ===
[p0267-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 9-2. An unlabeled dataset composed of five blobs of instances
[p0267-l0002] [10.5pt] Let’s train a K-Means clusterer on this dataset. It will try to find each blob’s center and
[p0267-l0003] [10.5pt] assign each instance to the closest blob:
[p0267-l0004] [8.5pt] from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
[p0267-l0005] [8.5pt] k = 5
[p0267-l0006] [8.5pt] kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=k)
[p0267-l0007] [8.5pt] y_pred = kmeans.fit_predict(X)
[p0267-l0008] [10.5pt] Note that you have to specify the number of clusters k that the algorithm must find.
[p0267-l0009] [10.5pt] In this example, it is pretty obvious from looking at the data that k should be set to 5,
[p0267-l0010] [10.5pt] but in general it is not that easy. We will discuss this shortly.
[p0267-l0011] [10.5pt] Each instance was assigned to one of the 5 clusters. In the context of clustering, an
[p0267-l0012] [10.5pt] instance’s label is the index of the cluster that this instance gets assigned to by the
[p0267-l0013] [10.5pt] algorithm: this is not to be confused with the class labels in classification (remember
[p0267-l0014] [10.5pt] that clustering is an unsupervised learning task). The KMeans instance preserves a
[p0267-l0015] [10.5pt] copy of the labels of the instances it was trained on, available via the labels_ instance
[p0267-l0016] [10.5pt] variable:
[p0267-l0017] [8.5pt] >>> y_pred
[p0267-l0018] [8.5pt] array([4, 0, 1, ..., 2, 1, 0], dtype=int32)
[p0267-l0019] [8.5pt] >>> y_pred is kmeans.labels_
[p0267-l0020] [8.5pt] True
[p0267-l0021] [10.5pt] We can also take a look at the 5 centroids that the algorithm found:
[p0267-l0022] [8.5pt] >>> kmeans.cluster_centers_
[p0267-l0023] [8.5pt] array([[-2.80389616,  1.80117999],
[p0267-l0024] [8.5pt]        [ 0.20876306,  2.25551336],
[p0267-l0025] [8.5pt]        [-2.79290307,  2.79641063],
[p0267-l0026] [8.5pt]        [-1.46679593,  2.28585348],
[p0267-l0027] [8.5pt]        [-2.80037642,  1.30082566]])
[p0267-l0028] [10.5pt] Of course, you can easily assign new instances to the cluster whose centroid is closest:
[p0267-l0029] [9.0pt] Clustering

[p0268-l0003] [8.5pt] array([1, 1, 2, 2], dtype=int32)
[p0268-l0004] [10.5pt] If you plot the cluster’s decision boundaries, you get a Voronoi tessellation (see
[p0268-l0005] [10.5pt] Figure 9-3, where each centroid is represented with an X):
[p0268-l0006] [10.5pt] Figure 9-3. K-Means decision boundaries (Voronoi tessellation)
[p0268-l0007] [10.5pt] The vast majority of the instances were clearly assigned to the appropriate cluster, but
[p0268-l0008] [10.5pt] a few instances were probably mislabeled (especially near the boundary between the
[p0268-l0009] [10.5pt] top left cluster and the central cluster). Indeed, the K-Means algorithm does not
[p0268-l0010] [10.5pt] behave very well when the blobs have very different diameters since all it cares about
[p0268-l0011] [10.5pt] when assigning an instance to a cluster is the distance to the centroid.
[p0268-l0012] [10.5pt] Instead of assigning each instance to a single cluster, which is called hard clustering, it
[p0268-l0013] [10.5pt] can be useful to just give each instance a score per cluster: this is called soft clustering.
[p0268-l0014] [10.5pt] For example, the score can be the distance between the instance and the centroid, or
[p0268-l0015] [10.5pt] conversely it can be a similarity score (or affinity) such as the Gaussian Radial Basis
[p0268-l0016] [10.5pt] Function (introduced in Chapter 5). In the KMeans class, the transform() method
[p0268-l0017] [10.5pt] measures the distance from each instance to every centroid:
[p0268-l0018] [8.5pt] >>> kmeans.transform(X_new)
[p0268-l0019] [8.5pt] array([[2.81093633, 0.32995317, 2.9042344 , 1.49439034, 2.88633901],
[p0268-l0020] [8.5pt]        [5.80730058, 2.80290755, 5.84739223, 4.4759332 , 5.84236351],
[p0268-l0021] [8.5pt]        [1.21475352, 3.29399768, 0.29040966, 1.69136631, 1.71086031],
[p0268-l0022] [8.5pt]        [0.72581411, 3.21806371, 0.36159148, 1.54808703, 1.21567622]])
[p0268-l0023] [10.5pt] In this example, the first instance in X_new is located at a distance of 2.81 from the
[p0268-l0024] [10.5pt] first centroid, 0.33 from the second centroid, 2.90 from the third centroid, 1.49 from
[p0268-l0025] [10.5pt] the fourth centroid and 2.87 from the fifth centroid. If you have a high-dimensional
[p0268-l0026] [10.5pt] dataset and you transform it this way, you end up with a k-dimensional dataset: this
[p0268-l0027] [10.5pt] can be a very efficient non-linear dimensionality reduction technique.

[p0269-l0001] [11.56pt] The K-Means Algorithm
[p0269-l0002] [10.5pt] So how does the algorithm work? Well it is really quite simple. Suppose you were
[p0269-l0003] [10.5pt] given the centroids: you could easily label all the instances in the dataset by assigning
[p0269-l0004] [10.5pt] each of them to the cluster whose centroid is closest. Conversely, if you were given all
[p0269-l0005] [10.5pt] the instance labels, you could easily locate all the centroids by computing the mean of
[p0269-l0006] [10.5pt] the instances for each cluster. But you are given neither the labels nor the centroids,
[p0269-l0007] [10.5pt] so how can you proceed? Well, just start by placing the centroids randomly (e.g., by
[p0269-l0008] [10.5pt] picking k instances at random and using their locations as centroids). Then label the
[p0269-l0009] [10.5pt] instances, update the centroids, label the instances, update the centroids, and so on
[p0269-l0010] [10.5pt] until the centroids stop moving. The algorithm is guaranteed to converge in a finite
[p0269-l0011] [10.5pt] number of steps (usually quite small), it will not oscillate forever2. You can see the
[p0269-l0012] [10.5pt] algorithm in action in Figure 9-4: the centroids are initialized randomly (top left),
[p0269-l0013] [10.5pt] then the instances are labeled (top right), then the centroids are updated (center left),
[p0269-l0014] [10.5pt] the instances are relabeled (center right), and so on. As you can see, in just 3 itera‐
[p0269-l0015] [10.5pt] tions the algorithm has reached a clustering that seems close to optimal.
[p0269-l0016] [10.5pt] Figure 9-4. The K-Means algorithm
[p0269-l0017] [8.0pt] 2 This can be proven by pointing out that the mean squared distance between the instances and their closest
[p0269-l0018] [8.0pt] centroid can only go down at each step.
[p0269-l0019] [9.0pt] Clustering
[p0269-l0020] [9.0pt] |
[p0269-l0021] [9.0pt] 243

=== PDF page 270 / printed label 244 ===
[p0270-l0001] [9.6pt] The computational complexity of the algorithm is generally linear
[p0270-l0002] [9.6pt] with regards to the number of instances m, the number of clusters
[p0270-l0003] [9.6pt] k and the number of dimensions n. However, this is only true when
[p0270-l0004] [9.6pt] the data has a clustering structure. If it does not, then in the worst
[p0270-l0005] [9.6pt] case scenario the complexity can increase exponentially with the
[p0270-l0006] [9.6pt] number of instances. In practice, however, this rarely happens, and
[p0270-l0007] [9.6pt] K-Means is generally one of the fastest clustering algorithms.
[p0270-l0008] [10.5pt] Unfortunately, although the algorithm is guaranteed to converge, it may not converge
[p0270-l0009] [10.5pt] to the right solution (i.e., it may converge to a local optimum): this depends on the
[p0270-l0010] [10.5pt] centroid initialization. For example, Figure 9-5 shows two sub-optimal solutions that
[p0270-l0011] [10.5pt] the algorithm can converge to if you are not lucky with the random initialization step:
[p0270-l0012] [10.5pt] Figure 9-5. Sub-optimal solutions due to unlucky centroid initializations
[p0270-l0013] [10.5pt] Let’s look at a few ways you can mitigate this risk by improving the centroid initializa‐
[p0270-l0014] [10.5pt] tion.
[p0270-l0015] [11.56pt] Centroid Initialization Methods
[p0270-l0016] [10.5pt] If you happen to know approximately where the centroids should be (e.g., if you ran
[p0270-l0017] [10.5pt] another clustering algorithm earlier), then you can set the init hyperparameter to a
[p0270-l0018] [10.5pt] NumPy array containing the list of centroids, and set n_init to 1:
[p0270-l0019] [8.5pt] good_init = np.array([[-3, 3], [-3, 2], [-3, 1], [-1, 2], [0, 2]])
[p0270-l0020] [8.5pt] kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=5, init=good_init, n_init=1)
[p0270-l0021] [10.5pt] Another solution is to run the algorithm multiple times with different random initial‐
[p0270-l0022] [10.5pt] izations and keep the best solution. This is controlled by the n_init hyperparameter:
[p0270-l0023] [10.5pt] by default, it is equal to 10, which means that the whole algorithm described earlier
[p0270-l0024] [10.5pt] actually runs 10 times when you call fit(), and Scikit-Learn keeps the best solution.
[p0270-l0025] [10.5pt] But how exactly does it know which solution is the best? Well of course it uses a per‐
[p0270-l0026] [10.5pt] formance metric! It is called the model’s inertia: this is the mean squared distance
[p0270-l0027] [10.5pt] between each instance and its closest centroid. It is roughly equal to 223.3 for the
[p0270-l0028] [10.5pt] model on the left of Figure 9-5, 237.5 for the model on the right of Figure 9-5, and
[p0270-l0029] [10.5pt] 211.6 for the model in Figure 9-3. The KMeans class runs the algorithm n_init times
[p0270-l0030] [10.5pt] and keeps the model with the lowest inertia: in this example, the model in Figure 9-3
[p0270-l0031] [10.5pt] will be selected (unless we are very unlucky with n_init consecutive random initiali‐
[p0270-l0032] [9.0pt] 244
[p0270-l0033] [9.0pt] |
[p0270-l0034] [9.0pt] Chapter 9: Unsupervised Learning Techniques

=== PDF page 271 / printed label 245 ===
[p0271-l0001] [10.5pt] zations). If you are curious, a model’s inertia is accessible via the inertia_ instance
[p0271-l0002] [10.5pt] variable:
[p0271-l0003] [8.5pt] >>> kmeans.inertia_
[p0271-l0004] [8.5pt] 211.59853725816856
[p0271-l0005] [10.5pt] The score() method returns the negative inertia. Why negative? Well, it is because a
[p0271-l0006] [10.5pt] predictor’s score() method must always respect the "great is better" rule.
[p0271-l0007] [8.5pt] >>> kmeans.score(X)
[p0271-l0008] [8.5pt] -211.59853725816856
[p0271-l0009] [10.5pt] An important improvement to the K-Means algorithm, called K-Means+\+, was pro‐
[p0271-l0010] [10.5pt] posed in a 2006 paper by David Arthur and Sergei Vassilvitskii:3 they introduced a
[p0271-l0011] [10.5pt] smarter initialization step that tends to select centroids that are distant from one
[p0271-l0012] [10.5pt] another, and this makes the K-Means algorithm much less likely to converge to a sub-
[p0271-l0013] [10.5pt] optimal solution. They showed that the additional computation required for the
[p0271-l0014] [10.5pt] smarter initialization step is well worth it since it makes it possible to drastically
[p0271-l0015] [10.5pt] reduce the number of times the algorithm needs to be run to find the optimal solu‐
[p0271-l0016] [10.5pt] tion. Here is the K-Means++ initialization algorithm:
[p0271-l0017] [10.5pt] • Take one centroid c(1), chosen uniformly at random from the dataset.
[p0271-l0018] [10.5pt] • Take a new centroid c(i), choosing an instance x(i) with probability: D �i
[p0271-l0019] [8.0pt] 2
[p0271-l0020] [10.5pt] ∑j = 1
[p0271-l0021] [8.0pt] m
[p0271-l0022] [10.5pt] D �j 2 where D(x(i)) is the distance between the instance x(i) and the closest
[p0271-l0023] [10.5pt] centroid that was already chosen. This probability distribution ensures that
[p0271-l0024] [10.5pt] instances further away from already chosen centroids are much more likely be
[p0271-l0025] [10.5pt] selected as centroids.
[p0271-l0026] [10.5pt] • Repeat the previous step until all k centroids have been chosen.
[p0271-l0027] [10.5pt] The KMeans class actually uses this initialization method by default. If you want to
[p0271-l0028] [10.5pt] force it to use the original method (i.e., picking k instances randomly to define the
[p0271-l0029] [10.5pt] initial centroids), then you can set the init hyperparameter to "random". You will
[p0271-l0030] [10.5pt] rarely need to do this.
[p0271-l0031] [11.56pt] Accelerated K-Means and Mini-batch K-Means
[p0271-l0032] [10.5pt] Another important improvement to the K-Means algorithm was proposed in a 2003
[p0271-l0033] [10.5pt] paper by Charles Elkan.4 It considerably accelerates the algorithm by avoiding many
[p0271-l0034] [10.5pt] unnecessary distance calculations: this is achieved by exploiting the triangle inequal‐
[p0271-l0035] [8.0pt] 3 “k-means\++: The advantages of careful seeding,” David Arthur and Sergei Vassilvitskii (2006).
[p0271-l0036] [8.0pt] 4 “Using the Triangle Inequality to Accelerate k-Means,” Charles Elkan (2003).
[p0271-l0037] [9.0pt] Clustering
[p0271-l0038] [9.0pt] |
[p0271-l0039] [9.0pt] 245

=== PDF page 272 / printed label 246 ===
[p0272-l0001] [10.5pt] ity (i.e., the straight line is always the shortest5) and by keeping track of lower and
[p0272-l0002] [10.5pt] upper bounds for distances between instances and centroids. This is the algorithm
[p0272-l0003] [10.5pt] used by default by the KMeans class (but you can force it to use the original algorithm
[p0272-l0004] [10.5pt] by setting the algorithm hyperparameter to "full", although you probably will
[p0272-l0005] [10.5pt] never need to).
[p0272-l0006] [10.5pt] Yet another important variant of the K-Means algorithm was proposed in a 2010
[p0272-l0007] [10.5pt] paper by David Sculley.6 Instead of using the full dataset at each iteration, the algo‐
[p0272-l0008] [10.5pt] rithm is capable of using mini-batches, moving the centroids just slightly at each iter‐
[p0272-l0009] [10.5pt] ation. This speeds up the algorithm typically by a factor of 3 or 4 and makes it
[p0272-l0010] [10.5pt] possible to cluster huge datasets that do not fit in memory. Scikit-Learn implements
[p0272-l0011] [10.5pt] this algorithm in the MiniBatchKMeans class. You can just use this class like the
[p0272-l0012] [10.5pt] KMeans class:
[p0272-l0013] [8.5pt] from sklearn.cluster import MiniBatchKMeans
[p0272-l0014] [8.5pt] minibatch_kmeans = MiniBatchKMeans(n_clusters=5)
[p0272-l0015] [8.5pt] minibatch_kmeans.fit(X)
[p0272-l0016] [10.5pt] If the dataset does not fit in memory, the simplest option is to use the memmap class, as
[p0272-l0017] [10.5pt] we did for incremental PCA in Chapter 8. Alternatively, you can pass one mini-batch
[p0272-l0018] [10.5pt] at a time to the partial_fit() method, but this will require much more work, since
[p0272-l0019] [10.5pt] you will need to perform multiple initializations and select the best one yourself (see
[p0272-l0020] [10.5pt] the notebook for an example).
[p0272-l0021] [10.5pt] Although the Mini-batch K-Means algorithm is much faster than the regular K-
[p0272-l0022] [10.5pt] Means algorithm, its inertia is generally slightly worse, especially as the number of
[p0272-l0023] [10.5pt] clusters increases. You can see this in Figure 9-6: the plot on the left compares the
[p0272-l0024] [10.5pt] inertias of Mini-batch K-Means and regular K-Means models trained on the previous
[p0272-l0025] [10.5pt] dataset using various numbers of clusters k. The difference between the two curves
[p0272-l0026] [10.5pt] remains fairly constant, but this difference becomes more and more significant as k
[p0272-l0027] [10.5pt] increases, since the inertia becomes smaller and smaller. However, in the plot on the
[p0272-l0028] [10.5pt] right, you can see that Mini-batch K-Means is much faster than regular K-Means, and
[p0272-l0029] [10.5pt] this difference increases with k.
[p0272-l0030] [8.0pt] 5 The triangle inequality is AC ≤ AB + BC where A, B and C are three points, and AB, AC and BC are the
[p0272-l0031] [8.0pt] distances between these points.
[p0272-l0032] [8.0pt] 6 “Web-Scale K-Means Clustering,” David Sculley (2010).
[p0272-l0033] [9.0pt] 246
[p0272-l0034] [9.0pt] |

[p0273-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 9-6. Mini-batch K-Means vs K-Means: worse inertia as k increases (left) but
[p0273-l0002] [10.5pt] much faster (right)
[p0273-l0003] [11.56pt] Finding the Optimal Number of Clusters
[p0273-l0004] [10.5pt] So far, we have set the number of clusters k to 5 because it was obvious by looking at
[p0273-l0005] [10.5pt] the data that this is the correct number of clusters. But in general, it will not be so
[p0273-l0006] [10.5pt] easy to know how to set k, and the result might be quite bad if you set it to the wrong
[p0273-l0007] [10.5pt] value. For example, as you can see in Figure 9-7, setting k to 3 or 8 results in fairly
[p0273-l0008] [10.5pt] bad models:
[p0273-l0009] [10.5pt] Figure 9-7. Bad choices for the number of clusters
[p0273-l0010] [10.5pt] You might be thinking that we could just pick the model with the lowest inertia,
[p0273-l0011] [10.5pt] right? Unfortunately, it is not that simple. The inertia for k=3 is 653.2, which is much
[p0273-l0012] [10.5pt] higher than for k=5 (which was 211.6), but with k=8, the inertia is just 119.1. The
[p0273-l0013] [10.5pt] inertia is not a good performance metric when trying to choose k since it keeps get‐
[p0273-l0014] [10.5pt] ting lower as we increase k. Indeed, the more clusters there are, the closer each
[p0273-l0015] [10.5pt] instance will be to its closest centroid, and therefore the lower the inertia will be. Let’s
[p0273-l0016] [10.5pt] plot the inertia as a function of k (see Figure 9-8):
[p0273-l0017] [9.0pt] Clustering
[p0273-l0018] [9.0pt] |
[p0273-l0019] [9.0pt] 247

=== PDF page 274 / printed label 248 ===
[p0274-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 9-8. Selecting the number of clusters k using the “elbow rule”
[p0274-l0002] [10.5pt] As you can see, the inertia drops very quickly as we increase k up to 4, but then it
[p0274-l0003] [10.5pt] decreases much more slowly as we keep increasing k. This curve has roughly the
[p0274-l0004] [10.5pt] shape of an arm, and there is an “elbow” at k=4 so if we did not know better, it would
[p0274-l0005] [10.5pt] be a good choice: any lower value would be dramatic, while any higher value would
[p0274-l0006] [10.5pt] not help much, and we might just be splitting perfectly good clusters in half for no
[p0274-l0007] [10.5pt] good reason.
[p0274-l0008] [10.5pt] This technique for choosing the best value for the number of clusters is rather coarse.
[p0274-l0009] [10.5pt] A more precise approach (but also more computationally expensive) is to use the sil‐
[p0274-l0010] [10.5pt] houette score, which is the mean silhouette coefficient over all the instances. An instan‐
[p0274-l0011] [10.5pt] ce’s silhouette coefficient is equal to (b – a) / max(a, b) where a is the mean distance
[p0274-l0012] [10.5pt] to the other instances in the same cluster (it is the mean intra-cluster distance), and b
[p0274-l0013] [10.5pt] is the mean nearest-cluster distance, that is the mean distance to the instances of the
[p0274-l0014] [10.5pt] next closest cluster (defined as the one that minimizes b, excluding the instance’s own
[p0274-l0015] [10.5pt] cluster). The silhouette coefficient can vary between -1 and +1: a coefficient close to
[p0274-l0016] [10.5pt] +1 means that the instance is well inside its own cluster and far from other clusters,
[p0274-l0017] [10.5pt] while a coefficient close to 0 means that it is close to a cluster boundary, and finally a
[p0274-l0018] [10.5pt] coefficient close to -1 means that the instance may have been assigned to the wrong
[p0274-l0019] [10.5pt] cluster. To compute the silhouette score, you can use Scikit-Learn’s silhou
[p0274-l0020] [10.5pt] ette_score() function, giving it all the instances in the dataset, and the labels they
[p0274-l0021] [10.5pt] were assigned:
[p0274-l0022] [8.5pt] >>> from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score
[p0274-l0023] [8.5pt] >>> silhouette_score(X, kmeans.labels_)
[p0274-l0024] [8.5pt] 0.655517642572828
[p0274-l0025] [10.5pt] Let’s compare the silhouette scores for different numbers of clusters (see Figure 9-9):
[p0274-l0026] [9.0pt] 248
[p0274-l0027] [9.0pt] |
[p0274-l0028] [9.0pt] Chapter 9: Unsupervised Learning Techniques

=== PDF page 275 / printed label 249 ===
[p0275-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 9-9. Selecting the number of clusters k using the silhouette score
[p0275-l0002] [10.5pt] As you can see, this visualization is much richer than the previous one: in particular,
[p0275-l0003] [10.5pt] although it confirms that k=4 is a very good choice, it also underlines the fact that
[p0275-l0004] [10.5pt] k=5 is quite good as well, and much better than k=6 or 7. This was not visible when
[p0275-l0005] [10.5pt] comparing inertias.
[p0275-l0006] [10.5pt] An even more informative visualization is obtained when you plot every instance’s
[p0275-l0007] [10.5pt] silhouette coefficient, sorted by the cluster they are assigned to and by the value of the
[p0275-l0008] [10.5pt] coefficient. This is called a silhouette diagram (see Figure 9-10):
[p0275-l0009] [10.5pt] Figure 9-10. Silouhette analysis: comparing the silhouette diagrams for various values of
[p0275-l0010] [10.5pt] k
[p0275-l0011] [10.5pt] The vertical dashed lines represent the silhouette score for each number of clusters.
[p0275-l0012] [10.5pt] When most of the instances in a cluster have a lower coefficient than this score (i.e., if
[p0275-l0013] [10.5pt] many of the instances stop short of the dashed line, ending to the left of it), then the
[p0275-l0014] [10.5pt] cluster is rather bad since this means its instances are much too close to other clus‐
[p0275-l0015] [9.0pt] Clustering
[p0275-l0016] [9.0pt] |
[p0275-l0017] [9.0pt] 249

=== PDF page 276 / printed label 250 ===
[p0276-l0001] [10.5pt] ters. We can see that when k=3 and when k=6, we get bad clusters. But when k=4 or
[p0276-l0002] [10.5pt] k=5, the clusters look pretty good – most instances extend beyond the dashed line, to
[p0276-l0003] [10.5pt] the right and closer to 1.0. When k=4, the cluster at index 1 (the third from the top),
[p0276-l0004] [10.5pt] is rather big, while when k=5, all clusters have similar sizes, so even though the over‐
[p0276-l0005] [10.5pt] all silhouette score from k=4 is slightly greater than for k=5, it seems like a good idea
[p0276-l0006] [10.5pt] to use k=5 to get clusters of similar sizes.
[p0276-l0007] [15.77pt] Limits of K-Means
[p0276-l0008] [10.5pt] Despite its many merits, most notably being fast and scalable, K-Means is not perfect.
[p0276-l0009] [10.5pt] As we saw, it is necessary to run the algorithm several times to avoid sub-optimal sol‐
[p0276-l0010] [10.5pt] utions, plus you need to specify the number of clusters, which can be quite a hassle.
[p0276-l0011] [10.5pt] Moreover, K-Means does not behave very well when the clusters have varying sizes,
[p0276-l0012] [10.5pt] different densities, or non-spherical shapes. For example, Figure 9-11 shows how K-
[p0276-l0013] [10.5pt] Means clusters a dataset containing three ellipsoidal clusters of different dimensions,
[p0276-l0014] [10.5pt] densities and orientations:
[p0276-l0015] [10.5pt] Figure 9-11. K-Means fails to cluster these ellipsoidal blobs properly
[p0276-l0016] [10.5pt] As you can see, neither of these solutions are any good. The solution on the left is
[p0276-l0017] [10.5pt] better, but it still chops off 25% of the middle cluster and assigns it to the cluster on
[p0276-l0018] [10.5pt] the right. The solution on the right is just terrible, even though its inertia is lower. So
[p0276-l0019] [10.5pt] depending on the data, different clustering algorithms may perform better. For exam‐
[p0276-l0020] [10.5pt] ple, on these types of elliptical clusters, Gaussian mixture models work great.
[p0276-l0021] [9.6pt] It is important to scale the input features before you run K-Means,
[p0276-l0022] [9.6pt] or else the clusters may be very stretched, and K-Means will per‐
[p0276-l0023] [9.6pt] form poorly. Scaling the features does not guarantee that all the
[p0276-l0024] [9.6pt] clusters will be nice and spherical, but it generally improves things.
[p0276-l0025] [10.5pt] Now let’s look at a few ways we can benefit from clustering. We will use K-Means, but
[p0276-l0026] [10.5pt] feel free to experiment with other clustering algorithms.

[p0277-l0001] [15.77pt] Using clustering for image segmentation
[p0277-l0002] [10.5pt] Image segmentation is the task of partitioning an image into multiple segments. In
[p0277-l0003] [10.5pt] semantic segmentation, all pixels that are part of the same object type get assigned to
[p0277-l0004] [10.5pt] the same segment. For example, in a self-driving car’s vision system, all pixels that are
[p0277-l0005] [10.5pt] part of a pedestrian’s image might be assigned to the “pedestrian” segment (there
[p0277-l0006] [10.5pt] would just be one segment containing all the pedestrians). In instance segmentation,
[p0277-l0007] [10.5pt] all pixels that are part of the same individual object are assigned to the same segment.
[p0277-l0008] [10.5pt] In this case there would be a different segment for each pedestrian. The state of the
[p0277-l0009] [10.5pt] art in semantic or instance segmentation today is achieved using complex architec‐
[p0277-l0010] [10.5pt] tures based on convolutional neural networks (see Chapter 14). Here, we are going to
[p0277-l0011] [10.5pt] do something much simpler: color segmentation. We will simply assign pixels to the
[p0277-l0012] [10.5pt] same segment if they have a similar color. In some applications, this may be sufficient,
[p0277-l0013] [10.5pt] for example if you want to analyze satellite images to measure how much total forest
[p0277-l0014] [10.5pt] area there is in a region, color segmentation may be just fine.
[p0277-l0015] [10.5pt] First, let’s load the image (see the upper left image in Figure 9-12) using Matplotlib’s
[p0277-l0016] [10.5pt] imread() function:
[p0277-l0017] [8.5pt] >>> from matplotlib.image import imread  # you could also use `imageio.imread()`
[p0277-l0018] [8.5pt] >>> image = imread(os.path.join("images","clustering","ladybug.png"))
[p0277-l0019] [8.5pt] >>> image.shape
[p0277-l0020] [8.5pt] (533, 800, 3)
[p0277-l0021] [10.5pt] The image is represented as a 3D array: the first dimension’s size is the height, the
[p0277-l0022] [10.5pt] second is the width, and the third is the number of color channels, in this case red,
[p0277-l0023] [10.5pt] green and blue (RGB). In other words, for each pixel there is a 3D vector containing
[p0277-l0024] [10.5pt] the intensities of red, green and blue, each between 0.0 and 1.0 (or between 0 and 255
[p0277-l0025] [10.5pt] if you use imageio.imread()). Some images may have less channels, such as gray‐
[p0277-l0026] [10.5pt] scale images (one channel), or more channels, such as images with an additional
[p0277-l0027] [10.5pt] alpha channel for transparency, or satellite images which often contain channels for
[p0277-l0028] [10.5pt] many light frequencies (e.g., infrared). The following code reshapes the array to get a
[p0277-l0029] [10.5pt] long list of RGB colors, then it clusters these colors using K-Means. For example, it
[p0277-l0030] [10.5pt] may identify a color cluster for all shades of green. Next, for each color (e.g., dark
[p0277-l0031] [10.5pt] green), it looks for the mean color of the pixel’s color cluster. For example, all shades
[p0277-l0032] [10.5pt] of green may be replaced with the same light green color (assuming the mean color of
[p0277-l0033] [10.5pt] the green cluster is light green). Finally it reshapes this long list of colors to get the
[p0277-l0034] [10.5pt] same shape as the original image. And we’re done!
[p0277-l0035] [8.5pt] X = image.reshape(-1, 3)
[p0277-l0036] [8.5pt] kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=8).fit(X)
[p0277-l0037] [8.5pt] segmented_img = kmeans.cluster_centers_[kmeans.labels_]
[p0277-l0038] [8.5pt] segmented_img = segmented_img.reshape(image.shape)
[p0277-l0039] [10.5pt] This outputs the image shown in the upper right of Figure 9-12. You can experiment
[p0277-l0040] [10.5pt] with various numbers of clusters, as shown in the figure. When you use less than 8
[p0277-l0041] [10.5pt] clusters, notice that the ladybug’s flashy red color fails to get a cluster of its own: it
[p0277-l0042] [9.0pt] Clustering
[p0277-l0043] [9.0pt] |
[p0277-l0044] [9.0pt] 251

=== PDF page 278 / printed label 252 ===
[p0278-l0001] [10.5pt] gets merged with colors from the environment. This is due to the fact that the lady‐
[p0278-l0002] [10.5pt] bug is quite small, much smaller than the rest of the image, so even though its color is
[p0278-l0003] [10.5pt] flashy, K-Means fails to dedicate a cluster to it: as mentioned earlier, K-Means prefers
[p0278-l0004] [10.5pt] clusters of similar sizes.
[p0278-l0005] [10.5pt] Figure 9-12. Image segmentation using K-Means with various numbers of color clusters

[p0278-l0008] [15.77pt] Using Clustering for Preprocessing
[p0278-l0009] [10.5pt] Clustering can be an efficient approach to dimensionality reduction, in particular as a
[p0278-l0010] [10.5pt] preprocessing step before a supervised learning algorithm. For example, let’s tackle
[p0278-l0011] [10.5pt] the digits dataset which is a simple MNIST-like dataset containing 1,797 grayscale 8×8
[p0278-l0012] [10.5pt] images representing digits 0 to 9. First, let’s load the dataset:
[p0278-l0013] [8.5pt] from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
[p0278-l0014] [8.5pt] X_digits, y_digits = load_digits(return_X_y=True)
[p0278-l0015] [10.5pt] Now, let’s split it into a training set and a test set:
[p0278-l0016] [8.5pt] from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
[p0278-l0017] [8.5pt] X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X_digits, y_digits)
[p0278-l0018] [10.5pt] Next, let’s fit a Logistic Regression model:
[p0278-l0019] [8.5pt] from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
[p0278-l0020] [8.5pt] log_reg = LogisticRegression(random_state=42)
[p0278-l0021] [8.5pt] log_reg.fit(X_train, y_train)
[p0278-l0022] [10.5pt] Let’s evaluate its accuracy on the test set:
[p0278-l0023] [8.5pt] >>> log_reg.score(X_test, y_test)
[p0278-l0024] [8.5pt] 0.9666666666666667
[p0278-l0025] [9.0pt] 252
[p0278-l0026] [9.0pt] |
[p0278-l0027] [9.0pt] Chapter 9: Unsupervised Learning Techniques

[p0279-l0001] [10.5pt] Okay, that’s our baseline: 96.7% accuracy. Let’s see if we can do better by using K-
[p0279-l0002] [10.5pt] Means as a preprocessing step. We will create a pipeline that will first cluster the
[p0279-l0003] [10.5pt] training set into 50 clusters and replace the images with their distances to these 50
[p0279-l0004] [10.5pt] clusters, then apply a logistic regression model.
[p0279-l0005] [9.6pt] Although it is tempting to define the number of clusters to 10,
[p0279-l0006] [9.6pt] since there are 10 different digits, it is unlikely to perform well,
[p0279-l0007] [9.6pt] because there are several different ways to write each digit.
[p0279-l0008] [8.5pt] from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
[p0279-l0009] [8.5pt] pipeline = Pipeline([
[p0279-l0010] [8.5pt]     ("kmeans", KMeans(n_clusters=50)),
[p0279-l0011] [8.5pt]     ("log_reg", LogisticRegression()),
[p0279-l0012] [8.5pt] ])
[p0279-l0013] [8.5pt] pipeline.fit(X_train, y_train)
[p0279-l0014] [10.5pt] Now let’s evaluate this classification pipeline:
[p0279-l0015] [8.5pt] >>> pipeline.score(X_test, y_test)
[p0279-l0016] [8.5pt] 0.9822222222222222
[p0279-l0017] [10.5pt] How about that? We almost divided the error rate by a factor of 2!
[p0279-l0018] [10.5pt] But we chose the number of clusters k completely arbitrarily, we can surely do better.
[p0279-l0019] [10.5pt] Since K-Means is just a preprocessing step in a classification pipeline, finding a good
[p0279-l0020] [10.5pt] value for k is much simpler than earlier: there’s no need to perform silhouette analysis
[p0279-l0021] [10.5pt] or minimize the inertia, the best value of k is simply the one that results in the best
[p0279-l0022] [10.5pt] classification performance during cross-validation. Let’s use GridSearchCV to find the
[p0279-l0023] [10.5pt] optimal number of clusters:
[p0279-l0024] [8.5pt] from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV
[p0279-l0025] [8.5pt] param_grid = dict(kmeans__n_clusters=range(2, 100))
[p0279-l0026] [8.5pt] grid_clf = GridSearchCV(pipeline, param_grid, cv=3, verbose=2)
[p0279-l0027] [8.5pt] grid_clf.fit(X_train, y_train)
[p0279-l0028] [10.5pt] Let’s look at best value for k, and the performance of the resulting pipeline:
[p0279-l0029] [8.5pt] >>> grid_clf.best_params_
[p0279-l0030] [8.5pt] {'kmeans__n_clusters': 90}
[p0279-l0031] [8.5pt] >>> grid_clf.score(X_test, y_test)
[p0279-l0032] [8.5pt] 0.9844444444444445
[p0279-l0033] [10.5pt] With k=90 clusters, we get a small accuracy boost, reaching 98.4% accuracy on the
[p0279-l0034] [10.5pt] test set. Cool!

[p0280-l0001] [15.77pt] Using Clustering for Semi-Supervised Learning
[p0280-l0002] [10.5pt] Another use case for clustering is in semi-supervised learning, when we have plenty
[p0280-l0003] [10.5pt] of unlabeled instances and very few labeled instances. Let’s train a logistic regression
[p0280-l0004] [10.5pt] model on a sample of 50 labeled instances from the digits dataset:
[p0280-l0005] [8.5pt] n_labeled = 50
[p0280-l0006] [8.5pt] log_reg = LogisticRegression()
[p0280-l0007] [8.5pt] log_reg.fit(X_train[:n_labeled], y_train[:n_labeled])
[p0280-l0008] [10.5pt] What is the performance of this model on the test set?
[p0280-l0009] [8.5pt] >>> log_reg.score(X_test, y_test)
[p0280-l0010] [8.5pt] 0.8266666666666667
[p0280-l0011] [10.5pt] The accuracy is just 82.7%: it should come as no surprise that this is much lower than
[p0280-l0012] [10.5pt] earlier, when we trained the model on the full training set. Let’s see how we can do
[p0280-l0013] [10.5pt] better. First, let’s cluster the training set into 50 clusters, then for each cluster let’s find
[p0280-l0014] [10.5pt] the image closest to the centroid. We will call these images the representative images:
[p0280-l0015] [8.5pt] k = 50
[p0280-l0016] [8.5pt] kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=k)
[p0280-l0017] [8.5pt] X_digits_dist = kmeans.fit_transform(X_train)
[p0280-l0018] [8.5pt] representative_digit_idx = np.argmin(X_digits_dist, axis=0)
[p0280-l0019] [8.5pt] X_representative_digits = X_train[representative_digit_idx]
[p0280-l0020] [10.5pt] Figure 9-13 shows these 50 representative images:
[p0280-l0021] [10.5pt] Figure 9-13. Fifty representative digit images (one per cluster)
[p0280-l0022] [10.5pt] Now let’s look at each image and manually label it:
[p0280-l0023] [8.5pt] y_representative_digits = np.array([4, 8, 0, 6, 8, 3, ..., 7, 6, 2, 3, 1, 1])
[p0280-l0024] [10.5pt] Now we have a dataset with just 50 labeled instances, but instead of being completely
[p0280-l0025] [10.5pt] random instances, each of them is a representative image of its cluster. Let’s see if the
[p0280-l0026] [10.5pt] performance is any better:
[p0280-l0027] [8.5pt] >>> log_reg = LogisticRegression()
[p0280-l0028] [8.5pt] >>> log_reg.fit(X_representative_digits, y_representative_digits)
[p0280-l0029] [8.5pt] >>> log_reg.score(X_test, y_test)
[p0280-l0030] [8.5pt] 0.9244444444444444
[p0280-l0031] [10.5pt] Wow! We jumped from 82.7% accuracy to 92.4%, although we are still only training
[p0280-l0032] [10.5pt] the model on 50 instances. Since it is often costly and painful to label instances, espe‐
[p0280-l0033] [9.0pt] 254
[p0280-l0034] [9.0pt] |
[p0280-l0035] [9.0pt] Chapter 9: Unsupervised Learning Techniques

=== PDF page 281 / printed label 255 ===
[p0281-l0001] [10.5pt] cially when it has to be done manually by experts, it is a good idea to label representa‐
[p0281-l0002] [10.5pt] tive instances rather than just random instances.
[p0281-l0003] [10.5pt] But perhaps we can go one step further: what if we propagated the labels to all the
[p0281-l0004] [10.5pt] other instances in the same cluster? This is called label propagation:
[p0281-l0005] [8.5pt] y_train_propagated = np.empty(len(X_train), dtype=np.int32)
[p0281-l0006] [8.5pt] for i in range(k):
[p0281-l0007] [8.5pt]     y_train_propagated[kmeans.labels_==i] = y_representative_digits[i]
[p0281-l0008] [10.5pt] Now let’s train the model again and look at its performance:
[p0281-l0009] [8.5pt] >>> log_reg = LogisticRegression()
[p0281-l0010] [8.5pt] >>> log_reg.fit(X_train, y_train_propagated)
[p0281-l0011] [8.5pt] >>> log_reg.score(X_test, y_test)
[p0281-l0012] [8.5pt] 0.9288888888888889
[p0281-l0013] [10.5pt] We got a tiny little accuracy boost. Better than nothing, but not astounding. The
[p0281-l0014] [10.5pt] problem is that we propagated each representative instance’s label to all the instances
[p0281-l0015] [10.5pt] in the same cluster, including the instances located close to the cluster boundaries,
[p0281-l0016] [10.5pt] which are more likely to be mislabeled. Let’s see what happens if we only propagate
[p0281-l0017] [10.5pt] the labels to the 20% of the instances that are closest to the centroids:
[p0281-l0018] [8.5pt] percentile_closest = 20
[p0281-l0019] [8.5pt] X_cluster_dist = X_digits_dist[np.arange(len(X_train)), kmeans.labels_]
[p0281-l0020] [8.5pt] for i in range(k):
[p0281-l0021] [8.5pt]     in_cluster = (kmeans.labels_ == i)
[p0281-l0022] [8.5pt]     cluster_dist = X_cluster_dist[in_cluster]
[p0281-l0023] [8.5pt]     cutoff_distance = np.percentile(cluster_dist, percentile_closest)
[p0281-l0024] [8.5pt]     above_cutoff = (X_cluster_dist > cutoff_distance)
[p0281-l0025] [8.5pt]     X_cluster_dist[in_cluster & above_cutoff] = -1
[p0281-l0026] [8.5pt] partially_propagated = (X_cluster_dist != -1)
[p0281-l0027] [8.5pt] X_train_partially_propagated = X_train[partially_propagated]
[p0281-l0028] [8.5pt] y_train_partially_propagated = y_train_propagated[partially_propagated]
[p0281-l0029] [10.5pt] Now let’s train the model again on this partially propagated dataset:
[p0281-l0030] [8.5pt] >>> log_reg = LogisticRegression()
[p0281-l0031] [8.5pt] >>> log_reg.fit(X_train_partially_propagated, y_train_partially_propagated)
[p0281-l0032] [8.5pt] >>> log_reg.score(X_test, y_test)
[p0281-l0033] [8.5pt] 0.9422222222222222
[p0281-l0034] [10.5pt] Nice! With just 50 labeled instances (only 5 examples per class on average!), we got
[p0281-l0035] [10.5pt] 94.2% performance, which is pretty close to the performance of logistic regression on
[p0281-l0036] [10.5pt] the fully labeled digits dataset (which was 96.7%). This is because the propagated
[p0281-l0037] [10.5pt] labels are actually pretty good, their accuracy is very close to 99%:
[p0281-l0038] [9.0pt] Clustering
[p0281-l0039] [9.0pt] |
[p0281-l0040] [9.0pt] 255

[p0282-l0001] [8.5pt] >>> np.mean(y_train_partially_propagated == y_train[partially_propagated])

[p0282-l0003] [15.0pt] Active Learning
[p0282-l0004] [10.0pt] To continue improving your model and your training set, the next step could be to do
[p0282-l0005] [10.0pt] a few rounds of active learning: this is when a human expert interacts with the learn‐
[p0282-l0006] [10.0pt] ing algorithm, providing labels when the algorithm needs them. There are many dif‐
[p0282-l0007] [10.0pt] ferent strategies for active learning, but one of the most common ones is called
[p0282-l0008] [10.0pt] uncertainty sampling:
[p0282-l0009] [10.0pt] • The model is trained on the labeled instances gathered so far, and this model is
[p0282-l0010] [10.0pt] used to make predictions on all the unlabeled instances.
[p0282-l0011] [10.0pt] • The instances for which the model is most uncertain (i.e., when its estimated
[p0282-l0012] [10.0pt] probability is lowest) must be labeled by the expert.
[p0282-l0013] [10.0pt] • Then you just iterate this process again and again, until the performance
[p0282-l0014] [10.0pt] improvement stops being worth the labeling effort.
[p0282-l0015] [10.0pt] Other strategies include labeling the instances that would result in the largest model
[p0282-l0016] [10.0pt] change, or the largest drop in the model’s validation error, or the instances that differ‐
[p0282-l0017] [10.0pt] ent models disagree on (e.g., an SVM, a Random Forest, and so on).
[p0282-l0018] [10.5pt] Before we move on to Gaussian mixture models, let’s take a look at DBSCAN,
[p0282-l0019] [10.5pt] another popular clustering algorithm that illustrates a very different approach based
[p0282-l0020] [10.5pt] on local density estimation. This approach allows the algorithm to identify clusters of
[p0282-l0021] [10.5pt] arbitrary shapes.
[p0282-l0022] [15.77pt] DBSCAN
[p0282-l0023] [10.5pt] This algorithm defines clusters as continuous regions of high density. It is actually
[p0282-l0024] [10.5pt] quite simple:
[p0282-l0025] [10.5pt] • For each instance, the algorithm counts how many instances are located within a
[p0282-l0026] [10.5pt] small distance ε (epsilon) from it. This region is called the instance’s ε-
[p0282-l0027] [10.5pt] neighborhood.
[p0282-l0028] [10.5pt] • If an instance has at least min_samples instances in its ε-neighborhood (includ‐
[p0282-l0029] [10.5pt] ing itself), then it is considered a core instance. In other words, core instances are
[p0282-l0030] [10.5pt] those that are located in dense regions.
[p0282-l0031] [10.5pt] • All instances in the neighborhood of a core instance belong to the same cluster.
[p0282-l0032] [10.5pt] This may include other core instances, therefore a long sequence of neighboring
[p0282-l0033] [10.5pt] core instances forms a single cluster.
[p0282-l0034] [9.0pt] 256
[p0282-l0035] [9.0pt] |
[p0282-l0036] [9.0pt] Chapter 9: Unsupervised Learning Techniques

=== PDF page 283 / printed label 257 ===
[p0283-l0001] [10.5pt] • Any instance that is not a core instance and does not have one in its neighbor‐
[p0283-l0002] [10.5pt] hood is considered an anomaly.
[p0283-l0003] [10.5pt] This algorithm works well if all the clusters are dense enough, and they are well sepa‐
[p0283-l0004] [10.5pt] rated by low-density regions. The DBSCAN class in Scikit-Learn is as simple to use as
[p0283-l0005] [10.5pt] you might expect. Let’s test it on the moons dataset, introduced in Chapter 5:
[p0283-l0006] [8.5pt] from sklearn.cluster import DBSCAN
[p0283-l0007] [8.5pt] from sklearn.datasets import make_moons
[p0283-l0008] [8.5pt] X, y = make_moons(n_samples=1000, noise=0.05)
[p0283-l0009] [8.5pt] dbscan = DBSCAN(eps=0.05, min_samples=5)
[p0283-l0010] [8.5pt] dbscan.fit(X)
[p0283-l0011] [10.5pt] The labels of all the instances are now available in the labels_ instance variable:
[p0283-l0012] [8.5pt] >>> dbscan.labels_
[p0283-l0013] [8.5pt] array([ 0,  2, -1, -1,  1,  0,  0,  0, ...,  3,  2,  3,  3,  4,  2,  6,  3])
[p0283-l0014] [10.5pt] Notice that some instances have a cluster index equal to -1: this means that they are
[p0283-l0015] [10.5pt] considered as anomalies by the algorithm. The indices of the core instances are avail‐
[p0283-l0016] [10.5pt] able in the core_sample_indices_ instance variable, and the core instances them‐
[p0283-l0017] [10.5pt] selves are available in the components_ instance variable:
[p0283-l0018] [8.5pt] >>> len(dbscan.core_sample_indices_)
[p0283-l0019] [8.5pt] 808
[p0283-l0020] [8.5pt] >>> dbscan.core_sample_indices_
[p0283-l0021] [8.5pt] array([ 0,  4,  5,  6,  7,  8, 10, 11, ..., 992, 993, 995, 997, 998, 999])
[p0283-l0022] [8.5pt] >>> dbscan.components_
[p0283-l0023] [8.5pt] array([[-0.02137124,  0.40618608],
[p0283-l0024] [8.5pt]        [-0.84192557,  0.53058695],
[p0283-l0025] [8.5pt]                   ...
[p0283-l0026] [8.5pt]        [-0.94355873,  0.3278936 ],
[p0283-l0027] [8.5pt]        [ 0.79419406,  0.60777171]])
[p0283-l0028] [10.5pt] This clustering is represented in the left plot of Figure 9-14. As you can see, it identi‐
[p0283-l0029] [10.5pt] fied quite a lot of anomalies, plus 7 different clusters. How disappointing! Fortunately,
[p0283-l0030] [10.5pt] if we widen each instance’s neighborhood by increasing eps to 0.2, we get the cluster‐
[p0283-l0031] [10.5pt] ing on the right, which looks perfect. Let’s continue with this model.
[p0283-l0032] [10.5pt] Figure 9-14. DBSCAN clustering using two different neighborhood radiuses

[p0284-l0001] [10.5pt] Somewhat surprisingly, the DBSCAN class does not have a predict() method,
[p0284-l0002] [10.5pt] although it has a fit_predict() method. In other words, it cannot predict which
[p0284-l0003] [10.5pt] cluster a new instance belongs to. The rationale for this decision is that several classi‐
[p0284-l0004] [10.5pt] fication algorithms could make sense here, and it is easy enough to train one, for
[p0284-l0005] [10.5pt] example a KNeighborsClassifier:
[p0284-l0006] [8.5pt] from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
[p0284-l0007] [8.5pt] knn = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=50)
[p0284-l0008] [8.5pt] knn.fit(dbscan.components_, dbscan.labels_[dbscan.core_sample_indices_])
[p0284-l0009] [10.5pt] Now, given a few new instances, we can predict which cluster they most likely belong
[p0284-l0010] [10.5pt] to, and even estimate a probability for each cluster. Note that we only trained them on
[p0284-l0011] [10.5pt] the core instances, but we could also have chosen to train them on all the instances,
[p0284-l0012] [10.5pt] or all but the anomalies: this choice depends on the final task.
[p0284-l0013] [8.5pt] >>> X_new = np.array([[-0.5, 0], [0, 0.5], [1, -0.1], [2, 1]])
[p0284-l0014] [8.5pt] >>> knn.predict(X_new)
[p0284-l0015] [8.5pt] array([1, 0, 1, 0])
[p0284-l0016] [8.5pt] >>> knn.predict_proba(X_new)
[p0284-l0017] [8.5pt] array([[0.18, 0.82],
[p0284-l0018] [8.5pt]        [1.  , 0.  ],
[p0284-l0019] [8.5pt]        [0.12, 0.88],
[p0284-l0020] [8.5pt]        [1.  , 0.  ]])
[p0284-l0021] [10.5pt] The decision boundary is represented on Figure 9-15 (the crosses represent the 4
[p0284-l0022] [10.5pt] instances in X_new). Notice that since there is no anomaly in the KNN’s training set,
[p0284-l0023] [10.5pt] the classifier always chooses a cluster, even when that cluster is far away. However, it
[p0284-l0024] [10.5pt] is fairly straightforward to introduce a maximum distance, in which case the two
[p0284-l0025] [10.5pt] instances that are far away from both clusters are classified as anomalies. To do this,
[p0284-l0026] [10.5pt] we can use the kneighbors() method of the KNeighborsClassifier: given a set of
[p0284-l0027] [10.5pt] instances, it returns the distances and the indices of the k nearest neighbors in the
[p0284-l0028] [10.5pt] training set (two matrices, each with k columns):
[p0284-l0029] [8.5pt] >>> y_dist, y_pred_idx = knn.kneighbors(X_new, n_neighbors=1)
[p0284-l0030] [8.5pt] >>> y_pred = dbscan.labels_[dbscan.core_sample_indices_][y_pred_idx]
[p0284-l0031] [8.5pt] >>> y_pred[y_dist > 0.2] = -1
[p0284-l0032] [8.5pt] >>> y_pred.ravel()
[p0284-l0033] [8.5pt] array([-1,  0,  1, -1])

[p0285-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 9-15. cluster_classification_diagram
[p0285-l0002] [10.5pt] In short, DBSCAN is a very simple yet powerful algorithm, capable of identifying any
[p0285-l0003] [10.5pt] number of clusters, of any shape, it is robust to outliers, and it has just two hyper‐
[p0285-l0004] [10.5pt] parameters (eps and min_samples). However, if the density varies significantly across
[p0285-l0005] [10.5pt] the clusters, it can be impossible for it to capture all the clusters properly. Moreover,
[p0285-l0006] [10.5pt] its computational complexity is roughly O(m log m), making it pretty close to linear
[p0285-l0007] [10.5pt] with regards to the number of instances. However, Scikit-Learn’s implementation can
[p0285-l0008] [10.5pt] require up to O(m2) memory if eps is large.
[p0285-l0009] [15.77pt] Other Clustering Algorithms
[p0285-l0010] [10.5pt] Scikit-Learn implements several more clustering algorithms that you should take a
[p0285-l0011] [10.5pt] look at. We cannot cover them all in detail here, but here is a brief overview:
[p0285-l0012] [10.5pt] • Agglomerative clustering: a hierarchy of clusters is built from the bottom up.
[p0285-l0013] [10.5pt] Think of many tiny bubbles floating on water and gradually attaching to each
[p0285-l0014] [10.5pt] other until there’s just one big group of bubbles. Similarly, at each iteration
[p0285-l0015] [10.5pt] agglomerative clustering connects the nearest pair of clusters (starting with indi‐
[p0285-l0016] [10.5pt] vidual instances). If you draw a tree with a branch for every pair of clusters that
[p0285-l0017] [10.5pt] merged, you get a binary tree of clusters, where the leaves are the individual
[p0285-l0018] [10.5pt] instances. This approach scales very well to large numbers of instances or clus‐
[p0285-l0019] [10.5pt] ters, it can capture clusters of various shapes, it produces a flexible and informa‐
[p0285-l0020] [10.5pt] tive cluster tree instead of forcing you to choose a particular cluster scale, and it
[p0285-l0021] [10.5pt] can be used with any pairwise distance. It can scale nicely to large numbers of
[p0285-l0022] [10.5pt] instances if you provide a connectivity matrix. This is a sparse m by m matrix
[p0285-l0023] [10.5pt] that indicates which pairs of instances are neighbors (e.g., returned by
[p0285-l0024] [10.5pt] sklearn.neighbors.kneighbors_graph()). Without a connectivity matrix, the
[p0285-l0025] [10.5pt] algorithm does not scale well to large datasets.
[p0285-l0026] [10.5pt] • Birch: this algorithm was designed specifically for very large datasets, and it can
[p0285-l0027] [10.5pt] be faster than batch K-Means, with similar results, as long as the number of fea‐
[p0285-l0028] [10.5pt] tures is not too large (<20). It builds a tree structure during training containing
[p0285-l0029] [9.0pt] Clustering
[p0285-l0030] [9.0pt] |
[p0285-l0031] [9.0pt] 259

=== PDF page 286 / printed label 260 ===
[p0286-l0001] [10.5pt] just enough information to quickly assign each new instance to a cluster, without
[p0286-l0002] [10.5pt] having to store all the instances in the tree: this allows it to use limited memory,
[p0286-l0003] [10.5pt] while handle huge datasets.
[p0286-l0004] [10.5pt] • Mean-shift: this algorithm starts by placing a circle centered on each instance,
[p0286-l0005] [10.5pt] then for each circle it computes the mean of all the instances located within it,
[p0286-l0006] [10.5pt] and it shifts the circle so that it is centered on the mean. Next, it iterates this
[p0286-l0007] [10.5pt] mean-shift step until all the circles stop moving (i.e., until each of them is cen‐
[p0286-l0008] [10.5pt] tered on the mean of the instances it contains). This algorithm shifts the circles
[p0286-l0009] [10.5pt] in the direction of higher density, until each of them has found a local density
[p0286-l0010] [10.5pt] maximum. Finally, all the instances whose circles have settled in the same place
[p0286-l0011] [10.5pt] (or close enough) are assigned to the same cluster. This has some of the same fea‐
[p0286-l0012] [10.5pt] tures as DBSCAN, in particular it can find any number of clusters of any shape, it
[p0286-l0013] [10.5pt] has just one hyperparameter (the radius of the circles, called the bandwidth) and
[p0286-l0014] [10.5pt] it relies on local density estimation. However, it tends to chop clusters into pieces
[p0286-l0015] [10.5pt] when they have internal density variations. Unfortunately, its computational
[p0286-l0016] [10.5pt] complexity is O(m2), so it is not suited for large datasets.
[p0286-l0017] [10.5pt] • Affinity propagation: this algorithm uses a voting system, where instances vote for
[p0286-l0018] [10.5pt] similar instances to be their representatives, and once the algorithm converges,
[p0286-l0019] [10.5pt] each representative and its voters form a cluster. This algorithm can detect any
[p0286-l0020] [10.5pt] number of clusters of different sizes. Unfortunately, this algorithm has a compu‐
[p0286-l0021] [10.5pt] tational complexity of O(m2), so it is not suited for large datasets.
[p0286-l0022] [10.5pt] • Spectral clustering: this algorithm takes a similarity matrix between the instances
[p0286-l0023] [10.5pt] and creates a low-dimensional embedding from it (i.e., it reduces its dimension‐
[p0286-l0024] [10.5pt] ality), then it uses another clustering algorithm in this low-dimensional space
[p0286-l0025] [10.5pt] (Scikit-Learn’s implementation uses K-Means). Spectral clustering can capture
[p0286-l0026] [10.5pt] complex cluster structures, and it can also be used to cut graphs (e.g., to identify
[p0286-l0027] [10.5pt] clusters of friends on a social network), however it does not scale well to large
[p0286-l0028] [10.5pt] number of instances, and it does not behave well when the clusters have very dif‐
[p0286-l0029] [10.5pt] ferent sizes.
[p0286-l0030] [10.5pt] Now let’s dive into Gaussian mixture models, which can be used for density estima‐
[p0286-l0031] [10.5pt] tion, clustering and anomaly detection.
[p0286-l0032] [18.92pt] Gaussian Mixtures
[p0286-l0033] [10.5pt] A Gaussian mixture model (GMM) is a probabilistic model that assumes that the
[p0286-l0034] [10.5pt] instances were generated from a mixture of several Gaussian distributions whose
[p0286-l0035] [10.5pt] parameters are unknown. All the instances generated from a single Gaussian distri‐
[p0286-l0036] [10.5pt] bution form a cluster that typically looks like an ellipsoid. Each cluster can have a dif‐
[p0286-l0037] [10.5pt] ferent ellipsoidal shape, size, density and orientation, just like in Figure 9-11. When
[p0286-l0038] [10.5pt] you observe an instance, you know it was generated from one of the Gaussian distri‐
[p0286-l0039] [9.0pt] 260
[p0286-l0040] [9.0pt] |
[p0286-l0041] [9.0pt] Chapter 9: Unsupervised Learning Techniques

=== PDF page 287 / printed label 261 ===
[p0287-l0001] [10.5pt] butions, but you are not told which one, and you do not know what the parameters of
[p0287-l0002] [10.5pt] these distributions are.
[p0287-l0003] [10.5pt] There are several GMM variants: in the simplest variant, implemented in the Gaus
[p0287-l0004] [10.5pt] sianMixture class, you must know in advance the number k of Gaussian distribu‐
[p0287-l0005] [10.5pt] tions. The dataset X is assumed to have been generated through the following
[p0287-l0006] [10.5pt] probabilistic process:
[p0287-l0007] [10.5pt] • For each instance, a cluster is picked randomly among k clusters. The probability
[p0287-l0008] [10.5pt] of choosing the jth cluster is defined by the cluster’s weight ϕ(j).7 The index of the
[p0287-l0009] [10.5pt] cluster chosen for the ith instance is noted z(i).
[p0287-l0010] [10.5pt] • If z(i)=j, meaning the ith instance has been assigned to the jth cluster, the location
[p0287-l0011] [10.5pt] x(i) of this instance is sampled randomly from the Gaussian distribution with
[p0287-l0012] [10.5pt] mean μ(j) and covariance matrix Σ(j). This is noted �i ∼�μ j , Σ j .
[p0287-l0013] [10.5pt] This generative process can be represented as a graphical model (see Figure 9-16).
[p0287-l0014] [10.5pt] This is a graph which represents the structure of the conditional dependencies
[p0287-l0015] [10.5pt] between random variables.
[p0287-l0016] [10.5pt] Figure 9-16. Gaussian mixture model
[p0287-l0017] [10.5pt] Here is how to interpret it:8
[p0287-l0018] [10.5pt] • The circles represent random variables.
[p0287-l0019] [10.5pt] • The squares represent fixed values (i.e., parameters of the model).
[p0287-l0020] [8.0pt] 7 Phi (ϕ or φ) is the 21st letter of the Greek alphabet.
[p0287-l0021] [8.0pt] 8 Most of these notations are standard, but a few additional notations were taken from the Wikipedia article on
[p0287-l0022] [8.0pt] plate notation.
[p0287-l0023] [9.0pt] Gaussian Mixtures
[p0287-l0024] [9.0pt] |
[p0287-l0025] [9.0pt] 261

=== PDF page 288 / printed label 262 ===
[p0288-l0001] [10.5pt] • The large rectangles are called plates: they indicate that their content is repeated
[p0288-l0002] [10.5pt] several times.
[p0288-l0003] [10.5pt] • The number indicated at the bottom right hand side of each plate indicates how
[p0288-l0004] [10.5pt] many times its content is repeated, so there are m random variables z(i) (from z(1)
[p0288-l0005] [10.5pt] to z(m)) and m random variables x(i), and k means μ(j) and k covariance matrices
[p0288-l0006] [10.5pt] Σ(j), but just one weight vector ϕ (containing all the weights ϕ(1) to ϕ(k)).
[p0288-l0007] [10.5pt] • Each variable z(i) is drawn from the categorical distribution with weights ϕ. Each
[p0288-l0008] [10.5pt] variable x(i) is drawn from the normal distribution with the mean and covariance
[p0288-l0009] [10.5pt] matrix defined by its cluster z(i).
[p0288-l0010] [10.5pt] • The solid arrows represent conditional dependencies. For example, the probabil‐
[p0288-l0011] [10.5pt] ity distribution for each random variable z(i) depends on the weight vector ϕ.
[p0288-l0012] [10.5pt] Note that when an arrow crosses a plate boundary, it means that it applies to all
[p0288-l0013] [10.5pt] the repetitions of that plate, so for example the weight vector ϕ conditions the
[p0288-l0014] [10.5pt] probability distributions of all the random variables x(1) to x(m).
[p0288-l0015] [10.5pt] • The squiggly arrow from z(i) to x(i) represents a switch: depending on the value of
[p0288-l0016] [10.5pt] z(i), the instance x(i) will be sampled from a different Gaussian distribution. For
[p0288-l0017] [10.5pt] example, if z(i)=j, then �i ∼�μ j , Σ j .
[p0288-l0018] [10.5pt] • Shaded nodes indicate that the value is known, so in this case only the random
[p0288-l0019] [10.5pt] variables x(i) have known values: they are called observed variables. The unknown
[p0288-l0020] [10.5pt] random variables z(i) are called latent variables.
[p0288-l0021] [10.5pt] So what can you do with such a model? Well, given the dataset X, you typically want
[p0288-l0022] [10.5pt] to start by estimating the weights ϕ and all the distribution parameters μ(1) to μ(k) and
[p0288-l0023] [10.5pt] Σ(1) to Σ(k). Scikit-Learn’s GaussianMixture class makes this trivial:
[p0288-l0024] [8.5pt] from sklearn.mixture import GaussianMixture
[p0288-l0025] [8.5pt] gm = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_init=10)
[p0288-l0026] [8.5pt] gm.fit(X)
[p0288-l0027] [10.5pt] Let’s look at the parameters that the algorithm estimated:
[p0288-l0028] [8.5pt] >>> gm.weights_
[p0288-l0029] [8.5pt] array([0.20965228, 0.4000662 , 0.39028152])
[p0288-l0030] [8.5pt] >>> gm.means_
[p0288-l0031] [8.5pt] array([[ 3.39909717,  1.05933727],
[p0288-l0032] [8.5pt]        [-1.40763984,  1.42710194],
[p0288-l0033] [8.5pt]        [ 0.05135313,  0.07524095]])
[p0288-l0034] [8.5pt] >>> gm.covariances_
[p0288-l0035] [8.5pt] array([[[ 1.14807234, -0.03270354],
[p0288-l0036] [8.5pt]         [-0.03270354,  0.95496237]],
[p0288-l0037] [8.5pt]        [[ 0.63478101,  0.72969804],
[p0288-l0038] [8.5pt]         [ 0.72969804,  1.1609872 ]],
[p0288-l0039] [9.0pt] 262
[p0288-l0040] [9.0pt] |
[p0288-l0041] [9.0pt] Chapter 9: Unsupervised Learning Techniques

=== PDF page 289 / printed label 263 ===
[p0289-l0001] [8.5pt]        [[ 0.68809572,  0.79608475],
[p0289-l0002] [8.5pt]         [ 0.79608475,  1.21234145]]])
[p0289-l0003] [10.5pt] Great, it worked fine! Indeed, the weights that were used to generate the data were
[p0289-l0004] [10.5pt] 0.2, 0.4 and 0.4, and similarly, the means and covariance matrices were very close to
[p0289-l0005] [10.5pt] those found by the algorithm. But how? This class relies on the Expectation-
[p0289-l0006] [10.5pt] Maximization (EM) algorithm, which has many similarities with the K-Means algo‐
[p0289-l0007] [10.5pt] rithm: it also initializes the cluster parameters randomly, then it repeats two steps
[p0289-l0008] [10.5pt] until convergence, first assigning instances to clusters (this is called the expectation
[p0289-l0009] [10.5pt] step) then updating the clusters (this is called the maximization step). Sounds famil‐
[p0289-l0010] [10.5pt] iar? Indeed, in the context of clustering you can think of EM as a generalization of K-
[p0289-l0011] [10.5pt] Means which not only finds the cluster centers (μ(1) to μ(k)), but also their size, shape
[p0289-l0012] [10.5pt] and orientation (Σ(1) to Σ(k)), as well as their relative weights (ϕ(1) to ϕ(k)). Unlike K-
[p0289-l0013] [10.5pt] Means, EM uses soft cluster assignments rather than hard assignments: for each
[p0289-l0014] [10.5pt] instance during the expectation step, the algorithm estimates the probability that it
[p0289-l0015] [10.5pt] belongs to each cluster (based on the current cluster parameters). Then, during the
[p0289-l0016] [10.5pt] maximization step, each cluster is updated using all the instances in the dataset, with
[p0289-l0017] [10.5pt] each instance weighted by the estimated probability that it belongs to that cluster.
[p0289-l0018] [10.5pt] These probabilities are called the responsibilities of the clusters for the instances. Dur‐
[p0289-l0019] [10.5pt] ing the maximization step, each cluster’s update will mostly be impacted by the
[p0289-l0020] [10.5pt] instances it is most responsible for.
[p0289-l0021] [9.6pt] Unfortunately, just like K-Means, EM can end up converging to
[p0289-l0022] [9.6pt] poor solutions, so it needs to be run several times, keeping only the
[p0289-l0023] [9.6pt] best solution. This is why we set n_init to 10. Be careful: by default
[p0289-l0024] [9.6pt] n_init is only set to 1.
[p0289-l0025] [10.5pt] You can check whether or not the algorithm converged and how many iterations it
[p0289-l0026] [10.5pt] took:
[p0289-l0027] [8.5pt] >>> gm.converged_
[p0289-l0028] [8.5pt] True
[p0289-l0029] [8.5pt] >>> gm.n_iter_
[p0289-l0030] [8.5pt] 3
[p0289-l0031] [10.5pt] Okay, now that you have an estimate of the location, size, shape, orientation and rela‐
[p0289-l0032] [10.5pt] tive weight of each cluster, the model can easily assign each instance to the most likely
[p0289-l0033] [10.5pt] cluster (hard clustering) or estimate the probability that it belongs to a particular
[p0289-l0034] [10.5pt] cluster (soft clustering). For this, just use the predict() method for hard clustering,
[p0289-l0035] [10.5pt] or the predict_proba() method for soft clustering:
[p0289-l0036] [8.5pt] >>> gm.predict(X)
[p0289-l0037] [8.5pt] array([2, 2, 1, ..., 0, 0, 0])
[p0289-l0038] [8.5pt] >>> gm.predict_proba(X)
[p0289-l0039] [8.5pt] array([[2.32389467e-02, 6.77397850e-07, 9.76760376e-01],
[p0289-l0040] [8.5pt]        [1.64685609e-02, 6.75361303e-04, 9.82856078e-01],
[p0289-l0041] [9.0pt] Gaussian Mixtures
[p0289-l0042] [9.0pt] |
[p0289-l0043] [9.0pt] 263

=== PDF page 290 / printed label 264 ===
[p0290-l0001] [8.5pt]        [2.01535333e-06, 9.99923053e-01, 7.49319577e-05],
[p0290-l0002] [8.5pt]        ...,
[p0290-l0003] [8.5pt]        [9.99999571e-01, 2.13946075e-26, 4.28788333e-07],
[p0290-l0004] [8.5pt]        [1.00000000e+00, 1.46454409e-41, 5.12459171e-16],
[p0290-l0005] [8.5pt]        [1.00000000e+00, 8.02006365e-41, 2.27626238e-15]])
[p0290-l0006] [10.5pt] It is a generative model, meaning you can actually sample new instances from it (note
[p0290-l0007] [10.5pt] that they are ordered by cluster index):
[p0290-l0008] [8.5pt] >>> X_new, y_new = gm.sample(6)
[p0290-l0009] [8.5pt] >>> X_new

[p0290-l0018] [10.5pt] It is also possible to estimate the density of the model at any given location. This is
[p0290-l0019] [10.5pt] achieved using the score_samples() method: for each instance it is given, this
[p0290-l0020] [10.5pt] method estimates the log of the probability density function (PDF) at that location.
[p0290-l0021] [10.5pt] The greater the score, the higher the density:
[p0290-l0022] [8.5pt] >>> gm.score_samples(X)
[p0290-l0023] [8.5pt] array([-2.60782346, -3.57106041, -3.33003479, ..., -3.51352783,
[p0290-l0024] [8.5pt]        -4.39802535, -3.80743859])
[p0290-l0025] [10.5pt] If you compute the exponential of these scores, you get the value of the PDF at the
[p0290-l0026] [10.5pt] location of the given instances. These are not probabilities, but probability densities:
[p0290-l0027] [10.5pt] they can take on any positive value, not just between 0 and 1. To estimate the proba‐
[p0290-l0028] [10.5pt] bility that an instance will fall within a particular region, you would have to integrate
[p0290-l0029] [10.5pt] the PDF over that region (if you do so over the entire space of possible instance loca‐
[p0290-l0030] [10.5pt] tions, the result will be 1).
[p0290-l0031] [10.5pt] Figure 9-17 shows the cluster means, the decision boundaries (dashed lines), and the
[p0290-l0032] [10.5pt] density contours of this model:

[p0291-l0003] [10.5pt] Nice! The algorithm clearly found an excellent solution. Of course, we made its task
[p0291-l0004] [10.5pt] easy by actually generating the data using a set of 2D Gaussian distributions (unfortu‐
[p0291-l0005] [10.5pt] nately, real life data is not always so Gaussian and low-dimensional), and we also gave
[p0291-l0006] [10.5pt] the algorithm the correct number of clusters. When there are many dimensions, or
[p0291-l0007] [10.5pt] many clusters, or few instances, EM can struggle to converge to the optimal solution.
[p0291-l0008] [10.5pt] You might need to reduce the difficulty of the task by limiting the number of parame‐
[p0291-l0009] [10.5pt] ters that the algorithm has to learn: one way to do this is to limit the range of shapes
[p0291-l0010] [10.5pt] and orientations that the clusters can have. This can be achieved by imposing con‐
[p0291-l0011] [10.5pt] straints on the covariance matrices. To do this, just set the covariance_type hyper‐
[p0291-l0012] [10.5pt] parameter to one of the following values:
[p0291-l0013] [10.5pt] • "spherical": all clusters must be spherical, but they can have different diameters
[p0291-l0014] [10.5pt] (i.e., different variances).
[p0291-l0015] [10.5pt] • "diag": clusters can take on any ellipsoidal shape of any size, but the ellipsoid’s
[p0291-l0016] [10.5pt] axes must be parallel to the coordinate axes (i.e., the covariance matrices must be
[p0291-l0017] [10.5pt] diagonal).
[p0291-l0018] [10.5pt] • "tied": all clusters must have the same ellipsoidal shape, size and orientation
[p0291-l0019] [10.5pt] (i.e., all clusters share the same covariance matrix).
[p0291-l0020] [10.5pt] By default, covariance_type is equal to "full", which means that each cluster can
[p0291-l0021] [10.5pt] take on any shape, size and orientation (it has its own unconstrained covariance
[p0291-l0022] [10.5pt] matrix). Figure 9-18 plots the solutions found by the EM algorithm when cova
[p0291-l0023] [10.5pt] riance_type is set to "tied" or "spherical“.

[p0291-l0025] [9.0pt] |
