[p0292-l0002] [9.6pt] The computational complexity of training a GaussianMixture
[p0292-l0003] [9.6pt] model depends on the number of instances m, the number of
[p0292-l0004] [9.6pt] dimensions n, the number of clusters k, and the constraints on the
[p0292-l0005] [9.6pt] covariance matrices. If covariance_type is "spherical or "diag",
[p0292-l0006] [9.6pt] it is O(kmn), assuming the data has a clustering structure. If cova
[p0292-l0007] [9.6pt] riance_type is "tied" or "full", it is O(kmn2 + kn3), so it will not
[p0292-l0008] [9.6pt] scale to large numbers of features.
[p0292-l0009] [10.5pt] Gaussian mixture models can also be used for anomaly detection. Let’s see how.
[p0292-l0010] [15.77pt] Anomaly Detection using Gaussian Mixtures
[p0292-l0011] [10.5pt] Anomaly detection (also called outlier detection) is the task of detecting instances that
[p0292-l0012] [10.5pt] deviate strongly from the norm. These instances are of course called anomalies or
[p0292-l0013] [10.5pt] outliers, while the normal instances are called inliers. Anomaly detection is very use‐
[p0292-l0014] [10.5pt] ful in a wide variety of applications, for example in fraud detection, or for detecting
[p0292-l0015] [10.5pt] defective products in manufacturing, or to remove outliers from a dataset before
[p0292-l0016] [10.5pt] training another model, which can significantly improve the performance of the
[p0292-l0017] [10.5pt] resulting model.
[p0292-l0018] [10.5pt] Using a Gaussian mixture model for anomaly detection is quite simple: any instance
[p0292-l0019] [10.5pt] located in a low-density region can be considered an anomaly. You must define what
[p0292-l0020] [10.5pt] density threshold you want to use. For example, in a manufacturing company that
[p0292-l0021] [10.5pt] tries to detect defective products, the ratio of defective products is usually well-
[p0292-l0022] [10.5pt] known. Say it is equal to 4%, then you can set the density threshold to be the value
[p0292-l0023] [10.5pt] that results in having 4% of the instances located in areas below that threshold den‐
[p0292-l0024] [10.5pt] sity. If you notice that you get too many false positives (i.e., perfectly good products
[p0292-l0025] [10.5pt] that are flagged as defective), you can lower the threshold. Conversely, if you have too
[p0292-l0026] [10.5pt] many false negatives (i.e., defective products that the system does not flag as defec‐
[p0292-l0027] [10.5pt] tive), you can increase the threshold. This is the usual precision/recall tradeoff (see
[p0292-l0028] [10.5pt] Chapter 3). Here is how you would identify the outliers using the 4th percentile low‐
[p0292-l0029] [9.0pt] 266
[p0292-l0030] [9.0pt] |
[p0292-l0031] [9.0pt] Chapter 9: Unsupervised Learning Techniques

=== PDF page 293 / printed label 267 ===
[p0293-l0001] [10.5pt] est density as the threshold (i.e., approximately 4% of the instances will be flagged as
[p0293-l0002] [10.5pt] anomalies):
[p0293-l0003] [8.5pt] densities = gm.score_samples(X)
[p0293-l0004] [8.5pt] density_threshold = np.percentile(densities, 4)
[p0293-l0005] [8.5pt] anomalies = X[densities < density_threshold]
[p0293-l0006] [10.5pt] These anomalies are represented as stars on Figure 9-19:
[p0293-l0007] [10.5pt] Figure 9-19. Anomaly detection using a Gaussian mixture model
[p0293-l0008] [10.5pt] A closely related task is novelty detection: it differs from anomaly detection in that the
[p0293-l0009] [10.5pt] algorithm is assumed to be trained on a “clean” dataset, uncontaminated by outliers,
[p0293-l0010] [10.5pt] whereas anomaly detection does not make this assumption. Indeed, outlier detection
[p0293-l0011] [10.5pt] is often precisely used to clean up a dataset.
[p0293-l0012] [9.6pt] Gaussian mixture models try to fit all the data, including the outli‐
[p0293-l0013] [9.6pt] ers, so if you have too many of them, this will bias the model’s view
[p0293-l0014] [9.6pt] of “normality”: some outliers may wrongly be considered as nor‐
[p0293-l0015] [9.6pt] mal. If this happens, you can try to fit the model once, use it to
[p0293-l0016] [9.6pt] detect and remove the most extreme outliers, then fit the model
[p0293-l0017] [9.6pt] again on the cleaned up dataset. Another approach is to use robust
[p0293-l0018] [9.6pt] covariance estimation methods (see the EllipticEnvelope class).
[p0293-l0019] [10.5pt] Just like K-Means, the GaussianMixture algorithm requires you to specify the num‐
[p0293-l0020] [10.5pt] ber of clusters. So how can you find it?
[p0293-l0021] [15.77pt] Selecting the Number of Clusters
[p0293-l0022] [10.5pt] With K-Means, you could use the inertia or the silhouette score to select the appro‐
[p0293-l0023] [10.5pt] priate number of clusters, but with Gaussian mixtures, it is not possible to use these
[p0293-l0024] [10.5pt] metrics because they are not reliable when the clusters are not spherical or have dif‐
[p0293-l0025] [10.5pt] ferent sizes. Instead, you can try to find the model that minimizes a theoretical infor‐
[p0293-l0026] [9.0pt] Gaussian Mixtures
[p0293-l0027] [9.0pt] |
[p0293-l0028] [9.0pt] 267

=== PDF page 294 / printed label 268 ===
[p0294-l0001] [10.5pt] mation criterion such as the Bayesian information criterion (BIC) or the Akaike
[p0294-l0002] [10.5pt] information criterion (AIC), defined in Equation 9-1.
[p0294-l0003] [10.5pt] Equation 9-1. Bayesian information criterion (BIC) and Akaike information
[p0294-l0004] [10.5pt] criterion (AIC)
[p0294-l0005] [10.0pt] BIC =
[p0294-l0006] [10.0pt] log m p −2 log L
[p0294-l0007] [10.0pt] AIC =
[p0294-l0008] [10.0pt] 2p −2 log L
[p0294-l0009] [10.5pt] • m is the number of instances, as always.
[p0294-l0010] [10.5pt] • p is the number of parameters learned by the model.
[p0294-l0011] [10.5pt] • L is the maximized value of the likelihood function of the model.
[p0294-l0012] [10.5pt] Both the BIC and the AIC penalize models that have more parameters to learn (e.g.,
[p0294-l0013] [10.5pt] more clusters), and reward models that fit the data well. They often end up selecting
[p0294-l0014] [10.5pt] the same model, but when they differ, the model selected by the BIC tends to be sim‐
[p0294-l0015] [10.5pt] pler (fewer parameters) than the one selected by the AIC, but it does not fit the data
[p0294-l0016] [10.5pt] quite as well (this is especially true for larger datasets).
[p0294-l0017] [15.0pt] Likelihood function
[p0294-l0018] [10.0pt] The terms “probability” and “likelihood” are often used interchangeably in the
[p0294-l0019] [10.0pt] English language, but they have very different meanings in statistics: given a statistical
[p0294-l0020] [10.0pt] model with some parameters θ, the word “probability” is used to describe how plausi‐
[p0294-l0021] [10.0pt] ble a future outcome x is (knowing the parameter values θ), while the word “likeli‐
[p0294-l0022] [10.0pt] hood” is used to describe how plausible a particular set of parameter values θ are,
[p0294-l0023] [10.0pt] after the outcome x is known.
[p0294-l0024] [10.0pt] Consider a one-dimensional mixture model of two Gaussian distributions centered at
[p0294-l0025] [10.0pt] -4 and +1. For simplicity, this toy model has a single parameter θ that controls the
[p0294-l0026] [10.0pt] standard deviations of both distributions. The top left contour plot in Figure 9-20
[p0294-l0027] [10.0pt] shows the entire model f(x; θ) as a function of both x and θ. To estimate the probabil‐
[p0294-l0028] [10.0pt] ity distribution of a future outcome x, you need to set the model parameter θ. For
[p0294-l0029] [10.0pt] example, if you set it to θ=1.3 (the horizontal line), you get the probability density
[p0294-l0030] [10.0pt] function f(x; θ=1.3) shown in the lower left plot. Say you want to estimate the proba‐
[p0294-l0031] [10.0pt] bility that x will fall between -2 and +2, you must calculate the integral of the PDF on
[p0294-l0032] [10.0pt] this range (i.e., the surface of the shaded region). On the other hand, if you have
[p0294-l0033] [10.0pt] observed a single instance x=2.5 (the vertical line in the upper left plot), you get the
[p0294-l0034] [10.0pt] likelihood function noted ℒ(θ|x=2.5)=f(x=2.5; θ) represented in the upper right plot.
[p0294-l0035] [10.0pt] In short, the PDF is a function of x (with θ fixed) while the likelihood function is a
[p0294-l0036] [10.0pt] function of θ (with x fixed). It is important to understand that the likelihood function
[p0294-l0037] [10.0pt] is not a probability distribution: if you integrate a probability distribution over all
[p0294-l0038] [9.0pt] 268
[p0294-l0039] [9.0pt] |
[p0294-l0040] [9.0pt] Chapter 9: Unsupervised Learning Techniques

=== PDF page 295 / printed label 269 ===
[p0295-l0001] [10.0pt] possible values of x, you always get 1, but if you integrate the likelihood function over
[p0295-l0002] [10.0pt] all possible values of θ, the result can be any positive value.
[p0295-l0003] [10.0pt] Figure 9-20. A model’s parametric function (top left), and some derived functions: a PDF
[p0295-l0004] [10.0pt] (lower left), a likelihood function (top right) and a log likelihood function (lower right)
[p0295-l0005] [10.0pt] Given a dataset X, a common task is to try to estimate the most likely values for the
[p0295-l0006] [10.0pt] model parameters. To do this, you must find the values that maximize the likelihood
[p0295-l0007] [10.0pt] function, given X. In this example, if you have observed a single instance x=2.5, the
[p0295-l0008] [10.0pt] maximum likelihood estimate (MLE) of θ is θ=1.5. If a prior probability distribution g
[p0295-l0009] [10.0pt] over θ exists, it is possible to take it into account by maximizing ℒ(θ|x)g(θ) rather
[p0295-l0010] [10.0pt] than just maximizing ℒ(θ|x). This is called maximum a-posteriori (MAP) estimation.
[p0295-l0011] [10.0pt] Since MAP constrains the parameter values, you can think of it as a regularized ver‐
[p0295-l0012] [10.0pt] sion of MLE.
[p0295-l0013] [10.0pt] Notice that it is equivalent to maximize the likelihood function or to maximize its
[p0295-l0014] [10.0pt] logarithm (represented in the lower right hand side of Figure 9-20): indeed, the loga‐
[p0295-l0015] [10.0pt] rithm is a strictly increasing function, so if θ maximizes the log likelihood, it also
[p0295-l0016] [10.0pt] maximizes the likelihood. It turns out that it is generally easier to maximize the log
[p0295-l0017] [10.0pt] likelihood. For example, if you observed several independent instances x(1) to x(m), you
[p0295-l0018] [10.0pt] would need to find the value of θ that maximizes the product of the individual likeli‐
[p0295-l0019] [10.0pt] hood functions. But it is equivalent, and much simpler, to maximize the sum (not the
[p0295-l0020] [10.0pt] product) of the log likelihood functions, thanks to the magic of the logarithm which
[p0295-l0021] [10.0pt] converts products into sums: log(ab)=log(a)+log(b).
[p0295-l0022] [10.0pt] Once you have estimated θ, the value of θ that maximizes the likelihood function,
[p0295-l0023] [10.0pt] then you are ready to compute L = ℒθ, �. This is the value which is used to com‐
[p0295-l0024] [10.0pt] pute the AIC and BIC: you can think of it as a measure of how well the model fits the
[p0295-l0025] [10.0pt] data.
[p0295-l0026] [10.5pt] To compute the BIC and AIC, just call the bic() or aic() methods:
[p0295-l0027] [9.0pt] Gaussian Mixtures

[p0296-l0011] [15.77pt] Bayesian Gaussian Mixture Models
[p0296-l0012] [10.5pt] Rather than manually searching for the optimal number of clusters, it is possible to
[p0296-l0013] [10.5pt] use instead the BayesianGaussianMixture class which is capable of giving weights
[p0296-l0014] [10.5pt] equal (or close) to zero to unnecessary clusters. Just set the number of clusters n_com
[p0296-l0015] [10.5pt] ponents to a value that you have good reason to believe is greater than the optimal
[p0296-l0016] [10.5pt] number of clusters (this assumes some minimal knowledge about the problem at
[p0296-l0017] [10.5pt] hand), and the algorithm will eliminate the unnecessary clusters automatically. For
[p0296-l0018] [10.5pt] example, let’s set the number of clusters to 10 and see what happens:
[p0296-l0019] [8.5pt] >>> from sklearn.mixture import BayesianGaussianMixture
[p0296-l0020] [8.5pt] >>> bgm = BayesianGaussianMixture(n_components=10, n_init=10, random_state=42)
[p0296-l0021] [8.5pt] >>> bgm.fit(X)
[p0296-l0022] [8.5pt] >>> np.round(bgm.weights_, 2)
[p0296-l0023] [8.5pt] array([0.4 , 0.21, 0.4 , 0.  , 0.  , 0.  , 0.  , 0.  , 0.  , 0.  ])
[p0296-l0024] [10.5pt] Perfect: the algorithm automatically detected that only 3 clusters are needed, and the
[p0296-l0025] [10.5pt] resulting clusters are almost identical to the ones in Figure 9-17.
[p0296-l0026] [10.5pt] In this model, the cluster parameters (including the weights, means and covariance
[p0296-l0027] [10.5pt] matrices) are not treated as fixed model parameters anymore, but as latent random
[p0296-l0028] [10.5pt] variables, like the cluster assignments (see Figure 9-22). So z now includes both the
[p0296-l0029] [10.5pt] cluster parameters and the cluster assignments.

[p0297-l0002] [10.5pt] Prior knowledge about the latent variables z can be encoded in a probability distribu‐
[p0297-l0003] [10.5pt] tion p(z) called the prior. For example, we may have a prior belief that the clusters are
[p0297-l0004] [10.5pt] likely to be few (low concentration), or conversely, that they are more likely to be
[p0297-l0005] [10.5pt] plentiful (high concentration). This can be adjusted using the weight_concentra
[p0297-l0006] [10.5pt] tion_prior hyperparameter. Setting it to 0.01 or 1000 gives very different clusterings
[p0297-l0007] [10.5pt] (see Figure 9-23). However, the more data we have, the less the priors matter. In fact,
[p0297-l0008] [10.5pt] to plot diagrams with such large differences, you must use very strong priors and lit‐
[p0297-l0009] [10.5pt] tle data.
[p0297-l0010] [10.5pt] Figure 9-23. Using different concentration priors
[p0297-l0011] [9.6pt] The fact that you see only 3 regions in the right plot although there
[p0297-l0012] [9.6pt] are 4 centroids is not a bug: the weight of the top-right cluster is
[p0297-l0013] [9.6pt] much larger than the weight of the lower-right cluster, so the prob‐
[p0297-l0014] [9.6pt] ability that any given point in this region belongs to the top-right
[p0297-l0015] [9.6pt] cluster is greater than the probability that it belongs to the lower-
[p0297-l0016] [9.6pt] right cluster, even near the lower-right cluster.
[p0297-l0017] [9.0pt] Gaussian Mixtures
[p0297-l0018] [9.0pt] |

[p0298-l0001] [10.5pt] Bayes’ theorem (Equation 9-2) tells us how to update the probability distribution over
[p0298-l0002] [10.5pt] the latent variables after we observe some data X. It computes the posterior distribu‐
[p0298-l0003] [10.5pt] tion p(z|X), which is the conditional probability of z given X.
[p0298-l0004] [10.5pt] Equation 9-2. Bayes’ theorem
[p0298-l0005] [10.0pt] p z X = Posterior = Likelihood×Prior
[p0298-l0006] [10.0pt] Evidence
[p0298-l0007] [10.0pt] = p X z p z
[p0298-l0008] [10.0pt] p X
[p0298-l0009] [10.5pt] Unfortunately, in a Gaussian mixture model (and many other problems), the denomi‐
[p0298-l0010] [10.5pt] nator p(x) is intractable, as it requires integrating over all the possible values of z
[p0298-l0011] [10.5pt] (Equation 9-3). This means considering all possible combinations of cluster parame‐
[p0298-l0012] [10.5pt] ters and cluster assignments.
[p0298-l0013] [10.5pt] Equation 9-3. The evidence p(X) is often intractable
[p0298-l0014] [20.0pt] p X =∫p X z p z dz
[p0298-l0015] [10.5pt] This is one of the central problems in Bayesian statistics, and there are several
[p0298-l0016] [10.5pt] approaches to solving it. One of them is variational inference, which picks a family of
[p0298-l0017] [10.5pt] distributions q(z; λ) with its own variational parameters λ (lambda), then it optimizes
[p0298-l0018] [10.5pt] these parameters to make q(z) a good approximation of p(z|X). This is achieved by
[p0298-l0019] [10.5pt] finding the value of λ that minimizes the KL divergence from q(z) to p(z|X), noted
[p0298-l0020] [10.5pt] DKL(q‖p). The KL divergence equation is shown in (see Equation 9-4), and it can be
[p0298-l0021] [10.5pt] rewritten as the log of the evidence (log p(X)) minus the evidence lower bound
[p0298-l0022] [10.5pt] (ELBO). Since the log of the evidence does not depend on q, it is a constant term, so
[p0298-l0023] [10.5pt] minimizing the KL divergence just requires maximizing the ELBO.
[p0298-l0024] [10.5pt] Equation 9-4. KL divergence from q(z) to p(z|X)
[p0298-l0025] [10.0pt] DKL q ∥p = �q log
[p0298-l0026] [10.0pt] q z
[p0298-l0027] [10.0pt] p z
[p0298-l0028] [10.0pt] X
[p0298-l0029] [10.0pt] = �q log q z −log p z
[p0298-l0030] [10.0pt] X
[p0298-l0031] [10.0pt] = �q log q z −log p z, X
[p0298-l0032] [10.0pt] p X
[p0298-l0033] [10.0pt] = �q log q z −log p z, X + log p X
[p0298-l0034] [10.0pt] = �q log q z
[p0298-l0035] [10.0pt] −�q log p z, X
[p0298-l0036] [10.0pt] + �q log p X
[p0298-l0037] [10.0pt] = �q log p X
[p0298-l0038] [10.0pt] −�q log p z, X
[p0298-l0039] [10.0pt] −�q log q z
[p0298-l0040] [10.0pt] =
[p0298-l0041] [10.0pt] log p X −ELBO
[p0298-l0042] [10.0pt] where ELBO = �q log p z, X
[p0298-l0043] [10.0pt] −�q log q z
[p0298-l0044] [9.0pt] 272
[p0298-l0045] [9.0pt] |
[p0298-l0046] [9.0pt] Chapter 9: Unsupervised Learning Techniques

=== PDF page 299 / printed label 273 ===
[p0299-l0001] [10.5pt] In practice, there are different techniques to maximize the ELBO. In mean field varia‐
[p0299-l0002] [10.5pt] tional inference, it is necessary to pick the family of distributions q(z; λ) and the prior
[p0299-l0003] [10.5pt] p(z) very carefully to ensure that the equation for the ELBO simplifies to a form that
[p0299-l0004] [10.5pt] can actually be computed. Unfortunately, there is no general way to do this, it
[p0299-l0005] [10.5pt] depends on the task and requires some mathematical skills. For example, the distribu‐
[p0299-l0006] [10.5pt] tions and lower bound equations used in Scikit-Learn’s BayesianGaussianMixture
[p0299-l0007] [10.5pt] class are presented in the documentation. From these equations it is possible to derive
[p0299-l0008] [10.5pt] update equations for the cluster parameters and assignment variables: these are then
[p0299-l0009] [10.5pt] used very much like in the Expectation-Maximization algorithm. In fact, the compu‐
[p0299-l0010] [10.5pt] tational complexity of the BayesianGaussianMixture class is similar to that of the
[p0299-l0011] [10.5pt] GaussianMixture class (but generally significantly slower). A simpler approach to
[p0299-l0012] [10.5pt] maximizing the ELBO is called black box stochastic variational inference (BBSVI): at
[p0299-l0013] [10.5pt] each iteration, a few samples are drawn from q and they are used to estimate the gra‐
[p0299-l0014] [10.5pt] dients of the ELBO with regards to the variational parameters λ, which are then used
[p0299-l0015] [10.5pt] in a gradient ascent step. This approach makes it possible to use Bayesian inference
[p0299-l0016] [10.5pt] with any kind of model (provided it is differentiable), even deep neural networks: this
[p0299-l0017] [10.5pt] is called Bayesian deep learning.
[p0299-l0018] [9.6pt] If you want to dive deeper into Bayesian statistics, check out the
[p0299-l0019] [9.6pt] Bayesian Data Analysis book by Andrew Gelman, John Carlin, Hal
[p0299-l0020] [9.6pt] Stern, David Dunson, Aki Vehtari, and Donald Rubin.
[p0299-l0021] [10.5pt] Gaussian mixture models work great on clusters with ellipsoidal shapes, but if you try
[p0299-l0022] [10.5pt] to fit a dataset with different shapes, you may have bad surprises. For example, let’s
[p0299-l0023] [10.5pt] see what happens if we use a Bayesian Gaussian mixture model to cluster the moons
[p0299-l0024] [10.5pt] dataset (see Figure 9-24):
[p0299-l0025] [10.5pt] Figure 9-24. moons_vs_bgm_diagram
[p0299-l0026] [10.5pt] Oops, the algorithm desperately searched for ellipsoids, so it found 8 different clus‐
[p0299-l0027] [10.5pt] ters instead of 2. The density estimation is not too bad, so this model could perhaps
[p0299-l0028] [10.5pt] be used for anomaly detection, but it failed to identify the two moons. Let’s now look
[p0299-l0029] [10.5pt] at a few clustering algorithms capable of dealing with arbitrarily shaped clusters.
[p0299-l0030] [9.0pt] Gaussian Mixtures
[p0299-l0031] [9.0pt] |
[p0299-l0032] [9.0pt] 273

=== PDF page 300 / printed label 274 ===
[p0300-l0001] [15.77pt] Other Anomaly Detection and Novelty Detection Algorithms
[p0300-l0002] [10.5pt] Scikit-Learn also implements a few algorithms dedicated to anomaly detection or
[p0300-l0003] [10.5pt] novelty detection:
[p0300-l0004] [10.5pt] • Fast-MCD (minimum covariance determinant), implemented by the EllipticEn
[p0300-l0005] [10.5pt] velope class: this algorithm is useful for outlier detection, in particular to
[p0300-l0006] [10.5pt] cleanup a dataset. It assumes that the normal instances (inliers) are generated
[p0300-l0007] [10.5pt] from a single Gaussian distribution (not a mixture), but it also assumes that the
[p0300-l0008] [10.5pt] dataset is contaminated with outliers that were not generated from this Gaussian
[p0300-l0009] [10.5pt] distribution. When it estimates the parameters of the Gaussian distribution (i.e.,
[p0300-l0010] [10.5pt] the shape of the elliptic envelope around the inliers), it is careful to ignore the
[p0300-l0011] [10.5pt] instances that are most likely outliers. This gives a better estimation of the elliptic
[p0300-l0012] [10.5pt] envelope, and thus makes it better at identifying the outliers.
[p0300-l0013] [10.5pt] • Isolation forest: this is an efficient algorithm for outlier detection, especially in
[p0300-l0014] [10.5pt] high-dimensional datasets. The algorithm builds a Random Forest in which each
[p0300-l0015] [10.5pt] Decision Tree is grown randomly: at each node, it picks a feature randomly, then
[p0300-l0016] [10.5pt] it picks a random threshold value (between the min and max value) to split the
[p0300-l0017] [10.5pt] dataset in two. The dataset gradually gets chopped into pieces this way, until all
[p0300-l0018] [10.5pt] instances end up isolated from the other instances. An anomaly is usually far
[p0300-l0019] [10.5pt] from other instances, so on average (across all the Decision Trees) it tends to get
[p0300-l0020] [10.5pt] isolated in less steps than normal instances.
[p0300-l0021] [10.5pt] • Local outlier factor (LOF): this algorithm is also good for outlier detection. It
[p0300-l0022] [10.5pt] compares the density of instances around a given instance to the density around
[p0300-l0023] [10.5pt] its neighbors. An anomaly is often more isolated than its k nearest neighbors.
[p0300-l0024] [10.5pt] • One-class SVM: this algorithm is better suited for novelty detection. Recall that a
[p0300-l0025] [10.5pt] kernelized SVM classifier separates two classes by first (implicitly) mapping all
[p0300-l0026] [10.5pt] the instances to a high-dimensional space, then separating the two classes using a
[p0300-l0027] [10.5pt] linear SVM classifier within this high-dimensional space (see Chapter 5). Since
[p0300-l0028] [10.5pt] we just have one class of instances, the one-class SVM algorithm instead tries to
[p0300-l0029] [10.5pt] separate the instances in high-dimensional space from the origin. In the original
[p0300-l0030] [10.5pt] space, this will correspond to finding a small region that encompasses all the
[p0300-l0031] [10.5pt] instances. If a new instance does not fall within this region, it is an anomaly.
[p0300-l0032] [10.5pt] There are a few hyperparameters to tweak: the usual ones for a kernelized SVM,
[p0300-l0033] [10.5pt] plus a margin hyperparameter that corresponds to the probability of a new
[p0300-l0034] [10.5pt] instance being mistakenly considered as novel, when it is in fact normal. It works
[p0300-l0035] [10.5pt] great, especially with high-dimensional datasets, but just like all SVMs, it does
[p0300-l0036] [10.5pt] not scale to large datasets.
[p0300-l0037] [9.0pt] 274

[p0303-l0001] [16.82pt] CHAPTER 10
[p0303-l0002] [25.22pt] Introduction to Artificial Neural Networks
[p0303-l0003] [25.22pt] with Keras
[p0303-l0004] [9.6pt] With Early Release ebooks, you get books in their earliest form—
[p0303-l0005] [9.6pt] the author’s raw and unedited content as he or she writes—so you
[p0303-l0006] [9.6pt] can take advantage of these technologies long before the official
[p0303-l0007] [9.6pt] release of these titles. The following will be Chapter 10 in the final
[p0303-l0008] [9.6pt] release of the book.
[p0303-l0009] [10.5pt] Birds inspired us to fly, burdock plants inspired velcro, and countless more inven‐
[p0303-l0010] [10.5pt] tions were inspired by nature. It seems only logical, then, to look at the brain’s archi‐
[p0303-l0011] [10.5pt] tecture for inspiration on how to build an intelligent machine. This is the key idea
[p0303-l0012] [10.5pt] that sparked artificial neural networks (ANNs). However, although planes were
[p0303-l0013] [10.5pt] inspired by birds, they don’t have to flap their wings. Similarly, ANNs have gradually
[p0303-l0014] [10.5pt] become quite different from their biological cousins. Some researchers even argue
[p0303-l0015] [10.5pt] that we should drop the biological analogy altogether (e.g., by saying “units” rather
[p0303-l0016] [10.5pt] than “neurons”), lest we restrict our creativity to biologically plausible systems.1
[p0303-l0017] [10.5pt] ANNs are at the very core of Deep Learning. They are versatile, powerful, and scala‐
[p0303-l0018] [10.5pt] ble, making them ideal to tackle large and highly complex Machine Learning tasks,
[p0303-l0019] [10.5pt] such as classifying billions of images (e.g., Google Images), powering speech recogni‐
[p0303-l0020] [10.5pt] tion services (e.g., Apple’s Siri), recommending the best videos to watch to hundreds
[p0303-l0021] [10.5pt] of millions of users every day (e.g., YouTube), or learning to beat the world champion
[p0303-l0022] [10.5pt] at the game of Go by playing millions of games against itself (DeepMind’s Alpha‐
[p0303-l0023] [10.5pt] Zero).
[p0303-l0024] [8.0pt] 1 You can get the best of both worlds by being open to biological inspirations without being afraid to create
[p0303-l0025] [8.0pt] biologically unrealistic models, as long as they work well.
[p0303-l0026] [9.0pt] 277

=== PDF page 304 / printed label 278 ===
[p0304-l0001] [10.5pt] In the first part of this chapter, we will introduce artificial neural networks, starting
[p0304-l0002] [10.5pt] with a quick tour of the very first ANN architectures, leading up to Multi-Layer Per‐
[p0304-l0003] [10.5pt] ceptrons (MLPs) which are heavily used today (other architectures will be explored in
[p0304-l0004] [10.5pt] the next chapters). In the second part, we will look at how to implement neural net‐
[p0304-l0005] [10.5pt] works using the popular Keras API. This is a beautifully designed and simple high-
[p0304-l0006] [10.5pt] level API for building, training, evaluating and running neural networks. But don’t be
[p0304-l0007] [10.5pt] fooled by its simplicity: it is expressive and flexible enough to let you build a wide
[p0304-l0008] [10.5pt] variety of neural network architectures. In fact, it will probably be sufficient for most
[p0304-l0009] [10.5pt] of your use cases. Moreover, should you ever need extra flexibility, you can always
[p0304-l0010] [10.5pt] write custom Keras components using its lower-level API, as we will see in Chap‐
[p0304-l0011] [10.5pt] ter 12.
[p0304-l0012] [10.5pt] But first, let’s go back in time to see how artificial neural networks came to be!
[p0304-l0013] [18.92pt] From Biological to Artificial Neurons
[p0304-l0014] [10.5pt] Surprisingly, ANNs have been around for quite a while: they were first introduced
[p0304-l0015] [10.5pt] back in 1943 by the neurophysiologist Warren McCulloch and the mathematician
[p0304-l0016] [10.5pt] Walter Pitts. In their landmark paper,2 “A Logical Calculus of Ideas Immanent in
[p0304-l0017] [10.5pt] Nervous Activity,” McCulloch and Pitts presented a simplified computational model
[p0304-l0018] [10.5pt] of how biological neurons might work together in animal brains to perform complex
[p0304-l0019] [10.5pt] computations using propositional logic. This was the first artificial neural network
[p0304-l0020] [10.5pt] architecture. Since then many other architectures have been invented, as we will see.
[p0304-l0021] [10.5pt] The early successes of ANNs until the 1960s led to the widespread belief that we
[p0304-l0022] [10.5pt] would soon be conversing with truly intelligent machines. When it became clear that
[p0304-l0023] [10.5pt] this promise would go unfulfilled (at least for quite a while), funding flew elsewhere
[p0304-l0024] [10.5pt] and ANNs entered a long winter. In the early 1980s there was a revival of interest in
[p0304-l0025] [10.5pt] connectionism (the study of neural networks), as new architectures were invented and
[p0304-l0026] [10.5pt] better training techniques were developed. But progress was slow, and by the 1990s
[p0304-l0027] [10.5pt] other powerful Machine Learning techniques were invented, such as Support Vector
[p0304-l0028] [10.5pt] Machines (see Chapter 5). These techniques seemed to offer better results and stron‐
[p0304-l0029] [10.5pt] ger theoretical foundations than ANNs, so once again the study of neural networks
[p0304-l0030] [10.5pt] entered a long winter.
[p0304-l0031] [10.5pt] Finally, we are now witnessing yet another wave of interest in ANNs. Will this wave
[p0304-l0032] [10.5pt] die out like the previous ones did? Well, there are a few good reasons to believe that
[p0304-l0033] [10.5pt] this wave is different and that it will have a much more profound impact on our lives:
[p0304-l0034] [8.0pt] 2 “A Logical Calculus of Ideas Immanent in Nervous Activity,” W. McCulloch and W. Pitts (1943).
[p0304-l0035] [9.0pt] 278
[p0304-l0036] [9.0pt] |
[p0304-l0037] [9.0pt] Chapter 10: Introduction to Artificial Neural Networks with Keras

=== PDF page 305 / printed label 279 ===
[p0305-l0001] [10.5pt] • There is now a huge quantity of data available to train neural networks, and
[p0305-l0002] [10.5pt] ANNs frequently outperform other ML techniques on very large and complex
[p0305-l0003] [10.5pt] problems.
[p0305-l0004] [10.5pt] • The tremendous increase in computing power since the 1990s now makes it pos‐
[p0305-l0005] [10.5pt] sible to train large neural networks in a reasonable amount of time. This is in
[p0305-l0006] [10.5pt] part due to Moore’s Law, but also thanks to the gaming industry, which has pro‐
[p0305-l0007] [10.5pt] duced powerful GPU cards by the millions.
[p0305-l0008] [10.5pt] • The training algorithms have been improved. To be fair they are only slightly dif‐
[p0305-l0009] [10.5pt] ferent from the ones used in the 1990s, but these relatively small tweaks have a
[p0305-l0010] [10.5pt] huge positive impact.
[p0305-l0011] [10.5pt] • Some theoretical limitations of ANNs have turned out to be benign in practice.
[p0305-l0012] [10.5pt] For example, many people thought that ANN training algorithms were doomed
[p0305-l0013] [10.5pt] because they were likely to get stuck in local optima, but it turns out that this is
[p0305-l0014] [10.5pt] rather rare in practice (or when it is the case, they are usually fairly close to the
[p0305-l0015] [10.5pt] global optimum).
[p0305-l0016] [10.5pt] • ANNs seem to have entered a virtuous circle of funding and progress. Amazing
[p0305-l0017] [10.5pt] products based on ANNs regularly make the headline news, which pulls more
[p0305-l0018] [10.5pt] and more attention and funding toward them, resulting in more and more pro‐
[p0305-l0019] [10.5pt] gress, and even more amazing products.
[p0305-l0020] [15.77pt] Biological Neurons
[p0305-l0021] [10.5pt] Before we discuss artificial neurons, let’s take a quick look at a biological neuron (rep‐
[p0305-l0022] [10.5pt] resented in Figure 10-1). It is an unusual-looking cell mostly found in animal cerebral
[p0305-l0023] [10.5pt] cortexes (e.g., your brain), composed of a cell body containing the nucleus and most
[p0305-l0024] [10.5pt] of the cell’s complex components, and many branching extensions called dendrites,
[p0305-l0025] [10.5pt] plus one very long extension called the axon. The axon’s length may be just a few
[p0305-l0026] [10.5pt] times longer than the cell body, or up to tens of thousands of times longer. Near its
[p0305-l0027] [10.5pt] extremity the axon splits off into many branches called telodendria, and at the tip of
[p0305-l0028] [10.5pt] these branches are minuscule structures called synaptic terminals (or simply synap‐
[p0305-l0029] [10.5pt] ses), which are connected to the dendrites (or directly to the cell body) of other neu‐
[p0305-l0030] [10.5pt] rons. Biological neurons receive short electrical impulses called signals from other
[p0305-l0031] [10.5pt] neurons via these synapses. When a neuron receives a sufficient number of signals
[p0305-l0032] [10.5pt] from other neurons within a few milliseconds, it fires its own signals.
[p0305-l0033] [9.0pt] From Biological to Artificial Neurons
[p0305-l0034] [9.0pt] |
[p0305-l0035] [9.0pt] 279

[p0306-l0002] [10.5pt] Thus, individual biological neurons seem to behave in a rather simple way, but they
[p0306-l0003] [10.5pt] are organized in a vast network of billions of neurons, each neuron typically connec‐
[p0306-l0004] [10.5pt] ted to thousands of other neurons. Highly complex computations can be performed
[p0306-l0005] [10.5pt] by a vast network of fairly simple neurons, much like a complex anthill can emerge
[p0306-l0006] [10.5pt] from the combined efforts of simple ants. The architecture of biological neural net‐
[p0306-l0007] [10.5pt] works (BNN)4 is still the subject of active research, but some parts of the brain have
[p0306-l0008] [10.5pt] been mapped, and it seems that neurons are often organized in consecutive layers, as
[p0306-l0009] [10.5pt] shown in Figure 10-2.

[p0307-l0001] [15.77pt] Logical Computations with Neurons
[p0307-l0002] [10.5pt] Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts proposed a very simple model of the biological
[p0307-l0003] [10.5pt] neuron, which later became known as an artificial neuron: it has one or more binary
[p0307-l0004] [10.5pt] (on/off) inputs and one binary output. The artificial neuron simply activates its out‐
[p0307-l0005] [10.5pt] put when more than a certain number of its inputs are active. McCulloch and Pitts
[p0307-l0006] [10.5pt] showed that even with such a simplified model it is possible to build a network of
[p0307-l0007] [10.5pt] artificial neurons that computes any logical proposition you want. For example, let’s
[p0307-l0008] [10.5pt] build a few ANNs that perform various logical computations (see Figure 10-3),
[p0307-l0009] [10.5pt] assuming that a neuron is activated when at least two of its inputs are active.
[p0307-l0010] [10.5pt] Figure 10-3. ANNs performing simple logical computations
[p0307-l0011] [10.5pt] • The first network on the left is simply the identity function: if neuron A is activa‐
[p0307-l0012] [10.5pt] ted, then neuron C gets activated as well (since it receives two input signals from
[p0307-l0013] [10.5pt] neuron A), but if neuron A is off, then neuron C is off as well.
[p0307-l0014] [10.5pt] • The second network performs a logical AND: neuron C is activated only when
[p0307-l0015] [10.5pt] both neurons A and B are activated (a single input signal is not enough to acti‐
[p0307-l0016] [10.5pt] vate neuron C).
[p0307-l0017] [10.5pt] • The third network performs a logical OR: neuron C gets activated if either neu‐
[p0307-l0018] [10.5pt] ron A or neuron B is activated (or both).
[p0307-l0019] [10.5pt] • Finally, if we suppose that an input connection can inhibit the neuron’s activity
[p0307-l0020] [10.5pt] (which is the case with biological neurons), then the fourth network computes a
[p0307-l0021] [10.5pt] slightly more complex logical proposition: neuron C is activated only if neuron A
[p0307-l0022] [10.5pt] is active and if neuron B is off. If neuron A is active all the time, then you get a
[p0307-l0023] [10.5pt] logical NOT: neuron C is active when neuron B is off, and vice versa.
[p0307-l0024] [10.5pt] You can easily imagine how these networks can be combined to compute complex
[p0307-l0025] [10.5pt] logical expressions (see the exercises at the end of the chapter).
[p0307-l0026] [15.77pt] The Perceptron
[p0307-l0027] [10.5pt] The Perceptron is one of the simplest ANN architectures, invented in 1957 by Frank
[p0307-l0028] [10.5pt] Rosenblatt. It is based on a slightly different artificial neuron (see Figure 10-4) called
[p0307-l0029] [9.0pt] From Biological to Artificial Neurons
[p0307-l0030] [9.0pt] |
[p0307-l0031] [9.0pt] 281

=== PDF page 308 / printed label 282 ===
[p0308-l0001] [10.5pt] a threshold logic unit (TLU), or sometimes a linear threshold unit (LTU): the inputs
[p0308-l0002] [10.5pt] and output are now numbers (instead of binary on/off values) and each input con‐
[p0308-l0003] [10.5pt] nection is associated with a weight. The TLU computes a weighted sum of its inputs
[p0308-l0004] [10.5pt] (z = w1 x1 + w2 x2 + ⋯ + wn xn = xT w), then applies a step function to that sum and
[p0308-l0005] [10.5pt] outputs the result: hw(x) = step(z), where z = xT w.
[p0308-l0006] [10.5pt] Figure 10-4. Threshold logic unit
[p0308-l0007] [10.5pt] The most common step function used in Perceptrons is the Heaviside step function
[p0308-l0008] [10.5pt] (see Equation 10-1). Sometimes the sign function is used instead.
[p0308-l0009] [10.5pt] Equation 10-1. Common step functions used in Perceptrons
[p0308-l0010] [10.0pt] heaviside z = 0 if z < 0
[p0308-l0011] [10.0pt] 1 if z ≥0
[p0308-l0012] [10.0pt] sgn z =
[p0308-l0013] [10.0pt] −1 if z < 0
[p0308-l0014] [10.0pt] 0
[p0308-l0015] [10.0pt] if z = 0
[p0308-l0016] [10.0pt] +1 if z > 0
[p0308-l0017] [10.5pt] A single TLU can be used for simple linear binary classification. It computes a linear
[p0308-l0018] [10.5pt] combination of the inputs and if the result exceeds a threshold, it outputs the positive
[p0308-l0019] [10.5pt] class or else outputs the negative class (just like a Logistic Regression classifier or a
[p0308-l0020] [10.5pt] linear SVM). For example, you could use a single TLU to classify iris flowers based on
[p0308-l0021] [10.5pt] the petal length and width (also adding an extra bias feature x0 = 1, just like we did in
[p0308-l0022] [10.5pt] previous chapters). Training a TLU in this case means finding the right values for w0,
[p0308-l0023] [10.5pt] w1, and w2 (the training algorithm is discussed shortly).
[p0308-l0024] [10.5pt] A Perceptron is simply composed of a single layer of TLUs,6 with each TLU connected
[p0308-l0025] [10.5pt] to all the inputs. When all the neurons in a layer are connected to every neuron in the
[p0308-l0026] [10.5pt] previous layer (i.e., its input neurons), it is called a fully connected layer or a dense
[p0308-l0027] [10.5pt] layer. To represent the fact that each input is sent to every TLU, it is common to draw
[p0308-l0028] [10.5pt] special passthrough neurons called input neurons: they just output whatever input
[p0308-l0029] [10.5pt] they are fed. All the input neurons form the input layer. Moreover, an extra bias fea‐
[p0308-l0030] [8.0pt] 6 The name Perceptron is sometimes used to mean a tiny network with a single TLU.
[p0308-l0031] [9.0pt] 282
[p0308-l0032] [9.0pt] |
[p0308-l0033] [9.0pt] Chapter 10: Introduction to Artificial Neural Networks with Keras

=== PDF page 309 / printed label 283 ===
[p0309-l0001] [10.5pt] ture is generally added (x0 = 1): it is typically represented using a special type of neu‐
[p0309-l0002] [10.5pt] ron called a bias neuron, which just outputs 1 all the time. A Perceptron with two
[p0309-l0003] [10.5pt] inputs and three outputs is represented in Figure 10-5. This Perceptron can classify
[p0309-l0004] [10.5pt] instances simultaneously into three different binary classes, which makes it a multi‐
[p0309-l0005] [10.5pt] output classifier.
[p0309-l0006] [10.5pt] Figure 10-5. Perceptron diagram
[p0309-l0007] [10.5pt] Thanks to the magic of linear algebra, it is possible to efficiently compute the outputs
[p0309-l0008] [10.5pt] of a layer of artificial neurons for several instances at once, by using Equation 10-2:
[p0309-l0009] [10.5pt] Equation 10-2. Computing the outputs of a fully connected layer
[p0309-l0010] [10.0pt] hW, b X = ϕ XW + b
[p0309-l0011] [10.5pt] • As always, X represents the matrix of input features. It has one row per instance,
[p0309-l0012] [10.5pt] one column per feature.
[p0309-l0013] [10.5pt] • The weight matrix W contains all the connection weights except for the ones
[p0309-l0014] [10.5pt] from the bias neuron. It has one row per input neuron and one column per artifi‐
[p0309-l0015] [10.5pt] cial neuron in the layer.
[p0309-l0016] [10.5pt] • The bias vector b contains all the connection weights between the bias neuron
[p0309-l0017] [10.5pt] and the artificial neurons. It has one bias term per artificial neuron.
[p0309-l0018] [10.5pt] • The function ϕ is called the activation function: when the artificial neurons are
[p0309-l0019] [10.5pt] TLUs, it is a step function (but we will discuss other activation functions shortly).
[p0309-l0020] [10.5pt] So how is a Perceptron trained? The Perceptron training algorithm proposed by
[p0309-l0021] [10.5pt] Frank Rosenblatt was largely inspired by Hebb’s rule. In his book The Organization of
[p0309-l0022] [10.5pt] Behavior, published in 1949, Donald Hebb suggested that when a biological neuron
[p0309-l0023] [10.5pt] often triggers another neuron, the connection between these two neurons grows
[p0309-l0024] [10.5pt] stronger. This idea was later summarized by Siegrid Löwel in this catchy phrase:
[p0309-l0025] [10.5pt] “Cells that fire together, wire together.” This rule later became known as Hebb’s rule
[p0309-l0026] [9.0pt] From Biological to Artificial Neurons
[p0309-l0027] [9.0pt] |
[p0309-l0028] [9.0pt] 283

=== PDF page 310 / printed label 284 ===
[p0310-l0001] [10.5pt] (or Hebbian learning); that is, the connection weight between two neurons is
[p0310-l0002] [10.5pt] increased whenever they have the same output. Perceptrons are trained using a var‐
[p0310-l0003] [10.5pt] iant of this rule that takes into account the error made by the network; it reinforces
[p0310-l0004] [10.5pt] connections that help reduce the error. More specifically, the Perceptron is fed one
[p0310-l0005] [10.5pt] training instance at a time, and for each instance it makes its predictions. For every
[p0310-l0006] [10.5pt] output neuron that produced a wrong prediction, it reinforces the connection
[p0310-l0007] [10.5pt] weights from the inputs that would have contributed to the correct prediction. The
[p0310-l0008] [10.5pt] rule is shown in Equation 10-3.
[p0310-l0009] [10.5pt] Equation 10-3. Perceptron learning rule (weight update)
[p0310-l0010] [10.0pt] wi, j
[p0310-l0011] [10.0pt] next step = wi, j + η yj −y j xi
[p0310-l0012] [10.5pt] • wi, j is the connection weight between the ith input neuron and the jth output neu‐
[p0310-l0013] [10.5pt] ron.
[p0310-l0014] [10.5pt] • xi is the ith input value of the current training instance.
[p0310-l0015] [10.5pt] • y j is the output of the jth output neuron for the current training instance.
[p0310-l0016] [10.5pt] • yj is the target output of the jth output neuron for the current training instance.
[p0310-l0017] [10.5pt] • η is the learning rate.
[p0310-l0018] [10.5pt] The decision boundary of each output neuron is linear, so Perceptrons are incapable
[p0310-l0019] [10.5pt] of learning complex patterns (just like Logistic Regression classifiers). However, if the
[p0310-l0020] [10.5pt] training instances are linearly separable, Rosenblatt demonstrated that this algorithm
[p0310-l0021] [10.5pt] would converge to a solution.7 This is called the Perceptron convergence theorem.
[p0310-l0022] [10.5pt] Scikit-Learn provides a Perceptron class that implements a single TLU network. It
[p0310-l0023] [10.5pt] can be used pretty much as you would expect—for example, on the iris dataset (intro‐
[p0310-l0024] [10.5pt] duced in Chapter 4):
[p0310-l0025] [8.5pt] import numpy as np
[p0310-l0026] [8.5pt] from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
[p0310-l0027] [8.5pt] from sklearn.linear_model import Perceptron
[p0310-l0028] [8.5pt] iris = load_iris()
[p0310-l0029] [8.5pt] X = iris.data[:, (2, 3)]  # petal length, petal width
[p0310-l0030] [8.5pt] y = (iris.target == 0).astype(np.int)  # Iris Setosa?
[p0310-l0031] [8.5pt] per_clf = Perceptron()
[p0310-l0032] [8.5pt] per_clf.fit(X, y)
[p0310-l0033] [8.0pt] 7 Note that this solution is generally not unique: in general when the data are linearly separable, there is an
[p0310-l0034] [8.0pt] infinity of hyperplanes that can separate them.
[p0310-l0035] [9.0pt] 284
[p0310-l0036] [9.0pt] |
[p0310-l0037] [9.0pt] Chapter 10: Introduction to Artificial Neural Networks with Keras

=== PDF page 311 / printed label 285 ===
[p0311-l0001] [8.5pt] y_pred = per_clf.predict([[2, 0.5]])
[p0311-l0002] [10.5pt] You may have noticed the fact that the Perceptron learning algorithm strongly resem‐
[p0311-l0003] [10.5pt] bles Stochastic Gradient Descent. In fact, Scikit-Learn’s Perceptron class is equivalent
[p0311-l0004] [10.5pt] to using an SGDClassifier with the following hyperparameters: loss="perceptron",
[p0311-l0005] [10.5pt] learning_rate="constant", eta0=1 (the learning rate), and penalty=None (no regu‐
[p0311-l0006] [10.5pt] larization).
[p0311-l0007] [10.5pt] Note that contrary to Logistic Regression classifiers, Perceptrons do not output a class
[p0311-l0008] [10.5pt] probability; rather, they just make predictions based on a hard threshold. This is one
[p0311-l0009] [10.5pt] of the good reasons to prefer Logistic Regression over Perceptrons.
[p0311-l0010] [10.5pt] In their 1969 monograph titled Perceptrons, Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert
[p0311-l0011] [10.5pt] highlighted a number of serious weaknesses of Perceptrons, in particular the fact that
[p0311-l0012] [10.5pt] they are incapable of solving some trivial problems (e.g., the Exclusive OR (XOR)
[p0311-l0013] [10.5pt] classification problem; see the left side of Figure 10-6). Of course this is true of any
[p0311-l0014] [10.5pt] other linear classification model as well (such as Logistic Regression classifiers), but
[p0311-l0015] [10.5pt] researchers had expected much more from Perceptrons, and their disappointment
[p0311-l0016] [10.5pt] was great, and many researchers dropped neural networks altogether in favor of
[p0311-l0017] [10.5pt] higher-level problems such as logic, problem solving, and search.
[p0311-l0018] [10.5pt] However, it turns out that some of the limitations of Perceptrons can be eliminated by
[p0311-l0019] [10.5pt] stacking multiple Perceptrons. The resulting ANN is called a Multi-Layer Perceptron
[p0311-l0020] [10.5pt] (MLP). In particular, an MLP can solve the XOR problem, as you can verify by com‐
[p0311-l0021] [10.5pt] puting the output of the MLP represented on the right of Figure 10-6: with inputs (0,
[p0311-l0022] [10.5pt] 0) or (1, 1) the network outputs 0, and with inputs (0, 1) or (1, 0) it outputs 1. All
[p0311-l0023] [10.5pt] connections have a weight equal to 1, except the four connections where the weight is
[p0311-l0024] [10.5pt] shown. Try verifying that this network indeed solves the XOR problem!
[p0311-l0025] [10.5pt] Figure 10-6. XOR classification problem and an MLP that solves it
[p0311-l0026] [9.0pt] From Biological to Artificial Neurons
[p0311-l0027] [9.0pt] |
[p0311-l0028] [9.0pt] 285

=== PDF page 312 / printed label 286 ===
[p0312-l0001] [15.77pt] Multi-Layer Perceptron and Backpropagation
[p0312-l0002] [10.5pt] An MLP is composed of one (passthrough) input layer, one or more layers of TLUs,
[p0312-l0003] [10.5pt] called hidden layers, and one final layer of TLUs called the output layer (see
[p0312-l0004] [10.5pt] Figure 10-7). The layers close to the input layer are usually called the lower layers,
[p0312-l0005] [10.5pt] and the ones close to the outputs are usually called the upper layers. Every layer
[p0312-l0006] [10.5pt] except the output layer includes a bias neuron and is fully connected to the next layer.
[p0312-l0007] [10.5pt] Figure 10-7. Multi-Layer Perceptron
[p0312-l0008] [9.6pt] The signal flows only in one direction (from the inputs to the out‐
[p0312-l0009] [9.6pt] puts), so this architecture is an example of a feedforward neural net‐
[p0312-l0010] [9.6pt] work (FNN).
[p0312-l0011] [10.5pt] When an ANN contains a deep stack of hidden layers8, it is called a deep neural net‐
[p0312-l0012] [10.5pt] work (DNN). The field of Deep Learning studies DNNs, and more generally models
[p0312-l0013] [10.5pt] containing deep stacks of computations. However, many people talk about Deep
[p0312-l0014] [10.5pt] Learning whenever neural networks are involved (even shallow ones).
[p0312-l0015] [10.5pt] For many years researchers struggled to find a way to train MLPs, without success.
[p0312-l0016] [10.5pt] But in 1986, David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton and Ronald Williams published a
[p0312-l0017] [10.5pt] groundbreaking paper9 introducing the backpropagation training algorithm, which is
[p0312-l0018] [10.5pt] still used today. In short, it is simply Gradient Descent (introduced in Chapter 4)
[p0312-l0019] [8.0pt] 8 In the 1990s, an ANN with more than two hidden layers was considered deep. Nowadays, it is common to see
[p0312-l0020] [8.0pt] ANNs with dozens of layers, or even hundreds, so the definition of “deep” is quite fuzzy.
[p0312-l0021] [8.0pt] 9 “Learning Internal Representations by Error Propagation,” D. Rumelhart, G. Hinton, R. Williams (1986).
[p0312-l0022] [9.0pt] 286
[p0312-l0023] [9.0pt] |
[p0312-l0024] [9.0pt] Chapter 10: Introduction to Artificial Neural Networks with Keras

=== PDF page 313 / printed label 287 ===
[p0313-l0001] [10.5pt] using an efficient technique for computing the gradients automatically10: in just two
[p0313-l0002] [10.5pt] passes through the network (one forward, one backward), the backpropagation algo‐
[p0313-l0003] [10.5pt] rithm is able to compute the gradient of the network’s error with regards to every sin‐
[p0313-l0004] [10.5pt] gle model parameter. In other words, it can find out how each connection weight and
[p0313-l0005] [10.5pt] each bias term should be tweaked in order to reduce the error. Once it has these gra‐
[p0313-l0006] [10.5pt] dients, it just performs a regular Gradient Descent step, and the whole process is
[p0313-l0007] [10.5pt] repeated until the network converges to the solution.
[p0313-l0008] [9.6pt] Automatically computing gradients is called automatic differentia‐
[p0313-l0009] [9.6pt] tion, or autodiff. There are various autodiff techniques, with differ‐
[p0313-l0010] [9.6pt] ent pros and cons. The one used by backpropagation is called
[p0313-l0011] [9.6pt] reverse-mode autodiff. It is fast and precise, and is well suited when
[p0313-l0012] [9.6pt] the function to differentiate has many variables (e.g., connection
[p0313-l0013] [9.6pt] weights) and few outputs (e.g., one loss). If you want to learn more
[p0313-l0014] [9.6pt] about autodiff, check out ???.
[p0313-l0015] [10.5pt] Let’s run through this algorithm in a bit more detail:
[p0313-l0016] [10.5pt] • It handles one mini-batch at a time (for example containing 32 instances each),
[p0313-l0017] [10.5pt] and it goes through the full training set multiple times. Each pass is called an
[p0313-l0018] [10.5pt] epoch, as we saw in Chapter 4.
[p0313-l0019] [10.5pt] • Each mini-batch is passed to the network’s input layer, which just sends it to the
[p0313-l0020] [10.5pt] first hidden layer. The algorithm then computes the output of all the neurons in
[p0313-l0021] [10.5pt] this layer (for every instance in the mini-batch). The result is passed on to the
[p0313-l0022] [10.5pt] next layer, its output is computed and passed to the next layer, and so on until we
[p0313-l0023] [10.5pt] get the output of the last layer, the output layer. This is the forward pass: it is
[p0313-l0024] [10.5pt] exactly like making predictions, except all intermediate results are preserved
[p0313-l0025] [10.5pt] since they are needed for the backward pass.
[p0313-l0026] [10.5pt] • Next, the algorithm measures the network’s output error (i.e., it uses a loss func‐
[p0313-l0027] [10.5pt] tion that compares the desired output and the actual output of the network, and
[p0313-l0028] [10.5pt] returns some measure of the error).
[p0313-l0029] [10.5pt] • Then it computes how much each output connection contributed to the error.
[p0313-l0030] [10.5pt] This is done analytically by simply applying the chain rule (perhaps the most fun‐
[p0313-l0031] [10.5pt] damental rule in calculus), which makes this step fast and precise.
[p0313-l0032] [10.5pt] • The algorithm then measures how much of these error contributions came from
[p0313-l0033] [10.5pt] each connection in the layer below, again using the chain rule—and so on until
[p0313-l0034] [10.5pt] the algorithm reaches the input layer. As we explained earlier, this reverse pass
[p0313-l0035] [10.5pt] efficiently measures the error gradient across all the connection weights in the
[p0313-l0036] [8.0pt] 10 This technique was actually independently invented several times by various researchers in different fields,
[p0313-l0037] [8.0pt] starting with P. Werbos in 1974.
[p0313-l0038] [9.0pt] From Biological to Artificial Neurons
[p0313-l0039] [9.0pt] |
[p0313-l0040] [9.0pt] 287

=== PDF page 314 / printed label 288 ===
[p0314-l0001] [10.5pt] network by propagating the error gradient backward through the network (hence
[p0314-l0002] [10.5pt] the name of the algorithm).
[p0314-l0003] [10.5pt] • Finally, the algorithm performs a Gradient Descent step to tweak all the connec‐
[p0314-l0004] [10.5pt] tion weights in the network, using the error gradients it just computed.
[p0314-l0005] [10.5pt] This algorithm is so important, it’s worth summarizing it again: for each training
[p0314-l0006] [10.5pt] instance the backpropagation algorithm first makes a prediction (forward pass),
[p0314-l0007] [10.5pt] measures the error, then goes through each layer in reverse to measure the error con‐
[p0314-l0008] [10.5pt] tribution from each connection (reverse pass), and finally slightly tweaks the connec‐
[p0314-l0009] [10.5pt] tion weights to reduce the error (Gradient Descent step).
[p0314-l0010] [9.6pt] It is important to initialize all the hidden layers’ connection weights
[p0314-l0011] [9.6pt] randomly, or else training will fail. For example, if you initialize all
[p0314-l0012] [9.6pt] weights and biases to zero, then all neurons in a given layer will be
[p0314-l0013] [9.6pt] perfectly identical, and thus backpropagation will affect them in
[p0314-l0014] [9.6pt] exactly the same way, so they will remain identical. In other words,
[p0314-l0015] [9.6pt] despite having hundreds of neurons per layer, your model will act
[p0314-l0016] [9.6pt] as if it had only one neuron per layer: it won’t be too smart. If
[p0314-l0017] [9.6pt] instead you randomly initialize the weights, you break the symme‐
[p0314-l0018] [9.6pt] try and allow backpropagation to train a diverse team of neurons.
[p0314-l0019] [10.5pt] In order for this algorithm to work properly, the authors made a key change to the
[p0314-l0020] [10.5pt] MLP’s architecture: they replaced the step function with the logistic function, σ(z) =
[p0314-l0021] [10.5pt] 1 / (1 + exp(–z)). This was essential because the step function contains only flat seg‐
[p0314-l0022] [10.5pt] ments, so there is no gradient to work with (Gradient Descent cannot move on a flat
[p0314-l0023] [10.5pt] surface), while the logistic function has a well-defined nonzero derivative every‐
[p0314-l0024] [10.5pt] where, allowing Gradient Descent to make some progress at every step. In fact, the
[p0314-l0025] [10.5pt] backpropagation algorithm works well with many other activation functions, not just
[p0314-l0026] [10.5pt] the logistic function. Two other popular activation functions are:
[p0314-l0027] [10.5pt] The hyperbolic tangent function tanh(z) = 2σ(2z) – 1
[p0314-l0028] [10.5pt] Just like the logistic function it is S-shaped, continuous, and differentiable, but its
[p0314-l0029] [10.5pt] output value ranges from –1 to 1 (instead of 0 to 1 in the case of the logistic func‐
[p0314-l0030] [10.5pt] tion), which tends to make each layer’s output more or less centered around 0 at
[p0314-l0031] [10.5pt] the beginning of training. This often helps speed up convergence.
[p0314-l0032] [10.5pt] The Rectified Linear Unit function: ReLU(z) = max(0, z)
[p0314-l0033] [10.5pt] It is continuous but unfortunately not differentiable at z = 0 (the slope changes
[p0314-l0034] [10.5pt] abruptly, which can make Gradient Descent bounce around), and its derivative is
[p0314-l0035] [10.5pt] 0 for z < 0. However, in practice it works very well and has the advantage of being
[p0314-l0036] [9.0pt] 288
[p0314-l0037] [9.0pt] |
[p0314-l0038] [9.0pt] Chapter 10: Introduction to Artificial Neural Networks with Keras

=== PDF page 315 / printed label 289 ===
[p0315-l0001] [10.5pt] fast to compute11. Most importantly, the fact that it does not have a maximum
[p0315-l0002] [10.5pt] output value also helps reduce some issues during Gradient Descent (we will
[p0315-l0003] [10.5pt] come back to this in Chapter 11).
[p0315-l0004] [10.5pt] These popular activation functions and their derivatives are represented in
[p0315-l0005] [10.5pt] Figure 10-8. But wait! Why do we need activation functions in the first place? Well, if
[p0315-l0006] [10.5pt] you chain several linear transformations, all you get is a linear transformation. For
[p0315-l0007] [10.5pt] example, say f(x) = 2 x + 3 and g(x) = 5 x - 1, then chaining these two linear functions
[p0315-l0008] [10.5pt] gives you another linear function: f(g(x)) = 2(5 x - 1) + 3 = 10 x + 1. So if you don’t
[p0315-l0009] [10.5pt] have some non-linearity between layers, then even a deep stack of layers is equivalent
[p0315-l0010] [10.5pt] to a single layer: you cannot solve very complex problems with that.
[p0315-l0011] [10.5pt] Figure 10-8. Activation functions and their derivatives
[p0315-l0012] [10.5pt] Okay! So now you know where neural nets came from, what their architecture is and
[p0315-l0013] [10.5pt] how to compute their outputs, and you also learned about the backpropagation algo‐
[p0315-l0014] [10.5pt] rithm. But what exactly can you do with them?
[p0315-l0015] [15.77pt] Regression MLPs
[p0315-l0016] [10.5pt] First, MLPs can be used for regression tasks. If you want to predict a single value (e.g.,
[p0315-l0017] [10.5pt] the price of a house given many of its features), then you just need a single output
[p0315-l0018] [10.5pt] neuron: its output is the predicted value. For multivariate regression (i.e., to predict
[p0315-l0019] [10.5pt] multiple values at once), you need one output neuron per output dimension. For
[p0315-l0020] [10.5pt] example, to locate the center of an object on an image, you need to predict 2D coordi‐
[p0315-l0021] [10.5pt] nates, so you need two output neurons. If you also want to place a bounding box
[p0315-l0022] [10.5pt] around the object, then you need two more numbers: the width and the height of the
[p0315-l0023] [10.5pt] object. So you end up with 4 output neurons.
[p0315-l0024] [8.0pt] 11 Biological neurons seem to implement a roughly sigmoid (S-shaped) activation function, so researchers stuck
[p0315-l0025] [8.0pt] to sigmoid functions for a very long time. But it turns out that ReLU generally works better in ANNs. This is
[p0315-l0026] [8.0pt] one of the cases where the biological analogy was misleading.
[p0315-l0027] [9.0pt] From Biological to Artificial Neurons
[p0315-l0028] [9.0pt] |
[p0315-l0029] [9.0pt] 289

=== PDF page 316 / printed label 290 ===
[p0316-l0001] [10.5pt] In general, when building an MLP for regression, you do not want to use any activa‐
[p0316-l0002] [10.5pt] tion function for the output neurons, so they are free to output any range of values.
[p0316-l0003] [10.5pt] However, if you want to guarantee that the output will always be positive, then you
[p0316-l0004] [10.5pt] can use the ReLU activation function, or the softplus activation function in the output
[p0316-l0005] [10.5pt] layer. Finally, if you want to guarantee that the predictions will fall within a given
[p0316-l0006] [10.5pt] range of values, then you can use the logistic function or the hyperbolic tangent, and
[p0316-l0007] [10.5pt] scale the labels to the appropriate range: 0 to 1 for the logistic function, or –1 to 1 for
[p0316-l0008] [10.5pt] the hyperbolic tangent.
[p0316-l0009] [10.5pt] The loss function to use during training is typically the mean squared error, but if you
[p0316-l0010] [10.5pt] have a lot of outliers in the training set, you may prefer to use the mean absolute
[p0316-l0011] [10.5pt] error instead. Alternatively, you can use the Huber loss, which is a combination of
[p0316-l0012] [10.5pt] both.
[p0316-l0013] [9.6pt] The Huber loss is quadratic when the error is smaller than a thres‐
[p0316-l0014] [9.6pt] hold δ (typically 1), but linear when the error is larger than δ. This
[p0316-l0015] [9.6pt] makes it less sensitive to outliers than the mean squared error, and
[p0316-l0016] [9.6pt] it is often more precise and converges faster than the mean abso‐
[p0316-l0017] [9.6pt] lute error.
[p0316-l0018] [10.5pt] Table 10-1 summarizes the typical architecture of a regression MLP.
[p0316-l0019] [10.0pt] Table 10-1. Typical Regression MLP Architecture
[p0316-l0020] [9.0pt] Hyperparameter
[p0316-l0021] [9.0pt] Typical Value
[p0316-l0022] [9.0pt] # input neurons
[p0316-l0023] [9.0pt] One per input feature (e.g., 28 x 28 = 784 for MNIST)
[p0316-l0024] [9.0pt] # hidden layers
[p0316-l0025] [9.0pt] Depends on the problem. Typically 1 to 5.
[p0316-l0026] [9.0pt] # neurons per hidden layer
[p0316-l0027] [9.0pt] Depends on the problem. Typically 10 to 100.
[p0316-l0028] [9.0pt] # output neurons
[p0316-l0029] [9.0pt] 1 per prediction dimension
[p0316-l0030] [9.0pt] Hidden activation
[p0316-l0031] [9.0pt] ReLU (or SELU, see Chapter 11)
[p0316-l0032] [9.0pt] Output activation
[p0316-l0033] [9.0pt] None or ReLU/Softplus (if positive outputs) or Logistic/Tanh (if bounded outputs)
[p0316-l0034] [9.0pt] Loss function
[p0316-l0035] [9.0pt] MSE or MAE/Huber (if outliers)
[p0316-l0036] [15.77pt] Classification MLPs
[p0316-l0037] [10.5pt] MLPs can also be used for classification tasks. For a binary classification problem,
[p0316-l0038] [10.5pt] you just need a single output neuron using the logistic activation function: the output
[p0316-l0039] [10.5pt] will be a number between 0 and 1, which you can interpret as the estimated probabil‐
[p0316-l0040] [10.5pt] ity of the positive class. Obviously, the estimated probability of the negative class is
[p0316-l0041] [10.5pt] equal to one minus that number.
[p0316-l0042] [10.5pt] MLPs can also easily handle multilabel binary classification tasks (see Chapter 3). For
[p0316-l0043] [10.5pt] example, you could have an email classification system that predicts whether each
[p0316-l0044] [10.5pt] incoming email is ham or spam, and simultaneously predicts whether it is an urgent
[p0316-l0045] [9.0pt] 290
[p0316-l0046] [9.0pt] |
[p0316-l0047] [9.0pt] Chapter 10: Introduction to Artificial Neural Networks with Keras

=== PDF page 317 / printed label 291 ===
[p0317-l0001] [10.5pt] or non-urgent email. In this case, you would need two output neurons, both using
[p0317-l0002] [10.5pt] the logistic activation function: the first would output the probability that the email is
[p0317-l0003] [10.5pt] spam and the second would output the probability that it is urgent. More generally,
[p0317-l0004] [10.5pt] you would dedicate one output neuron for each positive class. Note that the output
[p0317-l0005] [10.5pt] probabilities do not necessarily add up to one. This lets the model output any combi‐
[p0317-l0006] [10.5pt] nation of labels: you can have non-urgent ham, urgent ham, non-urgent spam, and
[p0317-l0007] [10.5pt] perhaps even urgent spam (although that would probably be an error).
[p0317-l0008] [10.5pt] If each instance can belong only to a single class, out of 3 or more possible classes
[p0317-l0009] [10.5pt] (e.g., classes 0 through 9 for digit image classification), then you need to have one
[p0317-l0010] [10.5pt] output neuron per class, and you should use the softmax activation function for the
[p0317-l0011] [10.5pt] whole output layer (see Figure 10-9). The softmax function (introduced in Chapter 4)
[p0317-l0012] [10.5pt] will ensure that all the estimated probabilities are between 0 and 1 and that they add
[p0317-l0013] [10.5pt] up to one (which is required if the classes are exclusive). This is called multiclass clas‐
[p0317-l0014] [10.5pt] sification.
[p0317-l0015] [10.5pt] Figure 10-9. A modern MLP (including ReLU and softmax) for classification
[p0317-l0016] [10.5pt] Regarding the loss function, since we are predicting probability distributions, the
[p0317-l0017] [10.5pt] cross-entropy (also called the log loss, see Chapter 4) is generally a good choice.
[p0317-l0018] [10.5pt] Table 10-2 summarizes the typical architecture of a classification MLP.

[p0318-l0014] [10.5pt] Now you have all the concepts you need to start implementing MLPs with Keras!
[p0318-l0015] [18.92pt] Implementing MLPs with Keras
[p0318-l0016] [10.5pt] Keras is a high-level Deep Learning API that allows you to easily build, train, evaluate
[p0318-l0017] [10.5pt] and execute all sorts of neural networks. Its documentation (or specification) is avail‐
[p0318-l0018] [10.5pt] able at https://keras.io. The reference implementation is simply called Keras as well, so
[p0318-l0019] [10.5pt] to avoid any confusion we will call it keras-team (since it is available at https://
[p0318-l0020] [10.5pt] github.com/keras-team/keras). It was developed by François Chollet as part of a
[p0318-l0021] [10.5pt] research project12 and released as an open source project in March 2015. It quickly
[p0318-l0022] [10.5pt] gained popularity owing to its ease-of-use, flexibility and beautiful design. To per‐
[p0318-l0023] [10.5pt] form the heavy computations required by neural networks, keras-team relies on a
[p0318-l0024] [10.5pt] computation backend. At the present, you can choose from three popular open
[p0318-l0025] [10.5pt] source deep learning libraries: TensorFlow, Microsoft Cognitive Toolkit (CNTK) or
[p0318-l0026] [10.5pt] Theano.
[p0318-l0027] [10.5pt] Moreover, since late 2016, other implementations have been released. You can now
[p0318-l0028] [10.5pt] run Keras on Apache MXNet, Apple’s Core ML, Javascript or Typescript (to run Keras
[p0318-l0029] [10.5pt] code in a web browser), or PlaidML (which can run on all sorts of GPU devices, not
[p0318-l0030] [10.5pt] just Nvidia). Moreover, TensorFlow itself now comes bundled with its own Keras
[p0318-l0031] [10.5pt] implementation called tf.keras. It only supports TensorFlow as the backend, but it has
[p0318-l0032] [10.5pt] the advantage of offering some very useful extra features (see Figure 10-10): for
[p0318-l0033] [10.5pt] example, it supports TensorFlow’s Data API which makes it quite easy to load and
[p0318-l0034] [10.5pt] preprocess data efficiently. For this reason, we will use tf.keras in this book. However,
[p0318-l0035] [10.5pt] in this chapter we will not use any of the TensorFlow-specific features, so the code
[p0318-l0036] [10.5pt] should run fine on other Keras implementations as well (at least in Python), with only
[p0318-l0037] [10.5pt] minor modifications, such as changing the imports.
[p0318-l0038] [8.0pt] 12 Project ONEIROS (Open-ended Neuro-Electronic Intelligent Robot Operating System).

[p0320-l0001] [10.5pt] The second version is the version of the Keras API implemented by tf.keras. Note that
[p0320-l0002] [10.5pt] it ends with -tf, highlighting the fact that tf.keras implements the Keras API, plus
[p0320-l0003] [10.5pt] some extra TensorFlow-specific features.
[p0320-l0004] [10.5pt] Now let’s use tf.keras! Let’s start by building a simple image classifier.
[p0320-l0005] [15.77pt] Building an Image Classifier Using the Sequential API
[p0320-l0006] [10.5pt] First, we need to load a dataset. We will tackle Fashion MNIST, which is a drop-in
[p0320-l0007] [10.5pt] replacement of MNIST (introduced in Chapter 3). It has the exact same format as
[p0320-l0008] [10.5pt] MNIST (70,000 grayscale images of 28×28 pixels each, with 10 classes), but the
[p0320-l0009] [10.5pt] images represent fashion items rather than handwritten digits, so each class is more
[p0320-l0010] [10.5pt] diverse and the problem turns out to be significantly more challenging than MNIST.
[p0320-l0011] [10.5pt] For example, a simple linear model reaches about 92% accuracy on MNIST, but only
[p0320-l0012] [10.5pt] about 83% on Fashion MNIST.
[p0320-l0013] [11.56pt] Using Keras to Load the Dataset
[p0320-l0014] [10.5pt] Keras provides some utility functions to fetch and load common datasets, including
[p0320-l0015] [10.5pt] MNIST, Fashion MNIST, the original California housing dataset, and more. Let’s load
[p0320-l0016] [10.5pt] Fashion MNIST:
[p0320-l0017] [8.5pt] fashion_mnist = keras.datasets.fashion_mnist
[p0320-l0018] [8.5pt] (X_train_full, y_train_full), (X_test, y_test) = fashion_mnist.load_data()
[p0320-l0019] [10.5pt] When loading MNIST or Fashion MNIST using Keras rather than Scikit-Learn, one
[p0320-l0020] [10.5pt] important difference is that every image is represented as a 28×28 array rather than a
[p0320-l0021] [10.5pt] 1D array of size 784. Moreover, the pixel intensities are represented as integers (from
[p0320-l0022] [10.5pt] 0 to 255) rather than floats (from 0.0 to 255.0). Here is the shape and data type of the
[p0320-l0023] [10.5pt] training set:
[p0320-l0024] [8.5pt] >>> X_train_full.shape
[p0320-l0025] [8.5pt] (60000, 28, 28)
[p0320-l0026] [8.5pt] >>> X_train_full.dtype
[p0320-l0027] [8.5pt] dtype('uint8')
[p0320-l0028] [10.5pt] Note that the dataset is already split into a training set and a test set, but there is no
[p0320-l0029] [10.5pt] validation set, so let’s create one. Moreover, since we are going to train the neural net‐
[p0320-l0030] [10.5pt] work using Gradient Descent, we must scale the input features. For simplicity, we just
[p0320-l0031] [10.5pt] scale the pixel intensities down to the 0-1 range by dividing them by 255.0 (this also
[p0320-l0032] [10.5pt] converts them to floats):
[p0320-l0033] [8.5pt] X_valid, X_train = X_train_full[:5000] / 255.0, X_train_full[5000:] / 255.0
[p0320-l0034] [8.5pt] y_valid, y_train = y_train_full[:5000], y_train_full[5000:]
[p0320-l0035] [10.5pt] With MNIST, when the label is equal to 5, it means that the image represents the
[p0320-l0036] [10.5pt] handwritten digit 5. Easy. However, for Fashion MNIST, we need the list of class
[p0320-l0037] [10.5pt] names to know what we are dealing with:
[p0320-l0038] [9.0pt] 294
[p0320-l0039] [9.0pt] |

[p0321-l0002] [8.5pt]                "Sandal", "Shirt", "Sneaker", "Bag", "Ankle boot"]
[p0321-l0003] [10.5pt] For example, the first image in the training set represents a coat:
[p0321-l0004] [8.5pt] >>> class_names[y_train[0]]

[p0321-l0008] [11.56pt] Creating the Model Using the Sequential API
[p0321-l0009] [10.5pt] Now let’s build the neural network! Here is a classification MLP with two hidden lay‐
[p0321-l0010] [10.5pt] ers:
[p0321-l0011] [8.5pt] model = keras.models.Sequential()
[p0321-l0012] [8.5pt] model.add(keras.layers.Flatten(input_shape=[28, 28]))
[p0321-l0013] [8.5pt] model.add(keras.layers.Dense(300, activation="relu"))
[p0321-l0014] [8.5pt] model.add(keras.layers.Dense(100, activation="relu"))
[p0321-l0015] [8.5pt] model.add(keras.layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax"))
[p0321-l0016] [10.5pt] Let’s go through this code line by line:
[p0321-l0017] [10.5pt] • The first line creates a Sequential model. This is the simplest kind of Keras
[p0321-l0018] [10.5pt] model, for neural networks that are just composed of a single stack of layers, con‐
[p0321-l0019] [10.5pt] nected sequentially. This is called the sequential API.
[p0321-l0020] [10.5pt] • Next, we build the first layer and add it to the model. It is a Flatten layer whose
[p0321-l0021] [10.5pt] role is simply to convert each input image into a 1D array: if it receives input data
[p0321-l0022] [10.5pt] X, it computes X.reshape(-1, 1). This layer does not have any parameters, it is
[p0321-l0023] [10.5pt] just there to do some simple preprocessing. Since it is the first layer in the model,
[p0321-l0024] [10.5pt] you should specify the input_shape: this does not include the batch size, only the
[p0321-l0025] [10.5pt] shape of the instances. Alternatively, you could add a keras.layers.InputLayer
[p0321-l0026] [10.5pt] as the first layer, setting shape=[28,28].
[p0321-l0027] [10.5pt] • Next we add a Dense hidden layer with 300 neurons. It will use the ReLU activa‐
[p0321-l0028] [10.5pt] tion function. Each Dense layer manages its own weight matrix, containing all the
[p0321-l0029] [10.5pt] connection weights between the neurons and their inputs. It also manages a vec‐
[p0321-l0030] [9.0pt] Implementing MLPs with Keras
[p0321-l0031] [9.0pt] |
[p0321-l0032] [9.0pt] 295

=== PDF page 322 / printed label 296 ===
[p0322-l0001] [10.5pt] tor of bias terms (one per neuron). When it receives some input data, it computes
[p0322-l0002] [10.5pt] Equation 10-2.
[p0322-l0003] [10.5pt] • Next we add a second Dense hidden layer with 100 neurons, also using the ReLU
[p0322-l0004] [10.5pt] activation function.
[p0322-l0005] [10.5pt] • Finally, we add a Dense output layer with 10 neurons (one per class), using the
[p0322-l0006] [10.5pt] softmax activation function (because the classes are exclusive).
[p0322-l0007] [9.6pt] Specifying
[p0322-l0008] [9.6pt] activation="relu"
[p0322-l0009] [9.6pt] is
[p0322-l0010] [9.6pt] equivalent
[p0322-l0011] [9.6pt] to
[p0322-l0012] [9.12pt] activa
[p0322-l0013] [9.6pt] tion=keras.activations.relu. Other activation functions are
[p0322-l0014] [9.6pt] available in the keras.activations package, we will use many of
[p0322-l0015] [9.6pt] them in this book. See https://keras.io/activations/ for the full list.
[p0322-l0016] [10.5pt] Instead of adding the layers one by one as we just did, you can pass a list of layers
[p0322-l0017] [10.5pt] when creating the Sequential model:
[p0322-l0018] [8.5pt] model = keras.models.Sequential([
[p0322-l0019] [8.5pt]     keras.layers.Flatten(input_shape=[28, 28]),
[p0322-l0020] [8.5pt]     keras.layers.Dense(300, activation="relu"),
[p0322-l0021] [8.5pt]     keras.layers.Dense(100, activation="relu"),
[p0322-l0022] [8.5pt]     keras.layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax")
[p0322-l0023] [8.5pt] ])
[p0322-l0024] [15.0pt] Using Code Examples From keras.io
[p0322-l0025] [10.0pt] Code examples documented on keras.io will work fine with tf.keras, but you need to
[p0322-l0026] [10.0pt] change the imports. For example, consider this keras.io code:
[p0322-l0027] [8.5pt] from keras.layers import Dense
[p0322-l0028] [8.5pt] output_layer = Dense(10)
[p0322-l0029] [10.0pt] You must change the imports like this:
[p0322-l0030] [8.5pt] from tensorflow.keras.layers import Dense
[p0322-l0031] [8.5pt] output_layer = Dense(10)
[p0322-l0032] [10.0pt] Or simply use full paths, if you prefer:
[p0322-l0033] [8.5pt] from tensorflow import keras
[p0322-l0034] [8.5pt] output_layer = keras.layers.Dense(10)
[p0322-l0035] [10.0pt] This is more verbose, but I use this approach in this book so you can easily see which
[p0322-l0036] [10.0pt] packages to use, and to avoid confusion between standard classes and custom classes.
[p0322-l0037] [10.0pt] In production code, I use the previous approach, as do most people.

[p0323-l0003] [10.5pt] output shape (None means the batch size can be anything), and its number of parame‐
[p0323-l0004] [10.5pt] ters. The summary ends with the total number of parameters, including trainable and
[p0323-l0005] [10.5pt] non-trainable parameters. Here we only have trainable parameters (we will see exam‐
[p0323-l0006] [10.5pt] ples of non-trainable parameters in Chapter 11):

[p0323-l0022] [10.5pt] Note that Dense layers often have a lot of parameters. For example, the first hidden
[p0323-l0023] [10.5pt] layer has 784 × 300 connection weights, plus 300 bias terms, which adds up to
[p0323-l0024] [10.5pt] 235,500 parameters! This gives the model quite a lot of flexibility to fit the training
[p0323-l0025] [10.5pt] data, but it also means that the model runs the risk of overfitting, especially when you
[p0323-l0026] [10.5pt] do not have a lot of training data. We will come back to this later.
[p0323-l0027] [10.5pt] You can easily get a model’s list of layers, to fetch a layer by its index, or you can fetch
[p0323-l0028] [10.5pt] it by name:
[p0323-l0029] [8.5pt] >>> model.layers
[p0323-l0030] [8.5pt] [<tensorflow.python.keras.layers.core.Flatten at 0x132414e48>,

[p0323-l0032] [8.5pt]  <tensorflow.python.keras.layers.core.Dense at 0x1356ba8d0>,
[p0323-l0033] [8.5pt]  <tensorflow.python.keras.layers.core.Dense at 0x13240d240>]
[p0323-l0034] [8.5pt] >>> model.layers[1].name
[p0323-l0035] [8.5pt] 'dense_3'
[p0323-l0036] [8.5pt] >>> model.get_layer('dense_3').name
[p0323-l0037] [8.5pt] 'dense_3'

[p0323-l0040] [10.5pt] and the bias terms:

[p0324-l0014] [10.5pt] Notice that the Dense layer initialized the connection weights randomly (which is
[p0324-l0015] [10.5pt] needed to break symmetry, as we discussed earlier), and the biases were just initial‐
