[p0324-l0017] [10.5pt] you can set kernel_initializer (kernel is another name for the matrix of connec‐
[p0324-l0018] [10.5pt] tion weights) or bias_initializer when creating the layer. We will discuss initializ‐
[p0324-l0019] [10.5pt] ers further in Chapter 11, but if you want the full list, see https://keras.io/initializers/.
[p0324-l0020] [9.6pt] The shape of the weight matrix depends on the number of inputs.
[p0324-l0021] [9.6pt] This is why it is recommended to specify the input_shape when
[p0324-l0022] [9.6pt] creating the first layer in a Sequential model. However, if you do
[p0324-l0023] [9.6pt] not specify the input shape, it’s okay: Keras will simply wait until it
[p0324-l0024] [9.6pt] knows the input shape before it actually builds the model. This will
[p0324-l0025] [9.6pt] happen either when you feed it actual data (e.g., during training),
[p0324-l0026] [9.6pt] or when you call its build() method. Until the model is really
[p0324-l0027] [9.6pt] built, the layers will not have any weights, and you will not be able
[p0324-l0028] [9.6pt] to do certain things (such as print the model summary or save the
[p0324-l0029] [9.6pt] model), so if you know the input shape when creating the model, it
[p0324-l0030] [9.6pt] is best to specify it.
[p0324-l0031] [11.56pt] Compiling the Model
[p0324-l0032] [10.5pt] After a model is created, you must call its compile() method to specify the loss func‐
[p0324-l0033] [10.5pt] tion and the optimizer to use. Optionally, you can also specify a list of extra metrics to
[p0324-l0034] [10.5pt] compute during training and evaluation:
[p0324-l0035] [8.5pt] model.compile(loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy",
[p0324-l0036] [8.5pt]               optimizer="sgd",
[p0324-l0037] [8.5pt]               metrics=["accuracy"])
[p0324-l0038] [9.0pt] 298
[p0324-l0039] [9.0pt] |
[p0324-l0040] [9.0pt] Chapter 10: Introduction to Artificial Neural Networks with Keras

=== PDF page 325 / printed label 299 ===
[p0325-l0001] [9.6pt] Using loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy" is equivalent to
[p0325-l0002] [9.6pt] loss=keras.losses.sparse_categorical_crossentropy.
[p0325-l0003] [9.6pt] Simi‐
[p0325-l0004] [9.6pt] larly, optimizer="sgd" is equivalent to optimizer=keras.optimiz
[p0325-l0005] [9.6pt] ers.SGD()
[p0325-l0006] [9.6pt] and
[p0325-l0007] [9.6pt] metrics=["accuracy"]
[p0325-l0008] [9.6pt] is
[p0325-l0009] [9.6pt] equivalent
[p0325-l0010] [9.6pt] to
[p0325-l0011] [9.6pt] metrics=[keras.metrics.sparse_categorical_accuracy] (when
[p0325-l0012] [9.6pt] using this loss). We will use many other losses, optimizers and met‐
[p0325-l0013] [9.6pt] rics in this book, but for the full lists see https://keras.io/losses/,
[p0325-l0014] [9.6pt] https://keras.io/optimizers/ and https://keras.io/metrics/.
[p0325-l0015] [10.5pt] This requires some explanation. First, we use the "sparse_categorical_crossen
[p0325-l0016] [10.5pt] tropy" loss because we have sparse labels (i.e., for each instance there is just a target
[p0325-l0017] [10.5pt] class index, from 0 to 9 in this case), and the classes are exclusive. If instead we had
[p0325-l0018] [10.5pt] one target probability per class for each instance (such as one-hot vectors, e.g. [0.,
[p0325-l0019] [10.5pt] 0., 0., 1., 0., 0., 0., 0., 0., 0.] to represent class 3), then we would need
[p0325-l0020] [10.5pt] to use the "categorical_crossentropy" loss instead. If we were doing binary classi‐
[p0325-l0021] [10.5pt] fication (with one or more binary labels), then we would use the "sigmoid" (i.e.,
[p0325-l0022] [10.5pt] logistic) activation function in the output layer instead of the "softmax" activation
[p0325-l0023] [10.5pt] function, and we would use the "binary_crossentropy" loss.
[p0325-l0024] [9.6pt] If you want to convert sparse labels (i.e., class indices) to one-hot
[p0325-l0025] [9.6pt] vector labels, you can use the keras.utils.to_categorical()
[p0325-l0026] [9.6pt] function. To go the other way round, you can just use the np.arg
[p0325-l0027] [9.6pt] max() function with axis=1.
[p0325-l0028] [10.5pt] Secondly, regarding the optimizer, "sgd" simply means that we will train the model
[p0325-l0029] [10.5pt] using simple Stochastic Gradient Descent. In other words, Keras will perform the
[p0325-l0030] [10.5pt] backpropagation algorithm described earlier (i.e., reverse-mode autodiff + Gradient
[p0325-l0031] [10.5pt] Descent). We will discuss more efficient optimizers in Chapter 11 (they improve the
[p0325-l0032] [10.5pt] Gradient Descent part, not the autodiff).
[p0325-l0033] [10.5pt] Finally, since this is a classifier, it’s useful to measure its "accuracy" during training
[p0325-l0034] [10.5pt] and evaluation.
[p0325-l0035] [11.56pt] Training and Evaluating the Model
[p0325-l0036] [10.5pt] Now the model is ready to be trained. For this we simply need to call its fit()
[p0325-l0037] [10.5pt] method. We pass it the input features (X_train) and the target classes (y_train), as
[p0325-l0038] [10.5pt] well as the number of epochs to train (or else it would default to just 1, which would
[p0325-l0039] [10.5pt] definitely not be enough to converge to a good solution). We also pass a validation set
[p0325-l0040] [10.5pt] (this is optional): Keras will measure the loss and the extra metrics on this set at the
[p0325-l0041] [10.5pt] end of each epoch, which is very useful to see how well the model really performs: if
[p0325-l0042] [10.5pt] the performance on the training set is much better than on the validation set, your

[p0326-l0024] [9.6pt] Instead of passing a validation set using the validation_data

[p0326-l0027] [10.5pt] If the training set was very skewed, with some classes being overrepresented and oth‐
[p0326-l0028] [10.5pt] ers underrepresented, it would be useful to set the class_weight argument when
[p0326-l0029] [10.5pt] calling the fit() method, giving a larger weight to underrepresented classes, and a
[p0326-l0030] [10.5pt] lower weight to overrepresented classes. These weights would be used by Keras when
[p0326-l0031] [10.5pt] computing the loss. If you need per-instance weights instead, you can set the sam
[p0326-l0032] [10.5pt] ple_weight argument (it supersedes class_weight). This could be useful for exam‐
[p0326-l0033] [10.5pt] ple if some instances were labeled by experts while others were labeled using a
[p0326-l0034] [10.5pt] crowdsourcing platform: you might want to give more weight to the former. You can
[p0326-l0035] [10.5pt] also provide sample weights (but not class weights) for the validation set by adding
[p0326-l0036] [10.5pt] them as a third item in the validation_data tuple.
[p0326-l0037] [10.5pt] The fit() method returns a History object containing the training parameters (his

[p0326-l0040] [10.5pt] measured at the end of each epoch on the training set and on the validation set (if

[p0329-l0004] [10.5pt] Now you know how to build, train, evaluate and use a classification MLP using the
[p0329-l0005] [10.5pt] Sequential API. But what about regression?
[p0329-l0006] [15.77pt] Building a Regression MLP Using the Sequential API
[p0329-l0007] [10.5pt] Let’s switch to the California housing problem and tackle it using a regression neural
[p0329-l0008] [10.5pt] network. For simplicity, we will use Scikit-Learn’s fetch_california_housing()
[p0329-l0009] [10.5pt] function to load the data: this dataset is simpler than the one we used in Chapter 2,
[p0329-l0010] [10.5pt] since it contains only numerical features (there is no ocean_proximity feature), and
[p0329-l0011] [10.5pt] there is no missing value. After loading the data, we split it into a training set, a vali‐
[p0329-l0012] [10.5pt] dation set and a test set, and we scale all the features:
[p0329-l0013] [8.5pt] from sklearn.datasets import fetch_california_housing
[p0329-l0014] [8.5pt] from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
[p0329-l0015] [8.5pt] from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
[p0329-l0016] [8.5pt] housing = fetch_california_housing()
[p0329-l0017] [8.5pt] X_train_full, X_test, y_train_full, y_test = train_test_split(
[p0329-l0018] [8.5pt]     housing.data, housing.target)
[p0329-l0019] [8.5pt] X_train, X_valid, y_train, y_valid = train_test_split(
[p0329-l0020] [8.5pt]     X_train_full, y_train_full)
[p0329-l0021] [8.5pt] scaler = StandardScaler()
[p0329-l0022] [8.5pt] X_train_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X_train)
[p0329-l0023] [8.5pt] X_valid_scaled = scaler.transform(X_valid)
[p0329-l0024] [8.5pt] X_test_scaled = scaler.transform(X_test)
[p0329-l0025] [10.5pt] Building, training, evaluating and using a regression MLP using the Sequential API to
[p0329-l0026] [10.5pt] make predictions is quite similar to what we did for classification. The main differ‐
[p0329-l0027] [10.5pt] ences are the fact that the output layer has a single neuron (since we only want to
[p0329-l0028] [10.5pt] predict a single value) and uses no activation function, and the loss function is the
[p0329-l0029] [10.5pt] mean squared error. Since the dataset is quite noisy, we just use a single hidden layer
[p0329-l0030] [10.5pt] with fewer neurons than before, to avoid overfitting:
[p0329-l0031] [8.5pt] model = keras.models.Sequential([
[p0329-l0032] [8.5pt]     keras.layers.Dense(30, activation="relu", input_shape=X_train.shape[1:]),
[p0329-l0033] [8.5pt]     keras.layers.Dense(1)
[p0329-l0034] [8.5pt] ])
[p0329-l0035] [8.5pt] model.compile(loss="mean_squared_error", optimizer="sgd")

[p0330-l0001] [10.5pt] As you can see, the Sequential API is quite easy to use. However, although sequential
[p0330-l0002] [10.5pt] models are extremely common, it is sometimes useful to build neural networks with
[p0330-l0003] [10.5pt] more complex topologies, or with multiple inputs or outputs. For this purpose, Keras
[p0330-l0004] [10.5pt] offers the Functional API.
[p0330-l0005] [15.77pt] Building Complex Models Using the Functional API
[p0330-l0006] [10.5pt] One example of a non-sequential neural network is a Wide & Deep neural network.
[p0330-l0007] [10.5pt] This neural network architecture was introduced in a 2016 paper by Heng-Tze Cheng
[p0330-l0008] [10.5pt] et al.14. It connects all or part of the inputs directly to the output layer, as shown in
[p0330-l0009] [10.5pt] Figure 10-13. This architecture makes it possible for the neural network to learn both
[p0330-l0010] [10.5pt] deep patterns (using the deep path) and simple rules (through the short path). In
[p0330-l0011] [10.5pt] contrast, a regular MLP forces all the data to flow through the full stack of layers, thus
[p0330-l0012] [10.5pt] simple patterns in the data may end up being distorted by this sequence of transfor‐
[p0330-l0013] [10.5pt] mations.
[p0330-l0014] [8.0pt] 14 “Wide & Deep Learning for Recommender Systems,” Heng-Tze Cheng et al. (2016).
[p0330-l0015] [9.0pt] 304
[p0330-l0016] [9.0pt] |
[p0330-l0017] [9.0pt] Chapter 10: Introduction to Artificial Neural Networks with Keras

=== PDF page 331 / printed label 305 ===
[p0331-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 10-13. Wide and Deep Neural Network
[p0331-l0002] [10.5pt] Let’s build such a neural network to tackle the California housing problem:
[p0331-l0003] [8.5pt] input = keras.layers.Input(shape=X_train.shape[1:])
[p0331-l0004] [8.5pt] hidden1 = keras.layers.Dense(30, activation="relu")(input)
[p0331-l0005] [8.5pt] hidden2 = keras.layers.Dense(30, activation="relu")(hidden1)
[p0331-l0006] [8.5pt] concat = keras.layers.Concatenate()[input, hidden2])
[p0331-l0007] [8.5pt] output = keras.layers.Dense(1)(concat)
[p0331-l0008] [8.5pt] model = keras.models.Model(inputs=[input], outputs=[output])
[p0331-l0009] [10.5pt] Let’s go through each line of this code:
[p0331-l0010] [10.5pt] • First, we need to create an Input object. This is needed because we may have
[p0331-l0011] [10.5pt] multiple inputs, as we will see later.
[p0331-l0012] [10.5pt] • Next, we create a Dense layer with 30 neurons and using the ReLU activation
[p0331-l0013] [10.5pt] function. As soon as it is created, notice that we call it like a function, passing it
[p0331-l0014] [10.5pt] the input. This is why this is called the Functional API. Note that we are just tell‐
[p0331-l0015] [9.0pt] Implementing MLPs with Keras
[p0331-l0016] [9.0pt] |
[p0331-l0017] [9.0pt] 305

=== PDF page 332 / printed label 306 ===
[p0332-l0001] [10.5pt] ing Keras how it should connect the layers together, no actual data is being pro‐
[p0332-l0002] [10.5pt] cessed yet.
[p0332-l0003] [10.5pt] • We then create a second hidden layer, and again we use it as a function. Note
[p0332-l0004] [10.5pt] however that we pass it the output of the first hidden layer.
[p0332-l0005] [10.5pt] • Next, we create a Concatenate() layer, and once again we immediately use it like
[p0332-l0006] [10.5pt] a function, to concatenate the input and the output of the second hidden layer
[p0332-l0007] [10.5pt] (you may prefer the keras.layers.concatenate() function, which creates a Con
[p0332-l0008] [10.5pt] catenate layer and immediately calls it with the given inputs).
[p0332-l0009] [10.5pt] • Then we create the output layer, with a single neuron and no activation function,
[p0332-l0010] [10.5pt] and we call it like a function, passing it the result of the concatenation.
[p0332-l0011] [10.5pt] • Lastly, we create a Keras Model, specifying which inputs and outputs to use.
[p0332-l0012] [10.5pt] Once you have built the Keras model, everything is exactly like earlier, so no need to
[p0332-l0013] [10.5pt] repeat it here: you must compile the model, train it, evaluate it and use it to make
[p0332-l0014] [10.5pt] predictions.
[p0332-l0015] [10.5pt] But what if you want to send a subset of the features through the wide path, and a
[p0332-l0016] [10.5pt] different subset (possibly overlapping) through the deep path (see Figure 10-14)? In
[p0332-l0017] [10.5pt] this case, one solution is to use multiple inputs. For example, suppose we want to
[p0332-l0018] [10.5pt] send 5 features through the deep path (features 0 to 4), and 6 features through the
[p0332-l0019] [10.5pt] wide path (features 2 to 7):
[p0332-l0020] [8.5pt] input_A = keras.layers.Input(shape=[5])
[p0332-l0021] [8.5pt] input_B = keras.layers.Input(shape=[6])
[p0332-l0022] [8.5pt] hidden1 = keras.layers.Dense(30, activation="relu")(input_B)
[p0332-l0023] [8.5pt] hidden2 = keras.layers.Dense(30, activation="relu")(hidden1)
[p0332-l0024] [8.5pt] concat = keras.layers.concatenate([input_A, hidden2])
[p0332-l0025] [8.5pt] output = keras.layers.Dense(1)(concat)
[p0332-l0026] [8.5pt] model = keras.models.Model(inputs=[input_A, input_B], outputs=[output])
[p0332-l0027] [9.0pt] 306
[p0332-l0028] [9.0pt] |

[p0333-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 10-14. Handling Multiple Inputs
[p0333-l0002] [10.5pt] The code is self-explanatory. Note that we specified inputs=[input_A, input_B]
[p0333-l0003] [10.5pt] when creating the model. Now we can compile the model as usual, but when we call
[p0333-l0004] [10.5pt] the fit() method, instead of passing a single input matrix X_train, we must pass a
[p0333-l0005] [10.5pt] pair of matrices (X_train_A, X_train_B): one per input. The same is true for
[p0333-l0006] [10.5pt] X_valid, and also for X_test and X_new when you call evaluate() or predict():
[p0333-l0007] [8.5pt] model.compile(loss="mse", optimizer="sgd")
[p0333-l0008] [8.5pt] X_train_A, X_train_B = X_train[:, :5], X_train[:, 2:]
[p0333-l0009] [8.5pt] X_valid_A, X_valid_B = X_valid[:, :5], X_valid[:, 2:]
[p0333-l0010] [8.5pt] X_test_A, X_test_B = X_test[:, :5], X_test[:, 2:]
[p0333-l0011] [8.5pt] X_new_A, X_new_B = X_test_A[:3], X_test_B[:3]
[p0333-l0012] [8.5pt] history = model.fit((X_train_A, X_train_B), y_train, epochs=20,
[p0333-l0013] [8.5pt]                     validation_data=((X_valid_A, X_valid_B), y_valid))
[p0333-l0014] [8.5pt] mse_test = model.evaluate((X_test_A, X_test_B), y_test)
[p0333-l0015] [8.5pt] y_pred = model.predict((X_new_A, X_new_B))

[p0334-l0001] [10.5pt] There are also many use cases in which you may want to have multiple outputs:
[p0334-l0002] [10.5pt] • The task may demand it, for example you may want to locate and classify the
[p0334-l0003] [10.5pt] main object in a picture. This is both a regression task (finding the coordinates of
[p0334-l0004] [10.5pt] the object’s center, as well as its width and height) and a classification task.
[p0334-l0005] [10.5pt] • Similarly, you may have multiple independent tasks to perform based on the
[p0334-l0006] [10.5pt] same data. Sure, you could train one neural network per task, but in many cases
[p0334-l0007] [10.5pt] you will get better results on all tasks by training a single neural network with
[p0334-l0008] [10.5pt] one output per task. This is because the neural network can learn features in the
[p0334-l0009] [10.5pt] data that are useful across tasks.
[p0334-l0010] [10.5pt] • Another use case is as a regularization technique (i.e., a training constraint whose
[p0334-l0011] [10.5pt] objective is to reduce overfitting and thus improve the model’s ability to general‐
[p0334-l0012] [10.5pt] ize). For example, you may want to add some auxiliary outputs in a neural net‐
[p0334-l0013] [10.5pt] work architecture (see Figure 10-15) to ensure that the underlying part of the
[p0334-l0014] [10.5pt] network learns something useful on its own, without relying on the rest of the
[p0334-l0015] [10.5pt] network.
[p0334-l0016] [10.5pt] Figure 10-15. Handling Multiple Outputs – Auxiliary Output for Regularization
[p0334-l0017] [10.5pt] Adding extra outputs is quite easy: just connect them to the appropriate layers and
[p0334-l0018] [10.5pt] add them to your model’s list of outputs. For example, the following code builds the
[p0334-l0019] [10.5pt] network represented in Figure 10-15:
[p0334-l0020] [9.0pt] 308
[p0334-l0021] [9.0pt] |

[p0335-l0001] [8.5pt] [...] # Same as above, up to the main output layer
[p0335-l0002] [8.5pt] output = keras.layers.Dense(1)(concat)
[p0335-l0003] [8.5pt] aux_output = keras.layers.Dense(1)(hidden2)
[p0335-l0004] [8.5pt] model = keras.models.Model(inputs=[input_A, input_B],
[p0335-l0005] [8.5pt]                            outputs=[output, aux_output])
[p0335-l0006] [10.5pt] Each output will need its own loss function, so when we compile the model we
[p0335-l0007] [10.5pt] should pass a list of losses (if we pass a single loss, Keras will assume that the same
[p0335-l0008] [10.5pt] loss must be used for all outputs). By default, Keras will compute all these losses and
[p0335-l0009] [10.5pt] simply add them up to get the final loss used for training. However, we care much
[p0335-l0010] [10.5pt] more about the main output than about the auxiliary output (as it is just used for reg‐
[p0335-l0011] [10.5pt] ularization), so we want to give the main output’s loss a much greater weight. Fortu‐
[p0335-l0012] [10.5pt] nately, it is possible to set all the loss weights when compiling the model:
[p0335-l0013] [8.5pt] model.compile(loss=["mse", "mse"], loss_weights=[0.9, 0.1], optimizer="sgd")
[p0335-l0014] [10.5pt] Now when we train the model, we need to provide some labels for each output. In
[p0335-l0015] [10.5pt] this example, the main output and the auxiliary output should try to predict the same
[p0335-l0016] [10.5pt] thing, so they should use the same labels. So instead of passing y_train, we just need
[p0335-l0017] [10.5pt] to pass (y_train, y_train) (and the same goes for y_valid and y_test):
[p0335-l0018] [8.5pt] history = model.fit(
[p0335-l0019] [8.5pt]     [X_train_A, X_train_B], [y_train, y_train], epochs=20,
[p0335-l0020] [8.5pt]     validation_data=([X_valid_A, X_valid_B], [y_valid, y_valid]))
[p0335-l0021] [10.5pt] When we evaluate the model, Keras will return the total loss, as well as all the individ‐
[p0335-l0022] [10.5pt] ual losses:
[p0335-l0023] [8.5pt] total_loss, main_loss, aux_loss = model.evaluate(
[p0335-l0024] [8.5pt]     [X_test_A, X_test_B], [y_test, y_test])
[p0335-l0025] [10.5pt] Similarly, the predict() method will return predictions for each output:
[p0335-l0026] [8.5pt] y_pred_main, y_pred_aux = model.predict([X_new_A, X_new_B])
[p0335-l0027] [10.5pt] As you can see, you can build any sort of architecture you want quite easily with the
[p0335-l0028] [10.5pt] Functional API. Let’s look at one last way you can build Keras models.
[p0335-l0029] [15.77pt] Building Dynamic Models Using the Subclassing API
[p0335-l0030] [10.5pt] Both the Sequential API and the Functional API are declarative: you start by declar‐
[p0335-l0031] [10.5pt] ing which layers you want to use and how they should be connected, and only then
[p0335-l0032] [10.5pt] can you start feeding the model some data for training or inference. This has many
[p0335-l0033] [10.5pt] advantages: the model can easily be saved, cloned, shared, its structure can be dis‐
[p0335-l0034] [10.5pt] played and analyzed, the framework can infer shapes and check types, so errors can
[p0335-l0035] [10.5pt] be caught early (i.e., before any data ever goes through the model). It’s also fairly easy
[p0335-l0036] [10.5pt] to debug, since the whole model is just a static graph of layers. But the flip side is just
[p0335-l0037] [10.5pt] that: it’s static. Some models involve loops, varying shapes, conditional branching,
[p0335-l0038] [10.5pt] and other dynamic behaviors. For such cases, or simply if you prefer a more impera‐
[p0335-l0039] [10.5pt] tive programming style, the Subclassing API is for you.
[p0335-l0040] [9.0pt] Implementing MLPs with Keras
[p0335-l0041] [9.0pt] |
[p0335-l0042] [9.0pt] 309

=== PDF page 336 / printed label 310 ===
[p0336-l0001] [10.5pt] Simply subclass the Model class, create the layers you need in the constructor, and use
[p0336-l0002] [10.5pt] them to perform the computations you want in the call() method. For example, cre‐
[p0336-l0003] [10.5pt] ating an instance of the following WideAndDeepModel class gives us an equivalent
[p0336-l0004] [10.5pt] model to the one we just built with the Functional API. You can then compile it, eval‐
[p0336-l0005] [10.5pt] uate it and use it to make predictions, exactly like we just did.
[p0336-l0006] [8.5pt] class WideAndDeepModel(keras.models.Model):
[p0336-l0007] [8.5pt]     def __init__(self, units=30, activation="relu", **kwargs):
[p0336-l0008] [8.5pt]         super().__init__(**kwargs) # handles standard args (e.g., name)
[p0336-l0009] [8.5pt]         self.hidden1 = keras.layers.Dense(units, activation=activation)
[p0336-l0010] [8.5pt]         self.hidden2 = keras.layers.Dense(units, activation=activation)
[p0336-l0011] [8.5pt]         self.main_output = keras.layers.Dense(1)
[p0336-l0012] [8.5pt]         self.aux_output = keras.layers.Dense(1)
[p0336-l0013] [8.5pt]     def call(self, inputs):
[p0336-l0014] [8.5pt]         input_A, input_B = inputs
[p0336-l0015] [8.5pt]         hidden1 = self.hidden1(input_B)
[p0336-l0016] [8.5pt]         hidden2 = self.hidden2(hidden1)
[p0336-l0017] [8.5pt]         concat = keras.layers.concatenate([input_A, hidden2])
[p0336-l0018] [8.5pt]         main_output = self.main_output(concat)
[p0336-l0019] [8.5pt]         aux_output = self.aux_output(hidden2)
[p0336-l0020] [8.5pt]         return main_output, aux_output
[p0336-l0021] [8.5pt] model = WideAndDeepModel()
[p0336-l0022] [10.5pt] This example looks very much like the Functional API, except we do not need to cre‐
[p0336-l0023] [10.5pt] ate the inputs, we just use the input argument to the call() method, and we separate
[p0336-l0024] [10.5pt] the creation of the layers15 in the constructor from their usage in the call() method.
[p0336-l0025] [10.5pt] However, the big difference is that you can do pretty much anything you want in the
[p0336-l0026] [10.5pt] call() method: for loops, if statements, low-level TensorFlow operations, your
[p0336-l0027] [10.5pt] imagination is the limit (see Chapter 12)! This makes it a great API for researchers
[p0336-l0028] [10.5pt] experimenting with new ideas.
[p0336-l0029] [10.5pt] However, this extra flexibility comes at a cost: your model’s architecture is hidden
[p0336-l0030] [10.5pt] within the call() method, so Keras cannot easily inspect it, it cannot save or clone it,
[p0336-l0031] [10.5pt] and when you call the summary() method, you only get a list of layers, without any
[p0336-l0032] [10.5pt] information on how they are connected to each other. Moreover, Keras cannot check
[p0336-l0033] [10.5pt] types and shapes ahead of time, and it is easier to make mistakes. So unless you really
[p0336-l0034] [10.5pt] need that extra flexibility, you should probably stick to the Sequential API or the
[p0336-l0035] [10.5pt] Functional API.
[p0336-l0036] [8.0pt] 15 Keras models have an output attribute, so we cannot use that name for the main output layer, which is why
[p0336-l0037] [8.0pt] we renamed it to main_output.
[p0336-l0038] [9.0pt] 310
[p0336-l0039] [9.0pt] |
[p0336-l0040] [9.0pt] Chapter 10: Introduction to Artificial Neural Networks with Keras

[p0337-l0001] [9.6pt] Keras models can be used just like regular layers, so you can easily
[p0337-l0002] [9.6pt] compose them to build complex architectures.
[p0337-l0003] [10.5pt] Now that you know how to build and train neural nets using Keras, you will want to
[p0337-l0004] [10.5pt] save them!
[p0337-l0005] [15.77pt] Saving and Restoring a Model
[p0337-l0006] [10.5pt] Saving a trained Keras model is as simple as it gets:
[p0337-l0007] [8.5pt] model.save("my_keras_model.h5")
[p0337-l0008] [10.5pt] Keras will save both the model’s architecture (including every layer’s hyperparame‐
[p0337-l0009] [10.5pt] ters) and the value of all the model parameters for every layer (e.g., connection
[p0337-l0010] [10.5pt] weights and biases), using the HDF5 format. It also saves the optimizer (including its
[p0337-l0011] [10.5pt] hyperparameters and any state it may have).
[p0337-l0012] [10.5pt] You will typically have a script that trains a model and saves it, and one or more
[p0337-l0013] [10.5pt] scripts (or web services) that load the model and use it to make predictions. Loading
[p0337-l0014] [10.5pt] the model is just as easy:
[p0337-l0015] [8.5pt] model = keras.models.load_model("my_keras_model.h5")
[p0337-l0016] [9.6pt] This will work when using the Sequential API or the Functional
[p0337-l0017] [9.6pt] API, but unfortunately not when using Model subclassing. How‐
[p0337-l0018] [9.6pt] ever, you can use save_weights() and load_weights() to at least
[p0337-l0019] [9.6pt] save and restore the model parameters (but you will need to save
[p0337-l0020] [9.6pt] and restore everything else yourself).
[p0337-l0021] [10.5pt] But what if training lasts several hours? This is quite common, especially when train‐
[p0337-l0022] [10.5pt] ing on large datasets. In this case, you should not only save your model at the end of
[p0337-l0023] [10.5pt] training, but also save checkpoints at regular intervals during training. But how can
[p0337-l0024] [10.5pt] you tell the fit() method to save checkpoints? The answer is: using callbacks.
[p0337-l0025] [15.77pt] Using Callbacks
[p0337-l0026] [10.5pt] The fit() method accepts a callbacks argument that lets you specify a list of objects
[p0337-l0027] [10.5pt] that Keras will call during training at the start and end of training, at the start and end
[p0337-l0028] [10.5pt] of each epoch and even before and after processing each batch. For example, the Mod
[p0337-l0029] [10.5pt] elCheckpoint callback saves checkpoints of your model at regular intervals during
[p0337-l0030] [10.5pt] training, by default at the end of each epoch:
[p0337-l0031] [9.0pt] Implementing MLPs with Keras
[p0337-l0032] [9.0pt] |
[p0337-l0033] [9.0pt] 311

=== PDF page 338 / printed label 312 ===
[p0338-l0001] [8.5pt] [...] # build and compile the model
[p0338-l0002] [8.5pt] checkpoint_cb = keras.callbacks.ModelCheckpoint("my_keras_model.h5")
[p0338-l0003] [8.5pt] history = model.fit(X_train, y_train, epochs=10, callbacks=[checkpoint_cb])
[p0338-l0004] [10.5pt] Moreover, if you use a validation set during training, you can set
[p0338-l0005] [10.5pt] save_best_only=True when creating the ModelCheckpoint. In this case, it will only
[p0338-l0006] [10.5pt] save your model when its performance on the validation set is the best so far. This
[p0338-l0007] [10.5pt] way, you do not need to worry about training for too long and overfitting the training
[p0338-l0008] [10.5pt] set: simply restore the last model saved after training, and this will be the best model
[p0338-l0009] [10.5pt] on the validation set. This is a simple way to implement early stopping (introduced in
[p0338-l0010] [10.5pt] Chapter 4):
[p0338-l0011] [8.5pt] checkpoint_cb = keras.callbacks.ModelCheckpoint("my_keras_model.h5",
[p0338-l0012] [8.5pt]                                                 save_best_only=True)
[p0338-l0013] [8.5pt] history = model.fit(X_train, y_train, epochs=10,
[p0338-l0014] [8.5pt]                     validation_data=(X_valid, y_valid),
[p0338-l0015] [8.5pt]                     callbacks=[checkpoint_cb])
[p0338-l0016] [8.5pt] model = keras.models.load_model("my_keras_model.h5") # rollback to best model
[p0338-l0017] [10.5pt] Another way to implement early stopping is to simply use the EarlyStopping call‐
[p0338-l0018] [10.5pt] back. It will interrupt training when it measures no progress on the validation set for
[p0338-l0019] [10.5pt] a number of epochs (defined by the patience argument), and it will optionally roll
[p0338-l0020] [10.5pt] back to the best model. You can combine both callbacks to both save checkpoints of
[p0338-l0021] [10.5pt] your model (in case your computer crashes), and actually interrupt training early
[p0338-l0022] [10.5pt] when there is no more progress (to avoid wasting time and resources):
[p0338-l0023] [8.5pt] early_stopping_cb = keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping(patience=10,
[p0338-l0024] [8.5pt]                                                   restore_best_weights=True)
[p0338-l0025] [8.5pt] history = model.fit(X_train, y_train, epochs=100,
[p0338-l0026] [8.5pt]                     validation_data=(X_valid, y_valid),
[p0338-l0027] [8.5pt]                     callbacks=[checkpoint_cb, early_stopping_cb])
[p0338-l0028] [10.5pt] The number of epochs can be set to a large value since training will stop automati‐
[p0338-l0029] [10.5pt] cally when there is no more progress. Moreover, there is no need to restore the best
[p0338-l0030] [10.5pt] model saved in this case since the EarlyStopping callback will keep track of the best
[p0338-l0031] [10.5pt] weights and restore them for us at the end of training.
[p0338-l0032] [9.6pt] There are many other callbacks available in the keras.callbacks
[p0338-l0033] [9.6pt] package. See https://keras.io/callbacks/.
[p0338-l0034] [10.5pt] If you need extra control, you can easily write your own custom callbacks. For exam‐
[p0338-l0035] [10.5pt] ple, the following custom callback will display the ratio between the validation loss
[p0338-l0036] [10.5pt] and the training loss during training (e.g., to detect overfitting):
[p0338-l0037] [9.0pt] 312
[p0338-l0038] [9.0pt] |

[p0339-l0001] [8.5pt] class PrintValTrainRatioCallback(keras.callbacks.Callback):
[p0339-l0002] [8.5pt]     def on_epoch_end(self, epoch, logs):
[p0339-l0003] [8.5pt]         print("\nval/train: {:.2f}".format(logs["val_loss"] / logs["loss"]))
[p0339-l0004] [10.5pt] As you might expect, you can implement on_train_begin(), on_train_end(),
[p0339-l0005] [10.5pt] on_epoch_begin(), on_epoch_begin(), on_batch_end() and on_batch_end().
[p0339-l0006] [10.5pt] Moreover, callbacks can also be used during evaluation and predictions, should you
[p0339-l0007] [10.5pt] ever need them (e.g., for debugging). In this case, you should implement
[p0339-l0008] [10.5pt] on_test_begin(),
[p0339-l0009] [10.5pt] on_test_end(),
[p0339-l0010] [10.5pt] on_test_batch_begin(),
[p0339-l0011] [10.5pt] or
[p0339-l0012] [10.5pt] on_test_batch_end() (called by evaluate()), or on_predict_begin(), on_pre
[p0339-l0013] [10.5pt] dict_end(), on_predict_batch_begin(), or on_predict_batch_end() (called by
[p0339-l0014] [10.5pt] predict()).
[p0339-l0015] [10.5pt] Now let’s take a look at one more tool you should definitely have in your toolbox
[p0339-l0016] [10.5pt] when using tf.keras: TensorBoard.
[p0339-l0017] [15.77pt] Visualization Using TensorBoard
[p0339-l0018] [10.5pt] TensorBoard is a great interactive visualization tool that you can use to view the
[p0339-l0019] [10.5pt] learning curves during training, compare learning curves between multiple runs, vis‐
[p0339-l0020] [10.5pt] ualize the computation graph, analyze training statistics, view images generated by
[p0339-l0021] [10.5pt] your model, visualize complex multidimensional data projected down to 3D and
[p0339-l0022] [10.5pt] automatically clustered for you, and more! This tool is installed automatically when
[p0339-l0023] [10.5pt] you install TensorFlow, so you already have it!
[p0339-l0024] [10.5pt] To use it, you must modify your program so that it outputs the data you want to visu‐
[p0339-l0025] [10.5pt] alize to special binary log files called event files. Each binary data record is called a
[p0339-l0026] [10.5pt] summary. The TensorBoard server will monitor the log directory, and it will automat‐
[p0339-l0027] [10.5pt] ically pick up the changes and update the visualizations: this allows you to visualize
[p0339-l0028] [10.5pt] live data (with a short delay), such as the learning curves during training. In general,
[p0339-l0029] [10.5pt] you want to point the TensorBoard server to a root log directory, and configure your
[p0339-l0030] [10.5pt] program so that it writes to a different subdirectory every time it runs. This way, the
[p0339-l0031] [10.5pt] same TensorBoard server instance will allow you to visualize and compare data from
[p0339-l0032] [10.5pt] multiple runs of your program, without getting everything mixed up.
[p0339-l0033] [10.5pt] So let’s start by defining the root log directory we will use for our TensorBoard logs,
[p0339-l0034] [10.5pt] plus a small function that will generate a subdirectory path based on the current date
[p0339-l0035] [10.5pt] and time, so that it is different at every run. You may want to include extra informa‐
[p0339-l0036] [10.5pt] tion in the log directory name, such as hyperparameter values that you are testing, to
[p0339-l0037] [10.5pt] make it easier to know what you are looking at in TensorBoard:
[p0339-l0038] [8.5pt] root_logdir = os.path.join(os.curdir, "my_logs")

[p0339-l0040] [8.5pt]     import time

[p0339-l0042] [8.5pt]     return os.path.join(root_logdir, run_id)

[p0341-l0016] [10.5pt] The flexibility of neural networks is also one of their main drawbacks: there are many
[p0341-l0017] [10.5pt] hyperparameters to tweak. Not only can you use any imaginable network architec‐
[p0341-l0018] [10.5pt] ture, but even in a simple MLP you can change the number of layers, the number of
[p0341-l0019] [10.5pt] neurons per layer, the type of activation function to use in each layer, the weight initi‐
[p0341-l0020] [9.0pt] Fine-Tuning Neural Network Hyperparameters
[p0341-l0021] [9.0pt] |

[p0342-l0001] [10.5pt] alization logic, and much more. How do you know what combination of hyperpara‐
[p0342-l0002] [10.5pt] meters is the best for your task?
[p0342-l0003] [10.5pt] One option is to simply try many combinations of hyperparameters and see which
[p0342-l0004] [10.5pt] one works best on the validation set (or using K-fold cross-validation). For this, one
[p0342-l0005] [10.5pt] approach is simply use GridSearchCV or RandomizedSearchCV to explore the hyper‐
[p0342-l0006] [10.5pt] parameter space, as we did in Chapter 2. For this, we need to wrap our Keras models
[p0342-l0007] [10.5pt] in objects that mimic regular Scikit-Learn regressors. The first step is to create a func‐
[p0342-l0008] [10.5pt] tion that will build and compile a Keras model, given a set of hyperparameters:
[p0342-l0009] [8.5pt] def build_model(n_hidden=1, n_neurons=30, learning_rate=3e-3, input_shape=[8]):
[p0342-l0010] [8.5pt]     model = keras.models.Sequential()
[p0342-l0011] [8.5pt]     options = {"input_shape": input_shape}
[p0342-l0012] [8.5pt]     for layer in range(n_hidden):
[p0342-l0013] [8.5pt]         model.add(keras.layers.Dense(n_neurons, activation="relu", **options))
[p0342-l0014] [8.5pt]         options = {}
[p0342-l0015] [8.5pt]     model.add(keras.layers.Dense(1, **options))
[p0342-l0016] [8.5pt]     optimizer = keras.optimizers.SGD(learning_rate)
[p0342-l0017] [8.5pt]     model.compile(loss="mse", optimizer=optimizer)
[p0342-l0018] [8.5pt]     return model
[p0342-l0019] [10.5pt] This function creates a simple Sequential model for univariate regression (only one
[p0342-l0020] [10.5pt] output neuron), with the given input shape and the given number of hidden layers
[p0342-l0021] [10.5pt] and neurons, and it compiles it using an SGD optimizer configured with the given
[p0342-l0022] [10.5pt] learning rate. The options dict is used to ensure that the first layer is properly given
[p0342-l0023] [10.5pt] the input shape (note that if n_hidden=0, the first layer will be the output layer). It is
[p0342-l0024] [10.5pt] good practice to provide reasonable defaults to as many hyperparameters as you can,
[p0342-l0025] [10.5pt] as Scikit-Learn does.
[p0342-l0026] [10.5pt] Next, let’s create a KerasRegressor based on this build_model() function:
[p0342-l0027] [8.5pt] keras_reg = keras.wrappers.scikit_learn.KerasRegressor(build_model)
[p0342-l0028] [10.5pt] The KerasRegressor object is a thin wrapper around the Keras model built using
[p0342-l0029] [10.5pt] build_model(). Since we did not specify any hyperparameter when creating it, it will
[p0342-l0030] [10.5pt] just use the default hyperparameters we defined in build_model(). Now we can use
[p0342-l0031] [10.5pt] this object like a regular Scikit-Learn regressor: we can train it using its fit()
[p0342-l0032] [10.5pt] method, then evaluate it using its score() method, and use it to make predictions
[p0342-l0033] [10.5pt] using its predict() method. Note that any extra parameter you pass to the fit()
[p0342-l0034] [10.5pt] method will simply get passed to the underlying Keras model. Also note that the
[p0342-l0035] [10.5pt] score will be the opposite of the MSE because Scikit-Learn wants scores, not losses
[p0342-l0036] [10.5pt] (i.e., higher should be better).
[p0342-l0037] [8.5pt] keras_reg.fit(X_train, y_train, epochs=100,
[p0342-l0038] [8.5pt]               validation_data=(X_valid, y_valid),
[p0342-l0039] [8.5pt]               callbacks=[keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping(patience=10)])
[p0342-l0040] [8.5pt] mse_test = keras_reg.score(X_test, y_test)
[p0342-l0041] [8.5pt] y_pred = keras_reg.predict(X_new)

[p0343-l0001] [10.5pt] However, we do not actually want to train and evaluate a single model like this, we
[p0343-l0002] [10.5pt] want to train hundreds of variants and see which one performs best on the validation
[p0343-l0003] [10.5pt] set. Since there are many hyperparameters, it is preferable to use a randomized search
[p0343-l0004] [10.5pt] rather than grid search (as we discussed in Chapter 2). Let’s try to explore the number
[p0343-l0005] [10.5pt] of hidden layers, the number of neurons and the learning rate:
[p0343-l0006] [8.5pt] from scipy.stats import reciprocal
[p0343-l0007] [8.5pt] from sklearn.model_selection import RandomizedSearchCV
[p0343-l0008] [8.5pt] param_distribs = {
[p0343-l0009] [8.5pt]     "n_hidden": [0, 1, 2, 3],
[p0343-l0010] [8.5pt]     "n_neurons": np.arange(1, 100),
[p0343-l0011] [8.5pt]     "learning_rate": reciprocal(3e-4, 3e-2),
[p0343-l0012] [8.5pt] }
[p0343-l0013] [8.5pt] rnd_search_cv = RandomizedSearchCV(keras_reg, param_distribs, n_iter=10, cv=3)
[p0343-l0014] [8.5pt] rnd_search_cv.fit(X_train, y_train, epochs=100,
[p0343-l0015] [8.5pt]                   validation_data=(X_valid, y_valid),
[p0343-l0016] [8.5pt]                   callbacks=[keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping(patience=10)])
[p0343-l0017] [10.5pt] As you can see, this is identical to what we did in Chapter 2, with the exception that
[p0343-l0018] [10.5pt] we pass extra parameters to the fit() method: they simply get relayed to the under‐
[p0343-l0019] [10.5pt] lying Keras models. Note that RandomizedSearchCV uses K-fold cross-validation, so it
[p0343-l0020] [10.5pt] does not use X_valid and y_valid. These are just used for early stopping.
[p0343-l0021] [10.5pt] The exploration may last many hours depending on the hardware, the size of the
[p0343-l0022] [10.5pt] dataset, the complexity of the model and the value of n_iter and cv. When it is over,
[p0343-l0023] [10.5pt] you can access the best parameters found, the best score, and the trained Keras model
[p0343-l0024] [10.5pt] like this:
[p0343-l0025] [8.5pt] >>> rnd_search_cv.best_params_
[p0343-l0026] [8.5pt] {'learning_rate': 0.0033625641252688094, 'n_hidden': 2, 'n_neurons': 42}
[p0343-l0027] [8.5pt] >>> rnd_search_cv.best_score_
[p0343-l0028] [8.5pt] -0.3189529188278931
[p0343-l0029] [8.5pt] >>> model = rnd_search_cv.best_estimator_.model
[p0343-l0030] [10.5pt] You can now save this model, evaluate it on the test set, and if you are satisfied with
[p0343-l0031] [10.5pt] its performance, deploy it to production. Using randomized search is not too hard,
[p0343-l0032] [10.5pt] and it works well for many fairly simple problems. However, when training is slow
[p0343-l0033] [10.5pt] (e.g., for more complex problems with larger datasets), this approach will only
[p0343-l0034] [10.5pt] explore a tiny portion of the hyperparameter space. You can partially alleviate this
[p0343-l0035] [10.5pt] problem by assisting the search process manually: first run a quick random search
[p0343-l0036] [10.5pt] using wide ranges of hyperparameter values, then run another search using smaller
[p0343-l0037] [10.5pt] ranges of values centered on the best ones found during the first run, and so on. This
[p0343-l0038] [10.5pt] will hopefully zoom in to a good set of hyperparameters. However, this is very time
[p0343-l0039] [10.5pt] consuming, and probably not the best use of your time.
[p0343-l0040] [10.5pt] Fortunately, there are many techniques to explore a search space much more effi‐
[p0343-l0041] [10.5pt] ciently than randomly. Their core idea is simple: when a region of the space turns out
[p0343-l0042] [9.0pt] Fine-Tuning Neural Network Hyperparameters
[p0343-l0043] [9.0pt] |
[p0343-l0044] [9.0pt] 317

=== PDF page 344 / printed label 318 ===
[p0344-l0001] [10.5pt] to be good, it should be explored more. This takes care of the “zooming” process for
[p0344-l0002] [10.5pt] you and leads to much better solutions in much less time. Here are a few Python
[p0344-l0003] [10.5pt] libraries you can use to optimize hyperparameters:
[p0344-l0004] [10.5pt] • Hyperopt: a popular Python library for optimizing over all sorts of complex
[p0344-l0005] [10.5pt] search spaces (including real values such as the learning rate, or discrete values
[p0344-l0006] [10.5pt] such as the number of layers).
[p0344-l0007] [10.5pt] • Hyperas, kopt or Talos: optimizing hyperparameters for Keras model (the first
[p0344-l0008] [10.5pt] two are based on Hyperopt).
[p0344-l0009] [10.5pt] • Scikit-Optimize (skopt): a general-purpose optimization library. The Bayes
[p0344-l0010] [10.5pt] SearchCV class performs Bayesian optimization using an interface similar to Grid
[p0344-l0011] [10.5pt] SearchCV.
[p0344-l0012] [10.5pt] • Spearmint: a Bayesian optimization library.
[p0344-l0013] [10.5pt] • Sklearn-Deap: a hyperparameter optimization library based on evolutionary
[p0344-l0014] [10.5pt] algorithms, also with a GridSearchCV-like interface.
[p0344-l0015] [10.5pt] • And many more!
[p0344-l0016] [10.5pt] Moreover, many companies offer services for hyperparameter optimization. For
[p0344-l0017] [10.5pt] example Google Cloud ML Engine has a hyperparameter tuning service. Other com‐
[p0344-l0018] [10.5pt] panies provide APIs for hyperparameter optimization, such as Arimo, SigOpt, Oscar
[p0344-l0019] [10.5pt] and many more.
[p0344-l0020] [10.5pt] Hyperparameter tuning is still an active area of research. Evolutionary algorithms are
[p0344-l0021] [10.5pt] making a comeback lately. For example, check out DeepMind’s excellent 2017 paper16,
[p0344-l0022] [10.5pt] where they jointly optimize a population of models and their hyperparameters. Goo‐
[p0344-l0023] [10.5pt] gle also used an evolutionary approach, not just to search for hyperparameters, but
[p0344-l0024] [10.5pt] also to look for the best neural network architecture for the problem. They call this
[p0344-l0025] [10.5pt] AutoML, and it is already available as a cloud service. Perhaps the days of building
[p0344-l0026] [10.5pt] neural networks manually will soon be over? Check out Google’s post on this topic. In
[p0344-l0027] [10.5pt] fact, evolutionary algorithms have also been used successfully to train individual neu‐
[p0344-l0028] [10.5pt] ral networks, replacing the ubiquitous Gradient Descent! See this 2017 post by Uber
[p0344-l0029] [10.5pt] where they introduce their Deep Neuroevolution technique.
[p0344-l0030] [10.5pt] Despite all this exciting progress, and all these tools and services, it still helps to have
[p0344-l0031] [10.5pt] an idea of what values are reasonable for each hyperparameter, so you can build a
[p0344-l0032] [10.5pt] quick prototype, and restrict the search space. Here are a few guidelines for choosing
[p0344-l0033] [10.5pt] the number of hidden layers and neurons in an MLP, and selecting good values for
[p0344-l0034] [10.5pt] some of the main hyperparameters.

[p0345-l0001] [15.77pt] Number of Hidden Layers
[p0345-l0002] [10.5pt] For many problems, you can just begin with a single hidden layer and you will get
[p0345-l0003] [10.5pt] reasonable results. It has actually been shown that an MLP with just one hidden layer
[p0345-l0004] [10.5pt] can model even the most complex functions provided it has enough neurons. For a
[p0345-l0005] [10.5pt] long time, these facts convinced researchers that there was no need to investigate any
[p0345-l0006] [10.5pt] deeper neural networks. But they overlooked the fact that deep networks have a much
[p0345-l0007] [10.5pt] higher parameter efficiency than shallow ones: they can model complex functions
[p0345-l0008] [10.5pt] using exponentially fewer neurons than shallow nets, allowing them to reach much
[p0345-l0009] [10.5pt] better performance with the same amount of training data.
[p0345-l0010] [10.5pt] To understand why, suppose you are asked to draw a forest using some drawing soft‐
[p0345-l0011] [10.5pt] ware, but you are forbidden to use copy/paste. You would have to draw each tree
[p0345-l0012] [10.5pt] individually, branch per branch, leaf per leaf. If you could instead draw one leaf,
[p0345-l0013] [10.5pt] copy/paste it to draw a branch, then copy/paste that branch to create a tree, and
[p0345-l0014] [10.5pt] finally copy/paste this tree to make a forest, you would be finished in no time. Real-
[p0345-l0015] [10.5pt] world data is often structured in such a hierarchical way and Deep Neural Networks
[p0345-l0016] [10.5pt] automatically take advantage of this fact: lower hidden layers model low-level struc‐
[p0345-l0017] [10.5pt] tures (e.g., line segments of various shapes and orientations), intermediate hidden
[p0345-l0018] [10.5pt] layers combine these low-level structures to model intermediate-level structures (e.g.,
[p0345-l0019] [10.5pt] squares, circles), and the highest hidden layers and the output layer combine these
[p0345-l0020] [10.5pt] intermediate structures to model high-level structures (e.g., faces).
[p0345-l0021] [10.5pt] Not only does this hierarchical architecture help DNNs converge faster to a good sol‐
[p0345-l0022] [10.5pt] ution, it also improves their ability to generalize to new datasets. For example, if you
[p0345-l0023] [10.5pt] have already trained a model to recognize faces in pictures, and you now want to
[p0345-l0024] [10.5pt] train a new neural network to recognize hairstyles, then you can kickstart training by
[p0345-l0025] [10.5pt] reusing the lower layers of the first network. Instead of randomly initializing the
[p0345-l0026] [10.5pt] weights and biases of the first few layers of the new neural network, you can initialize
[p0345-l0027] [10.5pt] them to the value of the weights and biases of the lower layers of the first network.
[p0345-l0028] [10.5pt] This way the network will not have to learn from scratch all the low-level structures
[p0345-l0029] [10.5pt] that occur in most pictures; it will only have to learn the higher-level structures (e.g.,
[p0345-l0030] [10.5pt] hairstyles). This is called transfer learning.
[p0345-l0031] [10.5pt] In summary, for many problems you can start with just one or two hidden layers and
[p0345-l0032] [10.5pt] it will work just fine (e.g., you can easily reach above 97% accuracy on the MNIST
[p0345-l0033] [10.5pt] dataset using just one hidden layer with a few hundred neurons, and above 98% accu‐
[p0345-l0034] [10.5pt] racy using two hidden layers with the same total amount of neurons, in roughly the
[p0345-l0035] [10.5pt] same amount of training time). For more complex problems, you can gradually ramp
[p0345-l0036] [10.5pt] up the number of hidden layers, until you start overfitting the training set. Very com‐
[p0345-l0037] [10.5pt] plex tasks, such as large image classification or speech recognition, typically require
[p0345-l0038] [10.5pt] networks with dozens of layers (or even hundreds, but not fully connected ones, as
[p0345-l0039] [10.5pt] we will see in Chapter 14), and they need a huge amount of training data. However,
[p0345-l0040] [10.5pt] you will rarely have to train such networks from scratch: it is much more common to
[p0345-l0041] [9.0pt] Fine-Tuning Neural Network Hyperparameters
[p0345-l0042] [9.0pt] |
[p0345-l0043] [9.0pt] 319

=== PDF page 346 / printed label 320 ===
[p0346-l0001] [10.5pt] reuse parts of a pretrained state-of-the-art network that performs a similar task.
[p0346-l0002] [10.5pt] Training will be a lot faster and require much less data (we will discuss this in Chap‐
[p0346-l0003] [10.5pt] ter 11).
[p0346-l0004] [15.77pt] Number of Neurons per Hidden Layer
[p0346-l0005] [10.5pt] Obviously the number of neurons in the input and output layers is determined by the
[p0346-l0006] [10.5pt] type of input and output your task requires. For example, the MNIST task requires 28
[p0346-l0007] [10.5pt] x 28 = 784 input neurons and 10 output neurons.
[p0346-l0008] [10.5pt] As for the hidden layers, it used to be a common practice to size them to form a pyra‐
[p0346-l0009] [10.5pt] mid, with fewer and fewer neurons at each layer—the rationale being that many low-
[p0346-l0010] [10.5pt] level features can coalesce into far fewer high-level features. For example, a typical
[p0346-l0011] [10.5pt] neural network for MNIST may have three hidden layers, the first with 300 neurons,
[p0346-l0012] [10.5pt] the second with 200, and the third with 100. However, this practice has been largely
[p0346-l0013] [10.5pt] abandoned now, as it seems that simply using the same number of neurons in all hid‐
[p0346-l0014] [10.5pt] den layers performs just as well in most cases, or even better, and there is just one
[p0346-l0015] [10.5pt] hyperparameter to tune instead of one per layer—for example, all hidden layers could
[p0346-l0016] [10.5pt] simply have 150 neurons. However, depending on the dataset, it can sometimes help
[p0346-l0017] [10.5pt] to make the first hidden layer bigger than the others.
[p0346-l0018] [10.5pt] Just like for the number of layers, you can try increasing the number of neurons grad‐
[p0346-l0019] [10.5pt] ually until the network starts overfitting. In general you will get more bang for the
[p0346-l0020] [10.5pt] buck by increasing the number of layers than the number of neurons per layer.
[p0346-l0021] [10.5pt] Unfortunately, as you can see, finding the perfect amount of neurons is still somewhat
[p0346-l0022] [10.5pt] of a dark art.
[p0346-l0023] [10.5pt] A simpler approach is to pick a model with more layers and neurons than you
[p0346-l0024] [10.5pt] actually need, then use early stopping to prevent it from overfitting (and other regu‐
[p0346-l0025] [10.5pt] larization techniques, such as dropout, as we will see in Chapter 11). This has been
[p0346-l0026] [10.5pt] dubbed the “stretch pants” approach:17 instead of wasting time looking for pants that
[p0346-l0027] [10.5pt] perfectly match your size, just use large stretch pants that will shrink down to the
[p0346-l0028] [10.5pt] right size.
[p0346-l0029] [15.77pt] Learning Rate, Batch Size and Other Hyperparameters
[p0346-l0030] [10.5pt] The number of hidden layers and neurons are not the only hyperparameters you can
[p0346-l0031] [10.5pt] tweak in an MLP. Here are some of the most important ones, and some tips on how
[p0346-l0032] [10.5pt] to set them:
[p0346-l0033] [10.5pt] • The learning rate is arguably the most important hyperparameter. In general, the
[p0346-l0034] [10.5pt] optimal learning rate is about half of the maximum learning rate (i.e., the learn‐
[p0346-l0035] [8.0pt] 17 By Vincent Vanhoucke in his Deep Learning class on Udacity.com.
[p0346-l0036] [9.0pt] 320
[p0346-l0037] [9.0pt] |
[p0346-l0038] [9.0pt] Chapter 10: Introduction to Artificial Neural Networks with Keras

=== PDF page 347 / printed label 321 ===
[p0347-l0001] [10.5pt] ing rate above which the training algorithm diverges, as we saw in Chapter 4). So
[p0347-l0002] [10.5pt] a simple approach for tuning the learning rate is to start with a large value that
[p0347-l0003] [10.5pt] makes the training algorithm diverge, then divide this value by 3 and try again,
[p0347-l0004] [10.5pt] and repeat until the training algorithm stops diverging. At that point, you gener‐
[p0347-l0005] [10.5pt] ally won’t be too far from the optimal learning rate. That said, it is sometimes
[p0347-l0006] [10.5pt] useful to reduce the learning rate during training: we will discuss this in Chap‐
[p0347-l0007] [10.5pt] ter 11.
[p0347-l0008] [10.5pt] • Choosing a better optimizer than plain old Mini-batch Gradient Descent (and
[p0347-l0009] [10.5pt] tuning its hyperparameters) is also quite important. We will discuss this in Chap‐
[p0347-l0010] [10.5pt] ter 11.
[p0347-l0011] [10.5pt] • The batch size can also have a significant impact on your model’s performance
[p0347-l0012] [10.5pt] and the training time. In general the optimal batch size will be lower than 32 (in
[p0347-l0013] [10.5pt] April 2018, Yann Lecun even tweeted "Friends don’t let friends use mini-batches
[p0347-l0014] [10.5pt] larger than 32“). A small batch size ensures that each training iteration is very
[p0347-l0015] [10.5pt] fast, and although a large batch size will give a more precise estimate of the gradi‐
[p0347-l0016] [10.5pt] ents, in practice this does not matter much since the optimization landscape is
[p0347-l0017] [10.5pt] quite complex and the direction of the true gradients do not point precisely in
[p0347-l0018] [10.5pt] the direction of the optimum. However, having a batch size greater than 10 helps
[p0347-l0019] [10.5pt] take advantage of hardware and software optimizations, in particular for matrix
[p0347-l0020] [10.5pt] multiplications, so it will speed up training. Moreover, if you use Batch Normal‐
[p0347-l0021] [10.5pt] ization (see Chapter 11), the batch size should not be too small (in general no less
[p0347-l0022] [10.5pt] than 20).
[p0347-l0023] [10.5pt] • We discussed the choice of the activation function earlier in this chapter: in gen‐
[p0347-l0024] [10.5pt] eral, the ReLU activation function will be a good default for all hidden layers. For
[p0347-l0025] [10.5pt] the output layer, it really depends on your task.
[p0347-l0026] [10.5pt] • In most cases, the number of training iterations does not actually need to be
[p0347-l0027] [10.5pt] tweaked: just use early stopping instead.
[p0347-l0028] [10.5pt] For more best practices, make sure to read Yoshua Bengio’s great 2012 paper18, which
[p0347-l0029] [10.5pt] presents many practical recommendations for deep networks.
[p0347-l0030] [10.5pt] This concludes this introduction to artificial neural networks and their implementa‐
[p0347-l0031] [10.5pt] tion with Keras. In the next few chapters, we will discuss techniques to train very
[p0347-l0032] [10.5pt] deep nets, we will see how to customize your models using TensorFlow’s lower-level
[p0347-l0033] [10.5pt] API and how to load and preprocess data efficiently using the Data API, and we will
[p0347-l0034] [10.5pt] dive into other popular neural network architectures: convolutional neural networks
[p0347-l0035] [10.5pt] for image processing, recurrent neural networks for sequential data, autoencoders for
[p0347-l0036] [8.0pt] 18 “Practical recommendations for gradient-based training of deep architectures,” Yoshua Bengio (2012).

[p0351-l0001] [16.82pt] CHAPTER 11
[p0351-l0002] [25.22pt] Training Deep Neural Networks
[p0351-l0003] [9.6pt] With Early Release ebooks, you get books in their earliest form—
[p0351-l0004] [9.6pt] the author’s raw and unedited content as he or she writes—so you
[p0351-l0005] [9.6pt] can take advantage of these technologies long before the official
[p0351-l0006] [9.6pt] release of these titles. The following will be Chapter 11 in the final
[p0351-l0007] [9.6pt] release of the book.
[p0351-l0008] [10.5pt] In Chapter 10 we introduced artificial neural networks and trained our first deep
[p0351-l0009] [10.5pt] neural networks. But they were very shallow nets, with just a few hidden layers. What
[p0351-l0010] [10.5pt] if you need to tackle a very complex problem, such as detecting hundreds of types of
[p0351-l0011] [10.5pt] objects in high-resolution images? You may need to train a much deeper DNN, per‐
[p0351-l0012] [10.5pt] haps with 10 layers or much more, each containing hundreds of neurons, connected
[p0351-l0013] [10.5pt] by hundreds of thousands of connections. This would not be a walk in the park:
[p0351-l0014] [10.5pt] • First, you would be faced with the tricky vanishing gradients problem (or the
[p0351-l0015] [10.5pt] related exploding gradients problem) that affects deep neural networks and makes
[p0351-l0016] [10.5pt] lower layers very hard to train.
[p0351-l0017] [10.5pt] • Second, you might not have enough training data for such a large network, or it
[p0351-l0018] [10.5pt] might be too costly to label.
[p0351-l0019] [10.5pt] • Third, training may be extremely slow.
[p0351-l0020] [10.5pt] • Fourth, a model with millions of parameters would severely risk overfitting the
[p0351-l0021] [10.5pt] training set, especially if there are not enough training instances, or they are too
[p0351-l0022] [10.5pt] noisy.
[p0351-l0023] [10.5pt] In this chapter, we will go through each of these problems in turn and present techni‐
[p0351-l0024] [10.5pt] ques to solve them. We will start by explaining the vanishing gradients problem and
[p0351-l0025] [10.5pt] exploring some of the most popular solutions to this problem. Next, we will look at
[p0351-l0026] [10.5pt] transfer learning and unsupervised pretraining, which can help you tackle complex
[p0351-l0027] [9.0pt] 325

=== PDF page 352 / printed label 326 ===
[p0352-l0001] [10.5pt] tasks even when you have little labeled data. Then we will discuss various optimizers
[p0352-l0002] [10.5pt] that can speed up training large models tremendously compared to plain Gradient
[p0352-l0003] [10.5pt] Descent. Finally, we will go through a few popular regularization techniques for large
[p0352-l0004] [10.5pt] neural networks.
[p0352-l0005] [10.5pt] With these tools, you will be able to train very deep nets: welcome to Deep Learning!
[p0352-l0006] [18.92pt] Vanishing/Exploding Gradients Problems
[p0352-l0007] [10.5pt] As we discussed in Chapter 10, the backpropagation algorithm works by going from
[p0352-l0008] [10.5pt] the output layer to the input layer, propagating the error gradient on the way. Once
[p0352-l0009] [10.5pt] the algorithm has computed the gradient of the cost function with regards to each
[p0352-l0010] [10.5pt] parameter in the network, it uses these gradients to update each parameter with a
[p0352-l0011] [10.5pt] Gradient Descent step.
[p0352-l0012] [10.5pt] Unfortunately, gradients often get smaller and smaller as the algorithm progresses
[p0352-l0013] [10.5pt] down to the lower layers. As a result, the Gradient Descent update leaves the lower
[p0352-l0014] [10.5pt] layer connection weights virtually unchanged, and training never converges to a good
[p0352-l0015] [10.5pt] solution. This is called the vanishing gradients problem. In some cases, the opposite
[p0352-l0016] [10.5pt] can happen: the gradients can grow bigger and bigger, so many layers get insanely
[p0352-l0017] [10.5pt] large weight updates and the algorithm diverges. This is the exploding gradients prob‐
[p0352-l0018] [10.5pt] lem, which is mostly encountered in recurrent neural networks (see ???). More gener‐
[p0352-l0019] [10.5pt] ally, deep neural networks suffer from unstable gradients; different layers may learn at
[p0352-l0020] [10.5pt] widely different speeds.
[p0352-l0021] [10.5pt] Although this unfortunate behavior has been empirically observed for quite a while
[p0352-l0022] [10.5pt] (it was one of the reasons why deep neural networks were mostly abandoned for a
[p0352-l0023] [10.5pt] long time), it is only around 2010 that significant progress was made in understand‐
[p0352-l0024] [10.5pt] ing it. A paper titled “Understanding the Difficulty of Training Deep Feedforward
[p0352-l0025] [10.5pt] Neural Networks” by Xavier Glorot and Yoshua Bengio1 found a few suspects, includ‐
[p0352-l0026] [10.5pt] ing the combination of the popular logistic sigmoid activation function and the
[p0352-l0027] [10.5pt] weight initialization technique that was most popular at the time, namely random ini‐
[p0352-l0028] [10.5pt] tialization using a normal distribution with a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1.
[p0352-l0029] [10.5pt] In short, they showed that with this activation function and this initialization scheme,
[p0352-l0030] [10.5pt] the variance of the outputs of each layer is much greater than the variance of its
[p0352-l0031] [10.5pt] inputs. Going forward in the network, the variance keeps increasing after each layer
[p0352-l0032] [10.5pt] until the activation function saturates at the top layers. This is actually made worse by
[p0352-l0033] [10.5pt] the fact that the logistic function has a mean of 0.5, not 0 (the hyperbolic tangent
[p0352-l0034] [10.5pt] function has a mean of 0 and behaves slightly better than the logistic function in deep
[p0352-l0035] [10.5pt] networks).
[p0352-l0036] [8.0pt] 1 “Understanding the Difficulty of Training Deep Feedforward Neural Networks,” X. Glorot, Y Bengio (2010).
[p0352-l0037] [9.0pt] 326
[p0352-l0038] [9.0pt] |
[p0352-l0039] [9.0pt] Chapter 11: Training Deep Neural Networks

=== PDF page 353 / printed label 327 ===
[p0353-l0001] [10.5pt] Looking at the logistic activation function (see Figure 11-1), you can see that when
[p0353-l0002] [10.5pt] inputs become large (negative or positive), the function saturates at 0 or 1, with a
[p0353-l0003] [10.5pt] derivative extremely close to 0. Thus when backpropagation kicks in, it has virtually
[p0353-l0004] [10.5pt] no gradient to propagate back through the network, and what little gradient exists
[p0353-l0005] [10.5pt] keeps getting diluted as backpropagation progresses down through the top layers, so
[p0353-l0006] [10.5pt] there is really nothing left for the lower layers.
[p0353-l0007] [10.5pt] Figure 11-1. Logistic activation function saturation
[p0353-l0008] [15.77pt] Glorot and He Initialization
[p0353-l0009] [10.5pt] In their paper, Glorot and Bengio propose a way to significantly alleviate this prob‐
[p0353-l0010] [10.5pt] lem. We need the signal to flow properly in both directions: in the forward direction
[p0353-l0011] [10.5pt] when making predictions, and in the reverse direction when backpropagating gradi‐
[p0353-l0012] [10.5pt] ents. We don’t want the signal to die out, nor do we want it to explode and saturate.
[p0353-l0013] [10.5pt] For the signal to flow properly, the authors argue that we need the variance of the
[p0353-l0014] [10.5pt] outputs of each layer to be equal to the variance of its inputs,2 and we also need the
[p0353-l0015] [10.5pt] gradients to have equal variance before and after flowing through a layer in the
[p0353-l0016] [10.5pt] reverse direction (please check out the paper if you are interested in the mathematical
[p0353-l0017] [10.5pt] details). It is actually not possible to guarantee both unless the layer has an equal
[p0353-l0018] [10.5pt] number of inputs and neurons (these numbers are called the fan-in and fan-out of the
[p0353-l0019] [10.5pt] layer), but they proposed a good compromise that has proven to work very well in
[p0353-l0020] [10.5pt] practice: the connection weights of each layer must be initialized randomly as
[p0353-l0021] [8.0pt] 2 Here’s an analogy: if you set a microphone amplifier’s knob too close to zero, people won’t hear your voice, but
[p0353-l0022] [8.0pt] if you set it too close to the max, your voice will be saturated and people won’t understand what you are say‐
[p0353-l0023] [8.0pt] ing. Now imagine a chain of such amplifiers: they all need to be set properly in order for your voice to come
[p0353-l0024] [8.0pt] out loud and clear at the end of the chain. Your voice has to come out of each amplifier at the same amplitude
[p0353-l0025] [8.0pt] as it came in.
[p0353-l0026] [9.0pt] Vanishing/Exploding Gradients Problems
[p0353-l0027] [9.0pt] |
[p0353-l0028] [9.0pt] 327

=== PDF page 354 / printed label 328 ===
[p0354-l0001] [10.5pt] described in Equation 11-1, where f anavg = f anin + f anout /2. This initialization
[p0354-l0002] [10.5pt] strategy is called Xavier initialization (after the author’s first name) or Glorot initiali‐
[p0354-l0003] [10.5pt] zation (after his last name).
[p0354-l0004] [10.5pt] Equation 11-1. Glorot initialization (when using the logistic activation function)
[p0354-l0005] [10.0pt] Normal distribution with mean 0 and variance σ2 =
[p0354-l0006] [8.0pt] 1
[p0354-l0007] [8.0pt] fanavg
[p0354-l0008] [10.0pt] Or a uniform distribution between −r and  + r, with r =
[p0354-l0009] [8.0pt] 3
[p0354-l0010] [8.0pt] fanavg
[p0354-l0011] [10.5pt] If you just replace fanavg with fanin in Equation 11-1, you get an initialization strategy
[p0354-l0012] [10.5pt] that was actually already proposed by Yann LeCun in the 1990s, called LeCun initiali‐
[p0354-l0013] [10.5pt] zation, which was even recommended in the 1998 book Neural Networks: Tricks of the
[p0354-l0014] [10.5pt] Trade by Genevieve Orr and Klaus-Robert Müller (Springer). It is equivalent to
[p0354-l0015] [10.5pt] Glorot initialization when fanin = fanout. It took over a decade for researchers to realize
[p0354-l0016] [10.5pt] just how important this trick really is. Using Glorot initialization can speed up train‐
[p0354-l0017] [10.5pt] ing considerably, and it is one of the tricks that led to the current success of Deep
[p0354-l0018] [10.5pt] Learning.
[p0354-l0019] [10.5pt] Some papers3 have provided similar strategies for different activation functions.
[p0354-l0020] [10.5pt] These strategies differ only by the scale of the variance and whether they use fanavg or
[p0354-l0021] [10.5pt] fanin, as shown in Table 11-1 (for the uniform distribution, just compute r =
[p0354-l0022] [10.5pt] 3σ2).
[p0354-l0023] [10.5pt] The initialization strategy for the ReLU activation function (and its variants, includ‐
[p0354-l0024] [10.5pt] ing the ELU activation described shortly) is sometimes called He initialization (after
[p0354-l0025] [10.5pt] the last name of its author). The SELU activation function will be explained later in
[p0354-l0026] [10.5pt] this chapter. It should be used with LeCun initialization (preferably with a normal
[p0354-l0027] [10.5pt] distribution, as we will see).
[p0354-l0028] [10.0pt] Table 11-1. Initialization parameters for each type of activation function
[p0354-l0029] [9.0pt] Initialization Activation functions
[p0354-l0030] [9.0pt] σ² (Normal)
[p0354-l0031] [9.0pt] Glorot
[p0354-l0032] [9.0pt] None, Tanh, Logistic, Softmax 1 / fanavg
[p0354-l0033] [9.0pt] He
[p0354-l0034] [9.0pt] ReLU & variants
[p0354-l0035] [9.0pt] 2 / fanin
[p0354-l0036] [9.0pt] LeCun
[p0354-l0037] [9.0pt] SELU
[p0354-l0038] [9.0pt] 1 / fanin
[p0354-l0039] [10.5pt] By default, Keras uses Glorot initialization with a uniform distribution. You can
[p0354-l0040] [10.5pt] change this to He initialization by setting kernel_initializer="he_uniform" or ker
[p0354-l0041] [10.5pt] nel_initializer="he_normal" when creating a layer, like this:
[p0354-l0042] [8.0pt] 3 Such as “Delving Deep into Rectifiers: Surpassing Human-Level Performance on ImageNet Classification,” K.
[p0354-l0043] [8.0pt] He et al. (2015).

[p0355-l0003] [10.5pt] than fanin, you can use the VarianceScaling initializer like this:
[p0355-l0004] [8.5pt] he_avg_init = keras.initializers.VarianceScaling(scale=2., mode='fan_avg',

[p0355-l0007] [15.77pt] Nonsaturating Activation Functions
[p0355-l0008] [10.5pt] One of the insights in the 2010 paper by Glorot and Bengio was that the vanishing/
[p0355-l0009] [10.5pt] exploding gradients problems were in part due to a poor choice of activation func‐
[p0355-l0010] [10.5pt] tion. Until then most people had assumed that if Mother Nature had chosen to use
[p0355-l0011] [10.5pt] roughly sigmoid activation functions in biological neurons, they must be an excellent
[p0355-l0012] [10.5pt] choice. But it turns out that other activation functions behave much better in deep
[p0355-l0013] [10.5pt] neural networks, in particular the ReLU activation function, mostly because it does
[p0355-l0014] [10.5pt] not saturate for positive values (and also because it is quite fast to compute).
[p0355-l0015] [10.5pt] Unfortunately, the ReLU activation function is not perfect. It suffers from a problem
[p0355-l0016] [10.5pt] known as the dying ReLUs: during training, some neurons effectively die, meaning
[p0355-l0017] [10.5pt] they stop outputting anything other than 0. In some cases, you may find that half of
[p0355-l0018] [10.5pt] your network’s neurons are dead, especially if you used a large learning rate. A neu‐
[p0355-l0019] [10.5pt] ron dies when its weights get tweaked in such a way that the weighted sum of its
[p0355-l0020] [10.5pt] inputs are negative for all instances in the training set. When this happens, it just
[p0355-l0021] [10.5pt] keeps outputting 0s, and gradient descent does not affect it anymore since the gradi‐
[p0355-l0022] [10.5pt] ent of the ReLU function is 0 when its input is negative.4
[p0355-l0023] [10.5pt] To solve this problem, you may want to use a variant of the ReLU function, such as
[p0355-l0024] [10.5pt] the leaky ReLU. This function is defined as LeakyReLUα(z) = max(αz, z) (see
[p0355-l0025] [10.5pt] Figure 11-2). The hyperparameter α defines how much the function “leaks”: it is the
[p0355-l0026] [10.5pt] slope of the function for z < 0, and is typically set to 0.01. This small slope ensures
[p0355-l0027] [10.5pt] that leaky ReLUs never die; they can go into a long coma, but they have a chance to
[p0355-l0028] [10.5pt] eventually wake up. A 2015 paper5 compared several variants of the ReLU activation
[p0355-l0029] [10.5pt] function and one of its conclusions was that the leaky variants always outperformed
[p0355-l0030] [10.5pt] the strict ReLU activation function. In fact, setting α = 0.2 (huge leak) seemed to
[p0355-l0031] [10.5pt] result in better performance than α = 0.01 (small leak). They also evaluated the
[p0355-l0032] [10.5pt] randomized leaky ReLU (RReLU), where α is picked randomly in a given range during
[p0355-l0033] [10.5pt] training, and it is fixed to an average value during testing. It also performed fairly well
[p0355-l0034] [10.5pt] and seemed to act as a regularizer (reducing the risk of overfitting the training set).
[p0355-l0035] [8.0pt] 4 Unless it is part of the first hidden layer, a dead neuron may sometimes come back to life: gradient descent
[p0355-l0036] [8.0pt] may indeed tweak neurons in the layers below in such a way that the weighted sum of the dead neuron’s
[p0355-l0037] [8.0pt] inputs is positive again.
[p0355-l0038] [8.0pt] 5 “Empirical Evaluation of Rectified Activations in Convolution Network,” B. Xu et al. (2015).
[p0355-l0039] [9.0pt] Vanishing/Exploding Gradients Problems
[p0355-l0040] [9.0pt] |
[p0355-l0041] [9.0pt] 329

=== PDF page 356 / printed label 330 ===
[p0356-l0001] [10.5pt] Finally, they also evaluated the parametric leaky ReLU (PReLU), where α is authorized
[p0356-l0002] [10.5pt] to be learned during training (instead of being a hyperparameter, it becomes a
[p0356-l0003] [10.5pt] parameter that can be modified by backpropagation like any other parameter). This
[p0356-l0004] [10.5pt] was reported to strongly outperform ReLU on large image datasets, but on smaller
[p0356-l0005] [10.5pt] datasets it runs the risk of overfitting the training set.
[p0356-l0006] [10.5pt] Figure 11-2. Leaky ReLU
[p0356-l0007] [10.5pt] Last but not least, a 2015 paper by Djork-Arné Clevert et al.6 proposed a new activa‐
[p0356-l0008] [10.5pt] tion function called the exponential linear unit (ELU) that outperformed all the ReLU
[p0356-l0009] [10.5pt] variants in their experiments: training time was reduced and the neural network per‐
[p0356-l0010] [10.5pt] formed better on the test set. It is represented in Figure 11-3, and Equation 11-2
[p0356-l0011] [10.5pt] shows its definition.
[p0356-l0012] [10.5pt] Equation 11-2. ELU activation function
[p0356-l0013] [10.0pt] ELUα z = α exp z −1 if z < 0
[p0356-l0014] [10.0pt] z
[p0356-l0015] [10.0pt] if z ≥0
[p0356-l0016] [8.0pt] 6 “Fast and Accurate Deep Network Learning by Exponential Linear Units (ELUs),” D. Clevert, T. Unterthiner,
[p0356-l0017] [8.0pt] S. Hochreiter (2015).
[p0356-l0018] [9.0pt] 330
[p0356-l0019] [9.0pt] |
[p0356-l0020] [9.0pt] Chapter 11: Training Deep Neural Networks

=== PDF page 357 / printed label 331 ===
[p0357-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 11-3. ELU activation function
[p0357-l0002] [10.5pt] It looks a lot like the ReLU function, with a few major differences:
[p0357-l0003] [10.5pt] • First it takes on negative values when z < 0, which allows the unit to have an
[p0357-l0004] [10.5pt] average output closer to 0. This helps alleviate the vanishing gradients problem,
[p0357-l0005] [10.5pt] as discussed earlier. The hyperparameter α defines the value that the ELU func‐
[p0357-l0006] [10.5pt] tion approaches when z is a large negative number. It is usually set to 1, but you
[p0357-l0007] [10.5pt] can tweak it like any other hyperparameter if you want.
[p0357-l0008] [10.5pt] • Second, it has a nonzero gradient for z < 0, which avoids the dead neurons prob‐
[p0357-l0009] [10.5pt] lem.
[p0357-l0010] [10.5pt] • Third, if α is equal to 1 then the function is smooth everywhere, including
[p0357-l0011] [10.5pt] around z = 0, which helps speed up Gradient Descent, since it does not bounce as
[p0357-l0012] [10.5pt] much left and right of z = 0.
[p0357-l0013] [10.5pt] The main drawback of the ELU activation function is that it is slower to compute
[p0357-l0014] [10.5pt] than the ReLU and its variants (due to the use of the exponential function), but dur‐
[p0357-l0015] [10.5pt] ing training this is compensated by the faster convergence rate. However, at test time
[p0357-l0016] [10.5pt] an ELU network will be slower than a ReLU network.
[p0357-l0017] [10.5pt] Moreover, in a 2017 paper7 by Günter Klambauer et al., called “Self-Normalizing
[p0357-l0018] [10.5pt] Neural Networks”, the authors showed that if you build a neural network composed
[p0357-l0019] [10.5pt] exclusively of a stack of dense layers, and if all hidden layers use the SELU activation
[p0357-l0020] [10.5pt] function (which is just a scaled version of the ELU activation function, as its name
[p0357-l0021] [10.5pt] suggests), then the network will self-normalize: the output of each layer will tend to
[p0357-l0022] [10.5pt] preserve mean 0 and standard deviation 1 during training, which solves the vanish‐
[p0357-l0023] [10.5pt] ing/exploding gradients problem. As a result, this activation function often outper‐
[p0357-l0024] [8.0pt] 7 “Self-Normalizing Neural Networks, " G. Klambauer, T. Unterthiner and A. Mayr (2017).
[p0357-l0025] [9.0pt] Vanishing/Exploding Gradients Problems
[p0357-l0026] [9.0pt] |
[p0357-l0027] [9.0pt] 331

=== PDF page 358 / printed label 332 ===
[p0358-l0001] [10.5pt] forms other activation functions very significantly for such neural nets (especially
[p0358-l0002] [10.5pt] deep ones). However, there are a few conditions for self-normalization to happen:
[p0358-l0003] [10.5pt] • The input features must be standardized (mean 0 and standard deviation 1).
[p0358-l0004] [10.5pt] • Every hidden layer’s weights must also be initialized using LeCun normal initiali‐
[p0358-l0005] [10.5pt] zation. In Keras, this means setting kernel_initializer="lecun_normal".
[p0358-l0006] [10.5pt] • The network’s architecture must be sequential. Unfortunately, if you try to use
[p0358-l0007] [10.5pt] SELU in non-sequential architectures, such as recurrent networks (see ???) or
[p0358-l0008] [10.5pt] networks with skip connections (i.e., connections that skip layers, such as in wide
[p0358-l0009] [10.5pt] & deep nets), self-normalization will not be guaranteed, so SELU will not neces‐
[p0358-l0010] [10.5pt] sarily outperform other activation functions.
[p0358-l0011] [10.5pt] • The paper only guarantees self-normalization if all layers are dense. However, in
[p0358-l0012] [10.5pt] practice the SELU activation function seems to work great with convolutional
[p0358-l0013] [10.5pt] neural nets as well (see Chapter 14).
[p0358-l0014] [9.6pt] So which activation function should you use for the hidden layers
[p0358-l0015] [9.6pt] of your deep neural networks? Although your mileage will vary, in
[p0358-l0016] [9.6pt] general SELU > ELU > leaky ReLU (and its variants) > ReLU > tanh
[p0358-l0017] [9.6pt] > logistic. If the network’s architecture prevents it from self-
[p0358-l0018] [9.6pt] normalizing, then ELU may perform better than SELU (since SELU
[p0358-l0019] [9.6pt] is not smooth at z = 0). If you care a lot about runtime latency, then
[p0358-l0020] [9.6pt] you may prefer leaky ReLU. If you don’t want to tweak yet another
[p0358-l0021] [9.6pt] hyperparameter, you may just use the default α values used by
[p0358-l0022] [9.6pt] Keras (e.g., 0.3 for the leaky ReLU). If you have spare time and
[p0358-l0023] [9.6pt] computing power, you can use cross-validation to evaluate other
[p0358-l0024] [9.6pt] activation functions, in particular RReLU if your network is over‐
[p0358-l0025] [9.6pt] fitting, or PReLU if you have a huge training set.
[p0358-l0026] [10.5pt] To use the leaky ReLU activation function, you must create a LeakyReLU instance like
[p0358-l0027] [10.5pt] this:
[p0358-l0028] [8.5pt] leaky_relu = keras.layers.LeakyReLU(alpha=0.2)
[p0358-l0029] [8.5pt] layer = keras.layers.Dense(10, activation=leaky_relu,
[p0358-l0030] [8.5pt]                            kernel_initializer="he_normal")
[p0358-l0031] [10.5pt] For PReLU, just replace LeakyRelu(alpha=0.2) with PReLU(). There is currently no
[p0358-l0032] [10.5pt] official implementation of RReLU in Keras, but you can fairly easily implement your
[p0358-l0033] [10.5pt] own (see the exercises at the end of Chapter 12).
[p0358-l0034] [10.5pt] For SELU activation, just set
[p0358-l0035] [10.5pt] activation="selu" and
[p0358-l0036] [9.98pt] kernel_initial
[p0358-l0037] [10.5pt] izer="lecun_normal" when creating a layer:
[p0358-l0038] [8.5pt] layer = keras.layers.Dense(10, activation="selu",
[p0358-l0039] [8.5pt]                            kernel_initializer="lecun_normal")
