[p0359-l0001] [15.77pt] Batch Normalization
[p0359-l0002] [10.5pt] Although using He initialization along with ELU (or any variant of ReLU) can signifi‐
[p0359-l0003] [10.5pt] cantly reduce the vanishing/exploding gradients problems at the beginning of train‐
[p0359-l0004] [10.5pt] ing, it doesn’t guarantee that they won’t come back during training.
[p0359-l0005] [10.5pt] In a 2015 paper,8 Sergey Ioffe and Christian Szegedy proposed a technique called
[p0359-l0006] [10.5pt] Batch Normalization (BN) to address the vanishing/exploding gradients problems.
[p0359-l0007] [10.5pt] The technique consists of adding an operation in the model just before or after the
[p0359-l0008] [10.5pt] activation function of each hidden layer, simply zero-centering and normalizing each
[p0359-l0009] [10.5pt] input, then scaling and shifting the result using two new parameter vectors per layer:
[p0359-l0010] [10.5pt] one for scaling, the other for shifting. In other words, this operation lets the model
[p0359-l0011] [10.5pt] learn the optimal scale and mean of each of the layer’s inputs. In many cases, if you
[p0359-l0012] [10.5pt] add a BN layer as the very first layer of your neural network, you do not need to
[p0359-l0013] [10.5pt] standardize your training set (e.g., using a StandardScaler): the BN layer will do it
[p0359-l0014] [10.5pt] for you (well, approximately, since it only looks at one batch at a time, and it can also
[p0359-l0015] [10.5pt] rescale and shift each input feature).
[p0359-l0016] [10.5pt] In order to zero-center and normalize the inputs, the algorithm needs to estimate
[p0359-l0017] [10.5pt] each input’s mean and standard deviation. It does so by evaluating the mean and stan‐
[p0359-l0018] [10.5pt] dard deviation of each input over the current mini-batch (hence the name “Batch
[p0359-l0019] [10.5pt] Normalization”). The whole operation is summarized in Equation 11-3.
[p0359-l0020] [10.5pt] Equation 11-3. Batch Normalization algorithm
[p0359-l0021] [8.0pt] mB
[p0359-l0022] [10.0pt] x i
[p0359-l0023] [10.0pt] 1 .
[p0359-l0024] [10.0pt] μB = 1
[p0359-l0025] [8.0pt] i = 1
[p0359-l0026] [14.14pt] mB ∑
[p0359-l0027] [8.0pt] mB
[p0359-l0028] [8.0pt] 2
[p0359-l0029] [10.0pt] 2 .
[p0359-l0030] [10.0pt] σB
[p0359-l0031] [10.0pt] x i −μB
[p0359-l0032] [8.0pt] i = 1
[p0359-l0033] [10.0pt] 2 = 1
[p0359-l0034] [14.14pt] mB ∑
[p0359-l0035] [10.0pt] x i −μB
[p0359-l0036] [10.0pt] 3 .
[p0359-l0037] [10.0pt] x i =
[p0359-l0038] [10.0pt] 2 + �
[p0359-l0039] [10.0pt] σB
[p0359-l0040] [10.0pt] 4 .
[p0359-l0041] [10.0pt] z i = γ ⊗x i + β
[p0359-l0042] [10.5pt] • μB is the vector of input means, evaluated over the whole mini-batch B (it con‐
[p0359-l0043] [10.5pt] tains one mean per input).
[p0359-l0044] [8.0pt] 8 “Batch Normalization: Accelerating Deep Network Training by Reducing Internal Covariate Shift,” S. Ioffe
[p0359-l0045] [8.0pt] and C. Szegedy (2015).
[p0359-l0046] [9.0pt] Vanishing/Exploding Gradients Problems
[p0359-l0047] [9.0pt] |
[p0359-l0048] [9.0pt] 333

=== PDF page 360 / printed label 334 ===
[p0360-l0001] [10.5pt] • σB is the vector of input standard deviations, also evaluated over the whole mini-
[p0360-l0002] [10.5pt] batch (it contains one standard deviation per input).
[p0360-l0003] [10.5pt] • mB is the number of instances in the mini-batch.
[p0360-l0004] [10.5pt] • x(i) is the vector of zero-centered and normalized inputs for instance i.
[p0360-l0005] [10.5pt] • γ is the output scale parameter vector for the layer (it contains one scale parame‐
[p0360-l0006] [10.5pt] ter per input).
[p0360-l0007] [10.5pt] • ⊗ represents element-wise multiplication (each input is multiplied by its corre‐
[p0360-l0008] [10.5pt] sponding output scale parameter).
[p0360-l0009] [10.5pt] • β is the output shift (offset) parameter vector for the layer (it contains one offset
[p0360-l0010] [10.5pt] parameter per input). Each input is offset by its corresponding shift parameter.
[p0360-l0011] [10.5pt] • ϵ is a tiny number to avoid division by zero (typically 10–5). This is called a
[p0360-l0012] [10.5pt] smoothing term.
[p0360-l0013] [10.5pt] • z(i) is the output of the BN operation: it is a rescaled and shifted version of the
[p0360-l0014] [10.5pt] inputs.
[p0360-l0015] [10.5pt] So during training, BN just standardizes its inputs then rescales and offsets them.
[p0360-l0016] [10.5pt] Good! What about at test time? Well it is not that simple. Indeed, we may need to
[p0360-l0017] [10.5pt] make predictions for individual instances rather than for batches of instances: in this
[p0360-l0018] [10.5pt] case, we will have no way to compute each input’s mean and standard deviation.
[p0360-l0019] [10.5pt] Moreover, even if we do have a batch of instances, it may be too small, or the instan‐
[p0360-l0020] [10.5pt] ces may not be independent and identically distributed (IID), so computing statistics
[p0360-l0021] [10.5pt] over the batch instances would be unreliable (during training, the batches should not
[p0360-l0022] [10.5pt] be too small, if possible more than 30 instances, and all instances should be IID, as we
[p0360-l0023] [10.5pt] saw in Chapter 4). One solution could be to wait until the end of training, then run
[p0360-l0024] [10.5pt] the whole training set through the neural network, and compute the mean and stan‐
[p0360-l0025] [10.5pt] dard deviation of each input of the BN layer. These “final” input means and standard
[p0360-l0026] [10.5pt] deviations can then be used instead of the batch input means and standard deviations
[p0360-l0027] [10.5pt] when making predictions. However, it is often preferred to estimate these final statis‐
[p0360-l0028] [10.5pt] tics during training using a moving average of the layer’s input means and standard
[p0360-l0029] [10.5pt] deviations. To sum up, four parameter vectors are learned in each batch-normalized
[p0360-l0030] [10.5pt] layer: γ (the ouput scale vector) and β (the output offset vector) are learned through
[p0360-l0031] [10.5pt] regular backpropagation, and μ (the final input mean vector), and σ (the final input
[p0360-l0032] [10.5pt] standard deviation vector) are estimated using an exponential moving average. Note
[p0360-l0033] [10.5pt] that μ and σ are estimated during training, but they are not used at all during train‐
[p0360-l0034] [10.5pt] ing, only after training (to replace the batch input means and standard deviations in
[p0360-l0035] [10.5pt] Equation 11-3).
[p0360-l0036] [10.5pt] The authors demonstrated that this technique considerably improved all the deep
[p0360-l0037] [10.5pt] neural networks they experimented with, leading to a huge improvement in the
[p0360-l0038] [10.5pt] ImageNet classification task (ImageNet is a large database of images classified into
[p0360-l0039] [10.5pt] many classes and commonly used to evaluate computer vision systems). The vanish‐
[p0360-l0040] [9.0pt] 334
[p0360-l0041] [9.0pt] |
[p0360-l0042] [9.0pt] Chapter 11: Training Deep Neural Networks

=== PDF page 361 / printed label 335 ===
[p0361-l0001] [10.5pt] ing gradients problem was strongly reduced, to the point that they could use saturat‐
[p0361-l0002] [10.5pt] ing activation functions such as the tanh and even the logistic activation function.
[p0361-l0003] [10.5pt] The networks were also much less sensitive to the weight initialization. They were
[p0361-l0004] [10.5pt] able to use much larger learning rates, significantly speeding up the learning process.
[p0361-l0005] [10.5pt] Specifically, they note that “Applied to a state-of-the-art image classification model,
[p0361-l0006] [10.5pt] Batch Normalization achieves the same accuracy with 14 times fewer training steps,
[p0361-l0007] [10.5pt] and beats the original model by a significant margin. […] Using an ensemble of
[p0361-l0008] [10.5pt] batch-normalized networks, we improve upon the best published result on ImageNet
[p0361-l0009] [10.5pt] classification: reaching 4.9% top-5 validation error (and 4.8% test error), exceeding
[p0361-l0010] [10.5pt] the accuracy of human raters.” Finally, like a gift that keeps on giving, Batch Normal‐
[p0361-l0011] [10.5pt] ization also acts like a regularizer, reducing the need for other regularization techni‐
[p0361-l0012] [10.5pt] ques (such as dropout, described later in this chapter).
[p0361-l0013] [10.5pt] Batch Normalization does, however, add some complexity to the model (although it
[p0361-l0014] [10.5pt] can remove the need for normalizing the input data, as we discussed earlier). More‐
[p0361-l0015] [10.5pt] over, there is a runtime penalty: the neural network makes slower predictions due to
[p0361-l0016] [10.5pt] the extra computations required at each layer. So if you need predictions to be
[p0361-l0017] [10.5pt] lightning-fast, you may want to check how well plain ELU + He initialization perform
[p0361-l0018] [10.5pt] before playing with Batch Normalization.
[p0361-l0019] [9.6pt] You may find that training is rather slow, because each epoch takes
[p0361-l0020] [9.6pt] much more time when you use batch normalization. However, this
[p0361-l0021] [9.6pt] is usually counterbalanced by the fact that convergence is much
[p0361-l0022] [9.6pt] faster with BN, so it will take fewer epochs to reach the same per‐
[p0361-l0023] [9.6pt] formance. All in all, wall time will usually be smaller (this is the
[p0361-l0024] [9.6pt] time measured by the clock on your wall).
[p0361-l0025] [11.56pt] Implementing Batch Normalization with Keras
[p0361-l0026] [10.5pt] As with most things with Keras, implementing Batch Normalization is quite simple.
[p0361-l0027] [10.5pt] Just add a BatchNormalization layer before or after each hidden layer’s activation
[p0361-l0028] [10.5pt] function, and optionally add a BN layer as well as the first layer in your model. For
[p0361-l0029] [10.5pt] example, this model applies BN after every hidden layer and as the first layer in the
[p0361-l0030] [10.5pt] model (after flattening the input images):
[p0361-l0031] [8.5pt] model = keras.models.Sequential([
[p0361-l0032] [8.5pt]     keras.layers.Flatten(input_shape=[28, 28]),
[p0361-l0033] [8.5pt]     keras.layers.BatchNormalization(),
[p0361-l0034] [8.5pt]     keras.layers.Dense(300, activation="elu", kernel_initializer="he_normal"),
[p0361-l0035] [8.5pt]     keras.layers.BatchNormalization(),
[p0361-l0036] [8.5pt]     keras.layers.Dense(100, activation="elu", kernel_initializer="he_normal"),
[p0361-l0037] [8.5pt]     keras.layers.BatchNormalization(),
[p0361-l0038] [8.5pt]     keras.layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax")
[p0361-l0039] [8.5pt] ])
[p0361-l0040] [9.0pt] Vanishing/Exploding Gradients Problems
[p0361-l0041] [9.0pt] |
[p0361-l0042] [9.0pt] 335

[p0362-l0001] [10.5pt] That’s all! In this tiny example with just two hidden layers, it’s unlikely that Batch
[p0362-l0002] [10.5pt] Normalization will have a very positive impact, but for deeper networks it can make a
[p0362-l0003] [10.5pt] tremendous difference.
[p0362-l0004] [10.5pt] Let’s zoom in a bit. If you display the model summary, you can see that each BN layer
[p0362-l0005] [10.5pt] adds 4 parameters per input: γ, β, μ and σ (for example, the first BN layer adds 3136
[p0362-l0006] [10.5pt] parameters, which is 4 times 784). The last two parameters, μ and σ, are the moving
[p0362-l0007] [10.5pt] averages, they are not affected by backpropagation, so Keras calls them “Non-
[p0362-l0008] [10.5pt] trainable”9 (if you count the total number of BN parameters, 3136 + 1200 + 400, and
[p0362-l0009] [10.5pt] divide by two, you get 2,368, which is the total number of non-trainable params in
[p0362-l0010] [10.5pt] this model).

[p0362-l0033] [10.5pt] Let’s look at the parameters of the first BN layer. Two are trainable (by backprop), and
[p0362-l0034] [10.5pt] two are not:
[p0362-l0035] [8.5pt] >>> [(var.name, var.trainable) for var in model.layers[1].variables]
[p0362-l0036] [8.5pt] [('batch_normalization_v2/gamma:0', True),
[p0362-l0037] [8.5pt]  ('batch_normalization_v2/beta:0', True),
[p0362-l0038] [8.5pt]  ('batch_normalization_v2/moving_mean:0', False),
[p0362-l0039] [8.5pt]  ('batch_normalization_v2/moving_variance:0', False)]
[p0362-l0040] [10.5pt] Now when you create a BN layer in Keras, it also creates two operations that will be
[p0362-l0041] [10.5pt] called by Keras at each iteration during training. These operations will update the
[p0362-l0042] [8.0pt] 9 However, they are estimated during training, based on the training data, so arguably they are trainable. In
[p0362-l0043] [8.0pt] Keras, “Non-trainable” really means “untouched by backpropagation”.

[p0363-l0001] [10.5pt] moving averages. Since we are using the TensorFlow backend, these operations are
[p0363-l0002] [10.5pt] TensorFlow operations (we will discuss TF operations in Chapter 12).
[p0363-l0003] [8.5pt] >>> model.layers[1].updates
[p0363-l0004] [8.5pt] [<tf.Operation 'cond_2/Identity' type=Identity>,
[p0363-l0005] [8.5pt]  <tf.Operation 'cond_3/Identity' type=Identity>]
[p0363-l0006] [10.5pt] The authors of the BN paper argued in favor of adding the BN layers before the acti‐
[p0363-l0007] [10.5pt] vation functions, rather than after (as we just did). There is some debate about this, as
[p0363-l0008] [10.5pt] it seems to depend on the task. So that’s one more thing you can experiment with to
[p0363-l0009] [10.5pt] see which option works best on your dataset. To add the BN layers before the activa‐
[p0363-l0010] [10.5pt] tion functions, we must remove the activation function from the hidden layers, and
[p0363-l0011] [10.5pt] add them as separate layers after the BN layers. Moreover, since a Batch Normaliza‐
[p0363-l0012] [10.5pt] tion layer includes one offset parameter per input, you can remove the bias term from
[p0363-l0013] [10.5pt] the previous layer (just pass use_bias=False when creating it):
[p0363-l0014] [8.5pt] model = keras.models.Sequential([
[p0363-l0015] [8.5pt]     keras.layers.Flatten(input_shape=[28, 28]),
[p0363-l0016] [8.5pt]     keras.layers.BatchNormalization(),
[p0363-l0017] [8.5pt]     keras.layers.Dense(300, kernel_initializer="he_normal", use_bias=False),
[p0363-l0018] [8.5pt]     keras.layers.BatchNormalization(),
[p0363-l0019] [8.5pt]     keras.layers.Activation("elu"),
[p0363-l0020] [8.5pt]     keras.layers.Dense(100, kernel_initializer="he_normal", use_bias=False),
[p0363-l0021] [8.5pt]     keras.layers.Activation("elu"),
[p0363-l0022] [8.5pt]     keras.layers.BatchNormalization(),
[p0363-l0023] [8.5pt]     keras.layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax")
[p0363-l0024] [8.5pt] ])
[p0363-l0025] [10.5pt] The BatchNormalization class has quite a few hyperparameters you can tweak. The
[p0363-l0026] [10.5pt] defaults will usually be fine, but you may occasionally need to tweak the momentum.
[p0363-l0027] [10.5pt] This hyperparameter is used when updating the exponential moving averages: given a
[p0363-l0028] [10.5pt] new value v (i.e., a new vector of input means or standard deviations computed over
[p0363-l0029] [10.5pt] the current batch), the running average � is updated using the following equation:
[p0363-l0030] [10.0pt] v
[p0363-l0031] [10.0pt] v × momentum + v × 1 −momentum
[p0363-l0032] [10.5pt] A good momentum value is typically close to 1—for example, 0.9, 0.99, or 0.999 (you
[p0363-l0033] [10.5pt] want more 9s for larger datasets and smaller mini-batches).
[p0363-l0034] [10.5pt] Another important hyperparameter is axis: it determines which axis should be nor‐
[p0363-l0035] [10.5pt] malized. It defaults to –1, meaning that by default it will normalize the last axis (using
[p0363-l0036] [10.5pt] the means and standard deviations computed across the other axes). For example,
[p0363-l0037] [10.5pt] when the input batch is 2D (i.e., the batch shape is [batch size, features]), this means
[p0363-l0038] [10.5pt] that each input feature will be normalized based on the mean and standard deviation
[p0363-l0039] [10.5pt] computed across all the instances in the batch. For example, the first BN layer in the
[p0363-l0040] [10.5pt] previous code example will independently normalize (and rescale and shift) each of
[p0363-l0041] [10.5pt] the 784 input features. However, if we move the first BN layer before the Flatten
[p0363-l0042] [9.0pt] Vanishing/Exploding Gradients Problems
[p0363-l0043] [9.0pt] |
[p0363-l0044] [9.0pt] 337

=== PDF page 364 / printed label 338 ===
[p0364-l0001] [10.5pt] layer, then the input batches will be 3D, with shape [batch size, height, width], there‐
[p0364-l0002] [10.5pt] fore the BN layer will compute 28 means and 28 standard deviations (one per column
[p0364-l0003] [10.5pt] of pixels, computed across all instances in the batch, and all rows in the column), and
[p0364-l0004] [10.5pt] it will normalize all pixels in a given column using the same mean and standard devi‐
[p0364-l0005] [10.5pt] ation. There will also be just 28 scale parameters and 28 shift parameters. If instead
[p0364-l0006] [10.5pt] you still want to treat each of the 784 pixels independently, then you should set
[p0364-l0007] [10.5pt] axis=[1, 2].
[p0364-l0008] [10.5pt] Notice that the BN layer does not perform the same computation during training and
[p0364-l0009] [10.5pt] after training: it uses batch statistics during training, and the “final” statistics after
[p0364-l0010] [10.5pt] training (i.e., the final value of the moving averages). Let’s take a peek at the source
[p0364-l0011] [10.5pt] code of this class to see how this is handled:
[p0364-l0012] [8.5pt] class BatchNormalization(Layer):
[p0364-l0013] [8.5pt]     [...]
[p0364-l0014] [8.5pt]     def call(self, inputs, training=None):
[p0364-l0015] [8.5pt]         if training is None:
[p0364-l0016] [8.5pt]             training = keras.backend.learning_phase()
[p0364-l0017] [8.5pt]         [...]
[p0364-l0018] [10.5pt] The call() method is the one that actually performs the computations, and as you
[p0364-l0019] [10.5pt] can see it has an extra training argument: if it is None it falls back to keras.back
[p0364-l0020] [10.5pt] end.learning_phase(), which returns 1 during training (the fit() method ensures
[p0364-l0021] [10.5pt] that). Otherwise, it returns 0. If you ever need to write a custom layer, and it needs to
[p0364-l0022] [10.5pt] behave differently during training and testing, simply use the same pattern (we will
[p0364-l0023] [10.5pt] discuss custom layers in Chapter 12).
[p0364-l0024] [10.5pt] Batch Normalization has become one of the most used layers in deep neural net‐
[p0364-l0025] [10.5pt] works, to the point that it is often omitted in the diagrams, as it is assumed that BN is
[p0364-l0026] [10.5pt] added after every layer. However, a very recent paper10 by Hongyi Zhang et al. may
[p0364-l0027] [10.5pt] well change this: the authors show that by using a novel fixed-update (fixup) weight
[p0364-l0028] [10.5pt] initialization technique, they manage to train a very deep neural network (10,000 lay‐
[p0364-l0029] [10.5pt] ers!) without BN, achieving state-of-the-art performance on complex image classifi‐
[p0364-l0030] [10.5pt] cation tasks.
[p0364-l0031] [15.77pt] Gradient Clipping
[p0364-l0032] [10.5pt] Another popular technique to lessen the exploding gradients problem is to simply
[p0364-l0033] [10.5pt] clip the gradients during backpropagation so that they never exceed some threshold.
[p0364-l0034] [10.5pt] This is called Gradient Clipping.11 This technique is most often used in recurrent neu‐
[p0364-l0035] [8.0pt] 10 “Fixup Initialization: Residual Learning Without Normalization,” Hongyi Zhang, Yann N. Dauphin, Tengyu
[p0364-l0036] [8.0pt] Ma (2019).
[p0364-l0037] [8.0pt] 11 “On the difficulty of training recurrent neural networks,” R. Pascanu et al. (2013).
[p0364-l0038] [9.0pt] 338
[p0364-l0039] [9.0pt] |
[p0364-l0040] [9.0pt] Chapter 11: Training Deep Neural Networks

=== PDF page 365 / printed label 339 ===
[p0365-l0001] [10.5pt] ral networks, as Batch Normalization is tricky to use in RNNs, as we will see in ???.
[p0365-l0002] [10.5pt] For other types of networks, BN is usually sufficient.
[p0365-l0003] [10.5pt] In Keras, implementing Gradient Clipping is just a matter of setting the clipvalue or
[p0365-l0004] [10.5pt] clipnorm argument when creating an optimizer. For example:
[p0365-l0005] [8.5pt] optimizer = keras.optimizers.SGD(clipvalue=1.0)
[p0365-l0006] [8.5pt] model.compile(loss="mse", optimizer=optimizer)
[p0365-l0007] [10.5pt] This will clip every component of the gradient vector to a value between –1.0 and 1.0.
[p0365-l0008] [10.5pt] This means that all the partial derivatives of the loss (with regards to each and every
[p0365-l0009] [10.5pt] trainable parameter) will be clipped between –1.0 and 1.0. The threshold is a hyper‐
[p0365-l0010] [10.5pt] parameter you can tune. Note that it may change the orientation of the gradient vec‐
[p0365-l0011] [10.5pt] tor: for example, if the original gradient vector is [0.9, 100.0], it points mostly in the
[p0365-l0012] [10.5pt] direction of the second axis, but once you clip it by value, you get [0.9, 1.0], which
[p0365-l0013] [10.5pt] points roughly in the diagonal between the two axes. In practice however, this
[p0365-l0014] [10.5pt] approach works well. If you want to ensure that Gradient Clipping does not change
[p0365-l0015] [10.5pt] the direction of the gradient vector, you should clip by norm by setting clipnorm
[p0365-l0016] [10.5pt] instead of clipvalue. This will clip the whole gradient if its ℓ2 norm is greater than
[p0365-l0017] [10.5pt] the threshold you picked. For example, if you set clipnorm=1.0, then the vector [0.9,
[p0365-l0018] [10.5pt] 100.0] will be clipped to [0.00899964, 0.9999595], preserving its orientation, but
[p0365-l0019] [10.5pt] almost eliminating the first component. If you observe that the gradients explode
[p0365-l0020] [10.5pt] during training (you can track the size of the gradients using TensorBoard), you may
[p0365-l0021] [10.5pt] want to try both clipping by value and clipping by norm, with different threshold,
[p0365-l0022] [10.5pt] and see which option performs best on the validation set.
[p0365-l0023] [18.92pt] Reusing Pretrained Layers
[p0365-l0024] [10.5pt] It is generally not a good idea to train a very large DNN from scratch: instead, you
[p0365-l0025] [10.5pt] should always try to find an existing neural network that accomplishes a similar task
[p0365-l0026] [10.5pt] to the one you are trying to tackle (we will discuss how to find them in Chapter 14),
[p0365-l0027] [10.5pt] then just reuse the lower layers of this network: this is called transfer learning. It will
[p0365-l0028] [10.5pt] not only speed up training considerably, but will also require much less training data.
[p0365-l0029] [10.5pt] For example, suppose that you have access to a DNN that was trained to classify pic‐
[p0365-l0030] [10.5pt] tures into 100 different categories, including animals, plants, vehicles, and everyday
[p0365-l0031] [10.5pt] objects. You now want to train a DNN to classify specific types of vehicles. These
[p0365-l0032] [10.5pt] tasks are very similar, even partly overlapping, so you should try to reuse parts of the
[p0365-l0033] [10.5pt] first network (see Figure 11-4).
[p0365-l0034] [9.0pt] Reusing Pretrained Layers
[p0365-l0035] [9.0pt] |
[p0365-l0036] [9.0pt] 339

=== PDF page 366 / printed label 340 ===
[p0366-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 11-4. Reusing pretrained layers
[p0366-l0002] [9.6pt] If the input pictures of your new task don’t have the same size as
[p0366-l0003] [9.6pt] the ones used in the original task, you will usually have to add a
[p0366-l0004] [9.6pt] preprocessing step to resize them to the size expected by the origi‐
[p0366-l0005] [9.6pt] nal model. More generally, transfer learning will work best when
[p0366-l0006] [9.6pt] the inputs have similar low-level features.
[p0366-l0007] [10.5pt] The output layer of the original model should usually be replaced since it is most
[p0366-l0008] [10.5pt] likely not useful at all for the new task, and it may not even have the right number of
[p0366-l0009] [10.5pt] outputs for the new task.
[p0366-l0010] [10.5pt] Similarly, the upper hidden layers of the original model are less likely to be as useful
[p0366-l0011] [10.5pt] as the lower layers, since the high-level features that are most useful for the new task
[p0366-l0012] [10.5pt] may differ significantly from the ones that were most useful for the original task. You
[p0366-l0013] [10.5pt] want to find the right number of layers to reuse.
[p0366-l0014] [9.6pt] The more similar the tasks are, the more layers you want to reuse
[p0366-l0015] [9.6pt] (starting with the lower layers). For very similar tasks, you can try
[p0366-l0016] [9.6pt] keeping all the hidden layers and just replace the output layer.
[p0366-l0017] [10.5pt] Try freezing all the reused layers first (i.e., make their weights non-trainable, so gradi‐
[p0366-l0018] [10.5pt] ent descent won’t modify them), then train your model and see how it performs.
[p0366-l0019] [10.5pt] Then try unfreezing one or two of the top hidden layers to let backpropagation tweak
[p0366-l0020] [10.5pt] them and see if performance improves. The more training data you have, the more
[p0366-l0021] [9.0pt] 340
[p0366-l0022] [9.0pt] |
[p0366-l0023] [9.0pt] Chapter 11: Training Deep Neural Networks

=== PDF page 367 / printed label 341 ===
[p0367-l0001] [10.5pt] layers you can unfreeze. It is also useful to reduce the learning rate when you unfreeze
[p0367-l0002] [10.5pt] reused layers: this will avoid wrecking their fine-tuned weights.
[p0367-l0003] [10.5pt] If you still cannot get good performance, and you have little training data, try drop‐
[p0367-l0004] [10.5pt] ping the top hidden layer(s) and freeze all remaining hidden layers again. You can
[p0367-l0005] [10.5pt] iterate until you find the right number of layers to reuse. If you have plenty of train‐
[p0367-l0006] [10.5pt] ing data, you may try replacing the top hidden layers instead of dropping them, and
[p0367-l0007] [10.5pt] even add more hidden layers.
[p0367-l0008] [15.77pt] Transfer Learning With Keras
[p0367-l0009] [10.5pt] Let’s look at an example. Suppose the fashion MNIST dataset only contained 8 classes,
[p0367-l0010] [10.5pt] for example all classes except for sandals and shirts. Someone built and trained a
[p0367-l0011] [10.5pt] Keras model on that set and got reasonably good performance (>90% accuracy). Let’s
[p0367-l0012] [10.5pt] call this model A. You now want to tackle a different task: you have images of sandals
[p0367-l0013] [10.5pt] and shirts, and you want to train a binary classifier (positive=shirts, negative=san‐
[p0367-l0014] [10.5pt] dals). However, your dataset is quite small, you only have 200 labeled images. When
[p0367-l0015] [10.5pt] you train a new model for this task (let’s call it model B), with the same architecture
[p0367-l0016] [10.5pt] as model A, it performs reasonably well (97.2% accuracy), but since it’s a much easier
[p0367-l0017] [10.5pt] task (there are just 2 classes), you were hoping for more. While drinking your morn‐
[p0367-l0018] [10.5pt] ing coffee, you realize that your task is quite similar to task A, so perhaps transfer
[p0367-l0019] [10.5pt] learning can help? Let’s find out!
[p0367-l0020] [10.5pt] First, you need to load model A, and create a new model based on the model A’s lay‐
[p0367-l0021] [10.5pt] ers. Let’s reuse all layers except for the output layer:
[p0367-l0022] [8.5pt] model_A = keras.models.load_model("my_model_A.h5")
[p0367-l0023] [8.5pt] model_B_on_A = keras.models.Sequential(model_A.layers[:-1])
[p0367-l0024] [8.5pt] model_B_on_A.add(keras.layers.Dense(1, activation="sigmoid"))
[p0367-l0025] [10.5pt] Note that model_A and model_B_on_A now share some layers. When you train
[p0367-l0026] [10.5pt] model_B_on_A, it will also affect model_A. If you want to avoid that, you need to clone
[p0367-l0027] [10.5pt] model_A before you reuse its layers. To do this, you must clone model A’s architecture,
[p0367-l0028] [10.5pt] then copy its weights (since clone_model() does not clone the weights):
[p0367-l0029] [8.5pt] model_A_clone = keras.models.clone_model(model_A)
[p0367-l0030] [8.5pt] model_A_clone.set_weights(model_A.get_weights())
[p0367-l0031] [10.5pt] Now we could just train model_B_on_A for task B, but since the new output layer was
[p0367-l0032] [10.5pt] initialized randomly, it will make large errors, at least during the first few epochs, so
[p0367-l0033] [10.5pt] there will be large error gradients that may wreck the reused weights. To avoid this,
[p0367-l0034] [10.5pt] one approach is to freeze the reused layers during the first few epochs, giving the new
[p0367-l0035] [10.5pt] layer some time to learn reasonable weights. To do this, simply set every layer’s train
[p0367-l0036] [10.5pt] able attribute to False and compile the model:
[p0367-l0037] [8.5pt] for layer in model_B_on_A.layers[:-1]:
[p0367-l0038] [8.5pt]     layer.trainable = False
[p0367-l0039] [9.0pt] Reusing Pretrained Layers
[p0367-l0040] [9.0pt] |
[p0367-l0041] [9.0pt] 341

=== PDF page 368 / printed label 342 ===
[p0368-l0001] [8.5pt] model_B_on_A.compile(loss="binary_crossentropy", optimizer="sgd",
[p0368-l0002] [8.5pt]                      metrics=["accuracy"])
[p0368-l0003] [9.6pt] You must always compile your model after you freeze or unfreeze
[p0368-l0004] [9.6pt] layers.
[p0368-l0005] [10.5pt] Next, we can train the model for a few epochs, then unfreeze the reused layers (which
[p0368-l0006] [10.5pt] requires compiling the model again) and continue training to fine-tune the reused
[p0368-l0007] [10.5pt] layers for task B. After unfreezing the reused layers, it is usually a good idea to reduce
[p0368-l0008] [10.5pt] the learning rate, once again to avoid damaging the reused weights:
[p0368-l0009] [8.5pt] history = model_B_on_A.fit(X_train_B, y_train_B, epochs=4,
[p0368-l0010] [8.5pt]                            validation_data=(X_valid_B, y_valid_B))
[p0368-l0011] [8.5pt] for layer in model_B_on_A.layers[:-1]:
[p0368-l0012] [8.5pt]     layer.trainable = True
[p0368-l0013] [8.5pt] optimizer = keras.optimizers.SGD(lr=1e-4) # the default lr is 1e-3
[p0368-l0014] [8.5pt] model_B_on_A.compile(loss="binary_crossentropy", optimizer=optimizer,
[p0368-l0015] [8.5pt]                      metrics=["accuracy"])
[p0368-l0016] [8.5pt] history = model_B_on_A.fit(X_train_B, y_train_B, epochs=16,
[p0368-l0017] [8.5pt]                            validation_data=(X_valid_B, y_valid_B))
[p0368-l0018] [10.5pt] So, what’s the final verdict? Well this model’s test accuracy is 99.25%, which means
[p0368-l0019] [10.5pt] that transfer learning reduced the error rate from 2.8% down to almost 0.7%! That’s a
[p0368-l0020] [10.5pt] factor of 4!
[p0368-l0021] [8.5pt] >>> model_B_on_A.evaluate(X_test_B, y_test_B)
[p0368-l0022] [8.5pt] [0.06887910133600235, 0.9925]
[p0368-l0023] [10.5pt] Are you convinced? Well you shouldn’t be: I cheated! :) I tried many configurations
[p0368-l0024] [10.5pt] until I found one that demonstrated a strong improvement. If you try to change the
[p0368-l0025] [10.5pt] classes or the random seed, you will see that the improvement generally drops, or
[p0368-l0026] [10.5pt] even vanishes or reverses. What I did is called “torturing the data until it confesses”.
[p0368-l0027] [10.5pt] When a paper just looks too positive, you should be suspicious: perhaps the flashy
[p0368-l0028] [10.5pt] new technique does not help much (in fact, it may even degrade performance), but
[p0368-l0029] [10.5pt] the authors tried many variants and reported only the best results (which may be due
[p0368-l0030] [10.5pt] to shear luck), without mentioning how many failures they encountered on the way.
[p0368-l0031] [10.5pt] Most of the time, this is not malicious at all, but it is part of the reason why so many
[p0368-l0032] [10.5pt] results in Science can never be reproduced.
[p0368-l0033] [10.5pt] So why did I cheat? Well it turns out that transfer learning does not work very well
[p0368-l0034] [10.5pt] with small dense networks: it works best with deep convolutional neural networks, so
[p0368-l0035] [10.5pt] we will revisit transfer learning in Chapter 14, using the same techniques (and this
[p0368-l0036] [10.5pt] time there will be no cheating, I promise!).
[p0368-l0037] [9.0pt] 342
[p0368-l0038] [9.0pt] |
[p0368-l0039] [9.0pt] Chapter 11: Training Deep Neural Networks

=== PDF page 369 / printed label 343 ===
[p0369-l0001] [15.77pt] Unsupervised Pretraining
[p0369-l0002] [10.5pt] Suppose you want to tackle a complex task for which you don’t have much labeled
[p0369-l0003] [10.5pt] training data, but unfortunately you cannot find a model trained on a similar task.
[p0369-l0004] [10.5pt] Don’t lose all hope! First, you should of course try to gather more labeled training
[p0369-l0005] [10.5pt] data, but if this is too hard or too expensive, you may still be able to perform unsuper‐
[p0369-l0006] [10.5pt] vised pretraining (see Figure 11-5). It is often rather cheap to gather unlabeled train‐
[p0369-l0007] [10.5pt] ing examples, but quite expensive to label them. If you can gather plenty of unlabeled
[p0369-l0008] [10.5pt] training data, you can try to train the layers one by one, starting with the lowest layer
[p0369-l0009] [10.5pt] and then going up, using an unsupervised feature detector algorithm such as Restric‐
[p0369-l0010] [10.5pt] ted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs; see ???) or autoencoders (see ???). Each layer is
[p0369-l0011] [10.5pt] trained on the output of the previously trained layers (all layers except the one being
[p0369-l0012] [10.5pt] trained are frozen). Once all layers have been trained this way, you can add the output
[p0369-l0013] [10.5pt] layer for your task, and fine-tune the final network using supervised learning (i.e.,
[p0369-l0014] [10.5pt] with the labeled training examples). At this point, you can unfreeze all the pretrained
[p0369-l0015] [10.5pt] layers, or just some of the upper ones.
[p0369-l0016] [10.5pt] Figure 11-5. Unsupervised pretraining
[p0369-l0017] [10.5pt] This is a rather long and tedious process, but it often works well; in fact, it is this
[p0369-l0018] [10.5pt] technique that Geoffrey Hinton and his team used in 2006 and which led to the
[p0369-l0019] [10.5pt] revival of neural networks and the success of Deep Learning. Until 2010, unsuper‐
[p0369-l0020] [10.5pt] vised pretraining (typically using RBMs) was the norm for deep nets, and it was only
[p0369-l0021] [10.5pt] after the vanishing gradients problem was alleviated that it became much more com‐
[p0369-l0022] [9.0pt] Reusing Pretrained Layers
[p0369-l0023] [9.0pt] |
[p0369-l0024] [9.0pt] 343

=== PDF page 370 / printed label 344 ===
[p0370-l0001] [10.5pt] mon to train DNNs purely using supervised learning. However, unsupervised pre‐
[p0370-l0002] [10.5pt] training (today typically using autoencoders rather than RBMs) is still a good option
[p0370-l0003] [10.5pt] when you have a complex task to solve, no similar model you can reuse, and little
[p0370-l0004] [10.5pt] labeled training data but plenty of unlabeled training data.
[p0370-l0005] [15.77pt] Pretraining on an Auxiliary Task
[p0370-l0006] [10.5pt] If you do not have much labeled training data, one last option is to train a first neural
[p0370-l0007] [10.5pt] network on an auxiliary task for which you can easily obtain or generate labeled
[p0370-l0008] [10.5pt] training data, then reuse the lower layers of that network for your actual task. The
[p0370-l0009] [10.5pt] first neural network’s lower layers will learn feature detectors that will likely be reusa‐
[p0370-l0010] [10.5pt] ble by the second neural network.
[p0370-l0011] [10.5pt] For example, if you want to build a system to recognize faces, you may only have a
[p0370-l0012] [10.5pt] few pictures of each individual—clearly not enough to train a good classifier. Gather‐
[p0370-l0013] [10.5pt] ing hundreds of pictures of each person would not be practical. However, you could
[p0370-l0014] [10.5pt] gather a lot of pictures of random people on the web and train a first neural network
[p0370-l0015] [10.5pt] to detect whether or not two different pictures feature the same person. Such a net‐
[p0370-l0016] [10.5pt] work would learn good feature detectors for faces, so reusing its lower layers would
[p0370-l0017] [10.5pt] allow you to train a good face classifier using little training data.
[p0370-l0018] [10.5pt] For natural language processing (NLP) applications, you can easily download millions
[p0370-l0019] [10.5pt] of text documents and automatically generate labeled data from it. For example, you
[p0370-l0020] [10.5pt] could randomly mask out some words and train a model to predict what the missing
[p0370-l0021] [10.5pt] words are (e.g., it should predict that the missing word in the sentence “What ___
[p0370-l0022] [10.5pt] you saying?” is probably “are” or “were”). If you can train a model to reach good per‐
[p0370-l0023] [10.5pt] formance on this task, then it will already know quite a lot about language, and you
[p0370-l0024] [10.5pt] can certainly reuse it for your actual task, and fine-tune it on your labeled data (we
[p0370-l0025] [10.5pt] will discuss more pretraining tasks in ???).
[p0370-l0026] [9.6pt] Self-supervised learning is when you automatically generate the
[p0370-l0027] [9.6pt] labels from the data itself, then you train a model on the resulting
[p0370-l0028] [9.6pt] “labeled” dataset using supervised learning techniques. Since this
[p0370-l0029] [9.6pt] approach requires no human labeling whatsoever, it is best classi‐
[p0370-l0030] [9.6pt] fied as a form of unsupervised learning.
[p0370-l0031] [18.92pt] Faster Optimizers
[p0370-l0032] [10.5pt] Training a very large deep neural network can be painfully slow. So far we have seen
[p0370-l0033] [10.5pt] four ways to speed up training (and reach a better solution): applying a good initiali‐
[p0370-l0034] [10.5pt] zation strategy for the connection weights, using a good activation function, using
[p0370-l0035] [10.5pt] Batch Normalization, and reusing parts of a pretrained network (possibly built on an
[p0370-l0036] [10.5pt] auxiliary task or using unsupervised learning). Another huge speed boost comes from
[p0370-l0037] [10.5pt] using a faster optimizer than the regular Gradient Descent optimizer. In this section
[p0370-l0038] [9.0pt] 344
[p0370-l0039] [9.0pt] |
[p0370-l0040] [9.0pt] Chapter 11: Training Deep Neural Networks

=== PDF page 371 / printed label 345 ===
[p0371-l0001] [10.5pt] we will present the most popular ones: Momentum optimization, Nesterov Acceler‐
[p0371-l0002] [10.5pt] ated Gradient, AdaGrad, RMSProp, and finally Adam and Nadam optimization.
[p0371-l0003] [15.77pt] Momentum Optimization
[p0371-l0004] [10.5pt] Imagine a bowling ball rolling down a gentle slope on a smooth surface: it will start
[p0371-l0005] [10.5pt] out slowly, but it will quickly pick up momentum until it eventually reaches terminal
[p0371-l0006] [10.5pt] velocity (if there is some friction or air resistance). This is the very simple idea behind
[p0371-l0007] [10.5pt] Momentum optimization, proposed by Boris Polyak in 1964.12 In contrast, regular
[p0371-l0008] [10.5pt] Gradient Descent will simply take small regular steps down the slope, so it will take
[p0371-l0009] [10.5pt] much more time to reach the bottom.
[p0371-l0010] [10.5pt] Recall that Gradient Descent simply updates the weights θ by directly subtracting the
[p0371-l0011] [10.5pt] gradient of the cost function J(θ) with regards to the weights (∇θJ(θ)) multiplied by
[p0371-l0012] [10.5pt] the learning rate η. The equation is: θ ← θ – η∇θJ(θ). It does not care about what the
[p0371-l0013] [10.5pt] earlier gradients were. If the local gradient is tiny, it goes very slowly.
[p0371-l0014] [10.5pt] Momentum optimization cares a great deal about what previous gradients were: at
[p0371-l0015] [10.5pt] each iteration, it subtracts the local gradient from the momentum vector m (multi‐
[p0371-l0016] [10.5pt] plied by the learning rate η), and it updates the weights by simply adding this
[p0371-l0017] [10.5pt] momentum vector (see Equation 11-4). In other words, the gradient is used for accel‐
[p0371-l0018] [10.5pt] eration, not for speed. To simulate some sort of friction mechanism and prevent the
[p0371-l0019] [10.5pt] momentum from growing too large, the algorithm introduces a new hyperparameter
[p0371-l0020] [10.5pt] β, simply called the momentum, which must be set between 0 (high friction) and 1
[p0371-l0021] [10.5pt] (no friction). A typical momentum value is 0.9.
[p0371-l0022] [10.5pt] Equation 11-4. Momentum algorithm
[p0371-l0023] [10.0pt] 1 .
[p0371-l0024] [10.0pt] m
[p0371-l0025] [10.0pt] βm −η∇θJ θ
[p0371-l0026] [10.0pt] 2 .
[p0371-l0027] [10.0pt] θ
[p0371-l0028] [10.0pt] θ + m
[p0371-l0029] [10.5pt] You can easily verify that if the gradient remains constant, the terminal velocity (i.e.,
[p0371-l0030] [10.5pt] the maximum size of the weight updates) is equal to that gradient multiplied by the
[p0371-l0031] [10.5pt] learning rate η multiplied by
[p0371-l0032] [8.0pt] 1
[p0371-l0033] [10.5pt] 1 −β (ignoring the sign). For example, if β = 0.9, then the
[p0371-l0034] [10.5pt] terminal velocity is equal to 10 times the gradient times the learning rate, so Momen‐
[p0371-l0035] [10.5pt] tum optimization ends up going 10 times faster than Gradient Descent! This allows
[p0371-l0036] [10.5pt] Momentum optimization to escape from plateaus much faster than Gradient Descent.
[p0371-l0037] [10.5pt] In particular, we saw in Chapter 4 that when the inputs have very different scales the
[p0371-l0038] [10.5pt] cost function will look like an elongated bowl (see Figure 4-7). Gradient Descent goes
[p0371-l0039] [10.5pt] down the steep slope quite fast, but then it takes a very long time to go down the val‐
[p0371-l0040] [8.0pt] 12 “Some methods of speeding up the convergence of iteration methods,” B. Polyak (1964).
[p0371-l0041] [9.0pt] Faster Optimizers
[p0371-l0042] [9.0pt] |
[p0371-l0043] [9.0pt] 345

=== PDF page 372 / printed label 346 ===
[p0372-l0001] [10.5pt] ley. In contrast, Momentum optimization will roll down the valley faster and faster
[p0372-l0002] [10.5pt] until it reaches the bottom (the optimum). In deep neural networks that don’t use
[p0372-l0003] [10.5pt] Batch Normalization, the upper layers will often end up having inputs with very dif‐
[p0372-l0004] [10.5pt] ferent scales, so using Momentum optimization helps a lot. It can also help roll past
[p0372-l0005] [10.5pt] local optima.
[p0372-l0006] [9.6pt] Due to the momentum, the optimizer may overshoot a bit, then
[p0372-l0007] [9.6pt] come back, overshoot again, and oscillate like this many times
[p0372-l0008] [9.6pt] before stabilizing at the minimum. This is one of the reasons why it
[p0372-l0009] [9.6pt] is good to have a bit of friction in the system: it gets rid of these
[p0372-l0010] [9.6pt] oscillations and thus speeds up convergence.
[p0372-l0011] [10.5pt] Implementing Momentum optimization in Keras is a no-brainer: just use the SGD
[p0372-l0012] [10.5pt] optimizer and set its momentum hyperparameter, then lie back and profit!
[p0372-l0013] [8.5pt] optimizer = keras.optimizers.SGD(lr=0.001, momentum=0.9)
[p0372-l0014] [10.5pt] The one drawback of Momentum optimization is that it adds yet another hyperpara‐
[p0372-l0015] [10.5pt] meter to tune. However, the momentum value of 0.9 usually works well in practice
[p0372-l0016] [10.5pt] and almost always goes faster than regular Gradient Descent.
[p0372-l0017] [15.77pt] Nesterov Accelerated Gradient
[p0372-l0018] [10.5pt] One small variant to Momentum optimization, proposed by Yurii Nesterov in 1983,13
[p0372-l0019] [10.5pt] is almost always faster than vanilla Momentum optimization. The idea of Nesterov
[p0372-l0020] [10.5pt] Momentum optimization, or Nesterov Accelerated Gradient (NAG), is to measure the
[p0372-l0021] [10.5pt] gradient of the cost function not at the local position but slightly ahead in the direc‐
[p0372-l0022] [10.5pt] tion of the momentum (see Equation 11-5). The only difference from vanilla
[p0372-l0023] [10.5pt] Momentum optimization is that the gradient is measured at θ + βm rather than at θ.
[p0372-l0024] [10.5pt] Equation 11-5. Nesterov Accelerated Gradient algorithm
[p0372-l0025] [10.0pt] 1 .
[p0372-l0026] [10.0pt] m
[p0372-l0027] [10.0pt] βm −η∇θJ θ + βm
[p0372-l0028] [10.0pt] 2 .
[p0372-l0029] [10.0pt] θ
[p0372-l0030] [10.0pt] θ + m
[p0372-l0031] [10.5pt] This small tweak works because in general the momentum vector will be pointing in
[p0372-l0032] [10.5pt] the right direction (i.e., toward the optimum), so it will be slightly more accurate to
[p0372-l0033] [10.5pt] use the gradient measured a bit farther in that direction rather than using the gradi‐
[p0372-l0034] [10.5pt] ent at the original position, as you can see in Figure 11-6 (where ∇1 represents the
[p0372-l0035] [10.5pt] gradient of the cost function measured at the starting point θ, and ∇2 represents the
[p0372-l0036] [8.0pt] 13 “A Method for Unconstrained Convex Minimization Problem with the Rate of Convergence O(1/k2),” Yurii
[p0372-l0037] [8.0pt] Nesterov (1983).
[p0372-l0038] [9.0pt] 346
[p0372-l0039] [9.0pt] |
[p0372-l0040] [9.0pt] Chapter 11: Training Deep Neural Networks

=== PDF page 373 / printed label 347 ===
[p0373-l0001] [10.5pt] gradient at the point located at θ + βm). As you can see, the Nesterov update ends up
[p0373-l0002] [10.5pt] slightly closer to the optimum. After a while, these small improvements add up and
[p0373-l0003] [10.5pt] NAG ends up being significantly faster than regular Momentum optimization. More‐
[p0373-l0004] [10.5pt] over, note that when the momentum pushes the weights across a valley, ∇1 continues
[p0373-l0005] [10.5pt] to push further across the valley, while ∇2 pushes back toward the bottom of the val‐
[p0373-l0006] [10.5pt] ley. This helps reduce oscillations and thus converges faster.
[p0373-l0007] [10.5pt] NAG will almost always speed up training compared to regular Momentum optimi‐
[p0373-l0008] [10.5pt] zation. To use it, simply set nesterov=True when creating the SGD optimizer:
[p0373-l0009] [8.5pt] optimizer = keras.optimizers.SGD(lr=0.001, momentum=0.9, nesterov=True)
[p0373-l0010] [10.5pt] Figure 11-6. Regular versus Nesterov Momentum optimization
[p0373-l0011] [15.77pt] AdaGrad
[p0373-l0012] [10.5pt] Consider the elongated bowl problem again: Gradient Descent starts by quickly going
[p0373-l0013] [10.5pt] down the steepest slope, then slowly goes down the bottom of the valley. It would be
[p0373-l0014] [10.5pt] nice if the algorithm could detect this early on and correct its direction to point a bit
[p0373-l0015] [10.5pt] more toward the global optimum.
[p0373-l0016] [10.5pt] The AdaGrad algorithm14 achieves this by scaling down the gradient vector along the
[p0373-l0017] [10.5pt] steepest dimensions (see Equation 11-6):
[p0373-l0018] [10.5pt] Equation 11-6. AdaGrad algorithm
[p0373-l0019] [10.0pt] 1 .
[p0373-l0020] [10.0pt] s
[p0373-l0021] [10.0pt] s + ∇θJ θ ⊗∇θJ θ
[p0373-l0022] [10.0pt] 2 .
[p0373-l0023] [10.0pt] θ
[p0373-l0024] [10.0pt] θ −η ∇θJ θ ⊘
[p0373-l0025] [10.0pt] s + �
[p0373-l0026] [8.0pt] 14 “Adaptive Subgradient Methods for Online Learning and Stochastic Optimization,” J. Duchi et al. (2011).
[p0373-l0027] [9.0pt] Faster Optimizers
[p0373-l0028] [9.0pt] |
[p0373-l0029] [9.0pt] 347

=== PDF page 374 / printed label 348 ===
[p0374-l0001] [10.5pt] The first step accumulates the square of the gradients into the vector s (recall that the
[p0374-l0002] [10.5pt] ⊗ symbol represents the element-wise multiplication). This vectorized form is equiv‐
[p0374-l0003] [10.5pt] alent to computing si ← si + (∂ J(θ) / ∂ θi)2 for each element si of the vector s; in other
[p0374-l0004] [10.5pt] words, each si accumulates the squares of the partial derivative of the cost function
[p0374-l0005] [10.5pt] with regards to parameter θi. If the cost function is steep along the ith dimension, then
[p0374-l0006] [10.5pt] si will get larger and larger at each iteration.
[p0374-l0007] [10.5pt] The second step is almost identical to Gradient Descent, but with one big difference:
[p0374-l0008] [10.5pt] the gradient vector is scaled down by a factor of �+ � (the ⊘ symbol represents the
[p0374-l0009] [10.5pt] element-wise division, and ϵ is a smoothing term to avoid division by zero, typically
[p0374-l0010] [10.5pt] set
[p0374-l0011] [10.5pt] to
[p0374-l0012] [10.5pt] 10–10).
[p0374-l0013] [10.5pt] This
[p0374-l0014] [10.5pt] vectorized
[p0374-l0015] [10.5pt] form
[p0374-l0016] [10.5pt] is
[p0374-l0017] [10.5pt] equivalent
[p0374-l0018] [10.5pt] to
[p0374-l0019] [10.5pt] computing
[p0374-l0020] [10.5pt] θi
[p0374-l0021] [10.5pt] θi −η ∂J θ / ∂θi/ si + � for all parameters θi (simultaneously).
[p0374-l0022] [10.5pt] In short, this algorithm decays the learning rate, but it does so faster for steep dimen‐
[p0374-l0023] [10.5pt] sions than for dimensions with gentler slopes. This is called an adaptive learning rate.
[p0374-l0024] [10.5pt] It helps point the resulting updates more directly toward the global optimum (see
[p0374-l0025] [10.5pt] Figure 11-7). One additional benefit is that it requires much less tuning of the learn‐
[p0374-l0026] [10.5pt] ing rate hyperparameter η.
[p0374-l0027] [10.5pt] Figure 11-7. AdaGrad versus Gradient Descent
[p0374-l0028] [10.5pt] AdaGrad often performs well for simple quadratic problems, but unfortunately it
[p0374-l0029] [10.5pt] often stops too early when training neural networks. The learning rate gets scaled
[p0374-l0030] [10.5pt] down so much that the algorithm ends up stopping entirely before reaching the
[p0374-l0031] [10.5pt] global optimum. So even though Keras has an Adagrad optimizer, you should not use
[p0374-l0032] [10.5pt] it to train deep neural networks (it may be efficient for simpler tasks such as Linear
[p0374-l0033] [10.5pt] Regression, though). However, understanding Adagrad is helpful to grasp the other
[p0374-l0034] [10.5pt] adaptive learning rate optimizers.
[p0374-l0035] [9.0pt] 348
[p0374-l0036] [9.0pt] |
[p0374-l0037] [9.0pt] Chapter 11: Training Deep Neural Networks

[p0375-l0001] [15.77pt] RMSProp
[p0375-l0002] [10.5pt] Although AdaGrad slows down a bit too fast and ends up never converging to the
[p0375-l0003] [10.5pt] global optimum, the RMSProp algorithm15 fixes this by accumulating only the gradi‐
[p0375-l0004] [10.5pt] ents from the most recent iterations (as opposed to all the gradients since the begin‐
[p0375-l0005] [10.5pt] ning of training). It does so by using exponential decay in the first step (see Equation
[p0375-l0006] [10.5pt] 11-7).
[p0375-l0007] [10.5pt] Equation 11-7. RMSProp algorithm
[p0375-l0008] [10.0pt] 1 .
[p0375-l0009] [10.0pt] s
[p0375-l0010] [10.0pt] βs + 1 −β ∇θJ θ ⊗∇θJ θ
[p0375-l0011] [10.0pt] 2 .
[p0375-l0012] [10.0pt] θ
[p0375-l0013] [10.0pt] θ −η ∇θJ θ ⊘
[p0375-l0014] [10.0pt] s + �
[p0375-l0015] [10.5pt] The decay rate β is typically set to 0.9. Yes, it is once again a new hyperparameter, but
[p0375-l0016] [10.5pt] this default value often works well, so you may not need to tune it at all.
[p0375-l0017] [10.5pt] As you might expect, Keras has an RMSProp optimizer:
[p0375-l0018] [8.5pt] optimizer = keras.optimizers.RMSprop(lr=0.001, rho=0.9)
[p0375-l0019] [10.5pt] Except on very simple problems, this optimizer almost always performs much better
[p0375-l0020] [10.5pt] than AdaGrad. In fact, it was the preferred optimization algorithm of many research‐
[p0375-l0021] [10.5pt] ers until Adam optimization came around.
[p0375-l0022] [15.77pt] Adam and Nadam Optimization
[p0375-l0023] [10.5pt] Adam,16 which stands for adaptive moment estimation, combines the ideas of Momen‐
[p0375-l0024] [10.5pt] tum optimization and RMSProp: just like Momentum optimization it keeps track of
[p0375-l0025] [10.5pt] an exponentially decaying average of past gradients, and just like RMSProp it keeps
[p0375-l0026] [10.5pt] track of an exponentially decaying average of past squared gradients (see Equation
[p0375-l0027] [10.5pt] 11-8).17
[p0375-l0028] [8.0pt] 15 This algorithm was created by Geoffrey Hinton and Tijmen Tieleman in 2012, and presented by Geoffrey
[p0375-l0029] [8.0pt] Hinton in his Coursera class on neural networks (slides: https://homl.info/57; video: https://homl.info/58).
[p0375-l0030] [8.0pt] Amusingly, since the authors did not write a paper to describe it, researchers often cite “slide 29 in lecture 6”
[p0375-l0031] [8.0pt] in their papers.
[p0375-l0032] [8.0pt] 16 “Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization,” D. Kingma, J. Ba (2015).
[p0375-l0033] [8.0pt] 17 These are estimations of the mean and (uncentered) variance of the gradients. The mean is often called the
[p0375-l0034] [8.0pt] first moment, while the variance is often called the second moment, hence the name of the algorithm.

[p0375-l0036] [9.0pt] |

[p0376-l0022] [10.5pt] • t represents the iteration number (starting at 1).
[p0376-l0023] [10.5pt] If you just look at steps 1, 2, and 5, you will notice Adam’s close similarity to both
[p0376-l0024] [10.5pt] Momentum optimization and RMSProp. The only difference is that step 1 computes
[p0376-l0025] [10.5pt] an exponentially decaying average rather than an exponentially decaying sum, but
[p0376-l0026] [10.5pt] these are actually equivalent except for a constant factor (the decaying average is just
[p0376-l0027] [10.5pt] 1 – β1 times the decaying sum). Steps 3 and 4 are somewhat of a technical detail: since
[p0376-l0028] [10.5pt] m and s are initialized at 0, they will be biased toward 0 at the beginning of training,
[p0376-l0029] [10.5pt] so these two steps will help boost m and s at the beginning of training.
[p0376-l0030] [10.5pt] The momentum decay hyperparameter β1 is typically initialized to 0.9, while the scal‐
[p0376-l0031] [10.5pt] ing decay hyperparameter β2 is often initialized to 0.999. As earlier, the smoothing
[p0376-l0032] [10.5pt] term ϵ is usually initialized to a tiny number such as 10–7. These are the default values
[p0376-l0033] [10.5pt] for the Adam class (to be precise, epsilon defaults to None, which tells Keras to use
[p0376-l0034] [10.5pt] keras.backend.epsilon(), which defaults to 10–7; you can change it using
[p0376-l0035] [10.5pt] keras.backend.set_epsilon()).
[p0376-l0036] [8.5pt] optimizer = keras.optimizers.Adam(lr=0.001, beta_1=0.9, beta_2=0.999)
[p0376-l0037] [10.5pt] Since Adam is an adaptive learning rate algorithm (like AdaGrad and RMSProp), it
[p0376-l0038] [10.5pt] requires less tuning of the learning rate hyperparameter η. You can often use the
[p0376-l0039] [10.5pt] default value η = 0.001, making Adam even easier to use than Gradient Descent.
[p0376-l0040] [9.6pt] If you are starting to feel overwhelmed by all these different techni‐
[p0376-l0041] [9.6pt] ques, and wondering how to choose the right ones for your task,
[p0376-l0042] [9.6pt] don’t worry: some practical guidelines are provided at the end of
[p0376-l0043] [9.6pt] this chapter.
[p0376-l0044] [10.5pt] Finally, two variants of Adam are worth mentioning:
[p0376-l0045] [9.0pt] 350
[p0376-l0046] [9.0pt] |
[p0376-l0047] [9.0pt] Chapter 11: Training Deep Neural Networks

=== PDF page 377 / printed label 351 ===
[p0377-l0001] [10.5pt] • Adamax, introduced in the same paper as Adam: notice that in step 2 of Equation
[p0377-l0002] [10.5pt] 11-8, Adam accumulates the squares of the gradients in s (with a greater weight
[p0377-l0003] [10.5pt] for more recent weights). In step 5, if we ignore ϵ and steps 3 and 4 (which are
[p0377-l0004] [10.5pt] technical details anyway), Adam just scales down the parameter updates by the
[p0377-l0005] [10.5pt] square root of s. In short, Adam scales down the parameter updates by the ℓ2
[p0377-l0006] [10.5pt] norm of the time-decayed gradients (recall that the ℓ2 norm is the square root of
[p0377-l0007] [10.5pt] the sum of squares). Adamax just replaces the ℓ2 norm with the ℓ∞ norm (a fancy
[p0377-l0008] [10.5pt] way of saying the max). Specifically, it replaces step 2 in Equation 11-8 with
[p0377-l0009] [10.5pt] �
[p0377-l0010] [10.5pt] max β2�, ∇θJ θ , it drops step 4, and in step 5 it scales down the gradient
[p0377-l0011] [10.5pt] updates by a factor of s, which is just the max of the time-decayed gradients. In
[p0377-l0012] [10.5pt] practice, this can make Adamax more stable than Adam, but this really depends
[p0377-l0013] [10.5pt] on the dataset, and in general Adam actually performs better. So it’s just one
[p0377-l0014] [10.5pt] more optimizer you can try if you experience problems with Adam on some task.
[p0377-l0015] [10.5pt] • Nadam optimization18 is more important: it is simply Adam optimization plus
[p0377-l0016] [10.5pt] the Nesterov trick, so it will often converge slightly faster than Adam. In his
[p0377-l0017] [10.5pt] report, Timothy Dozat compares many different optimizers on various tasks, and
[p0377-l0018] [10.5pt] finds that Nadam generally outperforms Adam, but is sometimes outperformed
[p0377-l0019] [10.5pt] by RMSProp.
[p0377-l0020] [9.6pt] Adaptive optimization methods (including RMSProp, Adam and
[p0377-l0021] [9.6pt] Nadam optimization) are often great, converging fast to a good sol‐
[p0377-l0022] [9.6pt] ution. However, a 2017 paper19 by Ashia C. Wilson et al. showed
[p0377-l0023] [9.6pt] that they can lead to solutions that generalize poorly on some data‐
[p0377-l0024] [9.6pt] sets. So when you are disappointed by your model’s performance,
[p0377-l0025] [9.6pt] try using plain Nesterov Accelerated Gradient instead: your dataset
[p0377-l0026] [9.6pt] may just be allergic to adaptive gradients. Also check out the latest
[p0377-l0027] [9.6pt] research, it is moving fast (e.g., AdaBound).
[p0377-l0028] [10.5pt] All the optimization techniques discussed so far only rely on the first-order partial
[p0377-l0029] [10.5pt] derivatives (Jacobians). The optimization literature contains amazing algorithms
[p0377-l0030] [10.5pt] based on the second-order partial derivatives (the Hessians, which are the partial
[p0377-l0031] [10.5pt] derivatives of the Jacobians). Unfortunately, these algorithms are very hard to apply
[p0377-l0032] [10.5pt] to deep neural networks because there are n2 Hessians per output (where n is the
[p0377-l0033] [10.5pt] number of parameters), as opposed to just n Jacobians per output. Since DNNs typi‐
[p0377-l0034] [10.5pt] cally have tens of thousands of parameters, the second-order optimization algorithms
[p0377-l0035] [8.0pt] 18 “Incorporating Nesterov Momentum into Adam,” Timothy Dozat (2015).
[p0377-l0036] [8.0pt] 19 “The Marginal Value of Adaptive Gradient Methods in Machine Learning,” A. C. Wilson et al. (2017).
[p0377-l0037] [9.0pt] Faster Optimizers
[p0377-l0038] [9.0pt] |
[p0377-l0039] [9.0pt] 351

=== PDF page 378 / printed label 352 ===
[p0378-l0001] [10.5pt] often don’t even fit in memory, and even when they do, computing the Hessians is
[p0378-l0002] [10.5pt] just too slow.
[p0378-l0003] [15.0pt] Training Sparse Models
[p0378-l0004] [10.0pt] All the optimization algorithms just presented produce dense models, meaning that
[p0378-l0005] [10.0pt] most parameters will be nonzero. If you need a blazingly fast model at runtime, or if
[p0378-l0006] [10.0pt] you need it to take up less memory, you may prefer to end up with a sparse model
[p0378-l0007] [10.0pt] instead.
[p0378-l0008] [10.0pt] One trivial way to achieve this is to train the model as usual, then get rid of the tiny
[p0378-l0009] [10.0pt] weights (set them to 0). However, this will typically not lead to a very sparse model,
[p0378-l0010] [10.0pt] and it may degrade the model’s performance.
[p0378-l0011] [10.0pt] A better option is to apply strong ℓ1 regularization during training, as it pushes the
[p0378-l0012] [10.0pt] optimizer to zero out as many weights as it can (as discussed in Chapter 4 about Lasso
[p0378-l0013] [10.0pt] Regression).
[p0378-l0014] [10.0pt] However, in some cases these techniques may remain insufficient. One last option is
[p0378-l0015] [10.0pt] to apply Dual Averaging, often called Follow The Regularized Leader (FTRL), a techni‐
[p0378-l0016] [10.0pt] que proposed by Yurii Nesterov.20 When used with ℓ1 regularization, this technique
[p0378-l0017] [10.0pt] often leads to very sparse models. Keras implements a variant of FTRL called FTRL-
[p0378-l0018] [10.0pt] Proximal21 in the FTRL optimizer.
[p0378-l0019] [15.77pt] Learning Rate Scheduling
[p0378-l0020] [10.5pt] Finding a good learning rate can be tricky. If you set it way too high, training may
[p0378-l0021] [10.5pt] actually diverge (as we discussed in Chapter 4). If you set it too low, training will
[p0378-l0022] [10.5pt] eventually converge to the optimum, but it will take a very long time. If you set it
[p0378-l0023] [10.5pt] slightly too high, it will make progress very quickly at first, but it will end up dancing
[p0378-l0024] [10.5pt] around the optimum, never really settling down. If you have a limited computing
[p0378-l0025] [10.5pt] budget, you may have to interrupt training before it has converged properly, yielding
[p0378-l0026] [10.5pt] a suboptimal solution (see Figure 11-8).
[p0378-l0027] [8.0pt] 20 “Primal-Dual Subgradient Methods for Convex Problems,” Yurii Nesterov (2005).
[p0378-l0028] [8.0pt] 21 “Ad Click Prediction: a View from the Trenches,” H. McMahan et al. (2013).
[p0378-l0029] [9.0pt] 352
[p0378-l0030] [9.0pt] |
[p0378-l0031] [9.0pt] Chapter 11: Training Deep Neural Networks

=== PDF page 379 / printed label 353 ===
[p0379-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 11-8. Learning curves for various learning rates η
[p0379-l0002] [10.5pt] As we discussed in Chapter 10, one approach is to start with a large learning rate, and
[p0379-l0003] [10.5pt] divide it by 3 until the training algorithm stops diverging. You will not be too far
[p0379-l0004] [10.5pt] from the optimal learning rate, which will learn quickly and converge to good solu‐
[p0379-l0005] [10.5pt] tion.
[p0379-l0006] [10.5pt] However, you can do better than a constant learning rate: if you start with a high
[p0379-l0007] [10.5pt] learning rate and then reduce it once it stops making fast progress, you can reach a
[p0379-l0008] [10.5pt] good solution faster than with the optimal constant learning rate. There are many dif‐
[p0379-l0009] [10.5pt] ferent strategies to reduce the learning rate during training. These strategies are called
[p0379-l0010] [10.5pt] learning schedules (we briefly introduced this concept in Chapter 4), the most com‐
[p0379-l0011] [10.5pt] mon of which are:
[p0379-l0012] [10.5pt] Power scheduling
[p0379-l0013] [10.5pt] Set the learning rate to a function of the iteration number t: η(t) = η0 / (1 + t/k)c.
[p0379-l0014] [10.5pt] The initial learning rate η0, the power c (typically set to 1) and the steps s are
[p0379-l0015] [10.5pt] hyperparameters. The learning rate drops at each step, and after s steps it is down
[p0379-l0016] [10.5pt] to η0 / 2. After s more steps, it is down to η0 / 3. Then down to η0 / 4, then η0 / 5,
[p0379-l0017] [10.5pt] and so on. As you can see, this schedule first drops quickly, then more and more
[p0379-l0018] [10.5pt] slowly. Of course, this requires tuning η0, s (and possibly c).
[p0379-l0019] [10.5pt] Exponential scheduling
[p0379-l0020] [10.5pt] Set the learning rate to: η(t) = η0 0.1t/s. The learning rate will gradually drop by a
[p0379-l0021] [10.5pt] factor of 10 every s steps. While power scheduling reduces the learning rate more
[p0379-l0022] [10.5pt] and more slowly, exponential scheduling keeps slashing it by a factor of 10 every
[p0379-l0023] [10.5pt] s steps.
[p0379-l0024] [10.5pt] Piecewise constant scheduling
[p0379-l0025] [10.5pt] Use a constant learning rate for a number of epochs (e.g., η0 = 0.1 for 5 epochs),
[p0379-l0026] [10.5pt] then a smaller learning rate for another number of epochs (e.g., η1 = 0.001 for 50
[p0379-l0027] [10.5pt] epochs), and so on. Although this solution can work very well, it requires fid‐
[p0379-l0028] [9.0pt] Faster Optimizers
[p0379-l0029] [9.0pt] |
[p0379-l0030] [9.0pt] 353

=== PDF page 380 / printed label 354 ===
[p0380-l0001] [10.5pt] dling around to figure out the right sequence of learning rates, and how long to
[p0380-l0002] [10.5pt] use each of them.
[p0380-l0003] [10.5pt] Performance scheduling
[p0380-l0004] [10.5pt] Measure the validation error every N steps (just like for early stopping) and
[p0380-l0005] [10.5pt] reduce the learning rate by a factor of λ when the error stops dropping.
[p0380-l0006] [10.5pt] A 2013 paper22 by Andrew Senior et al. compared the performance of some of the
[p0380-l0007] [10.5pt] most popular learning schedules when training deep neural networks for speech rec‐
[p0380-l0008] [10.5pt] ognition using Momentum optimization. The authors concluded that, in this setting,
[p0380-l0009] [10.5pt] both performance scheduling and exponential scheduling performed well. They
[p0380-l0010] [10.5pt] favored exponential scheduling because it was easy to tune and it converged slightly
[p0380-l0011] [10.5pt] faster to the optimal solution (they also mentioned that it was easier to implement
[p0380-l0012] [10.5pt] than performance scheduling, but in Keras both options are easy).
[p0380-l0013] [10.5pt] Implementing power scheduling in Keras is the easiest option: just set the decay
[p0380-l0014] [10.5pt] hyperparameter when creating an optimizer. The decay is the inverse of s (the num‐
[p0380-l0015] [10.5pt] ber of steps it takes to divide the learning rate by one more unit), and Keras assumes
[p0380-l0016] [10.5pt] that c is equal to 1. For example:
[p0380-l0017] [8.5pt] optimizer = keras.optimizers.SGD(lr=0.01, decay=1e-4)
[p0380-l0018] [10.5pt] Exponential scheduling and piecewise scheduling are quite simple too. You first need
[p0380-l0019] [10.5pt] to define a function that takes the current epoch and returns the learning rate. For
[p0380-l0020] [10.5pt] example, let’s implement exponential scheduling:
[p0380-l0021] [8.5pt] def exponential_decay_fn(epoch):
[p0380-l0022] [8.5pt]     return 0.01 * 0.1**(epoch / 20)
[p0380-l0023] [10.5pt] If you do not want to hard-code η0 and s, you can create a function that returns a
[p0380-l0024] [10.5pt] configured function:
[p0380-l0025] [8.5pt] def exponential_decay(lr0, s):
[p0380-l0026] [8.5pt]     def exponential_decay_fn(epoch):
[p0380-l0027] [8.5pt]         return lr0 * 0.1**(epoch / s)
[p0380-l0028] [8.5pt]     return exponential_decay_fn
[p0380-l0029] [8.5pt] exponential_decay_fn = exponential_decay(lr0=0.01, s=20)
[p0380-l0030] [10.5pt] Next, just create a LearningRateScheduler callback, giving it the schedule function,
[p0380-l0031] [10.5pt] and pass this callback to the fit() method:
[p0380-l0032] [8.5pt] lr_scheduler = keras.callbacks.LearningRateScheduler(exponential_decay_fn)
[p0380-l0033] [8.5pt] history = model.fit(X_train_scaled, y_train, [...], callbacks=[lr_scheduler])
[p0380-l0034] [8.0pt] 22 “An Empirical Study of Learning Rates in Deep Neural Networks for Speech Recognition,” A. Senior et al.
[p0380-l0035] [8.0pt] (2013).
[p0380-l0036] [9.0pt] 354
[p0380-l0037] [9.0pt] |
[p0380-l0038] [9.0pt] Chapter 11: Training Deep Neural Networks
