[p0409-l0001] [15.77pt] Custom Layers
[p0409-l0002] [10.5pt] You may occasionally want to build an architecture that contains an exotic layer for
[p0409-l0003] [10.5pt] which TensorFlow does not provide a default implementation. In this case, you will
[p0409-l0004] [10.5pt] need to create a custom layer. Or sometimes you may simply want to build a very
[p0409-l0005] [10.5pt] repetitive architecture, containing identical blocks of layers repeated many times, and
[p0409-l0006] [10.5pt] it would be convenient to treat each block of layers as a single layer. For example, if
[p0409-l0007] [10.5pt] the model is a sequence of layers A, B, C, A, B, C, A, B, C, then you might want to
[p0409-l0008] [10.5pt] define a custom layer D containing layers A, B, C, and your model would then simply
[p0409-l0009] [10.5pt] be D, D, D. Let’s see how to build custom layers.
[p0409-l0010] [10.5pt] First, some layers have no weights, such as keras.layers.Flatten or keras.lay
[p0409-l0011] [10.5pt] ers.ReLU. If you want to create a custom layer without any weights, the simplest
[p0409-l0012] [10.5pt] option is to write a function and wrap it in a keras.layers.Lambda layer. For exam‐
[p0409-l0013] [10.5pt] ple, the following layer will apply the exponential function to its inputs:
[p0409-l0014] [8.5pt] exponential_layer = keras.layers.Lambda(lambda x: tf.exp(x))
[p0409-l0015] [10.5pt] This custom layer can then be used like any other layer, using the sequential API, the
[p0409-l0016] [10.5pt] functional API, or the subclassing API. You can also use it as an activation function
[p0409-l0017] [10.5pt] (or you could just use activation=tf.exp, or activation=keras.activations.expo
[p0409-l0018] [10.5pt] nential, or simply activation="exponential"). The exponential layer is sometimes
[p0409-l0019] [10.5pt] used in the output layer of a regression model when the values to predict have very
[p0409-l0020] [10.5pt] different scales (e.g., 0.001, 10., 1000.).
[p0409-l0021] [10.5pt] As you probably guessed by now, to build a custom stateful layer (i.e., a layer with
[p0409-l0022] [10.5pt] weights), you need to create a subclass of the keras.layers.Layer class. For exam‐
[p0409-l0023] [10.5pt] ple, the following class implements a simplified version of the Dense layer:
[p0409-l0024] [8.5pt] class MyDense(keras.layers.Layer):
[p0409-l0025] [8.5pt]     def __init__(self, units, activation=None, **kwargs):
[p0409-l0026] [8.5pt]         super().__init__(**kwargs)
[p0409-l0027] [8.5pt]         self.units = units
[p0409-l0028] [8.5pt]         self.activation = keras.activations.get(activation)
[p0409-l0029] [8.5pt]     def build(self, batch_input_shape):
[p0409-l0030] [8.5pt]         self.kernel = self.add_weight(
[p0409-l0031] [8.5pt]             name="kernel", shape=[batch_input_shape[-1], self.units],
[p0409-l0032] [8.5pt]             initializer="glorot_normal")
[p0409-l0033] [8.5pt]         self.bias = self.add_weight(
[p0409-l0034] [8.5pt]             name="bias", shape=[self.units], initializer="zeros")
[p0409-l0035] [8.5pt]         super().build(batch_input_shape) # must be at the end
[p0409-l0036] [8.5pt]     def call(self, X):
[p0409-l0037] [8.5pt]         return self.activation(X @ self.kernel + self.bias)
[p0409-l0038] [8.5pt]     def compute_output_shape(self, batch_input_shape):
[p0409-l0039] [8.5pt]         return tf.TensorShape(batch_input_shape.as_list()[:-1] + [self.units])
[p0409-l0040] [9.0pt] Customizing Models and Training Algorithms
[p0409-l0041] [9.0pt] |
[p0409-l0042] [9.0pt] 383

=== PDF page 410 / printed label 384 ===
[p0410-l0001] [8.5pt]     def get_config(self):
[p0410-l0002] [8.5pt]         base_config = super().get_config()
[p0410-l0003] [8.5pt]         return {**base_config, "units": self.units,
[p0410-l0004] [8.5pt]                 "activation": keras.activations.serialize(self.activation)}
[p0410-l0005] [10.5pt] Let’s walk through this code:
[p0410-l0006] [10.5pt] • The constructor takes all the hyperparameters as arguments (in this example just
[p0410-l0007] [10.5pt] units and activation), and importantly it also takes a **kwargs argument. It
[p0410-l0008] [10.5pt] calls the parent constructor, passing it the kwargs: this takes care of standard
[p0410-l0009] [10.5pt] arguments such as input_shape, trainable, name, and so on. Then it saves the
[p0410-l0010] [10.5pt] hyperparameters as attributes, converting the activation argument to the
[p0410-l0011] [10.5pt] appropriate activation function using the keras.activations.get() function (it
[p0410-l0012] [10.5pt] accepts functions, standard strings like "relu" or "selu", or simply None)8.
[p0410-l0013] [10.5pt] • The build() method’s role is to create the layer’s variables, by calling the
[p0410-l0014] [10.5pt] add_weight() method for each weight. The build() method is called the first
[p0410-l0015] [10.5pt] time the layer is used. At that point, Keras will know the shape of this layer’s
[p0410-l0016] [10.5pt] inputs, and it will pass it to the build() method9, which is often necessary to cre‐
[p0410-l0017] [10.5pt] ate some of the weights. For example, we need to know the number of neurons in
[p0410-l0018] [10.5pt] the previous layer in order to create the connection weights matrix (i.e., the "ker
[p0410-l0019] [10.5pt] nel"): this corresponds to the size of the last dimension of the inputs. At the end
[p0410-l0020] [10.5pt] of the build() method (and only at the end), you must call the parent’s build()
[p0410-l0021] [10.5pt] method: this tells Keras that the layer is built (it just sets self.built = True).
[p0410-l0022] [10.5pt] • The call() method actually performs the desired operations. In this case, we
[p0410-l0023] [10.5pt] compute the matrix multiplication of the inputs X and the layer’s kernel, we add
[p0410-l0024] [10.5pt] the bias vector, we apply the activation function to the result, and this gives us the
[p0410-l0025] [10.5pt] output of the layer.
[p0410-l0026] [10.5pt] • The compute_output_shape() method simply returns the shape of this layer’s
[p0410-l0027] [10.5pt] outputs. In this case, it is the same shape as the inputs, except the last dimension
[p0410-l0028] [10.5pt] is replaced with the number of neurons in the layer. Note that in tf.keras, shapes
[p0410-l0029] [10.5pt] are instances of the tf.TensorShape class, which you can convert to Python lists
[p0410-l0030] [10.5pt] using as_list().
[p0410-l0031] [10.5pt] • The get_config() method is just like earlier. Note that we save the activation
[p0410-l0032] [10.5pt] function’s full configuration by calling keras.activations.serialize().
[p0410-l0033] [10.5pt] You can now use a MyDense layer just like any other layer!
[p0410-l0034] [8.0pt] 8 This function is specific to tf.keras. You could use keras.activations.Activation instead.
[p0410-l0035] [8.0pt] 9 The Keras API calls this argument input_shape, but since it also includes the batch dimension, I prefer to call
[p0410-l0036] [8.0pt] it batch_input_shape. Same for compute_output_shape().
[p0410-l0037] [9.0pt] 384
[p0410-l0038] [9.0pt] |
[p0410-l0039] [9.0pt] Chapter 12: Custom Models and Training with TensorFlow

=== PDF page 411 / printed label 385 ===
[p0411-l0001] [9.6pt] You can generally omit the compute_output_shape() method, as
[p0411-l0002] [9.6pt] tf.keras automatically infers the output shape, except when the
[p0411-l0003] [9.6pt] layer is dynamic (as we will see shortly). In other Keras implemen‐
[p0411-l0004] [9.6pt] tations, this method is either required or by default it assumes the
[p0411-l0005] [9.6pt] output shape is the same as the input shape.
[p0411-l0006] [10.5pt] To create a layer with multiple inputs (e.g., Concatenate), the argument to the call()
[p0411-l0007] [10.5pt] method should be a tuple containing all the inputs, and similarly the argument to the
[p0411-l0008] [10.5pt] compute_output_shape() method should be a tuple containing each input’s batch
[p0411-l0009] [10.5pt] shape. To create a layer with multiple outputs, the call() method should return the
[p0411-l0010] [10.5pt] list of outputs, and the compute_output_shape() should return the list of batch out‐
[p0411-l0011] [10.5pt] put shapes (one per output). For example, the following toy layer takes two inputs
[p0411-l0012] [10.5pt] and returns three outputs:
[p0411-l0013] [8.5pt] class MyMultiLayer(keras.layers.Layer):
[p0411-l0014] [8.5pt]     def call(self, X):
[p0411-l0015] [8.5pt]         X1, X2 = X
[p0411-l0016] [8.5pt]         return [X1 + X2, X1 * X2, X1 / X2]
[p0411-l0017] [8.5pt]     def compute_output_shape(self, batch_input_shape):
[p0411-l0018] [8.5pt]         b1, b2 = batch_input_shape
[p0411-l0019] [8.5pt]         return [b1, b1, b1] # should probably handle broadcasting rules
[p0411-l0020] [10.5pt] This layer may now be used like any other layer, but of course only using the func‐
[p0411-l0021] [10.5pt] tional and subclassing APIs, not the sequential API (which only accepts layers with
[p0411-l0022] [10.5pt] one input and one output).
[p0411-l0023] [10.5pt] If your layer needs to have a different behavior during training and during testing
[p0411-l0024] [10.5pt] (e.g., if it uses Dropout or BatchNormalization layers), then you must add a train
[p0411-l0025] [10.5pt] ing argument to the call() method and use this argument to decide what to do. For
[p0411-l0026] [10.5pt] example, let’s create a layer that adds Gaussian noise during training (for regulariza‐
[p0411-l0027] [10.5pt] tion), but does nothing during testing (Keras actually has a layer that does the same
[p0411-l0028] [10.5pt] thing: keras.layers.GaussianNoise):
[p0411-l0029] [8.5pt] class MyGaussianNoise(keras.layers.Layer):
[p0411-l0030] [8.5pt]     def __init__(self, stddev, **kwargs):
[p0411-l0031] [8.5pt]         super().__init__(**kwargs)
[p0411-l0032] [8.5pt]         self.stddev = stddev
[p0411-l0033] [8.5pt]     def call(self, X, training=None):
[p0411-l0034] [8.5pt]         if training:
[p0411-l0035] [8.5pt]             noise = tf.random.normal(tf.shape(X), stddev=self.stddev)
[p0411-l0036] [8.5pt]             return X + noise
[p0411-l0037] [8.5pt]         else:
[p0411-l0038] [8.5pt]             return X
[p0411-l0039] [8.5pt]     def compute_output_shape(self, batch_input_shape):
[p0411-l0040] [8.5pt]         return batch_input_shape
[p0411-l0041] [9.0pt] Customizing Models and Training Algorithms
[p0411-l0042] [9.0pt] |

[p0412-l0001] [10.5pt] With that, you can now build any custom layer you need! Now let’s create custom
[p0412-l0002] [10.5pt] models.
[p0412-l0003] [15.77pt] Custom Models
[p0412-l0004] [10.5pt] We already looked at custom model classes in Chapter 10 when we discussed the sub‐
[p0412-l0005] [10.5pt] classing API.10 It is actually quite straightforward, just subclass the keras.mod
[p0412-l0006] [10.5pt] els.Model class, create layers and variables in the constructor, and implement the
[p0412-l0007] [10.5pt] call() method to do whatever you want the model to do. For example, suppose you
[p0412-l0008] [10.5pt] want to build the model represented in Figure 12-3:
[p0412-l0009] [10.5pt] Figure 12-3. Custom Model Example
[p0412-l0010] [10.5pt] The inputs go through a first dense layer, then through a residual block composed of
[p0412-l0011] [10.5pt] two dense layers and an addition operation (as we will see in Chapter 14, a residual
[p0412-l0012] [10.5pt] block adds its inputs to its outputs), then through this same residual block 3 more
[p0412-l0013] [10.5pt] times, then through a second residual block, and the final result goes through a dense
[p0412-l0014] [10.5pt] output layer. Note that this model does not make much sense, it’s just an example to
[p0412-l0015] [10.5pt] illustrate the fact that you can easily build any kind of model you want, even contain‐
[p0412-l0016] [8.0pt] 10 The name “subclassing API” usually refers only to the creation of custom models by subclassing, although
[p0412-l0017] [8.0pt] many other things can be created by subclassing, as we saw in this chapter.
[p0412-l0018] [9.0pt] 386
[p0412-l0019] [9.0pt] |
[p0412-l0020] [9.0pt] Chapter 12: Custom Models and Training with TensorFlow

=== PDF page 413 / printed label 387 ===
[p0413-l0001] [10.5pt] ing loops and skip connections. To implement this model, it is best to first create a
[p0413-l0002] [10.5pt] ResidualBlock layer, since we are going to create a couple identical blocks (and we
[p0413-l0003] [10.5pt] might want to reuse it in another model):
[p0413-l0004] [8.5pt] class ResidualBlock(keras.layers.Layer):
[p0413-l0005] [8.5pt]     def __init__(self, n_layers, n_neurons, **kwargs):
[p0413-l0006] [8.5pt]         super().__init__(**kwargs)
[p0413-l0007] [8.5pt]         self.hidden = [keras.layers.Dense(n_neurons, activation="elu",
[p0413-l0008] [8.5pt]                                           kernel_initializer="he_normal")
[p0413-l0009] [8.5pt]                        for _ in range(n_layers)]
[p0413-l0010] [8.5pt]     def call(self, inputs):
[p0413-l0011] [8.5pt]         Z = inputs
[p0413-l0012] [8.5pt]         for layer in self.hidden:
[p0413-l0013] [8.5pt]             Z = layer(Z)
[p0413-l0014] [8.5pt]         return inputs + Z
[p0413-l0015] [10.5pt] This layer is a bit special since it contains other layers. This is handled transparently
[p0413-l0016] [10.5pt] by Keras: it automatically detects that the hidden attribute contains trackable objects
[p0413-l0017] [10.5pt] (layers in this case), so their variables are automatically added to this layer’s list of
[p0413-l0018] [10.5pt] variables. The rest of this class is self-explanatory. Next, let’s use the subclassing API
[p0413-l0019] [10.5pt] to define the model itself:
[p0413-l0020] [8.5pt] class ResidualRegressor(keras.models.Model):
[p0413-l0021] [8.5pt]     def __init__(self, output_dim, **kwargs):
[p0413-l0022] [8.5pt]         super().__init__(**kwargs)
[p0413-l0023] [8.5pt]         self.hidden1 = keras.layers.Dense(30, activation="elu",
[p0413-l0024] [8.5pt]                                           kernel_initializer="he_normal")
[p0413-l0025] [8.5pt]         self.block1 = ResidualBlock(2, 30)
[p0413-l0026] [8.5pt]         self.block2 = ResidualBlock(2, 30)
[p0413-l0027] [8.5pt]         self.out = keras.layers.Dense(output_dim)
[p0413-l0028] [8.5pt]     def call(self, inputs):
[p0413-l0029] [8.5pt]         Z = self.hidden1(inputs)
[p0413-l0030] [8.5pt]         for _ in range(1 + 3):
[p0413-l0031] [8.5pt]             Z = self.block1(Z)
[p0413-l0032] [8.5pt]         Z = self.block2(Z)
[p0413-l0033] [8.5pt]         return self.out(Z)
[p0413-l0034] [10.5pt] We create the layers in the constructor, and use them in the call() method. This
[p0413-l0035] [10.5pt] model can then be used like any other model (compile it, fit it, evaluate it and use it to
[p0413-l0036] [10.5pt] make predictions). If you also want to be able to save the model using the save()
[p0413-l0037] [10.5pt] method, and load it using the keras.models.load_model() function, you must
[p0413-l0038] [10.5pt] implement the get_config() method (as we did earlier) in both the ResidualBlock
[p0413-l0039] [10.5pt] class and the ResidualRegressor class. Alternatively, you can just save and load the
[p0413-l0040] [10.5pt] weights using the save_weights() and load_weights() methods.
[p0413-l0041] [10.5pt] The Model class is actually a subclass of the Layer class, so models can be defined and
[p0413-l0042] [10.5pt] used exactly like layers. But a model also has some extra functionalities, including of
[p0413-l0043] [10.5pt] course its compile(), fit(), evaluate() and predict() methods (and a few var‐
[p0413-l0044] [9.0pt] Customizing Models and Training Algorithms
[p0413-l0045] [9.0pt] |
[p0413-l0046] [9.0pt] 387

=== PDF page 414 / printed label 388 ===
[p0414-l0001] [10.5pt] iants, such as train_on_batch() or fit_generator()), plus the get_layers()
[p0414-l0002] [10.5pt] method (which can return any of the model’s layers by name or by index), and the
[p0414-l0003] [10.5pt] save() method (and support for keras.models.load_model() and keras.mod
[p0414-l0004] [10.5pt] els.clone_model()). So if models provide more functionalities than layers, why not
[p0414-l0005] [10.5pt] just define every layer as a model? Well, technically you could, but it is probably
[p0414-l0006] [10.5pt] cleaner to distinguish the internal components of your model (layers or reusable
[p0414-l0007] [10.5pt] blocks of layers) from the model itself. The former should subclass the Layer class,
[p0414-l0008] [10.5pt] while the latter should subclass the Model class.
[p0414-l0009] [10.5pt] With that, you can quite naturally and concisely build almost any model that you find
[p0414-l0010] [10.5pt] in a paper, either using the sequential API, the functional API, the subclassing API, or
[p0414-l0011] [10.5pt] even a mix of these. “Almost” any model? Yes, there are still a couple things that we
[p0414-l0012] [10.5pt] need to look at: first, how to define losses or metrics based on model internals, and
[p0414-l0013] [10.5pt] second how to build a custom training loop.
[p0414-l0014] [15.77pt] Losses and Metrics Based on Model Internals
[p0414-l0015] [10.5pt] The custom losses and metrics we defined earlier were all based on the labels and the
[p0414-l0016] [10.5pt] predictions (and optionally sample weights). However, you will occasionally want to
[p0414-l0017] [10.5pt] define losses based on other parts of your model, such as the weights or activations of
[p0414-l0018] [10.5pt] its hidden layers. This may be useful for regularization purposes, or to monitor some
[p0414-l0019] [10.5pt] internal aspect of your model.
[p0414-l0020] [10.5pt] To define a custom loss based on model internals, just compute it based on any part
[p0414-l0021] [10.5pt] of the model you want, then pass the result to the add_loss() method. For example,
[p0414-l0022] [10.5pt] the following custom model represents a standard MLP regressor with 5 hidden lay‐
[p0414-l0023] [10.5pt] ers, except it also implements a reconstruction loss (see ???): we add an extra Dense
[p0414-l0024] [10.5pt] layer on top of the last hidden layer, and its role is to try to reconstruct the inputs of
[p0414-l0025] [10.5pt] the model. Since the reconstruction must have the same shape as the model’s inputs,
[p0414-l0026] [10.5pt] we need to create this Dense layer in the build() method to have access to the shape
[p0414-l0027] [10.5pt] of the inputs. In the call() method, we compute both the regular output of the MLP,
[p0414-l0028] [10.5pt] plus the output of the reconstruction layer. We then compute the mean squared dif‐
[p0414-l0029] [10.5pt] ference between the reconstructions and the inputs, and we add this value (times
[p0414-l0030] [10.5pt] 0.05) to the model’s list of losses by calling add_loss(). During training, Keras will
[p0414-l0031] [10.5pt] add this loss to the main loss (which is why we scaled down the reconstruction loss,
[p0414-l0032] [10.5pt] to ensure the main loss dominates). As a result, the model will be forced to preserve
[p0414-l0033] [10.5pt] as much information as possible through the hidden layers, even information that is
[p0414-l0034] [10.5pt] not directly useful for the regression task itself. In practice, this loss sometimes
[p0414-l0035] [10.5pt] improves generalization; it is a regularization loss:
[p0414-l0036] [8.5pt] class ReconstructingRegressor(keras.models.Model):
[p0414-l0037] [8.5pt]     def __init__(self, output_dim, **kwargs):
[p0414-l0038] [8.5pt]         super().__init__(**kwargs)
[p0414-l0039] [8.5pt]         self.hidden = [keras.layers.Dense(30, activation="selu",
[p0414-l0040] [8.5pt]                                           kernel_initializer="lecun_normal")
[p0414-l0041] [9.0pt] 388
[p0414-l0042] [9.0pt] |
[p0414-l0043] [9.0pt] Chapter 12: Custom Models and Training with TensorFlow

=== PDF page 415 / printed label 389 ===
[p0415-l0001] [8.5pt]                        for _ in range(5)]
[p0415-l0002] [8.5pt]         self.out = keras.layers.Dense(output_dim)
[p0415-l0003] [8.5pt]     def build(self, batch_input_shape):
[p0415-l0004] [8.5pt]         n_inputs = batch_input_shape[-1]
[p0415-l0005] [8.5pt]         self.reconstruct = keras.layers.Dense(n_inputs)
[p0415-l0006] [8.5pt]         super().build(batch_input_shape)
[p0415-l0007] [8.5pt]     def call(self, inputs):
[p0415-l0008] [8.5pt]         Z = inputs
[p0415-l0009] [8.5pt]         for layer in self.hidden:
[p0415-l0010] [8.5pt]             Z = layer(Z)
[p0415-l0011] [8.5pt]         reconstruction = self.reconstruct(Z)
[p0415-l0012] [8.5pt]         recon_loss = tf.reduce_mean(tf.square(reconstruction - inputs))
[p0415-l0013] [8.5pt]         self.add_loss(0.05 * recon_loss)
[p0415-l0014] [8.5pt]         return self.out(Z)
[p0415-l0015] [10.5pt] Similarly, you can add a custom metric based on model internals by computing it in
[p0415-l0016] [10.5pt] any way you want, as long at the result is the output of a metric object. For example,
[p0415-l0017] [10.5pt] you can create a keras.metrics.Mean() object in the constructor, then call it in the
[p0415-l0018] [10.5pt] call() method, passing it the recon_loss, and finally add it to the model by calling
[p0415-l0019] [10.5pt] the model’s add_metric() method. This way, when you train the model, Keras will
[p0415-l0020] [10.5pt] display both the mean loss over each epoch (the loss is the sum of the main loss plus
[p0415-l0021] [10.5pt] 0.05 times the reconstruction loss) and the mean reconstruction error over each
[p0415-l0022] [10.5pt] epoch. Both will go down during training:
[p0415-l0023] [8.5pt] Epoch 1/5
[p0415-l0024] [8.5pt] 11610/11610 [=============] [...] loss: 4.3092 - reconstruction_error: 1.7360
[p0415-l0025] [8.5pt] Epoch 2/5
[p0415-l0026] [8.5pt] 11610/11610 [=============] [...] loss: 1.1232 - reconstruction_error: 0.8964
[p0415-l0027] [8.5pt] [...]
[p0415-l0028] [10.5pt] In over 99% of the cases, everything we have discussed so far will be sufficient to
[p0415-l0029] [10.5pt] implement whatever model you want to build, even with complex architectures, los‐
[p0415-l0030] [10.5pt] ses, metrics, and so on. However, in some rare cases you may need to customize the
[p0415-l0031] [10.5pt] training loop itself. However, before we get there, we need to look at how to compute
[p0415-l0032] [10.5pt] gradients automatically in TensorFlow.
[p0415-l0033] [15.77pt] Computing Gradients Using Autodiff
[p0415-l0034] [10.5pt] To understand how to use autodiff (see Chapter 10 and ???) to compute gradients
[p0415-l0035] [10.5pt] automatically, let’s consider a simple toy function:
[p0415-l0036] [8.5pt] def f(w1, w2):
[p0415-l0037] [8.5pt]     return 3 * w1 ** 2 + 2 * w1 * w2
[p0415-l0038] [10.5pt] If you know calculus, you can analytically find that the partial derivative of this func‐
[p0415-l0039] [10.5pt] tion with regards to w1 is 6 * w1 + 2 * w2. You can also find that its partial derivative
[p0415-l0040] [10.5pt] with regards to w2 is 2 * w1. For example, at the point (w1, w2) = (5, 3), these par‐
[p0415-l0041] [9.0pt] Customizing Models and Training Algorithms
[p0415-l0042] [9.0pt] |
[p0415-l0043] [9.0pt] 389

=== PDF page 416 / printed label 390 ===
[p0416-l0001] [10.5pt] tial derivatives are equal to 36 and 10, respectively, so the gradient vector at this point
[p0416-l0002] [10.5pt] is (36, 10). But if this were a neural network, the function would be much more com‐
[p0416-l0003] [10.5pt] plex, typically with tens of thousands of parameters, and finding the partial deriva‐
[p0416-l0004] [10.5pt] tives analytically by hand would be an almost impossible task. One solution could be
[p0416-l0005] [10.5pt] to compute an approximation of each partial derivative by measuring how much the
[p0416-l0006] [10.5pt] function’s output changes when you tweak the corresponding parameter:
[p0416-l0007] [8.5pt] >>> w1, w2 = 5, 3
[p0416-l0008] [8.5pt] >>> eps = 1e-6
[p0416-l0009] [8.5pt] >>> (f(w1 + eps, w2) - f(w1, w2)) / eps
[p0416-l0010] [8.5pt] 36.000003007075065
[p0416-l0011] [8.5pt] >>> (f(w1, w2 + eps) - f(w1, w2)) / eps
[p0416-l0012] [8.5pt] 10.000000003174137
[p0416-l0013] [10.5pt] Looks about right! This works rather well and it is trivial to implement, but it is just
[p0416-l0014] [10.5pt] an approximation, and importantly you need to call f() at least once per parameter
[p0416-l0015] [10.5pt] (not twice, since we could compute f(w1, w2) just once). This makes this approach
[p0416-l0016] [10.5pt] intractable for large neural networks. So instead we should use autodiff (see Chap‐
[p0416-l0017] [10.5pt] ter 10 and ???). TensorFlow makes this pretty simple:
[p0416-l0018] [8.5pt] w1, w2 = tf.Variable(5.), tf.Variable(3.)
[p0416-l0019] [8.5pt] with tf.GradientTape() as tape:
[p0416-l0020] [8.5pt]     z = f(w1, w2)
[p0416-l0021] [8.5pt] gradients = tape.gradient(z, [w1, w2])
[p0416-l0022] [10.5pt] We first define two variables w1 and w2, then we create a tf.GradientTape context
[p0416-l0023] [10.5pt] that will automatically record every operation that involves a variable, and finally we
[p0416-l0024] [10.5pt] ask this tape to compute the gradients of the result z with regards to both variables
[p0416-l0025] [10.5pt] [w1, w2]. Let’s take a look at the gradients that TensorFlow computed:
[p0416-l0026] [8.5pt] >>> gradients
[p0416-l0027] [8.5pt] [<tf.Tensor: id=828234, shape=(), dtype=float32, numpy=36.0>,
[p0416-l0028] [8.5pt]  <tf.Tensor: id=828229, shape=(), dtype=float32, numpy=10.0>]
[p0416-l0029] [10.5pt] Perfect! Not only is the result accurate (the precision is only limited by the floating
[p0416-l0030] [10.5pt] point errors), but the gradient() method only goes through the recorded computa‐
[p0416-l0031] [10.5pt] tions once (in reverse order), no matter how many variables there are, so it is incredi‐
[p0416-l0032] [10.5pt] bly efficient. It’s like magic!
[p0416-l0033] [9.6pt] Only put the strict minimum inside the tf.GradientTape() block,
[p0416-l0034] [9.6pt] to save memory. Alternatively, you can pause recording by creating
[p0416-l0035] [9.6pt] a with tape.stop_recording() block inside the tf.Gradient
[p0416-l0036] [9.6pt] Tape() block.
[p0416-l0037] [10.5pt] The tape is automatically erased immediately after you call its gradient() method, so
[p0416-l0038] [10.5pt] you will get an exception if you try to call gradient() twice:
[p0416-l0039] [9.0pt] 390
[p0416-l0040] [9.0pt] |
[p0416-l0041] [9.0pt] Chapter 12: Custom Models and Training with TensorFlow

=== PDF page 417 / printed label 391 ===
[p0417-l0001] [8.5pt] with tf.GradientTape() as tape:
[p0417-l0002] [8.5pt]     z = f(w1, w2)
[p0417-l0003] [8.5pt] dz_dw1 = tape.gradient(z, w1) # => tensor 36.0
[p0417-l0004] [8.5pt] dz_dw2 = tape.gradient(z, w2) # RuntimeError!
[p0417-l0005] [10.5pt] If you need to call gradient() more than once, you must make the tape persistent,
[p0417-l0006] [10.5pt] and delete it when you are done with it to free resources:
[p0417-l0007] [8.5pt] with tf.GradientTape(persistent=True) as tape:
[p0417-l0008] [8.5pt]     z = f(w1, w2)
[p0417-l0009] [8.5pt] dz_dw1 = tape.gradient(z, w1) # => tensor 36.0
[p0417-l0010] [8.5pt] dz_dw2 = tape.gradient(z, w2) # => tensor 10.0, works fine now!
[p0417-l0011] [8.5pt] del tape
[p0417-l0012] [10.5pt] By default, the tape will only track operations involving variables, so if you try to
[p0417-l0013] [10.5pt] compute the gradient of z with regards to anything else than a variable, the result will
[p0417-l0014] [10.5pt] be None:
[p0417-l0015] [8.5pt] c1, c2 = tf.constant(5.), tf.constant(3.)
[p0417-l0016] [8.5pt] with tf.GradientTape() as tape:
[p0417-l0017] [8.5pt]     z = f(c1, c2)
[p0417-l0018] [8.5pt] gradients = tape.gradient(z, [c1, c2]) # returns [None, None]
[p0417-l0019] [10.5pt] However, you can force the tape to watch any tensors you like, to record every opera‐
[p0417-l0020] [10.5pt] tion that involves them. You can then compute gradients with regards to these ten‐
[p0417-l0021] [10.5pt] sors, as if they were variables:
[p0417-l0022] [8.5pt] with tf.GradientTape() as tape:
[p0417-l0023] [8.5pt]     tape.watch(c1)
[p0417-l0024] [8.5pt]     tape.watch(c2)
[p0417-l0025] [8.5pt]     z = f(c1, c2)
[p0417-l0026] [8.5pt] gradients = tape.gradient(z, [c1, c2]) # returns [tensor 36., tensor 10.]
[p0417-l0027] [10.5pt] This can be useful in some cases, for example if you want to implement a regulariza‐
[p0417-l0028] [10.5pt] tion loss that penalizes activations that vary a lot when the inputs vary little: the loss
[p0417-l0029] [10.5pt] will be based on the gradient of the activations with regards to the inputs. Since the
[p0417-l0030] [10.5pt] inputs are not variables, you would need to tell the tape to watch them.
[p0417-l0031] [10.5pt] If you compute the gradient of a list of tensors (e.g., [z1, z2, z3]) with regards to
[p0417-l0032] [10.5pt] some variables (e.g., [w1, w2]), TensorFlow actually efficiently computes the sum of
[p0417-l0033] [10.5pt] the gradients of these tensors (i.e., gradient(z1, [w1, w2]), plus gradient(z2,
[p0417-l0034] [10.5pt] [w1, w2]), plus gradient(z3, [w1, w2])). Due to the way reverse-mode autodiff
[p0417-l0035] [10.5pt] works, it is not possible to compute the individual gradients (z1, z2 and z3) without
[p0417-l0036] [10.5pt] actually calling gradient() multiple times (once for z1, once for z2 and once for z3),
[p0417-l0037] [10.5pt] which requires making the tape persistent (and deleting it afterwards).
[p0417-l0038] [9.0pt] Customizing Models and Training Algorithms
[p0417-l0039] [9.0pt] |
[p0417-l0040] [9.0pt] 391

=== PDF page 418 / printed label 392 ===
[p0418-l0001] [10.5pt] Moreover, it is actually possible to compute second order partial derivatives (the Hes‐
[p0418-l0002] [10.5pt] sians, i.e., the partial derivatives of the partial derivatives)! To do this, we need to
[p0418-l0003] [10.5pt] record the operations that are performed when computing the first-order partial
[p0418-l0004] [10.5pt] derivatives (the Jacobians): this requires a second tape. Here is how it works:
[p0418-l0005] [8.5pt] with tf.GradientTape(persistent=True) as hessian_tape:
[p0418-l0006] [8.5pt]     with tf.GradientTape() as jacobian_tape:
[p0418-l0007] [8.5pt]         z = f(w1, w2)
[p0418-l0008] [8.5pt]     jacobians = jacobian_tape.gradient(z, [w1, w2])
[p0418-l0009] [8.5pt] hessians = [hessian_tape.gradient(jacobian, [w1, w2])
[p0418-l0010] [8.5pt]             for jacobian in jacobians]
[p0418-l0011] [8.5pt] del hessian_tape
[p0418-l0012] [10.5pt] The inner tape is used to compute the Jacobians, as we did earlier. The outer tape is
[p0418-l0013] [10.5pt] used to compute the partial derivatives of each Jacobian. Since we need to call gradi
[p0418-l0014] [10.5pt] ent() once for each Jacobian (or else we would get the sum of the partial derivatives
[p0418-l0015] [10.5pt] over all the Jabobians, as explained earlier), we need the outer tape to be persistent, so
[p0418-l0016] [10.5pt] we delete it at the end. The Jacobians are obviously the same as earlier (36 and 5), but
[p0418-l0017] [10.5pt] now we also have the Hessians:
[p0418-l0018] [8.5pt] >>> hessians # dz_dw1_dw1, dz_dw1_dw2, dz_dw2_dw1, dz_dw2_dw2
[p0418-l0019] [8.5pt] [[<tf.Tensor: id=830578, shape=(), dtype=float32, numpy=6.0>,
[p0418-l0020] [8.5pt]   <tf.Tensor: id=830595, shape=(), dtype=float32, numpy=2.0>],
[p0418-l0021] [8.5pt]  [<tf.Tensor: id=830600, shape=(), dtype=float32, numpy=2.0>, None]]
[p0418-l0022] [10.5pt] Let’s verify these Hessians. The first two are the partial derivatives of 6 * w1 + 2 * w2
[p0418-l0023] [10.5pt] (which is, as we saw earlier, the partial derivative of f with regards to w1), with
[p0418-l0024] [10.5pt] regards to w1 and w2. The result is correct: 6 for w1 and 2 for w2. The next two are the
[p0418-l0025] [10.5pt] partial derivatives of 2 * w1 (the partial derivative of f with regards to w2), with
[p0418-l0026] [10.5pt] regards to w1 and w2, which are 2 for w1 and 0 for w2. Note that TensorFlow returns
[p0418-l0027] [10.5pt] None instead of 0 since w2 does not appear at all in 2 * w1. TensorFlow also returns
[p0418-l0028] [10.5pt] None when you use an operation whose gradients are not defined (e.g., tf.argmax()).
[p0418-l0029] [10.5pt] In some rare cases you may want to stop gradients from backpropagating through
[p0418-l0030] [10.5pt] some part of your neural network. To do this, you must use the tf.stop_gradient()
[p0418-l0031] [10.5pt] function: it just returns its inputs during the forward pass (like tf.identity()), but
[p0418-l0032] [10.5pt] it does not let gradients through during backpropagation (it acts like a constant). For
[p0418-l0033] [10.5pt] example:
[p0418-l0034] [8.5pt] def f(w1, w2):
[p0418-l0035] [8.5pt]     return 3 * w1 ** 2 + tf.stop_gradient(2 * w1 * w2)
[p0418-l0036] [8.5pt] with tf.GradientTape() as tape:
[p0418-l0037] [8.5pt]     z = f(w1, w2) # same result as without stop_gradient()
[p0418-l0038] [8.5pt] gradients = tape.gradient(z, [w1, w2]) # => returns [tensor 30., None]
[p0418-l0039] [9.0pt] 392
[p0418-l0040] [9.0pt] |
[p0418-l0041] [9.0pt] Chapter 12: Custom Models and Training with TensorFlow

[p0419-l0001] [10.5pt] Finally, you may occasionally run into some numerical issues when computing gradi‐
[p0419-l0002] [10.5pt] ents. For example, if you compute the gradients of the my_softplus() function for
[p0419-l0003] [10.5pt] large inputs, the result will be NaN:
[p0419-l0004] [8.5pt] >>> x = tf.Variable([100.])
[p0419-l0005] [8.5pt] >>> with tf.GradientTape() as tape:
[p0419-l0006] [8.5pt] ...     z = my_softplus(x)
[p0419-l0007] [8.5pt] ...
[p0419-l0008] [8.5pt] >>> tape.gradient(z, [x])
[p0419-l0009] [8.5pt] <tf.Tensor: [...] numpy=array([nan], dtype=float32)>
[p0419-l0010] [10.5pt] This is because computing the gradients of this function using autodiff leads to some
[p0419-l0011] [10.5pt] numerical difficulties: due to floating point precision errors, autodiff ends up com‐
[p0419-l0012] [10.5pt] puting infinity divided by infinity (which returns NaN). Fortunately, we can analyti‐
[p0419-l0013] [10.5pt] cally find that the derivative of the softplus function is just 1 / (1 + 1 / exp(x)), which
[p0419-l0014] [10.5pt] is numerically stable. Next, we can tell TensorFlow to use this stable function when
[p0419-l0015] [10.5pt] computing the gradients of the my_softplus() function, by decorating it with
[p0419-l0016] [10.5pt] @tf.custom_gradient, and making it return both its normal output and the function
[p0419-l0017] [10.5pt] that computes the derivatives (note that it will receive as input the gradients that were
[p0419-l0018] [10.5pt] backpropagated so far, down to the softplus function, and according to the chain rule
[p0419-l0019] [10.5pt] we should multiply them with this function’s gradients):
[p0419-l0020] [8.5pt] @tf.custom_gradient
[p0419-l0021] [8.5pt] def my_better_softplus(z):
[p0419-l0022] [8.5pt]     exp = tf.exp(z)
[p0419-l0023] [8.5pt]     def my_softplus_gradients(grad):
[p0419-l0024] [8.5pt]         return grad / (1 + 1 / exp)
[p0419-l0025] [8.5pt]     return tf.math.log(exp + 1), my_softplus_gradients
[p0419-l0026] [10.5pt] Now when we compute the gradients of the my_better_softplus() function, we get
[p0419-l0027] [10.5pt] the proper result, even for large input values (however, the main output still explodes
[p0419-l0028] [10.5pt] because of the exponential: one workaround is to use tf.where() to just return the
[p0419-l0029] [10.5pt] inputs when they are large).
[p0419-l0030] [10.5pt] Congratulations! You can now compute the gradients of any function (provided it is
[p0419-l0031] [10.5pt] differentiable at the point where you compute it), you can even compute Hessians,
[p0419-l0032] [10.5pt] block backpropagation when needed and even write your own gradient functions!
[p0419-l0033] [10.5pt] This is probably more flexibility than you will ever need, even if you build your own
[p0419-l0034] [10.5pt] custom training loops, as we will see now.
[p0419-l0035] [15.77pt] Custom Training Loops
[p0419-l0036] [10.5pt] In some rare cases, the fit() method may not be flexible enough for what you need
[p0419-l0037] [10.5pt] to do. For example, the Wide and Deep paper we discussed in Chapter 10 actually
[p0419-l0038] [10.5pt] uses two different optimizers: one for the wide path and the other for the deep path.
[p0419-l0039] [10.5pt] Since the fit() method only uses one optimizer (the one that we specify when
[p0419-l0040] [9.0pt] Customizing Models and Training Algorithms
[p0419-l0041] [9.0pt] |

[p0420-l0001] [10.5pt] compiling the model), implementing this paper requires writing your own custom
[p0420-l0002] [10.5pt] loop.
[p0420-l0003] [10.5pt] You may also like to write your own custom training loops simply to feel more confi‐
[p0420-l0004] [10.5pt] dent that it does precisely what you intent it to do (perhaps you are unsure about
[p0420-l0005] [10.5pt] some details of the fit() method). It can sometimes feel safer to make everything
[p0420-l0006] [10.5pt] explicit. However, remember that writing a custom training loop will make your code
[p0420-l0007] [10.5pt] longer, more error prone and harder to maintain.
[p0420-l0008] [9.6pt] Unless you really need the extra flexibility, you should prefer using
[p0420-l0009] [9.6pt] the fit() method rather than implementing your own training
[p0420-l0010] [9.6pt] loop, especially if you work in a team.
[p0420-l0011] [10.5pt] First, let’s build a simple model. No need to compile it, since we will handle the train‐
[p0420-l0012] [10.5pt] ing loop manually:
[p0420-l0013] [8.5pt] l2_reg = keras.regularizers.l2(0.05)
[p0420-l0014] [8.5pt] model = keras.models.Sequential([
[p0420-l0015] [8.5pt]     keras.layers.Dense(30, activation="elu", kernel_initializer="he_normal",
[p0420-l0016] [8.5pt]                        kernel_regularizer=l2_reg),
[p0420-l0017] [8.5pt]     keras.layers.Dense(1, kernel_regularizer=l2_reg)
[p0420-l0018] [8.5pt] ])
[p0420-l0019] [10.5pt] Next, let’s create a tiny function that will randomly sample a batch of instances from
[p0420-l0020] [10.5pt] the training set (in Chapter 13 we will discuss the Data API, which offers a much bet‐
[p0420-l0021] [10.5pt] ter alternative):
[p0420-l0022] [8.5pt] def random_batch(X, y, batch_size=32):
[p0420-l0023] [8.5pt]     idx = np.random.randint(len(X), size=batch_size)
[p0420-l0024] [8.5pt]     return X[idx], y[idx]
[p0420-l0025] [10.5pt] Let’s also define a function that will display the training status, including the number
[p0420-l0026] [10.5pt] of steps, the total number of steps, the mean loss since the start of the epoch (i.e., we
[p0420-l0027] [10.5pt] will use the Mean metric to compute it), and other metrics:
[p0420-l0028] [8.5pt] def print_status_bar(iteration, total, loss, metrics=None):
[p0420-l0029] [8.5pt]     metrics = " - ".join(["{}: {:.4f}".format(m.name, m.result())
[p0420-l0030] [8.5pt]                          for m in [loss] + (metrics or [])])
[p0420-l0031] [8.5pt]     end = "" if iteration < total else "\n"
[p0420-l0032] [8.5pt]     print("\r{}/{} - ".format(iteration, total) + metrics,
[p0420-l0033] [8.5pt]           end=end)
[p0420-l0034] [10.5pt] This code is self-explanatory, unless you are unfamiliar with Python string format‐
[p0420-l0035] [10.5pt] ting: {:.4f} will format a float with 4 digits after the decimal point. Moreover, using
[p0420-l0036] [10.5pt] \r (carriage return) along with end="" ensures that the status bar always gets printed
[p0420-l0037] [10.5pt] on the same line. In the notebook, the print_status_bar() function also includes a
[p0420-l0038] [10.5pt] progress bar, but you could use the handy tqdm library instead.

[p0421-l0001] [10.5pt] With that, let’s get down to business! First, we need to define some hyperparameters,
[p0421-l0002] [10.5pt] choose the optimizer, the loss function and the metrics (just the MAE in this exam‐
[p0421-l0003] [10.5pt] ple):
[p0421-l0004] [8.5pt] n_epochs = 5
[p0421-l0005] [8.5pt] batch_size = 32
[p0421-l0006] [8.5pt] n_steps = len(X_train) // batch_size
[p0421-l0007] [8.5pt] optimizer = keras.optimizers.Nadam(lr=0.01)
[p0421-l0008] [8.5pt] loss_fn = keras.losses.mean_squared_error
[p0421-l0009] [8.5pt] mean_loss = keras.metrics.Mean()
[p0421-l0010] [8.5pt] metrics = [keras.metrics.MeanAbsoluteError()]
[p0421-l0011] [10.5pt] And now we are ready to build the custom loop!
[p0421-l0012] [8.5pt] for epoch in range(1, n_epochs + 1):
[p0421-l0013] [8.5pt]     print("Epoch {}/{}".format(epoch, n_epochs))
[p0421-l0014] [8.5pt]     for step in range(1, n_steps + 1):
[p0421-l0015] [8.5pt]         X_batch, y_batch = random_batch(X_train_scaled, y_train)
[p0421-l0016] [8.5pt]         with tf.GradientTape() as tape:
[p0421-l0017] [8.5pt]             y_pred = model(X_batch, training=True)
[p0421-l0018] [8.5pt]             main_loss = tf.reduce_mean(loss_fn(y_batch, y_pred))
[p0421-l0019] [8.5pt]             loss = tf.add_n([main_loss] + model.losses)
[p0421-l0020] [8.5pt]         gradients = tape.gradient(loss, model.trainable_variables)
[p0421-l0021] [8.5pt]         optimizer.apply_gradients(zip(gradients, model.trainable_variables))
[p0421-l0022] [8.5pt]         mean_loss(loss)
[p0421-l0023] [8.5pt]         for metric in metrics:
[p0421-l0024] [8.5pt]             metric(y_batch, y_pred)
[p0421-l0025] [8.5pt]         print_status_bar(step * batch_size, len(y_train), mean_loss, metrics)
[p0421-l0026] [8.5pt]     print_status_bar(len(y_train), len(y_train), mean_loss, metrics)
[p0421-l0027] [8.5pt]     for metric in [mean_loss] + metrics:
[p0421-l0028] [8.5pt]         metric.reset_states()
[p0421-l0029] [10.5pt] There’s a lot going on in this code, so let’s walk through it:
[p0421-l0030] [10.5pt] • We create two nested loops: one for the epochs, the other for the batches within
[p0421-l0031] [10.5pt] an epoch.
[p0421-l0032] [10.5pt] • Then we sample a random batch from the training set.
[p0421-l0033] [10.5pt] • Inside the tf.GradientTape() block, we make a prediction for one batch (using
[p0421-l0034] [10.5pt] the model as a function), and we compute the loss: it is equal to the main loss
[p0421-l0035] [10.5pt] plus the other losses (in this model, there is one regularization loss per layer).
[p0421-l0036] [10.5pt] Since the mean_squared_error() function returns one loss per instance, we
[p0421-l0037] [10.5pt] compute the mean over the batch using tf.reduce_mean() (if you wanted to
[p0421-l0038] [10.5pt] apply different weights to each instance, this is where you would do it). The regu‐
[p0421-l0039] [10.5pt] larization losses are already reduced to a single scalar each, so we just need to
[p0421-l0040] [10.5pt] sum them (using tf.add_n(), which sums multiple tensors of the same shape
[p0421-l0041] [10.5pt] and data type).
[p0421-l0042] [9.0pt] Customizing Models and Training Algorithms
[p0421-l0043] [9.0pt] |
[p0421-l0044] [9.0pt] 395

=== PDF page 422 / printed label 396 ===
[p0422-l0001] [10.5pt] • Next, we ask the tape to compute the gradient of the loss with regards to each
[p0422-l0002] [10.5pt] trainable variable (not all variables!), and we apply them to the optimizer to per‐
[p0422-l0003] [10.5pt] form a Gradient Descent step.
[p0422-l0004] [10.5pt] • Next we update the mean loss and the metrics (over the current epoch), and we
[p0422-l0005] [10.5pt] display the status bar.
[p0422-l0006] [10.5pt] • At the end of each epoch, we display the status bar again to make it look com‐
[p0422-l0007] [10.5pt] plete11 and to print a line feed, and we reset the states of the mean loss and the
[p0422-l0008] [10.5pt] metrics.
[p0422-l0009] [10.5pt] If you set the optimizer’s clipnorm or clipvalue hyperparameters, it will take care of
[p0422-l0010] [10.5pt] this for you. If you want to apply any other transformation to the gradients, simply do
[p0422-l0011] [10.5pt] so before calling the apply_gradients() method.
[p0422-l0012] [10.5pt] If you add weight constraints to your model (e.g., by setting kernel_constraint or
[p0422-l0013] [10.5pt] bias_constraint when creating a layer), you should update the training loop to
[p0422-l0014] [10.5pt] apply these constraints just after apply_gradients():
[p0422-l0015] [8.5pt] for variable in model.variables:
[p0422-l0016] [8.5pt]     if variable.constraint is not None:
[p0422-l0017] [8.5pt]         variable.assign(variable.constraint(variable))
[p0422-l0018] [10.5pt] Most importantly, this training loop does not handle layers that behave differently
[p0422-l0019] [10.5pt] during training and testing (e.g., BatchNormalization or Dropout). To handle these,
[p0422-l0020] [10.5pt] you need to call the model with training=True and make sure it propagates this to
[p0422-l0021] [10.5pt] every layer that needs it.12
[p0422-l0022] [10.5pt] As you can see, there are quite a lot of things you need to get right, it is easy to make a
[p0422-l0023] [10.5pt] mistake. But on the bright side, you get full control, so it’s your call.
[p0422-l0024] [10.5pt] Now that you know how to customize any part of your models13 and training algo‐
[p0422-l0025] [10.5pt] rithms, let’s see how you can use TensorFlow’s automatic graph generation feature: it
[p0422-l0026] [10.5pt] can speed up your custom code considerably, and it will also make it portable to any
[p0422-l0027] [10.5pt] platform supported by TensorFlow (see ???).
[p0422-l0028] [18.92pt] TensorFlow Functions and Graphs
[p0422-l0029] [10.5pt] In TensorFlow 1, graphs were unavoidable (as were the complexities that came with
[p0422-l0030] [10.5pt] them): they were a central part of TensorFlow’s API. In TensorFlow 2, they are still
[p0422-l0031] [8.0pt] 11 The truth is we did not process every single instance in the training set because we sampled instances ran‐
[p0422-l0032] [8.0pt] domly, so some were processed more than once while others were not processed at all. In practice that’s fine.
[p0422-l0033] [8.0pt] Moreover, if the training set size is not a multiple of the batch size, we will miss a few instances.

[p0423-l0001] [10.5pt] there, but not as central, and much (much!) simpler to use. To demonstrate this, let’s
[p0423-l0002] [10.5pt] start with a trivial function that just computes the cube of its input:
[p0423-l0003] [8.5pt] def cube(x):
[p0423-l0004] [8.5pt]     return x ** 3
[p0423-l0005] [10.5pt] We can obviously call this function with a Python value, such as an int or a float, or
[p0423-l0006] [10.5pt] we can call it with a tensor:
[p0423-l0007] [8.5pt] >>> cube(2)
[p0423-l0008] [8.5pt] 8
[p0423-l0009] [8.5pt] >>> cube(tf.constant(2.0))
[p0423-l0010] [8.5pt] <tf.Tensor: id=18634148, shape=(), dtype=float32, numpy=8.0>
[p0423-l0011] [10.5pt] Now, let’s use tf.function() to convert this Python function to a TensorFlow Func‐
[p0423-l0012] [10.5pt] tion:
[p0423-l0013] [8.5pt] >>> tf_cube = tf.function(cube)
[p0423-l0014] [8.5pt] >>> tf_cube
[p0423-l0015] [8.5pt] <tensorflow.python.eager.def_function.Function at 0x1546fc080>
[p0423-l0016] [10.5pt] This TF Function can then be used exactly like the original Python function, and it
[p0423-l0017] [10.5pt] will return the same result (but as tensors):
[p0423-l0018] [8.5pt] >>> tf_cube(2)
[p0423-l0019] [8.5pt] <tf.Tensor: id=18634201, shape=(), dtype=int32, numpy=8>
[p0423-l0020] [8.5pt] >>> tf_cube(tf.constant(2.0))
[p0423-l0021] [8.5pt] <tf.Tensor: id=18634211, shape=(), dtype=float32, numpy=8.0>
[p0423-l0022] [10.5pt] Under the hood, tf.function() analyzed the computations performed by the cube()
[p0423-l0023] [10.5pt] function and generated an equivalent computation graph! As you can see, it was
[p0423-l0024] [10.5pt] rather painless (we will see how this works shortly). Alternatively, we could have used
[p0423-l0025] [10.5pt] tf.function as a decorator; this is actually more common:
[p0423-l0026] [8.5pt] @tf.function
[p0423-l0027] [8.5pt] def tf_cube(x):
[p0423-l0028] [8.5pt]     return x ** 3
[p0423-l0029] [10.5pt] The original Python function is still available via the TF Function’s python_function
[p0423-l0030] [10.5pt] attribute, in case you ever need it:
[p0423-l0031] [8.5pt] >>> tf_cube.python_function(2)
[p0423-l0032] [8.5pt] 8
[p0423-l0033] [10.5pt] TensorFlow optimizes the computation graph, pruning unused nodes, simplifying
[p0423-l0034] [10.5pt] expressions (e.g., 1 + 2 would get replaced with 3), and more. Once the optimized
[p0423-l0035] [10.5pt] graph is ready, the TF Function efficiently executes the operations in the graph, in the
[p0423-l0036] [10.5pt] appropriate order (and in parallel when it can). As a result, a TF Function will usually
[p0423-l0037] [10.5pt] run much faster than the original Python function, especially if it performs complex
[p0423-l0038] [9.0pt] TensorFlow Functions and Graphs
[p0423-l0039] [9.0pt] |
[p0423-l0040] [9.0pt] 397

=== PDF page 424 / printed label 398 ===
[p0424-l0001] [10.5pt] computations.14 Most of the time you will not really need to know more than that:
[p0424-l0002] [10.5pt] when you want to boost a Python function, just transform it into a TF Function.
[p0424-l0003] [10.5pt] That’s all!
[p0424-l0004] [10.5pt] Moreover, when you write a custom loss function, a custom metric, a custom layer or
[p0424-l0005] [10.5pt] any other custom function, and you use it in a Keras model (as we did throughout
[p0424-l0006] [10.5pt] this chapter), Keras automatically converts your function into a TF Function, no need
[p0424-l0007] [10.5pt] to use tf.function(). So most of the time, all this magic is 100% transparent.
[p0424-l0008] [9.6pt] You can tell Keras not to convert your Python functions to TF
[p0424-l0009] [9.6pt] Functions by setting dynamic=True when creating a custom layer
[p0424-l0010] [9.6pt] or a custom model. Alternatively, you can set run_eagerly=True
[p0424-l0011] [9.6pt] when calling the model’s compile() method.
[p0424-l0012] [10.5pt] TF Function generates a new graph for every unique set of input shapes and data
[p0424-l0013] [10.5pt] types, and it caches it for subsequent calls. For example, if you call tf_cube(tf.con
[p0424-l0014] [10.5pt] stant(10)), a graph will be generated for int32 tensors of shape []. Then if you call
[p0424-l0015] [10.5pt] tf_cube(tf.constant(20)), the same graph will be reused. But if you then call
[p0424-l0016] [10.5pt] tf_cube(tf.constant([10, 20])), a new graph will be generated for int32 tensors
[p0424-l0017] [10.5pt] of shape [2]. This is how TF Functions handle polymorphism (i.e., varying argument
[p0424-l0018] [10.5pt] types and shapes). However, this is only true for tensor arguments: if you pass numer‐
[p0424-l0019] [10.5pt] ical Python values to a TF Function, a new graph will be generated for every distinct
[p0424-l0020] [10.5pt] value: for example, calling tf_cube(10) and tf_cube(20) will generate two graphs.
[p0424-l0021] [9.6pt] If you call a TF Function many times with different numerical
[p0424-l0022] [9.6pt] Python values, then many graphs will be generated, slowing down
[p0424-l0023] [9.6pt] your program and using up a lot of RAM. Python values should be
[p0424-l0024] [9.6pt] reserved for arguments that will have few unique values, such as
[p0424-l0025] [9.6pt] hyperparameters like the number of neurons per layer. This allows
[p0424-l0026] [9.6pt] TensorFlow to better optimize each variant of your model.
[p0424-l0027] [15.77pt] Autograph and Tracing
[p0424-l0028] [10.5pt] So how does TensorFlow generate graphs? Well, first it starts by analyzing the Python
[p0424-l0029] [10.5pt] function’s source code to capture all the control flow statements, such as for loops
[p0424-l0030] [10.5pt] and while loops, if statements, as well as break, continue and return statements.
[p0424-l0031] [10.5pt] This first step is called autograph. The reason TensorFlow has to analyze the source
[p0424-l0032] [10.5pt] code is that Python does not provide any other way to capture control flow state‐
[p0424-l0033] [10.5pt] ments: it offers magic methods like __add__() or __mul__() to capture operators like
[p0424-l0034] [8.0pt] 14 However, in this trivial example, the computation graph is so small that there is nothing at all to optimize, so
[p0424-l0035] [8.0pt] tf_cube() actually runs much slower than cube().
[p0424-l0036] [9.0pt] 398
[p0424-l0037] [9.0pt] |
[p0424-l0038] [9.0pt] Chapter 12: Custom Models and Training with TensorFlow

=== PDF page 425 / printed label 399 ===
[p0425-l0001] [10.5pt] + and *, but there are no __while__() or __if__() magic methods. After analyzing
[p0425-l0002] [10.5pt] the function’s code, autograph outputs an upgraded version of that function in which
[p0425-l0003] [10.5pt] all the control flow statements are replaced by the appropriate TensorFlow opera‐
[p0425-l0004] [10.5pt] tions, such as tf.while_loop() for loops and tf.cond() for if statements. For
[p0425-l0005] [10.5pt] example, in Figure 12-4, autograph analyzes the source code of the sum_squares()
[p0425-l0006] [10.5pt] Python function, and it generates the tf__sum_squares() function. In this function,
[p0425-l0007] [10.5pt] the for loop is replaced by the definition of the loop_body() function (containing
[p0425-l0008] [10.5pt] the body of the original for loop), followed by a call to the for_stmt() function. This
[p0425-l0009] [10.5pt] call will build the appropriate tf.while_loop() operation in the computation graph.
[p0425-l0010] [10.5pt] Figure 12-4. How TensorFlow generates graphs using autograph and tracing
[p0425-l0011] [10.5pt] Next, TensorFlow calls this “upgraded” function, but instead of passing the actual
[p0425-l0012] [10.5pt] argument, it passes a symbolic tensor, meaning a tensor without any actual value, only
[p0425-l0013] [10.5pt] a name, a data type, and a shape. For example, if you call sum_squares(tf.con
[p0425-l0014] [10.5pt] stant(10)), then the tf__sum_squares() function will actually be called with a sym‐
[p0425-l0015] [10.5pt] bolic tensor of type int32 and shape []. The function will run in graph mode, meaning
[p0425-l0016] [10.5pt] that each TensorFlow operation will just add a node in the graph to represent itself
[p0425-l0017] [10.5pt] and its output tensor(s) (as opposed to the regular mode, called eager execution, or
[p0425-l0018] [10.5pt] eager mode). In graph mode, TF operations do not perform any actual computations.
[p0425-l0019] [10.5pt] This should feel familiar if you know TensorFlow 1, as graph mode was the default
[p0425-l0020] [10.5pt] mode. In Figure 12-4, you can see the tf__sum_squares() function being called with
[p0425-l0021] [10.5pt] a symbolic tensor as argument (in this case, an int32 tensor of shape []), and the final
[p0425-l0022] [10.5pt] graph generated during tracing. The ellipses represent operations, and the arrows
[p0425-l0023] [10.5pt] represent tensors (both the generated function and the graph are simplified).
[p0425-l0024] [9.0pt] TensorFlow Functions and Graphs
[p0425-l0025] [9.0pt] |
[p0425-l0026] [9.0pt] 399

=== PDF page 426 / printed label 400 ===
[p0426-l0001] [9.6pt] To view the generated function’s source code, you can call tf.auto
[p0426-l0002] [9.6pt] graph.to_code(sum_squares.python_function). The code is not
[p0426-l0003] [9.6pt] meant to be pretty, but it can sometimes help for debugging.
[p0426-l0004] [15.77pt] TF Function Rules
[p0426-l0005] [10.5pt] Most of the time, converting a Python function that performs TensorFlow operations
[p0426-l0006] [10.5pt] into a TF Function is trivial: just decorate it with @tf.function or let Keras take care
[p0426-l0007] [10.5pt] of it for you. However, there are a few rules to respect:
[p0426-l0008] [10.5pt] • If you call any external library, including NumPy or even the standard library,
[p0426-l0009] [10.5pt] this call will run only during tracing, it will not be part of the graph. Indeed, a
[p0426-l0010] [10.5pt] TensorFlow graph can only include TensorFlow constructs (tensors, operations,
[p0426-l0011] [10.5pt] variables, datasets, and so on). So make sure you use tf.reduce_sum() instead of
[p0426-l0012] [10.5pt] np.sum(), and tf.sort() instead of the built-in sorted() function, and so on
[p0426-l0013] [10.5pt] (unless you really want the code to run only during tracing).
[p0426-l0014] [10.5pt] — For example, if you define a TF function f(x) that just returns np.ran
[p0426-l0015] [10.5pt] dom.rand(), a random number will only be generated when the function is
[p0426-l0016] [10.5pt] traced, so f(tf.constant(2.)) and f(tf.constant(3.)) will return the
[p0426-l0017] [10.5pt] same random number, but f(tf.constant([2., 3.])) will return a different
[p0426-l0018] [10.5pt] one. If you replace np.random.rand() with tf.random.uniform([]), then a
[p0426-l0019] [10.5pt] new random number will be generated upon every call, since the operation
[p0426-l0020] [10.5pt] will be part of the graph.
[p0426-l0021] [10.5pt] — If your non-TensorFlow code has side-effects (such as logging something or
[p0426-l0022] [10.5pt] updating a Python counter), then you should not expect that side-effect to
[p0426-l0023] [10.5pt] occur every time you call the TF Function, as it will only occur when the func‐
[p0426-l0024] [10.5pt] tion is traced.
[p0426-l0025] [10.5pt] — You can wrap arbitrary Python code in a tf.py_function() operation, but
[p0426-l0026] [10.5pt] this will hinder performance, as TensorFlow will not be able to do any graph
[p0426-l0027] [10.5pt] optimization on this code, and it will also reduce portability, as the graph will
[p0426-l0028] [10.5pt] only run on platforms where Python is available (and the right libraries
[p0426-l0029] [10.5pt] installed).
[p0426-l0030] [10.5pt] • You can call other Python functions or TF Functions, but they should follow the
[p0426-l0031] [10.5pt] same rules, as TensorFlow will also capture their operations in the computation
[p0426-l0032] [10.5pt] graph. Note that these other functions do not need to be decorated with
[p0426-l0033] [10.5pt] @tf.function.
[p0426-l0034] [10.5pt] • If the function creates a TensorFlow variable (or any other stateful TensorFlow
[p0426-l0035] [10.5pt] object, such as a dataset or a queue), it must do so upon the very first call, and
[p0426-l0036] [10.5pt] only then, or else you will get an exception. It is usually preferable to create vari‐
[p0426-l0037] [10.5pt] ables outside of the TF Function (e.g., in the build() method of a custom layer).
[p0426-l0038] [9.0pt] 400
[p0426-l0039] [9.0pt] |
[p0426-l0040] [9.0pt] Chapter 12: Custom Models and Training with TensorFlow

=== PDF page 427 / printed label 401 ===
[p0427-l0001] [10.5pt] • The source code of your Python function should be available to TensorFlow. If
[p0427-l0002] [10.5pt] the source code is unavailable (for example, if you define your function in the
[p0427-l0003] [10.5pt] Python shell, which does not give access to the source code, or if you deploy only
[p0427-l0004] [10.5pt] the compiled Python files *.pyc to production), then the graph generation pro‐
[p0427-l0005] [10.5pt] cess will fail or have limited functionality.
[p0427-l0006] [10.5pt] • TensorFlow will only capture for loops that iterate over a tensor or a Dataset. So
[p0427-l0007] [10.5pt] make sure you use for i in tf.range(10) rather than for i in range(10), or
[p0427-l0008] [10.5pt] else the loop will not be captured in the graph. Instead, it will run during tracing.
[p0427-l0009] [10.5pt] This may be what you want, if the for loop is meant to build the graph, for exam‐
[p0427-l0010] [10.5pt] ple to create each layer in a neural network.
[p0427-l0011] [10.5pt] • And as always, for performance reasons, you should prefer a vectorized imple‐
[p0427-l0012] [10.5pt] mentation whenever you can, rather than using loops.
[p0427-l0013] [10.5pt] It’s time to sum up! In this chapter we started with a brief overview of TensorFlow,
[p0427-l0014] [10.5pt] then we looked at TensorFlow’s low-level API, including tensors, operations, variables
[p0427-l0015] [10.5pt] and special data structures. We then used these tools to customize almost every com‐
[p0427-l0016] [10.5pt] ponent in tf.keras. Finally, we looked at how TF Functions can boost performance,
[p0427-l0017] [10.5pt] how graphs are generated using autograph and tracing, and what rules to follow when
[p0427-l0018] [10.5pt] you write TF Functions (if you would like to open the black box a bit further, for
[p0427-l0019] [10.5pt] example to explore the generated graphs, you will find further technical details
[p0427-l0020] [10.5pt] in ???).

[p0427-l0022] [10.5pt] TensorFlow.

[p0429-l0001] [16.82pt] CHAPTER 13
[p0429-l0002] [25.22pt] Loading and Preprocessing Data with
[p0429-l0003] [25.22pt] TensorFlow
[p0429-l0004] [9.6pt] With Early Release ebooks, you get books in their earliest form—
[p0429-l0005] [9.6pt] the author’s raw and unedited content as he or she writes—so you
[p0429-l0006] [9.6pt] can take advantage of these technologies long before the official
[p0429-l0007] [9.6pt] release of these titles. The following will be Chapter 13 in the final
[p0429-l0008] [9.6pt] release of the book.
[p0429-l0009] [10.5pt] So far we have used only datasets that fit in memory, but Deep Learning systems are
[p0429-l0010] [10.5pt] often trained on very large datasets that will not fit in RAM. Ingesting a large dataset
[p0429-l0011] [10.5pt] and preprocessing it efficiently can be tricky to implement with other Deep Learning
[p0429-l0012] [10.5pt] libraries, but TensorFlow makes it easy thanks to the Data API: you just create a data‐
[p0429-l0013] [10.5pt] set object, tell it where to get the data, then transform it in any way you want, and
[p0429-l0014] [10.5pt] TensorFlow takes care of all the implementation details, such as multithreading,
[p0429-l0015] [10.5pt] queuing, batching, prefetching, and so on.
[p0429-l0016] [10.5pt] Off the shelf, the Data API can read from text files (such as CSV files), binary files
[p0429-l0017] [10.5pt] with fixed-size records, and binary files that use TensorFlow’s TFRecord format,
[p0429-l0018] [10.5pt] which supports records of varying sizes. TFRecord is a flexible and efficient binary
[p0429-l0019] [10.5pt] format based on Protocol Buffers (an open source binary format). The Data API also
[p0429-l0020] [10.5pt] has support for reading from SQL databases. Moreover, many Open Source exten‐
[p0429-l0021] [10.5pt] sions are available to read from all sorts of data sources, such as Google’s BigQuery
[p0429-l0022] [10.5pt] service.
[p0429-l0023] [10.5pt] However, reading huge datasets efficiently is not the only difficulty: the data also
[p0429-l0024] [10.5pt] needs to be preprocessed. Indeed, it is not always composed strictly of convenient
[p0429-l0025] [10.5pt] numerical fields: sometimes there will be text features, categorical features, and so on.
[p0429-l0026] [10.5pt] To handle this, TensorFlow provides the Features API: it lets you easily convert these
[p0429-l0027] [10.5pt] features to numerical features that can be consumed by your neural network. For
[p0429-l0028] [9.0pt] 403

=== PDF page 430 / printed label 404 ===
[p0430-l0001] [10.5pt] example, categorical features with a large number of categories (such as cities, or
[p0430-l0002] [10.5pt] words) can be encoded using embeddings (as we will see, an embedding is a trainable
[p0430-l0003] [10.5pt] dense vector that represents a category).
[p0430-l0004] [9.6pt] Both the Data API and the Features API work seamlessly with
[p0430-l0005] [9.6pt] tf.keras.
[p0430-l0006] [10.5pt] In this chapter, we will cover the Data API, the TFRecord format and the Features
[p0430-l0007] [10.5pt] API in detail. We will also take a quick look at a few related projects from Tensor‐
[p0430-l0008] [10.5pt] Flow’s ecosystem:
[p0430-l0009] [10.5pt] • TF Transform (tf.Transform) makes it possible to write a single preprocessing
[p0430-l0010] [10.5pt] function that can be run both in batch mode on your full training set, before
[p0430-l0011] [10.5pt] training (to speed it up), and then exported to a TF Function and incorporated
[p0430-l0012] [10.5pt] into your trained model, so that once it is deployed in production, it can take
[p0430-l0013] [10.5pt] care of preprocessing new instances on the fly.
[p0430-l0014] [10.5pt] • TF Datasets (TFDS) provides a convenient function to download many common
[p0430-l0015] [10.5pt] datasets of all kinds, including large ones like ImageNet, and it provides conve‐
[p0430-l0016] [10.5pt] nient dataset objects to manipulate them using the Data API.
[p0430-l0017] [10.5pt] So let’s get started!
[p0430-l0018] [18.92pt] The Data API
[p0430-l0019] [10.5pt] The whole Data API revolves around the concept of a dataset: as you might suspect,
[p0430-l0020] [10.5pt] this represents a sequence of data items. Usually you will use datasets that gradually
[p0430-l0021] [10.5pt] read data from disk, but for simplicity let’s just create a dataset entirely in RAM using
[p0430-l0022] [10.5pt] tf.data.Dataset.from_tensor_slices():
[p0430-l0023] [8.5pt] >>> X = tf.range(10)  # any data tensor
[p0430-l0024] [8.5pt] >>> dataset = tf.data.Dataset.from_tensor_slices(X)
[p0430-l0025] [8.5pt] >>> dataset
[p0430-l0026] [8.5pt] <TensorSliceDataset shapes: (), types: tf.int32>
[p0430-l0027] [10.5pt] The from_tensor_slices() function takes a tensor and creates a tf.data.Dataset
[p0430-l0028] [10.5pt] whose elements are all the slices of X (along the first dimension), so this dataset con‐
[p0430-l0029] [10.5pt] tains 10 items: tensors 0, 1, 2, …, 9. In this case we would have obtained the same
[p0430-l0030] [10.5pt] dataset if we had used tf.data.Dataset.range(10).
[p0430-l0031] [10.5pt] You can simply iterate over a dataset’s items like this:
[p0430-l0032] [8.5pt] >>> for item in dataset:
[p0430-l0033] [8.5pt] ...     print(item)
[p0430-l0034] [9.0pt] 404
[p0430-l0035] [9.0pt] |

[p0431-l0001] [8.5pt] ...
[p0431-l0002] [8.5pt] tf.Tensor(0, shape=(), dtype=int32)
[p0431-l0003] [8.5pt] tf.Tensor(1, shape=(), dtype=int32)
[p0431-l0004] [8.5pt] tf.Tensor(2, shape=(), dtype=int32)
[p0431-l0005] [8.5pt] [...]
[p0431-l0006] [8.5pt] tf.Tensor(9, shape=(), dtype=int32)
[p0431-l0007] [15.77pt] Chaining Transformations
[p0431-l0008] [10.5pt] Once you have a dataset, you can apply all sorts of transformations to it by calling its
[p0431-l0009] [10.5pt] transformation methods. Each method returns a new dataset, so you can chain trans‐
[p0431-l0010] [10.5pt] formations like this (this chain is illustrated in Figure 13-1):
[p0431-l0011] [8.5pt] >>> dataset = dataset.repeat(3).batch(7)
[p0431-l0012] [8.5pt] >>> for item in dataset:
[p0431-l0013] [8.5pt] ...     print(item)
[p0431-l0014] [8.5pt] ...
[p0431-l0015] [8.5pt] tf.Tensor([0 1 2 3 4 5 6], shape=(7,), dtype=int32)
[p0431-l0016] [8.5pt] tf.Tensor([7 8 9 0 1 2 3], shape=(7,), dtype=int32)
[p0431-l0017] [8.5pt] tf.Tensor([4 5 6 7 8 9 0], shape=(7,), dtype=int32)
[p0431-l0018] [8.5pt] tf.Tensor([1 2 3 4 5 6 7], shape=(7,), dtype=int32)
[p0431-l0019] [8.5pt] tf.Tensor([8 9], shape=(2,), dtype=int32)
[p0431-l0020] [10.5pt] Figure 13-1. Chaining Dataset Transformations
[p0431-l0021] [10.5pt] In this example, we first call the repeat() method on the original dataset, and it
[p0431-l0022] [10.5pt] returns a new dataset that will repeat the items of the original dataset 3 times. Of
[p0431-l0023] [10.5pt] course, this will not copy the whole data in memory 3 times! In fact, if you call this
[p0431-l0024] [10.5pt] method with no arguments, the new dataset will repeat the source dataset forever.
[p0431-l0025] [10.5pt] Then we call the batch() method on this new dataset, and again this creates a new
[p0431-l0026] [10.5pt] dataset. This one will group the items of the previous dataset in batches of 7 items.
[p0431-l0027] [10.5pt] Finally, we iterate over the items of this final dataset. As you can see, the batch()
[p0431-l0028] [10.5pt] method had to output a final batch of size 2 instead of 7, but you can call it with
[p0431-l0029] [10.5pt] drop_remainder=True if you want it to drop this final batch so that all batches have
[p0431-l0030] [10.5pt] the exact same size.
[p0431-l0031] [9.0pt] The Data API
[p0431-l0032] [9.0pt] |
[p0431-l0033] [9.0pt] 405

=== PDF page 432 / printed label 406 ===
[p0432-l0001] [9.6pt] The dataset methods do not modify datasets, they create new ones,
[p0432-l0002] [9.6pt] so make sure to keep a reference to these new datasets (e.g., data
[p0432-l0003] [9.6pt] set = ...), or else nothing will happen.
[p0432-l0004] [10.5pt] You can also apply any transformation you want to the items by calling the map()
[p0432-l0005] [10.5pt] method. For example, this creates a new dataset with all items doubled:
[p0432-l0006] [8.5pt] >>> dataset = dataset.map(lambda x: x * 2) # Items: [0,2,4,6,8,10,12]
[p0432-l0007] [10.5pt] This function is the one you will call to apply any preprocessing you want to your
[p0432-l0008] [10.5pt] data. Sometimes, this will include computations that can be quite intensive, such as
[p0432-l0009] [10.5pt] reshaping or rotating an image, so you will usually want to spawn multiple threads to
[p0432-l0010] [10.5pt] speed things up: it’s as simple as setting the num_parallel_calls argument.
[p0432-l0011] [10.5pt] While the map() applies a transformation to each item, the apply() method applies a
[p0432-l0012] [10.5pt] transformation to the dataset as a whole. For example, the following code “unbatches”
[p0432-l0013] [10.5pt] the dataset, by applying the unbatch() function to the dataset (this function is cur‐
[p0432-l0014] [10.5pt] rently experimental, but it will most likely move to the core API in a future release).
[p0432-l0015] [10.5pt] Each item in the new dataset will be a single integer tensor instead of a batch of 7
[p0432-l0016] [10.5pt] integers:
[p0432-l0017] [8.5pt] >>> dataset = dataset.apply(tf.data.experimental.unbatch()) # Items: 0,2,4,...
[p0432-l0018] [10.5pt] It is also possible to simply filter the dataset using the filter() method:
[p0432-l0019] [8.5pt] >>> dataset = dataset.filter(lambda x: x < 10) # Items: 0 2 4 6 8 0 2 4 6...
[p0432-l0020] [10.5pt] You will often want to look at just a few items from a dataset. You can use the take()
[p0432-l0021] [10.5pt] method for that:
[p0432-l0022] [8.5pt] >>> for item in dataset.take(3):
[p0432-l0023] [8.5pt] ...     print(item)
[p0432-l0024] [8.5pt] ...
[p0432-l0025] [8.5pt] tf.Tensor(0, shape=(), dtype=int64)
[p0432-l0026] [8.5pt] tf.Tensor(2, shape=(), dtype=int64)
[p0432-l0027] [8.5pt] tf.Tensor(4, shape=(), dtype=int64)
[p0432-l0028] [15.77pt] Shuffling the Data
[p0432-l0029] [10.5pt] As you know, Gradient Descent works best when the instances in the training set are
[p0432-l0030] [10.5pt] independent and identically distributed (see Chapter 4). A simple way to ensure this
[p0432-l0031] [10.5pt] is to shuffle the instances. For this, you can just use the shuffle() method. It will
[p0432-l0032] [10.5pt] create a new dataset that will start by filling up a buffer with the first items of the
[p0432-l0033] [10.5pt] source dataset, then whenever it is asked for an item, it will pull one out randomly
[p0432-l0034] [10.5pt] from the buffer, and replace it with a fresh one from the source dataset, until it has
[p0432-l0035] [10.5pt] iterated entirely through the source dataset. At this point it continues to pull out
[p0432-l0036] [10.5pt] items randomly from the buffer until it is empty. You must specify the buffer size, and
[p0432-l0037] [9.0pt] 406
[p0432-l0038] [9.0pt] |
[p0432-l0039] [9.0pt] Chapter 13: Loading and Preprocessing Data with TensorFlow

=== PDF page 433 / printed label 407 ===
[p0433-l0001] [10.5pt] it is important to make it large enough or else shuffling will not be very efficient.1
[p0433-l0002] [10.5pt] However, obviously do not exceed the amount of RAM you have, and even if you
[p0433-l0003] [10.5pt] have plenty of it, there’s no need to go well beyond the dataset’s size. You can provide
[p0433-l0004] [10.5pt] a random seed if you want the same random order every time you run your program.
[p0433-l0005] [8.5pt] >>> dataset = tf.data.Dataset.range(10).repeat(3) # 0 to 9, three times
[p0433-l0006] [8.5pt] >>> dataset = dataset.shuffle(buffer_size=5, seed=42).batch(7)
[p0433-l0007] [8.5pt] >>> for item in dataset:
[p0433-l0008] [8.5pt] ...     print(item)
[p0433-l0009] [8.5pt] ...
[p0433-l0010] [8.5pt] tf.Tensor([0 2 3 6 7 9 4], shape=(7,), dtype=int64)
[p0433-l0011] [8.5pt] tf.Tensor([5 0 1 1 8 6 5], shape=(7,), dtype=int64)
[p0433-l0012] [8.5pt] tf.Tensor([4 8 7 1 2 3 0], shape=(7,), dtype=int64)
[p0433-l0013] [8.5pt] tf.Tensor([5 4 2 7 8 9 9], shape=(7,), dtype=int64)
[p0433-l0014] [8.5pt] tf.Tensor([3 6], shape=(2,), dtype=int64)
[p0433-l0015] [9.6pt] If you call repeat() on a shuffled dataset, by default it will generate
[p0433-l0016] [9.6pt] a new order at every iteration. This is generally a good idea, but if
[p0433-l0017] [9.6pt] you prefer to reuse the same order at each iteration (e.g., for tests
[p0433-l0018] [9.6pt] or debugging), you can set reshuffle_each_iteration=False.
[p0433-l0019] [10.5pt] For a large dataset that does not fit in memory, this simple shuffling-buffer approach
[p0433-l0020] [10.5pt] may not be sufficient, since the buffer will be small compared to the dataset. One sol‐
[p0433-l0021] [10.5pt] ution is to shuffle the source data itself (for example, on Linux you can shuffle text
[p0433-l0022] [10.5pt] files using the shuf command). This will definitely improve shuffling a lot! However,
[p0433-l0023] [10.5pt] even if the source data is shuffled, you will usually want to shuffle it some more, or
[p0433-l0024] [10.5pt] else the same order will be repeated at each epoch, and the model may end up being
[p0433-l0025] [10.5pt] biased (e.g., due to some spurious patterns present by chance in the source data’s
[p0433-l0026] [10.5pt] order). To shuffle the instances some more, a common approach is to split the source
[p0433-l0027] [10.5pt] data into multiple files, then read them in a random order during training. However,
[p0433-l0028] [10.5pt] instances located in the same file will still end up close to each other. To avoid this
[p0433-l0029] [10.5pt] you can pick multiple files randomly, and read them simultaneously, interleaving
[p0433-l0030] [10.5pt] their lines. Then on top of that you can add a shuffling buffer using the shuffle()
[p0433-l0031] [10.5pt] method. If all this sounds like a lot of work, don’t worry: the Data API actually makes
[p0433-l0032] [10.5pt] all this possible in just a few lines of code. Let’s see how to do this.
[p0433-l0033] [8.0pt] 1 Imagine a sorted deck of cards on your left: suppose you just take the top 3 cards and shuffle them, then pick
[p0433-l0034] [8.0pt] one randomly and put it to your right, keeping the other 2 in your hands. Take another card on your left,
[p0433-l0035] [8.0pt] shuffle the 3 cards in your hands and pick one of them randomly, and put it on your right. When you are
[p0433-l0036] [8.0pt] done going through all the cards like this, you will have a deck of cards on your right: do you think it will be
[p0433-l0037] [8.0pt] perfectly shuffled?
[p0433-l0038] [9.0pt] The Data API
[p0433-l0039] [9.0pt] |

[p0434-l0001] [11.56pt] Interleaving Lines From Multiple Files
[p0434-l0002] [10.5pt] First, let’s suppose that you loaded the California housing dataset, you shuffled it
[p0434-l0003] [10.5pt] (unless it was already shuffled), you split it into a training set, a validation set and a
[p0434-l0004] [10.5pt] test set, then you split each set into many CSV files that each look like this (each row
[p0434-l0005] [10.5pt] contains 8 input features plus the target median house value):
[p0434-l0006] [8.5pt] MedInc,HouseAge,AveRooms,AveBedrms,Popul,AveOccup,Lat,Long,MedianHouseValue
[p0434-l0007] [8.5pt] 3.5214,15.0,3.0499,1.1065,1447.0,1.6059,37.63,-122.43,1.442
[p0434-l0008] [8.5pt] 5.3275,5.0,6.4900,0.9910,3464.0,3.4433,33.69,-117.39,1.687
[p0434-l0009] [8.5pt] 3.1,29.0,7.5423,1.5915,1328.0,2.2508,38.44,-122.98,1.621
[p0434-l0010] [8.5pt] [...]
[p0434-l0011] [10.5pt] Let’s also suppose train_filepaths contains the list of file paths (and you also have
[p0434-l0012] [10.5pt] valid_filepaths and test_filepaths):
[p0434-l0013] [8.5pt] >>> train_filepaths
[p0434-l0014] [8.5pt] ['datasets/housing/my_train_00.csv', 'datasets/housing/my_train_01.csv',...]
[p0434-l0015] [10.5pt] Now let’s create a dataset containing only these file paths:
[p0434-l0016] [8.5pt] filepath_dataset = tf.data.Dataset.list_files(train_filepaths, seed=42)
[p0434-l0017] [10.5pt] By default, the list_files() function returns a dataset that shuffles the file paths. In
[p0434-l0018] [10.5pt] general this is a good thing, but you can set shuffle=False if you do not want that,
[p0434-l0019] [10.5pt] for some reason.
[p0434-l0020] [10.5pt] Next, we can call the interleave() method to read from 5 files at a time and inter‐
[p0434-l0021] [10.5pt] leave their lines (skipping the first line of each file, which is the header row, using the
[p0434-l0022] [10.5pt] skip() method):
[p0434-l0023] [8.5pt] n_readers = 5
[p0434-l0024] [8.5pt] dataset = filepath_dataset.interleave(
[p0434-l0025] [8.5pt]     lambda filepath: tf.data.TextLineDataset(filepath).skip(1),
[p0434-l0026] [8.5pt]     cycle_length=n_readers)
[p0434-l0027] [10.5pt] The interleave() method will create a dataset that will pull 5 file paths from the
[p0434-l0028] [10.5pt] filepath_dataset, and for each one it will call the function we gave it (a lambda in
[p0434-l0029] [10.5pt] this example) to create a new dataset, in this case a TextLineDataset. It will then
[p0434-l0030] [10.5pt] cycle through these 5 datasets, reading one line at a time from each until all datasets
[p0434-l0031] [10.5pt] are out of items. Then it will get the next 5 file paths from the filepath_dataset, and
[p0434-l0032] [10.5pt] interleave them the same way, and so on until it runs out of file paths.
[p0434-l0033] [9.6pt] For interleaving to work best, it is preferable to have files of identi‐
[p0434-l0034] [9.6pt] cal length, or else the end of the longest files will not be interleaved.
[p0434-l0035] [9.0pt] 408
[p0434-l0036] [9.0pt] |
