[p0435-l0001] [10.5pt] By default, interleave() does not use parallelism, it just reads one line at a time
[p0435-l0002] [10.5pt] from each file, sequentially. However, if you want it to actually read files in parallel,
[p0435-l0003] [10.5pt] you can set the num_parallel_calls argument to the number of threads you want.
[p0435-l0004] [10.5pt] You can even set it to tf.data.experimental.AUTOTUNE to make TensorFlow choose
[p0435-l0005] [10.5pt] the right number of threads dynamically based on the available CPU (however, this is
[p0435-l0006] [10.5pt] an experimental feature for now). Let’s look at what the dataset contains now:
[p0435-l0007] [8.5pt] >>> for line in dataset.take(5):
[p0435-l0008] [8.5pt] ...     print(line.numpy())
[p0435-l0009] [8.5pt] ...
[p0435-l0010] [8.5pt] b'4.2083,44.0,5.3232,0.9171,846.0,2.3370,37.47,-122.2,2.782'
[p0435-l0011] [8.5pt] b'4.1812,52.0,5.7013,0.9965,692.0,2.4027,33.73,-118.31,3.215'
[p0435-l0012] [8.5pt] b'3.6875,44.0,4.5244,0.9930,457.0,3.1958,34.04,-118.15,1.625'
[p0435-l0013] [8.5pt] b'3.3456,37.0,4.5140,0.9084,458.0,3.2253,36.67,-121.7,2.526'
[p0435-l0014] [8.5pt] b'3.5214,15.0,3.0499,1.1065,1447.0,1.6059,37.63,-122.43,1.442'
[p0435-l0015] [10.5pt] These are the first rows (ignoring the header row) of 5 CSV files, chosen randomly.
[p0435-l0016] [10.5pt] Looks good! But as you can see, these are just byte strings, we need to parse them,
[p0435-l0017] [10.5pt] and also scale the data.
[p0435-l0018] [15.77pt] Preprocessing the Data
[p0435-l0019] [10.5pt] Let’s implement a small function that will perform this preprocessing:
[p0435-l0020] [8.5pt] X_mean, X_std = [...] # mean and scale of each feature in the training set
[p0435-l0021] [8.5pt] n_inputs = 8
[p0435-l0022] [8.5pt] def preprocess(line):
[p0435-l0023] [8.5pt]   defs = [0.] * n_inputs + [tf.constant([], dtype=tf.float32)]
[p0435-l0024] [8.5pt]   fields = tf.io.decode_csv(line, record_defaults=defs)
[p0435-l0025] [8.5pt]   x = tf.stack(fields[:-1])
[p0435-l0026] [8.5pt]   y = tf.stack(fields[-1:])
[p0435-l0027] [8.5pt]   return (x - X_mean) / X_std, y
[p0435-l0028] [10.5pt] Let’s walk through this code:
[p0435-l0029] [10.5pt] • First, we assume that you have precomputed the mean and standard deviation of
[p0435-l0030] [10.5pt] each feature in the training set. X_mean and X_std are just 1D tensors (or NumPy
[p0435-l0031] [10.5pt] arrays) containing 8 floats, one per input feature.
[p0435-l0032] [10.5pt] • The preprocess() function takes one CSV line, and starts by parsing it. For this,
[p0435-l0033] [10.5pt] it uses the tf.io.decode_csv() function, which takes two arguments: the first is
[p0435-l0034] [10.5pt] the line to parse, and the second is an array containing the default value for each
[p0435-l0035] [10.5pt] column in the CSV file. This tells TensorFlow not only the default value for each
[p0435-l0036] [10.5pt] column, but also the number of columns and the type of each column. In this
[p0435-l0037] [10.5pt] example, we tell it that all feature columns are floats and missing values should
[p0435-l0038] [10.5pt] default to 0, but we provide an empty array of type tf.float32 as the default
[p0435-l0039] [10.5pt] value for the last column (the target): this tells TensorFlow that this column con‐
[p0435-l0040] [9.0pt] The Data API
[p0435-l0041] [9.0pt] |
[p0435-l0042] [9.0pt] 409

=== PDF page 436 / printed label 410 ===
[p0436-l0001] [10.5pt] tains floats, but that there is no default value, so it will raise an exception if it
[p0436-l0002] [10.5pt] encounters a missing value.
[p0436-l0003] [10.5pt] • The decode_csv() function returns a list of scalar tensors (one per column) but
[p0436-l0004] [10.5pt] we need to return 1D tensor arrays. So we call tf.stack() on all tensors except
[p0436-l0005] [10.5pt] for the last one (the target): this will stack these tensors into a 1D array. We then
[p0436-l0006] [10.5pt] do the same for the target value (this makes it a 1D tensor array with a single
[p0436-l0007] [10.5pt] value, rather than a scalar tensor).
[p0436-l0008] [10.5pt] • Finally, we scale the input features by subtracting the feature means and then
[p0436-l0009] [10.5pt] dividing by the feature standard deviations, and we return a tuple containing the
[p0436-l0010] [10.5pt] scaled features and the target.
[p0436-l0011] [10.5pt] Let’s test this preprocessing function:
[p0436-l0012] [8.5pt] >>> preprocess(b'4.2083,44.0,5.3232,0.9171,846.0,2.3370,37.47,-122.2,2.782')
[p0436-l0013] [8.5pt] (<tf.Tensor: id=6227, shape=(8,), dtype=float32, numpy=
[p0436-l0014] [8.5pt]  array([ 0.16579159,  1.216324  , -0.05204564, -0.39215982, -0.5277444 ,
[p0436-l0015] [8.5pt]         -0.2633488 ,  0.8543046 , -1.3072058 ], dtype=float32)>,
[p0436-l0016] [8.5pt]  <tf.Tensor: [...], numpy=array([2.782], dtype=float32)>)
[p0436-l0017] [10.5pt] We can now apply this preprocessing function to the dataset.
[p0436-l0018] [15.77pt] Putting Everything Together
[p0436-l0019] [10.5pt] To make the code reusable, let’s put together everything we have discussed so far into
[p0436-l0020] [10.5pt] a small helper function: it will create and return a dataset that will efficiently load Cal‐
[p0436-l0021] [10.5pt] ifornia housing data from multiple CSV files, then shuffle it, preprocess it and batch it
[p0436-l0022] [10.5pt] (see Figure 13-2):
[p0436-l0023] [8.5pt] def csv_reader_dataset(filepaths, repeat=None, n_readers=5,
[p0436-l0024] [8.5pt]                        n_read_threads=None, shuffle_buffer_size=10000,
[p0436-l0025] [8.5pt]                        n_parse_threads=5, batch_size=32):
[p0436-l0026] [8.5pt]     dataset = tf.data.Dataset.list_files(filepaths).repeat(repeat)
[p0436-l0027] [8.5pt]     dataset = dataset.interleave(
[p0436-l0028] [8.5pt]         lambda filepath: tf.data.TextLineDataset(filepath).skip(1),
[p0436-l0029] [8.5pt]         cycle_length=n_readers, num_parallel_calls=n_read_threads)
[p0436-l0030] [8.5pt]     dataset = dataset.shuffle(shuffle_buffer_size)
[p0436-l0031] [8.5pt]     dataset = dataset.map(preprocess, num_parallel_calls=n_parse_threads)
[p0436-l0032] [8.5pt]     dataset = dataset.batch(batch_size)
[p0436-l0033] [8.5pt]     return dataset.prefetch(1)

[p0437-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 13-2. Loading and Preprocessing Data From Multiple CSV Files
[p0437-l0002] [10.5pt] Everything should make sense in this code, except the very last line (prefetch(1)),
[p0437-l0003] [10.5pt] which is actually quite important for performance.
[p0437-l0004] [15.77pt] Prefetching
[p0437-l0005] [10.5pt] By calling prefetch(1) at the end, we are creating a dataset that will do its best to
[p0437-l0006] [10.5pt] always be one batch ahead2. In other words, while our training algorithm is working
[p0437-l0007] [10.5pt] on one batch, the dataset will already be working in parallel on getting the next batch
[p0437-l0008] [10.5pt] ready. This can improve performance dramatically, as is illustrated on Figure 13-3. If
[p0437-l0009] [10.5pt] we also ensure that loading and preprocessing are multithreaded (by setting num_par
[p0437-l0010] [10.5pt] allel_calls when calling interleave() and map()), we can exploit multiple cores
[p0437-l0011] [10.5pt] on the CPU and hopefully make preparing one batch of data shorter than running a
[p0437-l0012] [10.5pt] training step on the GPU: this way the GPU will be almost 100% utilized (except for
[p0437-l0013] [10.5pt] the data transfer time from the CPU to the GPU), and training will run much faster.
[p0437-l0014] [8.0pt] 2 In general, just prefetching one batch is fine, but in some cases you may need to prefetch a few more. Alterna‐
[p0437-l0015] [8.0pt] tively, you can let TensorFlow decide automatically by passing tf.data.experimental.AUTOTUNE (this is an
[p0437-l0016] [8.0pt] experimental feature for now).
[p0437-l0017] [9.0pt] The Data API
[p0437-l0018] [9.0pt] |
[p0437-l0019] [9.0pt] 411

[p0438-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 13-3. Speedup Training Thanks to Prefetching and Multithreading
[p0438-l0002] [9.6pt] If you plan to purchase a GPU card, its processing power and its
[p0438-l0003] [9.6pt] memory size are of course very important (in particular, a large
[p0438-l0004] [9.6pt] RAM is crucial for computer vision), but its memory bandwidth is
[p0438-l0005] [9.6pt] just as important as the processing power to get good performance:
[p0438-l0006] [9.6pt] this is the number of gigabytes of data it can get in or out of its
[p0438-l0007] [9.6pt] RAM per second.
[p0438-l0008] [10.5pt] With that, you can now build efficient input pipelines to load and preprocess data
[p0438-l0009] [10.5pt] from multiple text files. We have discussed the most common dataset methods, but
[p0438-l0010] [10.5pt] there are a few more you may want to look at: concatenate(), zip(), window(),
[p0438-l0011] [10.5pt] reduce(), cache(), shard(), flat_map() and padded_batch(). There are also a cou‐
[p0438-l0012] [10.5pt] ple more class methods: from_generator() and from_tensors(), which create a new
[p0438-l0013] [10.5pt] dataset from a Python generator or a list of tensors respectively. Please check the API
[p0438-l0014] [10.5pt] documentation for more details. Also note that there are experimental features avail‐
[p0438-l0015] [10.5pt] able in tf.data.experimental, many of which will most likely make it to the core
[p0438-l0016] [10.5pt] API in future releases (e.g., check out the CsvDataset class and the SqlDataset
[p0438-l0017] [10.5pt] classes).

[p0439-l0001] [15.77pt] Using the Dataset With tf.keras
[p0439-l0002] [10.5pt] Now we can use the csv_reader_dataset() function to create a dataset for the train‐
[p0439-l0003] [10.5pt] ing set (ensuring it repeats the data forever), the validation set and the test set:
[p0439-l0004] [8.5pt] train_set = csv_reader_dataset(train_filepaths, repeat=None)
[p0439-l0005] [8.5pt] valid_set = csv_reader_dataset(valid_filepaths)
[p0439-l0006] [8.5pt] test_set = csv_reader_dataset(test_filepaths)
[p0439-l0007] [10.5pt] And now we can simply build and train a Keras model using these datasets.3 All we
[p0439-l0008] [10.5pt] need to do is to call the fit() method with the datasets instead of X_train and
[p0439-l0009] [10.5pt] y_train, and specify the number of steps per epoch for each set:4
[p0439-l0010] [8.5pt] model = keras.models.Sequential([...])
[p0439-l0011] [8.5pt] model.compile([...])
[p0439-l0012] [8.5pt] model.fit(train_set, steps_per_epoch=len(X_train) // batch_size, epochs=10,
[p0439-l0013] [8.5pt]           validation_data=valid_set,
[p0439-l0014] [8.5pt]           validation_steps=len(X_valid) // batch_size)
[p0439-l0015] [10.5pt] Similarly, we can pass a dataset to the evaluate() and predict() methods (and again
[p0439-l0016] [10.5pt] specify the number of steps per epoch):
[p0439-l0017] [8.5pt] model.evaluate(test_set, steps=len(X_test) // batch_size)
[p0439-l0018] [8.5pt] model.predict(new_set, steps=len(X_new) // batch_size)
[p0439-l0019] [10.5pt] Unlike the other sets, the new_set will usually not contain labels (if it does, Keras will
[p0439-l0020] [10.5pt] just ignore them). Note that in all these cases, you can still use NumPy arrays instead
[p0439-l0021] [10.5pt] of datasets if you want (but of course they need to have been loaded and preprocessed
[p0439-l0022] [10.5pt] first).
[p0439-l0023] [10.5pt] If you want to build your own custom training loop (as in Chapter 12), you can just
[p0439-l0024] [10.5pt] iterate over the training set, very naturally:
[p0439-l0025] [8.5pt] for X_batch, y_batch in train_set:
[p0439-l0026] [8.5pt]     [...] # perform one gradient descent step
[p0439-l0027] [10.5pt] In fact, it is even possible to create a tf.function (see Chapter 12) that performs the
[p0439-l0028] [10.5pt] whole training loop!5
[p0439-l0029] [8.5pt] @tf.function
[p0439-l0030] [8.5pt] def train(model, optimizer, loss_fn, n_epochs, [...]):
[p0439-l0031] [8.5pt]     train_set = csv_reader_dataset(train_filepaths, repeat=n_epochs, [...])
[p0439-l0032] [8.5pt]     for X_batch, y_batch in train_set:
[p0439-l0033] [8.5pt]         with tf.GradientTape() as tape:
[p0439-l0034] [8.0pt] 3 Support for datasets is specific to tf.keras, it will not work on other implementations of the Keras API.
[p0439-l0035] [8.0pt] 4 The number of steps per epoch is optional if the dataset just goes through the data once, but if you do not
[p0439-l0036] [8.0pt] specify it, the progress bar will not be displayed during the first epoch.
[p0439-l0037] [8.0pt] 5 Note that for now the dataset must be created within the TF Function. This may be fixed by the time you read
[p0439-l0038] [8.0pt] these lines (see TensorFlow issue #25414).

[p0440-l0001] [8.5pt]             y_pred = model(X_batch)
[p0440-l0002] [8.5pt]             main_loss = tf.reduce_mean(loss_fn(y_batch, y_pred))
[p0440-l0003] [8.5pt]             loss = tf.add_n([main_loss] + model.losses)
[p0440-l0004] [8.5pt]         grads = tape.gradient(loss, model.trainable_variables)
[p0440-l0005] [8.5pt]         optimizer.apply_gradients(zip(grads, model.trainable_variables))
[p0440-l0006] [10.5pt] Congratulations, you now know how to build powerful input pipelines using the Data
[p0440-l0007] [10.5pt] API! However, so far we have used CSV files, which are common, simple and conve‐
[p0440-l0008] [10.5pt] nient, but they are not really efficient, and they do not support large or complex data
[p0440-l0009] [10.5pt] structures very well, such as images or audio. So let’s use TFRecords instead.
[p0440-l0010] [9.6pt] If you are happy with CSV files (or whatever other format you are
[p0440-l0011] [9.6pt] using), you do not have to use TFRecords. As the saying goes, if it
[p0440-l0012] [9.6pt] ain’t broke, don’t fix it! TFRecords are useful when the bottleneck
[p0440-l0013] [9.6pt] during training is loading and parsing the data.
[p0440-l0014] [18.92pt] The TFRecord Format
[p0440-l0015] [10.5pt] The TFRecord format is TensorFlow’s preferred format for storing large amounts of
[p0440-l0016] [10.5pt] data and reading it efficiently. It is a very simple binary format that just contains a
[p0440-l0017] [10.5pt] sequence of binary records of varying sizes (each record just has a length, a CRC
[p0440-l0018] [10.5pt] checksum to check that the length was not corrupted, then the actual data, and finally
[p0440-l0019] [10.5pt] a CRC checksum for the data). You can easily create a TFRecord file using the
[p0440-l0020] [10.5pt] tf.io.TFRecordWriter class:
[p0440-l0021] [8.5pt] with tf.io.TFRecordWriter("my_data.tfrecord") as f:
[p0440-l0022] [8.5pt]     f.write(b"This is the first record")
[p0440-l0023] [8.5pt]     f.write(b"And this is the second record")
[p0440-l0024] [10.5pt] And you can then use a tf.data.TFRecordDataset to read one or more TFRecord
[p0440-l0025] [10.5pt] files:
[p0440-l0026] [8.5pt] filepaths = ["my_data.tfrecord"]
[p0440-l0027] [8.5pt] dataset = tf.data.TFRecordDataset(filepaths)
[p0440-l0028] [8.5pt] for item in dataset:
[p0440-l0029] [8.5pt]     print(item)
[p0440-l0030] [10.5pt] This will output:
[p0440-l0031] [8.5pt] tf.Tensor(b'This is the first record', shape=(), dtype=string)
[p0440-l0032] [8.5pt] tf.Tensor(b'And this is the second record', shape=(), dtype=string)
[p0440-l0033] [9.6pt] By default, a TFRecordDataset will read files one by one, but you
[p0440-l0034] [9.6pt] can make it read multiple files in parallel and interleave their
[p0440-l0035] [9.6pt] records by setting num_parallel_reads. Alternatively, you could
[p0440-l0036] [9.6pt] obtain the same result by using list_files() and interleave()
[p0440-l0037] [9.6pt] as we did earlier to read multiple CSV files.
[p0440-l0038] [9.0pt] 414

[p0441-l0001] [15.77pt] Compressed TFRecord Files
[p0441-l0002] [10.5pt] It can sometimes be useful to compress your TFRecord files, especially if they need to
[p0441-l0003] [10.5pt] be loaded via a network connection. You can create a compressed TFRecord file by
[p0441-l0004] [10.5pt] setting the options argument:
[p0441-l0005] [8.5pt] options = tf.io.TFRecordOptions(compression_type="GZIP")
[p0441-l0006] [8.5pt] with tf.io.TFRecordWriter("my_compressed.tfrecord", options) as f:
[p0441-l0007] [8.5pt]   [...]
[p0441-l0008] [10.5pt] When reading a compressed TFRecord file, you need to specify the compression type:
[p0441-l0009] [8.5pt] dataset = tf.data.TFRecordDataset(["my_compressed.tfrecord"],
[p0441-l0010] [8.5pt]                                   compression_type="GZIP")
[p0441-l0011] [15.77pt] A Brief Introduction to Protocol Buffers
[p0441-l0012] [10.5pt] Even though each record can use any binary format you want, TFRecord files usually
[p0441-l0013] [10.5pt] contain serialized Protocol Buffers (also called protobufs). This is a portable, extensi‐
[p0441-l0014] [10.5pt] ble and efficient binary format developed at Google back in 2001 and Open Sourced
[p0441-l0015] [10.5pt] in 2008, and they are now widely used, in particular in gRPC, Google’s remote proce‐
[p0441-l0016] [10.5pt] dure call system. Protocol Buffers are defined using a simple language that looks like
[p0441-l0017] [10.5pt] this:
[p0441-l0018] [8.5pt] syntax = "proto3";
[p0441-l0019] [8.5pt] message Person {
[p0441-l0020] [8.5pt]   string name = 1;
[p0441-l0021] [8.5pt]   int32 id = 2;
[p0441-l0022] [8.5pt]   repeated string email = 3;
[p0441-l0023] [8.5pt] }
[p0441-l0024] [10.5pt] This definition says we are using the protobuf format version 3, and it specifies that
[p0441-l0025] [10.5pt] each Person object6 may (optionally) have a name of type string, an id of type int32,
[p0441-l0026] [10.5pt] and zero or more email fields, each of type string. The numbers 1, 2 and 3 are the
[p0441-l0027] [10.5pt] field identifiers: they will be used in each record’s binary representation. Once you
[p0441-l0028] [10.5pt] have a definition in a .proto file, you can compile it. This requires protoc, the proto‐
[p0441-l0029] [10.5pt] buf compiler, to generate access classes in Python (or some other language). Note that
[p0441-l0030] [10.5pt] the protobuf definitions we will use have already been compiled for you, and their
[p0441-l0031] [10.5pt] Python classes are part of TensorFlow, so you will not need to use protoc. All you
[p0441-l0032] [10.5pt] need to know is how to use protobuf access classes in Python. To illustrate the basics,
[p0441-l0033] [10.5pt] let’s look at a simple example that uses the access classes generated for the Person
[p0441-l0034] [10.5pt] protobuf (the code is explained in the comments):
[p0441-l0035] [8.5pt] >>> from person_pb2 import Person  # import the generated access class
[p0441-l0036] [8.5pt] >>> person = Person(name="Al", id=123, email=["a@b.com"])  # create a Person
[p0441-l0037] [8.5pt] >>> print(person)  # display the Person
[p0441-l0038] [8.0pt] 6 Since protobuf objects are meant to be serialized and transmitted, they are called messages.
[p0441-l0039] [9.0pt] The TFRecord Format
[p0441-l0040] [9.0pt] |
[p0441-l0041] [9.0pt] 415

=== PDF page 442 / printed label 416 ===
[p0442-l0001] [8.5pt] name: "Al"
[p0442-l0002] [8.5pt] id: 123
[p0442-l0003] [8.5pt] email: "a@b.com"
[p0442-l0004] [8.5pt] >>> person.name  # read a field
[p0442-l0005] [8.5pt] "Al"
[p0442-l0006] [8.5pt] >>> person.name = "Alice"  # modify a field
[p0442-l0007] [8.5pt] >>> person.email[0]  # repeated fields can be accessed like arrays
[p0442-l0008] [8.5pt] "a@b.com"
[p0442-l0009] [8.5pt] >>> person.email.append("c@d.com")  # add an email address
[p0442-l0010] [8.5pt] >>> s = person.SerializeToString()  # serialize the object to a byte string
[p0442-l0011] [8.5pt] >>> s
[p0442-l0012] [8.5pt] b'\n\x05Alice\x10{\x1a\x07a@b.com\x1a\x07c@d.com'
[p0442-l0013] [8.5pt] >>> person2 = Person()  # create a new Person
[p0442-l0014] [8.5pt] >>> person2.ParseFromString(s)  # parse the byte string (27 bytes long)
[p0442-l0015] [8.5pt] 27
[p0442-l0016] [8.5pt] >>> person == person2  # now they are equal
[p0442-l0017] [8.5pt] True
[p0442-l0018] [10.5pt] In short, we import the Person class generated by protoc, we create an instance and
[p0442-l0019] [10.5pt] we play with it, visualizing it, reading and writing some fields, then we serialize it
[p0442-l0020] [10.5pt] using the SerializeToString() method. This is the binary data that is ready to be
[p0442-l0021] [10.5pt] saved or transmitted over the network. When reading or receiving this binary data,
[p0442-l0022] [10.5pt] we can parse it using the ParseFromString() method, and we get a copy of the object
[p0442-l0023] [10.5pt] that was serialized.7
[p0442-l0024] [10.5pt] We could save the serialized Person object to a TFRecord file, then we could load and
[p0442-l0025] [10.5pt] parse it: everything would work fine. However, SerializeToString() and ParseFrom
[p0442-l0026] [10.5pt] String() are not TensorFlow operations (and neither are the other operations in this
[p0442-l0027] [10.5pt] code), so they cannot be included in a TensorFlow Function (except by wrapping
[p0442-l0028] [10.5pt] them in a tf.py_function() operation, which would make the code slower and less
[p0442-l0029] [10.5pt] portable, as we saw in Chapter 12). Fortunately, TensorFlow does include special pro‐
[p0442-l0030] [10.5pt] tobuf definitions for which it provides parsing operations.
[p0442-l0031] [15.77pt] TensorFlow Protobufs
[p0442-l0032] [10.5pt] The main protobuf typically used in a TFRecord file is the Example protobuf, which
[p0442-l0033] [10.5pt] represents one instance in a dataset. It contains a list of named features, where each
[p0442-l0034] [10.5pt] feature can either be a list of byte strings, a list of floats or a list of integers. Here is the
[p0442-l0035] [10.5pt] protobuf definition:
[p0442-l0036] [8.5pt] syntax = "proto3";
[p0442-l0037] [8.5pt] message BytesList { repeated bytes value = 1; }
[p0442-l0038] [8.5pt] message FloatList { repeated float value = 1 [packed = true]; }
[p0442-l0039] [8.5pt] message Int64List { repeated int64 value = 1 [packed = true]; }
[p0442-l0040] [8.0pt] 7 This chapter contains the bare minimum you need to know about protobufs to use TFRecords. To learn more
[p0442-l0041] [8.0pt] about protobufs, please visit https://homl.info/protobuf.
[p0442-l0042] [9.0pt] 416
[p0442-l0043] [9.0pt] |
[p0442-l0044] [9.0pt] Chapter 13: Loading and Preprocessing Data with TensorFlow

=== PDF page 443 / printed label 417 ===
[p0443-l0001] [8.5pt] message Feature {
[p0443-l0002] [8.5pt]     oneof kind {
[p0443-l0003] [8.5pt]         BytesList bytes_list = 1;
[p0443-l0004] [8.5pt]         FloatList float_list = 2;
[p0443-l0005] [8.5pt]         Int64List int64_list = 3;
[p0443-l0006] [8.5pt]     }
[p0443-l0007] [8.5pt] };
[p0443-l0008] [8.5pt] message Features { map<string, Feature> feature = 1; };
[p0443-l0009] [8.5pt] message Example { Features features = 1; };
[p0443-l0010] [10.5pt] The definitions of BytesList, FloatList and Int64List are straightforward enough
[p0443-l0011] [10.5pt] ([packed = true] is used for repeated numerical fields, for a more efficient encod‐
[p0443-l0012] [10.5pt] ing). A Feature either contains a BytesList, a FloatList or an Int64List. A Fea
[p0443-l0013] [10.5pt] tures (with an s) contains a dictionary that maps a feature name to the
[p0443-l0014] [10.5pt] corresponding feature value. And finally, an Example just contains a Features object.8
[p0443-l0015] [10.5pt] Here is how you could create a tf.train.Example representing the same person as
[p0443-l0016] [10.5pt] earlier, and write it to TFRecord file:
[p0443-l0017] [8.5pt] from tensorflow.train import BytesList, FloatList, Int64List
[p0443-l0018] [8.5pt] from tensorflow.train import Feature, Features, Example
[p0443-l0019] [8.5pt] person_example = Example(
[p0443-l0020] [8.5pt]     features=Features(
[p0443-l0021] [8.5pt]         feature={
[p0443-l0022] [8.5pt]             "name": Feature(bytes_list=BytesList(value=[b"Alice"])),
[p0443-l0023] [8.5pt]             "id": Feature(int64_list=Int64List(value=[123])),
[p0443-l0024] [8.5pt]             "emails": Feature(bytes_list=BytesList(value=[b"a@b.com",
[p0443-l0025] [8.5pt]                                                           b"c@d.com"]))
[p0443-l0026] [8.5pt]         }))
[p0443-l0027] [10.5pt] The code is a bit verbose and repetitive, but it’s rather straightforward (and you could
[p0443-l0028] [10.5pt] easily wrap it inside a small helper function). Now that we have an Example protobuf,
[p0443-l0029] [10.5pt] we can serialize it by calling its SerializeToString() method, then write the result‐
[p0443-l0030] [10.5pt] ing data to a TFRecord file:
[p0443-l0031] [8.5pt] with tf.io.TFRecordWriter("my_contacts.tfrecord") as f:
[p0443-l0032] [8.5pt]     f.write(person_example.SerializeToString())
[p0443-l0033] [10.5pt] Normally you would write much more than just one example! Typically, you would
[p0443-l0034] [10.5pt] create a conversion script that reads from your current format (say, CSV files), creates
[p0443-l0035] [10.5pt] an Example protobuf for each instance, serializes them and saves them to several
[p0443-l0036] [10.5pt] TFRecord files, ideally shuffling them in the process. This requires a bit of work, so
[p0443-l0037] [10.5pt] once again make sure it is really necessary (perhaps your pipeline works fine with
[p0443-l0038] [10.5pt] CSV files).
[p0443-l0039] [8.0pt] 8 Why was Example even defined since it contains no more than a Features object? Well, TensorFlow may one
[p0443-l0040] [8.0pt] day decide to add more fields to it. As long as the new Example definition still contains the features field,
[p0443-l0041] [8.0pt] with the same id, it will be backward compatible. This extensibility is one of the great features of protobufs.
[p0443-l0042] [9.0pt] The TFRecord Format
[p0443-l0043] [9.0pt] |

[p0444-l0001] [10.5pt] Now that we have a nice TFRecord file containing a serialized Example, let’s try to
[p0444-l0002] [10.5pt] load it.
[p0444-l0003] [15.77pt] Loading and Parsing Examples
[p0444-l0004] [10.5pt] To load the serialized Example protobufs, we will use a tf.data.TFRecordDataset
[p0444-l0005] [10.5pt] once again, and we will parse each Example using tf.io.parse_single_example().
[p0444-l0006] [10.5pt] This is a TensorFlow operation so it can be included in a TF Function. It requires at
[p0444-l0007] [10.5pt] least two arguments: a string scalar tensor containing the serialized data, and a
[p0444-l0008] [10.5pt] description of each feature. The description is a dictionary that maps each feature
[p0444-l0009] [10.5pt] name to either a tf.io.FixedLenFeature descriptor indicating the feature’s shape,
[p0444-l0010] [10.5pt] type and default value, or a tf.io.VarLenFeature descriptor indicating only the type
[p0444-l0011] [10.5pt] (if the length may vary, such as for the "emails" feature). For example:
[p0444-l0012] [8.5pt] feature_description = {
[p0444-l0013] [8.5pt]     "name": tf.io.FixedLenFeature([], tf.string, default_value=""),
[p0444-l0014] [8.5pt]     "id": tf.io.FixedLenFeature([], tf.int64, default_value=0),
[p0444-l0015] [8.5pt]     "emails": tf.io.VarLenFeature(tf.string),
[p0444-l0016] [8.5pt] }
[p0444-l0017] [8.5pt] for serialized_example in tf.data.TFRecordDataset(["my_contacts.tfrecord"]):
[p0444-l0018] [8.5pt]     parsed_example = tf.io.parse_single_example(serialized_example,
[p0444-l0019] [8.5pt]                                                 feature_description)
[p0444-l0020] [10.5pt] The fixed length features are parsed as regular tensors, but the variable length fea‐
[p0444-l0021] [10.5pt] tures are parsed as sparse tensors. You can convert a sparse tensor to a dense tensor
[p0444-l0022] [10.5pt] using tf.sparse.to_dense(), but in this case it is simpler to just access its values:
[p0444-l0023] [8.5pt] >>> tf.sparse.to_dense(parsed_example["emails"], default_value=b"")
[p0444-l0024] [8.5pt] <tf.Tensor: [...] dtype=string, numpy=array([b'a@b.com', b'c@d.com'], [...])>
[p0444-l0025] [8.5pt] >>> parsed_example["emails"].values
[p0444-l0026] [8.5pt] <tf.Tensor: [...] dtype=string, numpy=array([b'a@b.com', b'c@d.com'], [...])>
[p0444-l0027] [10.5pt] A BytesList can contain any binary data you want, including any serialized object.
[p0444-l0028] [10.5pt] For example, you can use tf.io.encode_jpeg() to encode an image using the JPEG
[p0444-l0029] [10.5pt] format, and put this binary data in a BytesList. Later, when your code reads the
[p0444-l0030] [10.5pt] TFRecord, it will start by parsing the Example, then you will need to call
[p0444-l0031] [10.5pt] tf.io.decode_jpeg() to parse the data and get the original image (or you can use
[p0444-l0032] [10.5pt] tf.io.decode_image(), which can decode any BMP, GIF, JPEG or PNG image). You
[p0444-l0033] [10.5pt] can also store any tensor you want in a BytesList by serializing the tensor using
[p0444-l0034] [10.5pt] tf.io.serialize_tensor(), then putting the resulting byte string in a BytesList
[p0444-l0035] [10.5pt] feature. Later, when you parse the TFRecord, you can parse this data using
[p0444-l0036] [10.5pt] tf.io.parse_tensor().
[p0444-l0037] [10.5pt] Instead of parsing examples one by one using tf.io.parse_single_example(), you
[p0444-l0038] [10.5pt] may want to parse them batch by batch using tf.io.parse_example():
[p0444-l0039] [9.0pt] 418
[p0444-l0040] [9.0pt] |

[p0445-l0001] [8.5pt] dataset = tf.data.TFRecordDataset(["my_contacts.tfrecord"]).batch(10)
[p0445-l0002] [8.5pt] for serialized_examples in dataset:
[p0445-l0003] [8.5pt]     parsed_examples = tf.io.parse_example(serialized_examples,
[p0445-l0004] [8.5pt]                                           feature_description)
[p0445-l0005] [10.5pt] As you can see, the Example proto will probably be sufficient for most use cases.
[p0445-l0006] [10.5pt] However, it may be a bit cumbersome to use when you are dealing with lists of lists.
[p0445-l0007] [10.5pt] For example, suppose you want to classify text documents. Each document may be
[p0445-l0008] [10.5pt] represented as a list of sentences, where each sentence is represented as a list of
[p0445-l0009] [10.5pt] words. And perhaps each document also has a list of comments, where each com‐
[p0445-l0010] [10.5pt] ment is also represented as a list of words. Moreover, there may be some contextual
[p0445-l0011] [10.5pt] data as well, such as the document’s author, title and publication date. TensorFlow’s
[p0445-l0012] [10.5pt] SequenceExample protobuf is designed for such use cases.
[p0445-l0013] [15.77pt] Handling Lists of Lists Using the SequenceExample Protobuf
[p0445-l0014] [10.5pt] Here is the definition of the SequenceExample protobuf:
[p0445-l0015] [8.5pt] message FeatureList { repeated Feature feature = 1; };
[p0445-l0016] [8.5pt] message FeatureLists { map<string, FeatureList> feature_list = 1; };
[p0445-l0017] [8.5pt] message SequenceExample {
[p0445-l0018] [8.5pt]     Features context = 1;
[p0445-l0019] [8.5pt]     FeatureLists feature_lists = 2;
[p0445-l0020] [8.5pt] };
[p0445-l0021] [10.5pt] A SequenceExample contains a Features object for the contextual data and a Fea
[p0445-l0022] [10.5pt] tureLists object which contains one or more named FeatureList objects (e.g., a
[p0445-l0023] [10.5pt] FeatureList named "content" and another named "comments"). Each FeatureList
[p0445-l0024] [10.5pt] just contains a list of Feature objects, each of which may be a list of byte strings, a list
[p0445-l0025] [10.5pt] of 64-bit integers or a list of floats (in this example, each Feature would represent a
[p0445-l0026] [10.5pt] sentence or a comment, perhaps in the form of a list of word identifiers). Building a
[p0445-l0027] [10.5pt] SequenceExample, serializing it and parsing it is very similar to building, serializing
[p0445-l0028] [10.5pt] and parsing an Example, but you must use tf.io.parse_single_sequence_exam
[p0445-l0029] [10.5pt] ple() to parse a single SequenceExample or tf.io.parse_sequence_example() to
[p0445-l0030] [10.5pt] parse a batch, and both functions return a tuple containing the context features (as a
[p0445-l0031] [10.5pt] dictionary) and the feature lists (also as a dictionary). If the feature lists contain
[p0445-l0032] [10.5pt] sequences of varying sizes (as in the example above), you may want to convert them
[p0445-l0033] [10.5pt] to ragged tensors using tf.RaggedTensor.from_sparse() (see the notebook for the
[p0445-l0034] [10.5pt] full code):
[p0445-l0035] [8.5pt] parsed_context, parsed_feature_lists = tf.io.parse_single_sequence_example(
[p0445-l0036] [8.5pt]     serialized_sequence_example, context_feature_descriptions,
[p0445-l0037] [8.5pt]     sequence_feature_descriptions)
[p0445-l0038] [8.5pt] parsed_content = tf.RaggedTensor.from_sparse(parsed_feature_lists["content"])
[p0445-l0039] [10.5pt] Now that you know how to efficiently store, load and parse data, the next step is to
[p0445-l0040] [10.5pt] prepare it so that it can be fed to a neural network. This means converting all features
[p0445-l0041] [9.0pt] The TFRecord Format
[p0445-l0042] [9.0pt] |
[p0445-l0043] [9.0pt] 419

=== PDF page 446 / printed label 420 ===
[p0446-l0001] [10.5pt] into numerical features (ideally not too sparse), scaling them, and more. In particular,
[p0446-l0002] [10.5pt] if your data contains categorical features or text features, they need to be converted to
[p0446-l0003] [10.5pt] numbers. For this, the Features API can help.
[p0446-l0004] [18.92pt] The Features API
[p0446-l0005] [10.5pt] Preprocessing your data can be performed in many ways: it can be done ahead of
[p0446-l0006] [10.5pt] time when preparing your data files, using any tool you like. Or you can preprocess
[p0446-l0007] [10.5pt] your data on the fly when loading it with the Data API (e.g., using the dataset’s map()
[p0446-l0008] [10.5pt] method, as we saw earlier). Or you can include a preprocessing layer directly in your
[p0446-l0009] [10.5pt] model. Whichever solution you prefer, the Features API can help you: it is a set of
[p0446-l0010] [10.5pt] functions available in the tf.feature_column package, which let you define how
[p0446-l0011] [10.5pt] each feature (or group of features) in your data should be preprocessed (therefore you
[p0446-l0012] [10.5pt] can think of this API as the analog of Scikit-Learn’s ColumnTransformer class). We
[p0446-l0013] [10.5pt] will start by looking at the different types of columns available, and then we will look
[p0446-l0014] [10.5pt] at how to use them.
[p0446-l0015] [10.5pt] Let’s go back to the variant of the California housing dataset that we used in Chap‐
[p0446-l0016] [10.5pt] ter 2, since it includes a categorical feature and missing data. Here is a simple numeri‐
[p0446-l0017] [10.5pt] cal column named "housing_median_age":
[p0446-l0018] [8.5pt] housing_median_age = tf.feature_column.numeric_column("housing_median_age")
[p0446-l0019] [10.5pt] Numeric columns let you specify a normalization function using the normalizer_fn
[p0446-l0020] [10.5pt] argument. For example, let’s tweak the "housing_median_age" column to define how
[p0446-l0021] [10.5pt] it should be scaled. Note that this requires computing ahead of time the mean and
[p0446-l0022] [10.5pt] standard deviation of this feature in the training set:
[p0446-l0023] [8.5pt] age_mean, age_std = X_mean[1], X_std[1]  # The median age is column in 1
[p0446-l0024] [8.5pt] housing_median_age = tf.feature_column.numeric_column(
[p0446-l0025] [8.5pt]     "housing_median_age", normalizer_fn=lambda x: (x - age_mean) / age_std)
[p0446-l0026] [10.5pt] In some cases, it might improve performance to bucketize some numerical features,
[p0446-l0027] [10.5pt] effectively transforming a numerical feature into a categorical feature. For example,
[p0446-l0028] [10.5pt] let’s create a bucketized column based on the median_income column, with 5 buckets:
[p0446-l0029] [10.5pt] less than 1.5 ($15,000), then 1.5 to 3, 3 to 4.5, 4.5 to 6., and above 6. (notice that when
[p0446-l0030] [10.5pt] you specify 4 boundaries, there are actually 5 buckets):
[p0446-l0031] [8.5pt] median_income = tf.feature_column.numeric_column("median_income")
[p0446-l0032] [8.5pt] bucketized_income = tf.feature_column.bucketized_column(
[p0446-l0033] [8.5pt]     median_income, boundaries=[1.5, 3., 4.5, 6.])
[p0446-l0034] [10.5pt] If the median_income feature is equal to, say, 3.2, then the bucketized_income feature
[p0446-l0035] [10.5pt] will automatically be equal to 2 (i.e., the index of the corresponding income bucket).
[p0446-l0036] [10.5pt] Choosing the right boundaries can be somewhat of an art, but one approach is to just
[p0446-l0037] [10.5pt] use percentiles of the data (e.g., the 10th percentile, the 20th percentile, and so on). If
[p0446-l0038] [10.5pt] a feature is multimodal, meaning it has separate peaks in its distribution, you may
[p0446-l0039] [9.0pt] 420
[p0446-l0040] [9.0pt] |
[p0446-l0041] [9.0pt] Chapter 13: Loading and Preprocessing Data with TensorFlow

=== PDF page 447 / printed label 421 ===
[p0447-l0001] [10.5pt] want to define a bucket for each mode, placing the boundaries in between the peaks.
[p0447-l0002] [10.5pt] Whether you use the percentiles or the modes, you need to analyze the distribution of
[p0447-l0003] [10.5pt] your data ahead of time, just like we had to measure the mean and standard deviation
[p0447-l0004] [10.5pt] ahead of time to normalize the housing_median_age column.
[p0447-l0005] [15.77pt] Categorical Features
[p0447-l0006] [10.5pt] For categorical features such as ocean_proximity, there are several options. If it is
[p0447-l0007] [10.5pt] already represented as a category ID (i.e., an integer from 0 to the max ID), then you
[p0447-l0008] [10.5pt] can use the categorical_column_with_identity() function (specifying the max
[p0447-l0009] [10.5pt] ID). If not, and you know the list of all possible categories, then you can use categori
[p0447-l0010] [10.5pt] cal_column_with_vocabulary_list():
[p0447-l0011] [8.5pt] ocean_prox_vocab = ['<1H OCEAN', 'INLAND', 'ISLAND', 'NEAR BAY', 'NEAR OCEAN']
[p0447-l0012] [8.5pt] ocean_proximity = tf.feature_column.categorical_column_with_vocabulary_list(
[p0447-l0013] [8.5pt]     "ocean_proximity", ocean_prox_vocab)
[p0447-l0014] [10.5pt] If you prefer to have TensorFlow load the vocabulary from a file, you can call catego
[p0447-l0015] [10.5pt] rical_column_with_vocabulary_file() instead. As you might expect, these two
[p0447-l0016] [10.5pt] functions will simply map each category to its index in the vocabulary (e.g., NEAR
[p0447-l0017] [10.5pt] BAY will be mapped to 3), and unknown categories will be mapped to -1.
[p0447-l0018] [10.5pt] For categorical columns with a large vocabulary (e.g., for zipcodes, cities, words,
[p0447-l0019] [10.5pt] products, users, etc.), it may not be convenient to get the full list of possible cate‐
[p0447-l0020] [10.5pt] gories, or perhaps categories may be added or removed so frequently that using cate‐
[p0447-l0021] [10.5pt] gory indices would be too unreliable. In this case, you may prefer to use a
[p0447-l0022] [10.5pt] categorical_column_with_hash_bucket(). If we had a "city" feature in the dataset,
[p0447-l0023] [10.5pt] we could encode it like this:
[p0447-l0024] [8.5pt] city_hash = tf.feature_column.categorical_column_with_hash_bucket(
[p0447-l0025] [8.5pt]     "city", hash_bucket_size=1000)
[p0447-l0026] [10.5pt] This feature will compute a hash for each category (i.e., for each city), modulo the
[p0447-l0027] [10.5pt] number of hash buckets (hash_bucket_size). You must set the number of buckets
[p0447-l0028] [10.5pt] high enough to avoid getting too many collisions (i.e., different categories ending up
[p0447-l0029] [10.5pt] in the same bucket), but the higher you set it, the more RAM will be used (by the
[p0447-l0030] [10.5pt] embedding table, as we will see shortly).
[p0447-l0031] [15.77pt] Crossed Categorical Features
[p0447-l0032] [10.5pt] If you suspect that two (or more) categorical features are more meaningful when used
[p0447-l0033] [10.5pt] jointly, then you can create a crossed column. For example, suppose people are partic‐
[p0447-l0034] [10.5pt] ularly fond of old houses inland and new houses near the ocean, then it might help to

[p0447-l0036] [9.0pt] |

[p0448-l0001] [10.5pt] create a bucketized column for the housing_median_age feature9, and cross it with
[p0448-l0002] [10.5pt] the ocean_proximity column. The crossed column will compute a hash of every age
[p0448-l0003] [10.5pt] & ocean proximity combination it comes across, modulo the hash_bucket_size, and
[p0448-l0004] [10.5pt] this will give it the cross category ID. You may then choose to use only this crossed
[p0448-l0005] [10.5pt] column in your model, or also include the individual columns.
[p0448-l0006] [8.5pt] bucketized_age = tf.feature_column.bucketized_column(
[p0448-l0007] [8.5pt]     housing_median_age, boundaries=[-1., -0.5, 0., 0.5, 1.]) # age was scaled
[p0448-l0008] [8.5pt] age_and_ocean_proximity = tf.feature_column.crossed_column(
[p0448-l0009] [8.5pt]     [bucketized_age, ocean_proximity], hash_bucket_size=100)
[p0448-l0010] [10.5pt] Another common use case for crossed columns is to cross latitude and longitude into
[p0448-l0011] [10.5pt] a single categorical feature: you start by bucketizing the latitude and longitude, for
[p0448-l0012] [10.5pt] example into 20 buckets each, then you cross these bucketized features into a loca
[p0448-l0013] [10.5pt] tion column. This will create a 20×20 grid over California, and each cell in the grid
[p0448-l0014] [10.5pt] will correspond to one category:
[p0448-l0015] [8.5pt] latitude = tf.feature_column.numeric_column("latitude")
[p0448-l0016] [8.5pt] longitude = tf.feature_column.numeric_column("longitude")
[p0448-l0017] [8.5pt] bucketized_latitude = tf.feature_column.bucketized_column(
[p0448-l0018] [8.5pt]     latitude, boundaries=list(np.linspace(32., 42., 20 - 1)))
[p0448-l0019] [8.5pt] bucketized_longitude = tf.feature_column.bucketized_column(
[p0448-l0020] [8.5pt]     longitude, boundaries=list(np.linspace(-125., -114., 20 - 1)))
[p0448-l0021] [8.5pt] location = tf.feature_column.crossed_column(
[p0448-l0022] [8.5pt]     [bucketized_latitude, bucketized_longitude], hash_bucket_size=1000)
[p0448-l0023] [15.77pt] Encoding Categorical Features Using One-Hot Vectors
[p0448-l0024] [10.5pt] No matter which option you choose to build a categorical feature (categorical col‐
[p0448-l0025] [10.5pt] umns, bucketized columns or crossed columns), it must be encoded before you can
[p0448-l0026] [10.5pt] feed it to a neural network. There are two options to encode a categorical feature:
[p0448-l0027] [10.5pt] one-hot vectors or embeddings. For the first option, simply use the indicator_col
[p0448-l0028] [10.5pt] umn() function:
[p0448-l0029] [8.5pt] ocean_proximity_one_hot = tf.feature_column.indicator_column(ocean_proximity)
[p0448-l0030] [10.5pt] A one-hot vector encoding has the size of the vocabulary length, which is fine if there
[p0448-l0031] [10.5pt] are just a few possible categories, but if the vocabulary is large, you will end up with
[p0448-l0032] [10.5pt] too many inputs fed to your neural network: it will have too many weights to learn
[p0448-l0033] [10.5pt] and it will probably not perform very well. In particular, this will typically be the case
[p0448-l0034] [10.5pt] when you use hash buckets. In this case, you should probably encode them using
[p0448-l0035] [10.5pt] embeddings instead.
[p0448-l0036] [8.0pt] 9 Since the housing_median_age feature was normalized, the boundaries are for normalized ages.
[p0448-l0037] [9.0pt] 422
[p0448-l0038] [9.0pt] |
[p0448-l0039] [9.0pt] Chapter 13: Loading and Preprocessing Data with TensorFlow

[p0449-l0001] [9.6pt] As a rule of thumb (but your mileage may vary!), if the number of
[p0449-l0002] [9.6pt] categories is lower than 10, then one-hot encoding is generally the
[p0449-l0003] [9.6pt] way to go. If the number of categories is greater than 50 (which is
[p0449-l0004] [9.6pt] often the case when you use hash buckets), then embeddings are
[p0449-l0005] [9.6pt] usually preferable. In between 10 and 50 categories, you may want
[p0449-l0006] [9.6pt] to experiment with both options and see which one works best for
[p0449-l0007] [9.6pt] your use case. Also, embeddings typically require more training
[p0449-l0008] [9.6pt] data, unless you can reuse pretrained embeddings.
[p0449-l0009] [15.77pt] Encoding Categorical Features Using Embeddings
[p0449-l0010] [10.5pt] An embedding is a trainable dense vector that represents a category. By default,
[p0449-l0011] [10.5pt] embeddings are initialized randomly, so for example the "NEAR BAY" category could
[p0449-l0012] [10.5pt] be represented initially by a random vector such as [0.131, 0.890], while the "NEAR
[p0449-l0013] [10.5pt] OCEAN" category may be represented by another random vector such as [0.631,
[p0449-l0014] [10.5pt] 0.791] (in this example, we are using 2D embeddings, but the number of dimensions
[p0449-l0015] [10.5pt] is a hyperparameter you can tweak). Since these embeddings are trainable, they will
[p0449-l0016] [10.5pt] gradually improve during training, and as they represent fairly similar categories,
[p0449-l0017] [10.5pt] Gradient Descent will certainly end up pushing them closer together, while it will
[p0449-l0018] [10.5pt] tend to move them away from the "INLAND" category’s embedding (see Figure 13-4).
[p0449-l0019] [10.5pt] Indeed, the better the representation, the easier it will be for the neural network to
[p0449-l0020] [10.5pt] make accurate predictions, so training tends to make embeddings useful representa‐
[p0449-l0021] [10.5pt] tions of the categories. This is called representation learning (we will see other types of
[p0449-l0022] [10.5pt] representation learning in ???).

[p0449-l0024] [9.0pt] |

[p0450-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 13-4. Embeddings Will Gradually Improve During Training
[p0450-l0002] [15.0pt] Word Embeddings
[p0450-l0003] [10.0pt] Not only will embeddings generally be useful representations for the task at hand, but
[p0450-l0004] [10.0pt] quite often these same embeddings can be reused successfully for other tasks as well.
[p0450-l0005] [10.0pt] The most common example of this is word embeddings (i.e., embeddings of individual
[p0450-l0006] [10.0pt] words): when you are working on a natural language processing task, you are often
[p0450-l0007] [10.0pt] better off reusing pretrained word embeddings than training your own. The idea of
[p0450-l0008] [10.0pt] using vectors to represent words dates back to the 1960s, and many sophisticated
[p0450-l0009] [10.0pt] techniques have been used to generate useful vectors, including using neural net‐
[p0450-l0010] [10.0pt] works, but things really took off in 2013, when Tomáš Mikolov and other Google
[p0450-l0011] [10.0pt] researchers published a paper10 describing how to learn word embeddings using deep
[p0450-l0012] [10.0pt] neural networks, much faster than previous attempts. This allowed them to learn
[p0450-l0013] [10.0pt] embeddings on a very large corpus of text: they trained a deep neural network to pre‐
[p0450-l0014] [10.0pt] dict the words near any given word. This allowed them to obtain astounding word
[p0450-l0015] [10.0pt] embeddings. For example, synonyms had very close embeddings, and semantically
[p0450-l0016] [10.0pt] related words such as France, Spain, Italy, and so on, ended up clustered together. But
[p0450-l0017] [10.0pt] it’s not just about proximity: word embeddings were also organized along meaningful
[p0450-l0018] [10.0pt] axes in the embedding space. Here is a famous example: if you compute King – Man
[p0450-l0019] [10.0pt] + Woman (adding and subtracting the embedding vectors of these words), then the
[p0450-l0020] [10.0pt] result will be very close to the embedding of the word Queen (see Figure 13-5). In
[p0450-l0021] [10.0pt] other words, the word embeddings encode the concept of gender! Similarly, you can
[p0450-l0022] [10.0pt] compute Madrid – Spain + France, and of course the result is close to Paris, which
[p0450-l0023] [10.0pt] seems to show that the notion of capital city was also encoded in the embeddings.
[p0450-l0024] [8.0pt] 10 “Distributed Representations of Words and Phrases and their Compositionality”, T. Mikolov et al. (2013).
[p0450-l0025] [9.0pt] 424
[p0450-l0026] [9.0pt] |
[p0450-l0027] [9.0pt] Chapter 13: Loading and Preprocessing Data with TensorFlow

=== PDF page 451 / printed label 425 ===
[p0451-l0001] [10.0pt] Figure 13-5. Word Embeddings
[p0451-l0002] [10.5pt] Let’s go back to the Features API. Here is how you could encode the ocean_proxim
[p0451-l0003] [10.5pt] ity categories as 2D embeddings:
[p0451-l0004] [8.5pt] ocean_proximity_embed = tf.feature_column.embedding_column(ocean_proximity,
[p0451-l0005] [8.5pt]                                                            dimension=2)
[p0451-l0006] [10.5pt] Each of the five ocean_proximity categories will now be represented as a 2D vector.
[p0451-l0007] [10.5pt] These vectors are stored in an embedding matrix with one row per category, and one
[p0451-l0008] [10.5pt] column per embedding dimension, so in this example it is a 5×2 matrix. When an
[p0451-l0009] [10.5pt] embedding column is given a category index as input (say, 3, which corresponds to
[p0451-l0010] [10.5pt] the category "NEAR BAY"), it just performs a lookup in the embedding matrix and
[p0451-l0011] [10.5pt] returns the corresponding row (say, [0.331, 0.190]). Unfortunately, the embedding
[p0451-l0012] [10.5pt] matrix can be quite large, especially when you have a large vocabulary: if this is the
[p0451-l0013] [10.5pt] case, the model can only learn good representations for the categories for which it has
[p0451-l0014] [10.5pt] sufficient training data. To reduce the size of the embedding matrix, you can of
[p0451-l0015] [10.5pt] course try lowering the dimension hyperparameter, but if you reduce this parameter
[p0451-l0016] [10.5pt] too much, the representations may not be as good. Another option is to reduce the
[p0451-l0017] [10.5pt] vocabulary size (e.g., if you are dealing with text, you can try dropping the rare words
[p0451-l0018] [10.5pt] from the vocabulary, and replace them all with a token like "<unknown>" or "<UNK>").
[p0451-l0019] [10.5pt] If you are using hash buckets, you can also try reducing the hash_bucket_size (but
[p0451-l0020] [10.5pt] not too much, or else you will get collisions).

[p0451-l0022] [9.0pt] |

[p0452-l0001] [9.6pt] If there are no pretrained embeddings that you can reuse for the
[p0452-l0002] [9.6pt] task you are trying to tackle, and if you do not have enough train‐
[p0452-l0003] [9.6pt] ing data to learn them, then you can try to learn them on some
[p0452-l0004] [9.6pt] auxiliary task for which it is easier to obtain plenty of training data.
[p0452-l0005] [9.6pt] After that, you can reuse the trained embeddings for your main
[p0452-l0006] [9.6pt] task.
[p0452-l0007] [15.77pt] Using Feature Columns for Parsing
[p0452-l0008] [10.5pt] Let’s suppose you have created feature columns for each of your input features, as well
[p0452-l0009] [10.5pt] as for the target. What can you do with them? Well, for one you can pass them to the
[p0452-l0010] [10.5pt] make_parse_example_spec() function to generate feature descriptions (so you don’t
[p0452-l0011] [10.5pt] have to do it manually, as we did earlier):
[p0452-l0012] [8.5pt] columns = [bucketized_age, ....., median_house_value] # all features + target
[p0452-l0013] [8.5pt] feature_descriptions = tf.feature_column.make_parse_example_spec(columns)
[p0452-l0014] [9.6pt] You don’t always have to create a separate feature column for each
[p0452-l0015] [9.6pt] and every feature. For example, instead of having 2 numerical fea‐
[p0452-l0016] [9.6pt] ture columns, you could choose to have a single 2D column: just
[p0452-l0017] [9.6pt] set shape=[2] when calling numerical_column().
[p0452-l0018] [10.5pt] You can then create a function that parses serialized examples using these feature
[p0452-l0019] [10.5pt] descriptions, and separates the target column from the input features:
[p0452-l0020] [8.5pt] def parse_examples(serialized_examples):
[p0452-l0021] [8.5pt]     examples = tf.io.parse_example(serialized_examples, feature_descriptions)
[p0452-l0022] [8.5pt]     targets = examples.pop("median_house_value") # separate the targets
[p0452-l0023] [8.5pt]     return examples, targets
[p0452-l0024] [10.5pt] Next, you can create a TFRecordDataset that will read batches of serialized examples
[p0452-l0025] [10.5pt] (assuming the TFRecord file contains serialized Example protobufs with the appropri‐
[p0452-l0026] [10.5pt] ate features):
[p0452-l0027] [8.5pt] batch_size = 32
[p0452-l0028] [8.5pt] dataset = tf.data.TFRecordDataset(["my_data_with_features.tfrecords"])
[p0452-l0029] [8.5pt] dataset = dataset.repeat().shuffle(10000).batch(batch_size).map(parse_examples)
[p0452-l0030] [15.77pt] Using Feature Columns in Your Models
[p0452-l0031] [10.5pt] Feature columns can also be used directly in your model, to convert all your input
[p0452-l0032] [10.5pt] features into a single dense vector which the neural network can then process. For
[p0452-l0033] [10.5pt] this, all you need to do is add a keras.layers.DenseFeatures layer as the first layer
[p0452-l0034] [10.5pt] in your model, passing it the list of feature columns (excluding the target column):
[p0452-l0035] [8.5pt] columns_without_target = columns[:-1]
[p0452-l0036] [8.5pt] model = keras.models.Sequential([
[p0452-l0037] [8.5pt]     keras.layers.DenseFeatures(feature_columns=columns_without_target),
[p0452-l0038] [9.0pt] 426

[p0453-l0002] [8.5pt] ])
[p0453-l0003] [8.5pt] model.compile(loss="mse", optimizer="sgd", metrics=["accuracy"])
[p0453-l0004] [8.5pt] steps_per_epoch = len(X_train) // batch_size

[p0453-l0006] [10.5pt] The DenseFeatures layer will take care of converting every input feature to a dense

[p0453-l0009] [10.5pt] can take a closer look at what the DenseFeatures layer does by calling it directly:

[p0453-l0014] [8.5pt] ...     "median_income": [[3.], [7.2], [1.]]
[p0453-l0015] [8.5pt] ... })
[p0453-l0016] [8.5pt] ...
[p0453-l0017] [8.5pt] <tf.Tensor: id=559790, shape=(3, 7), dtype=float32, numpy=
[p0453-l0018] [8.5pt] array([[ 0. , 0. , 1. , 0. , 0. ,-0.36277947 , 0.30109018],
[p0453-l0019] [8.5pt]        [ 0. , 0. , 0. , 0. , 1. , 0.22548223 , 0.33142096],
[p0453-l0020] [8.5pt]        [ 1. , 0. , 0. , 0. , 0. , 0.22548223 , 0.33142096]], dtype=float32)>
[p0453-l0021] [10.5pt] In this example, we create a DenseFeatures layer with just two columns, and we call
[p0453-l0022] [10.5pt] it with some data, in the form of a dictionary of features. In this case, since the bucke
[p0453-l0023] [10.5pt] tized_income column relies on the median_income column, the dictionary must
[p0453-l0024] [10.5pt] include the "median_income" key, and similarly since the ocean_proximity_embed
[p0453-l0025] [10.5pt] column is based on the ocean_proximity column, the dictionary must include the
[p0453-l0026] [10.5pt] "ocean_proximity" key. Columns are handled in alphabetical order, so first we look
[p0453-l0027] [10.5pt] at the bucketized income column (its name is the same as the median_income column
[p0453-l0028] [10.5pt] name, plus "_bucketized"). The incomes 3, 7.2 and 1 get mapped respectively to cat‐
[p0453-l0029] [10.5pt] egory 2 (for incomes between 1.5 and 3), category 0 (for incomes below 1.5), and cat‐
[p0453-l0030] [10.5pt] egory 4 (for incomes greater than 6). Then these category IDs get one-hot encoded:
[p0453-l0031] [10.5pt] category 2 gets encoded as [0., 0., 1., 0., 0.] and so on (note that bucketized
[p0453-l0032] [10.5pt] columns get one-hot encoded by default, no need to call indicator_column()). Now
[p0453-l0033] [10.5pt] on to the ocean_proximity_embed column. The "NEAR OCEAN" and "INLAND" cate‐
[p0453-l0034] [10.5pt] gories just get mapped to their respective embeddings (which were initialized ran‐
[p0453-l0035] [10.5pt] domly). The resulting tensor is the concatenation of the one-hot vectors and the
[p0453-l0036] [10.5pt] embeddings.
[p0453-l0037] [10.5pt] Now you can feed all kinds of features to a neural network, including numerical fea‐
[p0453-l0038] [10.5pt] tures, categorical features, and even text (by splitting the text into words, then using
[p0453-l0039] [10.5pt] word embedding)! However, performing all the preprocessing on the fly can slow
[p0453-l0040] [10.5pt] down training. Let’s see how this can be improved.

[p0453-l0042] [9.0pt] |

[p0454-l0001] [18.92pt] TF Transform
[p0454-l0002] [10.5pt] If preprocessing is computationally expensive, then handling it before training rather
[p0454-l0003] [10.5pt] than on the fly may give you a significant speedup: the data will be preprocessed just
[p0454-l0004] [10.5pt] once per instance before training, rather than once per instance and per epoch during
[p0454-l0005] [10.5pt] training. Tools like Apache Beam let you run efficient data processing pipelines over
[p0454-l0006] [10.5pt] large amounts of data, even distributed across multiple servers, so why not use it to
[p0454-l0007] [10.5pt] preprocess all the training data? This works great and indeed can speed up training,
[p0454-l0008] [10.5pt] but there is one problem: once your model is trained, suppose you want to deploy it
[p0454-l0009] [10.5pt] to a mobile app: you will need to write some code in your app to take care of prepro‐
[p0454-l0010] [10.5pt] cessing the data before it is fed to the model. And suppose you also want to deploy
[p0454-l0011] [10.5pt] the model to TensorFlow.js so it runs in a web browser? Once again, you will need to
[p0454-l0012] [10.5pt] write some preprocessing code. This can become a maintenance nightmare: when‐
[p0454-l0013] [10.5pt] ever you want to change the preprocessing logic, you will need to update your Apache
[p0454-l0014] [10.5pt] Beam code, your mobile app code and your Javascript code. It is not only time con‐
[p0454-l0015] [10.5pt] suming, but also error prone: you may end up with subtle differences between the
[p0454-l0016] [10.5pt] preprocessing operations performed before training and the ones performed in your
[p0454-l0017] [10.5pt] app or in the browser. This training/serving skew will lead to bugs or degraded perfor‐
[p0454-l0018] [10.5pt] mance.
[p0454-l0019] [10.5pt] One improvement would be to take the trained model (trained on data that was pre‐
[p0454-l0020] [10.5pt] processed by your Apache Beam code), and before deploying it to your app or the
[p0454-l0021] [10.5pt] browser, add an extra input layer to take care of preprocessing on the fly (either by
[p0454-l0022] [10.5pt] writing a custom layer or by using a DenseFeatures layer). That’s definitely better,
[p0454-l0023] [10.5pt] since now you just have two versions of your preprocessing code: the Apache Beam
[p0454-l0024] [10.5pt] code and the preprocessing layer’s code.
[p0454-l0025] [10.5pt] But what if you could define your preprocessing operations just once? This is what
[p0454-l0026] [10.5pt] TF Transform was designed for. It is part of TensorFlow Extended (TFX), an end-to-
[p0454-l0027] [10.5pt] end platform for productionizing TensorFlow models. First, to use a TFX component,
[p0454-l0028] [10.5pt] such as TF Transform, you must install it, it does not come bundled with TensorFlow.
[p0454-l0029] [10.5pt] You define your preprocessing function just once (in Python), by using TF Transform
[p0454-l0030] [10.5pt] functions for scaling, bucketizing, crossing features, and more. You can also use any
[p0454-l0031] [10.5pt] TensorFlow operation you need. Here is what this preprocessing function might look
[p0454-l0032] [10.5pt] like if we just had two features:
[p0454-l0033] [8.5pt] import tensorflow_transform as tft
[p0454-l0034] [8.5pt] def preprocess(inputs):  # inputs is a batch of input features
[p0454-l0035] [8.5pt]     median_age = inputs["housing_median_age"]
[p0454-l0036] [8.5pt]     ocean_proximity = inputs["ocean_proximity"]
[p0454-l0037] [8.5pt]     standardized_age = tft.scale_to_z_score(median_age - tft.mean(median_age))
[p0454-l0038] [8.5pt]     ocean_proximity_id = tft.compute_and_apply_vocabulary(ocean_proximity)
[p0454-l0039] [8.5pt]     return {
[p0454-l0040] [8.5pt]         "standardized_median_age": standardized_age,
[p0454-l0041] [9.0pt] 428
[p0454-l0042] [9.0pt] |
[p0454-l0043] [9.0pt] Chapter 13: Loading and Preprocessing Data with TensorFlow

=== PDF page 455 / printed label 429 ===
[p0455-l0001] [8.5pt]         "ocean_proximity_id": ocean_proximity_id
[p0455-l0002] [8.5pt]     }
[p0455-l0003] [10.5pt] Next, TF Transform lets you apply this preprocess() function to the whole training
[p0455-l0004] [10.5pt] set using Apache Beam (it provides an AnalyzeAndTransformDataset class that you
[p0455-l0005] [10.5pt] can use for this purpose in your Apache Beam pipeline). In the process, it will also
[p0455-l0006] [10.5pt] compute all the necessary statistics over the whole training set: in this example, the
[p0455-l0007] [10.5pt] mean and standard deviation of the housing_median_age feature, and the vocabulary
[p0455-l0008] [10.5pt] for the ocean_proximity feature. The components that compute these statistics are
[p0455-l0009] [10.5pt] called analyzers.
[p0455-l0010] [10.5pt] Importantly, TF Transform will also generate an equivalent TensorFlow Function that
[p0455-l0011] [10.5pt] you can plug into the model you deploy. This TF Function contains all the necessary
[p0455-l0012] [10.5pt] statistics computed by Apache Beam (the mean, standard deviation, and vocabulary),
[p0455-l0013] [10.5pt] simply included as constants.
[p0455-l0014] [9.6pt] At the time of this writing, TF Transform only supports Tensor‐
[p0455-l0015] [9.6pt] Flow 1. Moreover, Apache Beam only has partial support for
[p0455-l0016] [9.6pt] Python 3. That said, both these limitations will likely be fixed by
[p0455-l0017] [9.6pt] the time your read this.
[p0455-l0018] [10.5pt] With the Data API, TFRecords, the Features API and TF Transform, you can build
[p0455-l0019] [10.5pt] highly scalable input pipelines for training, and also benefit from fast and portable
[p0455-l0020] [10.5pt] data preprocessing in production.
[p0455-l0021] [10.5pt] But what if you just wanted to use a standard dataset? Well in that case, things are
[p0455-l0022] [10.5pt] much simpler: just use TFDS!
[p0455-l0023] [18.92pt] The TensorFlow Datasets (TFDS) Project
[p0455-l0024] [10.5pt] The TensorFlow Datasets project makes it trivial to download common datasets, from
[p0455-l0025] [10.5pt] small ones like MNIST or Fashion MNIST, to huge datasets like ImageNet11 (you will
[p0455-l0026] [10.5pt] need quite a bit of disk space!). The list includes image datasets, text datasets (includ‐
[p0455-l0027] [10.5pt] ing translation datasets), audio and video datasets, and more. You can visit https://
[p0455-l0028] [10.5pt] homl.info/tfds to view the full list, along with a description of each dataset.
[p0455-l0029] [10.5pt] TFDS is not bundled with TensorFlow, so you need to install the tensorflow-
[p0455-l0030] [10.5pt] datasets library (e.g., using pip). Then all you need to do is call the tfds.load()
[p0455-l0031] [10.5pt] function, and it will download the data you want (unless it was already downloaded
[p0455-l0032] [10.5pt] earlier), and return the data as a dictionary of Datasets (typically one for training,
[p0455-l0033] [8.0pt] 11 At the time of writing, TFDS requires you to download a few files manually for ImageNet (for legal reasons),
[p0455-l0034] [8.0pt] but this will hopefully get resolved soon.
[p0455-l0035] [9.0pt] The TensorFlow Datasets (TFDS) Project
[p0455-l0036] [9.0pt] |
[p0455-l0037] [9.0pt] 429

=== PDF page 456 / printed label 430 ===
[p0456-l0001] [10.5pt] and one for testing, but this depends on the dataset you choose). For example, let’s
[p0456-l0002] [10.5pt] download MNIST:
[p0456-l0003] [8.5pt] import tensorflow_datasets as tfds
[p0456-l0004] [8.5pt] dataset = tfds.load(name="mnist")
[p0456-l0005] [8.5pt] mnist_train, mnist_test = dataset["train"], dataset["test"]
[p0456-l0006] [10.5pt] You can then apply any transformation you want (typically repeating, batching and
[p0456-l0007] [10.5pt] prefetching), and you’re ready to train your model. Here is a simple example:
[p0456-l0008] [8.5pt] mnist_train = mnist_train.repeat(5).batch(32).prefetch(1)
[p0456-l0009] [8.5pt] for item in mnist_train:
[p0456-l0010] [8.5pt]     images = item["image"]
[p0456-l0011] [8.5pt]     labels = item["label"]
[p0456-l0012] [8.5pt]     [...]
[p0456-l0013] [9.6pt] In general, load() returns a shuffled training set, so there’s no need
[p0456-l0014] [9.6pt] to shuffle it some more.
[p0456-l0015] [10.5pt] Note that each item in the dataset is a dictionary containing both the features and the
[p0456-l0016] [10.5pt] labels. But Keras expects each item to be a tuple containing 2 elements (again, the fea‐
[p0456-l0017] [10.5pt] tures and the labels). You could transform the dataset using the map() method, like
[p0456-l0018] [10.5pt] this:
[p0456-l0019] [8.5pt] mnist_train = mnist_train.repeat(5).batch(32)
[p0456-l0020] [8.5pt] mnist_train = mnist_train.map(lambda items: (items["image"], items["label"]))
[p0456-l0021] [8.5pt] mnist_train = mnist_train.prefetch(1)
[p0456-l0022] [10.5pt] Or you can just ask the load() function to do this for you by setting as_super
[p0456-l0023] [10.5pt] vised=True (obviously this works only for labeled datasets). You can also specify the
[p0456-l0024] [10.5pt] batch size if you want. Then the dataset can be passed directly to your tf.keras model:
[p0456-l0025] [8.5pt] dataset = tfds.load(name="mnist", batch_size=32, as_supervised=True)
[p0456-l0026] [8.5pt] mnist_train = dataset["train"].repeat().prefetch(1)
[p0456-l0027] [8.5pt] model = keras.models.Sequential([...])
[p0456-l0028] [8.5pt] model.compile(loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy", optimizer="sgd")
[p0456-l0029] [8.5pt] model.fit(mnist_train, steps_per_epoch=60000 // 32, epochs=5)
[p0456-l0030] [10.5pt] This was quite a technical chapter, and you may feel that it is a bit far from the
[p0456-l0031] [10.5pt] abstract beauty of neural networks, but the fact is deep learning often involves large
[p0456-l0032] [10.5pt] amounts of data, and knowing how to load, parse and preprocess it efficiently is a
[p0456-l0033] [10.5pt] crucial skill to have. In the next chapter, we will look at Convolutional Neural Net‐
[p0456-l0034] [10.5pt] works, which are among the most successful neural net architectures for image pro‐
[p0456-l0035] [10.5pt] cessing, and many other applications.

[p0457-l0001] [16.82pt] CHAPTER 14
[p0457-l0002] [25.22pt] Deep Computer Vision Using Convolutional
[p0457-l0003] [25.22pt] Neural Networks
[p0457-l0004] [9.6pt] With Early Release ebooks, you get books in their earliest form—
[p0457-l0005] [9.6pt] the author’s raw and unedited content as he or she writes—so you
[p0457-l0006] [9.6pt] can take advantage of these technologies long before the official
[p0457-l0007] [9.6pt] release of these titles. The following will be Chapter 14 in the final
[p0457-l0008] [9.6pt] release of the book.
[p0457-l0009] [10.5pt] Although IBM’s Deep Blue supercomputer beat the chess world champion Garry Kas‐
[p0457-l0010] [10.5pt] parov back in 1996, it wasn’t until fairly recently that computers were able to reliably
[p0457-l0011] [10.5pt] perform seemingly trivial tasks such as detecting a puppy in a picture or recognizing
[p0457-l0012] [10.5pt] spoken words. Why are these tasks so effortless to us humans? The answer lies in the
[p0457-l0013] [10.5pt] fact that perception largely takes place outside the realm of our consciousness, within
[p0457-l0014] [10.5pt] specialized visual, auditory, and other sensory modules in our brains. By the time
[p0457-l0015] [10.5pt] sensory information reaches our consciousness, it is already adorned with high-level
[p0457-l0016] [10.5pt] features; for example, when you look at a picture of a cute puppy, you cannot choose
[p0457-l0017] [10.5pt] not to see the puppy, or not to notice its cuteness. Nor can you explain how you rec‐
[p0457-l0018] [10.5pt] ognize a cute puppy; it’s just obvious to you. Thus, we cannot trust our subjective
[p0457-l0019] [10.5pt] experience: perception is not trivial at all, and to understand it we must look at how
[p0457-l0020] [10.5pt] the sensory modules work.
[p0457-l0021] [10.5pt] Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) emerged from the study of the brain’s visual
[p0457-l0022] [10.5pt] cortex, and they have been used in image recognition since the 1980s. In the last few
[p0457-l0023] [10.5pt] years, thanks to the increase in computational power, the amount of available training
[p0457-l0024] [10.5pt] data, and the tricks presented in Chapter 11 for training deep nets, CNNs have man‐
[p0457-l0025] [10.5pt] aged to achieve superhuman performance on some complex visual tasks. They power
[p0457-l0026] [10.5pt] image search services, self-driving cars, automatic video classification systems, and
[p0457-l0027] [10.5pt] more. Moreover, CNNs are not restricted to visual perception: they are also successful
[p0457-l0028] [9.0pt] 431

=== PDF page 458 / printed label 432 ===
[p0458-l0001] [10.5pt] at many other tasks, such as voice recognition or natural language processing (NLP);
[p0458-l0002] [10.5pt] however, we will focus on visual applications for now.
[p0458-l0003] [10.5pt] In this chapter we will present where CNNs came from, what their building blocks
[p0458-l0004] [10.5pt] look like, and how to implement them using TensorFlow and Keras. Then we will dis‐
[p0458-l0005] [10.5pt] cuss some of the best CNN architectures, and discuss other visual tasks, including
[p0458-l0006] [10.5pt] object detection (classifying multiple objects in an image and placing bounding boxes
[p0458-l0007] [10.5pt] around them) and semantic segmentation (classifying each pixel according to the class
[p0458-l0008] [10.5pt] of the object it belongs to).
[p0458-l0009] [18.92pt] The Architecture of the Visual Cortex
[p0458-l0010] [10.5pt] David H. Hubel and Torsten Wiesel performed a series of experiments on cats in
[p0458-l0011] [10.5pt] 19581 and 19592 (and a few years later on monkeys3), giving crucial insights on the
[p0458-l0012] [10.5pt] structure of the visual cortex (the authors received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or
[p0458-l0013] [10.5pt] Medicine in 1981 for their work). In particular, they showed that many neurons in
[p0458-l0014] [10.5pt] the visual cortex have a small local receptive field, meaning they react only to visual
[p0458-l0015] [10.5pt] stimuli located in a limited region of the visual field (see Figure 14-1, in which the
[p0458-l0016] [10.5pt] local receptive fields of five neurons are represented by dashed circles). The receptive
[p0458-l0017] [10.5pt] fields of different neurons may overlap, and together they tile the whole visual field.
[p0458-l0018] [10.5pt] Moreover, the authors showed that some neurons react only to images of horizontal
[p0458-l0019] [10.5pt] lines, while others react only to lines with different orientations (two neurons may
[p0458-l0020] [10.5pt] have the same receptive field but react to different line orientations). They also
[p0458-l0021] [10.5pt] noticed that some neurons have larger receptive fields, and they react to more com‐
[p0458-l0022] [10.5pt] plex patterns that are combinations of the lower-level patterns. These observations
[p0458-l0023] [10.5pt] led to the idea that the higher-level neurons are based on the outputs of neighboring
[p0458-l0024] [10.5pt] lower-level neurons (in Figure 14-1, notice that each neuron is connected only to a
[p0458-l0025] [10.5pt] few neurons from the previous layer). This powerful architecture is able to detect all
[p0458-l0026] [10.5pt] sorts of complex patterns in any area of the visual field.
[p0458-l0027] [8.0pt] 1 “Single Unit Activity in Striate Cortex of Unrestrained Cats,” D. Hubel and T. Wiesel (1958).
[p0458-l0028] [8.0pt] 2 “Receptive Fields of Single Neurones in the Cat’s Striate Cortex,” D. Hubel and T. Wiesel (1959).
[p0458-l0029] [8.0pt] 3 “Receptive Fields and Functional Architecture of Monkey Striate Cortex,” D. Hubel and T. Wiesel (1968).
[p0458-l0030] [9.0pt] 432
[p0458-l0031] [9.0pt] |
[p0458-l0032] [9.0pt] Chapter 14: Deep Computer Vision Using Convolutional Neural Networks

=== PDF page 459 / printed label 433 ===
[p0459-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 14-1. Local receptive fields in the visual cortex
[p0459-l0002] [10.5pt] These studies of the visual cortex inspired the neocognitron, introduced in 1980,4
[p0459-l0003] [10.5pt] which gradually evolved into what we now call convolutional neural networks. An
[p0459-l0004] [10.5pt] important milestone was a 1998 paper5 by Yann LeCun, Léon Bottou, Yoshua Bengio,
[p0459-l0005] [10.5pt] and Patrick Haffner, which introduced the famous LeNet-5 architecture, widely used
[p0459-l0006] [10.5pt] to recognize handwritten check numbers. This architecture has some building blocks
[p0459-l0007] [10.5pt] that you already know, such as fully connected layers and sigmoid activation func‐
[p0459-l0008] [10.5pt] tions, but it also introduces two new building blocks: convolutional layers and pooling
[p0459-l0009] [10.5pt] layers. Let’s look at them now.
[p0459-l0010] [9.6pt] Why not simply use a regular deep neural network with fully con‐
[p0459-l0011] [9.6pt] nected layers for image recognition tasks? Unfortunately, although
[p0459-l0012] [9.6pt] this works fine for small images (e.g., MNIST), it breaks down for
[p0459-l0013] [9.6pt] larger images because of the huge number of parameters it
[p0459-l0014] [9.6pt] requires. For example, a 100 × 100 image has 10,000 pixels, and if
[p0459-l0015] [9.6pt] the first layer has just 1,000 neurons (which already severely
[p0459-l0016] [9.6pt] restricts the amount of information transmitted to the next layer),
[p0459-l0017] [9.6pt] this means a total of 10 million connections. And that’s just the first
[p0459-l0018] [9.6pt] layer. CNNs solve this problem using partially connected layers and
[p0459-l0019] [9.6pt] weight sharing.
[p0459-l0020] [8.0pt] 4 “Neocognitron: A Self-organizing Neural Network Model for a Mechanism of Pattern Recognition Unaffected
[p0459-l0021] [8.0pt] by Shift in Position,” K. Fukushima (1980).
[p0459-l0022] [8.0pt] 5 “Gradient-Based Learning Applied to Document Recognition,” Y. LeCun et al. (1998).
[p0459-l0023] [9.0pt] The Architecture of the Visual Cortex
[p0459-l0024] [9.0pt] |

[p0460-l0001] [18.92pt] Convolutional Layer
[p0460-l0002] [10.5pt] The most important building block of a CNN is the convolutional layer:6 neurons in
[p0460-l0003] [10.5pt] the first convolutional layer are not connected to every single pixel in the input image
[p0460-l0004] [10.5pt] (like they were in previous chapters), but only to pixels in their receptive fields (see
[p0460-l0005] [10.5pt] Figure 14-2). In turn, each neuron in the second convolutional layer is connected
[p0460-l0006] [10.5pt] only to neurons located within a small rectangle in the first layer. This architecture
[p0460-l0007] [10.5pt] allows the network to concentrate on small low-level features in the first hidden layer,
[p0460-l0008] [10.5pt] then assemble them into larger higher-level features in the next hidden layer, and so
[p0460-l0009] [10.5pt] on. This hierarchical structure is common in real-world images, which is one of the
[p0460-l0010] [10.5pt] reasons why CNNs work so well for image recognition.
[p0460-l0011] [10.5pt] Figure 14-2. CNN layers with rectangular local receptive fields
[p0460-l0012] [9.6pt] Until now, all multilayer neural networks we looked at had layers
[p0460-l0013] [9.6pt] composed of a long line of neurons, and we had to flatten input
[p0460-l0014] [9.6pt] images to 1D before feeding them to the neural network. Now each
[p0460-l0015] [9.6pt] layer is represented in 2D, which makes it easier to match neurons
[p0460-l0016] [9.6pt] with their corresponding inputs.
[p0460-l0017] [10.5pt] A neuron located in row i, column j of a given layer is connected to the outputs of the
[p0460-l0018] [10.5pt] neurons in the previous layer located in rows i to i + fh – 1, columns j to j + fw – 1,
[p0460-l0019] [10.5pt] where fh and fw are the height and width of the receptive field (see Figure 14-3). In
[p0460-l0020] [10.5pt] order for a layer to have the same height and width as the previous layer, it is com‐
[p0460-l0021] [8.0pt] 6 A convolution is a mathematical operation that slides one function over another and measures the integral of
[p0460-l0022] [8.0pt] their pointwise multiplication. It has deep connections with the Fourier transform and the Laplace transform,
[p0460-l0023] [8.0pt] and is heavily used in signal processing. Convolutional layers actually use cross-correlations, which are very
[p0460-l0024] [8.0pt] similar to convolutions (see https://homl.info/76 for more details).
[p0460-l0025] [9.0pt] 434
[p0460-l0026] [9.0pt] |
[p0460-l0027] [9.0pt] Chapter 14: Deep Computer Vision Using Convolutional Neural Networks

=== PDF page 461 / printed label 435 ===
[p0461-l0001] [10.5pt] mon to add zeros around the inputs, as shown in the diagram. This is called zero pad‐
[p0461-l0002] [10.5pt] ding.
[p0461-l0003] [10.5pt] Figure 14-3. Connections between layers and zero padding
[p0461-l0004] [10.5pt] It is also possible to connect a large input layer to a much smaller layer by spacing out
[p0461-l0005] [10.5pt] the receptive fields, as shown in Figure 14-4. The shift from one receptive field to the
[p0461-l0006] [10.5pt] next is called the stride. In the diagram, a 5 × 7 input layer (plus zero padding) is con‐
[p0461-l0007] [10.5pt] nected to a 3 × 4 layer, using 3 × 3 receptive fields and a stride of 2 (in this example
[p0461-l0008] [10.5pt] the stride is the same in both directions, but it does not have to be so). A neuron loca‐
[p0461-l0009] [10.5pt] ted in row i, column j in the upper layer is connected to the outputs of the neurons in
[p0461-l0010] [10.5pt] the previous layer located in rows i × sh to i × sh + fh – 1, columns j × sw to j × sw + fw –
[p0461-l0011] [10.5pt] 1, where sh and sw are the vertical and horizontal strides.
[p0461-l0012] [9.0pt] Convolutional Layer
[p0461-l0013] [9.0pt] |
