[p0462-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 14-4. Reducing dimensionality using a stride of 2
[p0462-l0002] [15.77pt] Filters
[p0462-l0003] [10.5pt] A neuron’s weights can be represented as a small image the size of the receptive field.
[p0462-l0004] [10.5pt] For example, Figure 14-5 shows two possible sets of weights, called filters (or convolu‐
[p0462-l0005] [10.5pt] tion kernels). The first one is represented as a black square with a vertical white line in
[p0462-l0006] [10.5pt] the middle (it is a 7 × 7 matrix full of 0s except for the central column, which is full of
[p0462-l0007] [10.5pt] 1s); neurons using these weights will ignore everything in their receptive field except
[p0462-l0008] [10.5pt] for the central vertical line (since all inputs will get multiplied by 0, except for the
[p0462-l0009] [10.5pt] ones located in the central vertical line). The second filter is a black square with a
[p0462-l0010] [10.5pt] horizontal white line in the middle. Once again, neurons using these weights will
[p0462-l0011] [10.5pt] ignore everything in their receptive field except for the central horizontal line.
[p0462-l0012] [10.5pt] Now if all neurons in a layer use the same vertical line filter (and the same bias term),
[p0462-l0013] [10.5pt] and you feed the network the input image shown in Figure 14-5 (bottom image), the
[p0462-l0014] [10.5pt] layer will output the top-left image. Notice that the vertical white lines get enhanced
[p0462-l0015] [10.5pt] while the rest gets blurred. Similarly, the upper-right image is what you get if all neu‐
[p0462-l0016] [10.5pt] rons use the same horizontal line filter; notice that the horizontal white lines get
[p0462-l0017] [10.5pt] enhanced while the rest is blurred out. Thus, a layer full of neurons using the same
[p0462-l0018] [10.5pt] filter outputs a feature map, which highlights the areas in an image that activate the
[p0462-l0019] [10.5pt] filter the most. Of course you do not have to define the filters manually: instead, dur‐
[p0462-l0020] [10.5pt] ing training the convolutional layer will automatically learn the most useful filters for
[p0462-l0021] [10.5pt] its task, and the layers above will learn to combine them into more complex patterns.
[p0462-l0022] [9.0pt] 436
[p0462-l0023] [9.0pt] |
[p0462-l0024] [9.0pt] Chapter 14: Deep Computer Vision Using Convolutional Neural Networks

=== PDF page 463 / printed label 437 ===
[p0463-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 14-5. Applying two different filters to get two feature maps
[p0463-l0002] [15.77pt] Stacking Multiple Feature Maps
[p0463-l0003] [10.5pt] Up to now, for simplicity, I have represented the output of each convolutional layer as
[p0463-l0004] [10.5pt] a thin 2D layer, but in reality a convolutional layer has multiple filters (you decide
[p0463-l0005] [10.5pt] how many), and it outputs one feature map per filter, so it is more accurately repre‐
[p0463-l0006] [10.5pt] sented in 3D (see Figure 14-6). To do so, it has one neuron per pixel in each feature
[p0463-l0007] [10.5pt] map, and all neurons within a given feature map share the same parameters (i.e., the
[p0463-l0008] [10.5pt] same weights and bias term). However, neurons in different feature maps use differ‐
[p0463-l0009] [10.5pt] ent parameters. A neuron’s receptive field is the same as described earlier, but it
[p0463-l0010] [10.5pt] extends across all the previous layers’ feature maps. In short, a convolutional layer
[p0463-l0011] [10.5pt] simultaneously applies multiple trainable filters to its inputs, making it capable of
[p0463-l0012] [10.5pt] detecting multiple features anywhere in its inputs.
[p0463-l0013] [9.6pt] The fact that all neurons in a feature map share the same parame‐
[p0463-l0014] [9.6pt] ters dramatically reduces the number of parameters in the model.
[p0463-l0015] [9.6pt] Moreover, once the CNN has learned to recognize a pattern in one
[p0463-l0016] [9.6pt] location, it can recognize it in any other location. In contrast, once
[p0463-l0017] [9.6pt] a regular DNN has learned to recognize a pattern in one location, it
[p0463-l0018] [9.6pt] can recognize it only in that particular location.
[p0463-l0019] [10.5pt] Moreover, input images are also composed of multiple sublayers: one per color chan‐
[p0463-l0020] [10.5pt] nel. There are typically three: red, green, and blue (RGB). Grayscale images have just
[p0463-l0021] [9.0pt] Convolutional Layer
[p0463-l0022] [9.0pt] |
[p0463-l0023] [9.0pt] 437

=== PDF page 464 / printed label 438 ===
[p0464-l0001] [10.5pt] one channel, but some images may have much more—for example, satellite images
[p0464-l0002] [10.5pt] that capture extra light frequencies (such as infrared).
[p0464-l0003] [10.5pt] Figure 14-6. Convolution layers with multiple feature maps, and images with three color
[p0464-l0004] [10.5pt] channels
[p0464-l0005] [10.5pt] Specifically, a neuron located in row i, column j of the feature map k in a given convo‐
[p0464-l0006] [10.5pt] lutional layer l is connected to the outputs of the neurons in the previous layer l – 1,
[p0464-l0007] [10.5pt] located in rows i × sh to i × sh + fh – 1 and columns j × sw to j × sw + fw – 1, across all
[p0464-l0008] [10.5pt] feature maps (in layer l – 1). Note that all neurons located in the same row i and col‐
[p0464-l0009] [10.5pt] umn j but in different feature maps are connected to the outputs of the exact same
[p0464-l0010] [10.5pt] neurons in the previous layer.
[p0464-l0011] [10.5pt] Equation 14-1 summarizes the preceding explanations in one big mathematical equa‐
[p0464-l0012] [10.5pt] tion: it shows how to compute the output of a given neuron in a convolutional layer.
[p0464-l0013] [9.0pt] 438
[p0464-l0014] [9.0pt] |
[p0464-l0015] [9.0pt] Chapter 14: Deep Computer Vision Using Convolutional Neural Networks

=== PDF page 465 / printed label 439 ===
[p0465-l0001] [10.5pt] It is a bit ugly due to all the different indices, but all it does is calculate the weighted
[p0465-l0002] [10.5pt] sum of all the inputs, plus the bias term.
[p0465-l0003] [10.5pt] Equation 14-1. Computing the output of a neuron in a convolutional layer
[p0465-l0004] [8.0pt] f h −1
[p0465-l0005] [8.0pt] f w −1
[p0465-l0006] [8.0pt] f n′ −1
[p0465-l0007] [10.0pt] i′ = i × sh + u
[p0465-l0008] [14.14pt] zi, j, k = bk + ∑
[p0465-l0009] [10.0pt] xi′, j′, k′ . wu, v, k′, k
[p0465-l0010] [10.0pt] with
[p0465-l0011] [8.0pt] u = 0
[p0465-l0012] [14.14pt] ∑
[p0465-l0013] [8.0pt] v = 0
[p0465-l0014] [14.14pt] ∑
[p0465-l0015] [8.0pt] k′ = 0
[p0465-l0016] [10.0pt] j′ = j × sw + v
[p0465-l0017] [10.5pt] • zi, j, k is the output of the neuron located in row i, column j in feature map k of the
[p0465-l0018] [10.5pt] convolutional layer (layer l).
[p0465-l0019] [10.5pt] • As explained earlier, sh and sw are the vertical and horizontal strides, fh and fw are
[p0465-l0020] [10.5pt] the height and width of the receptive field, and fn′ is the number of feature maps
[p0465-l0021] [10.5pt] in the previous layer (layer l – 1).
[p0465-l0022] [10.5pt] • xi′, j′, k′ is the output of the neuron located in layer l – 1, row i′, column j′, feature
[p0465-l0023] [10.5pt] map k′ (or channel k′ if the previous layer is the input layer).
[p0465-l0024] [10.5pt] • bk is the bias term for feature map k (in layer l). You can think of it as a knob that
[p0465-l0025] [10.5pt] tweaks the overall brightness of the feature map k.
[p0465-l0026] [10.5pt] • wu, v, k′ ,k is the connection weight between any neuron in feature map k of the layer
[p0465-l0027] [10.5pt] l and its input located at row u, column v (relative to the neuron’s receptive field),
[p0465-l0028] [10.5pt] and feature map k′.
[p0465-l0029] [15.77pt] TensorFlow Implementation
[p0465-l0030] [10.5pt] In TensorFlow, each input image is typically represented as a 3D tensor of shape
[p0465-l0031] [10.5pt] [height, width, channels]. A mini-batch is represented as a 4D tensor of shape
[p0465-l0032] [10.5pt] [mini-batch size, height, width, channels]. The weights of a convolutional
[p0465-l0033] [10.5pt] layer are represented as a 4D tensor of shape [fh, fw, fn′, fn]. The bias terms of a convo‐
[p0465-l0034] [10.5pt] lutional layer are simply represented as a 1D tensor of shape [fn].
[p0465-l0035] [10.5pt] Let’s look at a simple example. The following code loads two sample images, using
[p0465-l0036] [10.5pt] Scikit-Learn’s load_sample_images() (which loads two color images, one of a Chi‐
[p0465-l0037] [10.5pt] nese temple, and the other of a flower). The pixel intensities (for each color channel)
[p0465-l0038] [10.5pt] is represented as a byte from 0 to 255, so we scale these features simply by dividing by
[p0465-l0039] [10.5pt] 255, to get floats ranging from 0 to 1. Then we create two 7 × 7 filters (one with a
[p0465-l0040] [10.5pt] vertical white line in the middle, and the other with a horizontal white line in the
[p0465-l0041] [10.5pt] middle), and we apply them to both images using the tf.nn.conv2d() function,
[p0465-l0042] [10.5pt] which is part of TensorFlow’s low-level Deep Learning API. In this example, we use
[p0465-l0043] [10.5pt] zero padding (padding="SAME") and a stride of 2. Finally, we plot one of the resulting
[p0465-l0044] [10.5pt] feature maps (similar to the top-right image in Figure 14-5).
[p0465-l0045] [9.0pt] Convolutional Layer
[p0465-l0046] [9.0pt] |
[p0465-l0047] [9.0pt] 439

=== PDF page 466 / printed label 440 ===
[p0466-l0001] [8.5pt] from sklearn.datasets import load_sample_image
[p0466-l0002] [8.5pt] # Load sample images
[p0466-l0003] [8.5pt] china = load_sample_image("china.jpg") / 255
[p0466-l0004] [8.5pt] flower = load_sample_image("flower.jpg") / 255
[p0466-l0005] [8.5pt] images = np.array([china, flower])
[p0466-l0006] [8.5pt] batch_size, height, width, channels = images.shape
[p0466-l0007] [8.5pt] # Create 2 filters
[p0466-l0008] [8.5pt] filters = np.zeros(shape=(7, 7, channels, 2), dtype=np.float32)
[p0466-l0009] [8.5pt] filters[:, 3, :, 0] = 1  # vertical line
[p0466-l0010] [8.5pt] filters[3, :, :, 1] = 1  # horizontal line
[p0466-l0011] [8.5pt] outputs = tf.nn.conv2d(images, filters, strides=1, padding="SAME")
[p0466-l0012] [8.5pt] plt.imshow(outputs[0, :, :, 1], cmap="gray") # plot 1st image's 2nd feature map
[p0466-l0013] [8.5pt] plt.show()
[p0466-l0014] [10.5pt] Most of this code is self-explanatory, but the tf.nn.conv2d() line deserves a bit of
[p0466-l0015] [10.5pt] explanation:
[p0466-l0016] [10.5pt] • images is the input mini-batch (a 4D tensor, as explained earlier).
[p0466-l0017] [10.5pt] • filters is the set of filters to apply (also a 4D tensor, as explained earlier).
[p0466-l0018] [10.5pt] • strides is equal to 1, but it could also be a 1D array with 4 elements, where the
[p0466-l0019] [10.5pt] two central elements are the vertical and horizontal strides (sh and sw). The first
[p0466-l0020] [10.5pt] and last elements must currently be equal to 1. They may one day be used to
[p0466-l0021] [10.5pt] specify a batch stride (to skip some instances) and a channel stride (to skip some
[p0466-l0022] [10.5pt] of the previous layer’s feature maps or channels).
[p0466-l0023] [10.5pt] • padding must be either "VALID" or "SAME":
[p0466-l0024] [10.5pt] — If set to "VALID", the convolutional layer does not use zero padding, and may
[p0466-l0025] [10.5pt] ignore some rows and columns at the bottom and right of the input image,
[p0466-l0026] [10.5pt] depending on the stride, as shown in Figure 14-7 (for simplicity, only the hor‐
[p0466-l0027] [10.5pt] izontal dimension is shown here, but of course the same logic applies to the
[p0466-l0028] [10.5pt] vertical dimension).
[p0466-l0029] [10.5pt] — If set to "SAME", the convolutional layer uses zero padding if necessary. In this
[p0466-l0030] [10.5pt] case, the number of output neurons is equal to the number of input neurons
[p0466-l0031] [10.5pt] divided by the stride, rounded up (in this example, 13 / 5 = 2.6, rounded up to
[p0466-l0032] [10.5pt] 3). Then zeros are added as evenly as possible around the inputs.
[p0466-l0033] [9.0pt] 440
[p0466-l0034] [9.0pt] |
[p0466-l0035] [9.0pt] Chapter 14: Deep Computer Vision Using Convolutional Neural Networks

=== PDF page 467 / printed label 441 ===
[p0467-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 14-7. Padding options—input width: 13, filter width: 6, stride: 5
[p0467-l0002] [10.5pt] In this example, we manually defined the filters, but in a real CNN you would nor‐
[p0467-l0003] [10.5pt] mally define filters as trainable variables, so the neural net can learn which filters
[p0467-l0004] [10.5pt] work best, as explained earlier. Instead of manually creating the variables, however,
[p0467-l0005] [10.5pt] you can simply use the keras.layers.Conv2D layer:
[p0467-l0006] [8.5pt] conv = keras.layers.Conv2D(filters=32, kernel_size=3, strides=1,
[p0467-l0007] [8.5pt]                            padding="SAME", activation="relu")
[p0467-l0008] [10.5pt] This code creates a Conv2D layer with 32 filters, each 3 × 3, using a stride of 1 (both
[p0467-l0009] [10.5pt] horizontally and vertically), SAME padding, and applying the ReLU activation func‐
[p0467-l0010] [10.5pt] tion to its outputs. As you can see, convolutional layers have quite a few hyperpara‐
[p0467-l0011] [10.5pt] meters: you must choose the number of filters, their height and width, the strides, and
[p0467-l0012] [10.5pt] the padding type. As always, you can use cross-validation to find the right hyperpara‐
[p0467-l0013] [10.5pt] meter values, but this is very time-consuming. We will discuss common CNN archi‐
[p0467-l0014] [10.5pt] tectures later, to give you some idea of what hyperparameter values work best in
[p0467-l0015] [10.5pt] practice.
[p0467-l0016] [15.77pt] Memory Requirements
[p0467-l0017] [10.5pt] Another problem with CNNs is that the convolutional layers require a huge amount
[p0467-l0018] [10.5pt] of RAM. This is especially true during training, because the reverse pass of backpro‐
[p0467-l0019] [10.5pt] pagation requires all the intermediate values computed during the forward pass.
[p0467-l0020] [10.5pt] For example, consider a convolutional layer with 5 × 5 filters, outputting 200 feature
[p0467-l0021] [10.5pt] maps of size 150 × 100, with stride 1 and SAME padding. If the input is a 150 × 100
[p0467-l0022] [9.0pt] Convolutional Layer
[p0467-l0023] [9.0pt] |
[p0467-l0024] [9.0pt] 441

=== PDF page 468 / printed label 442 ===
[p0468-l0001] [10.5pt] RGB image (three channels), then the number of parameters is (5 × 5 × 3 + 1) × 200
[p0468-l0002] [10.5pt] = 15,200 (the +1 corresponds to the bias terms), which is fairly small compared to a
[p0468-l0003] [10.5pt] fully connected layer.7 However, each of the 200 feature maps contains 150 × 100 neu‐
[p0468-l0004] [10.5pt] rons, and each of these neurons needs to compute a weighted sum of its 5 × 5 × 3 =
[p0468-l0005] [10.5pt] 75 inputs: that’s a total of 225 million float multiplications. Not as bad as a fully con‐
[p0468-l0006] [10.5pt] nected layer, but still quite computationally intensive. Moreover, if the feature maps
[p0468-l0007] [10.5pt] are represented using 32-bit floats, then the convolutional layer’s output will occupy
[p0468-l0008] [10.5pt] 200 × 150 × 100 × 32 = 96 million bits (12 MB) of RAM.8 And that’s just for one
[p0468-l0009] [10.5pt] instance! If a training batch contains 100 instances, then this layer will use up 1.2 GB
[p0468-l0010] [10.5pt] of RAM!
[p0468-l0011] [10.5pt] During inference (i.e., when making a prediction for a new instance) the RAM occu‐
[p0468-l0012] [10.5pt] pied by one layer can be released as soon as the next layer has been computed, so you
[p0468-l0013] [10.5pt] only need as much RAM as required by two consecutive layers. But during training
[p0468-l0014] [10.5pt] everything computed during the forward pass needs to be preserved for the reverse
[p0468-l0015] [10.5pt] pass, so the amount of RAM needed is (at least) the total amount of RAM required by
[p0468-l0016] [10.5pt] all layers.
[p0468-l0017] [9.6pt] If training crashes because of an out-of-memory error, you can try
[p0468-l0018] [9.6pt] reducing the mini-batch size. Alternatively, you can try reducing
[p0468-l0019] [9.6pt] dimensionality using a stride, or removing a few layers. Or you can
[p0468-l0020] [9.6pt] try using 16-bit floats instead of 32-bit floats. Or you could distrib‐
[p0468-l0021] [9.6pt] ute the CNN across multiple devices.
[p0468-l0022] [10.5pt] Now let’s look at the second common building block of CNNs: the pooling layer.
[p0468-l0023] [18.92pt] Pooling Layer
[p0468-l0024] [10.5pt] Once you understand how convolutional layers work, the pooling layers are quite
[p0468-l0025] [10.5pt] easy to grasp. Their goal is to subsample (i.e., shrink) the input image in order to
[p0468-l0026] [10.5pt] reduce the computational load, the memory usage, and the number of parameters
[p0468-l0027] [10.5pt] (thereby limiting the risk of overfitting).
[p0468-l0028] [10.5pt] Just like in convolutional layers, each neuron in a pooling layer is connected to the
[p0468-l0029] [10.5pt] outputs of a limited number of neurons in the previous layer, located within a small
[p0468-l0030] [10.5pt] rectangular receptive field. You must define its size, the stride, and the padding type,
[p0468-l0031] [10.5pt] just like before. However, a pooling neuron has no weights; all it does is aggregate the
[p0468-l0032] [10.5pt] inputs using an aggregation function such as the max or mean. Figure 14-8 shows a
[p0468-l0033] [10.5pt] max pooling layer, which is the most common type of pooling layer. In this example,
[p0468-l0034] [8.0pt] 7 A fully connected layer with 150 × 100 neurons, each connected to all 150 × 100 × 3 inputs, would have 1502
[p0468-l0035] [8.0pt] × 1002 × 3 = 675 million parameters!
[p0468-l0036] [8.0pt] 8 In the international system of units (SI), 1 MB = 1,000 kB = 1,000 × 1,000 bytes = 1,000 × 1,000 × 8 bits.
[p0468-l0037] [9.0pt] 442
[p0468-l0038] [9.0pt] |
[p0468-l0039] [9.0pt] Chapter 14: Deep Computer Vision Using Convolutional Neural Networks

=== PDF page 469 / printed label 443 ===
[p0469-l0001] [10.5pt] we use a 2 × 2 _pooling kernel_9, with a stride of 2, and no padding. Only the max
[p0469-l0002] [10.5pt] input value in each receptive field makes it to the next layer, while the other inputs
[p0469-l0003] [10.5pt] are dropped. For example, in the lower left receptive field in Figure 14-8, the input
[p0469-l0004] [10.5pt] values are 1, 5, 3, 2, so only the max value, 5, is propagated to the next layer. Because
[p0469-l0005] [10.5pt] of the stride of 2, the output image has half the height and half the width of the input
[p0469-l0006] [10.5pt] image (rounded down since we use no padding).
[p0469-l0007] [10.5pt] Figure 14-8. Max pooling layer (2 × 2 pooling kernel, stride 2, no padding)
[p0469-l0008] [9.6pt] A pooling layer typically works on every input channel independ‐
[p0469-l0009] [9.6pt] ently, so the output depth is the same as the input depth.
[p0469-l0010] [10.5pt] Other than reducing computations, memory usage and the number of parameters, a
[p0469-l0011] [10.5pt] max pooling layer also introduces some level of invariance to small translations, as
[p0469-l0012] [10.5pt] shown in Figure 14-9. Here we assume that the bright pixels have a lower value than
[p0469-l0013] [10.5pt] dark pixels, and we consider 3 images (A, B, C) going through a max pooling layer
[p0469-l0014] [10.5pt] with a 2 × 2 kernel and stride 2. Images B and C are the same as image A, but shifted
[p0469-l0015] [10.5pt] by one and two pixels to the right. As you can see, the outputs of the max pooling
[p0469-l0016] [10.5pt] layer for images A and B are identical. This is what translation invariance means.
[p0469-l0017] [10.5pt] However, for image C, the output is different: it is shifted by one pixel to the right
[p0469-l0018] [10.5pt] (but there is still 75% invariance). By inserting a max pooling layer every few layers in
[p0469-l0019] [10.5pt] a CNN, it is possible to get some level of translation invariance at a larger scale.
[p0469-l0020] [10.5pt] Moreover, max pooling also offers a small amount of rotational invariance and a
[p0469-l0021] [10.5pt] slight scale invariance. Such invariance (even if it is limited) can be useful in cases
[p0469-l0022] [10.5pt] where the prediction should not depend on these details, such as in classification
[p0469-l0023] [10.5pt] tasks.
[p0469-l0024] [8.0pt] 9 Other kernels we discussed so far had weights, but pooling kernels do not: they are just stateless sliding win‐
[p0469-l0025] [8.0pt] dows.
[p0469-l0026] [9.0pt] Pooling Layer
[p0469-l0027] [9.0pt] |
[p0469-l0028] [9.0pt] 443

=== PDF page 470 / printed label 444 ===
[p0470-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 14-9. Invariance to small translations
[p0470-l0002] [10.5pt] But max pooling has some downsides: firstly, it is obviously very destructive: even
[p0470-l0003] [10.5pt] with a tiny 2 × 2 kernel and a stride of 2, the output will be two times smaller in both
[p0470-l0004] [10.5pt] directions (so its area will be four times smaller), simply dropping 75% of the input
[p0470-l0005] [10.5pt] values. And in some applications, invariance is not desirable, for example for seman‐
[p0470-l0006] [10.5pt] tic segmentation: this is the task of classifying each pixel in an image depending on the
[p0470-l0007] [10.5pt] object that pixel belongs to: obviously, if the input image is translated by 1 pixel to the
[p0470-l0008] [10.5pt] right, the output should also be translated by 1 pixel to the right. The goal in this case
[p0470-l0009] [10.5pt] is equivariance, not invariance: a small change to the inputs should lead to a corre‐
[p0470-l0010] [10.5pt] sponding small change in the output.
[p0470-l0011] [15.77pt] TensorFlow Implementation
[p0470-l0012] [10.5pt] Implementing a max pooling layer in TensorFlow is quite easy. The following code
[p0470-l0013] [10.5pt] creates a max pooling layer using a 2 × 2 kernel. The strides default to the kernel size,
[p0470-l0014] [10.5pt] so this layer will use a stride of 2 (both horizontally and vertically). By default, it uses
[p0470-l0015] [10.5pt] VALID padding (i.e., no padding at all):
[p0470-l0016] [8.5pt] max_pool = keras.layers.MaxPool2D(pool_size=2)
[p0470-l0017] [10.5pt] To create an average pooling layer, just use AvgPool2D instead of MaxPool2D. As you
[p0470-l0018] [10.5pt] might expect, it works exactly like a max pooling layer, except it computes the mean
[p0470-l0019] [10.5pt] rather than the max. Average pooling layers used to be very popular, but people
[p0470-l0020] [9.0pt] 444
[p0470-l0021] [9.0pt] |
[p0470-l0022] [9.0pt] Chapter 14: Deep Computer Vision Using Convolutional Neural Networks

=== PDF page 471 / printed label 445 ===
[p0471-l0001] [10.5pt] mostly use max pooling layers now, as they generally perform better. This may seem
[p0471-l0002] [10.5pt] surprising, since computing the mean generally loses less information than comput‐
[p0471-l0003] [10.5pt] ing the max. But on the other hand, max pooling preserves only the strongest feature,
[p0471-l0004] [10.5pt] getting rid of all the meaningless ones, so the next layers get a cleaner signal to work
[p0471-l0005] [10.5pt] with. Moreover, max pooling offers stronger translation invariance than average
[p0471-l0006] [10.5pt] pooling.
[p0471-l0007] [10.5pt] Note that max pooling and average pooling can be performed along the depth dimen‐
[p0471-l0008] [10.5pt] sion rather than the spatial dimensions, although this is not as common. This can
[p0471-l0009] [10.5pt] allow the CNN to learn to be invariant to various features. For example, it could learn
[p0471-l0010] [10.5pt] multiple filters, each detecting a different rotation of the same pattern, such as hand-
[p0471-l0011] [10.5pt] written digits (see Figure 14-10), and the depth-wise max pooling layer would ensure
[p0471-l0012] [10.5pt] that the output is the same regardless of the rotation. The CNN could similarly learn
[p0471-l0013] [10.5pt] to be invariant to anything else: thickness, brightness, skew, color, and so on.
[p0471-l0014] [10.5pt] Figure 14-10. Depth-wise max pooling can help the CNN learn any invariance
[p0471-l0015] [9.0pt] Pooling Layer
[p0471-l0016] [9.0pt] |
[p0471-l0017] [9.0pt] 445

=== PDF page 472 / printed label 446 ===
[p0472-l0001] [10.5pt] Keras does not include a depth-wise max pooling layer, but TensorFlow’s low-level
[p0472-l0002] [10.5pt] Deep Learning API does: just use the tf.nn.max_pool() function, and specify the
[p0472-l0003] [10.5pt] kernel size and strides as 4-tuples. The first three values of each should be 1: this indi‐
[p0472-l0004] [10.5pt] cates that the kernel size and stride along the batch, height and width dimensions
[p0472-l0005] [10.5pt] shoud be 1. The last value should be whatever kernel size and stride you want along
[p0472-l0006] [10.5pt] the depth dimension, for example 3 (this must be a divisor of the input depth; for
[p0472-l0007] [10.5pt] example, it will not work if the previous layer outputs 20 feature maps, since 20 is not
[p0472-l0008] [10.5pt] a multiple of 3):
[p0472-l0009] [8.5pt] output = tf.nn.max_pool(images,
[p0472-l0010] [8.5pt]                         ksize=(1, 1, 1, 3),
[p0472-l0011] [8.5pt]                         strides=(1, 1, 1, 3),
[p0472-l0012] [8.5pt]                         padding="VALID")
[p0472-l0013] [10.5pt] If you want to include this as a layer in your Keras models, you can simply wrap it in
[p0472-l0014] [10.5pt] a Lambda layer (or create a custom Keras layer):
[p0472-l0015] [8.5pt] depth_pool = keras.layers.Lambda(
[p0472-l0016] [8.5pt]     lambda X: tf.nn.max_pool(X, ksize=(1, 1, 1, 3), strides=(1, 1, 1, 3),
[p0472-l0017] [8.5pt]                              padding="VALID"))
[p0472-l0018] [10.5pt] One last type of pooling layer that you will often see in modern architectures is the
[p0472-l0019] [10.5pt] global average pooling layer. It works very differently: all it does is compute the mean
[p0472-l0020] [10.5pt] of each entire feature map (it’s like an average pooling layer using a pooling kernel
[p0472-l0021] [10.5pt] with the same spatial dimensions as the inputs). This means that it just outputs a sin‐
[p0472-l0022] [10.5pt] gle number per feature map and per instance. Although this is of course extremely
[p0472-l0023] [10.5pt] destructive (most of the information in the feature map is lost), it can be useful as the
[p0472-l0024] [10.5pt] output layer, as we will see later in this chapter. To create such a layer, simply use the
[p0472-l0025] [10.5pt] keras.layers.GlobalAvgPool2D class:
[p0472-l0026] [8.5pt] global_avg_pool = keras.layers.GlobalAvgPool2D()
[p0472-l0027] [10.5pt] It is actually equivalent to this simple Lamba layer, which computes the mean over the
[p0472-l0028] [10.5pt] spatial dimensions (height and width):
[p0472-l0029] [8.5pt] global_avg_pool = keras.layers.Lambda(lambda X: tf.reduce_mean(X, axis=[1, 2]))
[p0472-l0030] [10.5pt] Now you know all the building blocks to create a convolutional neural network. Let’s
[p0472-l0031] [10.5pt] see how to assemble them.
[p0472-l0032] [18.92pt] CNN Architectures
[p0472-l0033] [10.5pt] Typical CNN architectures stack a few convolutional layers (each one generally fol‐
[p0472-l0034] [10.5pt] lowed by a ReLU layer), then a pooling layer, then another few convolutional layers
[p0472-l0035] [10.5pt] (+ReLU), then another pooling layer, and so on. The image gets smaller and smaller
[p0472-l0036] [10.5pt] as it progresses through the network, but it also typically gets deeper and deeper (i.e.,
[p0472-l0037] [10.5pt] with more feature maps) thanks to the convolutional layers (see Figure 14-11). At the
[p0472-l0038] [10.5pt] top of the stack, a regular feedforward neural network is added, composed of a few
[p0472-l0039] [9.0pt] 446
[p0472-l0040] [9.0pt] |
[p0472-l0041] [9.0pt] Chapter 14: Deep Computer Vision Using Convolutional Neural Networks

=== PDF page 473 / printed label 447 ===
[p0473-l0001] [10.5pt] fully connected layers (+ReLUs), and the final layer outputs the prediction (e.g., a
[p0473-l0002] [10.5pt] softmax layer that outputs estimated class probabilities).
[p0473-l0003] [10.5pt] Figure 14-11. Typical CNN architecture
[p0473-l0004] [9.6pt] A common mistake is to use convolution kernels that are too large.
[p0473-l0005] [9.6pt] For example, instead of using a convolutional layer with a 5 × 5
[p0473-l0006] [9.6pt] kernel, it is generally preferable to stack two layers with 3 × 3 ker‐
[p0473-l0007] [9.6pt] nels: it will use less parameters and require less computations, and
[p0473-l0008] [9.6pt] it will usually perform better. One exception to this recommenda‐
[p0473-l0009] [9.6pt] tion is for the first convolutional layer: it can typically have a large
[p0473-l0010] [9.6pt] kernel (e.g., 5 × 5), usually with stride of 2 or more: this will reduce
[p0473-l0011] [9.6pt] the spatial dimension of the image without losing too much infor‐
[p0473-l0012] [9.6pt] mation, and since the input image only has 3 channels in general, it
[p0473-l0013] [9.6pt] will not be too costly.
[p0473-l0014] [10.5pt] Here is how you can implement a simple CNN to tackle the fashion MNIST dataset
[p0473-l0015] [10.5pt] (introduced in Chapter 10):
[p0473-l0016] [8.5pt] from functools import partial
[p0473-l0017] [8.5pt] DefaultConv2D = partial(keras.layers.Conv2D,
[p0473-l0018] [8.5pt]                         kernel_size=3, activation='relu', padding="SAME")
[p0473-l0019] [8.5pt] model = keras.models.Sequential([
[p0473-l0020] [8.5pt]     DefaultConv2D(filters=64, kernel_size=7, input_shape=[28, 28, 1]),
[p0473-l0021] [8.5pt]     keras.layers.MaxPooling2D(pool_size=2),
[p0473-l0022] [8.5pt]     DefaultConv2D(filters=128),
[p0473-l0023] [8.5pt]     DefaultConv2D(filters=128),
[p0473-l0024] [8.5pt]     keras.layers.MaxPooling2D(pool_size=2),
[p0473-l0025] [8.5pt]     DefaultConv2D(filters=256),
[p0473-l0026] [8.5pt]     DefaultConv2D(filters=256),
[p0473-l0027] [8.5pt]     keras.layers.MaxPooling2D(pool_size=2),
[p0473-l0028] [8.5pt]     keras.layers.Flatten(),
[p0473-l0029] [8.5pt]     keras.layers.Dense(units=128, activation='relu'),
[p0473-l0030] [8.5pt]     keras.layers.Dropout(0.5),
[p0473-l0031] [8.5pt]     keras.layers.Dense(units=64, activation='relu'),
[p0473-l0032] [8.5pt]     keras.layers.Dropout(0.5),
[p0473-l0033] [8.5pt]     keras.layers.Dense(units=10, activation='softmax'),
[p0473-l0034] [8.5pt] ])
[p0473-l0035] [9.0pt] CNN Architectures
[p0473-l0036] [9.0pt] |
[p0473-l0037] [9.0pt] 447

[p0474-l0001] [10.5pt] • In this code, we start by using the partial() function to define a thin wrapper
[p0474-l0002] [10.5pt] around the Conv2D class, called DefaultConv2D: it simply avoids having to repeat
[p0474-l0003] [10.5pt] the same hyperparameter values over and over again.
[p0474-l0004] [10.5pt] • The first layer uses a large kernel size, but no stride because the input images are
[p0474-l0005] [10.5pt] not very large. It also sets input_shape=[28, 28, 1], which means the images
[p0474-l0006] [10.5pt] are 28 × 28 pixels, with a single color channel (i.e., grayscale).
[p0474-l0007] [10.5pt] • Next, we have a max pooling layer, which divides each spatial dimension by a fac‐
[p0474-l0008] [10.5pt] tor of two (since pool_size=2).
[p0474-l0009] [10.5pt] • Then we repeat the same structure twice: two convolutional layers followed by a
[p0474-l0010] [10.5pt] max pooling layer. For larger images, we could repeat this structure several times
[p0474-l0011] [10.5pt] (the number of repetitions is a hyperparameter you can tune).
[p0474-l0012] [10.5pt] • Note that the number of filters grows as we climb up the CNN towards the out‐
[p0474-l0013] [10.5pt] put layer (it is initially 64, then 128, then 256): it makes sense for it to grow, since
[p0474-l0014] [10.5pt] the number of low level features is often fairly low (e.g., small circles, horizontal
[p0474-l0015] [10.5pt] lines, etc.), but there are many different ways to combine them into higher level
[p0474-l0016] [10.5pt] features. It is a common practice to double the number of filters after each pool‐
[p0474-l0017] [10.5pt] ing layer: since a pooling layer divides each spatial dimension by a factor of 2, we
[p0474-l0018] [10.5pt] can afford doubling the number of feature maps in the next layer, without fear of
[p0474-l0019] [10.5pt] exploding the number of parameters, memory usage, or computational load.
[p0474-l0020] [10.5pt] • Next is the fully connected network, composed of 2 hidden dense layers and a
[p0474-l0021] [10.5pt] dense output layer. Note that we must flatten its inputs, since a dense network
[p0474-l0022] [10.5pt] expects a 1D array of features for each instance. We also add two dropout layers,
[p0474-l0023] [10.5pt] with a dropout rate of 50% each, to reduce overfitting.
[p0474-l0024] [10.5pt] This CNN reaches over 92% accuracy on the test set. It’s not the state of the art, but it
[p0474-l0025] [10.5pt] is pretty good, and clearly much better than what we achieved with dense networks in
[p0474-l0026] [10.5pt] Chapter 10.
[p0474-l0027] [10.5pt] Over the years, variants of this fundamental architecture have been developed, lead‐
[p0474-l0028] [10.5pt] ing to amazing advances in the field. A good measure of this progress is the error rate
[p0474-l0029] [10.5pt] in competitions such as the ILSVRC ImageNet challenge. In this competition the
[p0474-l0030] [10.5pt] top-5 error rate for image classification fell from over 26% to less than 2.3% in just six
[p0474-l0031] [10.5pt] years. The top-five error rate is the number of test images for which the system’s top 5
[p0474-l0032] [10.5pt] predictions did not include the correct answer. The images are large (256 pixels high)
[p0474-l0033] [10.5pt] and there are 1,000 classes, some of which are really subtle (try distinguishing 120
[p0474-l0034] [10.5pt] dog breeds). Looking at the evolution of the winning entries is a good way to under‐
[p0474-l0035] [10.5pt] stand how CNNs work.
[p0474-l0036] [10.5pt] We will first look at the classical LeNet-5 architecture (1998), then three of the win‐
[p0474-l0037] [10.5pt] ners of the ILSVRC challenge: AlexNet (2012), GoogLeNet (2014), and ResNet
[p0474-l0038] [10.5pt] (2015).

[p0475-l0062] [10.5pt] There are a few extra details to be noted:
[p0475-l0063] [10.5pt] • MNIST images are 28 × 28 pixels, but they are zero-padded to 32 × 32 pixels and
[p0475-l0064] [10.5pt] normalized before being fed to the network. The rest of the network does not use
[p0475-l0065] [10.5pt] any padding, which is why the size keeps shrinking as the image progresses
[p0475-l0066] [10.5pt] through the network.
[p0475-l0067] [10.5pt] • The average pooling layers are slightly more complex than usual: each neuron
[p0475-l0068] [10.5pt] computes the mean of its inputs, then multiplies the result by a learnable coeffi‐
[p0475-l0069] [10.5pt] cient (one per map) and adds a learnable bias term (again, one per map), then
[p0475-l0070] [10.5pt] finally applies the activation function.
[p0475-l0071] [10.5pt] • Most neurons in C3 maps are connected to neurons in only three or four S2
[p0475-l0072] [10.5pt] maps (instead of all six S2 maps). See table 1 (page 8) in the original paper10 for
[p0475-l0073] [10.5pt] details.
[p0475-l0074] [10.5pt] • The output layer is a bit special: instead of computing the matrix multiplication
[p0475-l0075] [10.5pt] of the inputs and the weight vector, each neuron outputs the square of the Eucli‐
[p0475-l0076] [10.5pt] dian distance between its input vector and its weight vector. Each output meas‐
[p0475-l0077] [10.5pt] ures how much the image belongs to a particular digit class. The cross entropy
[p0475-l0078] [10.5pt] cost function is now preferred, as it penalizes bad predictions much more, pro‐
[p0475-l0079] [10.5pt] ducing larger gradients and converging faster.
[p0475-l0080] [8.0pt] 10 “Gradient-Based Learning Applied to Document Recognition”, Y. LeCun, L. Bottou, Y. Bengio and P. Haffner
[p0475-l0081] [8.0pt] (1998).

[p0476-l0003] [15.77pt] AlexNet
[p0476-l0004] [10.5pt] The AlexNet CNN architecture11 won the 2012 ImageNet ILSVRC challenge by a
[p0476-l0005] [10.5pt] large margin: it achieved 17% top-5 error rate while the second best achieved only
[p0476-l0006] [10.5pt] 26%! It was developed by Alex Krizhevsky (hence the name), Ilya Sutskever, and
[p0476-l0007] [10.5pt] Geoffrey Hinton. It is quite similar to LeNet-5, only much larger and deeper, and it
[p0476-l0008] [10.5pt] was the first to stack convolutional layers directly on top of each other, instead of
[p0476-l0009] [10.5pt] stacking a pooling layer on top of each convolutional layer. Table 14-2 presents this

[p0476-l0105] [10.5pt] To reduce overfitting, the authors used two regularization techniques: first they
[p0476-l0106] [10.5pt] applied dropout (introduced in Chapter 11) with a 50% dropout rate during training
[p0476-l0107] [10.5pt] to the outputs of layers F8 and F9. Second, they performed data augmentation by ran‐
[p0476-l0108] [10.5pt] domly shifting the training images by various offsets, flipping them horizontally, and
[p0476-l0109] [10.5pt] changing the lighting conditions.
[p0476-l0110] [15.0pt] Data Augmentation
[p0476-l0111] [10.0pt] Data augmentation artificially increases the size of the training set by generating
[p0476-l0112] [10.0pt] many realistic variants of each training instance. This reduces overfitting, making this
[p0476-l0113] [10.0pt] a regularization technique. The generated instances should be as realistic as possible:
[p0476-l0114] [8.0pt] 11 “ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks,” A. Krizhevsky et al. (2012).
[p0476-l0115] [9.0pt] 450
[p0476-l0116] [9.0pt] |
[p0476-l0117] [9.0pt] Chapter 14: Deep Computer Vision Using Convolutional Neural Networks

=== PDF page 477 / printed label 451 ===
[p0477-l0001] [10.0pt] ideally, given an image from the augmented training set, a human should not be able
[p0477-l0002] [10.0pt] to tell whether it was augmented or not. Moreover, simply adding white noise will not
[p0477-l0003] [10.0pt] help; the modifications should be learnable (white noise is not).
[p0477-l0004] [10.0pt] For example, you can slightly shift, rotate, and resize every picture in the training set
[p0477-l0005] [10.0pt] by various amounts and add the resulting pictures to the training set (see
[p0477-l0006] [10.0pt] Figure 14-12). This forces the model to be more tolerant to variations in the position,
[p0477-l0007] [10.0pt] orientation, and size of the objects in the pictures. If you want the model to be more
[p0477-l0008] [10.0pt] tolerant to different lighting conditions, you can similarly generate many images with
[p0477-l0009] [10.0pt] various contrasts. In general, you can also flip the pictures horizontally (except for
[p0477-l0010] [10.0pt] text, and other non-symmetrical objects). By combining these transformations you
[p0477-l0011] [10.0pt] can greatly increase the size of your training set.
[p0477-l0012] [10.0pt] Figure 14-12. Generating new training instances from existing ones
[p0477-l0013] [10.5pt] AlexNet also uses a competitive normalization step immediately after the ReLU step
[p0477-l0014] [10.5pt] of layers C1 and C3, called local response normalization. The most strongly activated
[p0477-l0015] [10.5pt] neurons inhibit other neurons located at the same position in neighboring feature
[p0477-l0016] [10.5pt] maps (such competitive activation has been observed in biological neurons). This
[p0477-l0017] [10.5pt] encourages different feature maps to specialize, pushing them apart and forcing them
[p0477-l0018] [9.0pt] CNN Architectures
[p0477-l0019] [9.0pt] |
[p0477-l0020] [9.0pt] 451

=== PDF page 478 / printed label 452 ===
[p0478-l0001] [10.5pt] to explore a wider range of features, ultimately improving generalization. Equation
[p0478-l0002] [10.5pt] 14-2 shows how to apply LRN.
[p0478-l0003] [10.5pt] Equation 14-2. Local response normalization
[p0478-l0004] [8.0pt] −β
[p0478-l0005] [8.0pt] jhigh
[p0478-l0006] [10.0pt] jhigh = min i + r
[p0478-l0007] [10.0pt] 2, f n −1
[p0478-l0008] [8.0pt] 2
[p0478-l0009] [10.0pt] with
[p0478-l0010] [10.0pt] aj
[p0478-l0011] [14.14pt] bi = ai k + α ∑
[p0478-l0012] [8.0pt] j = jlow
[p0478-l0013] [10.0pt] jlow = max 0, i −r
[p0478-l0014] [10.0pt] 2
[p0478-l0015] [10.5pt] • bi is the normalized output of the neuron located in feature map i, at some row u
[p0478-l0016] [10.5pt] and column v (note that in this equation we consider only neurons located at this
[p0478-l0017] [10.5pt] row and column, so u and v are not shown).
[p0478-l0018] [10.5pt] • ai is the activation of that neuron after the ReLU step, but before normalization.
[p0478-l0019] [10.5pt] • k, α, β, and r are hyperparameters. k is called the bias, and r is called the depth
[p0478-l0020] [10.5pt] radius.
[p0478-l0021] [10.5pt] • fn is the number of feature maps.
[p0478-l0022] [10.5pt] For example, if r = 2 and a neuron has a strong activation, it will inhibit the activation
[p0478-l0023] [10.5pt] of the neurons located in the feature maps immediately above and below its own.
[p0478-l0024] [10.5pt] In AlexNet, the hyperparameters are set as follows: r = 2, α = 0.00002, β = 0.75, and k
[p0478-l0025] [10.5pt] = 1. This step can be implemented using the tf.nn.local_response_normaliza
[p0478-l0026] [10.5pt] tion() function (which you can wrap in a Lambda layer if you want to use it in a
[p0478-l0027] [10.5pt] Keras model).
[p0478-l0028] [10.5pt] A variant of AlexNet called ZF Net was developed by Matthew Zeiler and Rob Fergus
[p0478-l0029] [10.5pt] and won the 2013 ILSVRC challenge. It is essentially AlexNet with a few tweaked
[p0478-l0030] [10.5pt] hyperparameters (number of feature maps, kernel size, stride, etc.).
[p0478-l0031] [15.77pt] GoogLeNet
[p0478-l0032] [10.5pt] The GoogLeNet architecture was developed by Christian Szegedy et al. from Google
[p0478-l0033] [10.5pt] Research,12 and it won the ILSVRC 2014 challenge by pushing the top-5 error rate
[p0478-l0034] [10.5pt] below 7%. This great performance came in large part from the fact that the network
[p0478-l0035] [10.5pt] was much deeper than previous CNNs (see Figure 14-14). This was made possible by
[p0478-l0036] [10.5pt] sub-networks called inception modules,13 which allow GoogLeNet to use parameters
[p0478-l0037] [8.0pt] 12 “Going Deeper with Convolutions,” C. Szegedy et al. (2015).
[p0478-l0038] [8.0pt] 13 In the 2010 movie Inception, the characters keep going deeper and deeper into multiple layers of dreams,
[p0478-l0039] [8.0pt] hence the name of these modules.
[p0478-l0040] [9.0pt] 452
[p0478-l0041] [9.0pt] |
[p0478-l0042] [9.0pt] Chapter 14: Deep Computer Vision Using Convolutional Neural Networks

=== PDF page 479 / printed label 453 ===
[p0479-l0001] [10.5pt] much more efficiently than previous architectures: GoogLeNet actually has 10 times
[p0479-l0002] [10.5pt] fewer parameters than AlexNet (roughly 6 million instead of 60 million).
[p0479-l0003] [10.5pt] Figure 14-13 shows the architecture of an inception module. The notation “3 × 3 +
[p0479-l0004] [10.5pt] 1(S)” means that the layer uses a 3 × 3 kernel, stride 1, and SAME padding. The input
[p0479-l0005] [10.5pt] signal is first copied and fed to four different layers. All convolutional layers use the
[p0479-l0006] [10.5pt] ReLU activation function. Note that the second set of convolutional layers uses differ‐
[p0479-l0007] [10.5pt] ent kernel sizes (1 × 1, 3 × 3, and 5 × 5), allowing them to capture patterns at different
[p0479-l0008] [10.5pt] scales. Also note that every single layer uses a stride of 1 and SAME padding (even
[p0479-l0009] [10.5pt] the max pooling layer), so their outputs all have the same height and width as their
[p0479-l0010] [10.5pt] inputs. This makes it possible to concatenate all the outputs along the depth dimen‐
[p0479-l0011] [10.5pt] sion in the final depth concat layer (i.e., stack the feature maps from all four top con‐
[p0479-l0012] [10.5pt] volutional layers). This concatenation layer can be implemented in TensorFlow using
[p0479-l0013] [10.5pt] the tf.concat() operation, with axis=3 (axis 3 is the depth).
[p0479-l0014] [10.5pt] Figure 14-13. Inception module
[p0479-l0015] [10.5pt] You may wonder why inception modules have convolutional layers with 1 × 1 ker‐
[p0479-l0016] [10.5pt] nels. Surely these layers cannot capture any features since they look at only one pixel
[p0479-l0017] [10.5pt] at a time? In fact, these layers serve three purposes:
[p0479-l0018] [10.5pt] • First, although they cannot capture spatial patterns, they can capture patterns
[p0479-l0019] [10.5pt] along the depth dimension.
[p0479-l0020] [10.5pt] • Second, they are configured to output fewer feature maps than their inputs, so
[p0479-l0021] [10.5pt] they serve as bottleneck layers, meaning they reduce dimensionality. This cuts the
[p0479-l0022] [10.5pt] computational cost and the number of parameters, speeding up training and
[p0479-l0023] [10.5pt] improving generalization.
[p0479-l0024] [10.5pt] • Lastly, each pair of convolutional layers ([1 × 1, 3 × 3] and [1 × 1, 5 × 5]) acts like
[p0479-l0025] [10.5pt] a single, powerful convolutional layer, capable of capturing more complex pat‐
[p0479-l0026] [10.5pt] terns. Indeed, instead of sweeping a simple linear classifier across the image (as a
[p0479-l0027] [9.0pt] CNN Architectures
[p0479-l0028] [9.0pt] |
[p0479-l0029] [9.0pt] 453

=== PDF page 480 / printed label 454 ===
[p0480-l0001] [10.5pt] single convolutional layer does), this pair of convolutional layers sweeps a two-
[p0480-l0002] [10.5pt] layer neural network across the image.
[p0480-l0003] [10.5pt] In short, you can think of the whole inception module as a convolutional layer on
[p0480-l0004] [10.5pt] steroids, able to output feature maps that capture complex patterns at various scales.
[p0480-l0005] [9.6pt] The number of convolutional kernels for each convolutional layer
[p0480-l0006] [9.6pt] is a hyperparameter. Unfortunately, this means that you have six
[p0480-l0007] [9.6pt] more hyperparameters to tweak for every inception layer you add.
[p0480-l0008] [10.5pt] Now let’s look at the architecture of the GoogLeNet CNN (see Figure 14-14). The
[p0480-l0009] [10.5pt] number of feature maps output by each convolutional layer and each pooling layer is
[p0480-l0010] [10.5pt] shown before the kernel size. The architecture is so deep that it has to be represented
[p0480-l0011] [10.5pt] in three columns, but GoogLeNet is actually one tall stack, including nine inception
[p0480-l0012] [10.5pt] modules (the boxes with the spinning tops). The six numbers in the inception mod‐
[p0480-l0013] [10.5pt] ules represent the number of feature maps output by each convolutional layer in the
[p0480-l0014] [10.5pt] module (in the same order as in Figure 14-13). Note that all the convolutional layers
[p0480-l0015] [10.5pt] use the ReLU activation function.
[p0480-l0016] [9.0pt] 454
[p0480-l0017] [9.0pt] |
[p0480-l0018] [9.0pt] Chapter 14: Deep Computer Vision Using Convolutional Neural Networks

=== PDF page 481 / printed label 455 ===
[p0481-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 14-14. GoogLeNet architecture
[p0481-l0002] [10.5pt] Let’s go through this network:
[p0481-l0003] [10.5pt] • The first two layers divide the image’s height and width by 4 (so its area is divided
[p0481-l0004] [10.5pt] by 16), to reduce the computational load. The first layer uses a large kernel size,
[p0481-l0005] [10.5pt] so that much of the information is still preserved.
[p0481-l0006] [10.5pt] • Then the local response normalization layer ensures that the previous layers learn
[p0481-l0007] [10.5pt] a wide variety of features (as discussed earlier).
[p0481-l0008] [10.5pt] • Two convolutional layers follow, where the first acts like a bottleneck layer. As
[p0481-l0009] [10.5pt] explained earlier, you can think of this pair as a single smarter convolutional
[p0481-l0010] [10.5pt] layer.
[p0481-l0011] [10.5pt] • Again, a local response normalization layer ensures that the previous layers cap‐
[p0481-l0012] [10.5pt] ture a wide variety of patterns.
[p0481-l0013] [9.0pt] CNN Architectures
[p0481-l0014] [9.0pt] |
[p0481-l0015] [9.0pt] 455

=== PDF page 482 / printed label 456 ===
[p0482-l0001] [10.5pt] • Next a max pooling layer reduces the image height and width by 2, again to speed
[p0482-l0002] [10.5pt] up computations.
[p0482-l0003] [10.5pt] • Then comes the tall stack of nine inception modules, interleaved with a couple
[p0482-l0004] [10.5pt] max pooling layers to reduce dimensionality and speed up the net.
[p0482-l0005] [10.5pt] • Next, the global average pooling layer simply outputs the mean of each feature
[p0482-l0006] [10.5pt] map: this drops any remaining spatial information, which is fine since there was
[p0482-l0007] [10.5pt] not much spatial information left at that point. Indeed, GoogLeNet input images
[p0482-l0008] [10.5pt] are typically expected to be 224 × 224 pixels, so after 5 max pooling layers, each
[p0482-l0009] [10.5pt] dividing the height and width by 2, the feature maps are down to 7 × 7. More‐
[p0482-l0010] [10.5pt] over, it is a classification task, not localization, so it does not matter where the
[p0482-l0011] [10.5pt] object is. Thanks to the dimensionality reduction brought by this layer, there is
[p0482-l0012] [10.5pt] no need to have several fully connected layers at the top of the CNN (like in
[p0482-l0013] [10.5pt] AlexNet), and this considerably reduces the number of parameters in the net‐
[p0482-l0014] [10.5pt] work and limits the risk of overfitting.
[p0482-l0015] [10.5pt] • The last layers are self-explanatory: dropout for regularization, then a fully con‐
[p0482-l0016] [10.5pt] nected layer with 1,000 units, since there are a 1,000 classes, and a softmax acti‐
[p0482-l0017] [10.5pt] vation function to output estimated class probabilities.
[p0482-l0018] [10.5pt] This diagram is slightly simplified: the original GoogLeNet architecture also included
[p0482-l0019] [10.5pt] two auxiliary classifiers plugged on top of the third and sixth inception modules.
[p0482-l0020] [10.5pt] They were both composed of one average pooling layer, one convolutional layer, two
[p0482-l0021] [10.5pt] fully connected layers, and a softmax activation layer. During training, their loss
[p0482-l0022] [10.5pt] (scaled down by 70%) was added to the overall loss. The goal was to fight the vanish‐
[p0482-l0023] [10.5pt] ing gradients problem and regularize the network. However, it was later shown that
[p0482-l0024] [10.5pt] their effect was relatively minor.
[p0482-l0025] [10.5pt] Several variants of the GoogLeNet architecture were later proposed by Google
[p0482-l0026] [10.5pt] researchers, including Inception-v3 and Inception-v4, using slightly different incep‐
[p0482-l0027] [10.5pt] tion modules, and reaching even better performance.
[p0482-l0028] [15.77pt] VGGNet
[p0482-l0029] [10.5pt] The runner up in the ILSVRC 2014 challenge was VGGNet14, developed by K. Simon‐
[p0482-l0030] [10.5pt] yan and A. Zisserman. It had a very simple and classical architecture, with 2 or 3 con‐
[p0482-l0031] [10.5pt] volutional layers, a pooling layer, then again 2 or 3 convolutional layers, a pooling
[p0482-l0032] [10.5pt] layer, and so on (with a total of just 16 convolutional layers), plus a final dense net‐
[p0482-l0033] [10.5pt] work with 2 hidden layers and the output layer. It used only 3 × 3 filters, but many
[p0482-l0034] [10.5pt] filters.
[p0482-l0035] [8.0pt] 14 “Very Deep Convolutional Networks for Large-Scale Image Recognition,” K. Simonyan and A. Zisserman
[p0482-l0036] [8.0pt] (2015).
[p0482-l0037] [9.0pt] 456
[p0482-l0038] [9.0pt] |
[p0482-l0039] [9.0pt] Chapter 14: Deep Computer Vision Using Convolutional Neural Networks

=== PDF page 483 / printed label 457 ===
[p0483-l0001] [15.77pt] ResNet
[p0483-l0002] [10.5pt] The ILSVRC 2015 challenge was won using a Residual Network (or ResNet), devel‐
[p0483-l0003] [10.5pt] oped by Kaiming He et al.,15 which delivered an astounding top-5 error rate under
[p0483-l0004] [10.5pt] 3.6%, using an extremely deep CNN composed of 152 layers. It confirmed the general
[p0483-l0005] [10.5pt] trend: models are getting deeper and deeper, with fewer and fewer parameters. The
[p0483-l0006] [10.5pt] key to being able to train such a deep network is to use skip connections (also called
[p0483-l0007] [10.5pt] shortcut connections): the signal feeding into a layer is also added to the output of a
[p0483-l0008] [10.5pt] layer located a bit higher up the stack. Let’s see why this is useful.
[p0483-l0009] [10.5pt] When training a neural network, the goal is to make it model a target function h(x).
[p0483-l0010] [10.5pt] If you add the input x to the output of the network (i.e., you add a skip connection),
[p0483-l0011] [10.5pt] then the network will be forced to model f(x) = h(x) – x rather than h(x). This is
[p0483-l0012] [10.5pt] called residual learning (see Figure 14-15).
[p0483-l0013] [10.5pt] Figure 14-15. Residual learning
[p0483-l0014] [10.5pt] When you initialize a regular neural network, its weights are close to zero, so the net‐
[p0483-l0015] [10.5pt] work just outputs values close to zero. If you add a skip connection, the resulting net‐
[p0483-l0016] [10.5pt] work just outputs a copy of its inputs; in other words, it initially models the identity
[p0483-l0017] [10.5pt] function. If the target function is fairly close to the identity function (which is often
[p0483-l0018] [10.5pt] the case), this will speed up training considerably.
[p0483-l0019] [10.5pt] Moreover, if you add many skip connections, the network can start making progress
[p0483-l0020] [10.5pt] even if several layers have not started learning yet (see Figure 14-16). Thanks to skip
[p0483-l0021] [10.5pt] connections, the signal can easily make its way across the whole network. The deep
[p0483-l0022] [10.5pt] residual network can be seen as a stack of residual units, where each residual unit is a
[p0483-l0023] [10.5pt] small neural network with a skip connection.
[p0483-l0024] [8.0pt] 15 “Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition,” K. He (2015).
[p0483-l0025] [9.0pt] CNN Architectures
[p0483-l0026] [9.0pt] |
[p0483-l0027] [9.0pt] 457

=== PDF page 484 / printed label 458 ===
[p0484-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 14-16. Regular deep neural network (left) and deep residual network (right)
[p0484-l0002] [10.5pt] Now let’s look at ResNet’s architecture (see Figure 14-17). It is actually surprisingly
[p0484-l0003] [10.5pt] simple. It starts and ends exactly like GoogLeNet (except without a dropout layer),
[p0484-l0004] [10.5pt] and in between is just a very deep stack of simple residual units. Each residual unit is
[p0484-l0005] [10.5pt] composed of two convolutional layers (and no pooling layer!), with Batch Normaliza‐
[p0484-l0006] [10.5pt] tion (BN) and ReLU activation, using 3 × 3 kernels and preserving spatial dimensions
[p0484-l0007] [10.5pt] (stride 1, SAME padding).
[p0484-l0008] [10.5pt] Figure 14-17. ResNet architecture
[p0484-l0009] [10.5pt] Note that the number of feature maps is doubled every few residual units, at the same
[p0484-l0010] [10.5pt] time as their height and width are halved (using a convolutional layer with stride 2).
[p0484-l0011] [10.5pt] When this happens the inputs cannot be added directly to the outputs of the residual
[p0484-l0012] [10.5pt] unit since they don’t have the same shape (for example, this problem affects the skip
[p0484-l0013] [9.0pt] 458
[p0484-l0014] [9.0pt] |
[p0484-l0015] [9.0pt] Chapter 14: Deep Computer Vision Using Convolutional Neural Networks

=== PDF page 485 / printed label 459 ===
[p0485-l0001] [10.5pt] connection represented by the dashed arrow in Figure 14-17). To solve this problem,
[p0485-l0002] [10.5pt] the inputs are passed through a 1 × 1 convolutional layer with stride 2 and the right
[p0485-l0003] [10.5pt] number of output feature maps (see Figure 14-18).
[p0485-l0004] [10.5pt] Figure 14-18. Skip connection when changing feature map size and depth
[p0485-l0005] [10.5pt] ResNet-34 is the ResNet with 34 layers (only counting the convolutional layers and
[p0485-l0006] [10.5pt] the fully connected layer) containing three residual units that output 64 feature maps,
[p0485-l0007] [10.5pt] 4 RUs with 128 maps, 6 RUs with 256 maps, and 3 RUs with 512 maps. We will imple‐
[p0485-l0008] [10.5pt] ment this architecture later in this chapter.
[p0485-l0009] [10.5pt] ResNets deeper than that, such as ResNet-152, use slightly different residual units.
[p0485-l0010] [10.5pt] Instead of two 3 × 3 convolutional layers with (say) 256 feature maps, they use three
[p0485-l0011] [10.5pt] convolutional layers: first a 1 × 1 convolutional layer with just 64 feature maps (4
[p0485-l0012] [10.5pt] times less), which acts as a bottleneck layer (as discussed already), then a 3 × 3 layer
[p0485-l0013] [10.5pt] with 64 feature maps, and finally another 1 × 1 convolutional layer with 256 feature
[p0485-l0014] [10.5pt] maps (4 times 64) that restores the original depth. ResNet-152 contains three such
[p0485-l0015] [10.5pt] RUs that output 256 maps, then 8 RUs with 512 maps, a whopping 36 RUs with 1,024
[p0485-l0016] [10.5pt] maps, and finally 3 RUs with 2,048 maps.
[p0485-l0017] [9.6pt] Google’s Inception-v416 architecture merged the ideas of GoogLe‐
[p0485-l0018] [9.6pt] Net and ResNet and achieved close to 3% top-5 error rate on
[p0485-l0019] [9.6pt] ImageNet classification.
[p0485-l0020] [15.77pt] Xception
[p0485-l0021] [10.5pt] Another variant of the GoogLeNet architecture is also worth noting: Xception17
[p0485-l0022] [10.5pt] (which stands for Extreme Inception) was proposed in 2016 by François Chollet (the
[p0485-l0023] [8.0pt] 16 “Inception-v4, Inception-ResNet and the Impact of Residual Connections on Learning,” C. Szegedy et al.
[p0485-l0024] [8.0pt] (2016).
[p0485-l0025] [8.0pt] 17 “Xception: Deep Learning with Depthwise Separable Convolutions,” François Chollet (2016)
[p0485-l0026] [9.0pt] CNN Architectures
[p0485-l0027] [9.0pt] |
[p0485-l0028] [9.0pt] 459

=== PDF page 486 / printed label 460 ===
[p0486-l0001] [10.5pt] author of Keras), and it significantly outperformed Inception-v3 on a huge vision task
[p0486-l0002] [10.5pt] (350 million images and 17,000 classes). Just like Inception-v4, it also merges the
[p0486-l0003] [10.5pt] ideas of GoogLeNet and ResNet, but it replaces the inception modules with a special
[p0486-l0004] [10.5pt] type of layer called a depthwise separable convolution (or separable convolution for
[p0486-l0005] [10.5pt] short18). These layers had been used before in some CNN architectures, but they were
[p0486-l0006] [10.5pt] not as central as in the Xception architecture. While a regular convolutional layer
[p0486-l0007] [10.5pt] uses filters that try to simultaneously capture spatial patterns (e.g., an oval) and cross-
[p0486-l0008] [10.5pt] channel patterns (e.g., mouth + nose + eyes = face), a separable convolutional layer
[p0486-l0009] [10.5pt] makes the strong assumption that spatial patterns and cross-channel patterns can be
[p0486-l0010] [10.5pt] modeled separately (see Figure 14-19). Thus, it is composed of two parts: the first part
[p0486-l0011] [10.5pt] applies a single spatial filter for each input feature map, then the second part looks
[p0486-l0012] [10.5pt] exclusively for cross-channel patterns—it is just a regular convolutional layer with 1 ×
[p0486-l0013] [10.5pt] 1 filters.
[p0486-l0014] [10.5pt] Figure 14-19. Depthwise Separable Convolutional Layer
[p0486-l0015] [10.5pt] Since separable convolutional layers only have one spatial filter per input channel,
[p0486-l0016] [10.5pt] you should avoid using them after layers that have too few channels, such as the input
[p0486-l0017] [10.5pt] layer (granted, that’s what Figure 14-19 represents, but it is just for illustration pur‐
[p0486-l0018] [10.5pt] poses). For this reason, the Xception architecture starts with 2 regular convolutional
[p0486-l0019] [10.5pt] layers, but then the rest of the architecture uses only separable convolutions (34 in
[p0486-l0020] [8.0pt] 18 This name can sometimes be ambiguous, since spatially separable convolutions are often called “separable
[p0486-l0021] [8.0pt] convolutions” as well.
[p0486-l0022] [9.0pt] 460
[p0486-l0023] [9.0pt] |
[p0486-l0024] [9.0pt] Chapter 14: Deep Computer Vision Using Convolutional Neural Networks

=== PDF page 487 / printed label 461 ===
[p0487-l0001] [10.5pt] all), plus a few max pooling layers and the usual final layers (a global average pooling
[p0487-l0002] [10.5pt] layer, and a dense output layer).
[p0487-l0003] [10.5pt] You might wonder why Xception is considered a variant of GoogLeNet, since it con‐
[p0487-l0004] [10.5pt] tains no inception module at all? Well, as we discussed earlier, an Inception module
[p0487-l0005] [10.5pt] contains convolutional layers with 1 × 1 filters: these look exclusively for cross-
[p0487-l0006] [10.5pt] channel patterns. However, the convolution layers that sit on top of them are regular
[p0487-l0007] [10.5pt] convolutional layers that look both for spatial and cross-channel patterns. So you can
[p0487-l0008] [10.5pt] think of an Inception module as an intermediate between a regular convolutional
[p0487-l0009] [10.5pt] layer (which considers spatial patterns and cross-channel patterns jointly) and a sepa‐
[p0487-l0010] [10.5pt] rable convolutional layer (which considers them separately). In practice, it seems that
[p0487-l0011] [10.5pt] separable convolutions generally perform better.
[p0487-l0012] [9.6pt] Separable convolutions use less parameters, less memory and less
[p0487-l0013] [9.6pt] computations than regular convolutional layers, and in general
[p0487-l0014] [9.6pt] they even perform better, so you should consider using them by
[p0487-l0015] [9.6pt] default (except after layers with few channels).
[p0487-l0016] [10.5pt] The ILSVRC 2016 challenge was won by the CUImage team from the Chinese Uni‐
[p0487-l0017] [10.5pt] versity of Hong Kong. They used an ensemble of many different techniques, includ‐
[p0487-l0018] [10.5pt] ing a sophisticated object-detection system called GBD-Net19, to achieve a top-5 error
[p0487-l0019] [10.5pt] rate below 3%. Although this result is unquestionably impressive, the complexity of
[p0487-l0020] [10.5pt] the solution contrasted with the simplicity of ResNets. Moreover, one year later
[p0487-l0021] [10.5pt] another fairly simple architecture performed even better, as we will see now.
[p0487-l0022] [15.77pt] SENet
[p0487-l0023] [10.5pt] The winning architecture in the ILSVRC 2017 challenge was the Squeeze-and-
[p0487-l0024] [10.5pt] Excitation Network (SENet)20. This architecture extends existing architectures such as
[p0487-l0025] [10.5pt] inception networks or ResNets, and boosts their performance. This allowed SENet to
[p0487-l0026] [10.5pt] win the competition with an astonishing 2.25% top-5 error rate! The extended ver‐
[p0487-l0027] [10.5pt] sions of inception networks and ResNet are called SE-Inception and SE-ResNet respec‐
[p0487-l0028] [10.5pt] tively. The boost comes from the fact that a SENet adds a small neural network, called
[p0487-l0029] [10.5pt] a SE Block, to every unit in the original architecture (i.e., every inception module or
[p0487-l0030] [10.5pt] every residual unit), as shown in Figure 14-20.
[p0487-l0031] [8.0pt] 19 “Crafting GBD-Net for Object Detection,” X. Zeng et al. (2016).
[p0487-l0032] [8.0pt] 20 “Squeeze-and-Excitation Networks,” Jie Hu et al. (2017)
[p0487-l0033] [9.0pt] CNN Architectures
[p0487-l0034] [9.0pt] |
[p0487-l0035] [9.0pt] 461

=== PDF page 488 / printed label 462 ===
[p0488-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 14-20. SE-Inception Module (left) and SE-ResNet Unit (right)
[p0488-l0002] [10.5pt] A SE Block analyzes the output of the unit it is attached to, focusing exclusively on
[p0488-l0003] [10.5pt] the depth dimension (it does not look for any spatial pattern), and it learns which fea‐
[p0488-l0004] [10.5pt] tures are usually most active together. It then uses this information to recalibrate the
[p0488-l0005] [10.5pt] feature maps, as shown in Figure 14-21. For example, a SE Block may learn that
[p0488-l0006] [10.5pt] mouths, noses and eyes usually appear together in pictures: if you see a mouth and a
[p0488-l0007] [10.5pt] nose, you should expect to see eyes as well. So if a SE Block sees a strong activation in
[p0488-l0008] [10.5pt] the mouth and nose feature maps, but only mild activation in the eye feature map, it
[p0488-l0009] [10.5pt] will boost the eye feature map (more accurately, it will reduce irrelevant feature
[p0488-l0010] [10.5pt] maps). If the eyes were somewhat confused with something else, this feature map
[p0488-l0011] [10.5pt] recalibration will help resolve the ambiguity.
[p0488-l0012] [9.0pt] 462
[p0488-l0013] [9.0pt] |
[p0488-l0014] [9.0pt] Chapter 14: Deep Computer Vision Using Convolutional Neural Networks

=== PDF page 489 / printed label 463 ===
[p0489-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 14-21. An SE Block Performs Feature Map Recalibration
[p0489-l0002] [10.5pt] A SE Block is composed of just 3 layers: a global average pooling layer, a hidden dense
[p0489-l0003] [10.5pt] layer using the ReLU activation function, and a dense output layer using the sigmoid
[p0489-l0004] [10.5pt] activation function (see Figure 14-22):
[p0489-l0005] [10.5pt] Figure 14-22. SE Block Architecture
[p0489-l0006] [9.0pt] CNN Architectures
[p0489-l0007] [9.0pt] |
[p0489-l0008] [9.0pt] 463

=== PDF page 490 / printed label 464 ===
[p0490-l0001] [10.5pt] As earlier, the global average pooling layer computes the mean activation for each fea‐
[p0490-l0002] [10.5pt] ture map: for example, if its input contains 256 feature maps, it will output 256 num‐
[p0490-l0003] [10.5pt] bers representing the overall level of response for each filter. The next layer is where
[p0490-l0004] [10.5pt] the “squeeze” happens: this layer has much less than 256 neurons, typically 16 times
[p0490-l0005] [10.5pt] less than the number of feature maps (e.g., 16 neurons), so the 256 numbers get com‐
[p0490-l0006] [10.5pt] pressed into a small vector (e.g., 16 dimensional). This is a low-dimensional vector
[p0490-l0007] [10.5pt] representation (i.e., an embedding) of the distribution of feature responses. This bot‐
[p0490-l0008] [10.5pt] tleneck step forces the SE Block to learn a general representation of the feature com‐
[p0490-l0009] [10.5pt] binations (we will see this principle in action again when we discuss autoencoders
[p0490-l0010] [10.5pt] in ???). Finally, the output layer takes the embedding and outputs a recalibration vec‐
[p0490-l0011] [10.5pt] tor containing one number per feature map (e.g., 256), each between 0 and 1. The
[p0490-l0012] [10.5pt] feature maps are then multiplied by this recalibration vector, so irrelevant features
[p0490-l0013] [10.5pt] (with a low recalibration score) get scaled down while relevant features (with a recali‐
[p0490-l0014] [10.5pt] bration score close to 1) are left alone.
[p0490-l0015] [18.92pt] Implementing a ResNet-34 CNN Using Keras
[p0490-l0016] [10.5pt] Most CNN architectures described so far are fairly straightforward to implement
[p0490-l0017] [10.5pt] (although generally you would load a pretrained network instead, as we will see). To
[p0490-l0018] [10.5pt] illustrate the process, let’s implement a ResNet-34 from scratch using Keras. First, let’s
[p0490-l0019] [10.5pt] create a ResidualUnit layer:
[p0490-l0020] [8.5pt] DefaultConv2D = partial(keras.layers.Conv2D, kernel_size=3, strides=1,
[p0490-l0021] [8.5pt]                         padding="SAME", use_bias=False)
[p0490-l0022] [8.5pt] class ResidualUnit(keras.layers.Layer):
[p0490-l0023] [8.5pt]     def __init__(self, filters, strides=1, activation="relu", **kwargs):
[p0490-l0024] [8.5pt]         super().__init__(**kwargs)
[p0490-l0025] [8.5pt]         self.activation = keras.activations.get(activation)
[p0490-l0026] [8.5pt]         self.main_layers = [
[p0490-l0027] [8.5pt]             DefaultConv2D(filters, strides=strides),
[p0490-l0028] [8.5pt]             keras.layers.BatchNormalization(),
[p0490-l0029] [8.5pt]             self.activation,
[p0490-l0030] [8.5pt]             DefaultConv2D(filters),
[p0490-l0031] [8.5pt]             keras.layers.BatchNormalization()]
[p0490-l0032] [8.5pt]         self.skip_layers = []
[p0490-l0033] [8.5pt]         if strides > 1:
[p0490-l0034] [8.5pt]             self.skip_layers = [
[p0490-l0035] [8.5pt]                 DefaultConv2D(filters, kernel_size=1, strides=strides),
[p0490-l0036] [8.5pt]                 keras.layers.BatchNormalization()]
[p0490-l0037] [8.5pt]     def call(self, inputs):
[p0490-l0038] [8.5pt]         Z = inputs
[p0490-l0039] [8.5pt]         for layer in self.main_layers:
[p0490-l0040] [8.5pt]             Z = layer(Z)
[p0490-l0041] [8.5pt]         skip_Z = inputs
[p0490-l0042] [8.5pt]         for layer in self.skip_layers:
[p0490-l0043] [9.0pt] 464
[p0490-l0044] [9.0pt] |
[p0490-l0045] [9.0pt] Chapter 14: Deep Computer Vision Using Convolutional Neural Networks

=== PDF page 491 / printed label 465 ===
[p0491-l0001] [8.5pt]             skip_Z = layer(skip_Z)
[p0491-l0002] [8.5pt]         return self.activation(Z + skip_Z)
[p0491-l0003] [10.5pt] As you can see, this code matches Figure 14-18 pretty closely. In the constructor, we
[p0491-l0004] [10.5pt] create all the layers we will need: the main layers are the ones on the right side of the
[p0491-l0005] [10.5pt] diagram, and the skip layers are the ones on the left (only needed if the stride is
[p0491-l0006] [10.5pt] greater than 1). Then in the call() method, we simply make the inputs go through
[p0491-l0007] [10.5pt] the main layers, and the skip layers (if any), then we add both outputs and we apply
[p0491-l0008] [10.5pt] the activation function.
[p0491-l0009] [10.5pt] Next, we can build the ResNet-34 simply using a Sequential model, since it is really
[p0491-l0010] [10.5pt] just a long sequence of layers (we can treat each residual unit as a single layer now
[p0491-l0011] [10.5pt] that we have the ResidualUnit class):
[p0491-l0012] [8.5pt] model = keras.models.Sequential()
[p0491-l0013] [8.5pt] model.add(DefaultConv2D(64, kernel_size=7, strides=2,
[p0491-l0014] [8.5pt]                         input_shape=[224, 224, 3]))
[p0491-l0015] [8.5pt] model.add(keras.layers.BatchNormalization())
[p0491-l0016] [8.5pt] model.add(keras.layers.Activation("relu"))
[p0491-l0017] [8.5pt] model.add(keras.layers.MaxPool2D(pool_size=3, strides=2, padding="SAME"))
[p0491-l0018] [8.5pt] prev_filters = 64
[p0491-l0019] [8.5pt] for filters in [64] * 3 + [128] * 4 + [256] * 6 + [512] * 3:
[p0491-l0020] [8.5pt]     strides = 1 if filters == prev_filters else 2
[p0491-l0021] [8.5pt]     model.add(ResidualUnit(filters, strides=strides))
[p0491-l0022] [8.5pt]     prev_filters = filters
[p0491-l0023] [8.5pt] model.add(keras.layers.GlobalAvgPool2D())
[p0491-l0024] [8.5pt] model.add(keras.layers.Flatten())
[p0491-l0025] [8.5pt] model.add(keras.layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax"))
[p0491-l0026] [10.5pt] The only slightly tricky part in this code is the loop that adds the ResidualUnit layers
[p0491-l0027] [10.5pt] to the model: as explained earlier, the first 3 RUs have 64 filters, then the next 4 RUs
[p0491-l0028] [10.5pt] have 128 filters, and so on. We then set the strides to 1 when the number of filters is
[p0491-l0029] [10.5pt] the same as in the previous RU, or else we set it to 2. Then we add the ResidualUnit,
[p0491-l0030] [10.5pt] and finally we update prev_filters.
[p0491-l0031] [10.5pt] It is quite amazing that in less than 40 lines of code, we can build the model that won
[p0491-l0032] [10.5pt] the ILSVRC 2015 challenge! It demonstrates both the elegance of the ResNet model,
[p0491-l0033] [10.5pt] and the expressiveness of the Keras API. Implementing the other CNN architectures
[p0491-l0034] [10.5pt] is not much harder. However, Keras comes with several of these architectures built in,
[p0491-l0035] [10.5pt] so why not use them instead?
[p0491-l0036] [18.92pt] Using Pretrained Models From Keras
[p0491-l0037] [10.5pt] In general, you won’t have to implement standard models like GoogLeNet or ResNet
[p0491-l0038] [10.5pt] manually, since pretrained networks are readily available with a single line of code, in
[p0491-l0039] [10.5pt] the keras.applications package. For example:
[p0491-l0040] [8.5pt] model = keras.applications.resnet50.ResNet50(weights="imagenet")
[p0491-l0041] [9.0pt] Using Pretrained Models From Keras
[p0491-l0042] [9.0pt] |
[p0491-l0043] [9.0pt] 465

[p0492-l0001] [10.5pt] That’s all! This will create a ResNet-50 model and download weights pretrained on
[p0492-l0002] [10.5pt] the ImageNet dataset. To use it, you first need to ensure that the images have the right
[p0492-l0003] [10.5pt] size. A ResNet-50 model expects 224 × 224 images (other models may expect other
[p0492-l0004] [10.5pt] sizes, such as 299 × 299), so let’s use TensorFlow’s tf.image.resize() function to
[p0492-l0005] [10.5pt] resize the images we loaded earlier:
[p0492-l0006] [8.5pt] images_resized = tf.image.resize(images, [224, 224])
[p0492-l0007] [9.6pt] The tf.image.resize() will not preserve the aspect ratio. If this is
[p0492-l0008] [9.6pt] a problem, you can try cropping the images to the appropriate
[p0492-l0009] [9.6pt] aspect ratio before resizing. Both operations can be done in one
[p0492-l0010] [9.6pt] shot with tf.image.crop_and_resize().
[p0492-l0011] [10.5pt] The pretrained models assume that the images are preprocessed in a specific way. In
[p0492-l0012] [10.5pt] some cases they may expect the inputs to be scaled from 0 to 1, or -1 to 1, and so on.
[p0492-l0013] [10.5pt] Each model provides a preprocess_input() function that you can use to preprocess
[p0492-l0014] [10.5pt] your images. These functions assume that the pixel values range from 0 to 255, so we
[p0492-l0015] [10.5pt] must multiply them by 255 (since earlier we scaled them to the 0–1 range):
[p0492-l0016] [8.5pt] inputs = keras.applications.resnet50.preprocess_input(images_resized * 255)
[p0492-l0017] [10.5pt] Now we can use the pretrained model to make predictions:
[p0492-l0018] [8.5pt] Y_proba = model.predict(inputs)
[p0492-l0019] [10.5pt] As usual, the output Y_proba is a matrix with one row per image and one column per
[p0492-l0020] [10.5pt] class (in this case, there are 1,000 classes). If you want to display the top K predic‐
[p0492-l0021] [10.5pt] tions, including the class name and the estimated probability of each predicted class,
[p0492-l0022] [10.5pt] you can use the decode_predictions() function. For each image, it returns an array
[p0492-l0023] [10.5pt] containing the top K predictions, where each prediction is represented as an array
[p0492-l0024] [10.5pt] containing the class identifier21, its name and the corresponding confidence score:
[p0492-l0025] [8.5pt] top_K = keras.applications.resnet50.decode_predictions(Y_proba, top=3)
[p0492-l0026] [8.5pt] for image_index in range(len(images)):
[p0492-l0027] [8.5pt]     print("Image #{}".format(image_index))
[p0492-l0028] [8.5pt]     for class_id, name, y_proba in top_K[image_index]:
[p0492-l0029] [8.5pt]         print("  {} - {:12s} {:.2f}%".format(class_id, name, y_proba * 100))
[p0492-l0030] [8.5pt]     print()
[p0492-l0031] [10.5pt] The output looks like this:
[p0492-l0032] [8.5pt] Image #0
[p0492-l0033] [8.5pt]   n03877845 - palace       42.87%
[p0492-l0034] [8.5pt]   n02825657 - bell_cote    40.57%
[p0492-l0035] [8.5pt]   n03781244 - monastery    14.56%
[p0492-l0036] [8.0pt] 21 In the ImageNet dataset, each image is associated to a word in the WordNet dataset: the class ID is just a
[p0492-l0037] [8.0pt] WordNet ID.

[p0493-l0007] [10.5pt] As you can see, it is very easy to create a pretty good image classifier using a pre‐
[p0493-l0008] [10.5pt] trained model. Other vision models are available in keras.applications, including
[p0493-l0009] [10.5pt] several ResNet variants, GoogLeNet variants like InceptionV3 and Xception,
[p0493-l0010] [10.5pt] VGGNet variants, MobileNet and MobileNetV2 (lightweight models for use in
[p0493-l0011] [10.5pt] mobile applications), and more.
[p0493-l0012] [10.5pt] But what if you want to use an image classifier for classes of images that are not part
[p0493-l0013] [10.5pt] of ImageNet? In that case, you may still benefit from the pretrained models to per‐

[p0493-l0015] [18.92pt] Pretrained Models for Transfer Learning
[p0493-l0016] [10.5pt] If you want to build an image classifier, but you do not have enough training data,
[p0493-l0017] [10.5pt] then it is often a good idea to reuse the lower layers of a pretrained model, as we dis‐
[p0493-l0018] [10.5pt] cussed in Chapter 11. For example, let’s train a model to classify pictures of flowers,
[p0493-l0019] [10.5pt] reusing a pretrained Xception model. First, let’s load the dataset using TensorFlow
[p0493-l0020] [10.5pt] Datasets (see Chapter 13):
[p0493-l0021] [8.5pt] import tensorflow_datasets as tfds
[p0493-l0022] [8.5pt] dataset, info = tfds.load("tf_flowers", as_supervised=True, with_info=True)
[p0493-l0023] [8.5pt] dataset_size = info.splits["train"].num_examples # 3670
[p0493-l0024] [8.5pt] class_names = info.features["label"].names # ["dandelion", "daisy", ...]
[p0493-l0025] [8.5pt] n_classes = info.features["label"].num_classes # 5
[p0493-l0026] [10.5pt] Note that you can get information about the dataset by setting with_info=True. Here,
[p0493-l0027] [10.5pt] we get the dataset size and the names of the classes. Unfortunately, there is only a
[p0493-l0028] [10.5pt] "train" dataset, no test set or validation set, so we need to split the training set. The
[p0493-l0029] [10.5pt] TF Datasets project provides an API for this. For example, let’s take the first 10% of
[p0493-l0030] [10.5pt] the dataset for testing, the next 15% for validation, and the remaining 75% for train‐
[p0493-l0031] [10.5pt] ing:
[p0493-l0032] [8.5pt] test_split, valid_split, train_split = tfds.Split.TRAIN.subsplit([10, 15, 75])
[p0493-l0033] [8.5pt] test_set = tfds.load("tf_flowers", split=test_split, as_supervised=True)
[p0493-l0034] [8.5pt] valid_set = tfds.load("tf_flowers", split=valid_split, as_supervised=True)
[p0493-l0035] [8.5pt] train_set = tfds.load("tf_flowers", split=train_split, as_supervised=True)
[p0493-l0036] [9.0pt] Pretrained Models for Transfer Learning
[p0493-l0037] [9.0pt] |
[p0493-l0038] [9.0pt] 467
