[p0494-l0001] [10.5pt] Next we must preprocess the images. The CNN expects 224 × 224 images, so we need
[p0494-l0002] [10.5pt] to resize them. We also need to run the image through Xception’s prepro
[p0494-l0003] [10.5pt] cess_input() function:
[p0494-l0004] [8.5pt] def preprocess(image, label):
[p0494-l0005] [8.5pt]     resized_image = tf.image.resize(image, [224, 224])
[p0494-l0006] [8.5pt]     final_image = keras.applications.xception.preprocess_input(resized_image)
[p0494-l0007] [8.5pt]     return final_image, label
[p0494-l0008] [10.5pt] Let’s apply this preprocessing function to all 3 datasets, and let’s also shuffle & repeat
[p0494-l0009] [10.5pt] the training set, and add batching & prefetching to all datasets:
[p0494-l0010] [8.5pt] batch_size = 32
[p0494-l0011] [8.5pt] train_set = train_set.shuffle(1000).repeat()
[p0494-l0012] [8.5pt] train_set = train_set.map(preprocess).batch(batch_size).prefetch(1)
[p0494-l0013] [8.5pt] valid_set = valid_set.map(preprocess).batch(batch_size).prefetch(1)
[p0494-l0014] [8.5pt] test_set = test_set.map(preprocess).batch(batch_size).prefetch(1)
[p0494-l0015] [10.5pt] If you want to perform some data augmentation, you can just change the preprocess‐
[p0494-l0016] [10.5pt] ing function for the training set, adding some random transformations to the training
[p0494-l0017] [10.5pt] images. For example, use tf.image.random_crop() to randomly crop the images, use
[p0494-l0018] [10.5pt] tf.image.random_flip_left_right() to randomly flip the images horizontally, and
[p0494-l0019] [10.5pt] so on (see the notebook for an example).
[p0494-l0020] [10.5pt] Next let’s load an Xception model, pretrained on ImageNet. We exclude the top of the
[p0494-l0021] [10.5pt] network (by setting include_top=False): this excludes the global average pooling
[p0494-l0022] [10.5pt] layer and the dense output layer. We then add our own global average pooling layer,
[p0494-l0023] [10.5pt] based on the output of the base model, followed by a dense output layer with 1 unit
[p0494-l0024] [10.5pt] per class, using the softmax activation function. Finally, we create the Keras Model:
[p0494-l0025] [8.5pt] base_model = keras.applications.xception.Xception(weights="imagenet",
[p0494-l0026] [8.5pt]                                                   include_top=False)
[p0494-l0027] [8.5pt] avg = keras.layers.GlobalAveragePooling2D()(base_model.output)
[p0494-l0028] [8.5pt] output = keras.layers.Dense(n_classes, activation="softmax")(avg)
[p0494-l0029] [8.5pt] model = keras.models.Model(inputs=base_model.input, outputs=output)
[p0494-l0030] [10.5pt] As explained in Chapter 11, it’s usually a good idea to freeze the weights of the pre‐
[p0494-l0031] [10.5pt] trained layers, at least at the beginning of training:
[p0494-l0032] [8.5pt] for layer in base_model.layers:
[p0494-l0033] [8.5pt]     layer.trainable = False
[p0494-l0034] [9.6pt] Since our model uses the base model’s layers directly, rather than
[p0494-l0035] [9.6pt] the base_model object itself, setting base_model.trainable=False
[p0494-l0036] [9.6pt] would have no effect.
[p0494-l0037] [10.5pt] Finally, we can compile the model and start training:
[p0494-l0038] [9.0pt] 468
[p0494-l0039] [9.0pt] |
[p0494-l0040] [9.0pt] Chapter 14: Deep Computer Vision Using Convolutional Neural Networks

[p0495-l0001] [8.5pt] optimizer = keras.optimizers.SGD(lr=0.2, momentum=0.9, decay=0.01)

[p0495-l0024] [10.5pt] It will take a while, but this model should reach around 95% accuracy on the test set.
[p0495-l0025] [10.5pt] With that, you can start training amazing image classifiers! But there’s more to com‐
[p0495-l0026] [10.5pt] puter vision than just classification. For example, what if you also want to know where
[p0495-l0027] [10.5pt] the flower is in the picture? Let’s look at this now.
[p0495-l0028] [18.92pt] Classification and Localization
[p0495-l0029] [10.5pt] Localizing an object in a picture can be expressed as a regression task, as discussed in
[p0495-l0030] [10.5pt] Chapter 10: to predict a bounding box around the object, a common approach is to
[p0495-l0031] [10.5pt] predict the horizontal and vertical coordinates of the object’s center, as well as its
[p0495-l0032] [10.5pt] height and width. This means we have 4 numbers to predict. It does not require much
[p0495-l0033] [10.5pt] change to the model, we just need to add a second dense output layer with 4 units
[p0495-l0034] [10.5pt] (typically on top of the global average pooling layer), and it can be trained using the
[p0495-l0035] [10.5pt] MSE loss:
[p0495-l0036] [8.5pt] base_model = keras.applications.xception.Xception(weights="imagenet",
[p0495-l0037] [8.5pt]                                                   include_top=False)
[p0495-l0038] [8.5pt] avg = keras.layers.GlobalAveragePooling2D()(base_model.output)
[p0495-l0039] [8.5pt] class_output = keras.layers.Dense(n_classes, activation="softmax")(avg)
[p0495-l0040] [9.0pt] Classification and Localization
[p0495-l0041] [9.0pt] |

[p0496-l0007] [10.5pt] But now we have a problem: the flowers dataset does not have bounding boxes
[p0496-l0008] [10.5pt] around the flowers. So we need to add them ourselves. This is often one of the hard‐
[p0496-l0009] [10.5pt] est and most costly part of a Machine Learning project: getting the labels. It’s a good
[p0496-l0010] [10.5pt] idea to spend time looking for the right tools. To annotate images with bounding
[p0496-l0011] [10.5pt] boxes, you may want to use an open source image labeling tool like VGG Image
[p0496-l0012] [10.5pt] Annotator, LabelImg, OpenLabeler or ImgLab, or perhaps a commercial tool like
[p0496-l0013] [10.5pt] LabelBox or Supervisely. You may also want to consider crowdsourcing platforms
[p0496-l0014] [10.5pt] such as Amazon Mechanical Turk or CrowdFlower if you have a very large number of
[p0496-l0015] [10.5pt] images to annotate. However, it is quite a lot of work to setup a crowdsourcing plat‐
[p0496-l0016] [10.5pt] form, prepare the form to be sent to the workers, to supervise them and ensure the
[p0496-l0017] [10.5pt] quality of the bounding boxes they produce is good, so make sure it is worth the
[p0496-l0018] [10.5pt] effort: if there are just a few thousand images to label, and you don’t plan to do this
[p0496-l0019] [10.5pt] frequently, it may be preferable to do it yourself. Adriana Kovashka et al. wrote a very
[p0496-l0020] [10.5pt] practical paper22 about crowdsourcing in Computer Vision, I recommend you check
[p0496-l0021] [10.5pt] it out, even if you do not plan to use crowdsourcing.
[p0496-l0022] [10.5pt] So let’s suppose you obtained the bounding boxes for every image in the flowers data‐
[p0496-l0023] [10.5pt] set (for now we will assume there is a single bounding box per image), you then need
[p0496-l0024] [10.5pt] to create a dataset whose items will be batches of preprocessed images along with
[p0496-l0025] [10.5pt] their class labels and their bounding boxes. Each item should be a tuple of the form:
[p0496-l0026] [10.5pt] (images, (class_labels, bounding_boxes)). Then you are ready to train your
[p0496-l0027] [10.5pt] model!
[p0496-l0028] [9.6pt] The bounding boxes should be normalized so that the horizontal
[p0496-l0029] [9.6pt] and vertical coordinates, as well as the height and width all range
[p0496-l0030] [9.6pt] from 0 to 1. Also, it is common to predict the square root of the
[p0496-l0031] [9.6pt] height and width rather than the height and width directly: this
[p0496-l0032] [9.6pt] way, a 10 pixel error for a large bounding box will not be penalized
[p0496-l0033] [9.6pt] as much as a 10 pixel error for a small bounding box.
[p0496-l0034] [10.5pt] The MSE often works fairly well as a cost function to train the model, but it is not a
[p0496-l0035] [10.5pt] great metric to evaluate how well the model can predict bounding boxes. The most
[p0496-l0036] [10.5pt] common metric for this is the Intersection over Union (IoU): it is the area of overlap
[p0496-l0037] [10.5pt] between the predicted bounding box and the target bounding box, divided by the
[p0496-l0038] [8.0pt] 22 “Crowdsourcing in Computer Vision,” A. Kovashka et al. (2016).
[p0496-l0039] [9.0pt] 470
[p0496-l0040] [9.0pt] |

[p0497-l0001] [10.5pt] area of their union (see Figure 14-23). In tf.keras, it is implemented by the
[p0497-l0002] [10.5pt] tf.keras.metrics.MeanIoU class.
[p0497-l0003] [10.5pt] Figure 14-23. Intersection over Union (IoU) Metric for Bounding Boxes
[p0497-l0004] [10.5pt] Classifying and localizing a single object is nice, but what if the images contain multi‐
[p0497-l0005] [10.5pt] ple objects (as is often the case in the flowers dataset)?
[p0497-l0006] [18.92pt] Object Detection
[p0497-l0007] [10.5pt] The task of classifying and localizing multiple objects in an image is called object
[p0497-l0008] [10.5pt] detection. Until a few years ago, a common approach was to take a CNN that was
[p0497-l0009] [10.5pt] trained to classify and locate a single object, then slide it across the image, as shown
[p0497-l0010] [10.5pt] in Figure 14-24. In this example, the image was chopped into a 6 × 8 grid, and we
[p0497-l0011] [10.5pt] show a CNN (the thick black rectangle) sliding across all 3 × 3 regions. When the
[p0497-l0012] [10.5pt] CNN was looking at the top left of the image, it detected part of the left-most rose,
[p0497-l0013] [10.5pt] and then it detected that same rose again when it was first shifted one step to the
[p0497-l0014] [10.5pt] right. At the next step, it started detecting part of the top-most rose, and then it detec‐
[p0497-l0015] [10.5pt] ted it again once it was shifted one more step to the right. You would then continue to
[p0497-l0016] [10.5pt] slide the CNN through the whole image, looking at all 3 × 3 regions. Moreover, since
[p0497-l0017] [10.5pt] objects can have varying sizes, you would also slide the CNN across regions of differ‐
[p0497-l0018] [10.5pt] ent sizes. For example, once you are done with the 3 × 3 regions, you might want to
[p0497-l0019] [10.5pt] slide the CNN across all 4 × 4 regions as well.
[p0497-l0020] [9.0pt] Object Detection
[p0497-l0021] [9.0pt] |
[p0497-l0022] [9.0pt] 471

=== PDF page 498 / printed label 472 ===
[p0498-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 14-24. Detecting Multiple Objects by Sliding a CNN Across the Image
[p0498-l0002] [10.5pt] This technique is fairly straightforward, but as you can see it will detect the same
[p0498-l0003] [10.5pt] object multiple times, at slightly different positions. Some post-processing will then
[p0498-l0004] [10.5pt] be needed to get rid of all the unnecessary bounding boxes. A common approach for
[p0498-l0005] [10.5pt] this is called non-max suppression:
[p0498-l0006] [10.5pt] • First, you need to add an extra objectness output to your CNN, to estimate the
[p0498-l0007] [10.5pt] probability that a flower is indeed present in the image (alternatively, you could
[p0498-l0008] [10.5pt] add a “no-flower” class, but this usually does not work as well). It must use the
[p0498-l0009] [10.5pt] sigmoid activation function and you can train it using the "binary_crossen
[p0498-l0010] [10.5pt] tropy" loss. Then just get rid of all the bounding boxes for which the objectness
[p0498-l0011] [10.5pt] score is below some threshold: this will drop all the bounding boxes that don’t
[p0498-l0012] [10.5pt] actually contain a flower.
[p0498-l0013] [10.5pt] • Second, find the bounding box with the highest objectness score, and get rid of
[p0498-l0014] [10.5pt] all the other bounding boxes that overlap a lot with it (e.g., with an IoU greater
[p0498-l0015] [10.5pt] than 60%). For example, in Figure 14-24, the bounding box with the max object‐
[p0498-l0016] [10.5pt] ness score is the thick bounding box over the top-most rose (the objectness score
[p0498-l0017] [10.5pt] is represented by the thickness of the bounding boxes). The other bounding box
[p0498-l0018] [10.5pt] over that same rose overlaps a lot with the max bounding box, so we will get rid
[p0498-l0019] [10.5pt] of it.
[p0498-l0020] [9.0pt] 472
[p0498-l0021] [9.0pt] |
[p0498-l0022] [9.0pt] Chapter 14: Deep Computer Vision Using Convolutional Neural Networks

=== PDF page 499 / printed label 473 ===
[p0499-l0001] [10.5pt] • Third, repeat step two until there are no more bounding boxes to get rid of.
[p0499-l0002] [10.5pt] This simple approach to object detection works pretty well, but it requires running
[p0499-l0003] [10.5pt] the CNN many times, so it is quite slow. Fortunately, there is a much faster way to
[p0499-l0004] [10.5pt] slide a CNN across an image: using a Fully Convolutional Network.
[p0499-l0005] [15.77pt] Fully Convolutional Networks (FCNs)
[p0499-l0006] [10.5pt] The idea of FCNs was first introduced in a 2015 paper23 by Jonathan Long et al., for
[p0499-l0007] [10.5pt] semantic segmentation (the task of classifying every pixel in an image according to
[p0499-l0008] [10.5pt] the class of the object it belongs to). They pointed out that you could replace the
[p0499-l0009] [10.5pt] dense layers at the top of a CNN by convolutional layers. To understand this, let’s look
[p0499-l0010] [10.5pt] at an example: suppose a dense layer with 200 neurons sits on top of a convolutional
[p0499-l0011] [10.5pt] layer that outputs 100 feature maps, each of size 7 × 7 (this is the feature map size, not
[p0499-l0012] [10.5pt] the kernel size). Each neuron will compute a weighted sum of all 100 × 7 × 7 activa‐
[p0499-l0013] [10.5pt] tions from the convolutional layer (plus a bias term). Now let’s see what happens if we
[p0499-l0014] [10.5pt] replace the dense layer with a convolution layer using 200 filters, each 7 × 7, and with
[p0499-l0015] [10.5pt] VALID padding. This layer will output 200 feature maps, each 1 × 1 (since the kernel
[p0499-l0016] [10.5pt] is exactly the size of the input feature maps and we are using VALID padding). In
[p0499-l0017] [10.5pt] other words, it will output 200 numbers, just like the dense layer did, and if you look
[p0499-l0018] [10.5pt] closely at the computations performed by a convolutional layer, you will notice that
[p0499-l0019] [10.5pt] these numbers will be precisely the same as the dense layer produced. The only differ‐
[p0499-l0020] [10.5pt] ence is that the dense layer’s output was a tensor of shape [batch size, 200] while the
[p0499-l0021] [10.5pt] convolutional layer will output a tensor of shape [batch size, 1, 1, 200].
[p0499-l0022] [9.6pt] To convert a dense layer to a convolutional layer, the number of fil‐
[p0499-l0023] [9.6pt] ters in the convolutional layer must be equal to the number of units
[p0499-l0024] [9.6pt] in the dense layer, the filter size must be equal to the size of the
[p0499-l0025] [9.6pt] input feature maps, and you must use VALID padding. The stride
[p0499-l0026] [9.6pt] may be set to 1 or more, as we will see shortly.
[p0499-l0027] [10.5pt] Why is this important? Well, while a dense layer expects a specific input size (since it
[p0499-l0028] [10.5pt] has one weight per input feature), a convolutional layer will happily process images of
[p0499-l0029] [10.5pt] any size24 (however, it does expect its inputs to have a specific number of channels,
[p0499-l0030] [10.5pt] since each kernel contains a different set of weights for each input channel). Since an
[p0499-l0031] [10.5pt] FCN contains only convolutional layers (and pooling layers, which have the same
[p0499-l0032] [10.5pt] property), it can be trained and executed on images of any size!
[p0499-l0033] [8.0pt] 23 “Fully Convolutional Networks for Semantic Segmentation,” J. Long, E. Shelhamer, T. Darrell (2015).
[p0499-l0034] [8.0pt] 24 There is one small exception: a convolutional layer using VALID padding will complain if the input size is
[p0499-l0035] [8.0pt] smaller than the kernel size.
[p0499-l0036] [9.0pt] Object Detection
[p0499-l0037] [9.0pt] |
[p0499-l0038] [9.0pt] 473

=== PDF page 500 / printed label 474 ===
[p0500-l0001] [10.5pt] For example, suppose we already trained a CNN for flower classification and localiza‐
[p0500-l0002] [10.5pt] tion. It was trained on 224 × 224 images and it outputs 10 numbers: outputs 0 to 4 are
[p0500-l0003] [10.5pt] sent through the softmax activation function, and this gives the class probabilities
[p0500-l0004] [10.5pt] (one per class); output 5 is sent through the logistic activation function, and this gives
[p0500-l0005] [10.5pt] the objectness score; outputs 6 to 9 do not use any activation function, and they rep‐
[p0500-l0006] [10.5pt] resent the bounding box’s center coordinates, and its height and width. We can now
[p0500-l0007] [10.5pt] convert its dense layers to convolutional layers. In fact, we don’t even need to retrain
[p0500-l0008] [10.5pt] it, we can just copy the weights from the dense layers to the convolutional layers!
[p0500-l0009] [10.5pt] Alternatively, we could have converted the CNN into an FCN before training.
[p0500-l0010] [10.5pt] Now suppose the last convolutional layer before the output layer (also called the bot‐
[p0500-l0011] [10.5pt] tleneck layer) outputs 7 × 7 feature maps when the network is fed a 224 × 224 image
[p0500-l0012] [10.5pt] (see the left side of Figure 14-25). If we feed the FCN a 448 × 448 image (see the right
[p0500-l0013] [10.5pt] side of Figure 14-25), the bottleneck layer will now output 14 × 14 feature maps.25
[p0500-l0014] [10.5pt] Since the dense output layer was replaced by a convolutional layer using 10 filters of
[p0500-l0015] [10.5pt] size 7 × 7, VALID padding and stride 1, the output will be composed of 10 features
[p0500-l0016] [10.5pt] maps, each of size 8 × 8 (since 14 - 7 + 1 = 8). In other words, the FCN will process
[p0500-l0017] [10.5pt] the whole image only once and it will output an 8 × 8 grid where each cell contains 10
[p0500-l0018] [10.5pt] numbers (5 class probabilities, 1 objectness score and 4 bounding box coordinates).
[p0500-l0019] [10.5pt] It’s exactly like taking the original CNN and sliding it across the image using 8 steps
[p0500-l0020] [10.5pt] per row and 8 steps per column: to visualize this, imagine chopping the original
[p0500-l0021] [10.5pt] image into a 14 × 14 grid, then sliding a 7 × 7 window across this grid: there will be 8
[p0500-l0022] [10.5pt] × 8 = 64 possible locations for the window, hence 8 × 8 predictions. However, the
[p0500-l0023] [10.5pt] FCN approach is much more efficient, since the network only looks at the image
[p0500-l0024] [10.5pt] once. In fact, You Only Look Once (YOLO) is the name of a very popular object detec‐
[p0500-l0025] [10.5pt] tion architecture!
[p0500-l0026] [8.0pt] 25 This assumes we used only SAME padding in the network: indeed, VALID padding would reduce the size of
[p0500-l0027] [8.0pt] the feature maps. Moreover, 448 can be neatly divided by 2 several times until we reach 7, without any round‐
[p0500-l0028] [8.0pt] ing error. If any layer uses a different stride than 1 or 2, then there may be some rounding error, so again the
[p0500-l0029] [8.0pt] feature maps may end up being smaller.

[p0501-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 14-25. A Fully Convolutional Network Processing a Small Image (left) and a
[p0501-l0002] [10.5pt] Large One (right)
[p0501-l0003] [15.77pt] You Only Look Once (YOLO)
[p0501-l0004] [10.5pt] YOLO is an extremely fast and accurate object detection architecture proposed by
[p0501-l0005] [10.5pt] Joseph Redmon et al. in a 2015 paper26, and subsequently improved in 201627
[p0501-l0006] [10.5pt] (YOLOv2) and in 201828 (YOLOv3). It is so fast that it can run in realtime on a video
[p0501-l0007] [10.5pt] (check out this nice demo).
[p0501-l0008] [10.5pt] YOLOv3’s architecture is quite similar to the one we just discussed, but with a few
[p0501-l0009] [10.5pt] important differences:
[p0501-l0010] [8.0pt] 26 “You Only Look Once: Unified, Real-Time Object Detection,” J. Redmon, S. Divvala, R. Girshick, A. Farhadi
[p0501-l0011] [8.0pt] (2015).
[p0501-l0012] [8.0pt] 27 “YOLO9000: Better, Faster, Stronger,” J. Redmon, A. Farhadi (2016).
[p0501-l0013] [8.0pt] 28 “YOLOv3: An Incremental Improvement,” J. Redmon, A. Farhadi (2018).
[p0501-l0014] [9.0pt] Object Detection
[p0501-l0015] [9.0pt] |
[p0501-l0016] [9.0pt] 475

=== PDF page 502 / printed label 476 ===
[p0502-l0001] [10.5pt] • First, it outputs 5 bounding boxes for each grid cell (instead of just 1), and each
[p0502-l0002] [10.5pt] bounding box comes with an objectness score. It also outputs 20 class probabili‐
[p0502-l0003] [10.5pt] ties per grid cell, as it was trained on the PASCAL VOC dataset, which contains
[p0502-l0004] [10.5pt] 20 classes. That’s a total of 45 numbers per grid cell (5 * 4 bounding box coordi‐
[p0502-l0005] [10.5pt] nates, plus 5 objectness scores, plus 20 class probabilities).
[p0502-l0006] [10.5pt] • Second, instead of predicting the absolute coordinates of the bounding box cen‐
[p0502-l0007] [10.5pt] ters, YOLOv3 predicts an offset relative to the coordinates of the grid cell, where
[p0502-l0008] [10.5pt] (0, 0) means the top left of that cell, and (1, 1) means the bottom right. For each
[p0502-l0009] [10.5pt] grid cell, YOLOv3 is trained to predict only bounding boxes whose center lies in
[p0502-l0010] [10.5pt] that cell (but the bounding box itself generally extends well beyond the grid cell).
[p0502-l0011] [10.5pt] YOLOv3 applies the logistic activation function to the bounding box coordinates
[p0502-l0012] [10.5pt] to ensure they remain in the 0 to 1 range.
[p0502-l0013] [10.5pt] • Third, before training the neural net, YOLOv3 finds 5 representative bounding
[p0502-l0014] [10.5pt] box dimensions, called anchor boxes (or bounding box priors): it does this by
[p0502-l0015] [10.5pt] applying the K-Means algorithm (see ???) to the height and width of the training
[p0502-l0016] [10.5pt] set bounding boxes. For example, if the training images contain many pedes‐
[p0502-l0017] [10.5pt] trians, then one of the anchor boxes will likely have the dimensions of a typical
[p0502-l0018] [10.5pt] pedestrian. Then when the neural net predicts 5 bounding boxes per grid cell, it
[p0502-l0019] [10.5pt] actually predicts how much to rescale each of the anchor boxes. For example,
[p0502-l0020] [10.5pt] suppose one anchor box is 100 pixels tall and 50 pixels wide, and the network
[p0502-l0021] [10.5pt] predicts, say, a vertical rescaling factor of 1.5 and a horizontal rescaling of 0.9 (for
[p0502-l0022] [10.5pt] one of the grid cells), this will result in a predicted bounding box of size 150 × 45
[p0502-l0023] [10.5pt] pixels. To be more precise, for each grid cell and each anchor box, the network
[p0502-l0024] [10.5pt] predicts the log of the vertical and horizontal rescaling factors. Having these pri‐
[p0502-l0025] [10.5pt] ors makes the network more likely to predict bounding boxes of the appropriate
[p0502-l0026] [10.5pt] dimensions, and it also speeds up training since it will more quickly learn what
[p0502-l0027] [10.5pt] reasonable bounding boxes look like.
[p0502-l0028] [10.5pt] • Fourth, the network is trained using images of different scales: every few batches
[p0502-l0029] [10.5pt] during training, the network randomly chooses a new image dimension (from
[p0502-l0030] [10.5pt] 330 × 330 to 608 × 608 pixels). This allows the network to learn to detect objects
[p0502-l0031] [10.5pt] at different scales. Moreover, it makes it possible to use YOLOv3 at different
[p0502-l0032] [10.5pt] scales: the smaller scale will be less accurate but faster than the larger scale, so
[p0502-l0033] [10.5pt] you can choose the right tradeoff for your use case.
[p0502-l0034] [10.5pt] There are a few more innovations you might be interested in, such as the use of skip
[p0502-l0035] [10.5pt] connections to recover some of the spatial resolution that is lost in the CNN (we will
[p0502-l0036] [10.5pt] discuss this shortly when we look at semantic segmentation). Moreover, in the 2016
[p0502-l0037] [10.5pt] paper, the authors introduce the YOLO9000 model that uses hierarchical classifica‐
[p0502-l0038] [10.5pt] tion: the model predicts a probability for each node in a visual hierarchy called Word‐
[p0502-l0039] [10.5pt] Tree. This makes it possible for the network to predict with high confidence that an
[p0502-l0040] [10.5pt] image represents, say, a dog, even though it is unsure what specific type of dog it is.
[p0502-l0041] [9.0pt] 476
[p0502-l0042] [9.0pt] |
[p0502-l0043] [9.0pt] Chapter 14: Deep Computer Vision Using Convolutional Neural Networks

[p0503-l0001] [10.5pt] So I encourage you to go ahead and read all three papers: they are quite pleasant to
[p0503-l0002] [10.5pt] read, and it is an excellent example of how Deep Learning systems can be incremen‐
[p0503-l0003] [10.5pt] tally improved.
[p0503-l0004] [15.0pt] Mean Average Precision (mAP)
[p0503-l0005] [10.0pt] A very common metric used in object detection tasks is the mean Average Precision
[p0503-l0006] [10.0pt] (mAP). “Mean Average” sounds a bit redundant, doesn’t it? To understand this met‐
[p0503-l0007] [10.0pt] ric, let’s go back to two classification metrics we discussed in Chapter 3: precision and
[p0503-l0008] [10.0pt] recall. Remember the tradeoff: the higher the recall, the lower the precision. You can
[p0503-l0009] [10.0pt] visualize this in a Precision/Recall curve (see Figure 3-5). To summarize this curve
[p0503-l0010] [10.0pt] into a single number, we could compute its Area Under the Curve (AUC). But note
[p0503-l0011] [10.0pt] that the Precision/Recall curve may contain a few sections where precision actually
[p0503-l0012] [10.0pt] goes up when recall increases, especially at low recall values (you can see this at the
[p0503-l0013] [10.0pt] top left of Figure 3-5). This is one of the motivations for the mAP metric.
[p0503-l0014] [10.0pt] Suppose the classifier has a 90% precision at 10% recall, but a 96% precision at 20%
[p0503-l0015] [10.0pt] recall: there’s really no tradeoff here: it simply makes more sense to use the classifier
[p0503-l0016] [10.0pt] at 20% recall rather than at 10% recall, as you will get both higher recall and higher
[p0503-l0017] [10.0pt] precision. So instead of looking at the precision at 10% recall, we should really be
[p0503-l0018] [10.0pt] looking at the maximum precision that the classifier can offer with at least 10% recall.
[p0503-l0019] [10.0pt] It would be 96%, not 90%. So one way to get a fair idea of the model’s performance is
[p0503-l0020] [10.0pt] to compute the maximum precision you can get with at least 0% recall, then 10%
[p0503-l0021] [10.0pt] recall, 20%, and so on up to 100%, and then calculate the mean of these maximum
[p0503-l0022] [10.0pt] precisions. This is called the Average Precision (AP) metric. Now when there are more
[p0503-l0023] [10.0pt] than 2 classes, we can compute the AP for each class, and then compute the mean AP
[p0503-l0024] [10.0pt] (mAP). That’s it!
[p0503-l0025] [10.0pt] However, in an object detection systems, there is an additional level of complexity:
[p0503-l0026] [10.0pt] what if the system detected the correct class, but at the wrong location (i.e., the
[p0503-l0027] [10.0pt] bounding box is completely off)? Surely we should not count this as a positive predic‐
[p0503-l0028] [10.0pt] tion. So one approach is to define an IOU threshold: for example, we may consider
[p0503-l0029] [10.0pt] that a prediction is correct only if the IOU is greater than, say, 0.5, and the predicted
[p0503-l0030] [10.0pt] class is correct. The corresponding mAP is generally noted mAP@0.5 (or mAP@50%,
[p0503-l0031] [10.0pt] or sometimes just AP50). In some competitions (such as the Pascal VOC challenge),
[p0503-l0032] [10.0pt] this is what is done. In others (such as the COCO competition), the mAP is computed
[p0503-l0033] [10.0pt] for different IOU thresholds (0.50, 0.55, 0.60, …, 0.95), and the final metric is the
[p0503-l0034] [10.0pt] mean of all these mAPs (noted AP@[.50:.95] or AP@[.50:0.05:.95]). Yes, that’s a mean
[p0503-l0035] [10.0pt] mean average.
[p0503-l0036] [10.5pt] Several YOLO implementations built using TensorFlow are available on github, some
[p0503-l0037] [10.5pt] with pretrained weights. At the time of writing, they are based on TensorFlow 1, but
[p0503-l0038] [10.5pt] by the time you read this, TF 2 implementations will certainly be available. Moreover,
[p0503-l0039] [10.5pt] other object detection models are available in the TensorFlow Models project, many
[p0503-l0040] [9.0pt] Object Detection
[p0503-l0041] [9.0pt] |
[p0503-l0042] [9.0pt] 477

=== PDF page 504 / printed label 478 ===
[p0504-l0001] [10.5pt] with pretrained weights, and some have even been ported to TF Hub, making them
[p0504-l0002] [10.5pt] extremely easy to use, such as SSD29 and Faster-RCNN.30, which are both quite popu‐
[p0504-l0003] [10.5pt] lar. SSD is also a “single shot” detection model, quite similar to YOLO, while Faster R-
[p0504-l0004] [10.5pt] CNN is more complex: the image first goes through a CNN, and the output is passed
[p0504-l0005] [10.5pt] to a Region Proposal Network (RPN) which proposes bounding boxes that are most
[p0504-l0006] [10.5pt] likely to contain an object, and a classifier is run for each bounding box, based on the
[p0504-l0007] [10.5pt] cropped output of the CNN.
[p0504-l0008] [10.5pt] The choice of detection system depends on many factors: speed, accuracy, available
[p0504-l0009] [10.5pt] pretrained models, training time, complexity, etc. The papers contain tables of met‐
[p0504-l0010] [10.5pt] rics, but there is quite a lot of variability in the testing environments, and the technol‐
[p0504-l0011] [10.5pt] ogies evolve so fast that it is difficulty to make a fair comparison that will be useful for
[p0504-l0012] [10.5pt] most people and remain valid for more than a few months.
[p0504-l0013] [10.5pt] Great! So we can locate objects by drawing bounding boxes around them. But per‐
[p0504-l0014] [10.5pt] haps you might want to be a bit more precise. Let’s see how to go down to the pixel
[p0504-l0015] [10.5pt] level.
[p0504-l0016] [18.92pt] Semantic Segmentation
[p0504-l0017] [10.5pt] In semantic segmentation, each pixel is classified according to the class of the object it
[p0504-l0018] [10.5pt] belongs to (e.g., road, car, pedestrian, building, etc.), as shown in Figure 14-26. Note
[p0504-l0019] [10.5pt] that different objects of the same class are not distinguished. For example, all the bicy‐
[p0504-l0020] [10.5pt] cles on the right side of the segmented image end up as one big lump of pixels. The
[p0504-l0021] [10.5pt] main difficulty in this task is that when images go through a regular CNN, they grad‐
[p0504-l0022] [10.5pt] ually lose their spatial resolution (due to the layers with strides greater than 1): so a
[p0504-l0023] [10.5pt] regular CNN may end up knowing that there’s a person in the image, somewhere in
[p0504-l0024] [10.5pt] the bottom left of the image, but it will not be much more precise than that.
[p0504-l0025] [8.0pt] 29 “SSD: Single Shot MultiBox Detector,” Wei Liu et al. (2015).
[p0504-l0026] [8.0pt] 30 “Faster R-CNN: Towards Real-Time Object Detection with Region Proposal Networks,” Shaoqing Ren et al.
[p0504-l0027] [8.0pt] (2015).
[p0504-l0028] [9.0pt] 478
[p0504-l0029] [9.0pt] |
[p0504-l0030] [9.0pt] Chapter 14: Deep Computer Vision Using Convolutional Neural Networks

=== PDF page 505 / printed label 479 ===
[p0505-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 14-26. Semantic segmentation
[p0505-l0002] [10.5pt] Just like for object detection, there are many different approaches to tackle this prob‐
[p0505-l0003] [10.5pt] lem, some quite complex. However, a fairly simple solution was proposed in the 2015
[p0505-l0004] [10.5pt] paper by Jonathan Long et al. we discussed earlier. They start by taking a pretrained
[p0505-l0005] [10.5pt] CNN and turning into an FCN, as discussed earlier. The CNN applies a stride of 32 to
[p0505-l0006] [10.5pt] the input image overall (i.e., if you add up all the strides greater than 1), meaning the
[p0505-l0007] [10.5pt] last layer outputs feature maps that are 32 times smaller than the input image. This is
[p0505-l0008] [10.5pt] clearly too coarse, so they add a single upsampling layer that multiplies the resolution
[p0505-l0009] [10.5pt] by 32. There are several solutions available for upsampling (increasing the size of an
[p0505-l0010] [10.5pt] image), such as bilinear interpolation, but it only works reasonably well up to ×4 or
[p0505-l0011] [10.5pt] ×8. Instead, they used a transposed convolutional layer:31 it is equivalent to first
[p0505-l0012] [10.5pt] stretching the image by inserting empty rows and columns (full of zeros), then per‐
[p0505-l0013] [10.5pt] forming a regular convolution (see Figure 14-27). Alternatively, some people prefer to
[p0505-l0014] [10.5pt] think of it as a regular convolutional layer that uses fractional strides (e.g., 1/2 in
[p0505-l0015] [10.5pt] Figure 14-27). The transposed convolutional layer can be initialized to perform some‐
[p0505-l0016] [10.5pt] thing close to linear interpolation, but since it is a trainable layer, it will learn to do
[p0505-l0017] [10.5pt] better during training.
[p0505-l0018] [8.0pt] 31 This type of layer is sometimes referred to as a deconvolution layer, but it does not perform what mathemati‐
[p0505-l0019] [8.0pt] cians call a deconvolution, so this name should be avoided.
[p0505-l0020] [9.0pt] Semantic Segmentation
[p0505-l0021] [9.0pt] |
[p0505-l0022] [9.0pt] 479

=== PDF page 506 / printed label 480 ===
[p0506-l0001] [10.5pt] Figure 14-27. Upsampling Using a Transpose Convolutional Layer
[p0506-l0002] [9.6pt] In a transposed convolution layer, the stride defines how much the
[p0506-l0003] [9.6pt] input will be stretched, not the size of the filter steps, so the larger
[p0506-l0004] [9.6pt] the stride, the larger the output (unlike for convolutional layers or
[p0506-l0005] [9.6pt] pooling layers).
[p0506-l0006] [15.0pt] TensorFlow Convolution Operations
[p0506-l0007] [10.0pt] TensorFlow also offers a few other kinds of convolutional layers:
[p0506-l0008] [10.0pt] • keras.layers.Conv1D creates a convolutional layer for 1D inputs, such as time
[p0506-l0009] [10.0pt] series or text (sequences of letters or words), as we will see in ???.
[p0506-l0010] [10.0pt] • keras.layers.Conv3D creates a convolutional layer for 3D inputs, such as 3D
[p0506-l0011] [10.0pt] PET scan.
[p0506-l0012] [10.0pt] • Setting the dilation_rate hyperparameter of any convolutional layer to a value
[p0506-l0013] [10.0pt] of 2 or more creates an à-trous convolutional layer (“à trous” is French for “with
[p0506-l0014] [10.0pt] holes”). This is equivalent to using a regular convolutional layer with a filter dila‐
[p0506-l0015] [10.0pt] ted by inserting rows and columns of zeros (i.e., holes). For example, a 1 × 3 filter
[p0506-l0016] [10.0pt] equal to [[1,2,3]] may be dilated with a dilation rate of 4, resulting in a dilated
[p0506-l0017] [10.0pt] filter [[1, 0, 0, 0, 2, 0, 0, 0, 3]]. This allows the convolutional layer to
[p0506-l0018] [9.0pt] 480
[p0506-l0019] [9.0pt] |
[p0506-l0020] [9.0pt] Chapter 14: Deep Computer Vision Using Convolutional Neural Networks

=== PDF page 507 / printed label 481 ===
[p0507-l0001] [10.0pt] have a larger receptive field at no computational price and using no extra param‐
[p0507-l0002] [10.0pt] eters.
[p0507-l0003] [10.0pt] • tf.nn.depthwise_conv2d() can be used to create a depthwise convolutional layer
[p0507-l0004] [10.0pt] (but you need to create the variables yourself). It applies every filter to every
[p0507-l0005] [10.0pt] individual input channel independently. Thus, if there are fn filters and fn′ input
[p0507-l0006] [10.0pt] channels, then this will output fn × fn′ feature maps.
[p0507-l0007] [10.5pt] This solution is okay, but still too imprecise. To do better, the authors added skip con‐
[p0507-l0008] [10.5pt] nections from lower layers: for example, they upsampled the output image by a factor
[p0507-l0009] [10.5pt] of 2 (instead of 32), and they added the output of a lower layer that had this double
[p0507-l0010] [10.5pt] resolution. Then they upsampled the result by a factor of 16, leading to a total upsam‐
[p0507-l0011] [10.5pt] pling factor of 32 (see Figure 14-28). This recovered some of the spatial resolution
[p0507-l0012] [10.5pt] that was lost in earlier pooling layers. In their best architecture, they used a second
[p0507-l0013] [10.5pt] similar skip connection to recover even finer details from an even lower layer: in
[p0507-l0014] [10.5pt] short, the output of the original CNN goes through the following extra steps: upscale
[p0507-l0015] [10.5pt] ×2, add the output of a lower layer (of the appropriate scale), upscale ×2, add the out‐
[p0507-l0016] [10.5pt] put of an even lower layer, and finally upscale ×8. It is even possible to scale up
[p0507-l0017] [10.5pt] beyond the size of the original image: this can be used to increase the resolution of an
[p0507-l0018] [10.5pt] image, which is a technique called super-resolution.
[p0507-l0019] [10.5pt] Figure 14-28. Skip layers recover some spatial resolution from lower layers
[p0507-l0020] [10.5pt] Once again, many github repositories provide TensorFlow implementations of
[p0507-l0021] [10.5pt] semantic segmentation (TensorFlow 1 for now), and you will even find a pretrained
[p0507-l0022] [10.5pt] instance segmentation model in the TensorFlow Models project. Instance segmenta‐
[p0507-l0023] [10.5pt] tion is similar to semantic segmentation, but instead of merging all objects of the
[p0507-l0024] [10.5pt] same class into one big lump, each object is distinguished from the others (e.g., it
[p0507-l0025] [10.5pt] identifies each individual bicycle). At the present, they provide multiple implementa‐
[p0507-l0026] [10.5pt] tions of the Mask R-CNN architecture, which was proposed in a 2017 paper: it
[p0507-l0027] [10.5pt] extends the Faster R-CNN model by additionally producing a pixel-mask for each
[p0507-l0028] [10.5pt] bounding box. So not only do you get a bounding box around each object, with a set
[p0507-l0029] [10.5pt] of estimated class probabilities, you also get a pixel mask that locates pixels in the
[p0507-l0030] [10.5pt] bounding box that belong to the object.

[p0507-l0032] [9.0pt] |

[p0508-l0001] [10.5pt] As you can see, the field of Deep Computer Vision is vast and moving fast, with all
[p0508-l0002] [10.5pt] sorts of architectures popping out every year, all based on Convolutional Neural Net‐
[p0508-l0003] [10.5pt] works. The progress made in just a few years has been astounding, and researchers
[p0508-l0004] [10.5pt] are now focusing on harder and harder problems, such as adversarial learning (which
[p0508-l0005] [10.5pt] attempts to make the network more resistant to images designed to fool it), explaina‐
[p0508-l0006] [10.5pt] bility (understanding why the network makes a specific classification), realistic image
[p0508-l0007] [10.5pt] generation (which we will come back to in ???), single-shot learning (a system that can
[p0508-l0008] [10.5pt] recognize an object after it has seen it just once), and much more. Some even explore
[p0508-l0009] [10.5pt] completely novel architectures, such as Geoffrey Hinton’s capsule networks32 (I pre‐
[p0508-l0010] [10.5pt] sented them in a couple videos, with the corresponding code in a notebook). Now on
[p0508-l0011] [10.5pt] to the next chapter, where we will look at how to process sequential data such as time
[p0508-l0012] [10.5pt] series using Recurrent Neural Networks and Convolutional Neural Networks.

[p0510-l0001] [15.75pt] About the Author
[p0510-l0002] [10.5pt] Aurélien Géron is a Machine Learning consultant. A former Googler, he led the You‐
[p0510-l0003] [10.5pt] Tube video classification team from 2013 to 2016. He was also a founder and CTO of
[p0510-l0004] [10.5pt] Wifirst from 2002 to 2012, a leading Wireless ISP in France; and a founder and CTO
[p0510-l0005] [10.5pt] of Polyconseil in 2001, the firm that now manages the electric car sharing service
[p0510-l0006] [10.5pt] Autolib’.
[p0510-l0007] [10.5pt] Before this he worked as an engineer in a variety of domains: finance (JP Morgan and
[p0510-l0008] [10.5pt] Société Générale), defense (Canada’s DOD), and healthcare (blood transfusion). He
[p0510-l0009] [10.5pt] published a few technical books (on C++, WiFi, and internet architectures), and was
[p0510-l0010] [10.5pt] a Computer Science lecturer in a French engineering school.
[p0510-l0011] [10.5pt] A few fun facts: he taught his three children to count in binary with their fingers (up
[p0510-l0012] [10.5pt] to 1023), he studied microbiology and evolutionary genetics before going into soft‐
[p0510-l0013] [10.5pt] ware engineering, and his parachute didn’t open on the second jump.
[p0510-l0014] [15.75pt] Colophon
[p0510-l0015] [10.5pt] The animal on the cover of Hands-On Machine Learning with Scikit-Learn and Ten‐
[p0510-l0016] [10.5pt] sorFlow is the fire salamander (Salamandra salamandra), an amphibian found across
[p0510-l0017] [10.5pt] most of Europe. Its black, glossy skin features large yellow spots on the head and
[p0510-l0018] [10.5pt] back, signaling the presence of alkaloid toxins. This is a possible source of this
[p0510-l0019] [10.5pt] amphibian’s common name: contact with these toxins (which they can also spray
[p0510-l0020] [10.5pt] short distances) causes convulsions and hyperventilation. Either the painful poisons
[p0510-l0021] [10.5pt] or the moistness of the salamander’s skin (or both) led to a misguided belief that these
[p0510-l0022] [10.5pt] creatures not only could survive being placed in fire but could extinguish it as well.
[p0510-l0023] [10.5pt] Fire salamanders live in shaded forests, hiding in moist crevices and under logs near
[p0510-l0024] [10.5pt] the pools or other freshwater bodies that facilitate their breeding. Though they spend
[p0510-l0025] [10.5pt] most of their life on land, they give birth to their young in water. They subsist mostly
[p0510-l0026] [10.5pt] on a diet of insects, spiders, slugs, and worms. Fire salamanders can grow up to a foot
[p0510-l0027] [10.5pt] in length, and in captivity, may live as long as 50 years.
[p0510-l0028] [10.5pt] The fire salamander’s numbers have been reduced by destruction of their forest habi‐
[p0510-l0029] [10.5pt] tat and capture for the pet trade, but the greatest threat is the susceptibility of their
[p0510-l0030] [10.5pt] moisture-permeable skin to pollutants and microbes. Since 2014, they have become
[p0510-l0031] [10.5pt] extinct in parts of the Netherlands and Belgium due to an introduced fungus.
[p0510-l0032] [10.5pt] Many of the animals on O’Reilly covers are endangered; all of them are important to
[p0510-l0033] [10.5pt] the world. To learn more about how you can help, go to animals.oreilly.com.
[p0510-l0034] [10.5pt] The cover image is from Wood’s Illustrated Natural History. The cover fonts are URW
[p0510-l0035] [10.5pt] Typewriter and Guardian Sans. The text font is Adobe Minion Pro; the heading font
[p0510-l0036] [10.5pt] is Adobe Myriad Condensed; and the code font is Dalton Maag’s Ubuntu Mono.
